# 03 — Round 2 对抗验证判决(34 组 × 3 票 = 102 票)

## V1 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I did not rely on the WebFetch summarizer's quotes. Because the pipeline has previously caught summarizers fabricating quotes, I downloaded the raw HTML of both PMC articles with curl, stripped tags with a local Python script, and located every quoted string by exact substring match in the resulting text myself. Every verbatim string in this report was confirmed that way. WebSearch budget was exhausted early in the session (200/200), so I used the Europe PMC REST API for literature discovery instead, which turned out to be more precise for exact-phrase checks.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Nadon et al., Age 2008, PMC2585647 — full text, confirming the four-way cross description, the 36F/44M-per-site sentence, the power-analysis sentence, and the three site names; (2) Cheng et al., Aging Cell 2019, PMC6516160 — full text, confirming 3,690 control mice, six cohorts with start years 2004/2005/2006/2007/2009/2010, and the exact medians 887 (879-898) and 803 (791-815); (3) Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024, PMC10828146 (astaxanthin/meclizine, ITP cohorts 2018-2019) via the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint — this is the key refutation source, giving actual current arm sizes and the explicit CByB6F1/J dam and C3D2F1/J sire stock numbers; (4) Warner, Age 2015, PMC4344944; (5) Zhavoronkov et al., Aging & Disease 2025, PMC13061545 (co-authored by ITP PI R.A. Miller); (6) the NIA ITP 'About' and 'FAQ' pages.

On the NIA pages: nia.nih.gov now returns HTTP 405 with a JavaScript CAPTCHA wall to non-browser clients. I did not attempt to solve or bypass it. I used Internet Archive snapshots instead and verified the snapshot timestamps against the Wayback CDX index: About page 20260723154802 (page's own 'Last updated: May 12, 2026'), FAQ 20260726134222 ('Last updated: October 23, 2024'). I re-fetched the timestamped About URL directly and re-confirmed the three load-bearing strings by substring match.

Refutation search: no erratum, correction or retraction attaches to Nadon 2008 or Cheng 2019 (Europe PMC citing-corrections query on PMID 30801953 returns 0; neither full text contains 'erratum' or 'retract'). I did find two GeroScience corrections to a different 2024 ITP paper, but both concern a compound name (16-hydroxyestriol vs 16-hydroxyestradiol) and do not bear on this claim group.

What remains uncertain: I could not reach Miller et al., Aging Cell 2007 in full text (not deposited in PMC; only the abstract via Europe PMC), which is the paper Nadon cites as the source of the power analysis. So the one-sided-vs-two-sided question and the exact assumed variance behind the 80% power figure are unverified at the primary level — I am relying on Nadon's and NIA's descriptions of it. I also could not obtain animal-level ITP data from the Mouse Phenome Database API to compute per-cohort arm sizes independently; my conclusion that arm sizes grew rests on the published per-arm n in Harrison et al. 2024, which is a primary ITP report but is one paper covering two cohorts. The direction and magnitude are unambiguous there (control arms of 282-298 cannot be reconciled with 2 x 108 = 216 females or 2 x 132 = 264 males), but I have not established exactly when the ITP changed the target or whether NIA has ever published a revised number — NIA's current pages give no arm sizes at all.

- **(a) UM-HET3 is a four-way cross, CByB6F1 dams x C3D2F1 sires, so no animal is inbred** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, with a wording caveat about the cited source. Nadon et al. 2008 (PMC2585647) states verbatim, and I read this string myself in the raw PMC HTML: 'The specific stock of HET mice used in the ITP is a cross of four inbred strains, generated by breeding two F1 hybrids, CB6F1 X C3D2F1. They are equivalent to the UM-HET3 mice described by Miller and Chrisp ( 1999 ).' Note Nadon writes CB6F1, NOT CByB6F1, and does not state which parent is the dam. The dam/sire direction the claim asserts IS correct, but it must be sourced elsewhere: Cheng et al. 2019 Methods 4.2 says verbatim 'UM-HET3 mice were bred at each of the three test sites from CByB6F1/J (JAX stock #100,009) mothers and C3D2F1/J (JAX stock #100,004) fathers.' Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience (PMC10828146) Experimental procedures says verbatim 'The dams of the test mice were CByB6F1/J, JAX stock #100,009 (dams, BALB/cByJ; sires, C57BL/6 J). The sires of the test mice were C3D2F1/J, JAX stock #100,004 (dams, C3H/HeJ; sires, DBA/2 J).' NIA's own About-the-ITP page says 'UM-HET3 mice are the progeny of CByB6F1 females and C3D2F1 males and are genetically heterogeneous, the equivalent of a large sibship.' One trap worth flagging: Cheng et al.'s own Introduction contradicts its own Methods, calling it a 'four-way cross between [BALB/cJ x C57BL/6J]F1 mothers and [C3H/HeJ x DBA/2J]F1 fathers' — BALB/cJ, not BALB/cByJ. The JAX stock number 100009 in the Methods (= CByB6F1/J = BALB/cByJ x C57BL/6J) is authoritative; do not cite Cheng's Introduction for the grandparental strains. 'No animal is inbred' is a fair gloss (each locus that differs among the four grandparental strains is obligately heterozygous), but it is my inference from the cross structure, not a verbatim source sentence.

- **(b) 36 females + 44 males per site = 108 females + 132 males total, sized a priori for 10% lifespan change at 80% power** — `corrected`
  The numbers are verbatim in Nadon 2008 but are the 2008-era design target and no longer describe what the ITP actually runs. WRONG (as a present-tense statement of ITP practice): 'each intervention arm is 36 females + 44 males per site = 108 females and 132 males total.' RIGHT: that was the design as specified in Nadon et al. 2008; current cohorts run larger arms. Nadon 2008 verbatim (read in raw HTML): 'Each experimental group includes 36 females and 44 males per site, for a total of 108 females and 132 males for each intervention tested. The males are over-represented because of the expectation that some cages will have to be culled due to fighting. The control lifespan group is twice the size of the experimental groups'. Warner 2015 (PMC4344944) still repeats 'usually 36 females and 44 males' but WITHOUT the phrase 'per site'. However, Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience (PMC10828146), reporting ITP cohorts 2018 and 2019, gives pooled treatment-arm n of 142-156 males and 132-144 females, with controls at 292/298 males and 286/282 females — i.e. roughly 48-50 males and 44-48 females PER SITE, not 44 and 36. A Europe PMC full-text phrase search for '44 males per site' returns exactly one hit in the entire corpus: Nadon 2008. The power claim itself is confirmed. Nadon 2008 verbatim: 'A power analysis was performed (by A. Galecki, University of Michigan, and S. Pletcher, Baylor College of Medicine) to determine the number of mice needed per experimental group to be able to detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power, as described in Miller et al. ( 2007 ).' The 'in either sex' qualifier is NOT in Nadon; it comes from NIA, whose About page says 'The study design includes sufficient numbers of mice to provide 80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites' and whose FAQ says '80% power to detect a 10% increase in average lifespan in either sex'. Two caliber points: the endpoint is MEAN/average lifespan (Warner 2015: 'a 10 % increase or decrease in mean life span with 80 % power'), not median; and NIA specifies the power applies when POOLING ACROSS SITES, not per site. Adversarial datapoint: a 2025 Aging & Disease protocol paper co-authored by ITP PI Richard Miller (PMC13061545) recalculates from ITP control data that 'the sample size to detect a 10% change in lifespan, 0.05 type I error and 80% power for male and female would be at least 176 and 72, respectively' — i.e. the ITP's own male arm may be under the nominal requirement.

- **(c) Three parallel sites running an identical protocol: Jackson Laboratory, University of Michigan, UT Health San Antonio** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed. Nadon 2008 verbatim: 'Testing is performed in triplicate at three independent sites: The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan, and the University of Texas Health Sciences Center—San Antonio.' Cheng et al. 2019 verbatim: 'pooled across all three sites (TJL = The Jackson Laboratory, UM = University of Michigan, UT = UT Health San Antonio)'. NIA About page (July 2026 snapshot) confirms this is still the structure: 'three U01s to the Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan, and the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio to support testing; and one U24 to the Jackson Laboratory to support a Data Coordinating Center (DCC).' Two minor notes: NIA still uses the full legal name 'University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio' (the institution's post-2017 brand is UT Health San Antonio; both are the same institution and Cheng 2019 uses the short form, so the claim's wording is fine). Also, 'identical protocol' is supported — Nadon: the ITP 'developed SOPs to ensure that environmental conditions at the three sites are as uniform as possible' — but the same paper documents that site-to-site control lifespan still varies materially ('For male control mice at the three sites, the mean median lifespan was 799 days, with a range (minimum to maximum) of 137 days, or 17% of the mean'). Do not let 'identical protocol' imply identical outcomes.

- **(d) 3,690 ITP control mice, six studies 2004-2013; control female median 887 d (95% CI 879-898), control male median 803 d (95% CI 791-815)** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim; I located these exact strings in the raw PMC HTML of Cheng et al. 2019 myself, not via a summarizer. 'Females had a longer median lifespan (887 days, 95% CI: 879–898) than males (803 days, 95% CI: 791–815) both when all the survival data were pooled and when the data were stratified by study cohort'. Also verbatim: 'Data analyzed in this study were from a total of 3,690 animals in the control groups at all three sites.' And: 'Survival data were obtained from six longevity studies conducted between the years of 2004 and 2013. Each study cohort is defined by start year (2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009, and 2010)'. And: '3,690 control (i.e., pharmacologically untreated) mice'. Precision notes for the article: the six COHORT START years are 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009 and 2010 (there is no 2008 cohort); 2004-2013 is the span of the studies, not of enrollment. Average cohort size was 'males n = 332, females n = 282'. These are MEDIAN lifespans only — the same paper reports 'there was no effect of sex on maximum lifespan in any study cohort', so do not extend the female advantage to maximum lifespan. No erratum, correction or retraction is attached to either Cheng 2019 or Nadon 2008 (Europe PMC citation search for corrections referencing PMID 30801953 returns 0 hits).

- **Does the ITP have a stated policy of publishing regardless of outcome? (article claims none could be found)** — `refuted`
  REFUTED — the claimed absence is wrong. NIA states the policy explicitly in two places on its own ITP pages. NIA 'About the ITP' page, under the heading 'Publication, Data Sharing, and Biospecimens', verbatim: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication. All data from the ITP are publicly available through the ITP Data Coordinating Center following publication.' NIA ITP FAQ, verbatim Q&A: 'If the agent shortens the lifespan or has negative effects, what will happen to the data? The ITP plans to publish all data, including data on agents that fail to increase lifespan or delay late-life illnesses, or interventions that have deleterious side effects.' I read both strings myself from Wayback snapshots (nia.nih.gov itself is CAPTCHA-gated and I did not bypass it): About page snapshot 20260723154802, FAQ snapshot 20260726134222. The About page carries 'Last updated: May 12, 2026'; the FAQ 'Last updated: October 23, 2024'. Corroborating evidence of the policy in practice: the ITP has published a long list of null results (Warner 2015 tabulates 'Aspirin, curcumin, green tea extract, NFP, 4-OH-PBN, oxaloacetic acid, resveratrol, simvastatin, median-chain TG, methylene blue — No or insignificant life span extension'), and PMC13061545 (2025) reports 'Eighty-five lifespan studies (Cohorts 2004 – 2020) are now complete and published in peer-reviewed journals' against 108 studies initiated as of Aug 2024. Caveat the article should keep: the wording is 'submitted for publication' / 'plans to publish', a program commitment on a website, not a binding pre-registration.

**修正:**
- Do not state the arm size in the present tense. Write: 'As originally designed (Nadon et al., Age 2008), each intervention arm was 36 females and 44 males per site — 108 females and 132 males in total.' Then add that current cohorts run larger arms: in ITP cohorts 2018-2019 (Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024, PMC10828146) pooled treatment-arm n was 142-156 males and 132-144 females, i.e. roughly 48-50 males and 44-48 females per site, with control groups of ~282-298 (the ITP control arm is twice the size of each treatment arm).
- Remove or rewrite the statement that no ITP publish-regardless-of-outcome policy could be found. NIA states it twice. Quote the About-the-ITP page: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication.' And the FAQ: 'The ITP plans to publish all data, including data on agents that fail to increase lifespan or delay late-life illnesses, or interventions that have deleterious side effects.' Characterize it as a stated program policy on NIA's website, not a binding pre-registration.
- Attribute the 'in either sex' qualifier to NIA, not to Nadon 2008. Nadon says only 'detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power'. NIA's About page adds the full caliber: '80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites' — note that the power applies to the three sites POOLED, not to any single site.
- The powered endpoint is a 10% change in MEAN (average) lifespan, not median. Warner 2015 (PMC4344944): 'to detect a 10 % increase or decrease in mean life span with 80 % power'; NIA FAQ: 'a 10% increase in average lifespan in either sex'. Do not write that the ITP is powered to detect a 10% change in median lifespan.
- For the parental cross, do not cite Nadon 2008 for 'CByB6F1 dams'. Nadon writes the loose shorthand 'CB6F1 X C3D2F1' and does not specify dam vs sire. Cite Cheng et al. 2019 Methods ('CByB6F1/J (JAX stock #100,009) mothers and C3D2F1/J (JAX stock #100,004) fathers') or Harrison et al. 2024, which additionally give the grandparental strains: dams BALB/cByJ x C57BL/6J, sires C3H/HeJ x DBA/2J.
- If the article names the four grandparental strains, use BALB/cByJ (not BALB/cJ). Cheng et al. 2019's own Introduction erroneously says 'BALB/cJ', contradicting its Methods' JAX stock #100009, which is CByB6F1/J = BALB/cByJ x C57BL/6J.
- When giving the Cheng control-lifespan figures, say the six cohorts have START years 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009 and 2010 (there is no 2008 cohort); '2004-2013' is the span over which the studies ran, not the span of cohort starts.
- If the 887 vs 803 day figures are used to make a point about the female survival advantage, note that Cheng found the advantage in MEDIAN lifespan only: 'there was no effect of sex on maximum lifespan in any study cohort'.
- Optional but strengthening: note that the ITP's arm size has been questioned on its own terms. A 2025 Aging & Disease protocol paper co-authored by ITP PI Richard Miller (PMC13061545) recomputes from ITP control data that detecting a 10% lifespan change at alpha=0.05 and 80% power requires at least 176 males and 72 females — i.e. the male arm is arguably underpowered relative to the nominal target because male lifespan is far more variable.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The 36F/44M-per-site figure is contradicted by the ITP's own recent primary data. Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024 (PMC10828146), Table 1 (pooled, cohorts 2018/2019) gives treatment-arm n of 150, 142, 153, 156, 148, 149, 149, 149, 152, 150 for males and 134, 144, 139, 132, 136, 135, 136, 133, 135, 134 for females, with controls at 292/298 (M) and 286/282 (F). Divided by three sites this is ~48-51 males and ~44-48 females per site, above the stated 44 and 36. A Europe PMC full-text search for the exact phrase '44 males per site' returns exactly one document in the whole corpus — Nadon 2008 itself — so no post-2008 ITP publication reaffirms the per-site figure.
- The claimed absence of a publish-regardless-of-outcome policy is directly contradicted by NIA's ITP About page and FAQ, both of which state the policy in plain language and were live as of July 2026 Wayback snapshots.
- Cheng et al. 2019 contradicts itself on the grandparental strains: Introduction says '[BALB/cJ x C57BL/6J]F1 mothers' while Methods 4.2 cites JAX stock #100,009 (CByB6F1/J = BALB/cByJ x C57BL/6J). Anyone citing Cheng's Introduction for the cross will get the substrain wrong.
- 'Identical protocol at three sites' should not be read as producing equivalent results. Nadon 2008 itself reports that among the three sites, 'For male control mice at the three sites, the mean median lifespan was 799 days, with a range (minimum to maximum) of 137 days, or 17% of the mean.' Harrison et al. 2024 shows the same effects splitting by site (meclizine: +11% median male lifespan at UM, +15% at JAX, 0 at UT).

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I reached both cited primary documents as raw HTML (curl with a browser UA to pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov), stripped tags locally, and grepped the actual article text rather than relying on any fetch-summarizer output — every quoted string below was read by me in the stripped document, not paraphrased by a summarizer. Local copies: /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/scratchpad/nadon.txt and cheng.txt.

Nadon 2008 (PMC2585647) confirms verbatim: the four-way cross ('a cross of four inbred strains, generated by breeding two F1 hybrids, CB6F1 X C3D2F1'), the group sizes ('36 females and 44 males per site, for a total of 108 females and 132 males'), the power analysis ('a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power'), and the three sites. Two caliber gaps: Nadon writes CB6F1 not CByB6F1 and gives no dam/sire direction, and the power sentence contains no 'either sex' qualifier.

Cheng 2019 (PMC6516160) confirms verbatim '3,690 control (i.e., pharmacologically untreated) mice', 'six longevity studies conducted between the years of 2004 and 2013', and 'Females had a longer median lifespan (887 days, 95% CI: 879–898) than males (803 days, 95% CI: 791–815)'. No erratum or retraction is linked to either PMID in PubMed (checked via eutils efetch).

Refutation hunting produced three real hits. (1) The publication-policy 'absence' is wrong: NIA blocks direct fetches with an AWS WAF challenge (both curl and WebFetch failed — 405 / human-verification page), so I went through the Wayback Machine and read the page capture. Both the 2022-10-09 and the 2026-07-23 captures contain, verbatim, 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication.' The 2026 capture's own footer reads 'Last updated: May 12, 2026'. (2) The same page supplies the missing power qualifier: '80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites' — so the article's 'either sex' is substantively right but misattributed, and 'pooling across sites' is a load-bearing omission. Harrison et al. 2014 (PMC3954939) independently states '>80% power to detect an increase or decrease of 10% in mean lifespan, with respect to controls of the same sex, even if only two of the three sites can contribute data to the pooled analysis.' (3) The 108/132 figure is superseded: the 2024 ITP paper (PMC11336000) Table 2 shows C2020 arms of 132 females and 150–153 males with a 272/302 control arm. I also caught Cheng 2019's own Methods misstating the cross as BALB/cJ, contradicted by Miller 2011 (PMC3021372), Harrison 2009 (PMC2786175), the 2024 ITP paper, and the NIA site (all: BALB/cByJ / CByB6F1 / JAX stock 100009).

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: I could NOT reach Miller et al. 2007, Aging Cell 6:565–575 — the original power-analysis paper that Nadon 2008 defers to for the sample-size derivation. It is not deposited in PMC (idconv returns 'Identifier not found in PMC' for PMID 17578509) and the Wiley DOI returned HTTP 402. So the underlying assumptions of the power calculation (variance estimate, one- vs two-sided, alpha, whether framed on mean or median) are unverified at source; I inferred the per-sex and pooled-site framing from the NIA program page and Harrison 2014 instead. I also could not date the transition from 36F/44M-per-site to the larger current arms — I can document the endpoints (2008 design vs C2020 actuals) but not the cohort in which it changed. My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the first search attempt, so all of the above was done by direct URL retrieval (curl, NCBI eutils, Wayback CDX/replay) rather than search.

- **(a) Mice are UM-HET3, a four-way cross (CByB6F1 dams x C3D2F1 sires), so no animal is inbred** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED, but NOT from the cited sentence in Nadon 2008. Nadon 2008 says verbatim: 'The specific stock of HET mice used in the ITP is a cross of four inbred strains, generated by breeding two F1 hybrids, CB6F1 X C3D2F1. They are equivalent to the UM-HET3 mice described by Miller and Chrisp ( 1999 ).' — note it writes CB6F1 (not CByB6F1) and does NOT state which parent is dam vs sire. The dam/sire direction and the CByB6 substrain are confirmed verbatim elsewhere: NIA ITP 'About the ITP' page (live, last updated May 12 2026): 'UM-HET3 mice are the progeny of CByB6F1 females and C3D2F1 males and are genetically heterogeneous, the equivalent of a large sibship.' Miller et al. 2011 (PMC3021372) Methods: '(BALB/cByJ × C57BL/6J)F1 mothers (JAX stock 100009) and (C3H/HeJ × DBA/2J)F1 fathers (JAX stock 100004).' 2024 ITP paper (PMC11336000): 'The study used UM-HET3 mice, the progeny of CByB6F1 mothers (JAX stock 100009), and C3D2F1 fathers (JAX stock 100004).' Harrison 2009 (PMC2786175): 'BALB/cByJ × C57BL/6J F1 (CB6F1) females and C3H/HeJ × DBA/2J F1 (C3D2F1) males are supplied to each site by The Jackson Laboratory.' TRAP FOR THE ARTICLE: the OTHER cited source, Cheng 2019, states the cross WRONG in its own Methods — 'a four‐way cross between [BALB/cJ × C57BL/6J]F1 mothers and [C3H/HeJ × DBA/2J]F1 fathers' (BALB/cJ, not BALB/cByJ). Do not cite Cheng 2019 for the strain composition. Also, 'no animal is inbred' is true but the more precise and more useful primary wording is Harrison 2009's: 'each animal is genetically unique, but a full sibling of all other mice in the population' — the stock samples only four inbred genomes, so heterogeneity is bounded.

- **(b) Each arm is 36 females + 44 males PER SITE = 108 females and 132 males total, sized a priori for 80% power to detect a 10% lifespan change in either sex** — `corrected`
  The numbers are verbatim correct FOR THE 2008 SOURCE but are (i) missing the 'pooled across sites' qualifier and (ii) superseded by current ITP practice. Nadon 2008 verbatim: 'A power analysis was performed (by A. Galecki, University of Michigan, and S. Pletcher, Baylor College of Medicine) to determine the number of mice needed per experimental group to be able to detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power, as described in Miller et al. ( 2007 ). Each experimental group includes 36 females and 44 males per site, for a total of 108 females and 132 males for each intervention tested. The males are over-represented because of the expectation that some cages will have to be culled due to fighting. The control lifespan group is twice the size of the experimental groups.' WRONG: 'in either sex' is not in Nadon's power sentence (Nadon never says 'sex' there); and the article implies per-arm power without saying the power is for the POOLED three-site analysis. RIGHT (NIA ITP site, live 2026): 'The study design includes sufficient numbers of mice to provide 80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites.' Harrison et al. 2014 (PMC3954939) is stronger still: 'Sufficient numbers of mice are used in each yearly cohort to give more than 80% power to detect an increase or decrease of 10% in mean lifespan, with respect to controls of the same sex, even if only two of the three sites can contribute data to the pooled analysis.' (note: MEAN lifespan there, not median). WRONG as a present-tense statement of ITP design: 108F/132M. RIGHT for the current era: the C2020 cohort (2024 ITP paper, PMC11336000, Table 2) enrolled 132 females and 150–153 males per treated arm, with a double-sized control arm of 272 females / 302 males — i.e. roughly 44F + 50M per site, not 36F + 44M. Individual-site subsets are explicitly acknowledged as underpowered: 'the low statistical power for each of these subsets of the C2020 cohort is too small to avoid Type II errors.'

- **(c) Three parallel sites run the identical protocol — Jackson Laboratory, University of Michigan, UT Health San Antonio** — `confirmed`
  Nadon 2008 verbatim: 'Testing is performed in triplicate at three independent sites: The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan, and the University of Texas Health Sciences Center—San Antonio.' Cheng 2019 uses the modern name verbatim: 'TJL = The Jackson Laboratory, UM = University of Michigan, UT = UT Health San Antonio'. Caution on 'identical protocol': the SOP is common but the sites are NOT environmentally identical, and both cited papers say so. Nadon 2008 flags site-to-site variation as a headline finding, and Cheng 2019 reports 'a significant interaction between sex and site... supporting a difference between males at UM compared to males at UT and TJL (HR = 0.661, p < 0.001)' — there is NO female survival advantage at UM at all. The 2024 ITP paper also notes each site 'used its own local water supply.' Also note protocol drift: Cana_16 in C2020 was run at 'UM, UT only' and Cana_6 at 'TJL only', so not every arm runs at all three sites.

- **(d) Across 3,690 ITP control mice from six studies 2004–2013, control female median lifespan 887 days (95% CI 879–898) and control male median 803 days (95% CI 791–815)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim confirmed in Cheng 2019 Results §2.1: 'Females had a longer median lifespan (887 days, 95% CI: 879–898) than males (803 days, 95% CI: 791–815) both when all the survival data were pooled and when the data were stratified by study cohort'. N and window verbatim: 'Kaplan–Meier survival curves of 3,690 control (i.e., pharmacologically untreated) mice pooled across all three sites'; Methods: 'Survival data were obtained from six longevity studies conducted between the years of 2004 and 2013. Each study cohort is defined by start year (2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009, and 2010)' — so the cohorts STARTED 2004–2010; 2004–2013 is the span including follow-up. Figure 1 legend: 'Average cohort size for males n = 332, females n = 282. Total number of animals n = 3,690.' No erratum, retraction or correction is registered in PubMed for PMID 30801953. Two caliber cautions the article must not drop: these are POOLED medians that mask a large site effect (no sex difference in median lifespan or overall survival at UM at all), and the same paper finds NO sex effect on MAXIMUM lifespan in any cohort ('there was no effect of sex on maximum lifespan in any study cohort (Survival at maximum lifespan in Females: 95% CI 0.079–0.121, Males: 95% CI 0.080–0.120)').

- **Claimed ABSENCE of a stated ITP policy of publishing regardless of outcome** — `refuted`
  REFUTED. The policy exists, is explicit, and is on the NIA's own ITP page. NIA, 'About the ITP', section headed 'Publication, Data Sharing, and Biospecimens', verbatim: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication. All data from the ITP are publicly available through the ITP Data Coordinating Center following publication.' I read this string in the Wayback capture of 2026-07-23 of https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp/about-itp, whose own footer reads 'Last updated: May 12, 2026', and confirmed the identical sentence in an independent 2022-10-09 capture — so it is a stable, current statement, not a one-off. (nia.nih.gov blocks direct automated fetches with an AWS WAF challenge, which is likely why the drafting pass 'could not find one'; the Wayback copies are byte-for-byte page captures.) Two honest caveats to preserve caliber: the policy says results are 'submitted for publication', which is a commitment to submit, not a guarantee of publication; and the data-release commitment is 'following publication', not pre-publication. Supporting behavioral evidence, not a substitute for the policy: the ITP routinely publishes nulls and harms — e.g. resveratrol and simvastatin nulls in Miller 2011, and in the 2024 C2020 paper nebivolol was reported as significantly HARMFUL in females (p = 0.03) and canagliflozin and 16-α-hydroxyestriol as significantly harmful in females while beneficial in males.

**修正:**
- Delete the sentence stating that the ITP has no findable policy of publishing regardless of outcome. The NIA ITP 'About the ITP' page (last updated May 12, 2026) states verbatim, under the heading 'Publication, Data Sharing, and Biospecimens': 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication. All data from the ITP are publicly available through the ITP Data Coordinating Center following publication.' If the article wants to keep a critical edge, the accurate hedge is that the commitment is to SUBMIT for publication and to release data only AFTER publication — not a guarantee of publication or of pre-publication data release.
- Do not attribute 'in either sex' to Nadon et al. 2008. Nadon's power sentence reads only 'to be able to detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power' and does not mention sex. Cite the per-sex framing to the NIA ITP page — '80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites' — or to Harrison et al. 2014, Aging Cell (PMC3954939): 'Sufficient numbers of mice are used in each yearly cohort to give more than 80% power to detect an increase or decrease of 10% in mean lifespan, with respect to controls of the same sex, even if only two of the three sites can contribute data to the pooled analysis.'
- Add the qualifier 'pooling across sites' to the power claim. The 80% power applies to the three-site pooled analysis, not to any single site. The 2024 ITP paper (PMC11336000) states that per-site subsets have 'low statistical power... too small to avoid Type II errors.' Any sentence implying each site independently detects a 10% effect is wrong.
- Do not state 36 females + 44 males per site (108F/132M total) in the present tense as 'the ITP design'. That is the 2008-era design as published in Nadon et al. 2008. Current arms are larger: in the C2020 cohort (2024 ITP paper, PMC11336000, Table 2), treated arms enrolled 132 females and 150–153 males in total across the three sites, with a double-sized control arm of 272 females and 302 males — roughly 44 females and 50 males per site. Either date-stamp the 108/132 figure ('as originally designed in 2008') or use the current numbers.
- If the article specifies the UM-HET3 cross, source it to the NIA ITP page ('UM-HET3 mice are the progeny of CByB6F1 females and C3D2F1 males'), Miller et al. 2011 ('(BALB/cByJ × C57BL/6J)F1 mothers (JAX stock 100009) and (C3H/HeJ × DBA/2J)F1 fathers (JAX stock 100004)'), or Harrison et al. 2009 — NOT to Cheng et al. 2019, whose Methods misstate the maternal grandparent as BALB/cJ rather than BALB/cByJ. Nadon 2008 writes only 'CB6F1 X C3D2F1' and does not specify which parent is the dam, so it cannot support the dam/sire direction on its own.
- Replace or supplement 'so no animal is inbred' with the sharper primary formulation from Harrison et al. 2009: mice are 'genetically unique, but a full sibling of all other mice in the population.' The stock is heterogeneous but draws on only four inbred genomes, so it is not a general-purpose model of genetic diversity — a distinction that matters in an evidence-grading argument.
- If the 887 / 803 day control medians are cited, note that they are pooled across sites and conceal a large site effect: Cheng 2019 found no difference in median lifespan or overall survival between males and females at the University of Michigan site (Cox sex-by-site interaction HR = 0.661, p < 0.001), and found no effect of sex on MAXIMUM lifespan in any of the six cohorts. Also note the cohorts STARTED in 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009 and 2010; '2004–2013' is the span including follow-up to death.
- Do not write that the three sites run an 'identical' protocol without qualification. The SOP is shared but sites differ (each uses its own local water supply, per the 2024 ITP paper) and site variation is a documented ITP finding. Individual arms are also not always run at all three sites — in C2020, canagliflozin-at-16-months ran at UM and UT only and canagliflozin-at-6-months at TJL only.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The NIA ITP's own 'About the ITP' page carries an explicit publication policy that the article claims does not exist: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication.' Read verbatim in the 2026-07-23 Wayback capture of the page, which self-reports 'Last updated: May 12, 2026', and independently in the 2022-10-09 capture.
- The article's per-arm sample sizes are stale. The 2024 ITP publication (PMC11336000, Table 2) reports C2020 arm counts of 132 females and 150–153 males per treated agent and 272 females / 302 males in the control arm — substantially larger than the 108 females / 132 males stated in Nadon 2008.
- Cheng et al. 2019, one of the two sources the claim cites, contradicts every other ITP primary source on the mouse cross: its Methods say '[BALB/cJ × C57BL/6J]F1 mothers' whereas Miller 2011, Harrison 2009, the 2024 ITP paper and the NIA ITP site all say BALB/cByJ (JAX stock 100009, CByB6F1). No erratum is registered in PubMed for PMID 30801953, so the error stands uncorrected in the literature.
- Harrison et al. 2014 states the ITP power target in terms of MEAN lifespan ('an increase or decrease of 10% in mean lifespan'), while the NIA site says '10% increase in lifespan' and Nadon 2008 says '10% change in lifespan'. The ITP's actual pre-specified primary test is neither a mean nor a median test: per the 2024 paper it is 'a log-rank test stratified by site and tested separately for each sex', with the Wang-Allison 90th-percentile test as the pre-specified secondary. An article about evidence grading should not describe the endpoint as a median- or mean-lifespan test.
- Nadon 2008 itself notes the reported p-values are unadjusted, and the 2024 ITP paper states it explicitly: 'P-values presented are nominal, i.e., they are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.' With up to six agents per year, two sexes and two endpoint tests, this is a live multiplicity concern for any evidence grade assigned to individual ITP hits.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

I did not rely on the WebFetch summarizer. Both summarizer outputs came back suspiciously clean, so I downloaded the primary documents with curl, stripped tags to plain text locally, and string-matched every quoted phrase in the raw text before treating it as verbatim. Everything I quote below was matched that way.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Nadon et al., Age 2008;30(4):187-199, PMC2585647 — full text, 63KB plain text. Confirmed exactly: the 36 females/44 males per site and 108/132 totals sentence; the power-analysis sentence naming Galecki and Pletcher; the three-sites-in-triplicate sentence; the four-inbred-strain cross sentence; plus two sentences the claim omits (controls are double-sized; males over-represented due to fighting culls) and the site-variation numbers (male control mean median 799 days, range 137 days = 17%; female 881 days, range 51 days = 6%). (2) Cheng et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(3):e12905, PMC6516160 — full text. Confirmed exactly: 3,690 control animals, six longevity studies 2004-2013, and the median lifespans 887 (879-898) and 803 (791-815). (3) Nadon et al., EBioMedicine 2017, PMC5514387 — this is where the 'in either sex' qualifier actually lives, together with the two qualifiers the claim drops ('mean lifespan', 'pooling data from as few as two sites'). (4) Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816, PMC10828146 — used for the full substrain breakdown and for current per-arm sample sizes. (5) NIA ITP website, four pages fetched with curl after WebFetch returned HTTP 405: the program homepage, About the ITP, the FAQ, and Supported Interventions.

The headline result is that the article's stated absence of a publication policy is simply wrong. Two explicit statements exist and I read both: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication' (About the ITP, updated 2026-05-12) and 'The ITP plans to publish all data, including data on agents that fail to increase lifespan or delay late-life illnesses, or interventions that have deleterious side effects' (FAQ). The Supported Interventions table corroborates this in practice, listing roughly twenty compounds whose outcome is 'none'.

The most consequential substantive correction is that 36 females + 44 males per site is the 2004-era design and is stale if written in present tense: recent ITP cohorts run arms of roughly 132-156 per sex pooled across sites. The rest are attribution and caliber slips — the dam/sire direction and CByB6F1 designation are not in the cited Nadon 2008 paper, and 'in either sex' is not in it either.

Limitations I want to be explicit about. I could NOT reach Miller et al. 2007, Aging Cell 6(4):565-575 (PMID 17578509), which is the original power calculation that both Nadon papers cite. It is not in PMC, Wiley returned HTTP 402, and the open-access copy in Michigan's Deep Blue repository is behind a Cloudflare challenge that blocked both the landing page and the DSpace REST API. So the underlying assumptions of the power analysis — one- versus two-sided test, alpha level, and the assumed lifespan variance — remain unverified by me. I inferred the design is two-sided from Harrison 2024's methods ('Significance tests about survival effects are based upon the two-tailed log-rank test at p < 0.05, stratified by the test site'), but that is the analysis test, not necessarily the power calculation, and I am not asserting them to be the same. My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task, so I could not run adversarial searches for critical letters or failed replications; I worked around it via NCBI E-utilities, which surfaced the Gehan-test critique and a formal correction to an ITP lifespan paper, but this is weaker coverage than a proper search sweep and I may have missed published criticism. One PMID I guessed for the canagliflozin paper (32998077) turned out to be an unrelated Lyme disease review; I discarded it rather than reporting anything from it, and I mention it because it shows the currency finding rests on the single Harrison 2024 dataset rather than on two independent recent papers as I had intended.

- **(a) Mice are UM-HET3, a four-way cross (CByB6F1 dams x C3D2F1 sires) so no animal is inbred** — `corrected`
  The biology is right but the ATTRIBUTION is wrong. Nadon et al. 2008 does NOT say 'CByB6F1 dams x C3D2F1 sires'. Its exact wording, which I read in the raw HTML, is: WRONG-to-cite-Nadon-for: 'The specific stock of HET mice used in the ITP is a cross of four inbred strains, generated by breeding two F1 hybrids, CB6F1 X C3D2F1. They are equivalent to the UM-HET3 mice described by Miller and Chrisp (1999).' Note it writes 'CB6F1' (not CByB6F1) and specifies NO dam/sire direction. The RIGHT source for the claim as written is Cheng et al. 2019 Methods 4.2, verbatim: 'UM-HET3 mice were bred at each of the three test sites from CByB6F1/J (JAX stock #100,009) mothers and C3D2F1/J (JAX stock #100,004) fathers.' Independently confirmed verbatim in Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience 46(1):795-816 (PMC10828146): 'The dams of the test mice were CByB6F1/J, JAX stock #100,009 (dams, BALB/cByJ; sires, C57BL/6 J). The sires of the test mice were C3D2F1/J, JAX stock #100,004 (dams, C3H/HeJ; sires, DBA/2 J).' LANDMINE: Cheng 2019's own Introduction CONTRADICTS its own Methods, saying 'a four-way cross between [BALB/cJ x C57BL/6J]F1 mothers and [C3H/HeJ x DBA/2J]F1 fathers' — BALB/cJ is wrong; JAX stock 100009 is BALB/cByJ. Do not cite Cheng's Introduction for the strain. 'No animal is inbred' is correct; NIA's own phrasing is that the mice are 'genetically heterogeneous, the equivalent of a large sibship' (i.e. unique but RELATED genotypes, not unrelated).

- **(b) Each intervention arm is 36 females + 44 males PER SITE = 108 females and 132 males total, sized a priori to detect a 10% change in lifespan in either sex at 80% power** — `corrected`
  The N figures are verbatim exact in Nadon 2008: 'Each experimental group includes 36 females and 44 males per site, for a total of 108 females and 132 males for each intervention tested.' TWO problems. (1) 'in either sex' is NOT in Nadon 2008. Nadon 2008's power sentence reads, verbatim: 'A power analysis was performed (by A. Galecki, University of Michigan, and S. Pletcher, Baylor College of Medicine) to determine the number of mice needed per experimental group to be able to detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power, as described in Miller et al. (2007).' The 'either sex' qualifier is real but comes from a DIFFERENT paper — Nadon et al. 2017 EBioMedicine (PMC5514387), verbatim: 'Population sizes are large enough that the protocol will detect a 10% change in mean lifespan, in either sex, with 80% power, pooling data from as few as two sites.' Two caliber details in that sentence the claim drops: it is MEAN lifespan (not median), and the 80% power is for data POOLED ACROSS SITES, not per site. NIA's current About page (updated 2026-05-12) says the same: 'The study design includes sufficient numbers of mice to provide 80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites.' (2) CURRENCY: 36/44 describes the ORIGINAL 2004-era design and no longer matches current ITP cohorts. Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience Table 1 (cohorts 2018 and 2019) reports per-arm n of 142-156 males and 132-144 females, pooled across the three sites, with the caption stating 'data from the 3 sites were pooled, about 1/3 of the mice were from each site' — i.e. roughly 44-52 per sex per site. Female arms in particular are now ~44-48/site, not 36. WRONG if stated in present tense; RIGHT as 'the design as published in 2008 called for 36 females and 44 males per site.' Also omitted from the claim, verbatim from Nadon 2008: 'The males are over-represented because of the expectation that some cages will have to be culled due to fighting' and 'The control lifespan group is twice the size of the experimental groups, and all experimental groups are compared to the same control group.'

- **(c) Three parallel sites run the identical protocol — Jackson Laboratory, University of Michigan, UT Health San Antonio** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim in Nadon 2008: 'Testing is performed in triplicate at three independent sites: The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan, and the University of Texas Health Sciences Center—San Antonio.' The institution names differ across sources by era only, not substance: Nadon 2008 uses the pre-2016 name; Cheng 2019 uses 'UT Health San Antonio'; NIA's current site uses 'University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio'. Any of these is defensible. One caliber caution on 'identical': the ITP's own wording is weaker. Nadon 2017 says tests are 'done in parallel, using the same protocol,' and NIA's About page says SOPs 'provide a consistent experimental protocol adhered to across the program' — but Nadon 2008 is explicitly hedged, saying SOPs ensure conditions 'are as uniform as possible' and that 'It is particularly challenging to provide uniform environmental conditions at independent institutions.' The same paper quantifies the residual variation: 'For male control mice at the three sites, the mean median lifespan was 799 days, with a range (minimum to maximum) of 137 days, or 17% of the mean. For females, the mean median lifespan was 881 days, with a range of 51 days, or 6% of the mean.' Prefer 'the same protocol'/'common SOPs' over 'identical protocol'.

- **(d) Across 3,690 ITP control mice from six studies 2004-2013, control female median lifespan 887 days (95% CI 879-898) and control male median 803 days (95% CI 791-815)** — `confirmed`
  Every element confirmed verbatim against the raw text of Cheng et al. 2019 (PMC6516160), which I stripped to plain text and string-matched. Verbatim: 'Females had a longer median lifespan (887 days, 95% CI: 879–898) than males (803 days, 95% CI: 791–815) both when all the survival data were pooled and when the data were stratified by study cohort (Supporting information Table S1).' Verbatim: 'Data analyzed in this study were from a total of 3,690 animals in the control groups at all three sites.' Verbatim: 'Survival data were obtained from six longevity studies conducted between the years of 2004 and 2013.' The mice are correctly described as controls — the paper says '3,690 control (i.e., pharmacologically untreated) mice pooled across all three sites'. Two precision notes that are not errors but could be misread: the six cohorts are defined by START year and those years are 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009 and 2010 (verbatim: 'Each study cohort is defined by start year (2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009, and 2010)'), with follow-up running to 2013 — so '2004-2013' is the span of the studies, not the span of enrollment start years. And these medians are POOLED across all three sites, not per-site figures. Title of the paper is 'Genetically heterogeneous mice exhibit a female survival advantage that is age- and site-specific: Results from a large multi-site study' — note the article's cited title/subtitle should match this.

- **Does the ITP have a stated policy of publishing regardless of outcome? (article claims no such policy could be found)** — `refuted`
  The stated absence is WRONG — an explicit policy exists in two places on nia.nih.gov, and I read both in raw fetched HTML. (1) 'About the ITP' page (nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp/about-itp, last updated 2026-05-12), section headed 'Publication, Data Sharing, and Biospecimens', verbatim: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication. All data from the ITP are publicly available through the ITP Data Coordinating Center following publication.' (2) The ITP FAQ page (.../frequently-asked-questions-about-itp), under the question 'If the agent shortens the lifespan or has negative effects, what will happen to the data?', verbatim: 'The ITP plans to publish all data, including data on agents that fail to increase lifespan or delay late-life illnesses, or interventions that have deleterious side effects.' Corroborating practice, not just policy: the public 'Supported Interventions' table lists every compound tested since 2004 with its outcome, including dozens explicitly marked 'none' (e.g. 4-OH-PBN, nitroflurbiprofen, CAPE at both doses, enalapril, resveratrol at all doses and start ages, simvastatin at both doses, curcumin, green tea extract, MCT oil, oxaloacetic acid, methylene blue, fish oil at both doses, ursodeoxycholic acid, HBX, INT-767, ursolic acid, aspirin 2014 at both doses). A published null-results paper title makes the same point: Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience is titled in part 'fisetin, SG1002 (hydrogen sulfide donor), dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used.' Note the policy is 'submitted for publication'/'plans to publish' — a commitment to submit and to archive via the DCC, not a guarantee of acceptance; phrase it that way rather than as 'guarantees publication'.

**修正:**
- Do not cite Nadon et al. 2008 for 'CByB6F1 dams x C3D2F1 sires'. That paper says only 'a cross of four inbred strains, generated by breeding two F1 hybrids, CB6F1 X C3D2F1' and never specifies which parent is the dam. Cite Cheng et al. 2019 Methods section 4.2 instead: 'UM-HET3 mice were bred at each of the three test sites from CByB6F1/J (JAX stock #100,009) mothers and C3D2F1/J (JAX stock #100,004) fathers.'
- Do not cite Cheng et al. 2019's Introduction for the strain composition. Its Introduction says '[BALB/cJ x C57BL/6J]F1 mothers', which is wrong and contradicts the paper's own Methods; JAX stock #100009 (CByB6F1/J) is BALB/cByJ x C57BL/6J. Use the Methods section, or Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience 46(1):795-816, which spells it out fully as 'dams, BALB/cByJ; sires, C57BL/6 J' and 'dams, C3H/HeJ; sires, DBA/2 J'.
- Attribute the phrase 'in either sex' to Nadon et al. 2017 (EBioMedicine 21:3-4, PMC5514387), not to Nadon et al. 2008. Nadon 2008's power sentence reads only 'to detect a 10% change in lifespan as compared to control groups, at 80% power'. The full 2017 sentence is: 'Population sizes are large enough that the protocol will detect a 10% change in mean lifespan, in either sex, with 80% power, pooling data from as few as two sites.'
- State that the 80% power is to detect a 10% change in MEAN lifespan and that it applies to data POOLED ACROSS SITES, not to any single site. NIA's current program page words it: '80% power to detect a 10% increase in lifespan for either sex, pooling across sites.' Dropping 'pooling across sites' overstates what one site's 36 females or 44 males can resolve.
- Put the 36 females + 44 males per site figure in the past tense or attribute it explicitly to the 2008 design description. It is no longer the operating size. Harrison et al. 2024 GeroScience Table 1 (cohorts 2018 and 2019) reports treatment arms of 142-156 males and 132-144 females pooled across three sites, with roughly one third from each site, i.e. about 44-52 per sex per site rather than 36 females per site.
- Add the detail that ITP control groups are double-sized, which the claim omits and which explains the large control N in Cheng 2019. Nadon 2008: 'The control lifespan group is twice the size of the experimental groups, and all experimental groups are compared to the same control group.' Nadon 2008 also gives the reason males outnumber females: 'The males are over-represented because of the expectation that some cages will have to be culled due to fighting.'
- Replace 'identical protocol' with 'the same protocol' or 'common standard operating procedures'. Nadon 2008 claims only that SOPs keep conditions 'as uniform as possible' and reports substantial residual site variation: 'For male control mice at the three sites, the mean median lifespan was 799 days, with a range (minimum to maximum) of 137 days, or 17% of the mean. For females, the mean median lifespan was 881 days, with a range of 51 days, or 6% of the mean.'
- Remove the statement that no ITP publication policy could be found. NIA's 'About the ITP' page states: 'All lifespan results, both positive and negative, are submitted for publication. All data from the ITP are publicly available through the ITP Data Coordinating Center following publication.' The ITP FAQ adds: 'The ITP plans to publish all data, including data on agents that fail to increase lifespan or delay late-life illnesses, or interventions that have deleterious side effects.' Describe it as a commitment to submit all results and archive them via the Data Coordinating Center, not as a guarantee of publication.
- When describing the Cheng 2019 cohorts, note the six cohorts are defined by start year — 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2009 and 2010 — with follow-up through 2013, so '2004-2013' is the study span, not the range of enrollment start years. Also state that the 887-day and 803-day medians are pooled across all three sites, since the paper's own title stresses that the female advantage is 'age- and site-specific'.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The claim's per-arm sample sizes are contradicted by current ITP practice. Harrison et al. 2024, GeroScience 46(1):795-816 (PMC10828146), Table 1, reports treatment-arm n for cohorts 2018 and 2019 of 142-156 males and 132-144 females with controls at 282-298, and the caption states 'data from the 3 sites were pooled, about 1/3 of the mice were from each site'. That implies roughly 44-52 mice per sex per site, materially above the 36 females per site the claim asserts.
- Cheng et al. 2019 contradicts itself internally on the parental strains: its Introduction says '[BALB/cJ x C57BL/6J]F1 mothers' while its Methods says 'CByB6F1/J (JAX stock #100,009) mothers'. BALB/cJ and BALB/cByJ are different substrains; the Methods and JAX stock number are correct and the Introduction is the error. Anyone verifying the claim against the Introduction alone would reach the wrong strain.
- The ITP's log-rank primary test — the basis on which the 10%/80% power design is framed — has been challenged in the peer-reviewed literature. Jiang et al., GeroScience 2024;46(5):4533-4541 (PMC11335987), 'The Gehan test identifies life-extending compounds overlooked by the log-rank test in the NIA Interventions Testing Program', reports that reanalysis with the Gehan test flags metformin, enalapril, CAPE, green tea extract and 17-DMAG, describing this as 'a nearly 50% increase in the number of compounds identified by the ITP that may enhance survival at least during part of the adult lifespan', while itself conceding 'We recognize that secondary analyses increase the risk of type 1 error'. This does not refute the design claims but means the ITP's null results are not as settled as a bare power statement implies.
- ITP lifespan papers do get formally corrected, so specific numbers should be checked against the latest version. Example: PMID 39004654, 'Correction to: Lifespan effects in male UM-HET3 mice treated with sodium thiosulfate, 16-hydroxyestriol, and late-start canagliflozin', GeroScience 2025.

## V2 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I reached the primary document directly rather than through a summarizer: I curled the PMC author manuscript of Harrison et al. 2009 (PMC2786175) to disk, stripped tags locally, and ran exact substring matches against the raw HTML for every string I report as verbatim. I separately pulled the PUBLISHED Nature abstract via NCBI eutils efetch (PMID 19587680) and diffed it against the manuscript — that is how I found the 'On the basis of' vs 'Based on' divergence. For the ITP ledger comparison I pulled full texts of Miller et al. 2014 (Europe PMC PMC4032600 fullTextXML), Strong et al. 2020 (PMC7681050 fullTextXML), and Miller et al. 2011 (PMC3021372 HTML), and read their survival tables and dose tables directly. Corrections/retractions were checked via the Europe PMC commentCorrectionList and PubMed esummary pubtype for PMID 19587680: only a News & Views comment, no erratum, as of 2026-07. The central assertion of the claim group HOLDS and is now verified word for word: 14%/9% is the age-at-90%-mortality (maximum-lifespan) figure, from Table 1 titled 'The effect of rapamycin on maximum lifespan', in mice started at 600 days, and the cancer-vs-aging hedge sentence is exact. Two supporting sub-claims fail: the 9%/13% pooled numbers are MEAN, not median lifespan (the paper reports no pooled median percentage at all), and the 'one of the smaller effects in the ITP ledger' aside is false on a like-for-like metric — it only works if you compare a 90th-percentile figure to other cohorts' median figures, which is the very error the paragraph condemns. Remaining uncertainty: I could not reach the 2009 supplementary PDF (PMC serves it behind a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge and my WebSearch budget was exhausted mid-task), so the 14 ppm dose is verified only indirectly, through the same authors' later statements, which give 14.7 ppm for this cohort and 14 ppm for the 9-month cohorts. I did not verify per-arm N or age-at-start distributions beyond the 1901-mouse total stated in the paper, because the per-arm counts are not in the main text either.

- **Quote 1 verbatim: Harrison et al. Nature 2009 headline 'an increase of 14% for females and 9% for males'** — `corrected`
  The fragment 'an increase of 14% for females and 9% for males' is verbatim in both versions. BUT the lead-in differs between the two texts. PUBLISHED Nature abstract (verified via PubMed efetch, PMID 19587680): 'On the basis of age at 90% mortality, rapamycin led to an increase of 14% for females and 9% for males.' PMC author-manuscript (PMC2786175, the URL the article cites): 'Based on age at 90% mortality, rapamycin led to an increase of 14% for females and 9% for males.' WRONG: quoting the full sentence as 'Based on age at 90% mortality...' while citing 'Nature 2009;460:392-395'. RIGHT: if citing the published Nature paper, the sentence begins 'On the basis of age at 90% mortality...'. I confirmed both strings by exact substring match against the raw fetched documents, not via a summarizer.

- **The 14%/9% figures are the increase in AGE AT 90% MORTALITY (a maximum-lifespan measure), not median lifespan** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED against Table 1 of the primary text, titled verbatim 'The effect of rapamycin on maximum lifespan'. Pooled across all sites: females, age at 90th percentile 1094 d (controls; 95% CI upper limit 1136) vs 1245 d (rapamycin) = 14%; males 1078 d (UL 1111) vs 1179 d = 9%. Site-level values (F: TJL 17%, UM 14%, UT 8%; M: TJL 10%, UM 4%, UT 16%) show the pooled numbers are not uniform across sites. Added precision the article may want: the percentages themselves are descriptive; statistical significance for maximal lifespan came from a Wang/Allison test on the proportion alive at the 90th-percentile age of the joint life table (females 4.8% of controls vs 21.5% of rapamycin, p<0.0001; males 5.9% vs 20.2%, p<0.0001), and the ITP design was powered for 'a 10% increase (or decrease) in mean lifespan' — so the 14%/9% are not the pre-specified primary endpoint statistic.

- **Median-lifespan figures from the 2009 cohort 'reported as roughly +9% males / +13% females pooled'** — `corrected`
  WRONG: those are median-lifespan figures. RIGHT: they are MEAN-lifespan figures. Verbatim from the paper: 'Expressed as mean lifespan, the effect sizes were 9% for males and 13% for females in the pooled dataset.' The paper reports NO pooled median-lifespan percentage anywhere in the main text or Methods Summary. The only median values given are control-female medians per site (881-895 days, compared to 858-909 d in Cohort 2004). The other pooled figure in that same sentence is life expectancy at 600 days: +28% males, +38% females. Site-level mean-lifespan increases: females 15%, 16%, 7% (TJL, UM, UT); males 5%, 8%, 15%.

- **Mice started on 14 ppm encapsulated rapamycin at 600 days of age** — `corrected`
  600 days: CONFIRMED verbatim ('...when fed beginning at 600 days of age'; Methods: 'until they were started on food containing rapamycin, in Purina 5LG6, at 600 days of age'). 14 ppm: NOT stated anywhere in the 2009 paper's main text or Methods Summary — no 'ppm' or 'mg/kg' string appears. The dose is in the supplementary PDF, which PMC serves behind a proof-of-work challenge I could not clear (so: unreachable at the primary level).
