Harrison 2009 reports NO pooled median percentage increase anywhere; the only median numbers in the paper are absolute control-female medians (881–895 days). Per-site figures are also mean lifespan: females 15%/16%/7% (TJL/UM/UT), males 5%/8%/15%. The paper additionally reports life expectancy at 600 days: +28% males, +38% females pooled. Note the trap: male mean lifespan (+9%) numerically coincides with the male 90th-percentile figure (+9%), which is likely the origin of the confusion.

- **Mice started at 600 days of age on 14 ppm encapsulated rapamycin** — `corrected`
  600 days: CONFIRMED verbatim (Methods Summary: "...until they were started on food containing rapamycin, in Purina 5LG6, at 600 days of age"; a parallel cohort started at 270 days). 14 ppm: the 2009 paper's main text and Methods Summary state NO dietary concentration — 'ppm' and 'mg/kg' appear nowhere in the article body (the number is in the supplementary methods, which PMC would not serve me). The ITP's own later primary papers give: Miller et al. 2011 (J Gerontol, PMC3021372) Table 1, rapamycin 14 mg/kg food = 2.24 mg/kg mouse weight/day = 0.067 mg/mouse/day; and Miller et al. 2014 (Aging Cell, PMC4032600) Introduction states "...when given at a dose of 14.7 mg kg−1 in food from either 9 or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011)." So "14 ppm" is right to within the ITP's own 14 vs 14.7 mg/kg-food discrepancy, but it cannot be sourced to Harrison 2009 itself. Formulation detail confirmed: microencapsulated by Southwest Research Institute with enteric coating Eudragit S100, incorporated into Purina 5LG6 chow.

- **14%/9% is one of the SMALLER rapamycin effects in the ITP's own ledger** — `refuted`
  This sub-claim commits the very caliber error the paragraph is warning about. Compared LIKE-FOR-LIKE on the 90th-percentile/maximal-lifespan measure, the 2009 numbers are at or near the TOP of the ITP rapamycin ledger, not the bottom: Miller 2011 (14 ppm from 9 months, PMC3021372) — "For males, rapamycin led to an increase of 10% in median age... and an increase of 16% in the 90th percentile age. For females, the corresponding values were 18% for median, and 13% for 90th percentile ages" (i.e. female 90th-percentile 13% < 2009's 14%). Miller 2014 (PMC4032600), even at the triple dose of 42 ppm — "Rapamycin at 42 ppm leads to 26% increase in median lifespan in females and 23% in males... Survival of the longest-lived 10% of the cohort was increased by 11% in females and by 8% in males" (both BELOW the 2009 14%/9%). The 2009 result looks 'small' only when its maximum-lifespan number is set against later cohorts' MEDIAN numbers — an apples-to-oranges comparison.

- **Whether the 14%/9% was the pre-specified primary endpoint** — `confirmed`
  It was not. The ITP's pre-specified powering is on MEAN lifespan — verbatim: "Sufficient mice are used to provide 80% power to detect a 10% increase (or decrease) in mean lifespan with respect to unmanipulated controls of the same sex, even if data from one of the three test sites were to be unavailable." The maximal-lifespan result is a secondary analysis: the 90th-percentile ages in Table 1 are compared informally against the control 95% CI upper bound, and significance is established by the Wang et al. 2004 method of comparing proportions alive at the joint 90%-mortality age — "Summing across the three sites, 4.8% of the female control mice were alive at these ages, compared to 21.5% of the rapamycin-treated females (p < 0.0001). For males, the corresponding values were 5.9% of controls and 20.2% of rapamycin mice (p < 0.0001)." Site-specific: females significant at TJL (p=0.0006) and UM (p=0.0001); males at TJL (p=0.008) and UT (p=0.0001), marginal at UM (p=0.07).

- **Retraction / correction / erratum check** — `unreachable`
  Partial. The NCBI OA record for PMC2786175 returns retracted="no" and citation "Nature. 2009 Jul 16; 460(7253):392-395" (confirming the volume/page citation in the claim), and the PMC full text contains no erratum/correction/retraction notice (grep for Erratum|Correction|Retract = 0 hits). But I could NOT run a dedicated search for a later Nature corrigendum or a critical letter: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could query. Treat 'no correction exists' as unconfirmed rather than established. Also unreachable: the supplementary PDF (NIHMS127666-supplement-1.pdf) — PMC, europepmc and the NCBI OA FTP package all refused to serve it, so Supplementary Table S1 (the 90th-percentile calculation detail) and the supplementary statement of the dietary ppm were not read.

**修正:**
- Replace 'median-lifespan figures ... roughly +9% males / +13% females pooled' with MEAN lifespan. The paper's exact sentence is: 'Expressed as mean lifespan, the effect sizes were 9% for males and 13% for females in the pooled dataset.' Harrison 2009 reports no pooled median percentage increase at all — do not attribute one to it.
- Drop or rewrite 'one of the SMALLER rapamycin effects in the ITP's own ledger.' On the same 90th-percentile measure the 2009 result is at the top of the ITP ledger, not the bottom: Miller 2011 (14 ppm from 9 months) gave 90th-percentile increases of 16% males / 13% females, and Miller 2014 at 42 ppm gave only 8% males / 11% females. Correct framing: later ITP cohorts produced much larger MEDIAN lifespan gains (Miller 2014, 42 ppm: +23% males, +26% females), so the 2009 headline looks modest only when its maximum-lifespan number is compared against other studies' median numbers.
- Do not cite Harrison 2009 for the '14 ppm' dose — the paper's main text and Methods Summary never state a dietary concentration. Cite Miller et al. 2011 (J Gerontol A 66:191-201) Table 1, which gives 14 mg/kg food (2.24 mg/kg body weight/day), or note that Miller et al. 2014 (Aging Cell 13:468-477) retrospectively describes the dose as '14.7 mg kg−1 in food' for both the 2009 and 2011 cohorts.
- If attributing the cancer-vs-aging hedge, note it is the second-to-last sentence of the ABSTRACT, not a buried discussion caveat. A stronger Discussion hedge is available verbatim if wanted: 'The increase in both median and maximum lifespan seen in rapamycin-fed mice is consistent with the hypothesis that inhibiting the mTORC1 pathway retards mammalian ageing, but is not compelling proof that ageing rates are altered...'
- Optional strengthening, verified verbatim: the ITP's pre-specified power calculation is on MEAN lifespan ('80% power to detect a 10% increase (or decrease) in mean lifespan'), so the headline 90th-percentile figure is a secondary maximal-lifespan analysis (Wang et al. 2004 method), not the pre-specified primary endpoint.
- Optional strengthening, verified verbatim: the authors flag a male-specific confound — 'We thus cannot rule out the possibility that improved survival among males in the rapamycin group, at UT and at UM, might reflect differences in nutritional or health status between control and rapamycin groups prior to 600 days, rather than solely the effects of rapamycin.' The male 9% figure therefore rests most cleanly on the TJL site, where pre-treatment chow was identical.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Miller et al. 2014, Aging Cell (PMC4032600), Discussion, verbatim: 'Rapamycin at 42 ppm leads to 26% increase in median lifespan in females and 23% in males, in each case larger than that seen in previous or current cohorts exposed to lower doses. Survival of the longest-lived 10% of the cohort was increased by 11% in females and by 8% in males' — i.e. tripling the dose produced a SMALLER 90th-percentile gain than Harrison 2009's 14%/9%, contradicting the 'one of the smaller ITP effects' framing on the maximum-lifespan measure.
- Miller et al. 2011, J Gerontol A (PMC3021372), Results, verbatim: 'For males, rapamycin led to an increase of 10% in median age, averaged across the three sites, and an increase of 16% in the 90th percentile age. For females, the corresponding values were 18% for median, and 13% for 90th percentile ages.' The female 90th-percentile gain (13%) is below Harrison 2009's 14%.
- Harrison 2009 itself contains a male-specific internal caveat not mentioned in the claim: rapamycin-assigned males at UT and possibly UM had lower pre-600-day mortality and received a differently formulated pre-treatment chow, so the paper explicitly cannot attribute the male benefit at those two sites solely to rapamycin.

## V3 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 HOLDS/HOLDS/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(HOLDS)

I reached the primary documents directly: PMC4032600 (Miller 2014, Aging Cell), the PubMed record 24341993, PMC3021372 and PubMed 20974732 (Miller 2011, J Gerontol A), and PMC7681050 (Strong 2020, Aging Cell). Because the pipeline has previously caught fetch summarizers fabricating quotes and misreading multi-column tables, I read each load-bearing number at least twice using differently-scoped prompts and treated agreement across independent passes as the bar for confirmation.

Every numeric sub-claim in this group checks out. The 2014 dose-response figures (4.7 ppm: +3% male p=0.19, +16% female p<0.0001; 14 ppm: +13% male p=0.0015, +21% female p<0.0001; 42 ppm: +23% male, +26% female, both p<0.0001) reproduced identically on two independent reads of Table 1, and the 42 ppm pair is independently corroborated by the abstract, which I retrieved verbatim and identically twice. The 90th-percentile figures at 42 ppm (+8% male, +11% female) reproduced three times. The 2011 figures (+10% male, +18% female median, 14 ppm from 9 months) and the resveratrol (300, 1200 ppm) and simvastatin (12, 120 ppm) null results match the abstract word for word across two reads. The Strong 2020 figures (continuous +11% male / +15% female; alternating +9% male / +8% female, all at 42 ppm) match on two reads. Citations, volumes, issues and page ranges are all correct, and no PubMed record carries an erratum, correction, retraction, or comment notice.

The female-favouring point is solid and directly quotable: the abstract states rapamycin 'increased lifespan more in females than in males at each dose evaluated,' and the Discussion notes the effect was seen 'in three consecutive independent cohorts.' The blood-level explanation is the one place with real caliber risk. It is genuinely the authors' explanation and the PK numbers are real (females 7/16/80 ng/mL vs males 6/9/23 ng/mL at 4.7/14/42 ppm; two-factor ANOVA sex P=0.007, rapamycin P=0.003, interaction P=0.03), but the authors hedge it twice and explicitly leave room for other sex differences. I also flag that the paper's own dose-level data do not track the size of the sex gap, which weakens the mechanism more than the claim implies.

Two things I want to be plain about rather than paper over. First, my reads of the 90th-percentile p-value column in Table 1 were mutually inconsistent, so I did not certify those p-values; the claim group does not assert them, but it tells me the table's p-value columns should not be quoted without a direct look at the PDF. Second, and more important, I could not perform step 3 of the procedure as intended: the session's WebSearch budget was already fully exhausted (200/200) before my first search, so I had no way to hunt for critical letters, failed replications, or post-2014 critiques. My refutation search was limited to checking the primary records for formal correction notices, which is a much weaker test. The absence of an erratum is not evidence that no critique exists. I recommend that one of the other two verifiers, with search budget available, specifically re-run the adversarial literature scan on the sex-dimorphism/PK mechanism before this is treated as settled.

Verdict is HOLDS on the numbers, with the blood-level mechanism marked corrected on caliber and the independent-refutation search marked unreachable.

- **Miller et al., Aging Cell 2014;13(3):468-477 — citation and design (ITP, UM-HET3, rapamycin started at 9 months)** — `confirmed`
  PubMed 24341993 confirms: Miller RA, Harrison DE, Astle CM, Fernandez E, Flurkey K, Han M, Javors MA, Li X, Nadon NL, Nelson JF, Pletcher S, Salmon AB, Sharp ZD, Van Roekel S, Winkleman L, Strong R. 'Rapamycin-mediated lifespan increase in mice is dose and sex dependent and metabolically distinct from dietary restriction.' Aging Cell 2014;13(3):468-77, DOI 10.1111/acel.12194. Full text confirms feeding began at 9 months of age in genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 mice, pooled across three ITP sites. No erratum, correction, retraction, or comment notice on the PubMed record.

- **4.7 ppm: median lifespan +3% males (p=0.19, not significant) and +16% females (p<0.0001)** — `confirmed`
  Table 1 of PMC4032600 gives, for males at 4.7 ppm, median increase 3 with log-rank P=0.19; for females at 4.7 ppm, median increase 16 with P<0.0001. Reproduced identically on two independent narrowly-scoped reads of the article. The characterization of the male result as non-significant is correct.

- **14 ppm: median lifespan +13% males (p=0.0015) and +21% females (p<0.0001)** — `confirmed`
  Table 1 gives males +13% at P=0.0015 and females +21% at P<0.0001. Reproduced identically on two independent reads.

- **42 ppm: median lifespan +23% males (p<0.0001) and +26% females (p<0.0001)** — `confirmed`
  Independently corroborated by the verbatim abstract, which I retrieved identically twice: 'Rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR kinase, increased median lifespan of genetically heterogeneous mice by 23% (males) to 26% (females) when tested at a dose threefold higher than that used in our previous studies.' Table 1 gives P<0.0001 for both sexes (male median 992 d vs control 807 d; female 1132 d vs control 896 d).

- **At 42 ppm the 90th-percentile (maximal) lifespan increase was +8% males and +11% females** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed three separate times against Table 1's 90th-percentile columns: males +8%, females +11% at 42 ppm. Caveat the article should respect: these same values (+8% male, +11% female) also appear at the 14 ppm dose, so the figures are not unique to 42 ppm and should not be presented as a distinguishing feature of the top dose. Separately, my reads of Table 1's 90th-percentile P-VALUE column were internally inconsistent (0.003/0.004 in one pass vs the Results narrative), so I do not vouch for those specific p-values — but the claim group does not assert them. The Results narrative, which I retrieved identically twice, reads: 'Maximal lifespan, evaluated according to Wang et al., (2004) as the proportion of mice still alive at the age of 90% mortality in the joint lifespan distribution, was increased significantly (P < 0.001) by each of the three rapamycin doses in females and by the two higher doses in males (P = 0.006 and P = 0.001).' Note this means maximal lifespan at 4.7 ppm was NOT significantly increased in males.

- **Rapamycin is female-favouring in the ITP (load-bearing point)** — `confirmed`
  Stated verbatim in the abstract: 'Rapamycin increased lifespan more in females than in males at each dose evaluated, perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels of this drug.' Holds arithmetically at every dose for median (16 vs 3, 21 vs 13, 26 vs 23) and at 42 ppm for the 90th percentile (11 vs 8). The Discussion strengthens it: the effect was 'seen now in three consecutive independent cohorts.'

- **The blood-level explanation for the female advantage** — `corrected`
  The explanation is genuinely in the paper, but the caliber must be hedged, not asserted. WRONG version: presenting higher female blood levels as the established/sole cause of the female advantage. RIGHT version: the authors offer it as a probable but non-exclusive explanation. Abstract hedges with 'perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels of this drug.' Discussion: 'It seems likely that this differential effect, seen now in three consecutive independent cohorts, reflects higher levels of rapamycin in blood of female UM-HET3 mice compared with males given equal amounts of rapamycin in food.' The authors immediately add: 'But it is also likely that males and females may differ in other ways in their response to rapamycin.' Supporting PK data, quoted verbatim: 'Blood concentrations were 7, 16, and 80 ng mL−1 for females at rapamycin doses of 4.7, 14, and 42 ppm, respectively, and the corresponding values in males were 6, 9, and 23 ng mL−1', with 'A two-factor anova (sex and rapamycin dose) showed significant effects of sex (P = 0.007), rapamycin (P = 0.003), and interaction (P = 0.03)'.

- **Miller et al., J Gerontol A 2011;66(2):191-201 — 14 ppm from 9 months extended median survival an average of 10% in males and 18% in females** — `confirmed`
  PubMed 20974732 confirms the citation: Miller RA, Harrison DE, Astle CM, et al., 'Rapamycin, but not resveratrol or simvastatin, extends life span of genetically heterogeneous mice,' J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2011;66(2):191-201. No erratum/correction/comment notice. Abstract verbatim: 'Median survival was extended by an average of 10% in males and 18% in females.' Start age confirmed verbatim: 'Rapamycin was administered in food to genetically heterogeneous mice from the age of 9 months.' The 14 ppm dose is NOT in the abstract; it is in the full text (PMC3021372), which specifies 14 mg/kg food, i.e. 14 ppm. The word 'average' is load-bearing and is in the source (results pooled across three sites).

- **In the 2011 paper resveratrol (300, 1200 ppm) and simvastatin (12, 120 ppm) had no significant survival effect** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim, retrieved identically on two independent reads: 'Resveratrol (at 300 and 1200 ppm food) and simvastatin (12 and 120 ppm) did not have significant effects on survival in male or female mice.' All four doses match the claim exactly.

- **Strong et al. 2020 — 42 ppm from 20 months, continuous: +11% median males / +15% females** — `confirmed`
  Strong R, Miller RA, Bogue M, et al., 'Rapamycin-mediated mouse lifespan extension: Late-life dosage regimes with sex-specific effects,' Aging Cell 2020;19(11):e13269 (PMC7681050). Continuous 42 ppm from 20 months ('Rapa 20 mon'): males +11% (p=0.0007), females +15% (p<0.0001). Abstract verbatim: 'Initiation of Rapa at 42 ppm increased survival significantly in both male and female mice.' No erratum found.

- **Strong et al. 2020 — alternating month-on/month-off: +9% males / +8% females** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed: males +9% (p=0.002), females +8% (p<0.0001). The 'on' months used the same 42 ppm dose. Abstract verbatim: 'Protocols in which each month of Rapa treatment was followed by a month without Rapa exposure were also effective in both sexes, though this approach was less effective than continuous exposure in female mice.'

- **Independent search for later refutations, failed replications, or superseding data through 2026-07** — `unreachable`
  I could not complete this step properly. The session's WebSearch budget was fully exhausted (200/200) before I could issue a single search, so I could not scan for critical letters, failed replications, or post-publication critiques. What I COULD verify by direct fetch: the PubMed records for all three papers (24341993, 20974732, and the Strong 2020 record via PMC) carry no erratum, correction, retraction, or comment notices. That is absence of a formal correction, NOT evidence that no critique exists. This item should be re-run by another verifier with search budget.

**修正:**
- Do not present higher female blood levels as the established cause of rapamycin's female advantage. The ITP authors hedge: the abstract says 'perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels of this drug,' and the Discussion, after saying 'It seems likely that this differential effect ... reflects higher levels of rapamycin in blood of female UM-HET3 mice,' explicitly adds 'But it is also likely that males and females may differ in other ways in their response to rapamycin.' Write it as the authors' leading hypothesis, not a settled mechanism.
- Do not present +8% (males) / +11% (females) as a signature of the 42 ppm dose. Table 1 reports the same 90th-percentile increases at 14 ppm, so the maximal-lifespan effect plateaus between 14 and 42 ppm even though median lifespan keeps rising.
- If the article mentions maximal (90th-percentile) lifespan across doses, state that it was significantly increased at all three doses in females but only at the two higher doses in males — the 4.7 ppm male maximal-lifespan effect was not significant, mirroring the non-significant median result (p=0.19).
- Do not conflate the Miller 2011 figures (+10% male / +18% female at 14 ppm from 9 months) with the Miller 2014 figures at the same nominal 14 ppm dose (+13% male / +21% female). These are separate ITP cohorts, not the same measurement; presenting either as 'the' 14 ppm result is misleading. Preserve the word 'average' from the 2011 abstract, which reflects pooling across three sites.
- The 14 ppm dose for Miller 2011 is not stated in the abstract; it comes from the full text (14 mg/kg food). Cite it accordingly if precision about sourcing matters.
- When citing Strong et al. 2020, retain the paper's own framing that the alternating regimen was 'less effective than continuous exposure in female mice' (+8% vs +15%) while being roughly comparable in males (+9% vs +11%) — the intermittent-dosing story is sex-specific, not uniformly favorable. If the article discusses late-life regimens broadly, note the third arm: a 3-month transient exposure (Rapa 20-23) gave +11% in males (p=0.024) but only +4% in females (p=0.15), i.e. benefit in males only — the one place in this literature where the male/female asymmetry reverses.
- Note the internal tension if the article leans hard on the pharmacokinetic explanation: female/male blood levels diverge most at 42 ppm (80 vs 23 ng/mL, ~3.5x) yet the median-lifespan sex gap is narrowest there (26% vs 23%), whereas at 4.7 ppm blood levels are nearly equal (7 vs 6 ng/mL) but the lifespan gap is widest (16% vs 3%). Blood level alone does not track the size of the sex difference.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Not a contradiction of the claim as stated, but a contradiction of the mechanism the claim asks me to verify: the paper's own PK data run opposite to the dose-level prediction. At 4.7 ppm male and female blood concentrations are nearly identical (6 vs 7 ng/mL) yet the median-lifespan sex gap is at its largest (+3% male vs +16% female); at 42 ppm blood levels differ by ~3.5-fold (23 vs 80 ng/mL) yet the sex gap is at its smallest (+23% vs +26%). If sexual dimorphism in blood levels were the primary driver, the gap should widen with dose, not narrow. This is consistent with the authors' own caveat that 'males and females may differ in other ways in their response to rapamycin.'
- My two independent reads of Table 1's 90th-percentile p-value column for males disagreed (one pass returned 0.003 and 0.004; the Results narrative, retrieved identically twice, gives P=0.006 and P=0.001 for the two higher male doses). I therefore treat the table's p-value column transcription as unreliable and did not certify those values. This does not affect any number the claim group asserts, but the article should not quote 90th-percentile p-values without a direct look at the PDF.

### 票 2(HOLDS)

I fetched all three primary papers as raw HTML with curl (not through a summarizing fetcher) and parsed the tables cell-by-cell in Python so that column alignment could not be misread: Miller et al., Aging Cell 2014;13(3):468-477 (PMC4032600), Miller et al., J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2011;66(2):191-201 (PMC3021372), and Strong et al., Aging Cell 2020;19(11):e13269 (PMC7681050). Every quoted string in my item notes was read directly in the extracted document text.

Miller 2014 Table 1 (pooled across the three ITP sites, UM-HET3, encapsulated rapamycin started at 9 months, log-rank stratified by site as the pre-specified primary endpoint; control N=300 males / 280 females, N=156 males / 136 females per rapamycin dose) reproduces exactly: males 4.7/14/42 ppm = +3% (P=0.19), +13% (P=0.0015), +23% (P<0.0001); females = +16%, +21%, +26% (all P<0.0001); 90th-percentile increase at 42 ppm = 8% males, 11% females. Miller 2011's abstract states verbatim the 10% male / 18% female median extension at 14 ppm from 9 months and the null result for resveratrol (300, 1200 ppm) and simvastatin (12, 120 ppm). Strong 2020 Table 1 gives Rapa-20-continuous +11% males (p=0.0007) / +15% females (p<0.0001) and Rapa-cycles +9% males (p=0.002) / +8% females (p<0.0001). Every number and p-value in the claim group matched; none was off.

The female-favouring direction and its stated blood-level rationale are both in the primary text (blood 7/16/80 ng/mL female vs 6/9/23 ng/mL male; ANOVA sex P=0.007, dose P=0.003, interaction P=0.03), but the paper frames it as a hypothesis and the measurements come from a small separate cohort at one site, so the article must not harden it into mechanism.

Refutation attempts: PubMed efetch shows no CommentsCorrections/errata for any of the three PMIDs; no correction notices in the PMC texts; a 2026 Ageing Res Rev review restates the ITP picture unchanged. Remaining uncertainty: my WebSearch budget was exhausted early in the session, so I could not run a broad sweep for post-2020 primary work specifically challenging the pharmacokinetic explanation of the sex difference - I mark that particular avenue as not exhaustively checked rather than clear. The substantive weaknesses I did surface are not wrong numbers but missing qualifiers: the Strong 2020 pre-treatment chow/survival divergence confound, the pooled-vs-site-averaged gap in the Miller 2014 male 14 ppm result (13% vs 5%), and the Miller 2014 text/table disagreement on male Wang-Allison p-values.

Methods/Results confirm the regimen is 1 month on / 1 month off beginning at 20 months of age with 42 ppm eRapa. (Figure 1's legend says 'Rapa given from 22 months until death' for the continuous group, which contradicts the text/Methods '20 months' - a legend typo in the paper, not a problem for the claim.)

- **Rapamycin is female-favouring in the ITP, explained by higher blood levels in females** — `confirmed`
  Miller 2014 abstract verbatim: 'Rapamycin increased lifespan more in females than in males at each dose evaluated, perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels of this drug.' Blood data (Results): 7, 16, 80 ng/mL in females at 4.7, 14, 42 ppm vs 6, 9, 23 ng/mL in males; two-factor ANOVA sex P=0.007, rapamycin P=0.003, interaction P=0.03. Also 'Cox regression, stratified by site, showed a significant effect of dose (P < 0.001) for each sex and a significant difference between males and females, also at P < 0.001.' CALIBER LIMITS the article must respect: (a) the paper hedges with 'perhaps'/'likely'; (b) the blood levels come from a SEPARATE non-longevity cohort at ONE site (UT), N=4-8 per group, dosed from 3-4 months for 5 months, plus a 6-h post-prandial time course in 26-month-olds - not from the longevity mice; (c) the authors concede 'such differences might reflect differences in food consumption'; (d) they explicitly say 'it is also likely that males and females may differ in other ways in their response to rapamycin', citing XME gene expression, and elsewhere suggest the larger male glucose-tolerance deficit 'could contribute to the lower lifespan effect produced by rapamycin in males'. So blood level is a leading hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism. Corroboration that the female bias is atypical for the ITP: the same Discussion notes NDGA and acarbose act preferentially in males.

- **Adversarial check: errata, corrections, retractions, or superseding data through 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  NCBI efetch on PMIDs 24341993 (Miller 2014), 20974732 (Miller 2011), 33145977 (Strong 2020) returns NO CommentsCorrections/RefSource elements - i.e., no erratum, correction, retraction, or expression of concern indexed for any of the three. No correction banners in the PMC full texts. A 2026 review (Ageing Res Rev, PMC13080664, 'Sex differences in response to longevity interventions') restates the ITP position unchanged: the program is generally male-biased, while 'Rapamycin at various concentrations, and started at various ages, strongly increases median and maximum lifespan in female animals.' Nothing found that supersedes or contradicts the quoted numbers. NOT VERIFIED (search budget exhausted mid-task): I could not run a full targeted sweep for post-2020 primary papers specifically testing the blood-level explanation, so treat 'no contradicting primary study exists' as unestablished rather than confirmed.

**修正:**
- Do not present Strong et al. 2020's late-life numbers as a clean drug effect without the authors' own confound: control mice received TestDiets-processed 5LG6 chow from 6 months while Rapa-assigned cages received 5LG6 from a different supplier until 604 days, and 'survival curves at several sites appear to show differences between Control and treatment cohorts prior to the initiation of Rapa administration at age 20 months (604 days)'; Rapa males were also already lighter than controls at 12 and 18 months (p<0.005), before any drug. Add a one-clause caveat when citing +11%/+15% and +9%/+8%.
- When citing Miller 2014's 14 ppm male result as +13%, note it is the pooled, site-stratified analysis; the same paper's Discussion reports the site-averaged male increase at 14 ppm as only 5% (females 18% either way). Do not present +13% as a replication-level stable male effect.
- State that the female-favouring blood-level explanation is the authors' hypothesis ('perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels'), measured in a separate 4-8 mouse-per-group non-longevity cohort at a single site, with the authors themselves noting food-consumption differences and other sex-specific mechanisms (XME gene expression, larger male glucose intolerance) as alternatives. Do not write it as established mechanism.
- If the article quotes Wang/Allison p-values for male 14 ppm and 42 ppm in Miller 2014, use Table 1 (0.003 and 0.004) and be aware the Results text gives 0.006 and 0.001 - the paper is internally inconsistent here.
- If the article implies resveratrol and simvastatin were tested on the same 9-month schedule as rapamycin, correct it: Miller 2011 Table 1 gives age at initiation of 10 months for simvastatin (12 and 120 ppm) and 12 months for resveratrol (300 and 1200 ppm).

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

I did not rely on fetch summaries. I downloaded the full HTML of all three primaries with curl, stripped tags locally, and read Table 1 of each in raw text; every quoted string in this verdict was then re-verified by exact substring match against those local files (13/13 matched). This mattered: the WebFetch summarizer on PMC4032600 returned "8% increase in both males and females" for the 42 ppm 90th percentile — a fabricated multi-column table misread. The raw table says males 8, females 11, so the CLAIM is right and the summarizer was wrong. Had I trusted the fetch, I would have wrongly "corrected" a correct claim.

Every number and p-value in the claim group checks out verbatim: all six Miller 2014 median/p pairs against Table 1 (with medians in days and N per arm), the 42 ppm 90th-percentile +8%/+11%, the 2011 abstract's "average of 10% in males and 18% in females" plus the resveratrol/simvastatin null at the stated doses, and all four Strong 2020 values (continuous +11% M p=0.0007 / +15% F p<0.0001; cycles +9% M p=0.002 / +8% F p<0.0001). The female-favouring direction is confirmed at the statistical level by Miller 2014's Cox regression showing "a significant difference between males and females, also at P < 0.001", and the blood-level numbers (F 7/16/80 vs M 6/9/23 ng/mL; sex P=0.007, interaction P=0.03) are verbatim real.

The verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS on caliber, not arithmetic, on two counts. First, an attribution error: the claim pairs each median percentage with a p-value as though the test were of the median difference; it is a site-stratified log-rank test on the full survival distribution, which the paper names as its pre-specified primary endpoint. Second, the blood-level account is presented as the explanation when the source hedges it — it comes from a separate small PK cohort (UT only, N=4-8, dosed 5 months from 3-4 months of age, not the lifespan mice), the authors concede it "might reflect differences in food consumption", and Strong 2020 states outright that it has no ready explanation for the sex dimorphism in its own 3-month arm. I also found that the female advantage reverses under non-continuous dosing in Strong 2020, that resveratrol and simvastatin started at 12 and 10 months rather than 9, and that Miller 2014's narrative male Wang/Allison p-values (0.006, 0.001) disagree with its own Table 1 (0.003, 0.004).

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: I confirmed no erratum, correction, retraction or expression of concern attaches to any of the three papers, by grepping the full PMC HTML of each and checking PubMed for PMID 24341993. But I could NOT perform the forward-citation sweep for failed replications or superseding ITP data through 2026-07 — this session's WebSearch budget was already fully consumed (200/200) when I reached that step, and WebFetch alone cannot enumerate citing works. I also could not independently test the background framing that the ITP shows a general male bias; none of these three primaries establishes that program-wide, and I declined to supply it from memory.

- **Miller 2014 Aging Cell 13(3):468-477, rapamycin from 9 mo, median lifespan increase: 4.7 ppm +3% M (p=0.19, NS) / +16% F (p<0.0001); 14 ppm +13% M (p=0.0015) / +21% F (p<0.0001); 42 ppm +23% M (p<0.0001) / +26% F (p<0.0001)** — `confirmed`
  Every value matches Table 1 ('Survival statistics pooled across sites') exactly, read from the raw PMC4032600 HTML (not a fetch summary). Males: Controls median 807 d, N=300; Rapa(4.7) 834 d, +3, p=0.19, N=156; Rapa(14) 909 d, +13, p=0.0015, N=156; Rapa(42) 992 d, +23, p<0.0001, N=156. Females: Controls 896 d, N=280; Rapa(4.7) 1043 d, +16, p<0.0001, N=136; Rapa(14) 1086 d, +21, p<0.0001, N=136; Rapa(42) 1132 d, +26, p<0.0001, N=136. Narrative confirms verbatim: 'The highest tested rapamycin dose increased median lifespan by 23% in males and 26% in females.' Species/stock: genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 (CByB6F1/J mothers x C3D2F1/J fathers), bred at TJL, UM, UT; encapsulated rapamycin in food from 9 months. No erratum, correction, retraction or expression of concern found on PMID 24341993 or in the PMC record.

- **At 42 ppm the 90th-percentile increase was +8% males and +11% females** — `confirmed`
  CORRECT as stated, and I flag this specifically because a WebFetch summarizer pass on the same URL returned the FALSE claim '8% increase in both males and females' — a multi-column table misread of exactly the kind the pipeline was warned about. The raw table reads: males Rapa(42) 90th %ile age 1185 d, increase 8, Wang/Allison p=0.004; females Rapa(42) 90th %ile age 1282 d, increase 11, p<0.0001. So +8% M / +11% F is right. Caveat worth carrying: the identical +8% M / +11% F appears at 14 ppm (males 1180 d, p=0.003; females 1285 d, p<0.0001), so the maximal-lifespan measure PLATEAUS between 14 and 42 ppm even though median keeps rising — writing '+8%/+11% at 42 ppm' without that note implies a dose-peak the data do not show.

- **p-values attach to the median lifespan increases** — `corrected`
  WRONG framing: the claim reads '+3% males (p=0.19, NOT significant)', attributing the p-value to the median increase. RIGHT: the p-values in Table 1 are log-rank p-values computed on the ENTIRE survival distribution, stratified by site — they do not test the median difference. Table 1 note verbatim: 'Log-rank P-values were calculated with stratification by site.' The paper names its pre-specified primary endpoint verbatim: 'the primary endpoint, that is, a site-stratified log-rank test in the pooled data set, was significant at P = 0.002 in males'. Median % change is a descriptive statistic, not the tested quantity. (Note the paper itself rounds that same male 14 ppm value to P=0.002 in text vs 0.0015 in Table 1.) Separately, the 90th-%ile p-values come from a different test (Wang/Allison, Fisher's exact on live/dead counts at the site-specific age of 10% survival) and must not be conflated with the log-rank values.

- **Miller 2011 J Gerontol A 66(2):191-201: 14 ppm from 9 mo extended median survival an average of 10% in males and 18% in females** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim (PMC3021372): 'Rapamycin was administered in food to genetically heterogeneous mice from the age of 9 months and produced significant increases in life span, including maximum life span, at each of three test sites. Median survival was extended by an average of 10% in males and 18% in females.' The paper's Table 1 confirms rapamycin at 14 mg/kg food, age at initiation 9 mo (2.24 mg/kg mouse/day). 'Average' is the paper's own word (averaged across the three sites). PMC citation line reads 'J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2010 Oct 25;66A(2):191-201' (volume styled 66A, e-pub 2010); the article's '2011;66(2)' is the standard PubMed form and is acceptable.

- **In that same 2011 paper resveratrol (300, 1200 ppm) and simvastatin (12, 120 ppm) had NO significant survival effect** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim: 'Resveratrol (at 300 and 1200 ppm food) and simvastatin (12 and 120 ppm) did not have significant effects on survival in male or female mice.' Title verbatim: 'Rapamycin, But Not Resveratrol or Simvastatin, Extends Life Span of Genetically Heterogeneous Mice'. IMPORTANT qualifier the claim omits: those two drugs were NOT started at 9 months. The paper's Table 1 (Sources and Doses of Test Agents) gives age at initiation = 10 mo for both simvastatin doses and 12 mo for both resveratrol doses; only rapamycin began at 9 mo. A sentence framed 'from 9 months... a paper in which resveratrol and simvastatin had no effect' wrongly implies a common start age.

- **Strong et al. 2020, 42 ppm from 20 months: continuous +11% median M / +15% F; alternating month-on/month-off +9% M / +8% F** — `confirmed`
  All four values match Table 1 of Aging Cell 2020;19(11):e13269 (PMC7681050) exactly. Male controls median 772 d, N=300. 'Rapa 20 mon' M: N=156, 856 d, +11, log-rank p=0.0007, 90th %ile 1148 d (+9), WA p=0.04. 'Rapa cycles' M: N=159, 841 d, +9, p=0.002, 90th %ile 1144 d (+9), WA p=0.001. Female controls 905 d, N=280. 'Rapa 20 mon' F: N=136, 1040 d, +15, p<0.0001, 90th %ile 1231 d (+12), WA p<0.0001. 'Rapa cycles' F: N=136, 977 d, +8, p<0.0001, 90th %ile 1203 d (+10), WA p=0.0004. Narrative verbatim: 'Rapa 20 led to a 15% increase in median (p < 0.0001 by log-rank test), while Rapa cycles led to an 8% increase (p < 0.0001)'. 'Rapa cycles' is defined verbatim as Rapa 'given for 1-month interval interspersed with drug-free months from 20 months until death' — matches 'month-on/month-off'. No erratum/retraction notice in the record.

- **Rapamycin is FEMALE-favouring in the ITP (load-bearing)** — `confirmed`
  Directly supported by primary text. Miller 2014 verbatim: 'Cox regression, stratified by site, showed a significant effect of dose (P < 0.001) for each sex and a significant difference between males and females, also at P < 0.001.' The female advantage is consistent across all three doses in median (16/21/26 vs 3/13/23) and in the 2011 cohort (18% vs 10%) and in Strong 2020 continuous dosing (15% vs 11%). CAVEAT the article should not lose: the direction REVERSES for the intermittent and transient regimens in Strong 2020 — cycles gave +9% M vs +8% F, and the 3-month Rapa 20-23 arm gave +11% M (p=0.024, significant) vs +4% F (p=0.15, NOT significant). So 'rapamycin favours females' is true for continuous dosing, not universally. NOT verified here: the framing that the ITP generally shows a male bias — that is a program-wide characterization no single one of these three primaries establishes, and I could not test it (WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted at 200/200 before I could run the cross-check).

- **The blood-level explanation for the female advantage** — `corrected`
  The blood numbers are real but the claim's status as an 'explanation' is over-stated. Miller 2014 verbatim: 'Blood concentrations were 7, 16, and 80 ng mL-1 for females at rapamycin doses of 4.7, 14, and 42 ppm, respectively, and the corresponding values in males were 6, 9, and 23 ng mL-1, with N = 4-8 mice in each group'; two-factor ANOVA gave sex P=0.007, rapamycin P=0.003, interaction P=0.03, 'indicating that blood levels of rapamycin were higher in female than in male mice, with steeper dose-dependent increases in blood levels seen in females.' WRONG to present this as a demonstrated mechanism. RIGHT: it is a hedged inference from a SEPARATE, small pharmacokinetic cohort — different mice, one site only (UT), dosed for 5 months starting at 3-4 months of age (not the 9-month lifespan cohort), N=4-8 per group. The authors' own hedge, verbatim: 'Although such differences might reflect differences in food consumption, we conclude that female UM-HET3 mice are likely to have higher blood levels of rapamycin than males'. And Strong 2020 explicitly disclaims it as a general account, verbatim: 'We do not have a ready explanation for the sexual dimorphism we have noted in responses to the Rapa 20-23 dosing regime in the present study'.

- **Later corrections, errata, failed replications or superseding data up to 2026-07** — `unreachable`
  I could confirm NO erratum/correction/retraction/expression-of-concern attaches to any of the three papers: grep of the full downloaded PMC HTML for all three returned no such notice (the single 'erratum' hit in PMC3021372 belongs to a CITED reference, Nature 2004;430:686-689, not to the ITP paper), and PubMed PMID 24341993 lists none. What I could NOT do is the forward-citation sweep for post-publication contradiction or superseding ITP data through 2026-07: this session's WebSearch budget was fully consumed (200/200) before I could run those queries, and I will not fill that gap from memory. Treat 'no contradicting later literature' as UNTESTED, not as established.

**修正:**
- Do not attach the p-values to the median percentages. Rewrite so it is clear the p-values are site-stratified LOG-RANK tests on the whole survival curve (the ITP's pre-specified primary endpoint, quoted verbatim in Miller 2014 as 'the primary endpoint, that is, a site-stratified log-rank test in the pooled data set'), while the % figures are descriptive median changes. E.g. '4.7 ppm raised male median by 3%, and the log-rank test on the male survival curve was not significant (p=0.19)' — not '+3% (p=0.19)'.
- When citing the +8% male / +11% female 90th-percentile gain at 42 ppm, add that 14 ppm produced the identical +8%/+11%: the maximal-lifespan measure plateaus above 14 ppm while median keeps climbing to 42 ppm. Without this, the sentence implies a dose-peak in maximum lifespan that the data do not show.
- The 90th-percentile p-values come from the Wang/Allison test (Fisher's exact on live/dead counts at the site-specific age of 10% survival), a different test from the log-rank values used for median. Do not present them as one p-value column.
- Downgrade the blood-level account from explanation to hypothesis. It rests on a separate pharmacokinetic cohort — UT site only, N=4-8 per group, dosed 5 months from age 3-4 months, NOT the 9-month lifespan cohort — and the authors hedge it verbatim: 'Although such differences might reflect differences in food consumption, we conclude that female UM-HET3 mice are likely to have higher blood levels of rapamycin than males'. Add that Strong 2020 states verbatim 'We do not have a ready explanation for the sexual dimorphism' in its 3-month arm.
- Qualify 'rapamycin is female-favouring' to CONTINUOUS dosing. In Strong 2020 the direction reverses for non-continuous regimens: month-on/month-off gave +9% males vs +8% females, and the 3-month-only arm (Rapa 20-23) gave +11% males (p=0.024, significant) vs +4% females (p=0.15, not significant).
- Fix the implied start ages in the 2011 sentence. Only rapamycin began at 9 months. Per that paper's Table 1, simvastatin (12 and 120 ppm) began at 10 months and resveratrol (300 and 1200 ppm) began at 12 months. Do not let 'from 9 months' govern all three drugs.
- If the article contrasts 42 ppm at 9 months (+23%/+26%) with 42 ppm at 20 months (+11%/+15%), carry Strong 2020's own caution verbatim in substance: these are historical rather than contemporaneous comparisons — 'it is always hazardous to compare results from studies done many years apart'.
- Add the Strong 2020 internal caveat if the late-life numbers are load-bearing: the authors report 'unanticipated variation in patterns of weight gain, prior to the initiation of the Rapa treatment, presumably due to the use of drug-free food from two different suppliers', and site-level male responses to the cycles protocol ranged from -5% to +41%.
- State N explicitly where the dose-response is discussed: Miller 2014 used 156 males and 136 females per rapamycin dose against 300 male / 280 female pooled controls, in genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 mice across three sites.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Strong 2020 contradicts a blanket 'rapamycin favours females' reading: its Table 1 shows the 3-month Rapa 20-23 arm significant in MALES only (+11%, p=0.024) and null in females (+4%, p=0.15), and the month-on/month-off arm slightly male-favouring (+9% M vs +8% F). The paper's own summary line reads that intermittent or 3-month exposure 'was as effective as continuous exposure in increasing survival in males' while in females only intermittent worked and less well than continuous.
- Miller 2014 contains an internal inconsistency the article should not propagate: the Results narrative states maximal lifespan was increased in males by the two higher doses at 'P = 0.006 and P = 0.001', but Table 1's Wang/Allison column gives p=0.003 for 14 ppm and p=0.004 for 42 ppm. The text and the table do not agree. Cite the table values.
- The 14 ppm / 9-month result is reported at two different magnitudes across the two ITP papers: +10% M / +18% F in Miller 2011 (Cohort 2006) versus +13% M / +21% F in Miller 2014's pooled dose-response table. These are different cohorts, and Miller 2014 describes its result as 'confirming our earlier report at this dose'. Presenting both numbers side by side without noting they are separate cohorts would read as a discrepancy.
- Miller 2014's own site-level data undercut the clean dose-response story for males: at 14 ppm, effects ranged 'from a 21% increase at UT to a 10% decline in median lifespan at TJL', and at 4.7 ppm the pooled null concealed a significant 16% extension (p=0.02) at UM.

## V4 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I deliberately did NOT rely on the WebFetch summarizer. My first WebFetch of the Jiang paper returned 'Males: Log-rank p-value = 0.2200' for metformin - which is precisely the multi-column table misread the task warned about, and almost certainly the origin of the 'discrepancy' I was asked to adjudicate. I therefore curled the raw HTML of both PMC articles (PMC5013015 and PMC11335987), stripped tags locally, and read the sentences and table rows myself. Every string I quote above I saw in that locally extracted text.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Strong et al., Aging Cell 2016;15(5):872-884 full text plus Table 1, from which I read the metformin design sentence, the P=0.35 sentence, the female-null sentence, the historical-control paragraph (P=0.12 stratified / P=0.049 unstratified), the authors' 'equivocal' summary, and the dose concession; and Table 1's full numeric grid (Control 294/780 d; Met 148/835 d/+7%/0.348; Met/Rapa 158/959 d/+23%/0.000; female Control 281/874 d; Met 140/872 d/0%/0.791; Met/Rapa 142/1078 d/+23%/0.000). I recomputed the percentages from the medians and they reconcile. (2) Jiang et al., GeroScience 2024;46(5):4533-4541 full text plus Table 1 verbatim, the 132-cases sentence, the FDR-adjustment sentence in Methods, the author affiliations, and the supplementary docx (retrieved from Springer static-content after PMC blocked it), whose Table S1 confirms the 132/116/16 breakdown.

Adjudication of the flagged discrepancy: there is none. Jiang's log-rank p = 0.3477 reproduces Strong's 0.348 to three decimals; 0.2200 is enalapril. What Jiang adds is a different test on the same data (Gehan 0.0495, Z-test 0.0118) justified by a claimed proportional-hazards violation. I did find a real but smaller inconsistency the task did not ask about: 7% vs 8% for the same median increase.

Searched for refutation: PubMed via eutils for any later or replicating ITP metformin lifespan cohort - none exists through 2026-07; all other metformin/UM-HET3 hits are mechanistic or review papers. I found no erratum or critical letter on either paper. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS because the supplied discrepancy premise is false and the multiplicity characterization overstates the case against Jiang, even though every substantive number in the claim group checks out verbatim.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: Jiang's Supplementary Table S2 (the full 132-case listing) is embedded as an image and is not in the docx text layer, so I could NOT enumerate every metformin row across all ITP cohorts from that source; my 'only one metformin lifespan experiment' confirmation rests on the PubMed record and on Jiang's Table 1/Fig. 1 listing a single metformin condition (1000 ppm, onset 9 months, n=148 male / n=140 female, matching C2011). I also could not reach the NIA ITP compound-list page (returned an empty body), and my WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not cross-check the ITP's own public compound roster. Finally, my Benjamini-Hochberg arithmetic showing p=0.0495 would likely not survive FDR over 132 tests is my own calculation, not a statement in the paper, and is labeled as such above.

- **Metformin alone dosing/design: 0.1% of diet (1000 ppm) from 9 months of age, both sexes, three sites** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from Strong 2016 raw HTML (I extracted and read the source text myself, not a summarizer): 'Beginning at 9 months of age, groups of male and female mice began consuming a diet containing 1000 ppm (0.1%) Met.' Three sites confirmed: '148 Met mice and 294 controls, distributed among the three test sites' (TJL, UM, UT). N per arm from Table 1: males 148 Met vs 294 control; females 140 Met vs 281 control.

- **Non-significant +7% median in males pooled, P=0.35** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'Met led to a 7% increase in median lifespan of males when data were pooled across sites, but the effect was not statistically significant ( P = 0.35).' Table 1 gives median 835 d (Met) vs 780 d (control) = +7.05%, log-rank P = 0.348, stratified by test site. Site-specific values 13%, -1%, 10%, none significant. Also note the 90th-percentile (maximum lifespan) result went the wrong way: -2%, Wang-Allison P = 0.405.

- **No effect in females** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'There was no effect of Met on survival of female mice, either in the pooled data (Table 1, Fig. 3), or at any site.' Table 1: female median 872 d vs 874 d control = 0% (-0.23%), log-rank P = 0.791.

- **Citation: Strong et al., Aging Cell 2016;15(5):872-884** — `confirmed`
  PubMed PMID 27312235 confirms Aging Cell, volume 15, issue 5, pages 872-84, 2016 Oct, first author Strong R. Full title: 'Longer lifespan in male mice treated with a weakly estrogenic agonist, an antioxidant, an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor or a Nrf2-inducer.' Note the title does not mention metformin, which is a reason this negative result is easy to miss in the literature.

- **The ITP has published exactly ONE metformin lifespan experiment - no higher dose, no later start, no replication** — `confirmed`
  Supported but requires one precision caveat. PubMed queries for ITP+metformin and for metformin+UM-HET3+lifespan return exactly one ITP lifespan paper, Strong 2016 (PMID 27312235); all other hits are mechanistic/companion studies (glucose intolerance PMID 29579736, brain protein synthesis PMID 30864661/32761290, juvenile-mouse phenotypes PMID 38227136) or reviews, none of which is a new metformin lifespan cohort. Nothing new through 2026-07. Strong 2016 itself concedes the dose question was never tested, verbatim: 'it is possible that evaluation of doses higher or lower than the 1000 ppm dose we used might have produced stronger eviden[ce]'. CAVEAT the article should respect: metformin appeared in TWO lifespan arms of the same C2011 cohort - Met alone and Met/Rapa. 'Exactly one metformin-ALONE lifespan experiment' is precise; 'exactly one metformin experiment' is loose.

- **Met+rapamycin combination: +23% median in both sexes, P<0.001, same paper** — `confirmed`
  Table 1: males Met/Rapa median 959 d vs 780 d control = +23% (22.95%), log-rank P = 0.000, n=158; females 1078 d vs 874 d = +23% (23.34%), P = 0.000, n=142. So P<0.001 for MEDIAN is correct per Table 1. One caliber warning: the prose sentence reads '...led to a 23% increase in survival compared with controls in both sexes, as well as to significant increases in maximum lifespan ( P < 0.001)' - in that sentence the P<0.001 grammatically attaches to MAXIMUM lifespan. Cite Table 1, not that sentence, when attaching P<0.001 to the median. Dose was Met 1000 ppm + Rapa 14 ppm from 9 months.

- **Combination-beats-rapamycin-alone rests on non-concurrent historical controls** — `confirmed`
  This is the strongest-supported item and the paper says it outright. Verbatim: 'Although the current (C2011) cohort did not contain any mice given Rapa alone, we thought it would be of interest to compare the survival of mice receiving both Rapa and Met to survival of mice treated with the same Rapa dose in previous years, C2006 and C2009.' Add the numbers, which make the point sharper than the claim does: male Met/Rapa +23% vs Rapa alone +10% (C2006) and +13% (C2009); pooling C2006+C2009 vs C2011, 'the difference did not reach statistical significance ( P = 0.12) using our standard calculation, which stratifies by site. An alternate analysis, omitting site stratification, found P = 0.049.' In females, Met/Rapa +23% vs rapamycin-alone +18% and +21%, and 'the difference did not reach significance by log-rank testing.' The authors' own summary calls it equivocal: 'statistical significance of this historical comparison was equivocal.' Note the P=0.049 is the analysis that DROPS the program's pre-specified site stratification - i.e. the only significant version is the non-standard one.

- **2024 reanalysis authors (Jiang, Gelfond, Liu, Strong, Nelson), Gehan test, compounds 'overlooked'** — `confirmed`
  Author list verbatim: Nisi Jiang, Jonathan Gelfond, Qianqian Liu, Randy Strong, James F Nelson. GeroScience 2024 Apr 17;46(5):4533-4541, doi 10.1007/s11357-024-01161-9, PMID 38630424. The word 'overlooked' is in the title itself. Strong and Nelson are both at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio - the ITP's UT test site - and Strong is first author of the very 2016 paper being reanalyzed, so 'the program's own site investigators' is accurate. Gehan p for metformin males = 0.0495 (Table 1), described verbatim in text as 'Analysis using the Gehan test showed a significant increase in survival of metformin-treated males ( p = 0.0495), but not in females.'

- **Characterized as a post-hoc test on the same data across many comparisons** — `corrected`

RIGHT: Jiang's Methods state verbatim 'To account for the multiplicity of testing (132 trials), the p-values were adjusted using a 5% FDR threshold'. The article must acknowledge this claim or the criticism is a straw man. The honest skeptical point is narrower and I flag it as MY OBSERVATION, not a source statement: the metformin Gehan value printed in Table 1 is 0.0495, a bare-threshold figure, and the paper prints no adjusted column, so it is unclear the FDR procedure was applied to the headline numbers; by Benjamini-Hochberg over 132 tests a p-value ranked ~50th would need to be below roughly 0.019 to survive. Do not assert that as fact - assert only that Table 1 reports raw-looking p-values while the Methods claim FDR, and that 0.0495 leaves no margin.

The only genuinely different metformin p-values in Jiang are from DIFFERENT TESTS on the same data, not a different estimate of the same test: Gehan p = 0.0495 and Z-test p = 0.0118. SEPARATE, REAL, MINOR DISCREPANCY that does exist: median lifespan change for metformin males is reported as +7% by Strong 2016 (Table 1: 835 vs 780 d = 7.05%) but as +8% by Jiang 2024 (Table 1 and text: 'increased the median lifespan of males by 8%'). The two ITP papers disagree by one percentage point on the same experiment; Strong's +7% is the one arithmetically consistent with the published medians.

Jiang's Methods state verbatim: 'To account for the multiplicity of testing (132 trials), the p-values were adjusted using a 5% FDR threshold.' The defensible skeptical framing is that the reported Gehan p = 0.0495 sits at the very edge of significance and Table 1 prints no adjusted column, so the margin is nil - not that multiplicity was ignored.

An article that dismisses the reanalysis as pure p-hacking without engaging the PH-violation argument is vulnerable. The honest framing is that the PH violation is a real statistical objection, but the resulting p = 0.0495 is too fragile to carry weight, and the reanalysis was performed by the same site investigators who produced the original null.

Note an internal tension worth flagging: the Methods state 'To account for the multiplicity of testing (132 trials), the p-values were adjusted using a 5% FDR threshold,' yet every newly-'significant' Gehan p in Table 1 sits just under 0.05 (0.0495, 0.0481, 0.0460, 0.0344, 0.0321, 0.0248) - none could survive Benjamini-Hochberg across 132 tests. The reported values are plainly raw.

- **IMPORTANT DISCREPANCY: Jiang 2024 table lists a different p-value than Strong 2016's P=0.35 for the same experiment** — `refuted`
  WRONG: that Jiang 2024 lists a different log-rank p-value for the metformin experiment. RIGHT: Jiang 2024 Table 1 lists metformin log-rank p = 0.3477, which MATCHES Strong 2016 (Table 1: 0.348; text: P = 0.35). There is no log-rank discrepancy. The apparent conflict is a TABLE MISREAD: 0.2200 is the log-rank p-value on the ENALAPRIL row, not metformin. The exact Table 1 rows read: 'GTE f 2000 4 +7% 0.3686 0.0344 0.0023 Violated | Met m 1000 9 +8% 0.3477 0.0495 0.0118 Violated | Enal m 120 4 +7% 0.2200 0.0460 0.0343 Violated'. Columns are: Treatment, Sex, Dosage(ppm), Age of onset(month), Median lifespan change, Log-rank p, Gehan p, Z-test p, PH assumption. The only genuinely NEW p-values Jiang reports for metformin are from DIFFERENT tests on the same data: Gehan p = 0.0495 and the proportional-hazards Z-test p = 0.0118 (PH assumption 'Violated').

- **Real inter-paper numeric discrepancy: median lifespan increase in males** — `corrected`
  WRONG (Jiang 2024): metformin 'increased the median lifespan of males by 8%' (stated twice in text plus '+8%' in Table 1). RIGHT (Strong 2016, the primary source): +7% - Table 1 gives median 835 days (Met, n=148) vs 780 days (control, n=294), which is +7.05%, and the text says '7% increase in median lifespan of males.' Both papers describe the identical experiment and identical Ns (Jiang Fig. 1C: 'Metformin treated (1000 ppm, from 9-month-old, n = 148) and control (n = 294) male mice'). The article's use of +7% is correct; Jiang's 8% is the outlier and should not be adopted.

- **Search for corrections, errata, or superseding data through 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  No erratum or correction found for either paper (Europe PMC: zero 'Published Erratum' records matching the ITP; DOIs 10.1111/acel.12496 and 10.1007/s11357-024-01161-9 each return a single research-article record). No failed replication exists because no replication was attempted. One superseding-adjacent item: a further post-hoc reanalysis of the same ITP data by the same group (Nat Commun 2025, 'temporal efficacy profiler,' PMC12630856) again lists metformin among compounds 'overlooked by the log-rank test,' but places its benefit only 'before the median lifespan' and, notably, also lists metformin among compounds that INCREASED the mortality hazard in females. This does not overturn the claim group; it reinforces that every positive metformin signal in the ITP dataset comes from post-hoc reanalysis of one 2011 cohort by the program's own investigators.

**修正:**
- Delete or rewrite any sentence asserting that Jiang 2024 reports a different p-value than Strong 2016 for the metformin log-rank test. Jiang 2024 Table 1 reports metformin log-rank p = 0.3477, which agrees with Strong 2016 (Table 1: 0.348; text: P = 0.35). The value 0.2200 belongs to the enalapril row of that table, not metformin. The only new metformin p-values in Jiang are from different tests: Gehan p = 0.0495 and proportional-hazards Z-test p = 0.0118.
- If citing the male metformin median effect, use +7% (Strong et al. 2016: median 835 vs 780 days, n=148 vs 294). Note if relevant that the Jiang 2024 reanalysis restates the same experiment as '+8%', an unexplained one-point discrepancy with the source it is reanalyzing; do not adopt the 8% figure.
- Strengthen the historical-controls point rather than leaving it as a bare caveat: Strong 2016 states outright that 'the current (C2011) cohort did not contain any mice given Rapa alone,' and the Met/Rapa-vs-rapamycin-alone contrast did NOT reach significance under the ITP's standard site-stratified analysis (P = 0.12). Only an alternate analysis that omits site stratification yields P = 0.049. In females the difference 'did not reach significance by log-rank testing.' The authors' own words: 'statistical significance of this historical comparison was equivocal.'
- When describing the Jiang 2024 multiple-comparisons problem, give the actual scale: the reanalysis covered 132 cases (drugs/conditions/sexes/cohorts) of ITP data from 2004-2022. Metformin's Gehan p = 0.0495 is nominal. Worth noting the internal tension: the Methods claim p-values 'were adjusted using a 5% FDR threshold' for the 132 trials, yet all six newly-significant Gehan p-values in Table 1 fall between 0.0248 and 0.0495, a pattern impossible after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 132 tests.
- If stating that the ITP ran exactly one metformin experiment, phrase it as one metformin-ALONE experiment: metformin appears in the ITP dataset only in cohort C2011, in two arms (metformin alone at 1000 ppm from 9 months, and metformin+rapamycin at 1000/14 ppm from 9 months). Confirmed against the Mouse Phenome Database ITP project and a scan of all ITP results papers through 2026-07.
- Optionally note that Strong 2016 itself concedes the dose limitation: 'it is possible that evaluation of doses higher or lower than the 1000 ppm dose we used might have produced stronger evidence of benefit.' This is a stronger version of the article's 'no higher dose' point because it is the ITP's own admission.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- A further post-hoc reanalysis of the same ITP dataset by the same UT Health San Antonio group (Nat Commun 2025, 'Deciphering the timing and impact of life-extending interventions: temporal efficacy profiler', PMC12630856) reports that metformin was among compounds that INCREASED the mortality hazard in females at some ages: 'Here the TEP revealed 15 trials with 14 compounds that increased the mortality hazard at one or more periods of treatment: 2 in males (HBX and INT-767) and 12 in females (CC, metformin, DMAG, ...)'. It also states metformin reduced mortality only 'before the median lifespan.' This cuts against any framing of metformin as a broadly beneficial ITP result and complicates the Jiang 2024 positive spin.
- Jiang 2024's own Table 1 records that metformin in males 'Violated' the proportional hazards assumption (Z-test p = 0.0118). This is the stated justification for switching to the Gehan test, but it is itself a post-hoc, data-dependent test-selection step: the test was chosen after observing that the pre-specified test's assumption failed on this particular dataset.
- Jiang 2024's stated multiplicity control is not reflected in its reported numbers. Methods: 'To account for the multiplicity of testing (132 trials), the p-values were adjusted using a 5% FDR threshold.' Yet the six newly-significant Gehan p-values in Table 1 are 0.0495, 0.0481, 0.0460, 0.0344, 0.0321 and 0.0248. Under Benjamini-Hochberg across 132 tests, a p of 0.0495 would need to rank near the very top of a very large discovery set to survive; with only 6 discoveries claimed, none of these would pass. The reported values are therefore nominal, and metformin's 'significance' is a bare p just under 0.05 out of 132 comparisons.

The refutation I was looking for: I attacked (d) by assuming the author had only consulted the MPD portal, which is a publication-lagged registry. That assumption was correct. The NIA page covers cohorts 2022-2025 that MPD does not, and it contains taurine and urolithin A as active lifespan interventions. Two of the seven absence claims are false as stated. Note also that urolithin A carries its own ITP abbreviation 'Uro' — which independently reinforces (c), since 'UA' is separately and unambiguously bound to ursolic acid.

Cross-checks that produced nothing: Europe PMC searches pairing each of taurine, spermidine, urolithin, nicotinamide mononucleotide, dasatinib, and berberine with 'UM-HET3' returned only reviews and unrelated primary work — no ITP lifespan paper for any of them, consistent with the 2025 arms being unreported.

Remaining uncertainty: (i) NIA's table and the MPD portal disagree on a few trivia (aspirin C2004 20 vs 21 ppm; 4-OH-PBN 315 vs 350 ppm; candesartan C2016 age 7 vs 8 mo) — none touch the claims here, but it means the two registries are not byte-identical and the peer-reviewed paper should win on any conflict. (ii) I could not rule out that a compound was proposed and dropped before enrollment, since neither registry records rejected proposals; that does not affect the claims as written. (iii) The C2025 arms are 'In Progress' with no interim data, so nothing can yet be said about whether taurine or urolithin A works — only that 'never tested' is the wrong frame.

- **(a) NR failed the ITP: NR chloride 1000 ppm from 8 months, three sites, males p=0.252 (median -3%), females p=0.612 (median 0%)** — `confirmed`
  Every number checks out verbatim against the primary source: Harrison DE et al., '17-a-estradiol late in life extends lifespan in aging UM-HET3 male mice; nicotinamide riboside and three other drugs do not affect lifespan in either sex.' Aging Cell 2021;20:e13328, PMID 33788371, PMC8135004. I read the Europe PMC full-text XML directly. Table 1 (pooled across the three sites), Males: 'NR 156 763 -3% 0.252'; Females: 'NR 136 875 0% 0.612'. n=156 males and n=136 females on NR vs Cont_16 n=303 males / n=304 females. Methods: NR 'was generously provided by ChromaDex ... as the chloride salt, and mixed at a dose of 1,000 mg NR Chloride per kilogram diet' — so 1000 ppm is of the chloride salt, exactly as the article states. Table 1 legend: 'Mice started on diets at 8 months of age were those fed: NR with 1,000 ppm nicotinamide riboside...'. Figure legend: 'CC, MIF098, and NR were fed from 8 months of age'. Cohort C2016; three sites = TJL, UM, UT. Result text: 'Lifespans for pooled data (across the three sites) were not significantly affected in UM-HET3 males or females fed diets with 1,000 ppm nicotinamide riboside (NR)...'. I checked for a retraction/erratum: there IS a 2022 corrigendum (Aging Cell 2022;21:e13672, PMID 35895871, PMC9649595), but I read it in full and it only adds Adrian Markewych as 11th author — 'In the original published article, the authorship list was not complete.' No data were revised. Optional strengthener the article could add: the paper itself pre-empts cherry-picking with 'The ITP primary endpoint is always the pooled data set, and NR had no significant effect, positive or negative, in the pooled data sets for either sex.' (site-level analyses did show one marginally significant female increase, offset by a marginally significant female decrease at another site and a marginally significant male decrease at one site).

- **(b) Fisetin failed the ITP: 600 ppm from 20 months, no significant increase in either sex** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, but the article should name the two schedules or it understates the test. Primary source: Harrison DE et al., 'Astaxanthin and meclizine extend lifespan in UM-HET3 male mice; fisetin, SG1002 (hydrogen sulfide donor), dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used.' GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816, PMID 38041783, PMC10828146 (note: GeroScience, NOT Aging Cell — check the article's citation). Read via Europe PMC full-text XML. Cohort 2018; dose verified at 99% ± 9 of target: 'Fisetin (Fis), 600 ppm, 99% ± 9 (5). Twenty months, fed continuously (Fis_On) or a repeat of 3 days on and 11 days off (Fis_Cyc)'. Pooled 3-site Table 1 numbers, males: Fis_Cyc n=150, median 799 d, +7%, p=0.54; Fis_On n=142, median 715 d, -5%, p=0.85. Females: Fis_Cyc n=134, 871 d, -1%, p=0.75; Fis_On n=144, 883 d, +1%, p=0.37. Abstract: 'None of these increased lifespan significantly at the dose and method of administration tested in either sex.' So '600 ppm from 20 months' is right but incomplete — it was 600 ppm from 20 months in TWO arms, continuous and cyclic (3 days on / 11 days off), and both failed. That matters because senolytic advocates specifically argue intermittent dosing is the correct regimen; the ITP already tested it.

- **(c) The ITP data portal's 'UA' is ursolic acid, not urolithin A** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against two independent primary listings. (1) MPD ITP data portal, https://phenome.jax.org/projects/ITP1, compound table row: 'ursolic acid (UA) | C2013 | 2000 ppm | 10 mo' with no significant lifespan effect flagged. I extracted all 74 rows of that table (cohorts C2004-C2021); 'urolithin' appears zero times anywhere on the page. (2) NIA's own Supported Interventions table: 'ursolic acid (UA) | 2013 | 2000 ppm | 10 mo | none'. Stronger still: NIA assigns urolithin A the distinct abbreviation 'Uro', not 'UA', so the two are separately coded in ITP records and the confusion is unambiguously an error.

- **(d) ITP has NEVER tested urolithin A** — `refuted`

Urolithin A is an enrolled ITP lifespan intervention in the 2025 cohort at 150 ppm in food from 7 months of age. The right statement is not 'never tested' but 'in progress, no results yet' — the C2025 cohort will not report for years, and the MPD data portal only carries published cohorts through C2021 (latest publication: Strong R et al., 'Extension of lifespan by epicatechin, halofuginone and mitoglitazone in male but not female genetically heterogeneous mice', GeroScience 2025, PMID 40973907). The article's absence claim was almost certainly built from the MPD portal alone, which is why it missed this.

  WRONG, same source. NIA ITP Supported Interventions table (updated April 13, 2026) contains: 'Taurine (Tau) | 2025 | 6000 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress'. Taurine is an enrolled ITP lifespan intervention in the 2025 cohort at 6000 ppm in food from 7 months of age. Results are pending, not absent. This one is especially damaging to leave uncorrected because the taurine longevity claim (Singh et al., Science 2023) is exactly the kind of finding readers expect the ITP to adjudicate, and the ITP is in fact adjudicating it.

- **(d) ITP has NEVER tested NMN, spermidine, berberine, CoQ10, or dasatinib+quercetin** — `confirmed`

Zero occurrences of 'nicotinamide mononucleotide'/'NMN', 'spermidine', 'berberine', 'coenzyme'/'CoQ'/'ubiquinol', 'dasatinib', or 'quercetin'. I also ran Europe PMC searches pairing each compound with 'UM-HET3' and found no ITP lifespan paper for any of them. The parentheticals are correct as far as they go — NR (C2016) is the only NAD precursor tested, and MitoQ (C2015, 100 ppm from 7 mo) is the only CoQ-family agent. ONE CITATION HAZARD on CoQ10: the ITP's own compounds-info page describes MitoQ as 'Small anti-oxidant molecule (also known as Coenzyme Q10)', which is chemically sloppy (MitoQ is mitoquinone mesylate, a TPP-conjugated ubiquinone derivative, not CoQ10). A hostile reader could quote the ITP against the article. The article should say MitoQ is a mitochondria-targeted ubiquinone derivative, not plain CoQ10, and not rest the distinction on the ITP's own wording.

**修正:**
- Delete urolithin A and taurine from the 'ITP has never tested' list. NIA's official ITP Supported Interventions page (updated 13 April 2026) lists 'Urolithin A (Uro), 2025 cohort, 150 ppm, from 7 months, In Progress' and 'Taurine (Tau), 2025 cohort, 6000 ppm, from 7 months, In Progress'. Replace the absence claim with: the ITP began lifespan testing of both urolithin A and taurine in its 2025 cohort; results are years away and no lifespan data exist yet.
- Do not infer ITP absence from the Jackson Lab MPD data portal (phenome.jax.org/projects/ITP1) alone. That table only carries cohorts with PUBLISHED results, currently C2004-C2021. Cohorts 2022-2025 (which include taurine, urolithin A, trametinib, alogliptin, glucosamine sulfate, BT2, sildenafil, alpelisib, L-deprenyl, mianserin, cinnarizine, lactoferrin, TPPU, and rapamycin+17aE2) appear only on NIA's Supported Interventions page. Any 'the ITP has never tested X' sentence must be checked against the NIA page.
- Fisetin: state that the ITP tested TWO schedules, not one. Cohort 2018, 600 ppm from 20 months of age, fed either continuously (Fis_On) or cyclically 3 days on / 11 days off (Fis_Cyc). Pooled 3-site log-rank results, males: cyclic +7% median, p=0.54; continuous -5%, p=0.85. Females: cyclic -1%, p=0.75; continuous +1%, p=0.37. Mentioning the cyclic arm is load-bearing because intermittent dosing is the standard senolytic rebuttal.
- Fix the fisetin citation journal if the article names one: the ITP fisetin result is in GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816 (PMID 38041783), not Aging Cell.
- Nicotinamide riboside: the ITP paper is Aging Cell 2021;20:e13328 (PMID 33788371). Note that a 2022 corrigendum exists (Aging Cell 2022;21:e13672, PMID 35895871) but it only adds a missing author and revises no data — say so if citing, so a reader who finds the corrigendum does not assume the numbers were retracted.

NR did show a marginally significant female increase at one of three sites, offset by a marginally significant female decrease at another and a male decrease at a third; naming this pre-empts the site-level cherry-pick.
- CoQ10: describe MitoQ as mitoquinone mesylate, a mitochondria-targeted (triphenylphosphonium-conjugated) ubiquinone derivative, and explicitly note it is not the same molecule as dietary CoQ10 / ubiquinone. Do not lean on the ITP's own compounds-info page for this distinction — that page wrongly glosses MitoQ as 'also known as Coenzyme Q10' and can be quoted against the article.

I also could not retrieve Wayback snapshots of the NIA page to check how recently taurine and urolithin A were added; I am relying on the page's own 'Last updated: April 13, 2026' stamp. Methods, verbatim: 'Nicotinamide riboside (NR) was generously provided by ChromaDex ... as the chloride salt, and mixed at a dose of 1,000 mg NR Chloride per kilogram diet (1,000 ppm). Table 1 is headed 'Effects of interventions on lifespan; data pooled from the 3 sites' and reads, verbatim, Females: 'NR 136 875 0% 0.612 1068 2% 0.99'; Males: 'NR 156 763 -3% 0.252 1019 -3% 0.99' (columns = n, median days, % change, log-rank p, 90th-percentile days, % change, Wang-Allison p). Two caliber details the article may want: the log-rank tests are two-tailed and stratified by site, and the 90th-percentile (Wang-Allison) p was 0.99 in BOTH sexes, so the null result covers maximum as well as median lifespan. ONE OMISSION worth fixing for caliber: the phrase '600 ppm from 20 months' implies a single arm, but the ITP ran TWO fisetin arms (continuous and intermittent 3-days-on/11-days-off) — this matters because intermittent dosing is exactly the senolytic-style regimen fisetin advocates argue for, and it also failed. - **(c) The ITP data portal's 'UA' is URSOLIC ACID, not urolithin A** — `confirmed`
