(2) The NIA ITP official compounds table (https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp/compounds-testing, last updated April 13, 2026), verbatim row: 'ursolic acid (UA) | 2013 | 2000 ppm | 10 mo | none'. The MPD 'Studied compounds' glossary also carries an entry for 'ursolic acid' and zero occurrences of the string 'urolithin' anywhere on either the compound list or the project page. The claim is not merely correct, it is now REINFORCED: urolithin A does appear on the NIA table but under a DIFFERENT abbreviation, 'Uro' (see item on urolithin A below). So UA and Uro are distinct codes in the ITP's own notation, which is the strongest possible form of this claim.

- **(d) The ITP has NEVER tested urolithin A** — `refuted`
  WRONG. The ITP is currently testing urolithin A as a lifespan intervention. The NIA ITP official compounds-in-testing table (last updated April 13, 2026) contains the verbatim row: 'Urolithin A (Uro) | 2025 | 150 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress'. That is a Stage I UM-HET3 lifespan study (the table's preamble states 'All testing is Stage I unless otherwise indicated' and the columns are Compound / Cohort / Concentration in Food / Age at Treatment Initiation / Increase in Median (Med) and Maximum (Max) Lifespan). The RIGHT version is: the ITP has not yet REPORTED a result for urolithin A — it entered the 2025 cohort at 150 ppm from 7 months of age and is listed 'In Progress'. The reason this was missed is almost certainly that the Mouse Phenome Database ITP data portal only covers cohorts C2004 through C2021 (I enumerated its cohort project links: 2004-2007, 2009-2021), so absence from the MPD portal does NOT establish absence from the ITP.

- **(d) The ITP has NEVER tested taurine** — `refuted`
  WRONG, same failure mode. The NIA ITP compounds table (updated April 13, 2026) contains the verbatim row: 'Taurine (Tau) | 2025 | 6000 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress'. The RIGHT version is: the ITP has not yet reported a taurine result — taurine entered the 2025 cohort at 6000 ppm from 7 months of age and is listed 'In Progress'. Given that taurine is one of the highest-profile longevity claims of the last few years, stating flatly that the ITP has never tested it is the kind of error a knowledgeable reader will catch immediately, and it inverts the article's likely point: the ITP replication attempt exists and is running, it just has not read out.

- **(d) The ITP has NEVER tested NMN (only NR), spermidine, berberine, CoQ10 (only MitoQ), or dasatinib+quercetin** — `confirmed`
  These five hold. I checked the full NIA ITP compounds table covering every cohort 2004 through 2025 (the authoritative list, including unreported in-progress studies) and the complete MPD 'Studied compounds' glossary. String counts on the NIA table: spermidine 0, berberine 0, 'nicotinamide mononucleotide' 0, 'NMN' 0, dasatinib 0, quercetin 0, 'coenzyme Q10' 0. Same on the MPD compound list: spermidine 0, berberine 0, nicotinamide mononucleotide 0, dasatinib 0, quercetin 0. The NAD-precursor arm really is NR only: 'nicotinamide riboside (NR) | 2016 | 1000 ppm | 8 mo | none'. The quinone arm really is MitoQ only: 'MitoQ (MitoQ) | 2015 | 100 ppm | 7 mo | none'. I also ran Europe PMC full-text searches pairing each of these compounds with 'UM-HET3' AND 'Interventions Testing Program' — every hit was a review, a C. elegans ITP (CITP) paper, or an unrelated primary study, never an ITP mouse lifespan test. ONE TRAP TO AVOID: the MPD compound glossary describes MitoQ, verbatim, as 'Small anti-oxidant molecule (also known as Coenzyme Q10) that accumulates in mitochondria' — that MPD blurb is chemically wrong (MitoQ is mitoquinone mesylate, a triphenylphosphonium-conjugated ubiquinone derivative, not CoQ10). If the article cites the ITP portal to support 'CoQ10 never tested', a hostile reader can quote that line back. Phrase it so the distinction is the article's own, not the portal's.

**修正:**
- Delete urolithin A and taurine from the 'ITP has never tested' list. The NIA ITP compounds-in-testing table (last updated April 13, 2026) lists both in the 2025 cohort as Stage I lifespan studies still running: 'Urolithin A (Uro) | 2025 | 150 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress' and 'Taurine (Tau) | 2025 | 6000 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress'.
- Replace the absence claim for those two with a not-yet-reported claim, e.g.: 'The ITP has not yet reported results for urolithin A or taurine; both entered the 2025 cohort (urolithin A at 150 ppm, taurine at 6000 ppm, each started at 7 months) and are listed In Progress as of the NIA table's April 2026 update.'
- Narrow the surviving absence list to the five that actually hold: NMN (the ITP's only NAD precursor is nicotinamide riboside), spermidine, berberine, CoQ10 (the ITP's only related compound is MitoQ, 100 ppm from 7 months, cohort 2015), and dasatinib+quercetin. None appears anywhere in the NIA table for cohorts 2004-2025.
- Do not source absence claims to the ITP data portal on Mouse Phenome Database. That portal only covers cohorts C2004-C2021 and therefore cannot establish that a compound was never tested. Source absence to the NIA ITP compounds-in-testing table instead, and date the assertion to that table's last-updated stamp.
- When stating that CoQ10 was never tested, do not lean on the MPD portal, whose MitoQ entry erroneously reads 'Small anti-oxidant molecule (also known as Coenzyme Q10)'. Note in the article's own voice that MitoQ is mitoquinone mesylate, a triphenylphosphonium-conjugated ubiquinone derivative, and is not CoQ10.
- Add that the ITP tested fisetin in TWO arms, not one: continuous (Fis_On) and intermittent 3-days-on/11-days-off (Fis_Cyc), both at 600 ppm from 20 months, and both null in both sexes. The intermittent arm is the senolytic-style regimen fisetin proponents advocate, so omitting it weakens the point.
- Add the anti-underdosing evidence for both null results: measured fisetin in the diet was 99% +/- 9 of the 600 ppm target across 5 preparations, and the NR diet assayed at 878 ppm NR plus nicotinamide. Neither null result can be attributed to the compound being absent from the food.
- Optionally strengthen the NR result by noting the null covers maximum as well as median lifespan: the 90th-percentile Wang-Allison p was 0.99 in both males and females.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The NIA ITP official compounds-in-testing table (https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp/compounds-testing, last updated April 13, 2026) contains the verbatim row 'Urolithin A (Uro) | 2025 | 150 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress', directly contradicting the claim that the ITP has never tested urolithin A.
- The same NIA table contains the verbatim row 'Taurine (Tau) | 2025 | 6000 ppm | 7 mo | In Progress', directly contradicting the claim that the ITP has never tested taurine.
- The Mouse Phenome Database ITP data portal, which appears to be the basis for the absence claims, only indexes cohorts C2004 through C2021 (its cohort project links are 2004-2007 and 2009-2021). Any 'never tested' inference drawn from that portal is structurally unable to see the 2022-2025 cohorts, which include taurine, urolithin A, trametinib, sildenafil, alpelisib, lactoferrin, BT2, alogliptin and others.
- The MPD compound glossary misdescribes MitoQ as 'also known as Coenzyme Q10'. This is chemically false and could be used to attack the article's 'CoQ10 was never tested, only MitoQ' framing if the article cites the portal as its authority.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Web search quota was exhausted at the start of this session, so I worked entirely through direct WebFetch against primary endpoints: PMC full text, the Europe PMC REST API (including raw fullTextXML, which bypasses the publisher's rendered page), the Mouse Phenome Database ITP portal, and the Semantic Scholar API.

Primary documents reached: (1) Harrison DE et al., Aging Cell 2021, PMID 33788371 / PMC8135004 — read both the rendered PMC article and the Europe PMC fullTextXML independently; both returned the same Table 1 values for NR (males N=156, median 763 d, -3%, p=0.252; females N=136, median 875 d, 0%, p=0.612), the same 1000 ppm chloride-salt dose, the same 8-month start, and the same three-site design. Because the pipeline has previously been caught fabricating quotes, I deliberately used two different retrieval routes and cross-checked the per-site Ns (51-54 males, 44-48 females per site) against the pooled Ns; they reconcile. (2) The 2022 Corrigendum, PMID 35895871 / PMC9649595 — authorship only, no data change, so it does not disturb the NR numbers. (3) Harrison DE et al., GeroScience 2024, PMID 38041783 / PMC10828146 — fullTextXML read; fisetin at 600 ppm from 20 months confirmed, but in two schedules with four separate p-values, none significant. (4) The Gehan-test reanalysis, GeroScience 2024, PMID 38630424 — checked specifically as a refutation route, since a compound null under log-rank can be positive under Gehan; NR and fisetin are not among the five rescued compounds, so this attempted refutation failed and the claim survives it. (5) The MPD ITP data portal, phenome.jax.org/projects/ITP1 and /compounds — the agent table lists 'Ursolic acid (UA)', and targeted string searches returned no occurrence of urolithin, NMN, nicotinamide mononucleotide, spermidine, taurine, berberine, coenzyme Q10, dasatinib or quercetin.

The refutation attempts that produced something: I found that the portal itself is incomplete — it lacks four agents the ITP published in January 2026 — which means the absence argument in (d) cannot rest on the portal alone. Europe PMC full-text searches for the seven compounds against 'UM-HET3' and 'Interventions Testing Program' returned only reviews and conference abstracts, no ITP primary lifespan report, so the absence holds for everything published.

What remains uncertain and is NOT resolved: I could not load the NIA's own 'compounds under testing' roster (HTTP 405 plus a CAPTCHA wall on a text proxy; web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment), and I could not read the full text of the January-2026 ITP paper, which reports eleven compounds while naming roughly eight or nine. Those two gaps are exactly where a counterexample to (d) would hide. I am reporting them as unreachable rather than papering over them, and the correction I recommend is to soften 'never tested' to 'no reported ITP lifespan test,' which is fully supported by what I did read.

Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: every number in (a), (b) and (c) checks out verbatim, but (b) omits the two-arm design and carries a real journal-attribution trap, and (d)'s absolute 'NEVER' exceeds what the reachable evidence licenses.

- **(a) NR protocol: NR chloride, 1000 ppm, started at 8 months, three test sites** — `confirmed`
  Verified in the primary paper: Harrison DE et al., '17-a-estradiol late in life extends lifespan in aging UM-HET3 male mice; nicotinamide riboside and three other drugs do not affect lifespan in either sex,' Aging Cell 2021, PMID 33788371 / PMC8135004. Methods state NR was supplied by ChromaDex 'as the chloride salt, and mixed at a dose of 1,000 mg NR Chloride per kilogram diet (1,000 ppm)' and that 'Mice were fed the NR diet continuously starting at 8 months of age.' Three sites (TJL, UM, UT), treated-group N 51-54/site males and 44-48/site females. One caveat the article may want to carry: assayed food content of NR plus nicotinamide totaled 878 ppm, not the nominal 1000 ppm.

- **(a) NR statistics: males p=0.252 (median -3%), females p=0.612 (median 0%)** — `confirmed`
  Table 1 of PMC8135004 read twice via independent extractions of the article text and of the Europe PMC full-text XML, both agreeing: males NR N=156, median 763 days, -3%, log-rank p=0.252; females NR N=136, median 875 days, 0%, p=0.612. These are the pooled three-site data, which the paper explicitly names as the pre-specified primary endpoint: 'The ITP primary endpoint is always the pooled data set, and NR had no significant effect, positive or negative, in the pooled data sets for either sex.' Two things the article should not omit: (i) 'NR led to a marginally significant increase in female lifespan at one site, but this was balanced by a marginally significant decline in female lifespan at another'; (ii) NR was not among the compounds rescued by the ITP's later Gehan-test reanalysis (GeroScience 2024, PMID 38630424, PMC11335987), which rescued only metformin, enalapril, 17-DMAG, CAPE and green tea extract. I also checked the 2022 Corrigendum (PMID 35895871 / PMC9649595): it adds Adrian Markewych as 11th author and changes no data.

- **(b) Fisetin: 600 ppm from 20 months, no significant increase in either sex** — `corrected`
  Substantively right but incomplete, and the attribution is easy to get wrong. Source is NOT Aging Cell: it is Harrison DE et al., 'Astaxanthin and meclizine extend lifespan in UM-HET3 male mice; fisetin, SG1002 (hydrogen sulfide donor), dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used,' GeroScience 2024, PMID 38041783 / PMC10828146 (online Dec 2023). Dose/start confirmed: 'We elected to use 600 ppm Fis, starting at 20 months of age.' WRONG version: a single fisetin arm. RIGHT version: TWO arms in cohort C2018 — continuous (Fis_On) and cyclic 3 days on / 11 days off (Fis_Cyc). Table 1: males Fis_Cyc N=150, median 799 d, +7%, p=0.54; males Fis_On N=142, median 715 d, -5%, p=0.85; females Fis_Cyc N=134, median 871 d, -1%, p=0.75; females Fis_On N=144, median 883 d, +1%, p=0.37. The paper also reports fisetin did not lower p16 mRNA in liver, kidney or brain, and that plasma fisetin was not reliably measurable — relevant because it means a null exposure cannot be excluded.

- **(c) ITP data portal 'UA' = ursolic acid, not urolithin A** — `confirmed`
  Verified directly on the Mouse Phenome Database ITP data portal, https://phenome.jax.org/projects/ITP1, whose agent table lists 'Ursolic acid (UA)'. Two separate targeted reads of that page returned no occurrence of 'urolithin' anywhere, and the compound-description page https://phenome.jax.org/projects/ITP1/compounds carries an entry for 'Ursolic acid' (described as present in many plants, reported to increase skeletal muscle mass etc.) with no urolithin entry. Lower-confidence detail, seen in only one extraction and worth re-checking before printing: the portal associates UA with cohort C2013 at 2000 ppm. Also note that ITP ursolic acid lifespan results appear to be portal-only/unpublished — a Europe PMC search for 'ursolic acid' AND 'UM-HET3' returns 2 hits, neither an ITP ursolic acid report.

- **(d) ITP has NEVER tested urolithin A, NMN, spermidine, taurine, berberine, CoQ10, or dasatinib+quercetin** — `corrected`
  The substance holds but the absolute qualifier 'NEVER' overstates what is verifiable. WRONG version: 'the ITP has never tested X.' RIGHT version: 'no ITP lifespan test of X has ever been reported, and none appears in the ITP data portal.' Evidence gathered: the MPD ITP1 agent table (62 agents, 16-a-hydroxyestriol through ursolic acid) contains nicotinamide riboside but no NMN/nicotinamide mononucleotide; MitoQ but no coenzyme Q10; and no urolithin, spermidine, taurine, berberine, dasatinib or quercetin — a targeted string search of that page returned 'Not found' for every one of those terms. Europe PMC searches ('Interventions Testing Program' AND 'urolithin', hitCount 7, all reviews/abstracts; 'UM-HET3' AND (spermidine OR taurine OR berberine OR dasatinib OR nicotinamide mononucleotide), hitCount 57, no ITP primary lifespan report among them) turned up no ITP test of any of the seven. WHY the qualifier must soften: the MPD portal demonstrably lags — it does not list pioglitazone, mifepristone, methotrexate or atorvastatin-telmisartan, all of which appear in the ITP's own January-2026 GeroScience report — so portal absence is not proof that a currently-running, unannounced cohort excludes these agents.

- **NIA ITP 'compounds under testing' list (the authoritative forward-looking roster)** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp/compounds-testing or the ITP publications page: nia.nih.gov returned HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed to direct fetch, a text-extraction proxy returned a CAPTCHA wall, and web.archive.org is not fetchable from this environment. This is the one page that could definitively refute (d) for cohorts not yet published, and I did not read it. I am not filling that gap from memory.

- **The three unnamed arms of the January-2026 ITP report (eleven compounds, ~8-9 named in the title)** — `unreachable`
  Korstanje R, Strong R, ... Miller RA, 'Astaxanthin, meclizine, mitoglitazone, pioglitazone, alpha-ketoglutarate, mifepristone, methotrexate, and atorvastatin-telmisartan do not increase lifespan in UM-HET3 mice,' GeroScience 2026, PMID 41843349, doi 10.1007/s11357-026-02201-2. Europe PMC reports isOpenAccess 'N' and inEPMC 'N', and the Springer page redirects to an auth gate, so I read the abstract only. The abstract says 'eleven compounds' but names only the title agents, so I could not verify that none of the three unlisted arms is one of the (d) compounds. Most likely they are extra dose/start-age variants of the named agents (a novel agent would normally appear in the title), but I did not confirm this and am flagging it rather than assuming.

**修正:**
- Attribute the fisetin null to GeroScience 2024 (Harrison DE et al., PMID 38041783), NOT to Aging Cell — Aging Cell 2021 (PMID 33788371) is the nicotinamide riboside paper. Confusing the two is the easiest error to make here because both are ITP multi-agent reports with Harrison as first author.
- State that fisetin was tested in TWO schedules at 600 ppm from 20 months in cohort C2018, not one: continuous (Fis_On) and cyclic 3 days on / 11 days off (Fis_Cyc). Give the four p-values if any are given: males 0.54 (cyclic, +7% median) and 0.85 (continuous, -5%); females 0.75 (cyclic, -1%) and 0.37 (continuous, +1%). Reporting only 'not significant' while omitting the +7% male cyclic point invites the objection that the article cherry-picked.
- Replace the absolute 'the ITP has NEVER tested' with 'no ITP lifespan test has ever been reported for, and none appears in the ITP data portal.' The portal is not a complete forward-looking roster: it omits pioglitazone, mifepristone, methotrexate and atorvastatin-telmisartan, which the ITP itself published in GeroScience in January 2026.
- When citing the NR result, say explicitly that p=0.252 (males) and p=0.612 (females) are log-rank tests on the POOLED three-site data, which the paper names as the ITP's pre-specified primary endpoint. The same paper reports a marginally significant female increase at one site offset by a marginally significant female decrease at another — omitting this leaves the article open to a 'you hid the positive site' rebuttal.
- If the article implies NR failed only under the log-rank test, note that the ITP's own Gehan-test reanalysis (GeroScience 2024, PMID 38630424) rescued metformin, enalapril, 17-DMAG, CAPE and green tea extract — and did NOT rescue nicotinamide riboside or fisetin. This strengthens the claim; leaving it out weakens it.
- Optionally note that assayed NR-plus-nicotinamide content of the treated chow was 878 ppm against a nominal 1000 ppm target, and that the paper detected no intact NR in serum (detection limit 500 ng/ml) though nicotinamide rose from 105 +/- 46 to 401 +/- 212 ng/ml. This is the standard 'was it even delivered?' objection and the paper addresses it.
- If the article states a cohort or dose for ITP ursolic acid, verify it independently first — the C2013 / 2000 ppm detail came from a single portal read and ITP ursolic acid lifespan results appear to be unpublished (portal data only, no journal report found).

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The Mouse Phenome Database ITP portal is NOT a complete list of what the ITP has tested. It omits pioglitazone, mifepristone, methotrexate and atorvastatin-telmisartan, all reported by the ITP in GeroScience in January 2026 (PMID 41843349). Any absence argument resting solely on that portal is therefore weaker than it looks.
- The January-2026 ITP report states it evaluated 'eleven compounds' while its title names only about eight or nine. I could not read the full text (paywalled, not in Europe PMC), so three arms are unaccounted for. This is a live, if small, hole in the (d) absence claim that I could not close.
- The fisetin cyclic-dosing arm in males showed a +7% median lifespan change (p=0.54). It is null, but an article that reports 'fisetin failed' without this number can be accused of suppressing the only directionally positive fisetin arm.
- The same fisetin paper reports that fisetin did not reduce p16 mRNA in liver, kidney or brain and that plasma fisetin was not reliably measurable. This is a confound cutting AGAINST the article's likely framing: the ITP null may partly reflect failed target engagement or exposure rather than a clean refutation of senolysis.

## V6 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I reached the primary document in full: PMID 41843349 = GeroScience 2026;48(3):3821-3830, DOI 10.1007/s11357-026-02201-2, free full text at PMC13356140, which I read directly (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13356140/). The PubMed HTML page itself was CAPTCHA-blocked, so I routed around it via NCBI E-utilities, Europe PMC REST and Semantic Scholar; the abstract came back byte-identical from Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar independently, which rules out a fetch-summarizer fabrication of the abstract. I also reached both prior ITP reports: PMID 38041783 (astaxanthin/meclizine, GeroScience 2024) and PMID 40973907 / PMC13355999 (epicatechin, halofuginone, mitoglitazone, e-pub 2025-09-19).

What the claim gets right: the sentence 'none of the tested compounds significantly increased lifespan in male or female mice' is verbatim from the abstract; astaxanthin, mitoglitazone and meclizine were indeed all prior ITP male-only hits; astaxanthin's +12% male median at p=0.003 and mitoglitazone's ~9% (8.7%) at p=0.015 are both exact against the source papers; and 'failed at other doses or later start ages' is the paper's own characterisation.

What is off: (1) 'eleven compounds' is eleven ARMS over eight agents; (2) meclizine's hit is from the 2024 paper, not '2024/2025' — mitoglitazone is the 2025 one; (3) the claim omits that the female results were significantly NEGATIVE for three arms pooled, with astaxanthin's negative signal disappearing once The Jackson Laboratory's long-lived control females were excluded; (4) two of the eleven arms (Asta_late, Mec_late) were male-only.

On the distinction the task flagged as mattering enormously: the ITP investigators do NOT present this as a failure to replicate the same regimen, and the underlying dose table proves they could not have — no arm repeated both the original dose and the original start age. Mitoglitazone is the closest (same 300 ppm, start moved 7 to 18 months) and it still ran +7.75% in males, merely non-significant. However, the authors do independently volunteer the chance-finding interpretation of their own earlier hits, and I verified those two sentences as literally present on a targeted second pass ('at or near the lower level of what is expected to be able to discover at 80% power'; 'chance effects can be expected in any series of studies for truly ineffective agents'). So the article can honestly say the ITP itself treats its earlier marginal hits as possibly spurious — it cannot say the ITP tried and failed to reproduce them.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not run an adversarial search for errata, critical correspondence or independent replications; none was linked on either PubMed record, but absence of a linked erratum is weak evidence. I could not confirm one- vs two-sided log-rank testing from the text. And every full-text number reached me through a summarizing fetch layer rather than raw document text — I mitigated this with repeated independent passes using different prompts (Table 1 male values and the dose/start-age table were self-consistent across passes, and the group label 'M160_late' correctly encodes mitoglitazone = MSDC-0160, an internal-consistency signal against fabrication), but the ACHIEVED-dose figures were NOT self-consistent across passes and I am explicitly marking those unreliable rather than reporting them as verified.

- **Source identity: 2026 GeroScience report by Korstanje R, Strong R, Salmon AB, et al. (PMID 41843349)** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed. Title: 'Astaxanthin, meclizine, mitoglitazone, pioglitazone, alpha-ketoglutarate, mifepristone, methotrexate, and atorvastatin-telmisartan do not increase lifespan in UM-HET3 mice.' GeroScience 2026 Jun;48(3):3821-3830, DOI 10.1007/s11357-026-02201-2, PMID 41843349, free full text at PMC13356140. Author list begins Korstanje R, Strong R, Salmon AB, Bogue MA, Curran SP... and ends Miller RA. Abstract text was retrieved identically from two independent APIs (Europe PMC REST and Semantic Scholar), so it is not a fetch-summarizer artifact.

- **The ITP 'tested eleven compounds'** — `corrected`
  WRONG framing if written as 'eleven compounds': the paper tested ELEVEN INTERVENTION ARMS covering only EIGHT distinct agents/combinations. The paper's own text says 'For Cohort 2022 (C2022), the ITP tested eleven interventions' and the abstract says 'evaluated eleven compounds' — but the title names just eight (astaxanthin, meclizine, mitoglitazone, pioglitazone, alpha-ketoglutarate, mifepristone, methotrexate, atorvastatin-telmisartan). The eleven arms, with target dose and start age, are: AKG_early 20,000 ppm @7mo; Asta_low 800 ppm @11mo; Asta_late 800 ppm @16mo; Atortel 120/30 ppm @7mo; M160_late (mitoglitazone) 300 ppm @18mo; Mec_high 2,400 ppm @16mo; Mec_late 800 ppm @16mo; Meth 0.2 ppm @14mo; Mife 30 ppm @7mo; Pio 100 ppm @7mo; Pio_late 100 ppm @20mo. RIGHT version: 'eleven intervention arms (eight distinct compounds/combinations), including three re-tests at new doses or later start ages.'

- **NONE significantly increased lifespan in either sex** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim from the abstract: 'none of the tested compounds significantly increased lifespan in male or female mice.' Male Table 1 values support it — the largest male median gain was Mec_high at +9.23% with log-rank p=0.396 (n=154, median 888 d); Asta_low +3.69% p=0.214; Asta_late +2.21% p=0.377; M160_late +7.75% p=0.176; Pio +5.54% p=0.172. One caveat the article should not blur: Asta_late and Mec_late were MALE-ONLY arms (no female rows), so 'in either sex' is true of the study as a whole but two of the eleven arms were never run in females.

- **Astaxanthin, mitoglitazone and meclizine were all previously reported BY THE ITP ITSELF as extending MALE lifespan** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, and all three prior effects were male-specific. Astaxanthin and meclizine: Harrison DE, Strong R, Reifsnyder P, et al., 'Astaxanthin and meclizine extend lifespan in UM-HET3 male mice; fisetin, SG1002..., dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used,' GeroScience 2024, PMID 38041783. Mitoglitazone: 'Extension of lifespan by epicatechin, halofuginone and mitoglitazone in male but not female genetically heterogeneous mice,' GeroScience 48(3):4139-4156, e-published 2025-09-19, PMID 40973907, PMC13355999.

- **Astaxanthin +12% male median, p=0.003, in the 2024 report** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim from the 2024 abstract (PMID 38041783): 'astaxanthin (Asta) extended the median male lifespan by 12% (p = 0.003, log-rank test)'. The 2026 paper restates the earlier regimen: 'Asta increased lifespan in a previous study when starting at 12 months at a target dose of 4000 ppm.' Note the 2024 paper also states neither Asta nor Mec significantly moved the 90th-percentile (Wang-Allison) endpoint — worth carrying if the article leans on the original hit.

- **Mitoglitazone ~+9%, p=0.015** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed from the primary source (PMC13355999): male median lifespan +8.7%, log-rank p=0.015, n=149 treated vs 298 controls, 300 ppm, started at 7 months. The paper's own text reads '...resulted in a ~ 9% increase in median lifespan in males (p = 0.015)'. Also relevant: mitoglitazone, unlike epicatechin and halofuginone, did NOT increase 90% survival.

- **'meclizine as male hits in 2024/2025' — attribution of report years** — `corrected`
  WRONG: lumping meclizine and mitoglitazone as '2024/2025'. RIGHT: meclizine's positive result came from the SAME 2024 report as astaxanthin (PMID 38041783) — +8% male median, p=0.03, 800 ppm started at 12 months. Mitoglitazone is the separate report (PMID 40973907, online 19 Sep 2025, print GeroScience 48(3) 2026). So it is 'the 2024 report (astaxanthin and meclizine) and the 2025 report (mitoglitazone)', not a blended 2024/2025 attribution for meclizine.

- **All three 'failed at other doses or later start ages' in the new report** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, and this is the decisive qualifier — NOT ONE re-test repeated both the dose and the start age of the original positive. Astaxanthin: prior 4,000 ppm target @12mo; re-tested at 800 ppm @11mo and 800 ppm @16mo — a ~5x LOWER dose in both arms. Meclizine: prior 800 ppm @12mo; re-tested at 2,400 ppm @16mo (higher dose, later start) and 800 ppm @16mo (same dose, later start, male-only). Mitoglitazone: prior 300 ppm @7mo; re-tested at 300 ppm @18mo — SAME dose, start age moved from 7 to 18 months. The paper states it plainly: 'Asta increased lifespan in a previous study when starting at 12 months at a target dose of 4000 ppm. However, both starting at 11 months at 880 ppm and starting at 16 months at 880 ppm did not show an effect.' (880 ppm is the achieved dose against an 800 ppm target.)

- **Do the ITP investigators characterise this as non-replication, or as a different regimen?** — `corrected`
  BOTH — and the article must not pick only the flattering half. PRIMARY framing is 'different regimen', not failed replication: the abstract says the three 'showed no benefit when administered at different doses or starting at later ages' and warns of 'the challenges of translating promising initial findings into consistent lifespan benefits at other doses or with alternate starting ages'; the Discussion says 'It is possible that for these compounds, intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' BUT the authors ALSO explicitly float the chance-finding reading of their own earlier hits: 'Their previously published increases in median lifespan (9%, 8%, and 12%, respectively) were at or near the lower level of what is expected to be able to discover at 80% power' (and none moved the Wang-Allison late-life statistic), plus 'chance effects can be expected in any series of studies for truly ineffective agents.' Each of these four strings was confirmed present verbatim on a targeted second read of the PMC text. So: the ITP does not claim a same-regimen replication failure, but it does self-flag the original effects as marginal and possibly spurious.

- **Female results / direction of effect in the new report** — `corrected`
  OMITTED by the claim and material. The 2026 report is not merely null in females — it is NEGATIVE. Abstract: 'In females, astaxanthin, late-start mitoglitazone, and pioglitazone were associated with significantly reduced lifespan when pooling the data from all three sites. However, site-specific analysis revealed unusually long lifespans in control females at The Jackson Laboratory, prompting reanalysis using data from the other two sites and only showed a negative effect for mitoglitazone and pioglitazone.' Table 1 female values: Asta_low -3.16% p=0.021; M160_late -5.76% p=0.001; Pio -9.41% p<0.0001. If the article cites this paper as 'null', that understates it for females; if it cites the female harm, it must carry the JAX-control caveat and the fact that astaxanthin's female signal did NOT survive the two-site reanalysis.

- **One- vs two-sided testing, confidence level, and existence of any correction/erratum or critical letter** — `unreachable`
  Could not verify. The WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before I could search for errata, critical correspondence, or independent replications, so I cannot certify that none exists — I simply found none via PubMed/Europe PMC/Semantic Scholar records reached, which showed no erratum link on either PMID. I also could not confirm from the text whether the log-rank p-values are one- or two-sided (ITP convention is two-sided log-rank plus a Fisher-exact Wang-Allison test for the 90th percentile, and the paper does describe 'the Wang-Allison ("WA") test, using the Fisher Exact test version', but I did not see an explicit sidedness statement). Separately, all full-text numbers reached me through a summarizing fetch layer rather than a raw byte-for-byte read; I mitigated this by re-reading Table 1 and the dose table on separate passes with different prompts and getting self-consistent values, and by cross-checking the abstract against two independent APIs. Achieved-dose figures (880 ppm astaxanthin, 1,727 ppm Mec_high, 126 ppm mitoglitazone, and a stray '68' for Mec_late) came back inconsistently across passes and should be treated as LOW CONFIDENCE — publish target doses (800 / 2,400 / 800 / 300 ppm), not achieved doses.

**修正:**
- Do not write 'the ITP tested eleven compounds.' Write 'eleven intervention arms covering eight distinct compounds or combinations.' The title names eight agents; the eleven arms include two astaxanthin arms, two meclizine arms, two pioglitazone arms and one late-start mitoglitazone arm.
- Do not write that the ITP 'failed to replicate its own hits.' No arm repeated the original regimen. State it as: every re-test changed the dose, the starting age, or both — astaxanthin was retried at roughly one-fifth the original dose (800 ppm target vs 4,000 ppm) at 11 and 16 months; meclizine at 2,400 ppm from 16 months and at its original 800 ppm but from 16 months instead of 12; mitoglitazone at its original 300 ppm but from 18 months instead of 7.
- Fix the attribution years: astaxanthin AND meclizine both come from the same 2024 GeroScience report (Harrison et al., PMID 38041783); mitoglitazone comes from a separate report published online 19 September 2025 (PMID 40973907, GeroScience 48(3):4139-4156). Do not describe meclizine as a '2024/2025' hit.
- Mitoglitazone's original effect is +8.7% male median lifespan, log-rank p=0.015, 300 ppm from 7 months, n=149 treated vs 298 controls. '~+9%, p=0.015' is fine; do not state a dose or start age other than 300 ppm from 7 months.
- Astaxanthin's original effect is '+12% median male lifespan (p = 0.003, log-rank test)' at a 4,000 ppm target dose started at 12 months. Meclizine's is +8% male median (p = 0.03) at 800 ppm started at 12 months. Neither moved the 90th-percentile (Wang-Allison) endpoint — say so if the article treats the original results as robust.
- If the article uses the ITP's own scepticism as support, quote what they actually said rather than paraphrasing it as non-replication. The paper states the earlier gains 'were at or near the lower level of what is expected to be able to discover at 80% power' and that 'chance effects can be expected in any series of studies for truly ineffective agents' — but it also offers the competing explanation that 'intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' Both must appear, or neither.
- Do not call the 2026 report simply 'null.' In females it was net negative: pooled across sites, astaxanthin (-3.16%, p=0.021), late-start mitoglitazone (-5.76%, p=0.001) and pioglitazone (-9.41%, p<0.0001) all significantly SHORTENED lifespan; after excluding The Jackson Laboratory (unusually long-lived control females), only mitoglitazone and pioglitazone remained negative.
- Note that Asta_late and Mec_late were male-only arms, so the phrase 'in either sex' applies to the study overall but those two follow-ups were never run in females.
- Publish target doses, not achieved doses. Achieved-dose figures read inconsistently across passes of the full text and should not appear in the article.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The paper itself supplies the counter-frame to 'the ITP cannot replicate its own hits': 'It is possible that for these compounds, intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' The abstract's own conclusion is about dose/timing sensitivity and multi-site rigor, not about the earlier results being wrong.
- Mitoglitazone is the only one of the three re-tested at its original dose (300 ppm), and it still showed a numerically POSITIVE male effect in the new report (+7.75% median, p=0.176, n=153) — statistically null but directionally consistent with the original +8.7%. That undercuts a strong 'the hit evaporated' reading for that compound; the honest reading is an underpowered late-start arm.
- Meclizine's high-dose arm produced the LARGEST male median gain in the whole 2026 cohort (+9.23%), larger than its own original +8% hit, yet with log-rank p=0.396 — a reminder that the 2026 arms are individually underpowered and that 'not significant' here is not evidence of absence.
- The prior positive results were already flagged as fragile in their own publications: neither astaxanthin nor meclizine moved the 90th-percentile Wang-Allison statistic in 2024, and mitoglitazone did not increase 90% survival in 2025. So the 2026 report is less a reversal than a continuation of a known weak signal.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I reached the primary document as raw JATS XML rather than as summarizer prose, which matters given the pipeline's history of fabricated quotes. Route: PubMed itself was CAPTCHA-blocked and my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the outset, so I went through NCBI eutils efetch (db=pmc, id=PMC13356140, retmode=xml) and pulled the abstract, the full Results section, the full Discussion section, Table 1 (pooled life-table statistics) and Table 3 (compound dose and starting times) as literal XML markup — complete with element ids (Abs1, Par19-Par30, Sec8-Sec12, Tab1, Tab3) and xref/pub-id tags. Text arriving inside intact structural markup with internal cross-reference ids is much harder to confabulate than prose, and the numbers I extracted from Table 1 are mutually consistent with the narrative sentences in Results and Discussion and with the abstract, so I treat these as genuinely read. I additionally reached both antecedent ITP papers independently: PMC10828146 (Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816) for the astaxanthin +12%/p=0.003 and meclizine +8%/p=0.03 figures and their doses, and PMC13355999 / PMID 40973907 (Strong et al.) for mitoglitazone ~+9%/p=0.015, whose MEDLINE record fixes it as GeroScience 2026 Jun;48(3):4139-4156, epub 2025 Sep 19.

The central assertion survives: eleven interventions in ITP cohort C2022, none significantly increased lifespan in either sex, and astaxanthin, meclizine and mitoglitazone — all three prior ITP male hits — showed nothing. Where the claim slips is caliber, in four places. (1) 'Eleven compounds' is the paper's own loose wording for eleven ARMS across eight agents, and only males got eleven; females got nine. (2) The date attributions are wrong for two of three compounds: meclizine was in the same 2024 Harrison paper as astaxanthin, and mitoglitazone's positive report is Strong et al. in the very same June 2026 GeroScience issue as the null paper, not a 2024/2025 report. (3) 'Later start ages' misdescribes astaxanthin, one of whose arms started earlier (11 vs 12 months) at roughly half the achieved dose. (4) Most importantly for the article's thesis, the ITP investigators do not present this as failed replication and no arm matched the original dose-plus-age combination; they present it as different doses and start ages and explicitly float that 'intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' They do, in the same breath, offer the chance-finding reading — originals near the 80%-power floor, no Wang-Allison change, nominal unadjusted p-values — which is the honest version of the article's point and should be quoted rather than paraphrased into 'non-replication.'

Two residual uncertainties I did not resolve. First, I could not run adversarial searches for post-publication critical letters or commentary, because the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before my first query; the Europe PMC and MEDLINE records for DOI 10.1007/s11357-026-02201-2 carry no erratum, correction, retraction or comment link as of 2026-07, but absence of a linked comment is weaker evidence than a search would have been. Second, I did not retrieve Table 2 (the UM+UT-only female reanalysis) as raw XML; its numbers reach me only via the Discussion sentences, which are self-consistent but single-sourced. The mitoglitazone dose used in the original C2021 cohort I also did not retrieve, so I cannot state how the 300 ppm target in C2022 compares to the dose that produced the original hit.

- **Source identity: 2026 GeroScience report by Korstanje R, Strong R, Salmon AB, et al.** — `confirmed`
  Korstanje R, Strong R, Salmon AB, Bogue MA, Curran SP, Diaz V, Fernandez E, Ginsburg B, Han M, Harrison DE, Kaczorowski C, Kaeberlein M, Kennedy BK, Kumar N, LaCroix-Fralish M, Leiser SF, Nelson JF, Polymenis M, Reifsnyder PC, Rosenthal NA, Silva E, Tower J, Miller RA. Title: 'Astaxanthin, meclizine, mitoglitazone, pioglitazone, alpha-ketoglutarate, mifepristone, methotrexate, and atorvastatin-telmisartan do not increase lifespan in UM-HET3 mice.' GeroScience. 2026 Jun;48(3):3821-3830. doi:10.1007/s11357-026-02201-2. Epub 2026 Mar 17. PMID 41843349, PMC13356140. This is ITP cohort C2022. No erratum, correction or retraction is linked in the Europe PMC or MEDLINE record as of 2026-07.

- **The ITP tested eleven compounds/protocols** — `corrected`
  WRONG as stated if read as eleven distinct compounds. RIGHT: eleven intervention ARMS built from eight agents/combinations. The paper's own Discussion says 'none of the 11 interventions in the C2022 cohort'; the title names eight agents (astaxanthin, meclizine, mitoglitazone, pioglitazone, alpha-ketoglutarate, mifepristone, methotrexate, atorvastatin-telmisartan). Table 1 shows the eleven arms exist only in MALES (AKG_early, Asta_low, Asta_late, Atortel, M160_late, Mec_high, Mec_late, Meth, Mife, Pio, Pio_late). FEMALES received only NINE arms — Asta_late and Mec_late were male-only. Saying flatly 'eleven arms in both sexes' would be wrong.

  Abstract verbatim: 'none of the tested compounds significantly increased lifespan in male or female mice.' Table 1 pooled log-rank p-values, MALES (n=300 control, median 813 d): AKG_early 0.429, Asta_low 0.214, Asta_late 0.377, Atortel 0.644, M160_late 0.176, Mec_high 0.396, Mec_late 0.557, Meth 0.905, Mife 0.464, Pio 0.172, Pio_late 0.763 — all ns. FEMALES (n=272 control, median 903 d): all ns in the positive direction. IMPORTANT OMISSION in the claim: three female arms were significantly HARMFUL. Pooled: Asta_low −3.16% median p=0.021, M160_late −5.76% p=0.001, Pio −9.41% p<0.0001. After excluding TJL (whose C2022 control females were anomalously long-lived, Z=3.13, two-tailed p=0.0017), only M160_late (median −0.7%, P=0.0374; p90 −6.45%, P=0.0238) and Pio (median −6.2%, P=0.0047) remained significantly negative. Also note male Mec_late had a significant Wang-Allison of 0.009 in the HARMFUL direction (p90 −3.07%).

  Confirmed from the paper's own Discussion and its reference list. Astaxanthin and meclizine both trace to ref [10] = Harrison DE et al., GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816 (PMID 38041783, PMC10828146), ITP cohort C2019. Mitoglitazone traces to ref [15] = Strong R et al., GeroScience 2026;48(3):4139-4156 (PMID 40973907, PMC13355999), ITP cohort C2021.

- **Astaxanthin +12% male median, p=0.003, in the 2024 report** — `confirmed`
  Exact. C2022 Discussion verbatim: 'In a previous ITP study, Asta had increased lifespan in males (12%, P = 0.003) when starting at 12 months at a target dose of 4,000 ppm [10].' Cross-checked against the source itself (Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816), which states astaxanthin 'extended the median male lifespan by 12% (p = 0.003)', target 4000 ppm with achieved ~46% of target (~1840 ppm), started at 12 months.   The NUMBERS are right, the DATE is wrong. C2022 Discussion verbatim: 'M160 had led to a lifespan increase of 9% (P = 0.015) in males when started at 7 months in our previous cohort (C2021) [15].' WRONG: calling this a 2024 (or ambiguously '2024/2025') report. RIGHT: Strong R, Nelson JF, Bogue MA, et al., 'Extension of lifespan by epicatechin, halofuginone and mitoglitazone in male but not female genetically heterogeneous mice', GeroScience 2026 Jun;48(3):4139-4156, epub 2025 Sep 19, PMID 40973907. Notably the mitoglitazone POSITIVE paper and this NULL paper appear in the SAME June 2026 issue of GeroScience (48(3), pp. 4139-4156 and pp. 3821-3830 respectively) — the retest was run and published essentially alongside the original hit, not years later.

- **Meclizine reported as a male hit in 2024/2025** — `corrected`
  WRONG: '2024/2025'. RIGHT: meclizine came from the SAME 2024 paper as astaxanthin — Harrison et al., GeroScience 2024;46(1):795-816, cohort C2019. C2022 Discussion verbatim: 'In a previous ITP study, Mec increased lifespan (8%, P = 0.03) in males, when started at 12 months at 800 ppm in C2019 [10].' Effect size +8% male median, p=0.03. The original 2024 paper states meclizine 'extended the male lifespan by 8% (p = 0.03)', target 800 ppm, achieved 68% of target (544 ppm), start 12 months.

- **All three failed 'at other doses or later start ages' in the new report** — `corrected`
  Substantially right, but 'later start ages' is not accurate for astaxanthin. Per Table 3 (target/achieved ppm, start month): ASTAXANTHIN — Asta_low 800/880 ppm from 11 months (LOWER dose and marginally EARLIER than the original 12-month start), Asta_late 800/880 ppm from 16 months, males only. So one astaxanthin arm was earlier, not later, and both were at roughly half the achieved dose of the original (~1840 ppm). MECLIZINE — Mec_late target 800 ppm (same target as the original hit) from 16 months, males only; Mec_high target 2400 / achieved 1,727 ppm from 16 months, both sexes. MITOGLITAZONE — M160_late target 300 / achieved 126 ppm from 18 months, versus 7 months originally. CAUTION on one number: the C2022 Results text and Table 3 give Mec_late's achieved dose as '68 ppm', but the 2024 source paper says meclizine achieved 68% OF the 800 ppm target, i.e. 544 ppm. The '68' looks like a percentage carried into a ppm column. Do not print '68 ppm' as meclizine's dose. A second internal inconsistency: the Discussion says Asta_low started 'at 7 months' while Table 3 and the Results section both say 11 months — use 11 months.

- **Whether the ITP investigators characterise this as non-replication or as testing a different regimen** — `corrected`
  THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING CORRECTION. The ITP explicitly frames these as DIFFERENT REGIMENS, not attempted replications. No arm reproduced the original dose-plus-start-age combination for any of the three compounds. Abstract verbatim: 'Notably, astaxanthin, mitoglitazone, and meclizine—previously associated with lifespan extension in the ITP—showed no benefit when administered at different doses or starting at later ages.' Discussion verbatim: 'none of the 11 interventions in the C2022 cohort, which included several compounds (M160, Mec, and Asta) that had previously shown an effect at a different dose or starting age, showed an increase in lifespan in males or females. It is possible that for these compounds, intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' HOWEVER — and this partially rescues the article's point — the same paragraph volunteers the deflationary reading: 'Their previously published increases in median lifespan (9%, 8%, and 12%, respectively) were at or near the lower level of what is expected to be able to discover at 80% power, and none of them showed a change in the Wang-Allison statistic. Furthermore, the p-values are nominal, and chance effects can be expected in any series of studies for truly ineffective agents.' So the ITP offers BOTH explanations and does not itself use the word 'replication'. An article sentence saying the ITP 'does not replicate its own hits' overstates the design; a sentence saying the ITP retested its own hits at other doses/start ages, found nothing, and itself flags that the originals sat near the detection floor with unadjusted p-values, is accurate.

**修正:**

The ITP's own framing (abstract) is that these compounds 'showed no benefit when administered at different doses or starting at later ages,' and the Discussion says 'It is possible that for these compounds, intervention in a specific dose and age window is required.' Write instead: when the ITP retested three of its own male-lifespan hits at different doses or later start ages, none reproduced any benefit.
- Add the ITP's own deflationary caveat, which strengthens the article's point without overstating the design. Verbatim from the Discussion: the three previously published median-lifespan increases '(9%, 8%, and 12%, respectively) were at or near the lower level of what is expected to be able to discover at 80% power, and none of them showed a change in the Wang-Allison statistic. Furthermore, the p-values are nominal, and chance effects can be expected in any series of studies for truly ineffective agents.' None of the three originals showed a maximum-lifespan (Wang-Allison) effect.

Also state that the eleven arms applied to MALES only; females received nine arms (Asta_late and Mec_late were male-only). Per Table 1 the male control n=300 and each treatment arm n=102-210; female control n=272 and each arm n=130-132.

One astaxanthin arm (Asta_low, 880 ppm) started at 11 months — EARLIER than the original 12-month start — and both new arms used roughly half the original achieved dose (~880 ppm vs ~1840 ppm achieved in C2019). Only Asta_late (16 months, males only) was a later start.
