- **Phase 3 population: non-smokers without COPD** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we recruited participants aged at least 65 years who did not have COPD and were not current smokers at 16 clinical sites in New Zealand and 15 clinical sites in Australia.' Note asthma was NOT excluded in phase 3 (exclusion is 'COPD or other clinically significant lung diseases other than asthma'), so 'lower-risk' does not mean 'healthy'.

- **Phase 3 conducted in NZ / AU / USA** — `corrected`
  WRONG: phase 3 was run in New Zealand, Australia and the USA. RIGHT: the phase 3 was run only in New Zealand and Australia — verbatim 'at 16 clinical sites in New Zealand and 15 clinical sites in Australia.' It was the PHASE 2B that used the USA: verbatim 'at ten clinical sites in New Zealand (part 1) and 17 clinical sites in the USA (part 2).' The 'New Zealand, Australia, and the USA at 54 sites' phrasing in the paper's abstract covers the two trials POOLED, and appears to be where this error entered. (The ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04668352 lists only one site, P3 Research Ltd., Wellington, New Zealand — the registry record is incomplete, so do not use it either.)

- **Phase 2b: OR 0.601, 90% CI 0.391-0.922, p=0.02** — `confirmed`
  The OR and the 90% CI are verbatim correct. Raw full text, Findings section: 'odds ratio [OR] 0·601 [90% CI 0·391–0·922]; p=0·02'. IMPORTANT CAVEAT the article must handle: the Results section of the SAME paper reports the identical comparison as 'OR 0·601 [90% CI 0·391–0·922]; p=0·025'. So p=0.02 is defensible (it is the abstract value) but the paper is internally inconsistent; safest wording is 'p=0.02 in the abstract, p=0.025 in the Results'. Numerators/denominators verified: RTB101 10 mg once daily 34 [19%] of 176 vs pooled placebo 50 [28%] of 180. The 90% CI is the correct caliber flag: the phase 2b was powered and tested at a ONE-SIDED alpha of 0.05, which is why a 90% two-sided interval is reported.

- **The 0.601 result came from a second analysis after a first endpoint analysis failed** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'In this step-down analysis, efficacy of RTB101 10 mg in combination with everolimus 0·1 mg once daily compared with placebo was first tested at a one-sided α level of 0·05 and did not meet statistical significance.' Then: 'Because this was an exploratory phase 2b dose-finding trial, an additional analysis of the primary endpoint was prespecified that did not adjust for multiplicity. This analysis evaluated the proportion of subjects with laboratory-confirmed RTIs in each of the active treatment groups compared with placebo, and included all data from Parts 1 and 2 of the study.' PRECISION POINT: the second analysis was PRE-SPECIFIED (unadjusted for multiplicity, pooling Parts 1+2), not post-hoc — the article must not call it post-hoc. The genuinely post-hoc step was elsewhere and is a stronger point: the phase 3 sample size was powered off a post-hoc re-analysis — verbatim 'This was done as a post-hoc analysis based on the FDA-recommended change in primary endpoint and patient population for the phase 3 trial', assuming 28.2% placebo vs 19.7% RTB101 and targeting 1066 participants for 90% power at two-sided 0.05. The trial enrolled 1024, i.e. under the 1066 target.

- **Phase 2b population was HIGH-risk (asthma, T2D, COPD, CHF, current smokers)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'Participants were aged 65–85 years with asthma, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), congestive heart failure, were current smokers, or had an emergency room or hospitalisation for an RTI within the past 12 months.' Two details the article omits: the phase 2b also allowed entry via 'emergency room or hospitalisation for an RTI within the past 12 months', and phase 2b had an upper age cap of 85 whereas phase 3 had none.

- **An independent commentary states the FDA required the endpoint change** — `corrected`
  WRONG (under-attributed): only an independent commentary says the FDA forced it. RIGHT: the trial's OWN primary publication says it, twice. Verbatim from Mannick et al. 2021 raw full text, Methods/phase 3 section: 'The change in participant enrollment criteria between the phase 2b and phase 3 trials was recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).' And in the outcomes section: 'The US FDA requested a change in primary endpoint between the Phase 2b and 3 trials because of concerns that laboratory confirmation of an infection was not relevant to how patients feel and function. Therefore, the FDA proposed a primary endpoint of the proportion of patients with at least one clinically symptomatic respiratory illness, defined as symptoms consistent with an RTI, irrespective of whether the symptoms were confirmed via laboratory testing to be due to an infection.' The accompanying commentary (Juricic & Partridge, 'Clinical trials of mTOR inhibitors to boost immunity to viral infection in older adults', Lancet Healthy Longev 2021, PMC8102037) repeats it and adds 'Compared with the phase 2b trial, the phase 3 trial was thus done in patients who were at lower overall risk of RTIs and with a primary endpoint that was less clearly linked to underlying immune function.' Attribute the FDA fact to the sponsor's own paper (stronger), and the 'lower-risk / weaker endpoint' judgement to the commentary.

- **resTORbio merged with Adicet Bio within about six months of the 2019-11-15 failure** — `corrected`
  WRONG: 'merging with Adicet Bio' within about six months. RIGHT: the MERGER AGREEMENT was signed April 28, 2020 and disclosed in an 8-K dated 'April 28, 2020' filed 2020-04-29 (SEC CIK 0001720580) — about 5.5 months after the Nov 15, 2019 failure. The MERGER CLOSED on September 15, 2020 — about 10 months after. Verbatim from Exhibit 99.1 to the 8-K filed 2020-09-15: 'Menlo Park, CA and Boston, MA – September 15, 2020 – Adicet Bio, Inc., ... today announced the completion of its previously announced merger with resTORbio, Inc. (previously trading on Nasdaq under the symbol "TORC").' EDGAR records the entity's former name 'resTORbio, Inc.' as running to 2020-08-21. Also, 'ceased to be an aging company within about six months' overstates: resTORbio kept running RTB101 clinical trials into late 2020 under the Restorbio Inc. sponsor name (NCT04409327, COVID-19 severity in nursing homes, start 2020-07-11, terminated at n=36; NCT04584710, COVID-19 post-exposure prophylaxis, start 2020-10-13 — i.e. after the merger closed). Safe phrasing: 'announced a reverse merger into oncology cell-therapy company Adicet Bio about five and a half months later; the deal closed 15 September 2020.'

- **What Joan Mannick is doing as of 2026** — `corrected`
  WRONG (if the article places her at Tornado Therapeutics in 2026): she left Tornado. RIGHT: Joan Mannick, MD is Senior Vice President, Chief Medical Officer and Head of Product Development at ALTOS LABS, announced in an Altos Labs press release (altoslabs.com) covered on 4-5 August 2025. Verbatim from the Altos press release: 'Altos Labs (Altos) today announced that Joan Mannick, M.D., has joined the company as Senior Vice President, Chief Medical Officer, and Head of Product Development.' and 'Dr. Mannick joins Altos from Tornado Therapeutics, where she served as Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder and led efforts to develop safer and more effective mTOR inhibitors for aging-related diseases.' Her Altos team page describes Tornado in the past tense: 'Joan brings extensive drug development expertise to Altos including from her time as the Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Tornado Therapeutics.' Independent corroboration: Endpoints News, 5 Aug 2025, 'Altos Labs hires a new medical chief with mTOR experience, Novartis chops'; Fierce Biotech Chutes & Ladders, 8 Aug 2025. Her last PubMed-indexed affiliation is 'Tornado Therapeutics, New York, NY, USA' on Mannick JB & Lamming DW, 'Targeting the biology of aging with mTOR inhibitors', Nat Aging 2023 (PMID 37142830) — she has no PubMed-indexed publications after 2023, so do not cite a 2026 publication affiliation.

- **TOR-101 (Tornado Therapeutics) has NOT entered human trials** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, and the article's belief is right. (1) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 returns ZERO studies for sponsor 'Tornado', ZERO for intervention 'TOR-101', ZERO for term 'TOR-101', ZERO for sponsor 'Cambrian'. (2) Cambrian Bio's current pipeline page (cambrianbio.com/pipeline, fetched 2026-07-28, and current — it links ADA 2026 posters 1782-P and 1788-P) lists TOR-101 twice, for 'Healthspan' and 'Intrinsic Capacity', both at stage 'Phase 1 Prepared'; TOR-103 is at 'Candidate'. Verbatim from that page: 'The platform received up to $30.8 million from ARPA-H's PROSPR program to advance a novel mTORC1-selective inhibitor toward clinical development.' (3) Tornado's own pipeline page (tornado-tx.com/pipeline) lists 'TOR-101 · Indication: Viral Respiratory Tract Infections · Phase: IND-enabling'. (4) Labiotech, 16 March 2026: TOR-101 'is moving into Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling' work. (5) Patsnap Synapse lists TOR-101's 'global highest R&D status' as Preclinical. Useful extra beat for the article: Cambrian's own July 18, 2023 blog said Tornado would be 'bringing one of these rapalogs (called TOR-101) into human clinical trials in 2024' — three years on it is still pre-IND. CAVEAT: the tornado-tx.com and tornadotherapeutics.com domains did not resolve/returned 520 from this machine, so the Tornado pipeline wording above comes from a search-engine index snapshot, not a page I loaded; the Cambrian and ClinicalTrials.gov evidence I did load directly.

- **Framing: RTB101 as a 'rapalog' and PROTECTOR 1 as the most decisive result 'in the rapalog field'** — `corrected`
  WRONG: calling the PROTECTOR 1 failure a result in 'the rapalog field'. RIGHT: RTB101 is NOT a rapalog. The paper states verbatim 'RTB101 (previously known as BEZ235), an oral mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor', and its own reference 11 describes BEZ235 as 'a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor' (BEZ235 = dactolisib; ClinicalTrials.gov lists the phase 3 arm as 'Dactolisib 10mg'). It is an ATP-competitive catalytic-site PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, mechanistically distinct from rapamycin/rapalogs. The rapalog in the program was everolimus (RAD001), which featured in the 2014 and 2018 phase 2a work and in one phase 2b combination arm — and that combination arm is exactly the comparison that FAILED the multiplicity-controlled first analysis. Recommended fix: describe PROTECTOR 1 as the most decisive human trial in the mTOR-inhibition-for-aging field, and note explicitly that the drug tested was a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, not rapamycin or a rapalog — otherwise the article imports a failure of dactolisib into the rapamycin evidence grade.

**修正:**
- Change the phase 3 geography: PROTECTOR 1 was run at 16 sites in New Zealand and 15 sites in Australia only — NOT the USA. The USA sites belonged to the phase 2b (10 NZ sites in part 1, 17 US sites in part 2). The paper's abstract phrase 'New Zealand, Australia, and the USA at 54 sites' describes the two trials pooled.
- Change the FDA attribution: do not say 'an independent commentary states the FDA required the endpoint change.' The sponsor's own primary publication (Mannick et al., Lancet Healthy Longev 2021;2:e250-e262) states it directly — 'The US FDA requested a change in primary endpoint between the Phase 2b and 3 trials because of concerns that laboratory confirmation of an infection was not relevant to how patients feel and function' — and separately that 'The change in participant enrollment criteria between the phase 2b and phase 3 trials was recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).' Attribute the FDA facts to the trial paper; attribute the interpretive verdict ('lower overall risk ... endpoint less clearly linked to underlying immune function') to the Juricic & Partridge commentary.
- Fix the p-value handling: p=0.02 is the value in the paper's abstract/Findings; the Results section of the same paper gives p=0.025 for the identical comparison (OR 0.601, 90% CI 0.391-0.922, 34/176 vs 50/180). Quote one and flag the discrepancy rather than presenting p=0.02 as unambiguous.
- Do not call the second phase 2b analysis 'post-hoc'. It was PRE-SPECIFIED but unadjusted for multiplicity and pooled Parts 1 and 2. The genuinely post-hoc step, and the stronger point, is that the phase 3 sample size was powered off a post-hoc re-analysis of phase 2b restricted to non-COPD non-smokers — verbatim 'This was done as a post-hoc analysis based on the FDA-recommended change in primary endpoint and patient population for the phase 3 trial' — targeting 1066 participants for 90% power against an assumed 28.2% vs 19.7% event rate; only 1024 were enrolled.
- Fix the merger timing: the merger agreement with Adicet Bio was signed 28 April 2020 (8-K filed 29 April 2020), about 5.5 months after the 15 November 2019 failure; the merger COMPLETED on 15 September 2020, about 10 months after. Also drop or soften 'ceased to be an aging company within about six months' — resTORbio was still sponsoring RTB101 COVID-19 trials under its own name into October 2020 (NCT04409327 started 2020-07-11; NCT04584710 started 2020-10-13).
- Update Joan Mannick's current role: as of 2026 she is Senior Vice President, Chief Medical Officer and Head of Product Development at ALTOS LABS, having joined in August 2025 from Tornado Therapeutics, where she had been CEO and co-founder. Do not describe TOR-101 as 'her' current program or place her at Tornado in the present tense.
- Keep the conclusion that TOR-101 has not entered human trials, and cite it precisely: Cambrian Bio's own pipeline page lists TOR-101 as 'Phase 1 Prepared' and Tornado's pipeline lists it as 'IND-enabling'; there is no ClinicalTrials.gov registration for TOR-101 or for Tornado Therapeutics as sponsor. Cambrian publicly said in July 2023 it would take TOR-101 into human trials in 2024, so the program has slipped roughly two years.
- Stop calling RTB101 a rapalog. RTB101 is dactolisib/BEZ235, an ATP-competitive dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor; the rapalog in the program was everolimus. Reframe PROTECTOR 1 as the most decisive human trial of mTOR inhibition for an aging-related outcome, and state the mechanism explicitly so the failure is not silently imported into the evidence grade for rapamycin itself.
- If the phase 3 confidence interval is quoted, note that the paper reports OR 1.07 with a '90% CI 0.80-1.42' in the abstract and a '95% CI 0.80-1.42' in the Results — the same interval, two different labels. Do not present either as the paper's settled caliber without noting the inconsistency.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04668352 (study code RTB-101-204, the 1024-participant phase 3) contradicts the publication on two facts: it gives Start Date 2019-04-15 (ACTUAL), not May 7, 2018, and it lists exactly one site (P3 Research Ltd., Wellington, New Zealand) with country New Zealand only. The record was registered retrospectively in December 2020. The paper registered the phase 3 with ANZCTR (ACTRN12619000628145), not ClinicalTrials.gov. Anyone checking the article's dates against ClinicalTrials.gov will see a mismatch, so the article should cite the publication and not imply registry agreement.
- The Mannick 2021 paper is internally inconsistent in three places that undercut quoting it as a clean number: p=0.02 (abstract) vs p=0.025 (Results) for the same phase 2b OR; '90% CI 0.80-1.42' (abstract) vs '95% CI 0.80-1.42' (Results) for the same phase 3 OR of 1.07; and randomisation counts of 513/510 (Results) vs 513/511 (Discussion) vs a full analysis set of 511/510.
- The phase 3 was under-enrolled relative to its own power calculation: the paper states 1066 participants were required for 90% power, and 1024 were enrolled. This slightly weakens (but does not overturn) the failure, and the article should not present the trial as over-powered.
- The phase 2b itself contained a signal that the phase 3 population change was likely to null out the effect, which the sponsor reports: the paper attributes the lack of benefit in current smokers and COPD patients to preclinical data that 'mTOR inhibitors increase cigarette smoke-induced inflammation' - i.e. the high-risk phase 2b population was heterogeneous, and the benefit was not uniform across it.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Primary documents I reached and read verbatim myself (not via a summarizer): (1) Europe PMC full-text XML of Mannick et al., 'Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials', Lancet Healthy Longev 2021;2(5):e250-e262, PMID 33977284 / PMC8102040 — downloaded the XML via the Europe PMC REST fullTextXML endpoint, stripped tags locally, and grepped the raw text. I confirmed by direct string match that the file contains '0·601', and I read the surrounding 3000 characters, the Methods 'Study design and participants' section, the full 'Statistical analysis' section, and every occurrence of 'FDA'. (2) The accompanying commentary, Juricic & Partridge, PMID 33977282 / PMC8102037, same method — it independently reproduces OR 0·601 [90% CI 0·391–0·922]; p=0·02. (3) SEC EDGAR filings for CIK 0001720580 (Adicet Bio, formerly resTORbio): the 2019-11-15 8-K exhibit 99.1 (PROTECTOR 1 topline), the 2020-04-29 8-K exhibit 99.1 (merger agreement), the 2020-09-16 8-K Item 2.01 (merger completed September 15, 2020), and the 2020-04-03 8-K (Parkinson's program status). (4) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 records for all five resTORbio-sponsored studies. (5) Cambrian Bio's live pipeline page and its February 24, 2026 ARPA-H PROSPR press release. (6) Altos Labs' live team page for Joan Mannick and the appointment press release. I searched for refutation: PubMed shows no erratum, correction or retraction linked to PMID 33977284, and an esearch for RTB101 plus erratum/correction/retraction returned zero. What remains uncertain: (a) I could not pin the exact date of the Altos Labs appointment from a primary source — Altos' page carries no dateline; the earliest Internet Archive capture of that URL is 2025-08-05 and trade press (Endpoints, Longevity.Technology, Fierce Biotech) dated it 2025-08-05 to 2025-08-08, so 'early August 2025' is the tightest defensible statement. (b) My check that TOR-101 has not entered humans covers ClinicalTrials.gov and ISRCTN (both zero hits) plus Cambrian's own 'Phase 1 Prepared' stage label and the February 2026 'toward clinical development' language; ANZCTR served a bot-challenge page and the EU CTIS API requires authentication, so a first-in-human study registered only in Australia or the EU cannot be fully excluded — though Cambrian's own February 2026 wording makes that very unlikely. (c) The ~0.36–1.00 reconstruction of the 95% CI for the phase 2b OR is my own arithmetic from the published 90% bounds, not a figure printed in the paper. My WebSearch quota was exhausted before I started, so all retrieval was done with direct HTTP via curl to registry, publisher, SEC and company endpoints; the one general web search that succeeded (Brave) was used only as a pointer, and every fact it suggested was then verified against the company's own site.

- **Phase 3 (PROTECTOR 1) enrolled 1024 adults and missed its primary endpoint with the point estimate on the wrong side of 1** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed twice over. Mannick et al., Lancet Healthy Longev 2021;2:e250-e262 (PMC8102040), abstract, verbatim: 'In the phase 3 trial, we enrolled 1024 patients between May 7, 2018, and July 19, 2019. 513 (50·1%) participants were randomly assigned to RTB101 10 mg once daily and 510 (49·9%) to placebo. In the full analysis set of the phase 3 trial, RTB101 did not reduce the proportion of patients with clinically symptomatic respiratory illness (134 [26%] of 511 patients in the RTB101 treatment group vs 125 [25%] 510 patients in the placebo treatment group; OR 1·07 [90% CI 0·80–1·42]; p=0·65).' Also confirmed in resTORbio's own 8-K exhibit 99.1 filed 2019-11-15 (SEC accession 0001193125-19-292868): 'The PROTECTOR 1 trial included 1024 patients... the odds of experiencing a CSRI were 0.44 in the placebo cohort and 0.46 in the RTB101 cohort (odds ratio 1.07, p=0.65).' NOTE for the writer: the paper's Results section prints the same figure as 'OR 1·07 [95% CI 0·80–1·42]; p=0·65' — the abstract's '90% CI' label is an internal inconsistency. Methods for phase 3 say '95% CIs' and 'a two-sided α of 0·05'. Quote the phase 3 as 95% CI.

- **Phase 3 start date 2018-05-07** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the paper: 'we enrolled 1024 patients between May 7, 2018, and July 19, 2019.' Caution: the retrospective ClinicalTrials.gov record for this trial (NCT04668352, org study ID RTB-101-204, registered Dec 2020) lists a start date of 2019-04-15 and enrollment 1024 — it contradicts the publication. The phase 3's primary registration is ANZCTR ACTRN12619000628145, not ClinicalTrials.gov.

- **Phase 3 population: adults aged >=65, non-smokers, without COPD** — `confirmed`
  Paper, Methods: 'we recruited participants aged at least 65 years who did not have COPD and were not current smokers.' Press release 2019-11-15: 'subjects 65 years of age and older, excluding current smokers and individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.' Note there is no upper age limit in phase 3, whereas phase 2b was capped at 85.

- **Phase 3 conducted in New Zealand, Australia and the USA** — `corrected`
  WRONG: 'NZ/AU/USA' for the phase 3. RIGHT: the phase 3 ran at '16 clinical sites in New Zealand and 15 clinical sites in Australia' (paper, Methods) — no US sites; ethics approvals were NZ (Northern A HDEC) and Australia (Bellberry) only. The USA sites belonged to the phase 2b: 'ten clinical sites in New Zealand (part 1) and 17 clinical sites in the USA (part 2).' The error almost certainly comes from the paper's abstract line 'enrolled in New Zealand, Australia, and the USA at 54 sites', which spans BOTH trials.

- **Phase 2b: OR 0.601, 90% CI 0.391-0.922, p=0.02** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim, seen by me in the Europe PMC full text of PMC8102040 (Lancet mid-dot style): 'odds ratio [OR] 0·601 [90% CI 0·391–0·922]; p=0·02', for 34 [19%] of 176 on RTB101 10 mg once daily vs 50 [28%] of 180 pooled placebo. Independently reproduced verbatim in the accompanying commentary (Juricic & Partridge, Lancet Healthy Longev 2021;2:e232, PMC8102037). The 90% CI is genuine and it is materially weaker than a 95% CI here: reconstructing the standard error from the reported bounds gives an approximate 95% CI of ~0.36–1.00, i.e. the interval would touch 1 (my calculation, not stated in the paper — label it as such if used).

- **Phase 2b population was HIGH-risk (asthma, T2D, COPD, CHF, current smokers)** — `confirmed`
  Paper, Methods, verbatim: 'Participants were aged 65–85 years with asthma, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), congestive heart failure, were current smokers, or had an emergency room or hospitalisation for an RTI within the past 12 months.' The article's list omits the sixth criterion (recent ER visit/hospitalisation for RTI) and the 65–85 age band. The paper's Discussion confirms the contrast: 'The phase 3 trial enrolled a healthier population than that of the phase 2b trial.'

- **The 0.601 came from a second analysis after a first endpoint failed** — `corrected`
  Substantially right but under-specified, and one word is wrong in the other direction. WRONG (implied): that the second analysis was an unplanned salvage. RIGHT: both analyses were PRESPECIFIED — 'Two different analyses of the key efficacy endpoints were prespecified.' The first was a fixed-sequence gatekeeping step-down restricted to part 2, ordered (1) RTB101 10 mg + everolimus 0.1 mg, (2) RTB101 10 mg twice daily, (3) RTB101 10 mg once daily; because gate (1) failed, the 10 mg once-daily comparison was never formally tested in that hierarchy at all. The second prespecified analysis 'did not adjust for multiplicity', pooled part 1 + part 2 data, and used 'a one-sided α of 0·05'. So the correct caliber statement is stronger than the article's: the winning number is (a) from a different arm than the one that failed, (b) from a pooled population, (c) unadjusted for multiplicity, and (d) one-sided. The '90% CI' is the direct consequence of the prespecified one-sided α=0.05.

- **An independent commentary states the FDA required the endpoint change** — `corrected`
  WRONG on both source and verb. RIGHT: the sponsors' own trial publication says it, in two places. Methods: 'The change in participant enrollment criteria between the phase 2b and phase 3 trials was recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).' Outcomes: 'The US FDA requested a change in primary endpoint between the Phase 2b and 3 trials because of concerns that laboratory confirmation of an infection was not relevant to how patients feel and function. Therefore, the FDA proposed a primary endpoint of the proportion of patients with at least one clinically symptomatic respiratory illness...'. The independent commentary (Juricic & Partridge) merely repeats this. Also: the FDA drove BOTH changes — endpoint AND patient population — which the article splits into an FDA item and a separate unattributed population item. And the paper's verbs are 'requested / recommended / proposed', not 'required'.

- **resTORbio ceased to be an aging company within about six months, merging with Adicet Bio (after the 2019-11-15 announcement)** — `corrected`
  Announcement date 2019-11-15 is CONFIRMED (8-K accession 0001193125-19-292868, press release headline: 'resTORbio Announces That the Phase 3 PROTECTOR 1 Trial of RTB101 in Clinically Symptomatic Respiratory Illness Did Not Meet the Primary Endpoint', dated 'BOSTON, MA, November 15, 2019'). WRONG: 'merging with Adicet Bio' within about six months. RIGHT: the merger AGREEMENT was announced April 29, 2020 (~5.5 months later; 8-K accession 0001193125-20-124620, exhibit 99.1 'resTORbio and Adicet Bio Announce Merger Agreement'); the merger CLOSED September 15, 2020 (~10 months later; 8-K accession 0001193125-20-246853: 'On September 15, 2020, the Company completed the Merger... the Company changed its name from resTORbio, Inc. to Adicet Bio, Inc.'). Two further caliber problems with 'ceased to be an aging company': (a) the Nov 15 2019 press release explicitly said the opposite at the time — subheadline: 'Company stops further development of clinically symptomatic respiratory illness indication but continues development of RTB101 in other aging-related diseases, including Parkinson's disease'; (b) resTORbio was still running RTB101 aging trials after the merger was announced — NCT04409327, a RTB101 COVID-19 phase 2 in nursing homes, sponsor 'Restorbio Inc.', started 2020-07-11, terminated 2020-12-27. Safest formulation: the pivot away from aging was announced ~5.5 months after the failure and completed with the Adicet merger close on 2020-09-15.

- **What Joan Mannick is doing as of 2026** — `refuted`
  The article's premise (that she is still at Tornado Therapeutics running the next-gen rapalog) is out of date. Altos Labs' own live team page (fetched 2026-07-28, footer '© 2026 Altos Labs'): 'Dr. Joan Mannick is the Senior Vice President, Chief Medical Officer and Head of Product Development at Altos Labs. Joan brings extensive drug development expertise to Altos including from her time as the Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Tornado Therapeutics.' — Tornado is in the past tense. Altos' own press release: 'Dr. Mannick joins Altos from Tornado Therapeutics, where she served as Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder.' Appointment was announced in early August 2025 (Endpoints News and Longevity.Technology coverage dated 2025-08-05, Fierce Biotech 2025-08-08; Internet Archive's first capture of the Altos press-release URL is 2025-08-05 — I could not pin the exact press-release date from Altos' own page, which carries no visible dateline). Her role at Altos is cellular rejuvenation reprogramming, not mTOR. She is not listed anywhere on Cambrian Bio's current team page and is not quoted in Cambrian's Feb 2026 TORnado press release.

- **TOR-101 (Tornado Therapeutics) has not entered human trials** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, with one naming correction. Cambrian Bio's live pipeline page (fetched 2026-07-28) lists TOR-101 for both 'Intrinsic Capacity' and 'Healthspan' at stage 'Phase 1 Prepared' — a pre-Phase-1 stage on their own progress bar, versus e.g. ATX-304 which is marked 'Phase 1b/2a'. TOR-103 is at 'Candidate'. Cambrian's press release of February 24, 2026 says the ARPA-H PROSPR award of 'up to $30.8 million' is 'to advance a novel mTORC1-selective inhibitor toward clinical development' — i.e. not yet clinical. No trial for TOR-101, Tornado Therapeutics or Cambrian exists on ClinicalTrials.gov (API queries by intervention and by sponsor returned zero) or ISRCTN (zero). I could NOT check ANZCTR (site returned a bot-challenge page) or EU CTIS (API requires auth), so registry coverage outside the US is incomplete. Naming correction: Cambrian now presents this as its own 'TORnado platform' rather than as the separate PipeCo 'Tornado Therapeutics' — the Feb 2026 release never uses the company name.

- **Framing: 'the rapalog field' / RTB101 as a rapalog** — `corrected`
  WRONG: calling PROTECTOR 1 the decisive result 'in the rapalog field'. RIGHT: RTB101 is not a rapamycin analogue. The paper itself states 'RTB101 (previously known as BEZ235)' — a catalytic-site mTOR inhibitor lineage, and resTORbio's own press release calls it 'an oral, selective, and potent TORC1 inhibitor', never a rapalog. The only true rapalog in the program was everolimus 0.1 mg, used in one phase 2b arm (the arm that failed the first gate) and absent entirely from the phase 3. Likewise TOR-101 is described by Cambrian as a 'highly selective mTORC1 inhibitor'. If the article wants the broad category, say 'mTOR-inhibitor field' or 'rapamycin-pathway field'; reserve 'rapalog' for sirolimus/everolimus.

**修正:**
- Delete the USA from the PROTECTOR 1 phase 3 description. The phase 3 ran at 16 clinical sites in New Zealand and 15 in Australia only. The 17 US sites belonged to part 2 of the phase 2b. (The paper's abstract line 'New Zealand, Australia, and the USA at 54 sites' covers both trials and must not be applied to the phase 3 alone.)
- Change the FDA attribution. Do not say 'an independent commentary states the FDA required the endpoint change.' The sponsors' own trial paper says it, in two places: 'The US FDA requested a change in primary endpoint between the Phase 2b and 3 trials because of concerns that laboratory confirmation of an infection was not relevant to how patients feel and function' and 'The change in participant enrollment criteria between the phase 2b and phase 3 trials was recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).' Use 'requested'/'recommended', not 'required'. Note that the FDA drove both the endpoint change and the shift to a lower-risk population — these are one FDA decision, not two separate facts.
- Fix the merger timing. resTORbio announced the merger AGREEMENT with Adicet Bio on April 29, 2020 (~5.5 months after the November 15, 2019 failure) and CLOSED it on September 15, 2020 (~10 months), at which point resTORbio was renamed Adicet Bio, Inc. 'Merged within about six months' is wrong; the announcement was at ~5.5 months, the merger at ~10.
- Soften 'ceased to be an aging company within about six months.' On the day of the failure the company said the opposite — the press release subheadline reads 'Company stops further development of clinically symptomatic respiratory illness indication but continues development of RTB101 in other aging-related diseases, including Parkinson's disease' — and it was still sponsoring an RTB101 aging/COVID trial (NCT04409327) that ran from July to December 2020. Say the pivot away from aging was announced at ~5.5 months and completed at the merger close.
- Strengthen and correct the phase 2b caliber statement. Both analyses were PRESPECIFIED (the paper: 'Two different analyses of the key efficacy endpoints were prespecified'), so do not call the second one post-hoc. But the true caliber problem is larger than a 90% CI: the first analysis was a fixed-sequence gatekeeping test whose first gate was RTB101 + everolimus, so when that gate failed the RTB101 10 mg once-daily comparison was never formally tested in the hierarchy at all; the winning 0.601 comes from a DIFFERENT arm, in a POOLED part 1 + part 2 population, in an analysis that 'did not adjust for multiplicity' and used 'a one-sided α of 0·05'. The 90% CI is a direct consequence of that one-sided alpha.
- Quote the phase 3 result as OR 1.07 (95% CI 0.80–1.42), p=0.65. The paper's Results section and Methods use 95% CI and a two-sided α of 0.05 for the phase 3; the abstract's '90% CI 0·80–1·42' for the phase 3 is an internal inconsistency in the paper. Do not present the phase 3 as having also used a 90% CI — the asymmetry between the two trials (phase 2b one-sided/90%, phase 3 two-sided/95%) is the real and more damning point.
- Stop calling RTB101 a rapalog. The paper states 'RTB101 (previously known as BEZ235)' and resTORbio described it as 'an oral, selective, and potent TORC1 inhibitor' — it is not a rapamycin analogue. The only rapalog in the program was everolimus 0.1 mg, used in the phase 2b arm that failed the first gate and absent from the phase 3 entirely. Use 'mTOR-inhibitor field' rather than 'rapalog field', and describe TOR-101 as a selective mTORC1 inhibitor.
- Update Joan Mannick's affiliation. As of 2026 she is Senior Vice President, Chief Medical Officer and Head of Product Development at Altos Labs (a cellular-rejuvenation-reprogramming company), a move announced in early August 2025. Altos' own team page describes Tornado Therapeutics in the past tense: 'from her time as the Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Tornado Therapeutics.' She is not on Cambrian Bio's team page and is not quoted in Cambrian's February 2026 TORnado press release. Do not present her as the person currently driving TOR-101.
- Attribute TOR-101 to Cambrian Bio's 'TORnado platform' rather than to 'Tornado Therapeutics'. Cambrian's February 24, 2026 press release and its current pipeline page both use the platform name and never the company name.
- Add the phase 2b sixth entry criterion and the age band when describing the high-risk population: 'aged 65–85 years with asthma, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), congestive heart failure, were current smokers, or had an emergency room or hospitalisation for an RTI within the past 12 months.' The phase 3, by contrast, had no upper age limit.
- If citing a trial registry for PROTECTOR 1, cite ANZCTR ACTRN12619000628145 (the registration named in the paper). Do not cite the retrospective ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04668352, which lists a start date of 2019-04-15 and New Zealand only, contradicting the publication's May 7, 2018 – July 19, 2019 window and its Australian sites.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Cambrian Bio's live pipeline page contains a second, unmentioned mTORC1 asset: TOR-103, listed at 'Candidate' stage for 'Respiratory Tract Infections' and for 'Oncology'. So the RTI indication that PROTECTOR 1 killed is being carried forward by a successor molecule. If the article's arc is 'the field abandoned the RTI endpoint after PROTECTOR 1', that is not quite what the successor company's own pipeline says.
- The paper's abstract and its Results section disagree on the confidence level for the phase 3 primary result: abstract says 'OR 1·07 [90% CI 0·80–1·42]', Results says 'OR 1·07 [95% CI 0·80–1·42]'. Anyone fact-checking the article against the abstract alone will reach a different conclusion about the phase 3 than one checking the body.
- The ClinicalTrials.gov record for the phase 3 (NCT04668352) reports a start date of 2019-04-15 and lists New Zealand as the only country, directly contradicting the publication's 'May 7, 2018' start and its 15 Australian sites. This is an independent registry source that disagrees with the paper on two facts the article asserts.
- A separate phase 3, NCT04139915 (RTB-101-205, 'PROTECTOR 2'), was registered with a start date of 2019-10-21 and was WITHDRAWN with 0 patients enrolled, primary completion recorded as 2019-11-15 — the exact day PROTECTOR 1's failure was announced. Worth a sentence: a second phase 3 was killed on the spot, which the article does not mention.
- resTORbio did not stop dosing RTB101 in older adults after PROTECTOR 1. NCT04409327 (RTB101 for COVID-19 severity in nursing-home residents aged >=65, sponsor Restorbio Inc.) ran 2020-07-11 to 2020-12-27 and was TERMINATED with 36 of a planned cohort enrolled; NCT04584710 (post-exposure prophylaxis, 60 planned) is still listed as ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING with a February 2021 estimated completion and no posted results. That is a second, quieter human failure of the same molecule that the article's narrative omits.

## V12 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 OVERTURNED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(OVERTURNED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so all verification was done through WebFetch against primary endpoints: NCBI E-utilities (esearch/efetch, returning raw PubMed XML), PubMed Central full text, Europe PMC's REST API, and the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2. I deliberately used the XML/JSON APIs rather than rendered pages so that the fetched content was the document itself rather than a rendered summary, and I re-fetched the two load-bearing numbers (RAPA-EX-01's HbA1c row and the trial's primary endpoint) through two differently-phrased requests to guard against summarizer fabrication; both returned identical spreadsheet-precision values (42.3125, 40.68421053, 1.739615191, 0.029612417), which is consistent with real table extraction rather than invention.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) PubMed XML abstract for PMID 41985884 — RAPA-EX-01, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 17(2), April 2026, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70274, PMC13082878 — including full Methods and Results abstract sections; (2) the PMC full text of the same paper, including Table 6 safety laboratory results and the multiplicity statement; (3) PubMed XML abstract for PMID 38310895, Lancet Healthy Longevity 2024 systematic review, containing the exact string 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies'; (4) PMC full text of the TRIAD design paper, PMID 39951177 / PMC12181551, GeroScience 47(3) 2025, containing the primary-outcome sentence, the 580-dog target with the 6%-lifespan power statement, and the 12-months-dosing-plus-24-months-monitoring design; (5) ClinicalTrials.gov API records for NCT06950385 and NCT03589976; (6) PubMed abstract for PEARL, PMID 40188830, Aging (Albany NY) 2025.

The adversarial search paid off twice. Against (c) I searched the registry specifically for rapamycin/sirolimus trials with mortality, survival, death, disability or incident-disease primary outcomes, and found both a historical counterexample (the MSA futility trial, where the primary endpoint is a disability-inclusive clinical rating scale) and a live one (the Phase 3 eRapa FAP trial, recruiting since July 2025, whose PFS primary endpoint explicitly incorporates death from any cause). Against the 'no long-term placebo-controlled data' claim I found the 24-month renal-transplant sirolimus-vs-placebo programme. Against (b)'s 'only trial in the entire rapamycin literature' superlative, the TRIAD authors' own abstract uses a much more careful formulation ('the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging ... outside of the laboratory in any species').

What remains uncertain: (i) the '~235 of 580 dogs enrolled as of 2026' figure — dogagingproject.org is a client-side-rendered application and every fetch of its pages returned only a logo reference with no text, and I would not attempt to defeat the reCAPTCHA that pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov intermittently served; the only enrollment figure I reached in a primary document is '150 dogs currently enrolled' from the 2025 design paper. (ii) The '~2029' reporting date — the design paper states no completion or reporting date, so this is an unsourced inference. (iii) The word 'only' applied to the Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review — I found no competing independent review in PubMed, but a null search is not proof of uniqueness and I am not treating it as verified. (iv) Whether the double-blind placebo phase of the Global renal-transplant trial extended the full 24 months for all patients: one fetch described the pivotal report as '6 months blinded; data also reported at 1 year' while the two-year report frames the trials as conducted over 24 months with a placebo comparator; the >12-month point stands but the exact blinding window should be checked against the Transplantation 2001 paper before the article leans hard on it.

- **(a) RAPA-EX-01 design facts: 40 sedentary adults 65-85, mean 72.2 y, 47.5% female, randomised 1:1 to sirolimus 6 mg once weekly vs placebo for 13 weeks (2026)** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from the PubMed abstract (PMID 41985884, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 17(2), April 2026, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70274, PMC13082878; Stanfield, Leroux, Kaeberlein, Jones, Lucas): 'In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 40 sedentary adults aged 65-85 years (mean 72.2 years; 47.5% female) were assigned (1:1) to sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg or matched placebo once weekly for 13 weeks.' Every design number in the claim matches.

- **(a) 'The trial did not show the hypothesised benefit' / primary endpoint** — `corrected`
  WRONG (as loosely stated): implies a clean null on the primary endpoint. RIGHT: the pre-specified primary endpoint was 'the change in 30-s chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks (intention-to-treat; ANCOVA adjusted for baseline performance, age stratum and sex)'. The ITT result was an adjusted mean difference (sirolimus-placebo) of -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p = 0.089) — NOT statistically significant. Statistical significance appeared only in the two PRE-SPECIFIED sensitivity analyses: complete-case (16 sirolimus, 19 placebo) -2.46 reps (95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045) and per-protocol (15 sirolimus, 16 placebo) -3.44 reps (95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007). So the result is directionally toward HARM, significant only on sensitivity analyses, not a plain null. The authors' own conclusion: sirolimus 'did not enhance, and in sensitivity analyses, it may have modestly attenuated' functional gains.

- **(a) 'Statistically significant increase in HbA1c in the sirolimus arm'** — `corrected`
  The finding is REAL but the caliber is off. Verified twice, independently, from the PMC full text Table 6 (safety laboratory results): HbA1c (mmol/mol) — rapamycin baseline 40.5, Week 13 42.3125; placebo baseline 41.7, Week 13 40.68421053; effect (rapamycin vs. placebo) 1.739615191; 95% CI 0.20142-3.2719; p = 0.029612417. Results text: 'HbA1c (+1.74 mmol/mol; p = 0.030) were slightly elevated compared with placebo.' WRONG framing: 'a statistically significant increase in HbA1c in the sirolimus arm' as if it were a headline safety endpoint. RIGHT: it is a nominally significant BETWEEN-GROUP difference of +1.74 mmol/mol (roughly +0.16 percentage points in NGSP/% units) on a safety laboratory panel, in an exploratory trial in which 'no adjustments were made for multiplicity'; part of the gap comes from placebo HbA1c falling (41.7 to 40.68) as well as sirolimus rising (40.5 to 42.31). It does not appear in the published abstract at all. Also note the trial excluded uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c >= 60 mmol/mol).

- **(a) 'The most important new human rapamycin result... tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly'** — `corrected`
  WRONG: RAPA-EX-01 does not test the central longevity/geroprotection hypothesis. RIGHT: per the Background, it tests the 'cycling hypothesis' — 'Preclinical models suggest alternating activation and inhibition of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) could enhance adaptation to exercise' — in an explicitly 'exploratory trial' of n=40 over 13 weeks with a functional-performance surrogate (30-s chair stand) as primary endpoint. Calling it a direct test of the central pharmacological hypothesis is an overreach; the authors themselves call for 'longer treatment duration or less frequent/lower dosing'.

- **(b) TRIAD has a hard clinical outcome (survival) as its primary endpoint** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from the TRIAD design paper full text (GeroScience 47(3), June 2025, DOI 10.1007/s11357-024-01484-7, PMID 39951177, PMC12181551): 'The primary outcome measure will be survival time from randomization, evaluated in the intention-to-treat subset.' Design: 'parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial'.

- **(b) TRIAD is the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  WRONG as written. RIGHT: TRIAD is the only trial testing rapamycin against BIOLOGICAL AGING with lifespan as the primary endpoint. The paper's own careful wording is 'the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan metrics as endpoints to be performed outside of the laboratory in any species' — 'first ... against biological aging', not 'only in the entire rapamycin literature'. Counterexamples with hard clinical primary endpoints in the rapamycin/rapalog literature: NCT06950385 (Phase 3, randomized, quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled eRapa in FAP, primary outcome 'Progression-free survival (PFS)', PFS definition includes 'Death from any cause; cancer/high-grade dysplasia; major FAP-related surgeries'); NCT03589976 (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled sirolimus in MSA, primary outcome 'Change From Baseline to 48 Weeks in United Multiple System Atrophy Rating Score (UMSARS) Total Score', which includes an activities-of-daily-living and a disability rating component); NCT00137345 (randomized sirolimus vs cyclosporine, composite graft loss/death); NCT00382109 (randomized tacrolimus/methotrexate +/- sirolimus, event-free survival).

- **(b) Target 580 dogs; ~235 enrolled as of 2026; will not report before roughly 2029** — `corrected`
  580 target CONFIRMED verbatim: 'A total of 580 dogs (290 rapamycin-treated and 290 placebo-treated) will be enrolled and randomized ... greater than 80% power to detect as small as a 6% difference in mean total lifespan'. Design duration CONFIRMED: 'Dogs are randomized in equal numbers to receive rapamycin or placebo by mouth once weekly for 12 months, with a subsequent 24-month post-treatment monitoring period, for a total study duration of 36 months.' The '~235 enrolled as of 2026' figure is UNVERIFIED — the only enrollment number I could reach in a primary document is from the design paper itself: 'the 150 dogs currently enrolled' (manuscript written ~2024). dogagingproject.org is a JavaScript-rendered app and returned no text to WebFetch. The reporting date is NOT STATED anywhere in the design paper; '~2029' is an inference from the 36-month per-dog design plus ongoing enrollment, not a sourced figure.

- **(c) NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever used a clinical outcome (mortality, incident disease, disability) as its primary endpoint, and none is currently registered** — `refuted`
  FALSE as written, on both halves. Ever-used: NCT03589976, 'A Single Center Randomized, Double Blind, Placebo-controlled Futility Trial to Determine if Sirolimus is of Sufficient Promise to Slow the Progression of Multiple System Atrophy' (n=47, sirolimus 2-6 mg/day vs placebo, 48 weeks; published Movement Disorders 2022, DOI 10.1002/mds.28923, PMID 35040506) had as its primary endpoint 'Change From Baseline to 48 Weeks in United Multiple System Atrophy Rating Score (UMSARS) Total Score' — a clinical disability/severity scale including an activities-of-daily-living section and a disability rating (UMSARS-4). Currently registered: NCT06950385, 'A Phase 3, Multi-Site, Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of eRapa to Improve Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Familial Adenomatous Polyposis', status RECRUITING, started 18 July 2025, primary completion July 2030, n=168, primary outcome 'Progression-free survival (PFS) in high-risk patients with FAP treated with eRapa versus placebo', where PFS explicitly includes 'Death from any cause', cancer/high-grade dysplasia, and major FAP-related surgeries. Beyond these, the registry is full of randomized sirolimus/rapalog trials with overall-survival, event-free-survival and MACE primary endpoints (e.g. NCT00297661, NCT00382109, NCT00137345). The claim survives ONLY if narrowed to 'no human randomised trial of rapamycin FOR AGEING/HEALTHSPAN has used a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint' — and even that narrowed version is strained by NCT01649960 (CARE trial, exercise + low-dose rapamycin in older adults with CAD, n=13, primary outcome measure listed as 'Frailty').

- **(c) The only independent systematic review of human rapamycin ageing evidence found 19 included studies from 18,400 screened** — `confirmed`
  Numbers CONFIRMED verbatim from the abstract of 'Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review', Lancet Healthy Longevity 5(2), Feb 2024, e152-e162, DOI 10.1016/S2666-7568(23)00258-1, PMID 38310895: 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' Two caveats on caliber, not on the numbers: (i) the review covers 'rapamycin and its derivatives (rapalogs)', not rapamycin alone, so '19 studies of rapamycin' overstates it; (ii) I could not verify the word 'only' — that is an unfalsifiable-by-search superlative and I did not find a competing review, but absence of a hit is not proof of uniqueness.

- **(c) There is no long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled human safety data; the longest is PEARL at 48 weeks** — `corrected`
  WRONG as an absolute. RIGHT with a population qualifier. (i) PEARL's 48 weeks is confirmed verbatim: 'This 48-week decentralized, double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04488601) evaluated the long-term safety of intermittent low-dose rapamycin in a healthy, normative-aging human cohort' (Aging (Albany NY) 2025, DOI 10.18632/aging.206235, PMID 40188830). (ii) But PEARL is not uniquely the longest even at 48 weeks: the MSA trial (NCT03589976) dosed sirolimus 2-6 mg/DAY versus placebo, double-blind, for 48 weeks — far higher cumulative exposure than PEARL's intermittent low dose. (iii) More decisively, >1 year double-blind placebo-controlled sirolimus safety data exists in transplant recipients: the worldwide phase III 'Global' trial (PMID 11213073, n=576, sirolimus vs PLACEBO on a cyclosporine/steroid background, double-blind) and its two-year report (PMID 12742466): 'Randomized clinical trials conducted over 24 months and including nearly 1300 renal transplant patients compared the efficacy and safety of two dose levels of sirolimus versus azathioprine (United States) or placebo (Global) comparators.' The defensible statement is: 'there is no long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled safety data in healthy, non-transplant older adults; the longest such trial is PEARL at 48 weeks.'

**修正:**
- Do not write that RAPA-EX-01 'did not show the hypothesised benefit' without stating that the pre-specified ITT primary endpoint (change in 30-s chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks) was NOT statistically significant: adjusted mean difference -2.13 repetitions, 95% CI -4.61 to 0.34, p = 0.089. Statistical significance favouring placebo appeared only in the two pre-specified sensitivity analyses: complete-case -2.46 reps (95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045) and per-protocol -3.44 reps (95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007).
- Restate the HbA1c finding at correct caliber: it is a nominally significant BETWEEN-GROUP difference of +1.74 mmol/mol (95% CI 0.20-3.27; p = 0.030) on the safety laboratory panel — approximately +0.16 percentage points in NGSP units — in a trial where the authors state 'no adjustments were made for multiplicity'. Note that placebo HbA1c fell (41.7 to 40.68 mmol/mol) while sirolimus rose (40.5 to 42.31 mmol/mol), so the gap is not entirely a sirolimus-arm rise. It is not reported in the published abstract.
- Do not describe RAPA-EX-01 as testing 'the central pharmacological hypothesis'. It is an explicitly exploratory n=40, 13-week trial of the mTORC1 'cycling hypothesis' — whether weekly sirolimus enhances adaptation to a home exercise programme — with a functional surrogate as primary endpoint. Attribute it correctly: Stanfield et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026;17(2), DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70274.
- Delete the claim that TRIAD is 'the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint.' Use the authors' own wording instead: TRIAD is 'the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan metrics as endpoints to be performed outside of the laboratory in any species' (GeroScience 2025, DOI 10.1007/s11357-024-01484-7).
- State TRIAD's primary endpoint precisely: 'The primary outcome measure will be survival time from randomization, evaluated in the intention-to-treat subset.' Target enrollment is 580 dogs (290 rapamycin, 290 placebo), powered at >80% to detect as small as a 6% difference in mean total lifespan. Per-dog design is 12 months of once-weekly dosing plus a 24-month post-treatment monitoring period, 36 months total.
- Drop or source the '~235 of 580 enrolled as of 2026' figure. The only enrollment number in a reachable primary document is 'the 150 dogs currently enrolled' in the 2025 design paper (written ~2024). Likewise, no completion or reporting date is stated in the design paper — '~2029' must be flagged as an inference from the 36-month design, not a published projection.
- Delete or rewrite 'NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever used a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint, and none is currently registered.' It is refuted by NCT03589976 (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled sirolimus 2-6 mg/day in multiple system atrophy; primary endpoint 'Change From Baseline to 48 Weeks in United Multiple System Atrophy Rating Score (UMSARS) Total Score', a disability scale; Movement Disorders 2022, DOI 10.1002/mds.28923) and by the currently RECRUITING NCT06950385 (Phase 3 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled eRapa in familial adenomatous polyposis, n=168, primary outcome progression-free survival, whose definition includes 'Death from any cause' and major FAP-related surgeries; started July 2025, primary completion July 2030). The narrowed, defensible version is: 'no human randomised trial of rapamycin FOR AGEING OR HEALTHSPAN has used a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint' — and even that should acknowledge NCT01649960 (CARE trial), whose registered primary outcome measure is 'Frailty'.
- Qualify the systematic review sentence: the Lancet Healthy Longevity 2024 review (DOI 10.1016/S2666-7568(23)00258-1) covers 'rapamycin and its derivatives' (rapalogs), not rapamycin alone. Its verbatim numbers are correct: 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' The word 'only' is an unverified superlative — either drop it or soften to 'the principal independent systematic review'.
- Add the population qualifier to the long-term safety claim: 'There is no long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled safety data in healthy, non-transplant older adults; the longest such trial is PEARL at 48 weeks.' As an unqualified statement it is false — the worldwide phase III Global sirolimus trial randomised 576 renal transplant recipients to sirolimus vs placebo double-blind on a cyclosporine/steroid background, with two-year results reported across ~1300 patients (PMIDs 11213073 and 12742466). Also note the MSA trial matched PEARL's 48 weeks at a much higher dose (2-6 mg/day vs PEARL's intermittent low dose).

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- NCT03589976 — 'A Single Center Randomized, Double Blind, Placebo-controlled Futility Trial to Determine if Sirolimus is of Sufficient Promise to Slow the Progression of Multiple System Atrophy'. Primary outcome measure (verbatim from ClinicalTrials.gov API v2): 'Change From Baseline to 48 Weeks in United Multiple System Atrophy Rating Score (UMSARS) Total Score'.
