### 票 2(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so I worked entirely from primary databases fetched directly: the Europe PMC REST API, the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, and publisher/PMC HTML pulled with curl and parsed locally. That turned out to matter: for the single most load-bearing number in this group (the HbA1c result), two WebFetch summariser passes over the same Europe PMC full-text XML returned flatly contradictory answers — one asserted 'HbA1c was used only as an exclusion criterion. No baseline or endpoint HbA1c results are reported', the other produced a specific quote. Per the fabrication warning I discarded both, downloaded the 174 KB full-text XML with curl, stripped tags locally and grepped it. The HbA1c finding is real: Section 3.6 'Lab Safety Analysis' and the Table 6 raw row give +1.739615191 mmol/mol, 95% CI 0.20142-3.2719, p = 0.029612417. Every quotation in this report was read by me in raw downloaded text, not taken from a fetch summary.

Primary documents reached verbatim: RAPA-EX-01 full text (PMC13082878, PMID 41985884) including its Methods, primary-outcome result, Safety and AEs subsection, Lab Safety Analysis subsection, Table 6 laboratory rows, and full Discussion; the RAPA-EX-01 protocol paper (PMID 39354527, ACTRN12624000790549); the TRIAD design paper full text (PMC12181551, PMID 39951177) including its 'Study outcome measures' and 'Power and sample size calculations' sections; the Lancet Healthy Longev systematic review abstract (PMID 38310895); the PEARL results abstract (PMID 40188830) and preprint; the Lamming 2026 GeroScience review full text via link.springer.com; the Ryave & Coleman J Vet Sci review full text (PMC12520851); and ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API records for NCT04488601, NCT01649960, NCT03373903, NCT04668352, NCT06960928, NCT02724332, NCT06950385, NCT00428064, NCT00133887 and NCT00414440.

(a) survives essentially intact — every design number matched verbatim, the primary endpoint is correctly characterised, and the HbA1c signal is genuine at p = 0.030. Its problems are caliber, not fact: the trial is self-described as exploratory and tested the exercise 'cycling hypothesis', not geroprotection; HbA1c was one of ~30 unadjusted comparisons with no multiplicity correction and is never mentioned again in the discussion; and both arm means stay in or near the normal range. Notably the article understates the negative result — the pre-specified sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo (PP p = 0.007).

(b) and (c) fail on over-broad universals rather than on substance. 'The ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature' and 'NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever' are both refuted by trials I read directly (NCT02724332 with overall survival as primary; NCT00133887 with SCC incidence as primary). The counterexample that genuinely threatens the argument rather than merely the wording is NCT03373903 — a 652-subject randomised placebo-controlled trial in healthy volunteers aged 65+ with a rapalog arm and an incident-disease primary endpoint — because the article cannot count rapalogs when citing the 'rapamycin and its derivatives' systematic review and then exclude them when claiming no clinical-endpoint trial exists.

The 19-from-18,400 figures are exactly correct verbatim; only the word 'only' is wrong. PEARL at 48 weeks is correct, but 'no >1 year placebo-controlled data' is false unscoped (NCT00414440, 24 months, n=431, placebo-controlled).

What remains uncertain: I could not reach any source for TRIAD enrollment of ~235 in 2026 or for a 2029 reporting date. The DAP's TRIAD page (whose Next.js data payload I inspected directly) publishes no counter, its WordPress API returns 403, and the Wayback CDX endpoint was down. The two published figures I did find, 210 (J Vet Sci, September 2025) and 158 (GeroScience 2026, 'as of 2025'), conflict with each other and neither supports 235. Given a 36-month per-dog follow-up and roughly a third of the target enrolled in 2025, a 2029 readout looks optimistic; I have marked both items unreachable rather than guessing. I also confirmed there is no erratum, correction or comment attached to the RAPA-EX-01 record, and that it has been cited exactly once (Lamming 2026), which does not dispute it.

- **(a) RAPA-EX-01 design facts: 40 sedentary adults 65-85, mean 72.2 y, 47.5% female, randomised 1:1 to sirolimus 6 mg once weekly vs placebo for 13 weeks** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the abstract of Stanfield B, Leroux B, Kaeberlein M, Jones J, Lucas R. 'Exercise and Weekly Sirolimus (Rapamycin) in Older Adults: RAPA-EX-01 Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.' J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026;17. PMID 41985884, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70274, PMC13082878: '40 sedentary adults aged 65-85 years (mean 72.2 years; 47.5% female) were assigned (1:1) to sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg or matched placebo once weekly for 13 weeks.' Registration is ACTRN12624000790549 (ANZCTR), not an NCT. Protocol paper: Trials 2024, PMID 39354527. Funding was crowdfunding via Lifespan.io; Kaeberlein (a TRIAD/Dog Aging Project PI) is an author, so this is not a hostile-source negative result.

- **(a) The trial did not show the hypothesised benefit; primary endpoint** — `confirmed`
  Pre-specified primary outcome was 'the change in 30-s chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks (intention-to-treat; ANCOVA adjusted for baseline performance, age stratum and sex).' Primary ITT result: adjusted mean difference (sirolimus-placebo) -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p = 0.089) — not significant, and directionally favouring placebo. If anything the article understates it: the pre-specified sensitivity analyses were significantly WORSE than null — complete-case -2.46 reps (95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045) and per-protocol -3.44 reps (95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007), i.e. suggesting sirolimus blunted training gains rather than merely failing to help.

- **(a) Statistically significant increase in HbA1c in the sirolimus arm** — `confirmed`
  REAL and nominally significant. I read the raw Europe PMC full-text XML myself (not a fetch summary — my first two summariser fetches gave contradictory answers, one of them falsely asserting HbA1c results were not reported). Section 3.6 'Lab Safety Analysis' states verbatim: 'Analysis of safety laboratory parameters revealed several statistically significant but clinically modest shifts in the sirolimus arm (Table 6). Mean corpuscular volume was lower (adjusted difference -2.90 fL; p < 0.001), whereas platelet count (+17.6 x 10^9/L; p = 0.025), alkaline phosphatase (+5.56 U/L; p = 0.012), LDL cholesterol (+0.32 mmol/L; p = 0.036) and HbA1c (+1.74 mmol/mol; p = 0.030) were slightly elevated compared with placebo.' Table 6 raw row: 'HbA1c (mmol/mol) 40.5 42.3125 41.7 40.68421053 1.739615191 0.20142-3.2719 0.029612417' (rapamycin baseline / rapamycin wk13 / placebo baseline / placebo wk13 / effect / 95% CI / p).

- **(a) Caliber: 'most important new human rapamycin result... tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly'; 'metabolic safety signal at exactly the intermittent regimen that is supposed to be metabolically clean'** — `corrected`
  WRONG as framed: this is not a direct test of the central geroprotection hypothesis. RIGHT: the authors call it an 'exploratory trial' and the hypothesis under test was the 'cycling hypothesis' — 'Preclinical models suggest alternating activation and inhibition of mTORC1 could enhance adaptation to exercise' — i.e. whether weekly sirolimus enhances functional gains from exercise. It is a 13-week, n=40 surrogate-endpoint trial of drug-on-top-of-exercise, not of the drug alone. Two further caliber corrections on the HbA1c framing: (i) HbA1c was one of ~30 unadjusted safety-laboratory comparisons; four were nominally significant (MCV, platelets, ALP, LDL) and no multiplicity correction is reported anywhere in the paper; the authors' own characterisation is 'statistically significant but clinically modest', and the discussion/limitations never mention HbA1c at all. (ii) Both arm means sit in or near the normal range (sirolimus 40.5 -> 42.31 mmol/mol; placebo 41.7 -> 40.68), so this is a within-normal-range shift, not incident dysglycaemia. Do not call it 'a metabolic safety signal' without those qualifiers.

- **(b) TRIAD design: primary endpoint is a hard clinical outcome; 580-dog target** — `confirmed`
  Coleman AE, Creevy KE, et al. 'Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD): study design and rationale...' GeroScience 2025;47(3):2851-77. PMID 39951177, DOI 10.1007/s11357-024-01484-7, PMC12181551. Verbatim: 'the primary outcome measure will be survival time from randomization, evaluated in the intention-to-treat subset'; 'A total of 580 dogs (290 rapamycin-treated and 290 placebo-treated) will be enrolled and randomized'; '>80% power to detect as small as a 6% difference in mean total lifespan, with greater than 80% power to detect an 11% difference in survival within the 3-year study timeframe'; 36-month study period with a 1-year treatment period and 7 in-person visits over 3 years.

- **(b) TRIAD is the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  WRONG: flatly false as written. RIGHT: TRIAD is the only trial testing rapamycin AS A GEROPROTECTOR with lifespan as the primary endpoint outside the laboratory. The paper's own claim is precisely scoped and should be quoted instead: 'the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan metrics as endpoints to be performed outside of the laboratory in any species.' Counterexamples I pulled from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, all randomised rapamycin/sirolimus trials with hard clinical primary endpoints: NCT02724332 'Adjuvant Anti-Recurrence Treatment With Rapamycin on Early-stage HCC' (intervention: Rapamycin; RANDOMIZED; N=300 actual; PRIMARY = 'Overall Survival', 3 years); NCT00133887 TUMORAPA 1 (rapamycin, RANDOMIZED, Phase 3, N=77; PRIMARY = 'To assess the incidence of new squamous cell carcinoma in kidney transplant recipients', 5 years); NCT00428064 (Sirolimus, RANDOMIZED, Phase 3, N=408; PRIMARY = 'Equivalence of graft survival at month 12'); NCT00795886 (rapamycin, PRIMARY = 'Number of Participants With Transplant-related Mortality' + 'Two Year Overall Survival'); NCT06950385 (eRapa, Phase 3, RANDOMIZED, QUADRUPLE-masked, placebo-controlled, N=168; PRIMARY = progression-free survival; currently RECRUITING).

- **(b) Enrollment about 235 of 580 as of 2026** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach any primary source stating 235, and the two published sources I did reach disagree with each other and with 235. Ryave J, Coleman A. 'Rapamycin as a potential intervention to promote longevity and extend healthspan in companion dogs.' J Vet Sci, first published 2025-09-19 (PMC12520851), states verbatim: 'At the time of writing, 210 dogs have been enrolled and randomized into the TRIAD RCT.' Lamming DW. 'Bench to bedside: is rapamycin headed for the docTOR?' GeroScience 2026;48(3):4547-4570 (DOI 10.1007/s11357-026-02306-8) states verbatim: 'One hundred fifty-eight animals were enrolled as of 2025, and the study is anticipated to run for 3 years'. The Dog Aging Project's own TRIAD page (dogagingproject.org/triad, Next.js payload inspected directly) carries no enrollment counter at all. Do not print 235 without a citable source; the defensible statement is 'roughly 160-210 of 580 as of 2025, per conflicting published figures'.

- **(b) TRIAD will not report before roughly 2029** — `unreachable`
  No primary source gives a reporting date; neither the design paper nor the DAP site states one. What the design paper does establish is a 36-month per-dog study period. With only ~158-210 of 580 dogs randomised as of 2025 and enrollment still open, last-dog-out is more plausibly 2030 or later, so 2029 is an optimistic floor rather than an expected date. Phrase it as 'not before the end of the decade' rather than asserting 2029.

- **(c) NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever used a clinical outcome (mortality, incident disease, disability) as its primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  WRONG as a universal. RIGHT: no human randomised trial of rapamycin AS A GEROPROTECTOR / for healthy ageing has used a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint. Direct counterexamples with rapamycin itself: NCT02724332 (RANDOMIZED, intervention Rapamycin, N=300 actual, PRIMARY = Overall Survival) and NCT00133887 TUMORAPA 1 (RANDOMIZED Phase 3, rapamycin, PRIMARY = incidence of new squamous cell carcinoma). The counterexample that actually threatens the article's argument, because it sits in an ageing-relevant healthy elderly population, is NCT03373903: 'A Multicenter, Dose-finding Study to Determine if Oral BEZ235 Alone or in Combination With RAD001 Decreases the Incidence of Respiratory Tract Infections in Elderly Subjects' — RANDOMIZED, TRIPLE-masked, placebo-controlled, Phase 2, N=652 actual, healthy volunteers aged 65+, one arm 'BEZ235 plus RAD001 once daily for 16 weeks' (RAD001 = everolimus, a rapalog), PRIMARY OUTCOME = 'The percentage of subjects with 1 or more laboratory-confirmed RTIs through Week 16' — an incident-disease primary endpoint. This is the Mannick-lineage programme (cf. PMID 29997249, Sci Transl Med 2018). Note the scope inconsistency the article must resolve: the systematic review it cites in the very same paragraph is titled 'rapamycin AND ITS DERIVATIVES', so it cannot simultaneously count rapalogs for the evidence base and exclude them from the endpoint claim.

- **(c) None is currently registered** — `corrected`
  Narrowly defensible today but fragile and must be dated. I searched the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API across rapamycin/sirolimus/everolimus x aging/frailty/healthspan/sarcopenia and found no geroscience trial with a clinical primary endpoint — the registered geroscience set is uniformly biomarker/surrogate (PEARL NCT04488601 visceral fat; RESTOR NCT06658093 PK/PD + sICAM-1; NCT06727305 PK/PD; NCT05237687 'phenotypic/functional biomarkers of aging'; NCT07475546 VO2max/cognition/iAge/lean mass; NCT05836025 ovarian reserve). BUT: (i) NCT06950385, a Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled eRapa trial with progression-free survival as primary, is currently RECRUITING; and (ii) two funded geroscience trials with clinical/functional primary endpoints are announced. Per Lamming 2026 verbatim: the ARPA-H PROSPR programme has funded a UT Health San Antonio trial — 'This $38 million randomized, double-blind trial will enroll a total of 726 adults between the ages of 60 and 65, all of whom will take one pill daily, and follow them for at least a year to assess the effects on intrinsic capacity'; and 'the University of Arizona has announced a $12 million study which will conduct a randomized, double-blind trial of rapamycin in adults 65 years of age and older for three years (2 years of treatment and 1-year follow-up). The primary outcomes of this study will be physical function and the transition to frailty, as well as inflammation as assessed by blood levels of IL-6.' I could find no ClinicalTrials.gov registration for either yet. Write 'none registered as of July 2026, though two funded trials with functional/clinical primary endpoints have been announced'.

- **(c) The only independent systematic review found 19 included studies from 18,400 screened** — `corrected`
  The NUMBERS are exactly right; the SUPERLATIVE is wrong. Verbatim from the abstract of Lee DJW, Hodzic Kuerec A, Maier AB. 'Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review.' Lancet Healthy Longev 2024. PMID 38310895, DOI 10.1016/S2666-7568(23)00258-1: 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' WRONG: 'the only independent systematic review of human rapamycin ageing evidence'. RIGHT: it is not the only one — e.g. 'The effect of rapamycin and its analogues on age-related musculoskeletal diseases: a systematic review', Aging Clin Exp Res 2022, PMID 35861940, overlaps the same question. Also note the review covers rapamycin AND rapalogs, and spans both healthy individuals and people with ageing-related diseases, so it is not a pure 'human rapamycin ageing' evidence base.

- **(c) No long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled human safety data; the longest is PEARL at 48 weeks** — `corrected`
  PEARL's 48 weeks is CONFIRMED: 'Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results', Aging 2025, PMID 40188830, DOI 10.18632/aging.206235 — 'This 48-week decentralized, double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04488601)... The primary outcome measure was visceral adiposity (by DXA scan)', which was null (eta_p^2 = 0.001, p = 0.942). But the surrounding claim is WRONG unscoped: >1-year placebo-controlled human mTOR-inhibitor safety data does exist — NCT00414440, 'A Multicenter, Randomized, Placebo-controlled, Double-blind Study on the Efficacy, Safety and Tolerability of Everolimus in Preventing End-stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in Patients With ADPKD', RANDOMIZED, TRIPLE-masked, N=431 actual, primary timepoint Baseline to Month 24. RIGHT: 'there is no placebo-controlled trial longer than one year of rapamycin in healthy, normative-ageing adults; the longest is PEARL at 48 weeks.'

**修正:**
- (a) Replace 'tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly' with an accurate description of what RAPA-EX-01 tested: the authors' own 'cycling hypothesis' — whether once-weekly sirolimus enhances functional adaptation to exercise — in a trial they explicitly label 'exploratory' (n=40, 13 weeks, surrogate functional endpoint). It is not a direct test of geroprotection.
- (a) State the primary endpoint and its result precisely: the pre-specified primary outcome was change in 30-second chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks (ITT, ANCOVA adjusted for baseline, age stratum and sex); the ITT result was an adjusted mean difference of -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p = 0.089) — not significant. Note that the pre-specified complete-case (-2.46 reps; 95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045) and per-protocol (-3.44 reps; 95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007) sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo, i.e. the signal is toward harm to training gains, not mere absence of benefit.
- (a) Report the HbA1c finding with its exact figure and its limits: +1.74 mmol/mol vs placebo (95% CI 0.20 to 3.27; p = 0.030), with the sirolimus arm moving 40.5 -> 42.31 mmol/mol and placebo 41.7 -> 40.68. Add that it was one of roughly 30 unadjusted safety-laboratory comparisons in an n=40 exploratory trial — three others were also nominally significant (platelets +17.6 x10^9/L, p = 0.025; alkaline phosphatase +5.56 U/L, p = 0.012; LDL +0.32 mmol/L, p = 0.036; MCV -2.90 fL, p < 0.001) — that no multiplicity correction is reported, that the authors characterise these as 'statistically significant but clinically modest', and that both arm means remain in or near the normal range. Also note the drug was given on top of an exercise programme, so this is not an isolated test of the regimen.
- (a) Cite the trial correctly: Stanfield B, Leroux B, Kaeberlein M, Jones J, Lucas R, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026;17, PMID 41985884, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70274; registration ACTRN12624000790549 (ANZCTR, not a ClinicalTrials.gov NCT); crowdfunded via Lifespan.io.
- (b) Delete 'the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint' — it is false. Randomised rapamycin trials with hard clinical primary endpoints include NCT02724332 (rapamycin in early-stage HCC, N=300, primary = overall survival), NCT00133887 TUMORAPA 1 (primary = incidence of new squamous cell carcinoma), NCT00428064 (sirolimus, primary = graft survival at 12 months) and NCT06950385 (eRapa Phase 3, primary = progression-free survival). Replace with the design paper's own precise claim: TRIAD is 'the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan metrics as endpoints to be performed outside of the laboratory in any species'.
- (b) Drop the unsourced '235 of 580 as of 2026'. The 580-dog target (290 rapamycin / 290 placebo) is confirmed, but published enrollment figures conflict: 210 enrolled and randomised per Ryave & Coleman, J Vet Sci (published 2025-09-19), versus 'One hundred fifty-eight animals were enrolled as of 2025' per Lamming, GeroScience 2026;48(3):4547-4570. The Dog Aging Project's TRIAD page publishes no count. Write 'roughly 160-210 of a 580-dog target as of 2025, with published figures in conflict'.
- (b) Do not assert a 2029 report date — no source states one. Say instead that each dog is followed for 36 months and that, with enrollment barely a third complete in 2025, results should not be expected before the end of the decade.
- (c) Do not write that NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever used a clinical primary endpoint. Scope it: no human randomised trial of rapamycin AS A GEROPROTECTOR has used a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint. Outside geroscience, NCT02724332 (primary = overall survival) and NCT00133887 (primary = incidence of squamous cell carcinoma) both do.
- (c) Address, rather than omit, NCT03373903: a randomised, triple-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial in 652 healthy volunteers aged 65+, with an arm of BEZ235 plus RAD001 (everolimus, a rapalog) and a primary outcome of 'the percentage of subjects with 1 or more laboratory-confirmed RTIs through Week 16' — an incident-disease primary endpoint in an ageing-relevant population. The article cannot count rapalogs when citing the 'rapamycin and its derivatives' systematic review and then exclude them when claiming no clinical-endpoint trial exists; pick one scope and apply it consistently.
- (c) Date and qualify 'none is currently registered': as of July 2026 no geroscience rapamycin trial with a clinical primary endpoint appears on ClinicalTrials.gov, but NCT06950385 (eRapa Phase 3, PFS primary) is recruiting, and two funded trials with functional/clinical primary endpoints have been announced — the ARPA-H PROSPR trial at UT Health San Antonio ($38M, 726 adults aged 60-65, followed at least a year, primary = intrinsic capacity) and a University of Arizona trial ($12M, adults 65+, 2 years treatment plus 1 year follow-up, primary outcomes physical function and transition to frailty).
- (c) Correct 'the only independent systematic review' to 'the most comprehensive systematic review' or similar — the 19-studies-from-18,400-screened figures are exactly right (Lee, Hodzic Kuerec & Maier, Lancet Healthy Longev 2024, PMID 38310895), but other systematic reviews of the same question exist (e.g. Aging Clin Exp Res 2022, PMID 35861940). Also note the review covers rapamycin and its derivatives, in both healthy people and people with ageing-related diseases.
- (c) Scope the long-term safety claim to healthy ageing: 'there is no placebo-controlled trial longer than one year of rapamycin in healthy, normative-ageing adults; the longest is PEARL at 48 weeks.' Unscoped it is false — NCT00414440 is a randomised, triple-masked, placebo-controlled everolimus trial in 431 patients with a 24-month primary timepoint. Add that PEARL's own primary endpoint (visceral adiposity by DXA) was null (p = 0.942).

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- NCT03373903 (ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API record read directly): randomised, TRIPLE-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2, N=652 actual, healthy volunteers aged 65+, arms include 'BEZ235 plus RAD001 once daily for 16 weeks' (RAD001 = everolimus, a rapamycin derivative), primary outcome 'The percentage of subjects with 1 or more laboratory-confirmed RTIs through Week 16'. This is a rapalog trial in a healthy elderly population with an incident-disease primary endpoint, contradicting (c) under the same broad scope the article's own cited systematic review uses.
- NCT02724332 'Adjuvant Anti-Recurrence Treatment With Rapamycin on Early-stage HCC': official title 'A Randomized Controlled Study...', intervention listed as DRUG: Rapamycin, allocation RANDOMIZED, N=300 actual, status COMPLETED, PRIMARY OUTCOME 'Overall Survival' at 3 years. A human randomised trial of rapamycin with mortality as its primary endpoint — directly contradicts both the (b) 'only trial in the entire rapamycin literature' superlative and the (c) 'never' universal.
- NCT00133887 TUMORAPA 1, Phase 3, RANDOMIZED, intervention rapamycin, primary outcome 'To assess the incidence of new squamous cell carcinoma in kidney transplant recipients' over 5 years — an incident-disease primary endpoint in a randomised rapamycin trial.
- NCT00414440: 'A Multicenter, Randomized, Placebo-controlled, Double-blind Study on the Efficacy, Safety and Tolerability of Everolimus in Preventing End-stage Renal Disease in Patients With ADPKD', RANDOMIZED, TRIPLE-masked, N=431 actual, primary timepoint Baseline to Month 24 — contradicts 'no long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled human safety data' unless scoped to healthy ageing.
- Published TRIAD enrollment figures contradict each other and both contradict the article's '235 as of 2026': Ryave & Coleman, J Vet Sci (2025-09-19) say 'At the time of writing, 210 dogs have been enrolled and randomized into the TRIAD RCT', while Lamming, GeroScience 2026;48(3):4547-4570 says 'One hundred fifty-eight animals were enrolled as of 2025'.
- Lamming DW, GeroScience 2026 (the only article citing RAPA-EX-01 so far) documents two funded, announced rapamycin geroscience trials with clinical/functional primary endpoints — ARPA-H PROSPR (726 adults aged 60-65, at least a year, intrinsic capacity) and a University of Arizona trial (adults 65+, 2 years treatment plus 1 year follow-up, primary outcomes physical function and transition to frailty) — which will make 'none is currently registered' and 'no >1 year data' stale imminently.
- Lamming 2026 also reports an independent metabolic signal in PEARL: 'a small increase in HbA1c for males on the lower dose of rapamycin'. This corroborates the direction of the RAPA-EX-01 HbA1c finding but in the opposite sex and at a lower dose, which argues for treating both as weak, non-replicating signals rather than a consistent metabolic effect.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

METHOD AND LIMITATION UP FRONT: my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the first call, so all verification was done by direct WebFetch against APIs and primary documents — NCBI E-utilities, the Europe PMC REST API (search + fullTextXML), the rendered PMC article HTML, and the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2. That is arguably better for this task than search, but it left one item unreachable (see below). Where a fetch returned a paraphrase rather than document text I re-fetched with a different, narrower prompt and cross-checked; I flag below exactly which strings I saw as raw field content versus summarizer output.

(a) RAPA-EX-01 IS REAL AND I REACHED IT. PMID 41985884, PMC13082878, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026;17(2), doi 10.1002/jcsm.70274, ACTRN12624000790549. The Wiley page returns HTTP 402, but the article is open access via Europe PMC. I pulled the abstractText field raw from the Europe PMC core API — it came back with the intact <h4>Background/Methods/Results/Conclusion</h4> structure, which is the genuine field content, not a summary. All of the article's design numbers match it word for word: 40 participants, 65-85 years, mean 72.2, 47.5% female, 1:1, 6 mg once weekly, 13 weeks. The primary outcome is 30-second chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks; ITT p = 0.089.

THE HbA1c CHECK, WHICH WAS THE CRUX. HbA1c does not appear in the abstract, and the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint truncates mid-table (it cuts off at 'Mean AEs per participant'), so I could not get the table from the XML. I got it from the rendered PMC HTML at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13082878/, and — because of the fabricated-quote and misread-table warning in my instructions — I did it twice with different prompts, the second one explicitly asking which column header each value sits under. Both reads agreed: HbA1c (mmol/mol), rapamycin 40.5 -> 42.3125, placebo 41.7 -> 40.68421053, effect +1.739615191, 95% CI 0.20142-3.2719, p = 0.029612417. I then ran an independent internal consistency check that does not depend on the summarizer: 42.3125 has a denominator of 16 and 40.68421053 has a denominator of 19, which exactly match the complete-case Ns (16 sirolimus, 19 placebo) reported in the abstract. A fabricated row would not carry that arithmetic. So the HbA1c finding is real and nominally significant. What the claim gets wrong is caliber: it is a safety-lab secondary in a trial the authors call exploratory, the paper states verbatim 'As this was an exploratory trial, no adjustments were made for multiplicity', and it sits among ~30 comparisons of which total cholesterol (p=0.004), LDL (p=0.036), ALP (p=0.012), platelets (p=0.025) and MCV (p=3.3e-06) were also nominally significant. The magnitude, 1.74 mmol/mol, is about 0.16 NGSP percentage points.

The claim's biggest problem in (a) is not a number at all — it is 'tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly'. The abstract's Background says the trial assessed 'whether once-weekly sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg enhances or inhibits functional gains from a home-based exercise programme', and both arms did the exercise programme. There is no drug-only arm. It is a drug x exercise interaction trial.

(b) TRIAD. Protocol paper reached in full: PMID 39951177 / PMC12181551, GeroScience 2025. Primary objective is lifespan, target is 580 dogs (290/290), 0.15 mg/kg weekly, 12 months on drug plus 24 months monitoring, >80% power for a 6% mean-lifespan difference. All confirmed. The 'ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as primary endpoint' claim is where I went hunting for refutation and found it easily: a ClinicalTrials.gov API query restricted to randomised sirolimus trials with survival/mortality/rejection primary outcomes returned, among others, NCT02724332 (adjuvant rapamycin in HCC, primary outcome overall survival), NCT00470665, NCT00321906 and NCT00141804. Notably the TRIAD authors themselves never make the article's claim — they say 'first clinical trial of the effects of a pharmacologic intervention on normative aging, with lifespan as the primary endpoint'. That qualifier is doing all the work and the article dropped it.

WHAT I COULD NOT REACH: the '235 of 580 enrolled as of 2026' figure and the '~2029' reporting date. The protocol paper contains neither; it only says recruitment of new clinical sites was ongoing as of February 2025. dogagingproject.org is JavaScript-rendered and returned no body text on any of three fetches. TRIAD has no ClinicalTrials.gov record (query returned an empty studies array), so there is no registry completion date. I am marking this unreachable rather than guessing. The 2029 figure is arithmetically consistent with a 36-month per-dog protocol, but that is inference.

(c) I attacked this hardest, as instructed. The systematic review is real and the numbers are exact: I found it as PMID 38310895, Lee DJW / Hodzic Kuerec A / Maier AB, Lancet Healthy Longevity 2024, and pulled the abstractText raw — 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' Two caveats the article must absorb: the review covers 'rapamycin and its derivatives (rapalogs)', not rapamycin alone, and it is a 2024 paper, so it cannot be the current state of the evidence in a piece written in 2026. 'The only independent systematic review' I could not confirm and would not print; PMID 40778880 (Aging, 2025) reviews the same question.

The absolute no-clinical-endpoint claim is refuted as written. Beyond the historical counterexamples, there is a live one: NCT06236022, sirolimus in KSHV-associated dilated cardiomyopathy, Phase 4, n=276, status RECRUITING, primary outcomes 'Cardiac mortality' and 'Rate of heart transplantation'. That single record falsifies 'none is currently registered'. However — and this matters for the article's actual argument — the ageing-scoped version of the claim survives my attempt to break it. I enumerated every sirolimus/mTOR-inhibitor study on ClinicalTrials.gov carrying aging/ageing/longevity/healthspan terms and read all their primary outcome measures: they are uniformly biomarkers, PK/PD, imaging, function tests or AE counts. The only thing resembling a clinical endpoint is 'Frailty' in NCT01649960, a Phase 1 with n=13. So the article's underlying point is sound; only its wording is indefensible.

PEARL: confirmed at 48 weeks from PMID 40188830's abstract, with visceral adiposity by DXA as the primary outcome and 5 mg / 10 mg weekly dosing (not 6 mg). The 'longest placebo-controlled human safety data' framing needs an ageing qualifier — MILES (NCT00414648) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis ran a 12-month placebo-controlled sirolimus period. I flag honestly that I could NOT reach the MILES primary publication: NEJM is paywalled, my search budget was gone, and I only saw it characterised as 'MILES was a phase III placebo-controlled trial' with its NCT number inside a 2023 secondary paper. I am not treating that as verified; I am treating it as a strongly indicated counterexample the article should check before printing an absolute.

NET: the article's thesis — that human rapamycin evidence is thin, biomarker-bound, short, and that the newest hard-ish human data point is negative — survives. Three specific universal quantifiers ('the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature', 'NO human randomised trial ... ever ... none currently registered', 'the longest is PEARL') are false as written and must be scoped to ageing indications. Two figures (235 enrolled, 2029) are unsourced and should be cut or sourced. And the HbA1c sentence needs its magnitude, its exploratory/no-multiplicity-adjustment status, and its lipid companions.

- **(a) RAPA-EX-01 design: 40 sedentary adults 65-85, mean 72.2 y, 47.5% female, randomised 1:1 to sirolimus 6 mg once weekly vs placebo for 13 weeks** — `confirmed`
  Every design number checks out verbatim against the Europe PMC abstract record for PMID 41985884 / PMC13082878 (J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, 2026;17(2), doi 10.1002/jcsm.70274, ACTRN12624000790549): 'In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 40 sedentary adults aged 65-85 years (mean 72.2 years; 47.5% female) were assigned (1:1) to sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg or matched placebo once weekly for 13 weeks.' Authors: Stanfield, Leroux, Kaeberlein, Jones, Lucas.

- **(a) The trial 'did not show the hypothesised benefit' on its primary endpoint** — `corrected`
  Directionally right but UNDERSTATED, and the primary endpoint must be named. WRONG (as written): a vague 'did not show the hypothesised benefit'. RIGHT: the pre-specified primary outcome was 'the change in 30-s chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks (intention-to-treat; ANCOVA adjusted for baseline performance, age stratum and sex)'. ITT result: adjusted mean difference (sirolimus-placebo) = -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p = 0.089) — not significant. But the two PRE-SPECIFIED sensitivity analyses significantly favoured PLACEBO: complete-case (16 sirolimus, 19 placebo) -2.46 reps (95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045); per-protocol (15 vs 16) -3.44 reps (95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007). So the result is not merely null — it points to harm on the primary functional measure.

- **(a) 'A statistically significant increase in HbA1c in the sirolimus arm'** — `corrected`
  The finding is REAL but the article's caliber is too high. I read the row myself in Table 6 ('Adverse events and laboratory summary') of PMC13082878, twice, from the rendered PMC HTML, with column headers confirmed as Parameter | Rapamycin baseline | Rapamycin Week 13 | Placebo baseline | Placebo Week 13 | Effect (rapamycin vs. placebo) | 95% CI | p. HbA1c (mmol/mol): rapamycin 40.5 -> 42.3125; placebo 41.7 -> 40.68421053; effect +1.739615191; 95% CI 0.20142-3.2719; p = 0.029612417. (Internal consistency check: the week-13 decimals resolve to n=16 and n=19, matching the reported complete-case Ns — the row is genuine, not a fetch artefact.) CORRECTIONS REQUIRED: (i) magnitude is +1.74 mmol/mol, roughly 0.16 percentage points in NGSP % — clinically trivial, and partly driven by the placebo arm's HbA1c FALLING; (ii) it is a safety-laboratory secondary, not the primary or any pre-specified key secondary, and it does not appear in the published abstract; (iii) the paper states verbatim 'As this was an exploratory trial, no adjustments were made for multiplicity', and HbA1c is one of ~30 lab comparisons in that table, several of which were also nominally significant (total cholesterol +0.49 mmol/L, p=0.004; LDL +0.32 mmol/L, p=0.036; alkaline phosphatase p=0.012; platelets p=0.025; MCV p=3.3e-06). Calling out HbA1c alone as 'a metabolic safety signal' without the multiplicity caveat and without the lipid findings is selective.

- **(a) The trial 'tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly'** — `refuted`
  WRONG. RAPA-EX-01 does not test rapamycin monotherapy against ageing. Per the abstract's own Background, it tested the 'cycling hypothesis': 'Preclinical models suggest alternating activation and inhibition of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) could enhance adaptation to exercise ... This exploratory trial assessed whether once-weekly sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg enhances or inhibits functional gains from a home-based exercise programme.' BOTH arms performed a standardised home resistance + endurance programme three times/week; there is no drug-alone arm. It is a drug x exercise interaction trial, n=40, self-described 'exploratory'. It is evidence that weekly sirolimus does not augment (and may blunt) exercise adaptation — not a direct test of the central geroprotection hypothesis.

- **(b) TRIAD design: lifespan as primary endpoint, 580-dog target** — `confirmed`
  Verified against the protocol paper (Lee/Dog Aging Project, GeroScience 2025, PMID 39951177 / PMC12181551, doi 10.1007/s11357-024-01484-7). Verbatim: 'The primary objective of this study is to determine whether once-weekly oral administration of rapamycin increases lifespan in medium-to-large- or large-breed, mature adult or senior companion dogs.' and 'A total of 580 dogs (290 rapamycin-treated and 290 placebo-treated) will be enrolled and randomized.' Also: dose 0.15 mg/kg once weekly; 'once weekly for 12 months, with a subsequent 24-month post-treatment monitoring period, for a total study duration of 36 months'; powered at >80% to detect a 6% difference in mean total lifespan and an 11% difference in 3-year survival.

- **(b) TRIAD is 'the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint'** — `refuted`
  FALSE as written. Rapamycin/sirolimus itself has been the intervention in randomised human trials whose PRIMARY endpoint is mortality or incident disease. From ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 records: NCT02724332 'Adjuvant Anti-Recurrence Treatment With Rapamycin on Early-stage HCC', n=300, primary outcome 'Overall Survival'; NCT00470665, n=460 Phase 3, primary outcome 'First biopsy-confirmed acute rejection, patient death or graft loss in the first 12 months following transplantation'; NCT00321906 sirolimus vs azathioprine in lung transplantation, n=181 Phase 4, primary 'Acute Rejection Rate at 12 Months'; NCT00141804, n=190 Phase 3, primary includes 'graft failure at month 12'. The TRIAD paper itself makes only the narrow, correct claim: TRIAD 'will be the first clinical trial of the effects of a pharmacologic intervention on normative aging, with lifespan as the primary endpoint and functional measures of aging as secondary endpoints' and 'the first rigorous test of a pharmacologic intervention against biological aging with lifespan and healthspan metrics as endpoints to be performed outside of the laboratory in any species.' Note also TRIAD is a DOG trial, so it cannot be 'the only trial in the rapamycin literature' with a hard endpoint under any reading that includes humans.

- **(b) 'Enrollment was about 235 of a 580-dog target as of 2026' and 'will not report before roughly 2029'** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach any primary source for either figure. The February 2025 protocol paper (PMC12181551) gives the 580 target and states only that 'at the time of writing, recruitment of new clinical sites is ongoing'; it contains no enrollment-to-date count and no projected completion or reporting date. dogagingproject.org is a JavaScript-rendered site and returned no text content on three separate fetches (/triad, /triad/, /blog). TRIAD is not on ClinicalTrials.gov (a query for it returned an empty studies array), so there is no registry record to read a completion date off. My WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could look for a news/annual-report source. The ~2029 date is at least ARITHMETICALLY consistent with the protocol (36-month per-dog duration from a 2025-26 enrollment window), but that is an inference, not a sourced fact. Do not print 235 or 2029 as verified without an independent source.

- **(c) 'The only independent systematic review of human rapamycin ageing evidence found 19 included studies from 18,400 screened'** — `corrected`
  The NUMBERS are confirmed verbatim; the DESCRIPTION is not. Source: Lee DJW, Hodzic Kuerec A, Maier AB, 'Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review', The Lancet Healthy Longevity, 2024 (PMID 38310895). Verbatim: 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' CORRECTIONS: (i) it is a review of 'rapamycin and its derivatives (rapalogs)', NOT rapamycin alone — so several of the 19 studies are everolimus/rapalog studies, which weakens using it as a count of the rapamycin evidence base; (ii) it is a 2024 publication and therefore PREDATES both the PEARL results paper (2025) and RAPA-EX-01 (2026) — the article should not present it as current; (iii) 'the only independent systematic review' is unverified and likely overstated: at minimum PMID 40778880, 'What is the clinical evidence to support off-label rapamycin therapy in healthy adults?' (Aging, 2025), reviews the same evidence base. Also worth quoting from the same review: it reported 'increased numbers of infections and increases in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides in individuals with ageing-related diseases' — lipids, not HbA1c.

- **(c) 'NO human randomised trial of rapamycin has ever used a clinical outcome (mortality, incident disease, disability) as its primary endpoint, and none is currently registered'** — `refuted`
  FALSE as literally written, on both halves. 'Ever': see the trials listed under (b) — e.g. NCT02724332 (adjuvant rapamycin in early-stage HCC, n=300) with primary outcome 'Overall Survival'. 'None currently registered': NCT06236022, 'The Effects of Sirolimus in Patients With Dilated Cardiomyopathy Infected With Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Virus', Phase 4, n=276, status RECRUITING, primary outcomes 'Cardiac mortality' and 'Rate of heart transplantation' — a currently-recruiting randomised human sirolimus trial with a mortality primary endpoint. THE DEFENSIBLE VERSION, which my own sweep supports: within AGEING/geroscience indications, no human rapamycin trial uses a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint. I pulled every sirolimus/mTOR-inhibitor study on ClinicalTrials.gov tagged aging/ageing/longevity/healthspan; the primary endpoints are exclusively biomarkers, PK/PD, imaging or function tests: visceral fat by DXA (NCT04488601 PEARL), P1NP (NCT07191353, NCT06789900), epigenetic markers (NCT04608448), Cmax/AUC/S6K activity (NCT06727305), PK + p-rpS6 + sICAM-1 (NCT06658093), insulin sensitivity (NCT05835999), ovarian reserve (NCT05836025), 'Phenotypic/functional biomarkers of aging' (NCT05237687), DLTs (NCT05949658), AE counts (NCT07058974). One borderline case the article should know about: NCT01649960 (CARE trial, exercise + low-dose rapamycin in older adults with CAD) lists 'Frailty' as its primary outcome — but it is Phase 1 with n=13.

- **(c) 'There is no long-term (>1 year) placebo-controlled human safety data; the longest is PEARL at 48 weeks'** — `corrected`
  PEARL's 48 weeks is confirmed verbatim (PMID 40188830): 'This 48-week decentralized, double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04488601) evaluated the long-term safety of intermittent low-dose rapamycin in a healthy, normative-aging human cohort. Participants received placebo, 5 mg or 10 mg compounded rapamycin weekly.' Primary outcome was visceral adiposity by DXA, which 'did not change significantly'. BUT the scope claim needs a qualifier. WRONG: 'the longest placebo-controlled human [rapamycin] data is PEARL at 48 weeks'. RIGHT: 'the longest placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin in healthy normative-ageing adults is PEARL, at 48 weeks'. Outside ageing, longer placebo-controlled sirolimus exposure exists — most obviously the MILES trial in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (NCT00414648), a phase III placebo-controlled sirolimus trial with a 12-month double-blind treatment period. CAVEAT: I could NOT reach the MILES primary publication text (NEJM is paywalled and my WebSearch budget was exhausted); I saw it described as 'MILES was a phase III placebo-controlled trial' with registration NCT00414648 only in a secondary 2023 paper surfaced by Europe PMC. Treat the MILES duration as strongly indicated but not verified by me at the primary source. Separately, note that PEARL used 5 mg and 10 mg weekly, not the 6 mg of RAPA-EX-01, so the two are not the same regimen.

**修正:**
- Name RAPA-EX-01's actual primary endpoint: change in 30-second chair-stand repetitions at 13 weeks, ITT ANCOVA adjusted for baseline performance, age stratum and sex.
- Replace 'did not show the hypothesised benefit' with the actual numbers: ITT adjusted mean difference -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p = 0.089), with pre-specified sensitivity analyses significantly favouring PLACEBO — complete-case -2.46 (95% CI -4.87 to -0.06; p = 0.045) and per-protocol -3.44 (95% CI -5.86 to -0.99; p = 0.007).
- Do not describe RAPA-EX-01 as testing 'the central pharmacological hypothesis directly'. It tested the 'cycling hypothesis' — whether weekly sirolimus enhances or inhibits gains from a home exercise programme. Both arms exercised three times weekly; there is no drug-alone arm.
- State the HbA1c result exactly: between-arm effect +1.74 mmol/mol (95% CI 0.20 to 3.27; p = 0.030), i.e. about 0.16 NGSP percentage points, from Table 6 'Adverse events and laboratory summary'.
- Add the multiplicity caveat to the HbA1c finding, quoting the paper: 'As this was an exploratory trial, no adjustments were made for multiplicity.' HbA1c is one of roughly 30 safety-lab comparisons; total cholesterol (+0.49 mmol/L, p = 0.004), LDL (+0.32 mmol/L, p = 0.036), alkaline phosphatase (p = 0.012), platelets (p = 0.025) and MCV (p = 3.3e-06) also differed nominally significantly.
- Label RAPA-EX-01 as an exploratory n=40 trial (registration ACTRN12624000790549, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026, doi 10.1002/jcsm.70274), not a definitive test.
- Delete the assertion that TRIAD is 'the ONLY trial in the entire rapamycin literature with a hard clinical outcome as its primary endpoint'. Use the protocol's own wording instead: TRIAD 'will be the first clinical trial of the effects of a pharmacologic intervention on normative aging, with lifespan as the primary endpoint'. Rapamycin/sirolimus RCTs with mortality or incident-disease primary endpoints already exist (e.g. NCT02724332, overall survival; NCT00470665, acute rejection/death/graft loss; NCT00321906, acute rejection rate).
- Add TRIAD's verified design details: 580 dogs (290 rapamycin, 290 placebo), 0.15 mg/kg once weekly for 12 months plus 24 months post-treatment monitoring (36 months total), powered >80% for a 6% difference in mean total lifespan (GeroScience 2025, doi 10.1007/s11357-024-01484-7).
- Remove or explicitly source the '235 of 580 enrolled as of 2026' and 'will not report before roughly 2029' figures. Neither appears in the TRIAD protocol paper, and TRIAD has no ClinicalTrials.gov record from which a completion date could be read.
- Qualify the no-clinical-endpoint claim to ageing indications: 'No human rapamycin trial in an ageing/geroscience indication uses a clinical outcome as its primary endpoint.' As an unqualified statement about all rapamycin trials it is false, and NCT06236022 (sirolimus in dilated cardiomyopathy, Phase 4, n=276, RECRUITING) currently lists 'Cardiac mortality' as a primary outcome.
- Correct the attribution of the systematic review: it is Lee, Hodzic Kuerec & Maier, Lancet Healthy Longevity 2024, and it covers 'rapamycin and its derivatives (rapalogs)', not rapamycin alone. The verbatim sentence is 'A search across five databases yielded 18 400 unique articles, resulting in 19 included studies.' Drop 'the only independent systematic review' — it is unverified, and it predates both PEARL and RAPA-EX-01.
- Qualify the PEARL duration claim: PEARL (48 weeks, NCT04488601, 5 mg or 10 mg weekly, primary outcome visceral adiposity by DXA) is the longest placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin in HEALTHY NORMATIVE-AGEING ADULTS. Do not claim it is the longest placebo-controlled human rapamycin exposure overall; the MILES trial in lymphangioleiomyomatosis ran a 12-month placebo-controlled treatment period.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The RAPA-EX-01 primary endpoint result is not merely null — both pre-specified sensitivity analyses were statistically significant in favour of placebo (per-protocol -3.44 repetitions, p = 0.007). The article's framing understates its own best evidence.
- RAPA-EX-01 has no rapamycin-monotherapy arm; both groups exercised. Any statement that it 'tests the central pharmacological hypothesis directly' is contradicted by the paper's own stated aim (the 'cycling hypothesis' of mTORC1 activation/inhibition and exercise adaptation).
- The same Table 6 that yields the HbA1c signal also shows significant increases in total cholesterol (p = 0.004) and LDL (p = 0.036) — which match what the Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review already reported ('increases in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides'). The lipid signal is the better-replicated one; singling out HbA1c inverts the weight of evidence.
- ClinicalTrials.gov currently lists NCT06236022 (sirolimus, dilated cardiomyopathy, Phase 4, n=276, RECRUITING) with primary outcomes 'Cardiac mortality' and 'Rate of heart transplantation' — a registered human sirolimus RCT with a mortality primary endpoint, directly contradicting 'none is currently registered'.
- NCT02724332 (adjuvant rapamycin, early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma, n=300) lists 'Overall Survival' as its primary outcome, contradicting the claim that no human rapamycin trial has ever used a clinical outcome as a primary endpoint.
- NCT01649960 (CARE trial, exercise + low-dose rapamycin in older adults with coronary artery disease) lists 'Frailty' as its primary outcome — a functional/clinical rather than biomarker endpoint, in an ageing population. It is tiny (Phase 1, n=13) but the article should not claim the category is empty without addressing it.

## V13 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session (200/200 used), so all verification was done by direct WebFetch and by curl-plus-local-read against raw APIs and the source PDF, which is the more reliable route anyway given the fabrication warning about fetch summarizers.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS ACTUALLY REACHED AND READ MYSELF (not summarizer output):
1. The Bannister 2014 full text. The Wiley version of record is paywalled (HTTP 402 on both onlinelibrary.wiley.com and dom-pubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com), and Unpaywall now reports zero OA locations. Semantic Scholar retained a green-OA pointer to Swansea University's Cronfa repository, but cronfa.swan.ac.uk is currently down (connection refused/timeout from both curl and WebFetch). I recovered the deposit from the Wayback Machine (snapshot 20231025171817), downloaded the PDF, ran pdftotext -layout, and read the extracted text directly with the Read tool. Every quotation in this report was read by me as an exact string in that file; I did not take any quote from a fetch summary. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is the peer-reviewed AUTHOR ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT, self-labelled 'This is the peer reviewed version of the following article... which has been published in final form at [DOI: 10.1111/dom.12354]', not the publisher's typeset version. Its abstract, author list, affiliations, pagination (16:1165-73) and all headline numbers match the PubMed and Crossref records of the published article, so I am confident the Methods text is the published Methods; but I cannot exclude small copy-edits between accepted MS and version of record. The accepted MS title also differs slightly in wording ('people without diabetes' / 'sulfonylurea') from the published title ('non-diabetic controls' / 'sulphonylurea').
2. PubMed record and raw efetch XML for PMID 25041462 (publication types, CommentsCorrections, grants, COI fields), parsed locally.
3. Crossref REST record and Crossref Labs record for 10.1111/dom.12354 (update-to, updated-by, funder), parsed locally.
4. Europe PMC core record raw JSON (grantsList, commentCorrectionList, OA status), parsed locally rather than via summarizer, precisely because an earlier WebFetch summary of the same endpoint needed checking.
5. Europe PMC citation list (245 citing works), scanned locally for critiques and replications.
6. Keys et al. IJE 2022 abstract, verified twice: once via PubMed and once against the raw Europe PMC API abstractText, which matched.
7. Stevenson-Hoare et al. BMC Public Health 2023: the first WebFetch returned a partly paraphrased 'abstract' with mixed quoted and unquoted material, exactly the failure mode warned about, so I discarded it and pulled the OA full-text XML from Europe PMC (PMC10155360) and extracted the abstract element locally. The verbatim text confirmed the substance.

WHAT HELD: the citation and date window, all three sample sizes, the incident-cases design, the log-logistic AFT model and the STR-as-median-survival-time-ratio machinery, the 15% / STR=0.85 (95% CI 0.81-0.90) figure, the median 2.4-year follow-up, the exact five non-adjusted variables, the existence of the 90-day post-regimen-change censoring rule, the AstraZeneca/BMS funding with a BMS employee co-author, and the absence of any retraction, erratum or expression of concern.

WHAT SLIPPED (hence CORRECTED rather than HOLDS): three caliber errors. (a) The non-adjustment reason is 'large proportions of missing data in controls', not data 'missing for' controls - Table 1 actually prints control means for systolic BP, cholesterol, creatinine and BMI, with only HbA1c blank. (b) The 90-day censoring is attributed to metformin patients when it governed both diabetic arms and propagated to controls via 'the censor date of their corresponding case'. (c) Most importantly, the claim says the authors 'named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry that could produce their result artefactually'. They named the asymmetry, but they explicitly declined to apply it to their headline contrast, restricting the missing-covariate concern to the metformin-vs-sulphonylurea comparison and concluding that metformin prophylaxis may benefit people without diabetes. Attributing the artefact concession to them would be a misattribution.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY: (1) I verified Methods/Discussion text against the accepted manuscript, not the Wiley version of record - if the article intends to quote Bannister's Methods verbatim, that caveat should be honoured or a library copy of the typeset PDF consulted. (2) Bannister's own Results text says 14.1 per 1,000 person-years for metformin while its Abstract and Table 2 say 14.4; I could not resolve which the published version carries, though the abstract/table figure of 14.4 is the one that appears in PubMed. (3) I could not fully sweep for critical letters published in Diabetes Obesity and Metabolism itself, since Wiley is paywalled and the WebSearch budget was gone; the Europe PMC citation scan surfaced no letters, but a letter that never got indexed as a citation would be invisible to my method. Everything else in this report I read with my own eyes in the source.

- **Citation, database and window: Bannister et al. 2014, Diabetes Obes Metab, UK CPRD, 2000 to July 2013** — `confirmed`
  Diabetes Obes Metab 2014 Nov;16(11):1165-73, doi 10.1111/dom.12354, PMID 25041462, confirmed via Crossref and PubMed. Full text (author accepted manuscript) Methods, verbatim: 'Data were available to July 2013.' and 'Patients subsequently initiated with sulfonylurea or metformin from 2000 were selected, providing they received treatment for a minimum of 180 days.' Both halves of '2000 to July 2013' check out.

- **N: 78,241 metformin monotherapy, 12,222 sulphonylurea monotherapy, 90,463 matched non-diabetic controls** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim: 'We identified 78,241 subjects treated with metformin, 12,222 treated with sulphonylurea, and 90,463 matched subjects without diabetes.' Table 1 confirms 78,241 metformin / 12,222 sulfonylurea / 78,241 metformin-matched controls. Worth noting for precision: the 90,463 is not one control pool but two 1:1-matched pools (78,241 + 12,222 = 90,463), one per treatment arm.

- **Cohort is INCIDENT type 2 diabetics** — `confirmed`
  Methods verbatim: 'Patients were defined as incident diabetes cases based on a wash-in period of at least 180 days from registration to diagnosis.' Additionally both cases and controls had to survive/persist 180 days: controls required '>=180 days' survival following index date', and the survival analysis start was 'the index date +180 days' treatment exposure.'

- **The ~15% figure is a MEDIAN SURVIVAL TIME RATIO from a log-logistic accelerated failure time (AFT) model, not observed lifespans** — `confirmed`
  Statistical methods verbatim: 'Modeling of survival was not performed with a Cox proportional hazards model because the proportional hazards assumption was violated. We therefore fitted a parametric accelerated failure time (AFT) survival model. Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic models were assessed for goodness of fit using the Akaike information criterion (AIC). The log-logistic model resulted in the best fit in terms of AIC'. And: 'Exponentiation of the beta coefficient gives the ratio between median survival times, known as the survival time ratio (STR), or acceleration factor.' Result verbatim: 'With reference to the observed survival in the group initiated with metformin, the median survival time was 15% lower in controls (STR=0.85; 95% CI 0.81-0.90)'. Two-sided 95% CI, adjusted model, not 90%. The 'not observed lifespans' characterisation is correct and is in fact understated: the UNADJUSTED comparison was null. Results verbatim: crude rates 'were lower in those treated with metformin compared with matched controls (14.1 vs 15.2 per 1,000 person-years respectively; p=0.054)' and the Kaplan-Meier curves 'show that overall there was little discernible difference between metformin cases and non-diabetic controls'. The entire 15% headline is model-dependent.

- **Median follow-up of roughly 2.4 years** — `confirmed`
  Results verbatim: 'Subjects were followed from their index date for an average of 2.8 (median 2.4) years, representing a censored total follow-up period of 503,384 years.' Restated in Study limitations verbatim: 'Our study included a large number of patients followed up for a median of 2.4 years.' Exactly 2.4 (median), 2.8 (mean); analysis hard-truncated at 5.5 years because 'the average duration of first-line monotherapy was three years.'

- **The paper did NOT adjust for BMI, HbA1c, systolic blood pressure, cholesterol or creatinine because those data were missing for the non-diabetic controls** — `corrected`
  The five variables are exactly right; the stated reason is overstated. Paper verbatim: 'Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, creatinine, and BMI were not considered because their large proportions of missing data in controls.' WRONG version: the data 'were missing for the non-diabetic controls' (implies absent). RIGHT version: they were excluded because of 'large proportions of missing data in controls' - i.e. largely, not wholly, missing. Table 1 in fact reports control-group means for systolic BP (136.2 mmHg), total cholesterol (5.1 umol/l), serum creatinine (89.1 umol/l) and BMI (27.4 kg/m2); only HbA1c is blank for controls. In the Discussion the authors phrase it as 'the understandably high percentage of missing data in controls.'

- **Design censored metformin patients 90 days after any regimen change, removing patients whose diabetes progressed** — `corrected`
  The censoring rule is real and quoted correctly in substance, but the scope is misattributed to metformin patients alone. Paper verbatim (Study endpoint): the censor date is 'defined as the earliest of a) the end of the recorded data, b) 90 days from regimen change, or c) five years plus 180 days from the index date.' WRONG version: 'censored metformin patients 90 days after any regimen change.' RIGHT version: this rule applied to ALL diabetic patients, both the metformin and the sulphonylurea arms; and it propagated to the comparison group, because controls were censored at 'the censor date of their corresponding case.' So follow-up ended for a matched control when their case's regimen changed. The claim's substantive point stands: follow-up covers only the monotherapy period and ends shortly after diabetes progression.

- **The authors themselves named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry that could produce their result artefactually** — `corrected`
  Half right: they named the asymmetry, but they never conceded it could produce their result artefactually. NAMED, verbatim: 'Due to the association between type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk, people with type 2 diabetes are likely to be receiving exercise and lifestyle interventions and close monitoring and control of blood pressure and cholesterol levels. Hypertension and hypercholesterolemia are risk factors for cardiovascular disease but are generally asymptomatic. Therefore, these conditions may be less well diagnosed in the control group.' Also verbatim: 'it is likely that some controls had undiagnosed type 2 diabetes.' NOT CONCEDED: they quarantined the unadjusted-confounder problem to the OTHER contrast, verbatim: 'we did not adjust for important covariates because they were unavailable in the non-diabetic subjects... This may impact on the comparison between metformin monotherapy and sulfonylurea monotherapy particularly.' And their Conclusion runs the opposite way, verbatim: 'these findings suggest that there may be a prognostic benefit of metformin prophylaxis in people without diabetes.' So the artefact inference is the article author's, not Bannister et al.'s, and must not be attributed to them.

- **Funding: AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb, with a BMS employee as co-author** — `confirmed`
  Funding/support verbatim: 'This study was supported by AstraZeneca and Bristol-Myers Squibb.' Conflict of interest disclosures verbatim: 'J.M. is an employee of Bristol-Myers Squibb.' Co-author Jayanti Mukherjee's affiliation is 'Global Health Economics and Outcomes Research, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Wallingford, CT, USA'. Crossref funder field records 'AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb'. Two under-stated additions available if wanted: (a) 'Role of the sponsors' verbatim: 'This article has been reviewed by AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb for scientific content'; (b) five of eight authors are tied to Pharmatelligence, verbatim: 'C.B. and C.Ll.M. are contractors of, S.E.H. and S.J.J. are employed by, and C.J.C. is a director of Pharmatelligence, a research consultancy receiving funding from pharmaceutical companies.' Note Europe PMC additionally indexes an MRC grant (1179296) that does not appear in the paper's own funding statement.

- **Has Bannister 2014 ever received a retraction, erratum or expression of concern? (belief: no)** — `confirmed`
  No, as of 2026-07-28. Table 1 does report control-group means for systolic BP (136.2 mmHg), total cholesterol (5.1 umol/l), creatinine (89.1 umol/l) and BMI (27.4 kg/m2); HbA1c alone is blank for controls. - Do not write that the 90-day censoring applied to 'metformin patients.' The rule applied to all diabetic patients in both arms, and it propagated to the comparison group: controls were censored at 'the censor date of their corresponding case.' Correct phrasing: diabetic patients in both arms were censored at the earliest of end of records, 90 days from a regimen change, or five years plus 180 days from index; each matched control was censored at their own case's censor date.
- Do not write that 'the authors themselves named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry that could produce their result artefactually.' Correct phrasing: the authors listed the asymmetry as a limitation - diabetics receive 'close monitoring and control of blood pressure and cholesterol levels' while in controls these asymptomatic conditions 'may be less well diagnosed' - without accepting that it undermines their headline result.

Two caliber slips force CORRECTED rather than HOLDS. First, the 90-day censoring was not metformin-specific: the rule as written applies to diabetic patients in both arms, and matched controls were censored at their corresponding case's censor date, so follow-up was truncated symmetrically. Second, and more consequentially for the article's rhetoric, the authors did NOT name the surveillance/treatment asymmetry as something that could produce their result artefactually. They named it as a limitation ('these conditions may be less well diagnosed in the control group'; 'it is likely that some controls had undiagnosed type 2 diabetes') and then concluded in the opposite direction ('there may be a prognostic benefit of metformin prophylaxis in people without diabetes'). Attributing the artefact inference to them is an overreach that a hostile reader would catch immediately.

I also checked whether the article was under-selling its own case and found it was: the strongest refutation of the 'metformin beats non-diabetics' headline is inside Bannister itself — crude rates 14.4 vs 15.2 with p=0.054, and the authors' own sentence that the Kaplan-Meier curves showed 'little discernible difference between metformin cases and non-diabetic controls'. The 15% survives only under adjustment by a model that omits a 5-point BMI gap and a doubling of cardioprotective drug exposure.

Published abstract (Europe PMC, final version) reads identically: 'adjusted median survival time was 15% lower (STR = 0.85, 95% CI 0.81-0.90) in matched individuals without diabetes'.   Verbatim Statistical methods: 'Modeling of survival was not performed with a Cox proportional hazards model because the proportional hazards assumption was violated. Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic models were assessed for goodness of fit using the Akaike information criterion (AIC). The log-logistic model resulted in the best fit in terms of AIC.' Covariates in the final model: age, modified Charlson comorbidity index, gender, smoking status, prior anti-platelet therapy, prior lipid-lowering therapy, prior anti-hypertensive therapy, index year, study arm. Verbatim: 'the censor date, defined as the earliest of a) the end of the recorded data, b) 90 days from regimen change, or c) five years plus 180 days from the index date.' Two related design features the article should add rather than omit: entry required at least 180 days of treatment, controls required at least 180 days' survival after index, and 'The start date for the survival analysis was defined as the index date +180 days' treatment exposure' — a 180-day landmark that removes early deaths from both arms.

- The paper's OWN unadjusted data do not support 'diabetics on metformin outlive non-diabetics'. Verbatim Results: unadjusted event rates 'were lower in those treated with metformin compared with matched controls (14.1 vs 15.2 per 1,000 person-years respectively; p=0.054)' — i.e. not significant at 0.05 — and the Kaplan-Meier comparison reads 'these survival curves show that overall there was little discernible difference between metformin cases and non-diabetic controls (p=0.037; Figure 2a)'. The entire 15% headline exists only inside the adjusted log-logistic AFT model. That is a sharper indictment than the article currently makes.
- The covariate the model could NOT adjust for is grossly imbalanced in exactly the arm being compared. Table 1: BMI 32.4 kg/m2 (SD 5.9) in the metformin group versus 27.4 (SD 5.0) in matched controls; GP contacts in the prior year 11.3 versus 6.0; prior lipid-lowering therapy 50% versus 20%; prior antihypertensive 66% versus 39%; prior antiplatelet 36% versus 19%; prior MACE 10% versus 6%. A 5 kg/m2 BMI gap and a doubling of prophylactic drug exposure between the compared groups sit entirely outside the adjustment set.
- An independent 2021 critical review reads the same paper as showing NO lifespan benefit. Mohammed et al., 'A Critical Review of the Evidence That Metformin Is a Putative Anti-Aging Drug That Enhances Healthspan and Extends Lifespan', Front Endocrinol 2021 (PMID 34421827, PMC8374068), Table 1, verbatim: 'Diabetic patients taking metformin had more co-morbidities, but their survival rates were comparable to the non-diabetic control group.' and 'Conclusion: Metformin extends healthspan, but not lifespan in humans.' The 'outlive' framing is not universal in the specialist literature.
- The comparison the paper itself flags as least trustworthy is the one most often quoted alongside the 15%. Verbatim Discussion: 'There also remained a difference in outcome between those taking metformin and sulfonylurea, although this needs to be interpreted with caution because we did not adjust for important covariates because they were unavailable in the non-diabetic subjects.' The sulphonylurea arm was also far older (mean 67.8 vs 61.2 years) and sicker (Charlson 2.3 vs 1.9, prior MACE 16% vs 10%), so the 38% figure carries the same unadjusted-confounding problem.
- Follow-up was structurally incapable of measuring lifespan: 'The survival analysis was truncated at 5½ years as the average duration of first-line monotherapy was three years.' Combined with a median follow-up of 2.4 years and censoring 90 days after regimen change, the study measures survival while on first-line monotherapy, not survival to death. The authors say so: patients 'can expect their survival to be at least as good as that of the non-diabetic population WHILST ON THIS SPECIFIC REGIMEN' (emphasis on the clause the longevity field routinely drops), followed by 'We remain unsure about how relative survival changes relative to those without diabetes once glucose-lowering treatment is intensified.'
