IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON WHAT I READ: the full text is the peer-reviewed AUTHOR ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT deposited by Swansea, not the final Wiley typeset PDF. Its own cover states 'This is the peer reviewed version of the following article... which has been published in final form at [DOI: 10.1111/dom.12354].' Every number I checked (78,241 / 12,222 / 90,463; 503,384 person-years; 7,498 deaths; rates 14.4, 15.2, 50.9, 28.7; STR 0.85 CI 0.81-0.90 and 0.62 CI 0.58-0.66) matches the published PubMed abstract exactly, so I am confident the substance is identical. Copy-editing differences do exist between the two versions: the accepted MS spells 'sulfonylurea' and titles the paper '...matched controls without diabetes', while the published version uses 'sulphonylurea' and '...matched, non-diabetic controls'. More materially, the accepted MS conclusion is hedged ('at least as good as') where the published abstract conclusion is assertive ('had longer survival than'). Anyone quoting Methods/Discussion wording verbatim from my report should ideally re-check against the Wiley typeset PDF; I could not reach it.

What is solidly confirmed: the log-logistic AFT model and the fact that the 15% is an exponentiated beta giving a ratio of MEDIAN SURVIVAL TIMES (the STR / acceleration factor) — this is the load-bearing element of the claim and it holds verbatim, including the reason for abandoning Cox ('the proportional hazards assumption was violated'). Median follow-up 2.4 years (mean 2.8) is exact. The non-adjustment list is exactly the five named variables. The 90-day-from-regimen-change censor is verbatim. Study window 'from 2000' with data 'available to July 2013' is verbatim. Funding by AstraZeneca and Bristol-Myers Squibb, Mukherjee as a BMS employee and BMS-affiliated co-author, and sponsor review of the article for scientific content are all verbatim.

What I corrected: three caliber slips. (1) The paper says the five lab/anthropometric variables had 'large proportions of missing data in controls', not that they were missing outright — Table 1 actually prints control means for systolic BP, cholesterol, creatinine and BMI, with only HbA1c blank. (2) The 90-day censor applied to all diabetic patients in both arms, not to metformin patients specifically. (3) The authors name the surveillance/treatment asymmetry but never call it a possible artefact; they conclude in the opposite direction ('Intriguingly, these findings suggest that there may be a prognostic benefit of metformin prophylaxis in people without diabetes'). That third one is the attribution error most likely to draw a fair objection, so I downgraded the group to CORRECTED rather than HOLDS.

Two facts I found that STRENGTHEN the article's critique and that it is currently missing: the survival clock started at index + 180 days and was truncated at 5.5 years; and cases had to receive 180 days of treatment to enter while controls needed only 180 days of survival — an entry asymmetry that is a cleaner statement of the selection problem than the 90-day censor.

Retraction status: verified none, from three independent registries (PubMed CommentsCorrections = CommentIn only; Crossref update-to and updated-by both null; Europe PMC commentCorrectionList = one 'Comment in' to a German news note). Your prior was right.

Remaining uncertainty: (a) I read the accepted manuscript, not the typeset article, as flagged above. (b) My search for a targeted published critique of Bannister returned nothing, but my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task (200/200 used before I ran a single query), so I worked entirely through WebFetch, curl and structured APIs (PubMed eutils, Crossref, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, OpenAIRE, Semantic Scholar, Wayback). The absence of a critique is therefore a weak null, not a demonstrated one — I would not have the article assert that the paper has gone uncriticised.

- **Citation, database and study window: Bannister et al. 2014, Diabetes Obes Metab, UK CPRD, 2000 to July 2013** — `confirmed`
  Reached primary document. Diabetes Obes Metab 2014 Nov;16(11):1165-73, doi 10.1111/dom.12354, PMID 25041462. Methods state verbatim: 'Patients subsequently initiated with sulfonylurea or metformin from 2000 were selected, providing they received treatment for a minimum of 180 days.' and 'Data were available to July 2013.' CPRD ISAC approval reference 12_151RAR. 'Incident' is also correct: 'Patients were defined as incident diabetes cases based on a wash-in period of at least 180 days from registration to diagnosis.'

- **Cohort sizes: 78,241 metformin monotherapy, 12,222 sulphonylurea monotherapy, 90,463 matched non-diabetic controls** — `confirmed`
  Exact, in both the published PubMed abstract and the full text: 'We identified 78,241 subjects treated with metformin, 12,222 treated with sulfonylurea, and matched 90,463 cases without diabetes. This resulted in a total, censored follow-up period of 503,384 years.' Results section adds '78,241 and 12,222 non-diabetic patients were matched to their respective cases' — i.e. 1:1 matching, and 78,241 + 12,222 = 90,463. Total deaths 7,498.

- **The ~15% figure is a MEDIAN SURVIVAL TIME RATIO from a log-logistic accelerated failure time model, not observed lifespans** — `confirmed`
  Fully confirmed verbatim, and this is the single most important element. Methods: 'Modeling of survival was not performed with a Cox proportional hazards model because the proportional hazards assumption was violated. We therefore fitted a parametric accelerated failure time (AFT) survival model. Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic models were assessed for goodness of fit using the Akaike information criterion (AIC). The log-logistic model resulted in the best fit in terms of AIC...' and 'Exponentiation of the beta coefficient gives the ratio between median survival times, known as the survival time ratio (STR), or acceleration factor.' Result: 'With reference to the observed survival in the group initiated with metformin, the median survival time was 15% lower in controls (STR=0.85; 95% CI 0.81-0.90) and 38% lower (0.62; 0.58-0.66) in patients with type 2 diabetes treated with sulfonylurea.' Two-sided 95% CI. Two further constraints the article should carry: the analysis clock started at index date + 180 days ('The start date for the survival analysis was defined as the index date +180 days' treatment exposure') and 'The survival analysis was truncated at 5½ years'. So the 15% is a modelled median-survival-time ratio inside a 5.5-year truncated window — nobody's lifespan was observed.

- **Median follow-up of roughly 2.4 years** — `confirmed`
  Exact, not merely 'roughly'. Results: 'Subjects were followed from their index date for an average of 2.8 (median 2.4) years, representing a censored total follow-up period of 503,384 years.' Repeated in limitations: 'Our study included a large number of patients followed up for a median of 2.4 years.' The article may state median 2.4 years (mean 2.8) as a hard number.

- **Paper did not adjust for BMI, HbA1c, systolic BP, cholesterol or creatinine because those data were missing for the non-diabetic controls** — `corrected`
  The five variables and the direction of the reason are right, but the qualifier is overstated. WRONG as written: the data 'were missing for the non-diabetic controls' (implies wholly absent). RIGHT, verbatim from Statistical methods: 'Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, creatinine, and BMI were not considered because their large proportions of missing data in controls.' — large proportions missing, not wholly missing. Table 1 in fact reports control-group means for systolic BP (136.2), total cholesterol (5.1), serum creatinine (89.1) and BMI (27.4); only HbA1c is blank for the control column. The Discussion repeats it as 'we could not adjust for some parameters due to the understandably high percentage of missing data in controls.' Also note the wording is 'were not considered' as candidate covariates — they were excluded at the candidate stage, not tried and dropped.

- **Design censored metformin patients 90 days after any regimen change, removing patients whose diabetes progressed** — `corrected`
  The 90-day rule is real and verbatim, but attributing it to metformin patients specifically is too narrow. WRONG as written: 'censored metformin patients 90 days after any regimen change.' RIGHT: the rule applied to ALL diabetic patients in both drug arms, and controls inherited their matched case's censor date. Verbatim Study endpoint section: 'For diabetic patients who died, the event date was defined as the patient's date of death provided that this occurred before the censor date, defined as the earliest of a) the end of the recorded data, b) 90 days from regimen change, or c) five years plus 180 days from the index date.' And for controls: 'The censor date here was defined as the earliest of the end of a patient's recorded data, the censor date of their corresponding case, or the end of the 5½ year follow-up period.' The inference that this removes patients whose diabetes progressed is sound and worth keeping, but state it as the article's reading, not as the paper's wording. A stronger, fully verbatim companion point the article should add: cases had to receive 'treatment for a minimum of 180 days' to enter, whereas 'Only individuals with ≥180 days' survival following index date were included as controls' — cases had to survive AND stay on monotherapy for 180 days, controls only had to survive.

- **The authors themselves named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry that could produce their result artefactually** — `corrected`
  The authors do name the asymmetry, but they never characterise it as capable of producing their result artefactually — that is the article's inference, and attributing it to the authors overstates them. WRONG as written: the authors 'named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry that could produce their result artefactually.' RIGHT: the authors name the asymmetry as a limitation while still endorsing a metformin benefit. Verbatim limitations text: 'Symptoms of type 2 diabetes can be mild and people with type 2 diabetes can remain undiagnosed for many years. Therefore, it is likely that some controls had undiagnosed type 2 diabetes. Due to the association between type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk, people with type 2 diabetes are likely to be receiving exercise and lifestyle interventions and close monitoring and control of blood pressure and cholesterol levels. Hypertension and hypercholesterolemia are risk factors for cardiovascular disease but are generally asymptomatic. Therefore, these conditions may be less well diagnosed in the control group.' Immediately after this the Conclusion reads: 'Intriguingly, these findings suggest that there may be a prognostic benefit of metformin prophylaxis in people without diabetes.' Note also Figure 1 of the paper plots use of antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, statins and antiplatelets by group over follow-up — the treatment asymmetry is documented in the paper's own figures, which is a stronger citation than the prose.

- **Funding: AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb, with a BMS employee as co-author** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim and then some. Funding/support: 'This study was supported by AstraZeneca and Bristol-Myers Squibb.' Conflict of interest disclosures: 'J.M. is an employee of Bristol-Myers Squibb.' Affiliation 5 is 'Global Health Economics and Outcomes Research, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Wallingford, CT, USA' (Jayanti Mukherjee). Crossref lists funder 'AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb'. Two additions that sharpen the COI point: (a) the sharpest verbatim fact is the sponsor-review sentence, 'Role of the sponsors: This article has been reviewed by AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb for scientific content. The funding agencies had no other role in the design and conduct of the study...' — the sponsors did review the manuscript for scientific content; (b) five of eight authors are tied to Pharmatelligence, a commercial research consultancy: 'C.B. and C.Ll.M. are contractors of, S.E.H. and S.J.J. are employed by, and C.J.C. is a director of Pharmatelligence, a research consultancy receiving funding from pharmaceutical companies.' Minor caveat: PubMed/Europe PMC additionally index an MRC grant (ID 1179296) against this PMID; the paper's own funding statement names only AstraZeneca and Bristol-Myers Squibb, so phrase it as the paper's stated funding.

- **Bannister 2014 has never received a retraction, erratum or expression of concern** — `confirmed`
  Checked three independent authoritative registries, all agree there is none, as of 2026-07-28. (1) PubMed efetch XML for PMID 25041462: CommentsCorrectionsList contains exactly one entry, RefType='CommentIn'; no ErratumIn, RetractionIn, or ExpressionOfConcernIn. (2) Crossref REST for 10.1111/dom.12354: 'update-to': null and 'updated-by': null — no correction, retraction or EoC has been registered against the DOI. (3) Europe PMC core record: commentCorrectionList holds a single item of type 'Comment in', referencing MMW Fortschr Med 2014 Oct 9;156(17):38, a short German-language news note, not a critique or correction. The paper remains in good standing and is heavily cited (Europe PMC 250, Crossref 329). Your belief that there is no retraction is correct.

**修正:**
- Change 'because those data were missing for the non-diabetic controls' to reflect the paper's actual wording: the five variables were excluded as candidate covariates 'because their large proportions of missing data in controls' — large proportions missing, not wholly missing. Table 1 does report control-group means for systolic BP, total cholesterol, creatinine and BMI; only HbA1c is blank for controls.
- Change 'censored metformin patients 90 days after any regimen change' to state that the 90-day-from-regimen-change censor applied to all diabetic patients in both the metformin and sulphonylurea arms, with controls censored at their matched case's censor date. The exact rule: the censor date was 'the earliest of a) the end of the recorded data, b) 90 days from regimen change, or c) five years plus 180 days from the index date.'
- Do not write that the authors named the surveillance/treatment asymmetry as something 'that could produce their result artefactually.' The authors name the asymmetry (undiagnosed diabetes among controls; hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia 'may be less well diagnosed in the control group'; people with diabetes receiving lifestyle intervention and closer BP/cholesterol monitoring) purely as a limitation, and immediately conclude 'there may be a prognostic benefit of metformin prophylaxis in people without diabetes.' Present the artefact reading as the article's own inference from the authors' stated limitation.
- Add the two design facts that make the 15% figure narrower than usually quoted: the survival clock started at index date + 180 days of treatment exposure, and 'The survival analysis was truncated at 5½ years.' The 15% is therefore a modelled median-survival-time ratio inside a truncated 5.5-year window, not a lifespan difference.
- Add the entry-criterion asymmetry, which is stronger evidence than the 90-day censor alone: metformin/sulphonylurea cases had to receive 'treatment for a minimum of 180 days' to be included, whereas 'Only individuals with ≥180 days' survival following index date were included as controls' — cases had to survive and stay on monotherapy, controls only had to survive.
- State the median follow-up as exactly 2.4 years (mean 2.8), not 'roughly 2.4' — the paper gives 'an average of 2.8 (median 2.4) years' and repeats 'a median of 2.4 years' in the limitations.
- Give the effect estimate with its interval and reference group: with metformin monotherapy as the reference, adjusted median survival time was 15% lower in non-diabetic controls (STR = 0.85, 95% CI 0.81-0.90) and 38% lower in sulphonylurea patients (STR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.58-0.66).
- If the COI point is made, use the strongest verbatim fact: 'Role of the sponsors: This article has been reviewed by AstraZeneca/Bristol-Myers Squibb for scientific content.' Optionally add that five of the eight authors are contractors, employees or a director of Pharmatelligence, 'a research consultancy receiving funding from pharmaceutical companies.' Attribute funding as the paper states it (AstraZeneca and Bristol-Myers Squibb); note PubMed additionally indexes an MRC grant (1179296) not named in the paper's funding statement.
- State plainly that Bannister 2014 carries no retraction, erratum or expression of concern as of July 2026, verified against PubMed CommentsCorrections (CommentIn only), Crossref (update-to and updated-by both null) and Europe PMC (single 'Comment in' to a German news note in MMW Fortschr Med 2014;156(17):38).

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Caution for the article, not a contradiction of the claim: the paper's own unadjusted mortality rates do NOT show diabetics outliving controls in the metformin comparison the way the headline implies — 14.4 vs 15.2 deaths per 1,000 person-years for metformin vs its matched controls is a very small raw gap, while the sulphonylurea comparison is enormous (50.9 vs 28.7). The 15% figure is model-generated from a near-overlapping pair of raw rates, which the article should say.
- Version discrepancy worth knowing: the peer-reviewed accepted manuscript I read concludes more cautiously than the published abstract. Accepted MS: 'our data suggest that patients with diabetes treated with metformin monotherapy can expect their survival to be at least as good as that of the non-diabetic population whilst on this specific regimen' and 'use of metformin ... was associated with survival that was at least as good as that of matched, non-diabetic controls.' The published PubMed abstract conclusion is stronger: 'Patients with type 2 diabetes initiated with metformin monotherapy had longer survival than did matched, non-diabetic controls.' The 'at least as good as' framing, plus the 'whilst on this specific regimen' restriction, undercuts the popular 'diabetics on metformin outlive non-diabetics' reading — and it is the authors' own hedge.
- The paper is not a post-hoc curiosity: comparing metformin patients with non-diabetic controls was a stated study objective and all-cause mortality was the declared study endpoint ('The study endpoint was all-cause mortality'), under CPRD ISAC protocol 12_151RAR. The article should not imply the metformin-vs-non-diabetic contrast was an unplanned subgroup finding; the honest critique is confounding and design asymmetry, not endpoint-fishing.
- I could not find any published letter, formal comment, erratum or failed-replication paper aimed specifically at Bannister 2014. A Europe PMC citation-restricted search (CITES:25041462_MED combined with title terms bias/immortal/comment/reply/letter) returned zero hits. This is a null result from one query strategy, not proof no critique exists; the general time-related-bias literature on metformin observational studies (e.g. Suissa and Azoulay) is extensive but I did not reach a document naming Bannister.

## V14 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start (200/200), so all work was done through WebFetch against primary hosts: NCBI E-utilities (esearch/efetch/elink), Europe PMC REST, and the publisher pages.\n\nPrimary documents reached: (1) Keys et al., Int J Epidemiol 2022;51(6):1886-1898, doi:10.1093/ije/dyac200 — the OUP article page returned actual body text (Methods, Results, Discussion), not just an abstract. (2) Stevenson-Hoare et al., BMC Public Health 2023;23(1):804, doi:10.1186/s12889-023-15764-y — full structured abstract retrieved verbatim from the PubMed XML record.\n\nAnti-fabrication procedure, given the pipeline's prior incident: I fetched the Keys Discussion passage three separate times with differently-worded prompts (an open summary, a demand for verbatim reproduction, and a pure string-presence check that asked only PRESENT/ABSENT per numeral). All three passes returned mutually consistent numbers, and the final pass confirmed the literal presence of '28.4', '28.7', '49.0', '50.9', '24.9', '14.4', '16.9', '15.2', the phrase 'sulfonylurea matched cohort without diabetes', and the full sentence 'Differences in crude mortality rates were only observed in those initiating metformin monotherapy'. The first (summary-style) pass actually omitted the sulfonylurea-control cell entirely and reported only three cells, which is what surfaced the drafting error — the verbatim pass recovered the missing fourth cell.\n\nWhat refutes our draft: the illustrative pair 'sulfonylurea 28.7 vs ~29' is wrong. 28.7 is Bannister's UK sulfonylurea-CONTROL rate, Denmark's is 28.4, and the actual sulfonylurea-TREATED cell (49.0 vs 50.9) was omitted from the draft altogether. Separately, our brief asked what the authors attribute the divergence to — the answer is nothing. Keys explicitly reports that sensitivity analyses showed the two Bannister biases they suspected 'likely had only marginal impact,' and concludes the contrast is 'unlikely to be the result of differences in epidemiological or methodological parameters.' An article that supplies a mechanism on Keys's behalf would misreport the paper.\n\nWhat survives: the load-bearing 'three of four cells replicate, one diverges' forensic is NOT overstated — it is the authors' own framing, in their own sentence, and the corrected grid supports it cleanly. The 7,842 vs 7,842 figure, the 1:1 birth-year-and-sex matching, and the 1 Jan 1996 to 31 Dec 2012 window are all exact. Both Stevenson-Hoare N values are exact and the crossover language is verbatim.\n\nAdversarial checks run: PubMed CommentsCorrectionsList for both PMIDs returned NONE — no erratum, retraction, republication, or published comment/rebuttal attached to either paper as of 2026-07. A PubMed sweep for follow-up literature on the 'survival advantage' question surfaced later records (incl. PMIDs 41893042 and 37540652) but none is registered as a comment on Keys.\n\nRemaining uncertainty, stated plainly: (i) Bannister et al. 2014 (doi:10.1111/dom.12354, PMID 25041462) is paywalled — Wiley returned HTTP 402, Europe PMC shows isOpenAccess 'N' with no PMCID — so the UK-side values 15.2 / 28.7 / 50.9 / 14.4 are verified only as Keys reports them, never against Bannister's own tables. If Keys transcribed any of them wrongly, I could not detect it. (ii) The Stevenson-Hoare BMC full text was not opened; that item rests on the structured abstract, so the twenty-year survival curves and the precise handling of the crossover point are unread. (iii) I did not see Keys's supplementary material, so I cannot rule out that a mechanism for the divergent cell is discussed there rather than in the main Discussion.

- **(a) Keys et al. 2022, Danish national registers 1996-2012, matched cohort 7,842 metformin monotherapy initiators vs 7,842 non-diabetics matched on birth year and sex; metformin initiators did NOT outlive non-diabetics** — `confirmed`
  Every element checks out verbatim. Keys MT, Thinggaard M, Larsen LA, Pedersen DA, Hallas J, Christensen K. 'Reassessing the evidence of a survival advantage in Type 2 diabetes treated with metformin compared with controls without diabetes: a retrospective cohort study.' Int J Epidemiol 2022;51(6):1886-1898, doi:10.1093/ije/dyac200, PMID 36287641. Verbatim from Methods: 'We identified 7842 singletons with incident Type 2 diabetes who were initiated on metformin monotherapy...' and 'For each exposed person, persons without diabetes were sampled without replacement from a risk set matched on birth year and sex, and then assigned the index date of their exposed match.' Table 1 gives 7842 metformin / 7842 matched without diabetes (1:1). Observation window verbatim: 'All eligible individuals were observed from cohort entry on 1 January 1996 until at the latest 31 December 2012.' Matched-cohort result: HR = 1.48 (95% CI 1.32, 1.64) unadjusted, attenuated to HR = 1.33 (95% CI 1.16, 1.54) fully adjusted. The abstract's headline figures (IRR 1.52 -> 1.32) are from the parallel nested case-control design, not the matched cohort - if the article cites 1.52 while describing the 7,842-vs-7,842 matched cohort, that is a design mismatch, though both point the same way. Note the finding is stronger than 'did not outlive': metformin initiators had significantly HIGHER mortality. A separate discordant-twin arm (976 pairs) gave IRR 1.90 -> 1.64. No erratum, retraction, or CommentIn attached to PMID 36287641 as of 2026-07.

- **(b) Forensic: Keys placed own crude mortality rates beside Bannister's; three of four cells replicate almost exactly (e.g. non-diabetic controls matched to metformin 16.9 DK vs 15.2 UK; sulfonylurea 28.7 vs ~29); disagreement localises to ONE cell** — `corrected`
  The STRUCTURE holds and is not overstated - but one of the two illustrative values is wrong. Verbatim from the Discussion (string-presence re-checked for every numeral): 'Interestingly, crude mortality rates per 1000 person-years for the matched cohorts without diabetes were almost identical (metformin matched cohort without diabetes, 16.9 vs 15.2; sulfonylurea matched cohort without diabetes, 28.4 vs 28.7), as well as for sulfonylurea monotherapy initiators (49.0 vs 50.9). Differences in crude mortality rates were only observed in those initiating metformin monotherapy (24.9 in our study vs 14.4 in Bannister et al.).' Ordering throughout is Denmark first, Bannister/UK second. So the four cells are: metformin-matched non-diabetic controls 16.9 DK vs 15.2 UK (replicates); sulfonylurea-matched non-diabetic controls 28.4 DK vs 28.7 UK (replicates); sulfonylurea monotherapy INITIATORS 49.0 DK vs 50.9 UK (replicates); metformin monotherapy INITIATORS 24.9 DK vs 14.4 UK (DIVERGES). WRONG version in our draft: 'sulfonylurea 28.7 vs ~29'. RIGHT version: the 28.x pair is the sulfonylurea-matched CONTROL-WITHOUT-DIABETES cell, and it is 28.4 Denmark vs 28.7 UK - our draft assigned Bannister's 28.7 to Denmark and invented '~29' for the UK, and mislabelled a control cell as the drug arm. The actual sulfonylurea-TREATED cell is 49.0 vs 50.9, which our draft omitted entirely. The 16.9 vs 15.2 example is correct as written. Two further caveats: (i) this is prose in the Discussion, not a formal side-by-side table, and it sits inside a longer replication list (mean age at baseline 60.1 vs 61.2, monotherapy duration 3.0 vs 3.0 years, men 53% vs 57%, prior lipid-lowering 46% vs 50%, prior antihypertensive 64% vs 66.0%, prior antiplatelet 31% vs 36%) - which strengthens rather than weakens the forensic; (ii) these are CRUDE rates with no confidence intervals and no formal heterogeneity test, so 'replicate almost exactly' is the authors' own descriptive characterisation ('almost identical'), not a tested equivalence. The 'one cell' framing is the authors' own: 'Differences in crude mortality rates were only observed in those initiating metformin monotherapy.' ATTRIBUTION - this is where our draft must not overreach: Keys et al. do NOT attribute the divergent cell to any identified cause. They had suspected two biases in Bannister and explicitly rule them out: 'Lastly, various sensitivity analyses suggested that the potential biases present in Bannister et al. (2014), specifically due to informative censoring of metformin initiators and a disadvantageous selection bias into the control group without diabetes, likely had only marginal impact.' Their closing position is 'Our contrasting findings compared with previous research are unlikely to be the result of differences in epidemiological or methodological parameters.' The divergence is left UNEXPLAINED. Any sentence saying Keys 'attributed' it to immortal-time bias, informative censoring, differing diagnostic thresholds, HbA1c screening practice, or CPRD-vs-Danish ascertainment would misreport the paper. One reachability gap: Bannister et al. 2014 (Diabetes Obes Metab 16(11):1165-73, doi:10.1111/dom.12354, PMID 25041462) is paywalled (Wiley returned HTTP 402; not open access in Europe PMC, no PMCID), so the UK-side values 15.2 / 28.7 / 50.9 / 14.4 are verified only as reported inside Keys, not against Bannister's own tables.

- **(c) Stevenson-Hoare et al. 2023, Wales SAIL, 129,140 metformin-treated and 68,563 sulphonylurea-treated type 2 diabetics plus non-diabetic controls; over a longer horizon the metformin advantage crosses over / disappears** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against the PubMed primary record. Stevenson-Hoare J, Leonenko G, Escott-Price V. 'Comparison of long-term effects of metformin on longevity between people with type 2 diabetes and matched non-diabetic controls.' BMC Public Health 2023;23(1):804, doi:10.1186/s12889-023-15764-y, PMID 37131166. Verbatim: 'We searched medical records for Wales, UK, using the Secure Anonymised Information Linkage dataset for type 2 diabetes patients treated with metformin (N = 129,140) and sulphonylurea (N = 68,563). Non-diabetic controls were matched on sex, age, smoking, and history of cancer and cardiovascular disease.' Both N values are exact. Crossover verbatim: 'Within the first three years, metformin therapy showed a benefit over matched controls, but this reversed after five years of treatment,' and over the full twenty-year window 'type 2 diabetes patients treated with metformin had shorter survival time than matched controls, as did sulfonylurea patients.' Two caliber points for the article: the matching variables are sex, age, smoking, cancer and CVD history - NOT birth year and sex as in Keys, so do not describe the two studies as identically matched; and the advantage that reverses is metformin vs NON-DIABETIC CONTROLS. The metformin-vs-sulphonylurea advantage does NOT reverse - 'Metformin patients had better survival than sulphonylurea patients, controlling for age' holds across the full period. Saying 'the metformin advantage disappears' without naming the comparator would blur these. Verified at abstract level from the PubMed XML record; the BMC full text was not separately opened, so the twenty-year survival curves themselves are unread. No erratum, retraction, or CommentIn attached to PMID 37131166 as of 2026-07.

**修正:**
- In the Keys forensic, replace 'sulfonylurea 28.7 vs ~29' with the correct cell: the sulfonylurea-matched CONTROL-WITHOUT-DIABETES rate is 28.4 per 1000 person-years in Denmark vs 28.7 in Bannister's UK cohort. Our draft assigned Bannister's 28.7 to Denmark, invented '~29' for the UK, and mislabelled a non-diabetic control cell as the sulfonylurea drug arm.
- Give the full four-cell grid as Keys reports it (Denmark first, UK second, crude rates per 1000 person-years): metformin-matched non-diabetic controls 16.9 vs 15.2; sulfonylurea-matched non-diabetic controls 28.4 vs 28.7; sulfonylurea monotherapy INITIATORS 49.0 vs 50.9; metformin monotherapy INITIATORS 24.9 vs 14.4. The sulfonylurea-initiator cell (49.0 vs 50.9) is missing from our draft and is the third replicating cell that makes the 'three of four' claim true.
- Do NOT write that Keys et al. attributed the divergent metformin cell to any cause. They explicitly rule out the biases they had suspected in Bannister: 'various sensitivity analyses suggested that the potential biases present in Bannister et al. (2014), specifically due to informative censoring of metformin initiators and a disadvantageous selection bias into the control group without diabetes, likely had only marginal impact.' Their conclusion is that the contrast is 'unlikely to be the result of differences in epidemiological or methodological parameters' — i.e. the divergence is left unexplained. Frame it as an unresolved anomaly, not a diagnosed artefact.
- Label the crude-rate comparison accurately: it is a prose passage in the Keys Discussion (not a published side-by-side table), reports crude rates with no confidence intervals, and applies no formal test of heterogeneity. 'Replicate almost exactly' should be attributed to the authors' own wording ('almost identical'), and the one-cell localisation should be attributed to their sentence 'Differences in crude mortality rates were only observed in those initiating metformin monotherapy.'
- If citing an effect size alongside the 7,842-vs-7,842 matched cohort, use the MATCHED COHORT hazard ratios: HR 1.48 (95% CI 1.32–1.64) unadjusted and HR 1.33 (95% CI 1.16–1.54) fully adjusted. The abstract's IRR 1.52 (95% CI 1.37–1.68) / 1.32 (95% CI 1.16–1.50) come from the parallel nested case-control design; pairing those IRRs with the matched-cohort description is a design mismatch.

BOTTOM LINE: the load-bearing forensic survives — three of four cells align, the disagreement localises to the metformin-initiator cell alone (24.9 vs 14.4), and the framing 'almost identical' is the authors' own. It is NOT overstated. But our worked example mis-assigns 28.7 to the sulfonylurea-treated arm when it is the sulfonylurea CONTROL arm (partner 28.4), and invents a '~29'; the true sulfonylurea-treated pair is 49.0 vs 50.9. 'Reassessing the evidence of a survival advantage in Type 2 diabetes treated with metformin compared with controls without diabetes: a retrospective cohort study.' **新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Keys et al. 2022 has attracted no published rebuttal, correspondence, erratum or correction as of 2026-07. I enumerated all 11 citing works in Europe PMC and separately searched all metformin papers in International Journal of Epidemiology: nothing from Currie, Bannister, Holden or Morgan, and no letter or reply. The reversal stands unchallenged in the literature — but note this is a null finding from citation indexes, not proof that no critique exists.
- Not a contradiction of Keys, but a caution against over-reading it as 'metformin is useless': Shadyab AH et al., 'Comparative Effectiveness of Metformin Versus Sulfonylureas on Exceptional Longevity in Women With Type 2 Diabetes: Target Trial Emulation', J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2025, doi:10.1093/gerona/glaf095 (PMID 40388602), found metformin initiation associated with 30% lower risk of death before age 90 versus sulfonylurea (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56-0.88; death rates 3.7 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years). This is an ACTIVE-COMPARATOR contrast (metformin vs sulfonylurea), which is exactly the contrast that survives in both Keys and Stevenson-Hoare. It says nothing about the metformin-vs-non-diabetic claim that Keys overturns. Also note the propensity-matched analytic sample is only 438 women, so the wide-seeming precision rests on a small matched set; the authors themselves state causality cannot be inferred.
- The same senior authors published a broader retraction-of-enthusiasm review: Keys MT, Hallas J, Miller RA, Suissa S, Christensen K, 'Emerging uncertainty on the anti-aging potential of metformin', Ageing Res Rev 2025, doi:10.1016/j.arr.2025.102817 (PMID 40582648). Verbatim from the abstract: 'These developments generally illustrate an emerging uncertainty in the anti-aging potential of metformin.' Note for the article's independence accounting: this review shares authors with the 2022 Danish study, so it is a continuation of the same critique, not corroboration from an independent group. Stevenson-Hoare (Cardiff/SAIL) IS an independent group.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Method note first: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I started, so I worked entirely through raw HTTP via Bash curl against primary APIs (Europe PMC REST, NCBI eutils, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar) plus WebFetch where curl was blocked. Where I could get raw bytes I extracted and grepped the text myself rather than trusting any summarizer.

DOCUMENTS I REACHED AS RAW TEXT (no summarizer in the loop): (1) Stevenson-Hoare et al. 2023 full text XML from Europe PMC PMC10155360 — downloaded, stripped tags, grepped for every N and every STR; all figures in item (c) are verbatim strings from that file. (2) Bannister et al. 2014 PubMed record via eutils efetch — contains the four unadjusted mortality rates explicitly. (3) Keys, Hallas, Miller, Suissa & Christensen, Ageing Res Rev 2025;111:102817 — open-access PDF from the SDU repository, downloaded and converted with pdftotext; Box 3 and section 3.7 read directly. (4) Keys et al. 2022 PubMed abstract via eutils.

DOCUMENT I COULD NOT REACH AS RAW TEXT: Keys et al. 2022 IJE full text. It is genuinely closed (OpenAlex oa_status 'closed', Unpaywall is_oa false with zero oa_locations, Semantic Scholar openAccessPdf empty, no PMC deposit, no medRxiv preprint, curl to academic.oup.com returns 403, the SDU repository record carries abstract only). I read it through two independent WebFetch renderings of the OUP article page, issued with different prompts.

Given the pipeline's history of fabricated quotes, I did not accept those renderings on trust. I built an external anchor: Bannister's own PubMed abstract, which I fetched myself, states 'unadjusted mortality rates of 14.4 and 15.2, and 50.9 and 28.7 deaths per 1000 person-years for metformin monotherapy and their matched controls, and sulphonylurea monotherapy and their matched controls, respectively.' All four values Keys attributes to Bannister match that raw string exactly, in the correct group order. A hallucinating summarizer reproducing four numbers in correct order against an independently-fetched source is not credible. Second anchor: the 2025 review PDF I extracted myself says metformin-initiator mortality was '43% lower in Bannister et al. than Keys et al.' — 14.4/24.9 gives 42.2%, and the same Box states 'parity of mortality across all other groups, including metformin matched controls, sulfonylurea initiators, and sulfonylurea matched controls', independently confirming the three-of-four-cells structure. Third: the two WebFetch reads returned 24.93 (23.23, 26.64) and 16.86 (15.46, 18.27) with confidence intervals that round consistently to the 24.9 and 16.9 in the Discussion paragraph. I treat the Danish-side values (24.9 / 16.9 / 49.0 / 28.4) as verified to high but not absolute confidence; the UK-side values are verified outright.

VERDICT REASONING. (a) survives intact — every element is verbatim-confirmed, with the only caliber risk being that the famous 1.52 belongs to the case-control arm rather than the 7,842-pair matched cohort. (b) is the reason this is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: the underlying forensic is not overstated — it is real, and our version actually undersells it by omitting the fourth cell and never naming the diverging one — but our sulfonylurea example inverts the country attribution (28.4 is Denmark, 28.7 is the UK, and '~29' does not exist), and our framing implies the authors localised and then explained the divergence when in fact they state twice, across two papers, that no explanation could be found. That distinction matters for how strongly the article can lean on it: the forensic establishes that the disagreement is not a country or control-selection artefact, but it does not establish why Bannister's metformin arm looks the way it does. (c) is CORRECTED on one number: 68,563 is real but comes only from the paper's abstract and is contradicted by its own Results text and Table 1 (68,108); the paper also contradicts itself on whether the reversal occurs at four or five years.

REFUTATION SEARCH. I checked Europe PMC citation lists for both Keys 2022 and Stevenson-Hoare 2023 and PubMed comment/erratum linkage for all three papers. No erratum, correction, retraction, expression of concern, or published rebuttal from the Bannister/Currie group exists for either replication as of 2026-07. Bannister 2014 carries only a German-language 'Comment in' (MMW Fortschr Med 2014). Nothing supersedes these numbers.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY, stated plainly: I have not personally seen the Keys 2022 PDF, so the four Danish crude rates rest on WebFetch rendering corroborated by three independent cross-checks rather than on my own reading of the document. If the article is going to put the exact strings 24.9, 16.9, 49.0 and 28.4 in print as a centrepiece, someone with institutional access to Int J Epidemiol 51(6):1886-1898 should eyeball the Discussion paragraph once. The four Bannister-side values need no such check.

- **(a) Keys et al. 2022, Danish national registers 1996-2012, matched cohort of 7,842 metformin monotherapy initiators vs 7,842 non-diabetics matched on birth year and sex, metformin initiators did NOT outlive non-diabetics** — `confirmed`
  Keys MT, Thinggaard M, Larsen LA, Pedersen DA, Hallas J, Christensen K. Int J Epidemiol 2022 Dec 13;51(6):1886-1898, doi:10.1093/ije/dyac200, PMID 36287641. Every element checks out. Study window verbatim: 'cohort entry on 1 January 1996 until at the latest 31 December 2012'. Cohort verbatim: 'We identified 7842 singletons with incident Type 2 diabetes who were initiated on metformin monotherapy and 976 twin pairs discordant on diabetes where metformin monotherapy was the initiating treatment in the first exposed twin.'   The FORENSIC STRUCTURE IS CORRECT and if anything understated — but one of the two example cells is misstated and the diverging cell is never named. Keys' Discussion reads: 'Interestingly, crude mortality rates per 1000 person-years for the matched cohorts without diabetes were almost identical (metformin matched cohort without diabetes, 16.9 vs 15.2; sulfonylurea matched cohort without diabetes, 28.4 vs 28.7), as well as for sulfonylurea monotherapy initiators (49.0 vs 50.9). Differences in crude mortality rates were only observed in those initiating metformin monotherapy (24.9 in our study vs 14.4 in Bannister et al.).' Order is Denmark-first in every pair. The full 2x2, deaths per 1000 person-years, Denmark vs UK: metformin initiators 24.9 vs 14.4 (+72.9% — THE ONE DIVERGING CELL); metformin controls 16.9 vs 15.2 (+11.2%); sulfonylurea initiators 49.0 vs 50.9 (-3.7%); sulfonylurea controls 28.4 vs 28.7 (-1.0%). Our claim omitted the sulfonylurea-INITIATOR cell (49.0 vs 50.9) entirely, which is one of the three replicating cells, and never states the diverging cell's numbers — which is the whole point. VERIFICATION CHAIN: I could not obtain Keys 2022 as raw document text (closed access, OpenAlex/Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar all report oa_status 'closed'; curl to OUP returns 403). ATTRIBUTION — the load-bearing part our claim did not ask precisely enough: the authors attribute the divergence to NOTHING. The 2025 review is blunter: 'No epidemiological or methodological explanation could be determined for the differential findings across studies, despite extensive efforts.' Do not write that Keys explained the gap; they explicitly could not.

- **(c) Stevenson-Hoare et al. 2023, Wales SAIL, 129,140 metformin and 68,563 sulphonylurea T2D patients plus non-diabetic controls; over a longer horizon the metformin advantage crosses over / disappears** — `corrected`
  Stevenson-Hoare J, Leonenko G, Escott-Price V. 'Comparison of long-term effects of metformin on longevity between people with type 2 diabetes and matched non-diabetic controls.' BMC Public Health 2023, doi:10.1186/s12889-023-15764-y, PMID 37131166, PMC10155360. I pulled the full text XML myself via Europe PMC and grepped the raw text, so these are true verbatim strings. 129,140 metformin CONFIRMED. 68,563 IS NOT SAFE AS A BARE FACT: it appears only in the paper's own abstract ('type 2 diabetes patients treated with metformin (N = 129,140) and sulphonylurea (N = 68,563)'), while the Results text and Table 1 both say 68,108 ('We extracted 129,140 T2D patients treated with metformin and 68,108 T2D patients treated with sulphonylurea'; Table 1 'N individuals 129,140 68,108'). This is an unresolved internal inconsistency in the published paper. Write '~68,000' or cite both figures with the discrepancy noted; do not assert 68,563 flatly. Crossover CONFIRMED, and the exact shape is: Table 2 STR vs matched controls by truncated study length — 1 year 1.237 (p=1.06e-10), 2 years 1.098 (p=2.57e-5), 3 years 1.014 (p=0.435, non-significant), 4 years 0.972 (p=0.049, reversed), 5 years 0.943 (p=3.78e-6), full 20 years 0.819 (p<1e-50). SECOND INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: the abstract says the benefit 'reversed after five years of treatment' while the Results say it 'became non-significant after three years, and reversed after four years (STR = 0.972, p = 0.049)'. If a year is quoted, quote the Results ('non-significant by year 3, reversed at year 4') and note the abstract disagrees. Sulphonylurea over 20 years STR = 0.778. Controls matched 1:1 on 'sex, date of birth (± 1 year), history of cancer, history of CVD, hypertension ..., deprivation index, and smoking status'. CAUTION the article should carry: Keys et al.'s 2025 review argues the SHORT-TERM metformin advantage in this paper is itself an artefact — controls were additionally matched on baseline cardiovascular disease, 'of which 90 % of patients were affected', and using never-diabetic controls there 'results in a selection bias that inflates mortality in the control groups, and is likely responsible for the modest first year effects of both drugs.' So do not present the year-1 STR 1.237 as evidence of a genuine early metformin benefit.

**修正:**
- In claim (b), the sulfonylurea cell is misstated. Replace 'sulfonylurea 28.7 vs ~29' with: sulfonylurea-matched non-diabetic controls, 28.4 per 1000 person-years in Denmark vs 28.7 in the UK. 28.7 is Bannister's UK value, not Denmark's; there is no '~29' figure in either paper.
- State the full 2x2 rather than two examples. Keys et al. 2022, crude mortality per 1000 person-years, Denmark vs Bannister's UK: metformin initiators 24.9 vs 14.4; metformin-matched non-diabetic controls 16.9 vs 15.2; sulfonylurea initiators 49.0 vs 50.9; sulfonylurea-matched non-diabetic controls 28.4 vs 28.7. The claim currently omits the sulfonylurea-initiator cell (49.0 vs 50.9), which is one of the three replicating cells.
- Name the diverging cell explicitly: it is the METFORMIN MONOTHERAPY INITIATOR cell — 24.9/1000 py in Denmark against 14.4/1000 py in the UK, i.e. 73% higher in Denmark, or as Keys' own 2025 review puts it, 'mortality in metformin initiators was 43% lower in Bannister et al. than Keys et al.'
- Do not say the three replicating cells match 'almost exactly' without qualification. The metformin-control cell (16.9 vs 15.2) differs by 11%, versus 1.0% and 3.7% for the two sulfonylurea cells. Keys' own wording is 'almost identical'; use that and note the metformin-control pair is the loosest of the three.
- Correct the attribution. Keys et al. attribute the divergence to NOTHING — they explicitly report they could not explain it. Quote or paraphrase: 'our contrasting findings are unlikely to be the result of differences in methodological or epidemiological parameters' (2022), and 'No epidemiological or methodological explanation could be determined for the differential findings across studies, despite extensive efforts' (Keys et al., Ageing Res Rev 2025;111:102817). Their tests of Bannister's suspected biases moved HR only from 1.48 to 1.39.
- In claim (a), do not attach IRR 1.52 to the 7,842-pair matched cohort. IRR 1.52 (95% CI 1.37, 1.68) is from the nested CASE-CONTROL design. The matched-cohort estimate is HR 1.48 (95% CI 1.32, 1.64) unadjusted, 1.33 (1.16, 1.54) fully adjusted. The twin estimate IRR 1.90 (1.35, 2.67) rests on 976 discordant pairs.
- In claim (c), do not assert 68,563 sulphonylurea patients as a bare fact. That figure appears only in the Stevenson-Hoare abstract; the paper's own Results text and Table 1 both say 68,108. Write '~68,000' or cite both and flag the paper's internal inconsistency.
- In claim (c), if a crossover year is named, use the Results section, not the abstract: the metformin advantage became non-significant at 3 years (STR 1.014, p=0.435) and reversed at 4 years (STR 0.972, p=0.049), reaching STR 0.819 over the full 20 years. The paper's abstract says 'reversed after five years', contradicting its own Results.
- If the article cites Stevenson-Hoare's first-year metformin advantage (STR 1.237), add the caveat that Keys et al. 2025 attribute it to selection bias: controls were matched on baseline cardiovascular disease, which 90% of patients had, and never-diabetic control selection 'is likely responsible for the modest first year effects of both drugs.'
- Add the scale asymmetry so the replication is not oversold: Bannister studied 78,241 metformin and 12,222 sulphonylurea initiators against 90,463 non-diabetic controls in UK CPRD; Keys' matched cohort was 7,842 pairs. Keys is a smaller, differently-designed replication in a different country, not a larger one.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**

This does NOT contradict Keys or Stevenson-Hoare, because it is an active-comparator (metformin vs sulfonylurea) comparison, not a comparison against non-diabetics — the very distinction Keys' one-cell forensic turns on. If the article uses it, it must not be presented as reinstating a general-population survival advantage. Note also the abstract's '438 propensity score-matched women' is implausibly small relative to the reported CIs and looks like a typo in the source.
- Keys et al.'s own 2025 review notes that Stevenson-Hoare's ratio of the metformin to sulfonylurea first-year estimates 'is less than what is usually observed when directly comparing sulfonylureas versus metformin in appropriately designed observational studies', i.e. they regard the Welsh replication's internals as also distorted — so (c) supports (a) directionally but is not an independent clean confirmation.
- Minor discrepancy worth not propagating: the Keys 2025 review reports Stevenson-Hoare's first-year metformin figure as STR = 1.21 and the sulfonylurea figure as 0.99, whereas the primary paper's Table 2 gives 1.237 and 0.991. Cite the primary paper.

## V15 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against literature APIs and primary documents. I reached the primary in full: Lee CG et al., Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782 (PMID 34697033, DOI 10.2337/dc21-1046) is open access at PMC8669534, so the researcher's ADA 403 was not a real obstacle and the article should not be relying on a search-reported abstract.

On fabrication guard: I obtained the Results sentence through three independent routes (Europe PMC core record, the PubMed abstract page, and the PMC full text) and all three returned cardiovascular HR 1.08, never 1.09. I additionally ran an arithmetic consistency check that a fabricating summarizer would be unlikely to satisfy: the by-arm deaths from Table 2 (placebo 143, metformin 152, lifestyle 158) sum to exactly 453, the reported total. The three metformin HRs, the arm sizes summing to 3,234, and the median/IQR all cross-check. I treat the HR string as verbatim-verified; I treat the Table 2 by-arm death counts as well-supported but single-route, since only the PMC fetch surfaced them.

What is right: 3,234 randomized 1996-1999; metformin 850 mg twice daily, n=1,073; median 21 years (IQR 20-21) through 31 December 2018; 453 deaths, cancer 170, CVD 131; all-cause HR 0.99 (0.79-1.25); cancer HR 1.04 (0.72-1.52). The 31% diabetes reduction is confirmed against the 2002 NEJM primary (PMID 11832527) at 95% CI 17-43%, over an average follow-up of 2.8 years.

What is wrong: the CVD HR is 1.08, not 1.09, and the placebo arm was 1,082, not 1,073 (the claim duplicated the metformin n). Both are small but they are exactly the kind of slippage this pass exists to catch.

The serious finding is the population claim. I refused to assert a TAME mismatch from memory and instead reached the TAME design paper (Barzilai et al., Cell Metabolism 2016, PMID 27304507, PMC5943638), which states '3,000 subjects, ages 65-79.' Against DPP's mean age of 50.6 with eligibility from age 25, the assertion that DPPOS treated 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat' is false. TAME's endpoint is also a composite including dementia and non-fatal events, not mortality. Since this sentence is described as load-bearing, it needs rewriting rather than a footnote — the underlying dissociation argument survives, but the identity-of-populations framing does not.

I also flag caliber on 'decisive' and 'demonstrably moves nothing': mortality was an adjudicated secondary analysis, not a pre-specified primary endpoint, and the all-cause CI admits up to a 21% reduction. And the primary itself concedes a dilution problem the article omits — placebo stopped in 2001 while metformin continued unmasked, with provider-prescribed metformin drop-in across all arms.

Supersession check through 2026-07: no erratum or correction is indexed, and no newer DPPOS paper reports updated mortality HRs. The 2025 reanalysis robust to treatment departures (PMID 40857175) reinforces rather than overturns the null.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not independently confirm the Table 2 by-arm death counts from a second route, and I could not verify whether TAME's 65-79 age range has been revised in any protocol update since 2016 — the trial does not appear to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov under a retrievable NCT record, and my search budget was gone. If the article leans hard on TAME's design specifics, that age range should be re-confirmed against a more recent source.

- **Primary source reachability (researcher reported ADA site 403, abstract only)** — `confirmed`
  The primary IS fully reachable and open access. Lee CG, Heckman-Stoddard B, Dabelea D, et al., 'Effect of Metformin and Lifestyle Interventions on Mortality in the Diabetes Prevention Program and Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study,' Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, PMID 34697033, DOI 10.2337/dc21-1046, PMCID PMC8669534. The ADA paywall is bypassable via PubMed Central. The article should cite the primary directly, not a search-reported abstract.

- **DPP randomized 3,234 adults, 1996-1999** — `confirmed`
  Abstract states verbatim: 'From 1996 to 1999, 3,234 adults at high risk for type 2 diabetes were randomized to an intensive lifestyle intervention, masked metformin, or placebo.'

- **Placebo arm n=1,073** — `corrected`
  WRONG: placebo n=1,073. RIGHT: placebo n=1,082. The correct three-arm split is placebo 1,082 / metformin 1,073 / lifestyle 1,079 (sums to 3,234). The claim appears to have copied the metformin n onto the placebo arm.

- **Metformin arm n=1,073 at 850 mg twice daily** — `confirmed`
  Metformin n=1,073 and dose 850 mg twice daily both confirmed against the 2021 paper and the 2002 DPP primary (NEJM, PMID 11832527).

- **Metformin reduced diabetes incidence ~31% vs placebo in the original trial** — `confirmed`
  DPP 2002 (PMID 11832527) states metformin reduced incidence by 'metformin by 31 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 17 to 43 percent)' vs placebo, with lifestyle at 58% (95% CI 48-66). The WINDOW the claim asked to verify: 'The average follow-up was 2.8 years.' The article must state the 2.8-year window, because a 31% relative reduction over 2.8 years is a much weaker statement than an unqualified '31%'.

- **Median ~21 years follow-up, 453 deaths, cancer 170, cardiovascular 131** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'Over a median of 21 years (interquartile range 20-21), 453 participants died. Cancer was the leading cause of death (n = 170), followed by cardiovascular disease (n = 131).' Deaths through 31 December 2018, causes adjudicated by blinded review. By-arm deaths from Table 2 are placebo 143, metformin 152, lifestyle 158, which sums to exactly 453.

- **All-cause mortality HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.79-1.25), metformin vs placebo** — `confirmed`
  Exact match to the primary.

- **Cancer mortality HR 1.04 (95% CI 0.72-1.52)** — `confirmed`
  Exact match to the primary.

- **Cardiovascular mortality HR 1.09 (approximately)** — `corrected`
  WRONG: HR 1.09. RIGHT: HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.70, 1.66). Verbatim from the primary: 'Compared with placebo, metformin did not influence mortality from all causes (HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.79, 1.25]), cancer (HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.72, 1.52]), or cardiovascular disease (HR 1.08 [95% CI 0.70, 1.66]).' The article must also carry the CI, which is very wide.

- **Population described as 'adults with impaired glucose tolerance'** — `corrected`
  Incomplete. Eligibility required IGT AND elevated fasting glucose, not IGT alone: 'fasting plasma glucose 95-125 mg/dL (<=125 mg/dL for American Indians), and 2-h glucose 140-199 mg/dL after a 75-g oral glucose load.' The cohort was also markedly obese (mean BMI 34.0 +/- 6.7) and 68% female.

- **DPP/DPPOS is 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat'** — `refuted`
  This is false and it is the load-bearing sentence, so it matters most. DPP baseline: mean age 50.6 +/- 10.7 years, age eligibility >=25 years, mean BMI 34.0, 68% female, all prediabetic by OGTT. TAME as designed by Barzilai et al. (Cell Metabolism 2016, PMID 27304507, PMC5943638) states verbatim: '3,000 subjects, ages 65-79, in ~14 centers across the U.S.' with the endpoint 'time to a new occurrence of a composite outcome that includes cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality.' A middle-aged obese prediabetic cohort is not the 65-79 geroscience cohort. DPPOS is strong evidence against a mortality benefit in middle-aged prediabetics; it does not test TAME's population, and TAME's composite endpoint (which includes dementia and non-fatal events) is not mortality.

- **Framing: 'decisive randomized evidence', 'demonstrably moves nothing'** — `corrected`
  Overstated caliber for an evidence-grading article. Mortality was NOT a pre-specified primary endpoint of DPP or DPPOS; it was a later adjudicated secondary analysis, and the trial was not powered for it. The all-cause CI (0.79-1.25) is compatible with anything from a 21% mortality reduction to a 25% increase. That is a null result, not a demonstration of no effect. 'Demonstrably moves nothing' asserts proof of the null and should be softened to 'showed no detectable effect, with confidence intervals excluding any large benefit.'

- **Confounding by treatment crossover / dilution** — `corrected`
  The article omits a limitation the primary itself flags. Placebo and lifestyle interventions stopped in 2001 (only ~3 years into a 21-year window) while unmasked metformin continued in the metformin arm, and the authors state: 'Throughout DPP and DPPOS, study participants who developed diabetes in all randomized groups were frequently prescribed metformin as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes by their health care providers,' conceding 'the drop-in use of provider-prescribed metformin in all randomized groups when participants developed diabetes may not have been fully controlled for in our sensitivity analyses.' The 21-year comparison is therefore not 21 years of metformin vs no metformin.

- **Whether the 2021 HRs have been superseded or corrected through 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  No erratum or correction is indexed for PMID 34697033, and no newer DPPOS publication through July 2026 reports updated all-cause or cause-specific mortality HRs. The nearest relevant newer work, Diabetes Care 2025 (PMID 40857175), reanalyzes DPPOS accounting for departures from assigned treatment and REINFORCES the null: 'All of the analytic methods used resulted in similar metformin effect estimates with 95% CIs for hazard ratios including 1.0 (no effect) for all outcomes except for diabetes incidence.' A 2026 post-hoc paper (PMID 41397402) on prediabetes remission and CV outcomes is not a randomized arm comparison and does not bear on this.

**修正:**
- Change the cardiovascular mortality figure from 'HR 1.09' to 'HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.70-1.66)'. Carry the confidence interval, which is wide enough that the CVD result alone is nearly uninformative.
- Change the placebo arm size from n=1,073 to n=1,082. The correct split of the 3,234 randomized is placebo 1,082 / metformin 1,073 / lifestyle 1,079.
- Delete or rewrite the phrase 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat.' DPP enrolled adults with mean age 50.6 years (eligibility >=25), mean BMI 34.0, 68% female. TAME as designed (Barzilai et al., Cell Metabolism 2016, PMID 27304507) plans 3,000 subjects 'ages 65-79.' Replace with something like: 'in a younger, obese, prediabetic population — not the 65-79-year-old cohort TAME targets, though the burden of proof this places on TAME is considerable.'
- Qualify 'decisive' and 'demonstrably moves nothing.' Mortality was not a pre-specified primary endpoint of DPP or DPPOS and the trial was not powered for it. The all-cause CI of 0.79-1.25 is compatible with up to a 21% mortality reduction. State it as 'no detectable mortality signal, with confidence intervals excluding any large benefit' rather than as proof of no effect.
- Attach the time window to the 31% figure: metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% (95% CI 17-43%) over an average follow-up of 2.8 years in the original DPP (NEJM 2002, PMID 11832527), not over the 21-year period.
- Note that TAME's primary endpoint is a composite of cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality — not mortality alone. DPPOS being null on mortality does not by itself predict a null on TAME's composite, and the article should not imply a one-to-one refutation.
- Add the crossover limitation the primary itself concedes: placebo and lifestyle arms stopped in 2001 while unmasked metformin continued in the metformin arm, and participants in all arms who developed diabetes were frequently prescribed metformin by outside providers. The authors state this 'may not have been fully controlled for in our sensitivity analyses.' The 21-year contrast is diluted, which biases toward the null the article is leaning on.
- Describe the cohort correctly: eligibility required impaired glucose tolerance (2-h glucose 140-199 mg/dL) PLUS elevated fasting plasma glucose (95-125 mg/dL), not IGT alone.
- Cite the primary directly — Lee CG, et al., Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, PMID 34697033, PMCID PMC8669534 — rather than a search-reported abstract. The full text is open access at PubMed Central; the ADA 403 is not a real barrier.
- Optionally strengthen the argument by citing the 2025 DPPOS reanalysis (Diabetes Care, PMID 40857175), which used methods robust to treatment departures and still found all hazard ratio CIs including 1.0 for every outcome except diabetes incidence. This is independent support for the dissociation thesis and is more recent.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The population-match assertion is contradicted by the primary sources themselves. DPP baseline mean age is 50.6 +/- 10.7 years with eligibility >=25 years (Diabetes Care 2021, PMC8669534), while the TAME design paper (Barzilai et al., Cell Metabolism 2016, PMC5943638) specifies '3,000 subjects, ages 65-79.' The claim that DPPOS treated 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat' is refuted by a roughly 15-25 year age gap and a very different comorbidity profile.
- TAME's stated primary endpoint is not mortality. The design paper says 'we will measure time to a new occurrence of a composite outcome that includes cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality.' A null on mortality in DPPOS does not directly test a composite that is dominated by non-fatal incident events, and DPPOS never assessed dementia in this analysis at all.
- The 21-year 'metformin vs placebo' contrast is substantially diluted by design and by drop-in. Placebo dosing ceased in 2001 while the metformin arm continued unmasked, and the authors concede that participants in all arms who developed diabetes were 'frequently prescribed metformin as first-line therapy' by outside providers, an effect they admit 'may not have been fully controlled for in our sensitivity analyses.' This cuts against reading the null as a clean demonstration that metformin does nothing.
- The confidence intervals undercut the strength of the claimed demonstration. All-cause 0.79-1.25 and cardiovascular 0.70-1.66 mean the study can exclude a large mortality benefit but cannot exclude a moderate one. Mortality was not a pre-specified primary endpoint and the trial was not powered for it, so 'decisive' overstates what an underpowered secondary analysis can establish.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

My web-search budget was exhausted before I made a single call, so I verified entirely by direct URL fetches against PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC full text, eutils, clinicaltrials.gov and afar.org. That constrains what I could rule out (see the unreachable item) but did not prevent reaching the primaries.

PRIMARY REACHED. The researcher's ADA 403 is bypassable: the paper is Lee CG et al., 'Effect of Metformin and Lifestyle Interventions on Mortality in the Diabetes Prevention Program and Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study,' Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, PMID 34697033, PMCID PMC8669534, free full text at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8669534/. Given the pipeline's history of fabricated quotes, I deliberately fetched the mortality numbers by three independent routes (PMC article page, PubMed record, Europe PMC/eutils record) and required agreement before accepting any figure. The following two sentences came back byte-identical on multiple independent passes and I am treating them as genuinely verbatim: 'Over a median of 21 years (interquartile range 20-21), 453 participants died. Cancer was the leading cause of death (n = 170), followed by cardiovascular disease (n = 131).' and 'Compared with placebo, metformin did not influence mortality from all causes (HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.79, 1.25]), cancer (HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.72, 1.52]), or cardiovascular disease (HR 1.08 [95% CI 0.70, 1.66]).' Lifestyle versus placebo, same paper: all-cause 1.02 (0.81-1.28), cancer 1.07 (0.74-1.55), CV 1.18 (0.77-1.81).

So the numeric spine holds with one digit wrong: cardiovascular mortality is 1.08, not 1.09. Everything else in the mortality set is exact.

Two things I flag as SINGLE-SOURCE and therefore not certified verbatim even though I believe the substance: the Knowler 2002 sentence containing '31 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 17 to 43 percent)' and the DPPOS sentence 'While mortality was not a primary outcome in DPP or DPPOS, mortality was assessed with rigorous adjudication.' Each was seen on one fetch. The underlying facts (31% over average 2.8 years; mortality not pre-specified) are consistent with the trials' design and with incidence rates of 11.0 / 7.8 / 4.8 per 100 person-years, but the article should not quote those strings as verbatim without a second look.

WHERE THE DRAFT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, beyond the 1.08/1.09 slip. First, the placebo arm is 1,082, not 1,073 — the draft duplicated the metformin N. Second, and much more consequential, 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat' is refuted by both trials' own criteria: DPP's mean age at randomization was 50.6 +/- 10.7 with a floor of 25, while TAME proposes 65-79. That is not the same population, and the sentence is doing load-bearing rhetorical work in the article, so it will be the first thing a hostile reader attacks. Third, the draft says 'metformin versus placebo over 21 years' when the masked placebo-controlled phase ended 1 July 2001 — about 3 of the 21 years. After that, placebo stopped, lifestyle was offered to everyone, and metformin continued open-label. Fourth, 'demonstrably moves nothing' is a caliber jump from absence of evidence to evidence of absence; with 131 CV deaths the interval 0.70-1.66 cannot support 'demonstrably.' The all-cause interval 0.79-1.25 can support a much more careful version of the claim, and that is the one to lean on.

I actively hunted for the refutation and did not find one. No erratum or correction notice appears on the PubMed record. No later randomized dataset contradicts the HRs through 2026-07. The strongest thing I found actually cuts the article's way: Diabetes Care 2025 (PMID 40857175, PMCID PMC12451852) re-analyzed DPPOS specifically to handle departures from assigned treatment using ITT, as-treated, instrumental-variable and IPCW estimators, and reports that every 95% CI included 1.0 except for diabetes incidence — which pre-empts the standard 'the null is just non-adherence' rebuttal. Its as-treated mortality point estimate of 1.21 moves toward harm, not benefit. I could NOT retrieve that paper's Supplementary Table 3 (hosted at doi:10.2337/figshare.29591417), so the per-method CIs are unverified and the 1.21 should be cited as the paper's in-text statement with no CI attached.

Residual uncertainty, stated plainly: because I had zero search calls, I could not sweep for critical letters or commentaries that only keyword search would surface, and I could not verify the TAME design against a peer-reviewed protocol paper — the 65-79 age range comes from AFAR's own trial page on a single fetch. The age mismatch conclusion is robust regardless, since DPP's mean age of 50.6 is incompatible with any 65+ floor.

Net: the article's load-bearing dissociation — metformin prevents diabetes, and does not reduce 21-year mortality in the trial population — survives adversarial checking and is well-sourced. What does not survive is the surrounding calibration: one wrong HR digit, one wrong N, an overstated placebo contrast, an overstated 'demonstrably,' and a population-identity claim to TAME that is false.
