  Exact. Verbatim from the primary abstract on three independent fetches: 'metformin did not influence mortality from all causes (HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.79, 1.25])'.

- **Metformin vs placebo cancer mortality HR 1.04 (0.72-1.52)** — `confirmed`
  Exact. Same verbatim sentence: 'cancer (HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.72, 1.52])'.

- **Metformin vs placebo cardiovascular mortality HR ~1.09** — `corrected`
  WRONG: HR 1.09. RIGHT: HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.66. Verbatim from the primary abstract, identical across three independent fetches: 'or cardiovascular disease (HR 1.08 [95% CI 0.70, 1.66])'. The draft's flagged uncertainty was warranted — it is 1.08, and the CI must be printed because 0.70-1.66 is very wide.

- **Framing: 'demonstrably moves nothing downstream in mortality'** — `corrected`
  Caliber slippage from 'no evidence of effect' to 'evidence of no effect.' The primary itself states mortality was not a pre-specified endpoint: 'While mortality was not a primary outcome in DPP or DPPOS, mortality was assessed with rigorous adjudication' (single-fetch quote; substance is consistent with the paper's design section). With only 131 CV deaths across three arms, the CV CI of 0.70-1.66 is compatible with a 30% reduction OR a 66% increase in CV mortality. WRONG: 'demonstrably moves nothing downstream in mortality.' RIGHT: 'showed no reduction in all-cause, cancer, or cardiovascular mortality, in an adjudicated but non-prespecified analysis whose confidence intervals still admit clinically meaningful benefit or harm on the cause-specific endpoints.' The all-cause CI (0.79-1.25) is the tightest and does the most work; lean on that one, not the CV one.

- **Framing: 'metformin versus placebo over 21 years'** — `corrected`
  Overstates the contrast. The masked placebo-controlled phase ENDED 1 July 2001, i.e. after roughly 3 of the 21 years, when diabetes-prevention efficacy was met. Thereafter placebo was discontinued, ALL participants (including the placebo arm) were offered a modified group lifestyle intervention, and only the metformin arm continued open-label metformin. WRONG: 'metformin versus placebo over 21 years.' RIGHT: 'intention-to-treat by original randomized assignment over 21 years, of which only the first ~3 years were masked and placebo-controlled; thereafter placebo was stopped, lifestyle education was offered to all arms, and metformin continued open-label.' This is the single most important caveat the draft is missing, because it is the standard objection a metformin advocate will raise ('the null is dilution, not absence of effect').

- **Framing: 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat'** — `refuted`
  This is not correct and should be struck. TAME proposes to enroll adults aged 65-79 (AFAR: 'between the ages of 65-79', ~3,000 participants, ~6 years, composite of incident age-related disease and death). DPP enrolled adults aged >=25 with a mean age of 50.6 +/- 10.7 years at randomization, 68% female, selected for dysglycemia and overweight rather than for age or for existing age-related disease. A trial with a mean enrollment age of 50 is not 'the exact population' of a trial whose floor is 65. Separately, TAME's endpoint is a composite first-event endpoint over ~6 years, not 21-year cause-specific mortality. RIGHT framing: 'in a younger, dysglycemic population that overlaps only partially with TAME's proposed 65-79 cohort, and on mortality rather than TAME's composite morbidity endpoint.' Also note TAME remains unfunded and not enrolling as of this writing (AFAR is still soliciting donors to launch it), so 'proposes' is the right verb — do not imply it is running.

- **Framing: evidence 'in NON-diabetics'** — `corrected`
  True at randomization only. With placebo-arm diabetes incidence of 11.0 cases per 100 person-years, a large majority of all three arms developed type 2 diabetes during the 21-year follow-up. WRONG: 'randomized human evidence on metformin in non-diabetics.' RIGHT: 'in adults who were non-diabetic at randomization,' with the acknowledgment that most had converted to diabetes long before the mortality endpoints accrued. This matters because it partly explains the null: the arms converge metabolically over time.

- **Whether the 2021 HRs have been superseded or contradicted by anything through 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  Not superseded; independently reinforced. I searched for later DPPOS mortality analyses, corrections, and critical letters and found no erratum and no contradicting randomized dataset. The most relevant newer work is Diabetes Care 2025, 'Analysis of Long-term Follow-up of a Randomized Clinical Trial With Departures From Assigned Treatments: Estimation of Metformin Effects on Diabetes and Its Complications in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study' (PMID 40857175, PMCID PMC12451852), which re-analyzes DPPOS with intention-to-treat, as-treated, instrumental-variable and IPCW methods precisely to address the non-adherence/contamination objection above. Its reported conclusion is that all 95% CIs for hazard ratios included 1.0 for every outcome except diabetes incidence. This is a strong citation for the article because it pre-empts the 'the null is just dilution' rebuttal. One directional note: the paper's text states that for mortality the HR was highest in the as-treated analysis at 1.21 — i.e. the adherence-corrected point estimate drifts toward harm, not benefit.

- **Exact per-method mortality HRs and CIs in the 2025 DPPOS re-analysis** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach these. The per-method mortality hazard ratios live in Supplementary Table 3, hosted separately at doi:10.2337/figshare.29591417, which I was not able to retrieve. I have the paper's in-text characterization (all CIs include 1.0 except diabetes incidence; as-treated mortality HR 1.21) but NOT the verified CI bounds for that 1.21 or for the ITT/IV/IPCW mortality estimates. If the article cites the 1.21, cite it as the paper's in-text statement and do not attach a CI to it. Separately: my web-search budget was exhausted at the start of this task, so I worked entirely through direct URL fetches of PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC and clinicaltrials.gov. I therefore cannot rule out a critical letter or commentary that only a keyword search would have surfaced, though the PubMed record for PMID 34697033 showed no erratum or correction notice.

**修正:**
- Change the cardiovascular mortality hazard ratio from 'approximately 1.09' to 'HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.70-1.66)'. Print the confidence interval — it is wide enough to matter.
- Change the placebo arm size from n=1,073 to n=1,082. Correct arm sizes are: placebo 1,082, metformin 1,073, lifestyle 1,079 (total 3,234).
- State the window for the 31% figure: metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% (95% CI 17-43%) over an average follow-up of 2.8 years in the original DPP (Knowler et al., NEJM 2002;346:393-403). Do not let '31%' float next to '21 years' without making clear they are different time frames.
- Cite the primary correctly and by date: Lee CG et al., Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, doi:10.2337/dc21-1046, PMID 34697033. Free full text at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8669534/ — the ADA 403 is bypassable via PMC, so there is no need to source this from a search-reported abstract.
- Add the masking caveat, which is currently absent and is the strongest objection to the article's reading: the placebo-controlled masked phase ended 1 July 2001, after roughly 3 of the 21 years. Placebo was then discontinued, group lifestyle intervention was offered to ALL arms, and only the metformin arm continued open-label metformin. The 21-year HRs are intention-to-treat by original assignment, not 21 years of metformin versus placebo.
- Strike 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat.' DPP's mean age at randomization was 50.6 +/- 10.7 years with an eligibility floor of 25; TAME proposes adults aged 65-79. Replace with language acknowledging partial overlap, and note that TAME's endpoint is a ~6-year composite of incident age-related disease and death, not 21-year cause-specific mortality.
- Downgrade 'demonstrably moves nothing downstream in mortality' to 'showed no reduction in all-cause, cancer, or cardiovascular mortality.' Mortality was not a pre-specified primary endpoint in DPP or DPPOS, and with 131 cardiovascular deaths the CV interval (0.70-1.66) does not license 'demonstrably.' Rest the weight on the all-cause estimate, HR 0.99 (0.79-1.25), which is the tightest.
- Qualify 'non-diabetics' as 'non-diabetic at randomization.' At 11.0 cases per 100 person-years in the placebo arm, most participants had developed diabetes well before the mortality endpoints accrued.
- Add the 2025 adherence re-analysis as supporting citation, because it directly answers the 'the null is just non-adherence' rebuttal: Diabetes Care 2025, PMID 40857175, PMCID PMC12451852, which applied ITT, as-treated, instrumental-variable and IPCW methods and reported that all 95% CIs included 1.0 for every outcome except diabetes incidence. Note that its as-treated mortality point estimate was 1.21 — the adherence correction moves toward harm, not benefit. Do not attach a confidence interval to that 1.21; the supplementary table was not verified.
- Report the median follow-up as 'a median of 21 years (IQR 20-21)' rather than 'about 21 years' — the IQR is narrow and strengthens the claim.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- 'The exact population TAME proposes to treat' is contradicted by the two trials' own enrollment criteria. AFAR's TAME description specifies participants 'between the ages of 65-79'; DPP enrolled adults aged 25 and up with a mean age of 50.6 +/- 10.7 years, selected for impaired glucose tolerance plus elevated fasting glucose plus overweight. These are different cohorts selected on different axes (dysglycemia versus chronological age), and TAME additionally targets a composite morbidity endpoint over ~6 years rather than 21-year mortality.
- The 21-year comparison is not a 21-year placebo-controlled comparison. The masked phase stopped on 1 July 2001 once diabetes-prevention efficacy was met; placebo was discontinued, all arms were offered a modified group lifestyle intervention, and the metformin arm continued open-label. Roughly 18 of the 21 years are unmasked, treatment-contaminated follow-up analyzed by original assignment. Any 'decisive' framing has to survive this.
- Mortality was not a pre-specified primary outcome of either DPP or DPPOS — the primary paper says so itself. The article treats an adequately-powered-sounding null as if it were a pre-registered negative primary result. The all-cause interval (0.79-1.25) is genuinely informative; the cause-specific ones (cancer 0.72-1.52, CV 0.70-1.66) are not tight enough to support 'demonstrably moves nothing.'
- Partial counter-pressure on the 'metformin does nothing' direction, worth disclosing rather than hiding: the DPPOS mortality analysis is a null, but the accompanying literature includes observational work pointing the other way (e.g. a 2025 J Gerontol A study comparing metformin versus sulfonylureas on exceptional longevity, PMID 40388602). The article should say explicitly that the randomized evidence is null while the favorable metformin-longevity signal is observational and confounded by indication — otherwise a reader who knows that literature will think the article suppressed it.
- Directionally awkward for the pro-metformin reading, and therefore useful to the article: in the 2025 DPPOS departures-from-assignment re-analysis, the as-treated mortality hazard ratio was the highest across methods at 1.21. Correcting for non-adherence does not rescue a benefit; it nudges the point estimate toward harm.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted (200/200) before I started, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against literature APIs, which turned out to be sufficient and arguably more reliable.

Primary documents I reached and read:
1. Lee CG et al., "Effect of Metformin and Lifestyle Interventions on Mortality in the Diabetes Prevention Program and Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study," Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, PMID 34697033, PMCID PMC8669534, DOI 10.2337/dc21-1046. I retrieved the abstract through TWO independent routes — the Europe PMC REST core-result API and the PubMed record page — and compared the returned strings. They matched character-for-character on every hazard ratio, confidence interval, death count and follow-up figure. I then opened the PMC full text for Table 1 arm sizes, baseline age, dose, pre-specification language and crossover discussion. Because of the pipeline's history of fabricated quotes, I treated the two-route agreement as the verification bar; every string I have marked verbatim appeared identically in at least two retrievals, except the Knowler 2025 abstract, which I flag as single-sourced in its item note.
2. DPP Research Group, NEJM 2002;346:393-403, PMID 11832527, DOI 10.1056/nejmoa012512, via Europe PMC core result — for the 31% figure, its CI, the 2.8-year window, the dose, and the entry criteria.
3. Barzilai N et al., "Metformin as a Tool to Target Aging," Cell Metab 2016, PMID 27304507, PMCID PMC5943638, full text via PMC — for TAME's planned age range and composite endpoint. Note I first fetched a wrong PMCID (PMC4906314) which returned an unrelated Na,K-ATPase paper; I caught this because the fetch tool correctly reported the mismatch, and I re-fetched the right one. This is worth recording as evidence that at least one fetch route does not silently confabulate.
4. Knowler WC et al., Diabetes Care 2025;48(10), PMID 40857175, DOI 10.2337/dci25-0032 — the departures-from-assigned-treatment re-analysis, reached via Europe PMC. Single route only; full text not opened.

What the adversarial pass found. The core quantitative spine of the claim survives intact and verbatim: 3,234 randomised 1996-99, metformin 850 mg twice daily, 31% (17-43%) diabetes reduction, median 21 years, 453 deaths, cancer 170, CVD 131, all-cause HR 0.99 (0.79-1.25), cancer HR 1.04 (0.72-1.52). Three things are wrong. The placebo arm is 1,082 not 1,073. The cardiovascular HR is 1.08 not 1.09. And the rhetorical bridge — that DPPOS treated "the exact population TAME proposes to treat" — is refuted by both trials' own design documents: TAME is ages 65-79, DPP had a mean age of 50.6.

Three further caliber problems the claim does not acknowledge, all of which cut against the article rather than for it. Mortality was never a pre-specified endpoint of DPP or DPPOS and the paper says so in its own words. The placebo arm was discontinued in 2001, so calling this a 21-year randomised comparison overstates the design; it is ITT on original assignment with acknowledged open-label metformin contamination across all arms. And the cause-specific figures are Fine-Gray subdistribution HRs, not Cox HRs.

I also actively hunted for a refutation and did not find one: no erratum or correction is attached to the PubMed or PMC records, and the one substantive later re-analysis (Knowler 2025) explicitly reports that correcting for treatment departures does not substantially change the intention-to-treat conclusions. That strengthens the article's null, and I have recommended citing it.

Remaining uncertainty. I could not locate any ClinicalTrials.gov registration for TAME, which is consistent with it never having been funded and launched, but absence from my query is not proof of absence — I searched the registry API once with a term query. The Barzilai 2016 paper gives TAME's age range and endpoint but does not state its diabetes/prediabetes exclusion criteria, so I cannot say from primary sources whether TAME would exclude the prediabetic participants DPP enrolled; the article should not assert either way. The Knowler 2025 finding rests on a single retrieval of its abstract and should be re-verified before it is quoted in print.

Verdict is CORRECTED rather than OVERTURNED: the central assertion — that the best randomised human evidence shows metformin preventing diabetes while failing to move mortality over two decades — holds against the primary source. But the draft overstates its force in three separate ways ("decisive," "demonstrably moves nothing," "exact population"), and an article whose whole subject is evidence grading cannot afford to grade its own load-bearing citation more generously than it grades others. The honest version of this paragraph is stronger, not weaker, because the pre-specification and placebo-discontinuation caveats are exactly the kind of thing the article is presumably teaching readers to look for.

- **Participants characterised as having 'impaired glucose tolerance'** — `corrected`
  WRONG as stated (IGT alone). RIGHT: entry required BOTH impaired glucose tolerance AND an elevated fasting glucose. NEJM 2002 abstract, verbatim: 'We randomly assigned 3234 nondiabetic persons with elevated fasting and post-load plasma glucose concentrations to placebo, metformin (850 mg twice daily), or a lifestyle-modification program.' Writing 'impaired glucose tolerance' alone describes a broader and less metabolically impaired group than DPP actually enrolled.

- **Arm sizes: placebo n=1,073, metformin n=1,073/1,073-ish** — `corrected`
  WRONG: placebo n=1,073. RIGHT: placebo n=1,082, metformin n=1,073, intensive lifestyle n=1,079 (sums to 3,234). Taken from the Table 1 column headers of the 2021 Diabetes Care full text (PMC8669534). The claim's hedge '1,073/1,073-ish' collapsed two different numbers into one; only the metformin arm is 1,073.

  Verbatim in NEJM 2002 abstract: 'metformin (850 mg twice daily)'. The 2021 full text likewise gives 'metformin 850 mg twice daily with standard diet and exercise recommendations'.

  Verbatim, NEJM 2002 (346:393-403, PMID 11832527): 'The lifestyle intervention reduced the incidence by 58 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 48 to 66 percent) and metformin by 31 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 17 to 43 percent), as compared with placebo.' WINDOW, which the claim left blank: 'The average follow-up was 2.8 years.' Incidence rates were 11.0 (placebo), 7.8 (metformin), 4.8 (lifestyle) cases per 100 person-years; NNT for metformin was 13.9 over 3 years. The article must state the 2.8-year window — 31% is not a lifetime or 21-year figure.

- **DPPOS follow-up median ~21 years, 453 deaths, cancer 170, cardiovascular 131** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the 2021 abstract: 'Over a median of 21 years (interquartile range 20-21), 453 participants died. Cancer was the leading cause of death (n = 170), followed by cardiovascular disease (n = 131).' The IQR (20-21) is a free precision gain the article can add. Deaths were adjudicated by blinded review through 31 December 2018.

- **All-cause mortality HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.79-1.25)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'Compared with placebo, metformin did not influence mortality from all causes (HR 0.99 [95% CI 0.79, 1.25])'. Confirmed identically through two independent retrieval routes (Europe PMC API, PubMed). Note for calibration: the lower bound of 0.79 means the trial does not exclude a true 21% relative reduction in all-cause mortality — this is a failure to demonstrate benefit, not a demonstration of no benefit.

- **Cancer mortality HR 1.04 (0.72-1.52)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'cancer (HR 1.04 [95% CI 0.72, 1.52])'. Confirmed via two independent routes.

  WRONG: 1.09. RIGHT: HR 1.08, and the CI the claim omitted is 95% CI 0.70, 1.66. Verbatim from the abstract: 'or cardiovascular disease (HR 1.08 [95% CI 0.70, 1.66])'. Same string returned by both Europe PMC and PubMed. Print 1.08 (0.70-1.66), not 1.09.

  Caliber slippage the claim does not flag: the cancer and cardiovascular HRs are NOT Cox hazard ratios. Verbatim: 'All-cause and cause-specific mortality hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated from Cox proportional hazards regression models and Fine-Gray models, respectively.' So all-cause HR 0.99 is a Cox HR; cancer 1.04 and CVD 1.08 are Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios accounting for competing risks. If the article presents all three as the same quantity it misstates the estimand.

- **Framing: 'decisive randomized human evidence' / a maintained 21-year randomised comparison** — `corrected`
  WRONG implication: that a placebo-controlled randomised comparison ran for 21 years and was designed to answer this. RIGHT, verbatim from the abstract: 'Placebo and lifestyle interventions stopped in 2001, and unmasked study metformin continued in those originally randomized.' The placebo control therefore ended after roughly 3 years; the 21-year result is intention-to-treat on the original 1996-99 assignment across ~18 further years without a placebo arm. And mortality was never a designed endpoint — verbatim from the full text (PMC8669534): 'While mortality was not a primary outcome in DPP or DPPOS, mortality was assessed with rigorous adjudication of causes to account for the competing risk of deaths on key outcomes measured in DPPOS.' It is a post-trial, non-pre-specified, unpowered analysis. Additional confound stated in the full text: 'Throughout DPP and DPPOS, study participants who developed diabetes in all randomized groups were frequently prescribed metformin as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes by their health care providers' — i.e. substantial contamination of the placebo arm with open-label metformin.

  No erratum or correction notice found on the PubMed record or the PMC full text. 'Analysis of Long-term Follow-up of a Randomized Clinical Trial With Departures From Assigned Treatments: Estimation of Metformin Effects on Diabetes and Its Complications in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study.' Diabetes Care 2025;48(10). PMID 40857175, PMCID PMC12451852, DOI 10.2337/dci25-0032. It applies methods correcting for the treatment departures described above and reports that doing so 'did not substantially change the conclusions from those of the simpler intention-to-treat analysis,' with complication-outcome intervals including 1.0. This is a strong citation for the article because it pre-empts the obvious 'the null is just contamination' objection. TAME's age FLOOR of 65 sits well above DPP's mean age; the populations differ by roughly 15 years and by selection on age-related morbidity rather than on obesity plus dysglycemia. TAME's endpoint also differs: verbatim, 'we will measure time to a new occurrence of a composite outcome that includes cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality' — a composite including incident dementia and non-fatal events, which DPPOS mortality analysis does not address at all. Separately, I could not locate any ClinicalTrials.gov registration for TAME (a query for 'Targeting Aging with Metformin' returned only NCT04264897 and NCT07302932, neither of which is TAME), so as of 2026-07 TAME appears still to be a proposed rather than registered trial — the article should not imply it is enrolling.

- Change the placebo arm size: placebo n=1,082, not 1,073. The correct trio is placebo 1,082 / metformin 1,073 / intensive lifestyle 1,079, summing to 3,234. Remove the '1,073/1,073-ish' hedge.
- Change the cardiovascular mortality hazard ratio from 1.09 to 1.08, and print the confidence interval the draft omits: HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.70, 1.66).
- State the window on the 31% diabetes-prevention figure. Correct form: metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% (95% CI 17-43%) versus placebo over an average follow-up of 2.8 years (DPP, NEJM 2002;346:393-403). Do not let 31% float free as though it were a long-run figure.
- Correct the population description: DPP required BOTH an elevated fasting glucose AND impaired glucose tolerance ('elevated fasting and post-load plasma glucose concentrations'), not impaired glucose tolerance alone.
- Delete or rewrite 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat.' TAME plans to enroll 3,000 subjects ages 65-79 (Barzilai et al., Cell Metab 2016); DPP enrolled adults aged 25+ with a mean baseline age of 50.6 years and mean BMI 34.0. Honest phrasing: 'a younger, obese, prediabetic population — not the older cohort TAME targets, which weakens rather than settles the extrapolation.'
- Qualify 'decisive randomized human evidence.' The placebo and lifestyle interventions stopped in 2001; only the originally randomized metformin group continued on unmasked drug. The 21-year result is an intention-to-treat comparison on 1996-99 assignment carried through ~18 years without an active placebo control, not a maintained 21-year randomised comparison.
- Add that mortality was not a pre-specified endpoint. Quote available: 'While mortality was not a primary outcome in DPP or DPPOS, mortality was assessed with rigorous adjudication of causes to account for the competing risk of deaths on key outcomes measured in DPPOS.' This is a non-pre-specified, unpowered post-trial analysis and should be graded as such by an article whose subject is evidence grading.
- Soften 'demonstrably moves nothing downstream in mortality.' The 95% CI for all-cause mortality runs 0.79 to 1.25, so a true 21% relative reduction in death is not excluded. Correct caliber: the trial failed to demonstrate a mortality benefit and rules out large benefits, but it does not demonstrate the absence of a moderate one.
- Distinguish the estimands: all-cause HR 0.99 is from a Cox proportional hazards model; the cancer (1.04) and cardiovascular (1.08) figures are Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios accounting for competing risks. The paper states 'Cox proportional hazards regression models and Fine-Gray models, respectively.'
- Cite the primary directly rather than a search-reported abstract: Lee CG et al., Diabetes Care 2021;44(12):2775-2782, PMID 34697033, DOI 10.2337/dc21-1046. The ADA 403 is bypassable via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8669534/.
- Optionally strengthen the argument by citing Knowler WC et al., Diabetes Care 2025;48(10), PMID 40857175, DOI 10.2337/dci25-0032, which re-analyses DPPOS correcting for departures from assigned treatment and reports the conclusions are not substantially changed from intention-to-treat. This answers the 'the null is just placebo-arm contamination' objection.
- Add the interquartile range now that it is free: median 21 years (IQR 20-21), 453 deaths, causes adjudicated by blinded review through 31 December 2018.
- Do not describe TAME as underway or enrolling. No ClinicalTrials.gov registration for TAME was locatable as of 2026-07.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- TAME's target population is ages 65-79 (Barzilai et al., Cell Metab 2016, PMCID PMC5943638, verbatim: 'we plan to enroll 3,000 subjects, ages 65-79'), whereas DPP's baseline mean age was 50.6 +/- 10.7 years with mean BMI 34.0. The article's claim that DPPOS treated 'the exact population TAME proposes to treat' is contradicted by the primary design documents of both trials.
- TAME's proposed primary endpoint is a composite of cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality — verbatim: 'time to a new occurrence of a composite outcome that includes cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, and mortality'. DPPOS mortality analysis addresses only the fatal components and says nothing about incident dementia or non-fatal cardiovascular events, so it cannot by itself pre-empt TAME's endpoint.
- The 21-year comparison is not a placebo-controlled randomised comparison for most of its duration. The paper itself states placebo stopped in 2001 while unmasked metformin continued in the originally randomized metformin group, and that participants in all arms who developed diabetes were frequently prescribed metformin clinically. This undercuts the word 'decisive'.
- Mortality was explicitly not a primary outcome of either DPP or DPPOS (stated in the paper's own discussion), so the strongest available human randomised evidence on this question is a non-pre-specified secondary analysis — a point an article about evidence grading is obliged to make about its own load-bearing citation.
- The all-cause mortality confidence interval (0.79-1.25) is compatible with a 21% relative mortality reduction, which contradicts the article's stronger phrasing that metformin 'demonstrably moves nothing downstream'.

3. STAT, 9 Aug 2022, via Wayback capture 20221214164313. Read the Barzilai quote in full: 'I'm on the record saying I'm pretty sure it will start this year, for the last seven years... I have no credibility anymore.' Seven years back from Aug 2022 = 2015; the claim's 'roughly 2015' is right.

4. Lifespan Research Institute interview, 12 Aug 2025, https://lifespan.io/nir-barzilai-positive-evidence-for-metformin-is-mounting/ — raw HTML fetched, tags stripped, exact sentences located. This is where the claim slips: the real sentence is 'I cannot give you a perfect update because it's now being handled within ARPA-H', and the Lilly GLP-1 study is framed as one of two expected trials with metformin still championed, not as a replacement.

What remains uncertain, stated plainly: (a) I could not exhaustively clear WHO ICTRP or EudraCT — ICTRP's query API returned empty and its search UI is JS-gated, and the EUCTR search page returned only its own form markup. My non-CTG registry result is 'no record found', not 'proven absent'. (b) I could not verify the '2028 readout' sub-claim at all. My WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200 calls) at the fourth step of this task, and every fallback search engine I tried — DuckDuckGo HTML, DuckDuckGo Lite, Mojeek, searx.be, search.bus-hit.me, priv.au — returned a bot-challenge, CAPTCHA, or 429, and I did not attempt to solve any CAPTCHA. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: the central assertion — TAME was announced ~2015, is still unregistered and unenrolled as of 2026-07, and at least one site reports its results as fact — survives every attempt I made to refute it, and AFAR's own live page affirmatively corroborates non-enrollment. But the ARPA-H quotation is misquoted, 'instead' misstates Barzilai's position on Lilly/GLP-1, the query count is understated, and the '~3,000' figure is wrongly labeled a fabrication when it is the sponsor's own published target.

- **TAME has no ClinicalTrials.gov registration as of 2026-07-28** — `confirmed`
  I ran eight independent CTG API v2 query formulations (not three): (1) query.term='TAME metformin aging'; (2) query.titles='Targeting Aging with Metformin'; (3) query.term exact phrase '"Targeting Aging with Metformin"'; (4) query.term='Barzilai'; (5) query.spons='American Federation for Aging Research'; (6) query.intr=metformin AND query.cond=aging; (7) AREA[Acronym]TAME; (8) query.intr=metformin filtered to EnrollmentCount RANGE[2000,MAX]; plus query.spons='Albert Einstein College of Medicine'+metformin, query.spons='Wake Forest'+metformin, query.term='ARPA-H', and query.cond=aging with enrollment >=1000. NONE returns a TAME aging trial. Einstein's only registered metformin longevity study is NCT02432287 MILES, n=16, COMPLETED. IMPORTANT TRAP the article must avoid: the acronym 'TAME' IS registered on CTG by ~15 unrelated trials, including NCT02656017 'Metformin as a Novel Therapy for Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease', acronym TAME, COMPLETED. A careless reader/searcher will find a real metformin trial called TAME that has nothing to do with aging. ISRCTN and WHO ICTRP returned no TAME aging record either (ICTRP's API returned empty; I could not get a clean negative from its search UI, so treat non-CTG registries as 'no record found' rather than exhaustively excluded).

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Not a contradiction of the claim but a live trap for it: ClinicalTrials.gov DOES contain registered trials with the acronym 'TAME', including a metformin trial — NCT02656017, 'Metformin as a Novel Therapy for Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease', acronym TAME, status COMPLETED, sponsor Kyongtae Ty Bae. About fifteen TAME-acronym trials exist (ALS memantine, cardiac arrest hypercapnia, anger management, etc.). Anyone spot-checking the claim with a naive registry search will surface a completed metformin trial called TAME and conclude the article is wrong.
- Barzilai's 'handled within ARPA-H' framing does not correspond to any registered ARPA-H trial. I queried CTG for ARPA-H-associated studies and got nine records (Daré Bioscience HPV, Aalto INGA sensors, Northwestern smart band-aid, Mayo HAIQU, UNC EVOLVE-BDT, and two false-positive matches on a Thai investigator named 'arpa'). No metformin trial, no aging trial. So the ARPA-H handoff has produced no registered protocol either — this strengthens rather than weakens the article, but the article should not let readers infer ARPA-H has started something.
- The imedic.health fabrication is load-bearing on a second fabricated number the article may inherit: it invents 'a 2014 UK study of over 180,000 patients that found metformin-treated diabetics had approximately 15% lower all-cause mortality than matched non-diabetic controls'. There is a real 2014 Bannister et al. study of metformin-treated diabetics versus matched non-diabetic controls, but the '15%' and '180,000' figures on that page should not be reused without independent verification — I did not verify them.
- AFAR describes TAME as 'a series of nationwide, six-year clinical trials' (plural) at 14 institutions with Wake Forest as coordinating center. If the article calls TAME 'the trial' (singular), that is defensible shorthand but diverges from the sponsor's own current description.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I tried to overturn this group and could not. What I did reach, verbatim, in primary or first-party form:

(1) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, queried live on 2026-07-28 via eight independent formulations (title, free-text, exact-phrase, intervention+condition, AREA[Acronym], sponsor=Wake Forest+metformin, AREA[LeadSponsorName]='American Federation for Aging Research', sponsor=Albert Einstein+metformin). Barzilai's TAME appears in none. The AFAR lead-sponsor query returns an empty JSON array — AFAR sponsors zero registered studies. The strongest near-miss, and the one the article must inoculate against, is NCT02656017: a completed metformin trial whose registered acronym is TAME, for polycystic kidney disease.

(2) EU Clinical Trials Register, queried directly: 'targeting aging with metformin' = 0; 'metformin AND aging' = 4, none TAME; 'TAME AND metformin' = 1, EudraCT 2021-003299-15 (METFORAGING, HIV, Hospital La Paz).

(3) afar.org/tame-trial, raw HTML parsed myself rather than through a summarizer. Footer '©2026'. Every reference to the trial is future-tense: '6 — Years of trials, once launched'; 'Raising Funds to Launch'; WHAT'S NEEDED lists donors, '3,000 individuals... to participate', and 'An "indication" for aging'. The 3,000 figure is a recruitment target on the sponsor's own site.

(4) STAT News, 9 August 2022, Megan Molteni — full article body read (the page served the complete text). Verbatim: 'I'm on the record saying I'm pretty sure it will start this year, for the last seven years,' said Barzilai. 'I have no credibility anymore. It's just incredibly frustrating. But it's going to happen, because it has to happen.' The article carries a correction, but it concerns statins/cholesterol, not TAME.

(5) Lifespan.io, 12 August 2025, Arkadi Mazin interview — raw HTML parsed myself. Verbatim: 'I cannot give you a perfect update because it's now being handled within ARPA-H. I think there will be two major trials that come out of this. One is going to be from Eli Lilly; they're going to do a TAME-like study but with their GLP-1 agonist.' And: 'we're holding everything because I would love for all four major drug classes to be tested so we can get comparisons.' Date independently cross-checked by decoding the timestamp embedded in the LinkedIn activity id that cites it (2025-08-13 01:33 UTC = 12 Aug 2025 US time).

(6) imedic.health, raw HTML: published 2 March 2026, badged 'Evidence level: 1A', reports TAME results as accomplished fact, and cites five references none of which is a TAME results paper.

Caliber slippage found, hence CORRECTED not HOLDS: the ARPA-H quote drops Barzilai's hedge 'perfect' and alters "it's" to "is" inside quotation marks; the Eli Lilly sentence's word 'instead' inverts his actual position (he wants all four drug classes tested and calls TAME 'a template', not a thing being replaced); the 'every year since roughly 2015' line is the article's arithmetic on his 'for the last seven years', not his phrasing; and the flat 'no ClinicalTrials.gov registration' is literally refutable because a different registered trial is acronymed TAME.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: WHO ICTRP is UNREACHABLE — its API endpoints returned 'The resource you are looking for has been removed' and its portal pages timed out past 120 seconds. EU CTIS's public search API returned 'Missing Authentication Token'. I did not verify either myself and the article must not claim they were checked. I also exhausted the session's web-search budget partway through, so I could not exhaustively canvass post-August-2025 podcast or conference statements; the 12 August 2025 interview is the most recent primary statement I located, not provably the most recent that exists. Finally, 'never enrolled a patient' is a universal negative that no document can affirmatively state; it rests on the sponsor's own prospective language, registry absence, and Barzilai's silence on enrollment.

  CONFIRMED for the trial in question, but the flat phrasing 'no ClinicalTrials.gov registration for TAME' is refutable on a literal read and needs a qualifier. ### 票 3(CORRECTED)

I attacked the claim registry-first, since a single registration would overturn it. I hit the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 with eight structurally different queries (free text, title field, sponsor field, acronym AREA filter, quoted phrase, PI surname, intervention+condition cross, and an enrollment>=1500 filter on metformin). None returns a TAME aging trial; the acronym query returns 15 unrelated TAME trials, which is the trap a sloppy search would fall into. I then reached EudraCT/EU CTR via its ctr-search summary REST endpoint (negative; only METFORAGING 2021-003299-15, an unrelated HIV-aging metformin trial in Madrid) and ISRCTN via its query API (empty result set). WHO ICTRP and EU CTIS I could NOT reach — ICTRP's endpoints returned a removal notice and a connection failure, CTIS returned 'Missing Authentication Token' — and I am flagging that rather than papering over it.

For the primary documents I deliberately avoided the WebFetch summarizer and pulled raw HTML, stripping tags locally, so that every string I call verbatim is one I actually saw. This mattered: WebFetch's first pass on the AFAR page returned a plausible-looking quote set, and a WebFetch of a Bing search URL returned wholly unrelated cached content about love-poem generators — a live instance of the fabrication failure mode I was warned about. afar.org itself 403s to curl, so I used the Wayback capture 20260704152538 (24 days before the as-of date) and de-tagged it myself. STAT is paywalled live; I used Wayback capture 20220809141926, taken the day of publication. The lifespan.io interview I fetched live at HTTP 200.

What holds: no registration anywhere I could reach; AFAR's own July-2026 page is uniformly future-tense and explicitly fundraising ('once launched', 'to be engaged', 'Raising Funds to Launch'); the imedic.health page is a real, live, dated fabrication reporting TAME results with a self-applied '1A' evidence badge.

What slips: three caliber errors. The 2025 quote is 'I cannot give you a perfect update', not 'an update' — a small word that changes the register from stonewalling to hedging. The Eli Lilly sentence's 'instead' is not supported; Barzilai describes two parallel trials and wants all four drug classes compared. And the 2022 line should be quoted, not paraphrased, because 'for the last seven years' is the load-bearing phrase.

  I ran EIGHT independent CTG API v2 query formulations against clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies on 2026-07-28: (1) query.term='TAME metformin'; (2) query.titles='Targeting Aging with Metformin'; (3) query.spons='American Federation for Aging Research'; (4) query.term='AREA[Acronym]TAME'; (5) query.term='"Targeting Aging with Metformin"' (quoted full-text); (6) query.term='Barzilai'; (7) query.intr=metformin + query.cond=aging; (8) query.intr=metformin filtered to AREA[EnrollmentCount]RANGE[1500,MAX]. No record for the TAME aging trial appears in any of them. Query (4) returns 15 unrelated trials that use the TAME acronym (ADPKD metformin NCT02656017, memantine ALS NCT01020331, therapeutic mild hypercapnia NCT03114033, etc.) — none is the aging trial. Query (3) returns only AFAR-grantee-affiliated trials with other lead sponsors; AFAR is not the lead sponsor of any registered study.
