**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The article's own framing that ARPA-H has taken TAME over could be read as 'the trial is finally moving'. The primary document cuts the other way: Columbia Mailman's 25 Feb 2026 ARPA-H PROSPR announcement says the Barzilai-co-led FAST project will, verbatim, 'analyze data and biospecimens from already-completed clinical trials' and that FAST 'has incorporated trials involving four of five priority drug classes identified by the research team: metformin, SGLT-2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, and rapamycin.' There is no TAME trial inside PROSPR; PROSPR is upstream biomarker work whose stated purpose (per PM Andrew Brack) is 'to allow the first clinical trials for aging to be possible' — i.e., the first such trial is still described as not yet possible as of Feb 2026.
- Barzilai's own 12 Aug 2025 language undercuts any imminence reading: 'we're holding everything'. That is an explicit statement of continued non-start, eleven months before the article's as-of date.
- A near-miss that could be mistaken for TAME in a careless registry search: NCT02960711, 'Metformin and Dietary Restriction to Prevent Age-related Morbid Events in People', enrollment 1600, COMPLETED, start 2014-02. It is an Italian trial (MeMeMe), not TAME. Anyone reporting 'a completed metformin aging trial with >1,000 participants' is likely conflating these.
- imedic.health's fabricated page cites Bannister CA et al. 2014 (Diabetes Obes Metab 16:1165) as showing metformin-treated diabetics outlived matched non-diabetic controls, and glosses it as '~15% lower all-cause mortality'. That 15% figure is imedic's own invention layered onto a real paper; if the article repeats any effect size in connection with that citation, it should come from the Bannister paper itself, not from the content-farm page.

## V17 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

Primary documents I reached and read myself:

1. Konopka AR et al., Aging Cell 2019, PMID 30548390, PMC6351883 — full text via PMC. I confirmed the randomisation (n=26 placebo / n=27 metformin = 53), age '(62 ± 1 years)', the dose-titration sentence including the 11 dose reductions to 1,500 mg/day, the VO2max sentence with its explicit 'p = 0.08', the insulin-sensitivity interaction (p<0.05) and inhibition (p=0.02), and the exact '~25%' sentence, which is specific to 'maximal CI-linked respiration ... during the ADP titration'. I also confirmed the placebo within-group mitochondrial increases were only p=0.07. PubMed lists no erratum, comment, retraction or expression of concern.

2. Walton RG et al. (MASTERS), Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039, PMID 31557380, PMC6826125 — full text via PMC. Confirmed 'Of 109 randomized subjects...' verbatim, Table 1 randomised N=55 placebo / N=54 metformin, dose 1,700 mg/day, the pre-specified augmentation hypothesis in both abstract and body, registration NCT02308228, and the opposite-direction primary results. PMC carries the correction notice.

3. Corrigendum, Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098, PMID 32141718, PMC7059173 — read directly, twice with differently-phrased prompts to guard against summariser fabrication; both reads returned the same baseline values (3.89 / 4.60), confirming the corrected Relative strength row: placebo +18.9 (19.1) vs metformin +14.8 (18.3), p = 0.30, N=44 per arm. The superseded original values (19.7 / 14.5, p=0.188) are still visible in the PMC copy of the original article, letting me confirm what actually changed.

4. Yang Y et al., Cell 2024;187(22):6358-6378.e29, PMID 39270656 — cell.com blocked WebFetch (403) and the DOI resolver bounced to the homepage, so I loaded the article in the browser pane and extracted text from the DOM directly. This let me read the RESOURCE label, the 'proof-of-concept' sentence, the 13-16 year age range, the 20 mg/kg/day dose (drinking water, 40 months, 1,200 days), the control-monkey death on day 1,126, the '36 monkeys' clock-training sentence, and the Limitations section verbatim. Group sizes are only in the Figure 1 legend, which the page renders collapsed; I expanded that specific caption programmatically and read 'Y-Ctrl, n = 6; M-Ctrl, n = 3; O-Ctrl, n = 5; O-Met, n = 6 monkeys.' I then enumerated every 'N years' string in the full text to test the 'eight years' claim — there is no eight-year figure anywhere.

5. Lifespan.io interview 'Nir Barzilai: "Positive Evidence for Metformin is Mounting"', 12 August 2025 — cell text via browser DOM. Both the 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' line and the under-50 line are verbatim from this page. I also searched the same page text for 'six year'/'6-year' and got zero hits.

Everything I have marked verbatim above I saw as an exact string in the source, either in a WebFetch return that quoted the document or, for the Cell and Lifespan.io pages, in raw DOM innerText I extracted myself. Where a WebFetch returned prose rather than quoted text I did not treat it as a quote.

What remains uncertain: (i) the 'six years younger' brain quote attributed to Barzilai — I could not locate any primary Barzilai source containing it, and it is absent from the only Barzilai interview I could reach; it looks like the paper's own abstract wording misattributed to him, but I cannot exclude that he said it in an unreached podcast. My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task and the DuckDuckGo/Mojeek fallbacks degraded to CAPTCHA and 403, which I did not bypass, so my search coverage for Barzilai's other public statements is thin. (ii) The Cell paper's internal '36 monkeys' vs Figure-1 group-size discrepancy is unexplained in the article; I could not resolve it from the text or from Table S3, which I could not open. (iii) I did not find any failed replication or critical letter for Konopka 2019 or MASTERS, but given the search limitation I would not call that an exhaustive negative — I can only say PubMed lists no linked erratum, comment, or expression of concern for either PMID beyond the MASTERS corrigendum.

Overall verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: the trial architecture, N's, doses, the pre-specification of the MASTERS hypothesis, the corrigendum's existence and exact values, the monkey study's design and limitations, and the Barzilai under-50 statement all survive scrutiny — but the mitochondrial '~25%' needs a significance qualifier, the metformin dose in (a) needs the 1,500 mg caveat, Barzilai's 'eight years' is contradicted by the paper it describes, the 'six years younger' Barzilai attribution is unsupported, and (d) misstates his stated rationale.

- **(a) Konopka 2019: 53 older adults, mean age 62, randomised to metformin or placebo alongside aerobic exercise training** — `confirmed`
  Konopka AR et al., 'Metformin inhibits mitochondrial adaptations to aerobic exercise training in older adults', Aging Cell 2019, PMID 30548390, PMC6351883. Abstract verbatim: 'In a double-blinded fashion, participants were randomized to placebo (n = 26) or metformin (n = 27) treatment during 12 weeks of AET.' 26+27 = 53. Age stated verbatim as '(62 ± 1 years)' — this is mean ± SEM, so 'mean age 62' is correct.

- **(a) Metformin titrated to 2,000 mg/day** — `corrected`
  Substantially right but incomplete. Methods verbatim: 'The dose for both placebo and metformin was 500 mg/day the first week and increased by 500 mg each week until reaching 2000 mg/day (1,000 mg twice daily) by week 4.' CORRECTION: not everyone stayed at 2,000 mg — eleven participants had the dose reduced to 1,500 mg/day for gastrointestinal discomfort. WRONG version: 'titrated to 2,000 mg/day' full stop. RIGHT version: 'titrated to a target of 2,000 mg/day, with 11 participants reduced to 1,500 mg/day for GI intolerance.'

- **(a) Metformin attenuated the training-induced improvement in insulin sensitivity** — `confirmed`
  Results verbatim: 'There was a significant interaction (p < 0.05, time by treatment) for an increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity, evaluated by the Matsuda index, after AET with placebo but not metformin' and 'On average, the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity after AET was inhibited (p = 0.02) by metformin.' Note the paper stresses heterogeneity: 'In the metformin group, there was no overall change in whole-body insulin sensitivity after AET due to positive and negative responders.'

- **(a) Metformin abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration** — `corrected`
  The '~25%' string is real and verbatim — the paper says: 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration.' CORRECTION on caliber: this is NOT a ~25% increase that was itself statistically significant in placebo. The paper also states verbatim: 'With placebo, AET nonsignificantly increased CIP and CI+FAOP (both p = 0.07) and this trend was not apparent with metformin.' The significant finding is the between-group difference in change: 'the change in CI+II&FAOP was greater (p < 0.05) in placebo versus metformin.' WRONG version: 'abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration' (implies a significant placebo gain in mitochondrial respiration generally). RIGHT version: 'abolished the ~25% increase in maximal complex-I-linked respiration during the ADP titration; the within-placebo increases in CI_P and CI+FAO_P were themselves only trends (p = 0.07), with the placebo-vs-metformin difference in change significant at p < 0.05.'

- **(a) NOTE TO VERIFY: the VO2max result was p=0.08 and is routinely miscited as significant** — `confirmed`
  The article's own caution is correct and should be kept. Results verbatim: 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO2max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.08).' Also verbatim: 'VO2max (L/min) was significantly increased after 12 weeks of AET (p < 0.05, main effect for time) with a significant increase within the placebo group (p < 0.01) but not metformin.' So the within-placebo gain was significant; the metformin-vs-placebo attenuation was not (p = 0.08). Note the ABSTRACT itself is the source of the miscitation: it says flatly 'metformin attenuated the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO2 max after AET' with no p-value, which is how the non-significant result propagates as significant. No erratum or comment is listed on PubMed for PMID 30548390.

- **(b) MASTERS: 109 randomised (55 placebo, 54 metformin) older adults in progressive resistance training** — `confirmed`
  Walton RG et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039, PMID 31557380, PMC6826125. Verbatim: 'Of 109 randomized subjects, 15 participants discontinued the study (n = 6 due to adverse events), resulting in a final analytic sample of 94 (86%) who completed the study (n = 46 Metformin; n = 48 Placebo).' Table 1 header gives Randomized N = 55 Placebo, N = 54 Metformin. Registered NCT02308228. Note for the article's precision: the abstract reports the ANALYSED numbers (metformin N=46, placebo N=48), not the randomised ones, so do not mix the two. Dose was 1,700 mg/day (850 mg x2), NOT 2,000 mg — verbatim: 'titrated up to the target dose by taking 1 tablet per day (850 mg) for 7 days, followed by 2 tablets per day (1,700 mg) for the remainder of the trial.' Training was 14 weeks of supervised PRT.

- **(b) The investigators' pre-specified hypothesis was that metformin would ENHANCE the response, and they found the opposite** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim: 'Metformin reduces inflammation, so we hypothesized that metformin would augment the muscle response to PRT in healthy women and men aged 65 and older.' Body verbatim: 'we hypothesized that metformin would augment the muscle response to RT by increasing the abundance of M2 macrophages, thereby reducing muscle inflammation.' The hypothesis was published in advance in the protocol paper (Long DE et al., Trials 2017;18:192, PMID 28441958) and the trial was pre-registered (NCT02308228), so 'pre-specified' is fair. Opposite result confirmed verbatim: 'placebo gained more lean body mass (p = .003) and thigh muscle mass (p < .001) than metformin.' This is a genuine and unusually clean case of a hypothesis-contradicting result, and the framing is accurate.

- **(b) Table 2 relative-strength values were wrong in the original publication and were replaced by corrigendum (corrected: placebo +18.9% vs metformin +14.8%, p=0.30)** — `confirmed`
  Corrigendum EXISTS and the numbers are exactly right. Corrigendum, Aging Cell 2020 Jan 15;19(3):e13098, doi 10.1111/acel.13098, PMID 32141718, PMC7059173. It corrects vol 18, e13039, specifically the 'Relative strength (kg/kg)' row of Table 2. Corrected values: Placebo N=44, baseline 3.89 (1.48), 14-week PRT 4.62 (1.74), % change 18.9 (19.1); Metformin N=44, baseline 4.60 (1.39), 14-week PRT 5.23 (1.58), % change 14.8 (18.3); p = 0.30. The corrigendum also states related measures in Appendix S2 were updated online. For contrast, the still-visible original Table 2 on PMC6826125 shows 19.7 (19.0) vs 14.5 (17.9), p = 0.188 — i.e. the original overstated the placebo advantage and understated the p-value, which is a good detail for the article. PMC6826125 carries the notice 'This article has been corrected. See Aging Cell. 2020 Jan 15;19(3):e13098.'

- **(c) Yang et al. Cell 2024 is a proof-of-concept Resource article in MALE cynomolgus monkeys aged 13-16 at start, 20 mg/kg/day metformin, with SIX treated animals** — `confirmed`
  Yang Y et al., 'Metformin decelerates aging clock in male monkeys', Cell 2024;187(22):6358-6378.e29, PMID 39270656, PII S0092-8674(24)00914-0. Read the full text directly on cell.com. Article type label at top of the page is 'RESOURCE'. Body verbatim: 'we conducted a proof-of-concept study involving male cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) aged between 13 and 16 years, roughly equivalent to approximately 40-50 years in humans.' Dose verbatim: 'The monkeys in the O-Met group were administered a daily dose of 20 mg/kg metformin, a standard dosage used in diabetes management for humans' — STAR Methods adds it was 'administered through drinking water over the duration of the study (40 months).' Group sizes, verbatim from the Figure 1 legend (obtained by expanding the collapsed caption): 'Y-Ctrl, n = 6; M-Ctrl, n = 3; O-Ctrl, n = 5; O-Met, n = 6 monkeys.' So SIX treated animals is correct, and the aged control arm is only FIVE — verbatim: 'One participant in the O-Ctrl group succumbed to kidney failure on the 1,126th day of the study.' Treatment ran 1,200 days ('approximately 3.3 years, which corresponds to about 10 years in humans').

- **(c) The authors' own limitations state they did NOT measure survival** — `confirmed`
  Limitations of the study, verbatim: 'The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation.' The same section also concedes, verbatim: 'We have noted that metformin potentially slows aging at molecular and tissue levels in males, but conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse, and a full understanding of its side effects in humans remains elusive.' That second sentence is arguably even more damaging to the hype and is worth quoting.

- **(c) Barzilai publicly restated it as 'Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level'** — `confirmed`
  Quote is REAL and I read it at the primary source. Nir Barzilai interview, 'Nir Barzilai: "Positive Evidence for Metformin is Mounting"', Lifespan.io, dated August 12, 2025 (https://www.lifespan.io/news/nir-barzilai-positive-evidence-for-metformin-is-mounting/). Verbatim: 'Then there's the monkey study published in Cell, which was a big deal. Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level. There are so many other good studies on metformin.' The number is NOT in the paper — see the separate itemVerdict below.

- **(c) Whether the paper supports 'eight years on the transcriptomic level'** — `refuted`
  It does not. I grepped every 'years' figure in the full text. The paper's transcriptAge (bulk RNA-seq) ΔAgeDiff values, verbatim: 'the transcriptAge of all thirteen tissues was restored to a younger state, including the Achilles tendon (ΔAgeDiff -5.31 years), liver (ΔAgeDiff -4.14 years), bronchus (ΔAgeDiff -3.71 years), muscle (ΔAgeDiff -3.56 years), and lung (ΔAgeDiff -3.40 years).' The single largest number anywhere in the paper, across ALL clocks and layers, is -6.86 years (microglia sn-transcriptAge). Others: proteinAge -6.41 y; frontal-lobe DNAmAge -6.10 y; frontal-lobe integrated sn-transcriptAge -5.90 y; liver integrated sn-transcriptAge 4.28 y. NOTHING reaches eight years, and nothing at the transcriptomic level exceeds -6.86 y. Barzilai's 'eight years' overstates the paper's own top transcriptomic figure by roughly 50% and its headline transcriptAge figure (-5.31 y) by about 50%. Suggestive detail for the article: in the SAME interview Barzilai says of his centenarian-offspring proteomics, verbatim, 'They were, on average, eight years younger on a proteomic level than their spouses' — the 'eight years' looks like a cross-contamination from his own unrelated human proteomic dataset.

- **(c) Barzilai restated the brain result as 'six years younger'** — `unreachable`
  I could NOT verify this attribution. The string 'six years' / '6-year' does not appear anywhere in the Lifespan.io interview of 12 Aug 2025 — I searched the rendered page text directly for it and got zero hits; his only quantitative statement about the monkey study there is the 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' line. He may have said 'six years younger' in some podcast or talk I could not reach (my WebSearch budget was exhausted and DuckDuckGo/Mojeek fallbacks hit rate limits and CAPTCHAs, which I did not attempt to bypass). CAUTION: the ~6-year brain figure IS the PAPER's own abstract wording, verbatim: 'The results highlighted a significant slowing of aging indicators, notably a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging.' So the article may have mistakenly attributed the paper's own abstract line to Barzilai as a quote. Do not present 'six years younger' as a Barzilai quotation unless a dated primary recording/transcript is produced.

- **(c) Whether the aging clocks were trained by the same laboratory on a small monkey cohort** — `confirmed`
  Yes, and the circularity is worse than 'small cohort' implies. Verbatim: 'By integrating data from the Y-Ctrl, M-Ctrl, and O-Ctrl cohorts (a total of 36 monkeys), we were able to formulate a penalized linear model (see STAR Methods).' The clocks (DNAmAge, transcriptAge, proteinAge, metabAge, sn-transcriptAge) were all newly constructed by the authors for this study using ElasticNet, trained on the study's own untreated control monkeys — i.e. the O-Ctrl comparison arm is inside the training set, and ΔAgeDiff is measured against a model those same controls defined. There is no external validation cohort and no pre-existing published monkey clock used as a check. FLAG AN INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY the article can use: the stated training cohort of '36 monkeys' cannot be reconciled with the Figure 1 group sizes (Y-Ctrl 6 + M-Ctrl 3 + O-Ctrl 5 = 14, or 20 including the 6 O-Met). The paper does not explain the discrepancy. Either way the clock training base is far below what clock validation normally requires. No erratum, retraction, comment, or expression of concern is listed on PubMed for PMID 39270656 as of 2026-07.

- **(d) Barzilai has stated that people under 50 without diabetes should not take metformin because of the exercise interaction** — `corrected`
  Substantially right, with two caliber slips. Verbatim from the same Lifespan.io interview (12 Aug 2025): 'This relates to the antagonistic pleiotropy hypothesis of aging, where not everything that's good for you when you're young is good for you when you're old, and it's the other way around with drugs. Not every drug for aging is good for the young, and metformin is a perfect example. Whoever takes metformin who doesn't have diabetes and is not at least 50 years old is making a mistake, in particular if they're trying to build their muscle or increase their VO2max.' SLIP 1 — his stated PRIMARY rationale is antagonistic pleiotropy, not the exercise interaction; exercise enters as an aggravating condition ('in particular if'). WRONG version: 'should not take metformin BECAUSE OF the exercise interaction.' RIGHT version: 'said non-diabetics under 50 taking metformin are "making a mistake" on antagonistic-pleiotropy grounds, "in particular" if they are trying to build muscle or raise VO2max.' SLIP 2 — his phrasing is 'is not at least 50 years old', and it is conjunctive with 'doesn't have diabetes'; 'people under 50 without diabetes' is a faithful rendering but should not be tightened into a blanket prohibition, since he frames it as a mistake rather than a contraindication. Also worth noting the irony for the article: the VO2max caveat he invokes rests on Konopka 2019, whose VO2max attenuation was p = 0.08.

**修正:**
- (a) Do not say metformin was simply 'titrated to 2,000 mg/day'. Konopka 2019 Methods: dose started at 500 mg/day and rose 500 mg weekly to 2,000 mg/day (1,000 mg twice daily) by week 4, BUT eleven participants were reduced to 1,500 mg/day for gastrointestinal discomfort. Write: 'titrated to a target of 2,000 mg/day (11 participants reduced to 1,500 mg/day for GI intolerance).'
- (a) Tighten the mitochondrial claim. The paper's exact sentence is 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration' — the ~25% applies specifically to maximal complex-I-linked respiration during the ADP titration, not to mitochondrial respiration in general. The paper also states 'With placebo, AET nonsignificantly increased CI_P and CI+FAO_P (both p = 0.07)', so the placebo gain was itself only a trend on those measures; the significant result was the between-group difference in change for CI+II&FAO_P (p < 0.05). Write it as: 'abolished the ~25% increase in maximal complex-I-linked respiration; the placebo-vs-metformin difference in change was significant (p < 0.05), though the within-placebo increases were themselves trends (p = 0.07).'
- (a) Keep and sharpen the VO2max caution. Konopka 2019 verbatim: 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO2max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.08).' Add the reason the miscitation propagates: the paper's own ABSTRACT states 'metformin attenuated the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO2 max after AET' with no p-value attached, so readers who stop at the abstract cannot tell that one of those two was non-significant. The insulin-sensitivity half WAS significant (time x treatment interaction p < 0.05; inhibition p = 0.02); the VO2max half was not.
- (b) Give MASTERS randomised and analysed numbers separately and do not mix them. Randomised: 109 (55 placebo, 54 metformin). Analysed/completers: 94 (48 placebo, 46 metformin); 15 discontinued, 6 for adverse events. The published abstract reports only the analysed numbers, so quoting '46 vs 48' as the randomisation is a common error.
- (b) State the MASTERS metformin dose correctly as 1,700 mg/day (850 mg once daily for 7 days, then 850 mg twice daily), across 14 weeks of supervised progressive resistance training. Do not carry the 2,000 mg/day figure over from Konopka 2019 — the two trials used different doses.
- (b) Cite the corrigendum precisely: Corrigendum, Aging Cell 2020 Jan 15;19(3):e13098, doi 10.1111/acel.13098, PMID 32141718, correcting Walton RG et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039 (PMID 31557380), NCT02308228. Corrected Table 2 'Relative strength (kg/kg)': placebo N=44, 3.89 (1.48) to 4.62 (1.74), +18.9% (19.1); metformin N=44, 4.60 (1.39) to 5.23 (1.58), +14.8% (18.3); p = 0.30. The superseded original values were 19.7% (19.0) vs 14.5% (17.9), p = 0.188 — worth naming explicitly, since the correction moved the p-value from 0.188 to 0.30 and shrank the placebo advantage.
- (c) Describe the Cell 2024 monkey study with all of: article type RESOURCE (not a standard Article); the authors' own words 'proof-of-concept study'; MALE cynomolgus monkeys only; aged 13-16 years at start (16-19 at endpoint); 20 mg/kg/day metformin delivered in drinking water; 1,200 days of dosing within a 40-month study. Group sizes from the Figure 1 legend: 'Y-Ctrl, n = 6; M-Ctrl, n = 3; O-Ctrl, n = 5; O-Met, n = 6 monkeys.' Note the aged control arm is n=5, not 6, because one control monkey died of kidney failure on day 1,126.
- (c) Quote the limitations verbatim: 'The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation.' Consider pairing it with the adjacent sentence, also verbatim: 'We have noted that metformin potentially slows aging at molecular and tissue levels in males, but conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse, and a full understanding of its side effects in humans remains elusive.'
- (c) Barzilai's 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' is a real quote — source it precisely as the Lifespan.io interview 'Nir Barzilai: "Positive Evidence for Metformin is Mounting"', 12 August 2025 — and state flatly that the paper contains no such number. The paper's largest bulk transcriptAge effect is Achilles tendon at -5.31 years; the largest figure anywhere in the paper across all omic layers is -6.86 years (microglia single-nucleus transcriptAge); the headline is 'a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging.' The gap is roughly 50%.
- (c) REMOVE or reattribute the 'six years younger' brain quote. I could not find Barzilai saying 'six years younger' in the Lifespan.io interview, which is the only primary Barzilai source I could reach; the ~6-year brain figure is the PAPER's own abstract wording ('a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging'). Attribute the 6-year brain number to Yang et al. 2024, not to Barzilai, unless a dated primary transcript of him saying it is produced.
- (c) When describing the clocks, say they were built de novo by the same laboratory using ElasticNet and trained on the study's own control animals — verbatim: 'By integrating data from the Y-Ctrl, M-Ctrl, and O-Ctrl cohorts (a total of 36 monkeys), we were able to formulate a penalized linear model.' The key methodological point is that the O-Ctrl comparison arm sits inside the training set and there is no external validation cohort or pre-existing published monkey clock used as a check. If the article states a training-cohort size, flag that the paper's '36 monkeys' cannot be reconciled with its own Figure 1 group sizes (6 + 3 + 5 = 14 controls, 20 including the treated arm), and the paper does not explain the discrepancy.
- (d) Correct the framing of Barzilai's under-50 statement. Verbatim: 'Whoever takes metformin who doesn't have diabetes and is not at least 50 years old is making a mistake, in particular if they're trying to build their muscle or increase their VO2max.' He grounds it in antagonistic pleiotropy, with the exercise interaction as an aggravating case ('in particular if'), not as the reason. Do not write 'because of the exercise interaction'; write that he calls it a mistake on antagonistic-pleiotropy grounds, 'in particular' for those trying to build muscle or raise VO2max. Source: Lifespan.io, 12 August 2025.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The '8 years' figure Barzilai used publicly is contradicted by the paper he was describing. Yang et al. Cell 2024 reports NO effect estimate of eight years at any omic layer. Bulk transcriptAge ΔAgeDiff maxima, verbatim: Achilles tendon -5.31 y, liver -4.14 y, bronchus -3.71 y, muscle -3.56 y, lung -3.40 y. The single largest value anywhere in the paper is -6.86 y (microglia sn-transcriptAge). The abstract's headline is 'a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging.' Barzilai's number exceeds the paper's own top transcriptomic figure by ~50%.
- Plausible source of Barzilai's error, from the SAME interview: describing his unrelated centenarian-offspring human proteomics he says verbatim, 'They were, on average, eight years younger on a proteomic level than their spouses.' The 'eight years' appears to be imported from that human dataset into the monkey study.
- Konopka 2019's mitochondrial result is weaker than the abstract implies. The abstract asserts 'Metformin also abrogated the exercise-mediated increase in skeletal muscle mitochondrial respiration', but the Results state 'With placebo, AET nonsignificantly increased CI_P and CI+FAO_P (both p = 0.07)' — i.e. the exercise-mediated increase that metformin supposedly abrogated did not itself reach significance on those measures. Any article claiming metformin 'blocked a significant training gain in mitochondrial respiration' is over-reading the paper.
- The MASTERS strength story was weaker after correction than before. The corrigendum moved relative strength from +19.7% vs +14.5%, p=0.188 to +18.9% vs +14.8%, p=0.30 — i.e. the corrected data are LESS supportive of a metformin penalty on relative strength than the originally published table. Any secondary source citing 19.7/14.5 or p=0.188 is citing retracted numbers.
- The two metformin-plus-exercise trials used different doses (Konopka target 2,000 mg/day; MASTERS 1,700 mg/day), different modalities (aerobic vs progressive resistance), different durations (12 vs 14 weeks) and different age floors (mean 62 vs 65 and older). They should not be pooled or described as replications of each other.
- On Barzilai's own logic there is an internal tension worth noting: he invokes the VO2max concern as a reason for under-50 non-diabetics to avoid metformin, but the VO2max attenuation in Konopka 2019 was p = 0.08 and did not reach significance. The insulin-sensitivity and mitochondrial findings are the statistically supported parts of that trial; VO2max is not.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

Method note: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before my first call, so I worked primary-document-first through NCBI E-utilities, the Europe PMC REST full-text XML API, the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, and a real browser for the Cell Open Archive page. Several search front-ends (DuckDuckGo HTML, Mojeek, Brave) served CAPTCHAs or 429s; I did not attempt to solve any CAPTCHA. Because of the pipeline's prior fabrication incident, I did not accept summarizer output for any load-bearing number: every quoted string below was extracted by running string searches against the actual document text in the browser, and both Table 2 rows were parsed cell-by-cell through the XML DOM rather than read off a rendered table.

Documents reached verbatim: (1) Konopka et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(1):e12880, full text via Europe PMC PMC6351883 — confirmed 26+27=53 randomised, 62±1 y, titration to 2000 mg/day, insulin-sensitivity interaction p<0.05 with inhibition at p=0.02, and the exact string 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO2max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.08, Figure 1b)'. The article's own warning about the VO2max p-value is correct and should stay. The only slippage is that the ~25% figure is specific to maximal CI-linked respiration during the ADP titration. (2) MASTERS, PMC6826125 plus NCT02308228 via API — 109 randomised confirmed in the paper text, and the 55/54 split confirmed structurally from the participant-flow milestones (STARTED: metformin 54, placebo 55). The pre-specified directional hypothesis is confirmed twice, in the paper and in the registry's primary-outcome description. (3) Corrigendum PMC7059173 (Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098, JATS article-type='correction') — exists, and its corrected relative-strength row matches the claim digit for digit: placebo 18.9 (19.1), metformin 14.8 (18.3), p = 0.30; I additionally pulled the original erroneous row (19.7 / 14.5, p = 0.188) for contrast. (4) Yang et al., Cell 2024, read in full on cell.com where it is Open Archive — 'RESOURCE' label, 'proof-of-concept study', males aged 13-16 at start, 20 mg/kg/day in drinking water, O-Met = 6 wherever specified, clocks trained on the study's own 36 control monkeys by ElasticNet with LOOCV, and the limitations section stating the study 'omitted assessments of monkey mortality'. (5) The Barzilai quotes traced to their actual source: the Lifespan.io interview of 12 August 2025, where both the 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' line and the under-50 line appear verbatim.

What remains uncertain: I could not verify that Barzilai ever restated the brain result as 'six years younger'. The interview that carries the eight-year quote contains no six-year figure at all, and with search engines unavailable I could not canvass podcasts or other interviews. I am marking that sub-claim unreachable rather than guessing. The substantive point stands on firmer ground anyway: the ~6-year brain figure is the paper's own abstract language, so the article should attribute 6 years to the paper and 8 years to Barzilai. Two further caliber issues emerged that the claim group did not anticipate and that I judge more consequential than anything it did flag: MASTERS' registered primary endpoint was null for metformin, so 'they found the opposite' is true only of secondary body-composition measures; and the Konopka trial was a 2x2 with a co-randomised beverage factor, with peak aerobic capacity registered as a primary outcome — which makes the p=0.08 VO2max result a primary-endpoint null.

- **(a) Konopka 2019: 53 older adults, mean age 62, randomised to metformin vs placebo alongside aerobic exercise training** — `confirmed`
  Aging Cell 2019;18(1):e12880 (PMID 30548390, PMC6351883), read as Europe PMC full-text XML. Abstract verbatim: 'participants were randomized to placebo (n = 26) or metformin (n = 27) treatment during 12 weeks of AET' = 53, and 'older adults (62 ± 1 years)'. Table 1 shows the two arms separately as 63 ± 1 and 62 ± 1. One omission worth knowing: the registration (NCT02552355, 'Milk Protein Feeding After Aerobic Exercise in Older Adults With Pre-diabetes Taking the Biguanide Metformin', actual enrollment 56) is a 2x2 design in which subjects were ALSO randomised to a protein vs carbohydrate beverage — four arms, not two.

- **(a) metformin titrated to 2,000 mg/day** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the paper: 'The dose for both placebo and metformin was 500 mg/day the first week and increased by 500 mg each week until reaching 2000 mg/day (1,000 mg twice daily) by week 4.' (paper writes '2000 mg/day', no comma — cosmetic only).

- **(a) metformin attenuated the training-induced improvement in insulin sensitivity** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'There was a significant interaction (p < 0.05, time by treatment) for an increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity, evaluated by the Matsuda index, after AET with placebo but not metformin' and 'On average, the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity after AET was inhibited (p = 0.02) by metformin'. So this one IS significant (p=0.02), unlike VO2max. 58% of metformin subjects were positive responders, 42% negative.

- **(a) NOTE TO VERIFY: the VO2max result was p=0.08 and is routinely miscited as significant** — `confirmed`
  The note is correct and should be kept. Verbatim from Results: 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO2max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.08, Figure 1b).' The abstract's looser wording ('metformin attenuated the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO2 max after AET') is what drives the miscitation. Note also that Peak Aerobic Capacity was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as one of several primary outcome measures, so the non-significant VO2max result is a null on a registered primary outcome, not a secondary.

- **(a) metformin abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration** — `corrected`
  WRONG (as generically stated): 'abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration'. RIGHT: the verbatim sentence is 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration.' The ~25% figure applies specifically to MAXIMAL COMPLEX-I-LINKED respiration measured during the ADP titration, not to mitochondrial respiration in general. (I confirmed this string byte-for-byte in the Europe PMC full-text XML, not via a summarizer.)

- **(b) MASTERS: 109 randomised (55 placebo, 54 metformin) older adults in progressive resistance training** — `confirmed`
  Walton et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039 (PMID 31557380, PMC6826125). Paper verbatim: 'Of 109 randomized subjects, 15 participants discontinued the study (n = 6 due to adverse events), resulting in a final analytic sample of 94 (86%) who completed the study (n = 46 Metformin; n = 48 Placebo).' The 55/54 split comes from the NCT02308228 results participant-flow module, parsed structurally from the ClinicalTrials.gov API: STARTED = Metformin 54, Placebo 55; COMPLETED = 46 / 48. Beware that the published abstract quotes only 'N = 46 / N = 48', so a reader checking the abstract alone will think the trial was 94.

- **(b) the investigators' PRE-SPECIFIED hypothesis was that metformin would enhance the response, and they found the opposite** — `corrected`
  The DIRECTION of the pre-specified hypothesis is confirmed verbatim: 'Metformin reduces inflammation, so we hypothesized that metformin would augment the muscle response to PRT in healthy women and men aged 65 and older', and the registry's own primary-outcome description reads 'The ability of metformin to improve the hypertrophic response to resistance training will be determined.' BUT the caliber is off on what 'found the opposite' rests on. WRONG implication: that the pre-specified primary endpoint went the other way. RIGHT: the single registered PRIMARY outcome was 'Percent Change in Type 2 Myofiber Cross Sectional Area' at 16 weeks, and metformin had NO effect on it — the abstract states 'metformin did not affect fiber hypertrophy'. The opposite-direction findings are on DXA lean body mass (p=.003), thigh muscle mass (p<.001), and CT thigh muscle area (p=.005) and density (p=.020), none of which is the registered primary endpoint. Dose was 1,700 mg/day (not 2,000).

- **(b) Table 2 relative-strength values were wrong in the original publication and were replaced by corrigendum (corrected: placebo +18.9% vs metformin +14.8%, p=0.30)** — `confirmed`
  Corrigendum exists and the numbers are exactly right. Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098, doi 10.1111/acel.13098, PMID 32141718, PMC7059173, JATS article-type='correction', epub 15 Jan 2020 / print March 2020. Notice verbatim: 'In Table 2, data in row Relative strength (kg/kg)c mean (SD) were incorrect. The correct data is shown as follow:'. I parsed the corrected table row through the XML DOM (cell-by-cell, not by reading a rendered table) to avoid column-misalignment: Placebo N=44, baseline 3.89 (1.48), 14-week 4.62 (1.74), %change 18.9 (19.1); Metformin N=44, baseline 4.60 (1.39), 14-week 5.23 (1.58), %change 14.8 (18.3); p = 0.30. The ORIGINAL (still uncorrected in PMC6826125) read: Placebo N=45, 3.43 (3.27), 3.99 (3.70), 19.7 (19.0); Metformin N=44, 4.40 (4.49), 4.72 (4.70), 14.5 (17.9); p = 0.188. Footnote c defines 'relative strength' as 'kg knee extension/kg thigh muscle mass'. The corrigendum adds that related measures in Appendix S2 were updated online.

- **(c) Yang et al., Cell 2024 is a proof-of-concept Resource article in MALE cynomolgus monkeys aged 13-16 at start, 20 mg/kg/day, with SIX treated animals** — `confirmed`
  Read the Open Archive full text on cell.com directly (article ID S0092-8674(24)00914-0; Cell 2024;187(22):6358-6378.e29). The page header reads 'RESOURCE Volume 187, Issue 22'. Verbatim: 'we conducted a proof-of-concept study involving male cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) aged between 13 and 16 years, roughly equivalent to approximately 40-50 years in humans' and 'The monkeys in the O-Met group were administered a daily dose of 20 mg/kg metformin'. STAR Methods: 'the O-Met group was treated every day with 20 mg/kg metformin administered through drinking water over the duration of the study (40 months)'. On N: the paper never states a single headline group size, but every place it is specified O-Met = 6 — 'The structural MRI analysis in this study involved 6 young monkeys in the Y-Ctrl group, 3 mature monkeys in the M-Ctrl group, 8 old monkeys in the O-Ctrl group, and 6 old monkeys in the O-Met group' and 'In the cognitive testing phase, 5 monkeys from the O-Ctrl group and 6 from the O-Met group participated'. snRNA-seq used only 3 monkeys per group. One O-Ctrl monkey died of kidney failure on day 1,126; treatment ran 1,200 days (~3.3 years).

- **(c) the authors' own limitations state they did NOT measure survival** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from 'Limitations of the study': 'We have noted that metformin potentially slows aging at molecular and tissue levels in males, but conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse, and a full understanding of its side effects in humans remains elusive. The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation.' So: no survival/mortality endpoint, and the authors themselves call functional-rejuvenation evidence 'sparse'.

- **(c) Barzilai publicly restated it as 'Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level'** — `confirmed`
  He said it — and the paper does not support it. Primary source located: Lifespan.io interview 'Nir Barzilai: "Positive Evidence for Metformin is Mounting"', 12 August 2025. Verbatim: 'Then there's the monkey study published in Cell, which was a big deal. Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level.' No figure of 8 years appears anywhere in the Cell paper. The paper's transcriptAge ΔAgeDiff values are Achilles tendon -5.31 years (the largest), liver -4.14, bronchus -3.71, muscle -3.56, lung -3.40; frontal-lobe single-nucleus transcriptAge averaged -5.90 years; the largest single number anywhere in the paper is proteinAge -6.41 years (proteome, not transcriptome) and microglia sn-transcriptAge -6.86 years. Likely source of the error: in the SAME interview Barzilai says centenarian offspring were 'on average, eight years younger on a proteomic level than their spouses' — a different study, a different omic layer, a different eight.

- **(c) Barzilai restated the brain result as 'six years younger'** — `unreachable`
  Could not reach any Barzilai statement using 'six years' for the brain. I searched the full text of the Lifespan.io interview where the 'eight years' quote lives: it contains no 'six years' or '6 years' string anywhere, and its only mentions of 'brain' are about organ-specific proteomics and GLP-1 agonists, not the monkey study. Web search was largely unavailable to me (the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I started, and DuckDuckGo/Mojeek/Brave fell back to CAPTCHAs or rate limits, which I did not attempt to bypass), so I cannot rule out that he said it elsewhere. What I CAN state: the ~6-year brain figure is the PAPER'S OWN headline, verbatim in the Cell abstract — 'The results highlighted a significant slowing of aging indicators, notably a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging' — so framing '6 years' as a Barzilai overstatement inverts the attribution.

- **(c) whether the clocks were trained by the same laboratory on a small monkey cohort** — `corrected`
  Substantially right, but 'the same laboratory' is loose. RIGHT: the clocks were bespoke models trained de novo on the study's OWN control animals and never externally validated. Verbatim: 'By integrating data from the Y-Ctrl, M-Ctrl, and O-Ctrl cohorts (a total of 36 monkeys), we were able to formulate a penalized linear model'. STAR Methods for both the DNA-methylation and the multi-model clocks: aging-associated features were selected in the Y-Ctrl/M-Ctrl/O-Ctrl groups, an ElasticNet was trained on those same three groups with leave-one-out cross-validation, and then 'the O-Met group was used as an input to predict transcriptAge' — i.e. the treated animals were never part of training, but the clock's entire notion of monkey age comes from ~36 in-house controls. WRONG in the strict sense: it was not one laboratory. Author contributions read 'Z. Zheng and P.R. performed the aging clock construction. X.L., A.H., and S.H. performed bioinformatics analysis of the aging clock', and the declaration of interests states P.R., A.H., S.H. (Steve Horvath) and others are Altos Labs employees, with Horvath a founder of the Epigenetic Clock Development Foundation.

- **(d) Barzilai has stated that people under 50 without diabetes should not take metformin because of the exercise interaction** — `corrected`
  The age-50 claim is confirmed verbatim; the 'because of the exercise interaction' rationale is only partly right. Same Lifespan.io interview (12 Aug 2025), verbatim: 'metformin is not for young people; it's only for old people' and 'Whoever takes metformin who doesn't have diabetes and is not at least 50 years old is making a mistake, in particular if they're trying to build their muscle or increase their VO2max.' WRONG: that the exercise interaction is his reason. RIGHT: his stated primary reason is antagonistic pleiotropy plus a new ITP re-analysis — 'there's a new study from the ITP, which re-analyzes their own data and shows that metformin wasn't good in the first half of the animals' lives but performed significantly better in the second half of life' — with muscle-building and VO2max introduced as an aggravating case ('in particular if...'), not the basis of the rule.

**修正:**
- Konopka 2019, mitochondrial result: change 'abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration' to the paper's actual scope — 'abolished the ~25% increase in maximal complex-I-linked respiration during the ADP titration'. The paper's verbatim sentence is: 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration.'
- Konopka 2019, insulin sensitivity: state the statistic, because it is the contrast that makes the VO2max caveat land. Significant time-by-treatment interaction (p < 0.05) for the Matsuda index increasing with placebo but not metformin, and metformin inhibited the average increase at p = 0.02 — unlike VO2max at p = 0.08.
- Konopka 2019, design: the trial (NCT02552355) was a 2x2 in which participants were co-randomised to a protein vs carbohydrate beverage as well as to metformin vs placebo. If the article describes it as a simple two-arm metformin-vs-placebo trial, add the beverage factor or say 'metformin vs placebo arm of a 2x2 trial'.
- MASTERS: do not imply the pre-specified primary endpoint went the opposite way. The single registered primary outcome (NCT02308228) was 'Percent Change in Type 2 Myofiber Cross Sectional Area' at 16 weeks, and metformin had NO effect on it — the paper states 'metformin did not affect fiber hypertrophy'. The opposite-direction results are DXA lean body mass (p=.003), thigh muscle mass (p<.001), CT thigh muscle area (p=.005) and density (p=.020). Phrase it as: the pre-specified DIRECTIONAL HYPOTHESIS was that metformin would augment the response, and the secondary body-composition endpoints went the other way while the primary myofiber endpoint was null.
- MASTERS: state the dose as 1,700 mg/day (titrated: 850 mg/day for 7 days, then 1,700 mg/day), and define 'relative strength' as kg knee extension per kg thigh muscle mass — otherwise the +18.9% vs +14.8% figures read as raw strength gains.
- MASTERS corrigendum: cite it precisely as Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098, doi 10.1111/acel.13098 (PMID 32141718), and note the original erroneous values for contrast — original: placebo 19.7% (19.0) vs metformin 14.5% (17.9), p = 0.188; corrected: placebo 18.9% (19.1) vs metformin 14.8% (18.3), p = 0.30. Also note the corrected baselines (placebo 3.89, metformin 4.60) differ from the originals (3.43, 4.40) and that the PMC copy of the original article still shows the uncorrected row.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: do NOT attribute the 'six years' brain figure to Barzilai as an overstatement. 'A roughly 6-year regression in brain aging' is the paper's own abstract wording. I found no Barzilai statement using a six-year brain figure. Attribute the 6 years to the paper and the 8 years to Barzilai.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: when saying the eight-year figure is unsupported, give the paper's actual transcriptomic numbers. Tissue-level transcriptAge ΔAgeDiff maxes out at -5.31 years (Achilles tendon), with liver -4.14, bronchus -3.71, muscle -3.56, lung -3.40; frontal-lobe single-nucleus transcriptAge averaged -5.90 years. The largest number anywhere in the paper is proteinAge -6.41 years (proteome, not transcriptome). No eight-year figure exists in the paper.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: if the article speculates about where Barzilai's 'eight years' came from, the same interview supplies a candidate — he separately says centenarian offspring were 'on average, eight years younger on a proteomic level than their spouses'. Present this as a plausible conflation, not as established fact.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024, clocks: replace 'trained by the same laboratory' with the accurate and stronger point — the clocks were bespoke ElasticNet models trained de novo on the study's own control animals (36 monkeys across Y-Ctrl, M-Ctrl and O-Ctrl) with leave-one-out cross-validation, then applied to the treated group; they were never externally validated. Note that clock construction and analysis involved Altos Labs personnel including Steve Horvath, so it was not a single lab marking its own homework in the narrow sense.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: quote the limitations accurately. The authors write that 'conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse' and that 'The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation.' Also worth stating: treatment ran 1,200 days (~3.3 years) within a 40-month study, and one control monkey died of kidney failure on day 1,126.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024, N: say that the paper never reports a single headline group size, and that six is the O-Met number wherever it is specified (6 in the MRI analysis, 6 in cognitive testing, against 8 O-Ctrl for MRI and 5 O-Ctrl for cognition), while the single-nucleus RNA-seq used only 3 animals per group.
- Barzilai's under-50 statement: source it and get the rationale right. Lifespan.io interview, 12 August 2025 — 'Whoever takes metformin who doesn't have diabetes and is not at least 50 years old is making a mistake, in particular if they're trying to build their muscle or increase their VO2max.' His stated basis is antagonistic pleiotropy plus an ITP re-analysis showing metformin 'wasn't good in the first half of the animals' lives but performed significantly better in the second half of life'; the exercise/muscle/VO2max interaction is an aggravating case he flags, not the reason for the age threshold. Do not write 'because of the exercise interaction' without that qualification.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Barzilai's 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' is contradicted by the paper's own numbers, which I read in the Open Archive full text: the largest tissue-level transcriptAge ΔAgeDiff is -5.31 years (Achilles tendon), and the largest figure of any kind in the paper is proteinAge -6.41 years. There is no 8-year result in the paper on any omic layer.
- The same Lifespan.io interview contains a different, unrelated 'eight years' — centenarian offspring being 'on average, eight years younger on a proteomic level than their spouses' — which independently suggests the monkey figure is a conflation rather than a citation.
- MASTERS' registered primary endpoint (percent change in type 2 myofiber cross-sectional area, NCT02308228) was null for metformin; the paper's abstract states 'metformin did not affect fiber hypertrophy'. Any framing that the trial's primary endpoint showed metformin blunting hypertrophy is contradicted by the registry and the paper together.
- The Konopka trial registration (NCT02552355) reveals a 2x2 design with a co-randomised protein vs carbohydrate beverage and an actual enrollment of 56, which is not evident from the paper's framing as a metformin-vs-placebo trial in 53 people.
- Konopka's registration lists Peak Aerobic Capacity among the primary outcome measures, which makes the p = 0.08 VO2max result a null on a registered primary outcome — a stronger point against the drug-blunts-fitness narrative than the article's current framing, and one that cuts against citing the study as positive evidence of a VO2max effect at all.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Primary documents reached and read directly, not via summary: (1) Konopka et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(1):e12880 — I downloaded the PMC full text (PMC6351883) to disk, stripped the markup, and grepped it so every quoted string is one I saw in the raw text. (2) Walton et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039 — same procedure on PMC6826125, including Table 1 and Table 2 as rendered. (3) The corrigendum, Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098 / PMID 32141718 / PMC7059173, read on two independent routes (PMC page and the Europe PMC full-text XML endpoint) which returned identical corrected values. (4) ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308228 pulled as raw JSON from the v2 API and parsed locally, giving the official title, actual enrollment, and the single registered primary outcome. (5) Yang et al., Cell 2024;187(22):6358-6378.e29 — paywalled on cell.com (403 direct, closed in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar), so I retrieved it as plain text through a text-extraction proxy, saved 134 KB to disk, and grepped it locally for group sizes, dose, the Limitations section, the clock-training cohort, and every year-figure. All 'verbatim' strings in this report were matched in files on disk, not lifted from a fetch summary — I did this deliberately because two of my early WebFetch summaries were unreliable (one returned an unrelated autophagy review for a PMC ID, another quoted a Limitations passage whose keywords my first grep could not find until I located the section by line number). What holds: Konopka's 53 randomised (26/27), age 62 ± 1, the ~25% CI-linked respiration abolition, and — importantly — the p = 0.08 VO2max warning, which is exactly right and traceable to the paper's own unqualified abstract. MASTERS' 109 randomised split 55/54, the registry-confirmed pre-specified enhancement hypothesis, and the corrigendum values 18.9% vs 14.8%, p = 0.30 all check out verbatim. The Cell 2024 descriptors — Resource, proof-of-concept, male, 13-16 years at start, 20 mg/kg/day, six treated, no mortality assessment, in-house clocks on 36 of the authors' own monkeys — all check out. What does not: 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' has no counterpart in the Cell paper (max -5.31 years), while 'six years younger' brain is the paper's own abstract claim rather than an inflation. Two additions the article needs: Konopka's dose was a 2,000 mg/day target that a fifth of participants did not hold, and MASTERS' registered primary endpoint (type 2 myofiber CSA) was null at p = .610, so the headline rests on secondary outcomes in completers. A live hazard: PMC still serves the uncorrected MASTERS Table 2. What remains uncertain and I refuse to guess at: both Barzilai attributions — the 'eight years' quote and the under-50 recommendation in (d). The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before my first call, and every fallback engine blocked me — DuckDuckGo HTML and Lite served an image CAPTCHA I will not solve, Mojeek gave 403 then a CAPTCHA, Brave 429, Ecosia 403, four SearXNG instances CAPTCHA/429/403, and Bing returned unrelated boilerplate. I reached no transcript, article, or post in which Barzilai says either thing, so both are marked unreachable rather than filled from memory. The scientific substance of (c) is settled independently of who said it; the attribution is not.

- **(a) Konopka 2019: 53 older adults (mean age 62) randomised to metformin or placebo alongside aerobic exercise training** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in the PMC full text (Aging Cell 2019;18(1):e12880, PMC6351883): 'in older adults (62 ± 1 years). In a double-blinded fashion, participants were randomized to placebo (n = 26) or metformin (n = 27) treatment during 12 weeks of AET.' 26+27 = 53. Note 62 ± 1 is mean ± SEM, not SD. Training was 12 weeks of AET.

- **(a) metformin titrated to 2,000 mg/day** — `corrected`
  The TARGET dose was 2,000 mg/day, but a flat '(titrated to 2,000 mg/day)' overstates what participants actually took. Verbatim: 'The dose for both placebo and metformin was 500 mg/day the first week and increased by 500 mg each week until reaching 2000 mg/day (1,000 mg twice daily) by week 4. If participants weighed <75 kg, the maximum dose was 1,500 mg/day (n = 5).' And: 'The dose was decreased from 2,000 to 1,500 mg/day in 11 participants who reported gastrointestinal discomfort (placebo n = 3; metformin n = 8).' RIGHT version: titrated to a target of 2,000 mg/day, capped at 1,500 mg/day for participants under 75 kg (n=5) and reduced to 1,500 mg/day in 11 more for GI intolerance.

- **(a) metformin attenuated the training-induced improvement in insulin sensitivity** — `corrected`
  Directionally right, but the measure is not what most readers assume. Verbatim: 'There was a significant interaction (p < 0.05, time by treatment) for an increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity, evaluated by the Matsuda index, after AET with placebo but not metformin (Figure 1c). On average, the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity after AET was inhibited (p = 0.02) by metformin (Figure 1d).' WRONG if written as clamp-measured insulin sensitivity; RIGHT version: Matsuda index derived from an oral glucose tolerance test, not a hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, and this outcome was available in only 24 placebo / 25 metformin (figure legend: 'PLA (n = 24), MET (n = 25)'), not the full 53. Also: 58% of the metformin arm were positive responders and 42% negative — the group mean masks a split response.

- **(a) metformin abolished the ~25% training increase in mitochondrial respiration** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration.' Precision point: this is maximal complex-I-linked respiration during the ADP titration in permeabilised muscle fibres, not mitochondrial respiration in general.

- **(a) The VO2max result was p=0.08 and is routinely miscited as significant** — `confirmed`
  The warning is correct and I read the sentence myself. Verbatim from the Results: 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO 2 max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.08, Figure 1 b).' The origin of the miscitation is the paper's own abstract, which says without qualification: 'However, metformin attenuated the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO 2 max after AET.' A second trap in the same paragraph is a within-group vs between-group fallacy: 'VO 2 max (L/min) was significantly increased after 12 weeks of AET (p < 0.05, main effect for time) with a significant increase within the placebo group (p < 0.01) but not metformin.' Significant in one arm and not the other is NOT a significant difference between arms.

- **(b) MASTERS: 109 randomised, 55 placebo and 54 metformin, older adults in progressive resistance training** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in Table 1 of the PMC full text (Walton et al., Aging Cell 2019;18(6):e13039, PMC6826125): 'Randomized N = 55' (Placebo) and 'N = 54' (Metformin). Text: 'Of 109 randomized subjects, 15 participants discontinued the study (n = 6 due to adverse events), resulting in a final analytic sample of 94 (86%) who completed the study (n = 46 Metformin; n = 48 Placebo).' ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308228 lists enrollment 109 ACTUAL. Note the reported analysis is of the 94 completers, not intention-to-treat. Dose was 1,700 mg/day; 14 weeks of supervised PRT within a 16-week drug period.

- **(b) The investigators' pre-specified hypothesis was that metformin would ENHANCE the response, and they found the opposite** — `confirmed`
  Pre-specification verified from the registry, not just the paper. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308228 official title: 'Novel Actions of Metformin to Augment Resistance Training Adaptations in Older Adults'; registry primary-outcome description: 'The ability of metformin to improve the hypertrophic response to resistance training will be determined.' Paper abstract verbatim: 'Metformin reduces inflammation, so we hypothesized that metformin would augment the muscle response to PRT in healthy women and men aged 65 and older.' Result was the opposite direction: 'placebo gained more lean body mass (p = .003) and thigh muscle mass (p < .001) than metformin.'

- **(b) A corrigendum replaced the Table 2 relative-strength values; corrected values placebo +18.9% vs metformin +14.8%, p=0.30** — `confirmed`
  Corrigendum exists and the numbers match exactly. Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098, doi 10.1111/acel.13098, PMID 32141718, PMC7059173, e-published 15 Jan 2020. It states: 'In Table 2, data in row Relative strength (kg/kg) mean (SD) were incorrect.' Corrected row, read on two independent routes (PMC page and Europe PMC full-text XML), identical both times: Placebo N=44, baseline 3.89 (1.48), 14 wk PRT 4.62 (1.74), % change 18.9 (19.1); Metformin N=44, baseline 4.60 (1.39), 14 wk PRT 5.23 (1.58), % change 14.8 (18.3); p = 0.30. It adds that 'related measures presented in Appendix S2 under Supporting Information have been updated online.' The corrigendum also changes the placebo N from 45 to 44.

- **(b) Live trap: the UNCORRECTED relative-strength values are still what a reader of the article itself will find** — `corrected`
  Not asserted in the claim, but it will bite the article if unstated. The PMC copy of the original paper (PMC6826125) STILL displays the pre-correction values in both the running text and Table 2. Body text verbatim: 'Relative strength (knee extension kg/bilateral thigh muscle mass kg) gains following PRT were similar in both groups, with placebo improving 19.7% (SD 19.0) and metformin improving 14.5% (SD 17.9) (between groups p = .188).' Table 2 as displayed: 'Relative strength (kg/kg) mean (SD) 45 3.43 (3.27) 3.99 (3.70) 19.7 (19.0) 44 4.40 (4.49) 4.72 (4.70) 14.5 (17.9) 0.188'. WRONG (uncorrected, still live on PMC): 19.7% vs 14.5%, p=.188. RIGHT (corrigendum): 18.9% vs 14.8%, p=0.30.

- **(b) Material omission: the PRE-SPECIFIED PRIMARY ENDPOINT of MASTERS was null** — `corrected`
  The claim group frames MASTERS as a clean pre-specified-hypothesis reversal, which understates a problem for the 'metformin blunts hypertrophy' headline. NCT02308228 registers exactly ONE primary outcome: 'Percent Change in Type 2 Myofiber Cross Sectional Area', time frame 16 weeks. That endpoint was NOT significant. Paper verbatim: 'Metformin also did not affect type II fiber hypertrophy with PRT; mean type II CSA change in placebo was 18.5% (SD 31.5) versus 14.5% (SD 29...)' with 'p = .610' reported in the Figure 3 legend, and immunohistochemistry performed in only 30 subjects/group. The significant results carrying the title — lean body mass (p = .003), thigh muscle mass (p < .001), total thigh muscle area by CT 6.43% vs 2.27% (p = .005) — are SECONDARY outcomes. Strength outcomes were all null: 1RM 23.1% vs 15.3% (p = .055), isometric 11.8% vs 6.7% (p = .082), power 29.4% vs 14.3% (p = .064).

- **(c) Yang et al., Cell 2024 is a proof-of-concept Resource article in male cynomolgus monkeys aged 13-16 at start, 20 mg/kg/day, with six treated animals** — `confirmed`
  All four elements verified against the full text of Cell 2024;187(22):6358-6378.e29, doi 10.1016/j.cell.2024.08.021 (retrieved as raw text and grepped locally, not read through a summarizer). Article-type label on the journal page: 'RESOURCE Volume 187, Issue 22 P6358-6378.E29 October 31, 2024 Open Archive'. Verbatim: 'we conducted a proof-of-concept study involving male cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) aged between 13 and 16 years, roughly equivalent to approximately 40-50 years in humans.' Dose verbatim: 'The monkeys in the O-Met group were administered a daily dose of 20 mg/kg metformin' and, in STAR Methods, 'treated every day with 20 mg/kg metformin administered through drinking water over the duration of the study (40 months).' Treated-group size: the paper never states an overall N for the treated (O-Met) arm anywhere in text, but every O-Met count it does give is six — 'The structural MRI analysis in this study involved 6 young monkeys in the Y-Ctrl group, 3 mature monkeys in the M-Ctrl group, 8 old monkeys in the O-Ctrl group, and 6 old monkeys in the O-Met group' and 'In the cognitive testing phase, 5 monkeys from the O-Ctrl group and 6 from the O-Met group participated.' Duration 1,200 days ≈ 3.3 years; one O-Ctrl monkey 'succumbed to kidney failure on the 1,126th day'.

- **(c) The authors' own limitations state they did NOT measure survival** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from the 'Limitations of the study' section: 'The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation.' One wording nuance: the paper says 'mortality', not 'survival'. The same paragraph also concedes 'conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse' and 'a current emphasis on male subjects'.

- **(c) The aging clocks were trained by the same laboratory on a small monkey cohort** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: 'By integrating data from the Y-Ctrl, M-Ctrl, and O-Ctrl cohorts (a total of 36 monkeys), we were able to formulate a penalized linear model (see STAR Methods).' The clocks (DNAmAge, transcriptAge, proteinAge, metabolAge) are ElasticNet/glmnet models built in-house on the authors' own 36 control monkeys spanning three age bands (Y-Ctrl 3-5 y, M-Ctrl 10-12 y, O-Ctrl and O-Met 16-19 y at endpoint), then applied to the treated arm: 'the O-Met group was used as an input to pre[dict]...'. For the single-nucleus models the training set was a 60/40 split of metacells. There is no external validation cohort and no independently developed primate clock used as a check.

- **(c) Barzilai's restatement 'Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level'** — `refuted`
  Refuted as a description of the paper. I searched the complete retrieved full text for 'eight', '8 years', '8.0', '7.9' and any 7-8 year figure: no such number exists anywhere in the article. The paper's actual transcriptomic numbers, verbatim: 'the transcriptAge of all thirteen tissues was restored to a younger state, including the Achilles tendon (ΔAgeDiff -5.31 years), liver (ΔAgeDiff -4.14 years), bronchus (ΔAgeDiff -3.71 years), muscle (ΔAgeDiff -3.56 years), and lung (ΔAgeDiff -3.40 years).' The largest transcriptomic effect reported anywhere is -5.31 years. The only figure approaching 6+ years are proteinAge ('resets the proteinAge of treated monkeys by an average of -6.41 years') and frontal-lobe DNAmAge (-6.10 years) — neither is transcriptomic. WHETHER BARZILAI SAID IT is a separate matter I could not check (see the attribution item).

- **(c) Barzilai's restatement of the brain result as 'six years younger'** — `confirmed`
  This one is NOT an exaggeration relative to the paper — it is the paper's own headline number, so an article that presents it as Barzilai inflating the finding would be attacking the wrong target. Cell abstract verbatim: 'The results highlighted a significant slowing of aging indicators, notably a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging.' Supporting values in the body: frontal-lobe DNAmAge 'restored by an average of -6.10' years, and frontal-lobe single-nucleus transcriptAge 'metformin treatment rescued the frontal lobe of monkeys by an average of 5.90 years'. The criticism to make is of the underlying number (n=6 treated, in-house clocks trained on 36 of the authors' own monkeys, no survival data), not of the restatement.

- **(c) Attribution of both quotes to Barzilai (that he publicly said them, in those words)** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach any primary record of Barzilai uttering either sentence and I am not going to supply one from memory. Before publishing, the article needs a citable Barzilai source (dated interview, transcript with timestamp, or post) for each quote.

  Not verified — I reached no primary Barzilai statement. Same blocked-search situation as above. The only things that surfaced were third-party SEO/aggregator pages (stackingyears.com, blog.aihavit.com, thewellsourced.com, progevita.com, biologicalx.com) that I would not cite: one of them asserts a 'TAME trial 2025 interim data' reshaping the debate, which is a strong tell for AI-generated filler given TAME's funding status, and none quoted Barzilai directly on an under-50 threshold. **修正:**
- Konopka 2019 VO2max: do not write that metformin significantly blunted the VO2max gain. The paper says verbatim: 'Metformin attenuated the increase in VO 2 max following 12 weeks of AET by ~50%, although this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.08, Figure 1b).' If the article wants to flag the miscitation, note that the paper's own abstract states the attenuation without the caveat, and that the Results also commit a within- vs between-group slip ('a significant increase within the placebo group (p < 0.01) but not metformin').
- Konopka 2019 dose: change 'titrated to 2,000 mg/day' to 'titrated toward a 2,000 mg/day target'. Participants under 75 kg were capped at 1,500 mg/day (n = 5) and the dose was cut from 2,000 to 1,500 mg/day in 11 further participants for GI intolerance (placebo n = 3, metformin n = 8).
- Konopka 2019 insulin sensitivity: specify the measure. It is the Matsuda index from an oral glucose tolerance test, NOT a hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, and it was available in 24 placebo / 25 metformin, not all 53. The between-group inhibition was p = 0.02. Add that the metformin arm split 58% positive / 42% negative responders, so the group mean is not the whole story.
- Konopka 2019 mitochondria: the '~25%' figure is specific. Verbatim: 'Metformin abolished the ~25% increase in maximal CI-linked respiration after AET during the ADP titration.' Write 'maximal complex-I-linked respiration', not 'mitochondrial respiration' generally.
- MASTERS: the corrigendum claim is exactly right and can be stated with confidence — Aging Cell 2020;19(3):e13098 (doi 10.1111/acel.13098, PMID 32141718, PMC7059173) corrects Table 2 to placebo 18.9% (SD 19.1) vs metformin 14.8% (SD 18.3), p = 0.30, both arms N = 44. Add the reason it matters: the uncorrected values 19.7% vs 14.5%, p = .188 are STILL displayed in the running text and Table 2 of the article on PubMed Central, so anyone verifying against PMC will reproduce the error.
- MASTERS: add the primary-endpoint qualifier, or the article overstates the trial. The single registered primary outcome (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308228) was percent change in type 2 myofiber cross-sectional area at 16 weeks, and it was NULL: 18.5% (SD 31.5) placebo vs 14.5% metformin, p = .610, in 30 subjects per group. The 'metformin blunts hypertrophy' conclusion rests on secondary outcomes — lean body mass (p = .003), thigh muscle mass (p < .001), CT total thigh muscle area 6.43% vs 2.27% (p = .005) — analysed in the 94 completers rather than intention-to-treat, while every strength outcome was null (1RM p = .055, isometric p = .082, power p = .064, relative strength p = 0.30).
- MASTERS pre-specification is strong and should be cited to the registry, not only the paper: the trial's official title is 'Novel Actions of Metformin to Augment Resistance Training Adaptations in Older Adults' and the registered primary-outcome description reads 'The ability of metformin to improve the hypertrophic response to resistance training will be determined.' The dose was 1,700 mg/day and the training was 14 weeks of supervised PRT within a 16-week drug period.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: delete or rewrite 'Aging was delayed by eight years on the transcriptomic level'. No 8-year figure appears anywhere in the paper. The transcriptomic values are ΔAgeDiff -5.31 years (Achilles tendon), -4.14 (liver), -3.71 (bronchus), -3.56 (muscle), -3.40 (lung). The 6+ year figures are proteinAge (-6.41 years) and frontal-lobe DNAmAge (-6.10 years), neither of which is 'the transcriptomic level'.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: do not present 'six years younger' brain as a Barzilai exaggeration. It is the paper's own abstract claim, verbatim: 'notably a roughly 6-year regression in brain aging'. Aim the criticism at the number's provenance instead: six treated males, in-house ElasticNet clocks trained on the same laboratory's 36 control monkeys across three age bands with no external validation cohort, and no survival data.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024: the 'no survival' point is correct but quote it accurately. The Limitations section says 'The study also omitted assessments of monkey mortality and the long-term effects following metformin cessation' — the word is 'mortality', not 'survival'. Useful adjacent concessions in the same paragraph: 'conclusive evidence of functional rejuvenation is sparse' and 'a current emphasis on male subjects'.
- Yang et al. Cell 2024 group size: the paper never states an overall N for the treated arm. Every O-Met count it does report is six ('6 old monkeys in the O-Met group' for structural MRI; '6 from the O-Met group' in cognitive testing). Phrase it as 'six treated animals in every analysis for which the paper reports a number' rather than implying a stated cohort N. Note also that the control arm size varies by analysis (8 for MRI, 5 for cognition) and one control monkey died of kidney failure on day 1,126.
- Both Barzilai quotes and the under-50 recommendation are currently UNSOURCED in this pipeline. Do not publish either the 'eight years' quote, the 'six years younger' attribution, or the under-50/exercise-interaction recommendation without a dated primary citation (interview transcript with timestamp, article, or verified post). I was unable to reach any such source; the article must not present them as established simply because they sound like things he has said.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The Cell 2024 monkey paper contains no 8-year or ~8-year figure of any kind. Grepping the complete retrieved full text for 'eight', '8 years', '8.0' and '7.9' in proximity to 'year' returns nothing. The maximum transcriptomic rescue reported is ΔAgeDiff -5.31 years (Achilles tendon). Any public restatement of 'eight years on the transcriptomic level' therefore has no anchor in the paper.
- MASTERS' registered primary endpoint failed. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02308228 lists one primary outcome, percent change in type 2 myofiber cross-sectional area at 16 weeks; the paper reports placebo 18.5% (SD 31.5) vs metformin 14.5%, p = .610. This substantially weakens MASTERS as evidence that metformin blunts hypertrophy — the positive findings are secondary outcomes.
- The corrigendum has not propagated. The PubMed Central copy of Walton et al. (PMC6826125) still shows the erroneous pre-correction relative-strength values in both the narrative text and Table 2 (19.7% vs 14.5%, p = .188, placebo N = 45), despite the 2020 corrigendum. Independent verifiers going to PMC will 'confirm' the wrong numbers.
- Konopka's own paper abstract is the vector for the VO2max miscitation: it asserts 'metformin attenuated the increase in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO 2 max after AET' with no mention of the p = 0.08 that appears in the Results. Downstream citations inherit the error from the abstract, not from careless secondary writers.
- The Cell 2024 clocks are not independent instruments. The same group built them from its own 36 control monkeys and then applied them to its own six treated monkeys, with no external primate clock or independent cohort used as a check. The reported 'years younger' effects are therefore internal to one laboratory's model.
- Konopka's insulin-sensitivity finding is not a uniform group effect: 58% of the metformin arm improved and 42% worsened, and the outcome was measured in only 24 and 25 participants per arm. A blanket statement that metformin blocks the exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gain is stronger than the data.
- Search-layer hazard worth recording for the pipeline: several pages that surface for 'Barzilai metformin non-diabetic' queries appear to be AI-generated filler, including one asserting 'TAME trial's 2025 interim data is reshaping the metformin longevity debate'. Any TAME interim-results claim entering the article from that stratum should be treated as fabricated until traced to a registry or journal record.
