### 票 1(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so all work was done via WebFetch against literature APIs (Europe PMC REST, PubMed, PMC, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall) and publisher pages.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM:
- Massudi et al., PLoS ONE 2012, PMID 22848760 / PMC3407129 — full abstract retrieved verbatim from the Europe PMC core record, including the sample sentence ('Human pelvic skin samples ... (n = 49)') and the sex-split correlation coefficients. (a) checks out; the sex-split and newborn-inclusion caveats are additions, not corrections.
- Zhu et al., PNAS 2015, PMID 25730862 / PMC4352772 — full text on PMC read twice on separate fetches, returning identical strings: 'Seventeen human volunteers (age: 21-68 y; 10 males and 7 females) participated in this study' and 'younger (21-26 y old; n = 7), middle (33-36 y old; n = 4), and older (59-68 y old; n = 6)'. Occipital lobe, 7 T. Every number in sub-claim (b)'s parenthetical is exactly right.
- Trętowicz et al., Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290, PMID 42135539 — abstract retrieved verbatim by two INDEPENDENT routes (Europe PMC core record and the nature.com article page after following the idp.nature.com redirect chain) and the two strings matched character-for-character, which is my confidence basis for quoting it. Author list (32 names) and full affiliation list from Europe PMC core. Publication date 2026-05-14. Figure captions from nature.com: only two figures, Fig. 2 titled 'Whole-blood NAD+ levels remain unchanged across age and lifestyle interventions.'
- Vinten et al., Nature Metabolism 2025;7(10):1974-1990, PMID 41083806 — full abstract retrieved verbatim from PubMed, containing the exact sentence the article paraphrases.

THE REFUTATION HUNT PAID OFF TWICE. First, a Europe PMC search for in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD studies surfaced at least six distinct studies, one of which (Cuenoud 2020, n=50) is nearly three times the size of Zhu 2015 and also examined age — so (b)'s 'entire' is false. Second, pulling the author list of the October 2025 review showed it is the same Amsterdam UMC lab as the May 2026 paper, so (e)'s 'independent' is false.

WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN. The per-cohort and total N for the May 2026 paper. Unpaywall returns is_oa false / oa_status 'closed' / zero OA locations, Semantic Scholar returns an empty openAccessPdf, and no preprint exists in Europe PMC. One WebFetch pass on the nature.com page returned a detailed, confident seven-cohort roster with n values and a ~347 total; a second pass on the identical URL established that the Main text is paywalled and that only abstract, figure captions, references and author info are visible. Because the pipeline has previously caught fetch summarizers fabricating specifics, and because the figure-caption pass contradicts the possibility of the Main text having been read, I am treating that roster as confabulated and reporting the N as unreachable rather than guessing. Someone with institutional access should read the PDF before the article prints any N.

I also cannot exhaustively prove the negative in (c), but I verified positively that the two candidate primary sources both report correlation coefficients and no percentage, and that the field's own current review calls the human tissue data 'sparse'.

Net: the article's strongest claim (d) survives, but only in a narrower form — whole blood, biomarker utility, not tissue NAD+ — and the two supporting claims (b) and (e) each contain a falsifiable overstatement that must be fixed.

- **(a) Massudi et al. 2012 — human pelvic skin, n=49, cross-sectional** — `confirmed`
  Reached the primary source (PLoS ONE 2012, PMID 22848760, PMCID PMC3407129, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0042357). Abstract verbatim: "Human pelvic skin samples were obtained from consenting patients aged between 15-77 and newborn babies (0-1 year old) (n = 49) previously scheduled for an unrelated surgical procedure." and "A strong negative correlation was observed between NAD(+) levels and age in both males (p = 0.001; r = -0.706) and females (p = 0.01; r = -0.537)." Cross-sectional is correct (single surgical-waste sample per donor). Semantic Scholar citationCount = 530, supporting 'most-cited human tissue datapoint'. TWO CALIBER CAVEATS the article should carry: (1) n=49 is the TOTAL; every NAD+/age correlation was run SEPARATELY BY SEX, so each reported r rests on roughly half that (~20-25 donors), not 49. (2) The 49 includes newborns (0-1 y) pooled with adults aged 15-77, which mechanically inflates a 'decline with age' slope. (3) The paper reports correlation coefficients only — NO percentage decline figure appears anywhere in it.

- **(b) Entire in-vivo human BRAIN evidence = a single 31P-MRS occipital study, n=17 (7 aged 21-26; 4 aged 33-36; 6 aged 59-68)** — `refuted`
  The n=17 study is real and every number in the parenthetical is exactly right — but the word 'entire' is false. THE STUDY: Zhu, Lu, Lee, Ugurbil, Chen, PNAS 2015 (PMID 25730862, PMCID PMC4352772). Verbatim from full text, confirmed on two independent fetches: "Seventeen human volunteers (age: 21-68 y; 10 males and 7 females) participated in this study" and "younger (21-26 y old; n = 7), middle (33-36 y old; n = 4), and older (59-68 y old; n = 6)". Occipital lobe, 7 T. Reported r = -0.75 for [NAD+] vs age; NO percent-decline figure is given. WHAT IS WRONG: it is NOT the only in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD dataset, and not even the only one that looked at age. Cuenoud et al., Front Aging Neurosci 2020 (PMID 33390929) ran 31P-MRS brain NAD in 50 healthy participants across a young group (mean age 27.1) and a middle-aged group (mean age 56.4) — verbatim from the abstract: "An inverted trend between age and NAD level was detected." That is nearly 3x the sample of Zhu 2015. Further in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD studies exist: Guo et al., Front Neurosci 2024 (PMID 38911598, whole-brain 31P-MRSI at 7 T); Nanga et al., Magn Reson Med 2024 (PMID 39044608); Cuenoud et al., Front Physiol 2023 (PMID 38028810); Arias-Mendoza et al., Adv Exp Med Biol 2022 (PMID 36527656); Lu, Zhu, Chen, NMR Biomed 2016 (PMID 27257783). The defensible sentence is narrower and must be rewritten.

- **(c) 'NAD+ falls ~50% by age 50' has no clean human primary source** — `confirmed`
  Supported, with the honest limit that one cannot exhaustively prove a negative. What I did verify directly: neither of the two candidate primaries reports any percentage. Massudi 2012 reports only r and p values (abstract read verbatim; no % figure). Zhu 2015 full text on PMC reports correlation coefficients and group means; on direct query the full text yields no stated percent decline. Independent corroboration from the field itself: the Nature Metabolism October 2025 review states verbatim "the published body of data on NAD+ dynamics in human tissues remains sparse, and the extrapolation of rodent-based data is not straightforward" — i.e. the specialists writing the current review do not cite any human study supporting a quantified ~50%-by-50 figure. The 'fuses incompatible calibers' charge is well founded: the two datasets being blended are cross-sectional skin biopsies (Massudi, n=49, sex-split) and 31P-MRS occipital brain (Zhu, n=17, three bins) — different tissues, different assays, different age ranges, neither yielding a percentage.

- **(d) May 2026, 32 authors, Amsterdam UMC/Helsinki/Leiden/Valencia, validated UHPLC-HRMS, seven independent human cohorts, whole-blood NAD+ does not decline with age** — `corrected`
  The study is real and the headline is right, but the article overstates its reach and one detail. VERIFIED: Trętowicz MM, Scantlebery AML, Schomakers BV, et al., 'Human whole-blood NAD+ levels do not vary with age or lifestyle interventions', Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01537-5, PMID 42135539, firstPublicationDate 2026-05-14 (so 'May 2026' is correct). Europe PMC author list contains exactly 32 names — 32 authors CONFIRMED. Affiliations confirm Amsterdam UMC (UvA and VU), University of Helsinki, Leiden University Medical Center and University of Valencia — but the article's four-institution list is INCOMPLETE and reads as if that were the whole set; the affiliation list also includes Universidad Catolica de Murcia (UCAM), University of Oulu, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and Deakin University. Abstract retrieved verbatim and IDENTICALLY on two independent routes (Europe PMC core record and the nature.com article page): "Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) levels in blood and tissues are widely proposed to decline with age, yet evidence in human blood is inconsistent. Using a rigorously validated ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry system that accounts for real-world analytical variability, we quantify NAD+ across seven independent human cohorts. We find that whole-blood NAD+ levels remain remarkably stable with age and across lifestyle interventions, but change in response to nicotinamide riboside supplementation, as expected. Our results challenge the utility of blood NAD+ levels as a biomarker of ageing or lifestyle factors." So: UHPLC-HRMS confirmed, seven independent human cohorts confirmed, 'does not decline with age' confirmed. WHAT MUST BE CORRECTED: (1) WHOLE BLOOD ONLY — no human tissue. Fig. 2 caption verbatim: 'Whole-blood NAD+ levels remain unchanged across age and lifestyle interventions.' The paper does NOT measure skin, brain or muscle NAD+ and therefore does NOT contradict Massudi 2012 or Zhu 2015; it contradicts blood NAD+ as an ageing biomarker. Calling it 'DECISIVE' against the founding premise, or saying the premise 'has been contradicted' full stop, is caliber inflation. (2) The paper's own framed conclusion is about biomarker UTILITY ('challenge the utility of blood NAD+ levels as a biomarker'), not about whether tissue NAD+ falls. (3) 'Consortium' is the article's word, not the paper's — it is a multi-centre collaboration, not a named consortium. (4) The paper is short-format (2 figures, 9 journal pages), not a large multi-cohort flagship. N PER COHORT AND TOTAL N: UNREACHABLE. The article is closed access (Unpaywall: is_oa false, oa_status 'closed', zero OA locations); no preprint exists in Europe PMC. Only the abstract, figure titles and reference list are public. One WebFetch pass returned a confident-looking list of seven named cohorts with n values (a cross-sectional ageing cohort, CardioHT, ELITE, LLS, TEAMS, 'MEJNES2019', a twin-pair NR study; ~347 total) — a second pass on the SAME URL established that the Main text is paywalled and not visible, so I treat that cohort roster and the ~347 figure as UNVERIFIED and possibly confabulated. Do not print any per-cohort N or total N unless someone reads the paywalled PDF.

- **(e) An INDEPENDENT expert review in Nature Metabolism (October 2025) says the human NAD+ age decline has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies** — `corrected`
  The quoted content is exactly right; the word 'independent' is wrong and must be deleted. THE REVIEW: Vinten KT, Tretowicz MM, Coskun E, van Weeghel M, Canto C, Zapata-Perez R, Janssens GE, Houtkooper RH, 'NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges', Nature Metabolism 2025;7(10):1974-1990, DOI 10.1038/s42255-025-01387-7, PMID 41083806, firstPublicationDate 2025-10-13. October 2025 and Nature Metabolism both confirmed. Abstract sentence retrieved verbatim from PubMed: "However, evidence for an age-related decline in NAD+ levels in humans has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies." — a near-exact match to the article's paraphrase. THE PROBLEM: this is the SAME LAB as claim (d). Five of the review's eight authors are also authors on the May 2026 whole-blood paper: Kasper T Vinten, Maria M Tretowicz (first author of the 2026 paper), Evrim Coskun, Michel van Weeghel, Ruben Zapata-Perez, plus Georges E Janssens and Riekelt H Houtkooper (senior authors of both). Same primary affiliation: Laboratory Genetic Metabolic Diseases, Amsterdam UMC. Presenting (e) as independent corroboration of (d) is a real attribution error — it is the same group setting up its own result. Note also the review does NOT say the decline is absent; it says it is thinly evidenced.

**修正:**
- Delete 'independent' from the description of the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review. Vinten et al. 2025 (Nat Metab 7:1974-1990, PMID 41083806) shares seven of eight authors' institutional home and five individual authors — including first author Tretowicz and senior authors Janssens and Houtkooper — with the May 2026 whole-blood paper. It is the same Amsterdam UMC group, not independent corroboration. Rewrite as: 'The same Amsterdam UMC group had already written, in an October 2025 Nature Metabolism review, that...'
- Restrict claim (d) to whole blood explicitly and drop the word 'DECISIVE'. Trętowicz et al., Nat Metab 2026;8(6):1282-1290 measured NAD+ in WHOLE BLOOD only across seven human cohorts; it contains no human tissue measurement. It therefore does not contradict Massudi 2012 (skin) or Zhu 2015 (brain). The paper's own stated conclusion is that the results 'challenge the utility of blood NAD+ levels as a biomarker of ageing or lifestyle factors' — a biomarker claim, not a refutation of tissue NAD+ decline. Say 'the blood arm of the premise has been contradicted', not 'the founding premise has been contradicted'.
- Do not state any N (per-cohort or total) for the May 2026 paper. The article is closed access (Unpaywall: oa_status 'closed', zero OA locations) with no preprint; only the abstract, two figure captions and references are public. A cohort roster with n values surfaced in one automated fetch and could not be corroborated on a second pass of the same page — treat it as unverified. Write 'seven independent human cohorts' and stop there.
- Fix claim (b): it is false that the n=17 study is the ENTIRE in-vivo human brain NAD+ evidence. Cuenoud et al., Front Aging Neurosci 2020 (PMID 33390929) ran 31P-MRS brain NAD in 50 healthy participants across a young (mean 27.1 y) and middle-aged (mean 56.4 y) group and reported 'an inverted trend between age and NAD level'. Further in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD studies: Guo 2024 (PMID 38911598), Nanga 2024 (PMID 39044608), Cuenoud 2023 (PMID 38028810), Arias-Mendoza 2022 (PMID 36527656), Lu 2016 (PMID 27257783). Rewrite as: 'The in-vivo human brain literature is tiny — the most-cited age-dependence result, Zhu et al. PNAS 2015, rests on 17 volunteers scanned at the occipital lobe (7 aged 21-26, 4 aged 33-36, 6 aged 59-68); the one larger attempt, Cuenoud et al. 2020 with n=50, found only a trend.'
- Add the sex-split caveat to Massudi 2012. The n=49 is the total; every NAD+ vs age correlation in that paper was computed separately within males and within females (males r = -0.706, p = 0.001; females r = -0.537, p = 0.01), so each coefficient rests on roughly half the sample. The 49 also pools newborns (0-1 y) with adults aged 15-77.
- When making point (c), state the positive fact rather than only the absence: neither Massudi 2012 nor Zhu 2015 reports ANY percentage decline — both report correlation coefficients only. That is the concrete basis for saying the '~50% by age 50' figure has no clean primary source.
- Correct the institution list for the May 2026 paper, or mark it as partial. Beyond Amsterdam UMC, Helsinki, Leiden and Valencia, the affiliations include Universidad Catolica de Murcia (UCAM), University of Oulu, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Deakin University. Also drop 'consortium' — it is a multi-centre collaboration with 32 authors, not a named consortium.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Cuenoud et al., Front Aging Neurosci 2020 (PMID 33390929) is a larger in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD dataset (n=50) than the n=17 study the article treats as the whole brain literature, and it found only 'an inverted trend between age and NAD level' — i.e. it both breaks the 'single study' framing and reports a weaker effect.
- The October 2025 Nature Metabolism review invoked in (e) as independent support shares five authors and its senior authorship (Janssens, Houtkooper) with the May 2026 paper in (d). Using it to corroborate (d) is circular.
- The May 2026 paper's own abstract opens by conceding that NAD+ decline is 'widely proposed' in 'blood AND TISSUES' and then restricts its own evidence to whole blood — so the paper itself does not claim to have refuted the tissue-level premise.
- Massudi 2012's reported NAD+/age correlations are sex-stratified, so the effective n behind each coefficient is roughly 20-25, not 49; and the sample mixes newborns (0-1 y) with adults up to 77, which inflates any age slope.

- **(a) Massudi et al. 2012: human pelvic skin, n=49, cross-sectional — the most-cited human tissue datapoint** — `confirmed`
  Primary source reached: Massudi H, Grant R, Braidy N, Guest J, Farnsworth B, Guillemin GJ. 'Age-associated changes in oxidative stress and NAD+ metabolism in human tissue.' PLoS One 2012;7(7):e42357. PMID 22848760, PMC3407129. Methods verbatim: 'Human skin tissues were obtained with informed consent from patients (n = 49) who were scheduled for surgery at the Sydney Adventist Hospital.' and 'Skin tissues were obtained from non-sun exposed areas of the pelvic region.' Cross-sectional confirmed (single sampling, ages spanning newborns 0–1 y plus patients 15–77 y). Two caveats the article should not lose: (1) the n=49 is not 49 adults — Table 1 includes 8 newborns; the post-pubescent male regression is n=19 (r=-0.706, p=0.0001) and the female analysis spans ages 36–76 (p=0.01, n=22); (2) 'most-cited' is an editorial characterization I cannot verify against any primary document — it is defensible but is not a fact drawn from a source.

- **(b) Entire in-vivo human brain evidence = single 31P-MRS occipital-lobe study, n=17, bins 7 (21-26) / 4 (33-36) / 6 (59-68)** — `corrected`
  All numbers CORRECT. Primary source: Zhu XH, Lu M, Lee BY, Ugurbil K, Chen W. 'In vivo NAD assay reveals the intracellular NAD contents and redox state in healthy human brain and their age dependences.' PNAS 2015;112(9). PMID 25730862, PMC4352772. Verbatim: 'Seventeen human volunteers (age: 21–68 y; 10 males and 7 females) participated in this study'; brain region verbatim: 'The 31P spectra were obtained from the human occipital lobes'; age bins verbatim from the Fig. 3 caption: 'younger (21–26 y old; n = 7), middle (33–36 y old; n = 4), and older (59–68 y old; n = 6)'. WRONG version: 'the entire in-vivo human BRAIN evidence is a single study'. RIGHT version: it is the only in-vivo human brain study of NAD+ AND AGE. Other in-vivo human brain 31P-MRS NAD measurements exist and would falsify the unqualified sentence — e.g. Xin L et al., 'Nutritional Ketosis Increases NAD+/NADH Ratio in Healthy Human Brain: An in Vivo Study by 31P-MRS,' Front Nutr 2018 (PMID 30050907), human brain, not an aging study. (Lu/Zhu/Chen, Magn Reson Med 2014, PMID 23843330, is the method paper and is cat brain, not human.) Also worth stating: Zhu reports correlations only (NAD+ vs age r = -0.75; NADH r = 0.68; total NAD r = -0.57; redox potential r = -0.76), and 7 of the 17 were scanned twice.

- **(c) '~50% by age 50' has no clean human primary source** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against both candidate primaries. Massudi 2012 (PMC3407129): no percentage or fold-change for NAD+ vs age appears anywhere; the paper reports only significance/correlations ('NAD+ levels decreased significantly in males aged between 0–77 years (line a; p = 0.0007; n = 27)'). Zhu 2015 (PMC4352772): no 50% figure for NAD+ vs age; only Pearson r values. The percentages that DO appear in Zhu are cited rodent/other-modality numbers (15–34% respiratory complex activity in aged MOUSE brain, ~30% neuronal oxidative glucose metabolism, ~40% mitochondrial oxidative/phosphorylation activity) — which is precisely the caliber-fusion the article describes. Honest limit: this is a negative existential; I verified the two documents the figure is usually pinned to, not every possible source, and I did not have WebSearch budget to canvass the grey literature. Phrase it as 'no primary human measurement in either of the two studies it is normally attributed to states this number' rather than 'no source exists anywhere'.

- **(d) May 2026, 32-author consortium, Amsterdam UMC/Helsinki/Leiden/Valencia, validated UHPLC-HRMS, seven independent human cohorts, whole-blood NAD+ does not decline with age** — `corrected`
  Substantially CORRECT and it is the strongest item, but three qualifiers need fixing and one number is unreachable. CONFIRMED verbatim from the PubMed record (PMID 42135539) and the Nature landing page: Trętowicz MM et al., 'Human whole-blood NAD+ levels do not vary with age or lifestyle interventions,' Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01537-5, e-published 14 May 2026. Author count is exactly 32 (I counted the full PubMed AuthorList; OpenAlex's '35' and Semantic Scholar's '31' are indexing artifacts — use 32). Abstract verbatim: 'Using a rigorously validated ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry system that accounts for real-world analytical variability, we quantify NAD+ across seven independent human cohorts. We find that whole-blood NAD+ levels remain remarkably stable with age and across lifestyle interventions, but change in response to nicotinamide riboside supplementation, as expected. Our results challenge the utility of blood NAD+ levels as a biomarker of ageing or lifestyle factors.' CORRECTIONS: (1) 'consortium' is wrong — there is no named consortium; it is a multi-centre collaboration led by Riekelt Houtkooper's Laboratory Genetic Metabolic Diseases at Amsterdam UMC. (2) The institution list is incomplete: alongside Amsterdam UMC, University of Helsinki, Leiden UMC and University of Valencia, the affiliations include Universidad Católica de Murcia (UCAM), University of Oulu / Oulu University Hospital, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences, and Deakin University. (3) MOST IMPORTANT: the measurement is WHOLE BLOOD ONLY. No human tissue was measured. The paper therefore does not contradict Massudi's skin data or Zhu's brain data, and its own stated conclusion is about biomarker utility of BLOOD NAD+, not about NAD+ decline in general. The paper also shows the assay does detect the expected rise after nicotinamide riboside — so this is a null result from a demonstrably sensitive assay, which strengthens it, but only for blood. UNREACHABLE: total N and per-cohort N. Nature Metabolism is closed access; a targeted re-fetch confirmed 'Methods body not present' and the Fig. 1/Fig. 2 caption bodies and Extended Data Table 1 do not render. Cohort NAMES are visible in the Extended Data captions: a cross-sectional aging cohort, CardioHT, ELITE, LLS (Leiden Longevity Study), TEAMS, MEJNES2019, and a twin-pair NR supplementation cohort (n=24, the only per-cohort n I saw printed, in the Extended Data Fig. 3 caption). Do NOT publish a total-N figure — see newContradictions for why.

- **(e) Independent expert review in Nature Metabolism (Oct 2025) says the human NAD+ decline has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies** — `corrected`
  The QUOTED SUBSTANCE is verbatim correct; the word 'independent' is FALSE. Source: Vinten KT, Trętowicz MM, Coskun E, van Weeghel M, Cantó C, Zapata-Pérez R, Janssens GE, Houtkooper RH. 'NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges.' Nature Metabolism 2025;7(10):1974-1990, DOI 10.1038/s42255-025-01387-7, PMID 41083806, e-published 13 October 2025, PublicationType 'Review'. Abstract verbatim: 'However, evidence for an age-related decline in NAD+ levels in humans has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies.' WRONG version: 'An independent expert review.' RIGHT version: a review from the same laboratory that produced the 2026 whole-blood paper — Amsterdam UMC (Houtkooper lab). Seven of its eight authors (Vinten, Trętowicz, Coskun, van Weeghel, Zapata-Pérez, Janssens, Houtkooper) are also authors on the May 2026 Nature Metabolism paper; only Carles Cantó (EPFL) is external. Secondary correction: its scope is NAD+ precursor supplementation in ageing, not a general review of the NAD+-decline literature.

**修正:**
- Replace '32-author consortium (Amsterdam UMC, Helsinki, Leiden, Valencia)' with: a 32-author multi-centre collaboration led by the Houtkooper lab at Amsterdam UMC, with co-authors at Leiden UMC, the University of Helsinki, the University of Valencia, Universidad Católica de Murcia, the University of Oulu, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and Deakin University. Cite it as: Trętowicz MM et al., 'Human whole-blood NAD+ levels do not vary with age or lifestyle interventions,' Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290, published online 14 May 2026, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01537-5.
- State explicitly that the 2026 finding is confined to WHOLE BLOOD. The study measured no human tissue, so it does not contradict Massudi's skin data or Zhu's brain data. The paper's own conclusion is that blood NAD+ is not a useful biomarker of ageing or lifestyle, not that NAD+ does not decline in tissue. Do not let the section header imply the tissue premise has been refuted.
- Add the point that strengthens the null: the same assay did detect the expected increase in whole-blood NAD+ after nicotinamide riboside supplementation, so the flat age curve is not an insensitivity artifact.
- Do NOT state a total N or per-cohort N for the 2026 paper. The Methods and Extended Data Table 1 are behind Nature's paywall and I could not reach them. If an N is needed, say 'seven independent human cohorts' (verbatim from the abstract) and stop there. The only per-cohort n visible on the free page is the twin-pair NR supplementation cohort, n=24.
- Delete 'independent' from the description of the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review. It is by Vinten, Trętowicz, Coskun, van Weeghel, Cantó, Zapata-Pérez, Janssens and Houtkooper — seven of the eight are also authors of the May 2026 paper. Describe it as the same group's own review, and note its title is 'NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges' (Nat Metab 2025;7(10):1974-1990, online 13 Oct 2025).
- Because (d) and (e) come from the same laboratory, do not present them as two converging independent lines of evidence. Rewrite the passage so the reader sees one research group making a consistent case, and note that no independent replication of the seven-cohort null has been published as of July 2026.
- Scope the brain claim: say Zhu et al. 2015 (PNAS 112(9), PMID 25730862) is the only in-vivo human brain study of NAD+ AND AGE, not the entire in-vivo human brain NAD+ literature — Xin et al., Front Nutr 2018 (PMID 30050907) also measured NAD+/NADH in healthy human brain by 31P-MRS, though not as a function of age.
- Optionally sharpen (a): the n=49 in Massudi 2012 includes 8 newborns (0–1 y); the post-pubescent male regression is n=19 and the female analysis covers ages 36–76 only. This makes the 'small and contested' point stronger, not weaker.
- Optionally sharpen (c): note that Massudi 2012 reports no percentage at all (only p-values and r), and Zhu 2015 reports only correlation coefficients (NAD+ vs age r = -0.75) — the percentage figures that appear in Zhu (15–34%, ~30%, ~40%) are cited rodent or other-modality numbers, which is exactly the caliber fusion being described.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The article's two 'independent' pillars are one lab. The May 2026 Nature Metabolism paper and the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review share Houtkooper, Janssens, van Weeghel, Zapata-Pérez, Vinten, Trętowicz and Coskun. Presenting (e) as independent corroboration of (d) is a real error of evidentiary structure, not a wording nitpick.
- The 2026 paper cannot bear the weight the article puts on it for the TISSUE premise. Its own abstract opens by conceding the premise is about 'blood and tissues' and then narrows the challenge to blood: 'evidence in human blood is inconsistent.' Massudi (skin) and Zhu (brain) are untouched by it.
- A prior WebFetch of the Nature landing page returned a confident, fully itemised cohort breakdown (CardioHT N=26, ELITE N=47, LLS N=70, TEAMS N=65, MEJNES2019 N=31, cross-sectional N=40, twin NR N=24, 'approximately 303 individuals'). A follow-up fetch demanding literal text established that the Methods body and the figure caption bodies are NOT on the page. The cohort names are real (they appear in Extended Data captions), but the N values were not verifiable from the page and I treat them as fabricated by the summarizer. Flagging this because these numbers are exactly the kind that could leak into the article as if verified.
- Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290 is not open access, has no PMCID, no preprint I could locate under any author name, and no open-access PDF in OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar (best_oa_location null). Anyone re-checking the N will hit the same wall.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

WebSearch was exhausted before I started (200/200 used by this session), so I worked entirely through WebFetch against literature APIs and publisher pages: Europe PMC REST (search, core records, citations), PubMed, PMC full texts, PLOS, Semantic Scholar Graph API, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, and the nature.com landing page via its IdP redirect chain.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS I REACHED AND READ MYSELF:
- Massudi H et al., PLoS One 2012;7(7):e42357 (PMID 22848760) — read the full abstract and Methods/Results on journals.plos.org. Confirms 'Human pelvic skin samples ... aged between 15–77 and newborn babies (0–1 year old) (n = 49)' and 'non-sun exposed areas of the pelvic region'. Also surfaced two things the claim omits: newborns are inside the n=49, and the paper's own abstract (r = −0.706 males) conflicts with its Results text (r = 0.769 males).
- Zhu XH et al., PNAS 2015;112(9):2876-2881 (PMID 25730862, PMC4352772) — read Methods/Results in PMC. Every number in sub-claim (b) matched verbatim: 'Seventeen human volunteers (age: 21–68 y; 10 males and 7 females)', 'younger (21–26 y old; n = 7), middle (33–36 y old; n = 4), and older (59–68 y old; n = 6)', '31P spectra were obtained from the human occipital lobes'. This is the one sub-claim whose arithmetic is exactly right.
- Guo R et al., Front Neurosci 2024;18:1389111 (PMC11190064) — read in PMC. This is the refutation of (b)'s word 'entire'.
- Vinten KT et al., Nat Metab 2025;7(10):1974-1990 (PMID 41083806) — read the abstract verbatim on PubMed along with author affiliations. The quoted sentence is exact. The author overlap with the 2026 paper is what breaks the 'independent' framing.
- Trętowicz MM et al., Nat Metab 2026;8(6):1282-1290 (PMID 42135539) — reached the nature.com landing page and obtained the abstract verbatim (cross-checked against the Europe PMC core record, which matched word for word), the article-type label 'Brief Communication', the dates (received 23 Oct 2025 / accepted 24 Apr 2026 / published 14 May 2026), the figure and Extended Data figure titles, and the Data availability statement. I counted the 32 authors independently from two sources (Europe PMC core and Semantic Scholar) and they agree. OpenAlex supplied the institution list, which is broader than the four the claim names.

WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN: the paper is closed access with no repository copy (Unpaywall: is_oa false, has_repository_copy false, no PMCID) and the ResearchGate PDF returned 403. The Methods are behind the paywall; the landing page explicitly offers only 'a preview of subscription content'. One fetch returned a tidy list of seven cohort names with per-arm n's, but a second stricter fetch of the same page could not reproduce those names verbatim, so I am treating them as unverified rather than passing them through — this pipeline has been burned by fetch summarizers inventing exactly that kind of structured detail. I verified only the sample sizes that a strict verbatim pass reproduced (n = 20 / n = 20 young-vs-old, n = 70, n = 26, n = 24, n = 15). I also checked for a rebuttal: Europe PMC's citation endpoint for PMID 42135539 returns hitCount 0, and a 2026 Comment/Letter/Erratum sweep on NAD-blood-age found nothing responsive. The paper is only ~2.5 months old, so absence of criticism is weak evidence.

NET: the group's central factual spine survives — the human NAD+-decline literature really is tiny, the 2026 Nature Metabolism paper really does exist and really does report stable whole-blood NAD+ across seven cohorts by validated UHPLC-HRMS, and its author count of 32 is exact. Three things need fixing before publication: (e) is not independent, (b)'s 'entire' is false, and (d) is about blood and not tissue, so 'the founding premise ... has been contradicted' overreaches unless scoped to the blood version of the premise.

- **(a) Massudi et al. 2012: human pelvic skin, n=49, cross-sectional** — `corrected`
  Substantially right; two caliber slips. VERIFIED verbatim from the PLoS One abstract: "Human pelvic skin samples were obtained from consenting patients aged between 15–77 and newborn babies (0–1 year old) (n = 49) previously scheduled for an unrelated surgical procedure." Methods add: "Skin tissues were obtained from non-sun exposed areas of the pelvic region." Cross-sectional is correct by design (the paper never uses the word). WRONG if the article implies n=49 adults aged 15–77: the n=49 INCLUDES newborns (0–1 y), and the newborn-vs-adult contrast is what drives the largest step change ("A significant decrease in total NAD+ content was observed in adults (p<0.05), older adult (p<0.05) and elderly (p<0.05) subjects compared to newborns"). RIGHT: n=49 spans newborns (0–1 y) plus patients aged 15–77, and they were surgical patients, not healthy volunteers. Second slip: there is no single pooled NAD+-vs-age statistic — results are split by sex (abstract: males p=0.001, r=−0.706; females p=0.01, r=−0.537). The paper is also internally inconsistent: the abstract gives r=−0.706 for males while the Results text gives "r = 0.769 males, versus r = 0.537 females" (sign dropped) for post-pubescent males. "Most-cited human tissue datapoint" is plausible but I did not verify a citation ranking — do not assert it as fact. Cite: Massudi H et al., PLoS One 2012;7(7):e42357, PMID 22848760.

- **(b) Entire in-vivo human brain evidence = a single 31P-MRS occipital study, n=17 (7 aged 21-26; 4 aged 33-36; 6 aged 59-68)** — `corrected`
  The NUMBERS ARE EXACTLY RIGHT; the word "entire" is FALSE. Verified verbatim from PMC4352772 (Zhu XH, Lu M, Lee BY, Ugurbil K, Chen W, PNAS 2015;112(9):2876-2881, PMID 25730862): "Seventeen human volunteers (age: 21–68 y; 10 males and 7 females) participated in this study"; "younger (21–26 y old; n = 7), middle (33–36 y old; n = 4), and older (59–68 y old; n = 6) subjects"; "The 31P spectra were obtained from the human occipital lobes using the single-pulse acquire sequence". Reported age correlations: "a positive age correlation for [NADH] (Pearson's correlation coefficient r = 0.68) and negative age correlations for [NAD+] (r = −0.75), [NAD]total (r = −0.57)". WRONG: it is not the only in-vivo human brain 31P NAD study. At least three others exist — Lu M, Zhu XH, Chen W, NMR Biomed 2016 (PMID 27257783, human brain NAD at 4T/3T); Zhu XH et al., Metabolites 2021;11(3):145 (PMID 33804401, occipital NAD in Parkinson's patients vs controls at 7T); and Guo R et al., Front Neurosci 2024;18:1389111 (PMID 38911598, PMC11190064) which mapped NAD across the ENTIRE brain by 31P-MRSI at 7T in two datasets (7 volunteers, then 14 subjects) and reported "Cluster of the data with ages below 30 showed the highest overall NAD levels, and the NAD levels declined with ages above 30." RIGHT phrasing: the foundational and most-cited in-vivo human brain measurement is a single n=17 occipital-lobe 31P-MRS study; the whole in-vivo human brain literature still amounts to a handful of small studies from essentially one Minnesota group (Zhu/Chen), which is a common-source problem, not an independence problem.

- **(c) "NAD+ falls ~50% by age 50" has no clean human primary source** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed as far as a negative can be confirmed, and I checked the two candidate sources directly. Massudi 2012 reports NO percentage decline anywhere — only per-sex correlation coefficients and a categorical newborn-vs-adult contrast. Zhu 2015 PNAS reports NO percentage either — only pooled concentrations ([NAD+] = 0.30 ± 0.02 mM, [NADH] = 0.06 ± 0.01 mM, total NAD = 0.37 ± 0.02 mM across all 17 subjects) and correlation coefficients; the Results text explicitly gives no group-wise numbers, which appear only in a figure. So the popular "~50% by 50" cannot be read off either. Independent support for the fusion charge: the Nature Metabolism review (Vinten et al. 2025) states verbatim "the published body of data on NAD+ dynamics in human tissues remains sparse". CAVEAT: I cannot exhaustively prove no paper anywhere states it; the article should say "we could not locate a human primary source reporting this figure" rather than "there is none".

- **(d) May 2026, 32-author consortium (Amsterdam UMC, Helsinki, Leiden, Valencia), validated UHPLC-HRMS, seven independent human cohorts, whole-blood NAD+ does not decline with age** — `corrected`
  Core assertion HOLDS and is stronger than most such claims, but four qualifiers need fixing. VERIFIED: Trętowicz MM, Scantlebery AML, Schomakers BV, ... Janssens GE, Houtkooper RH. "Human whole-blood NAD+ levels do not vary with age or lifestyle interventions." Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290. PMID 42135539, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01537-5. Received 23 Oct 2025, Accepted 24 Apr 2026, Published online 14 May 2026 (print June 2026). I counted the full author list from the Europe PMC core record and Semantic Scholar independently: exactly 32 authors. Abstract verbatim from the nature.com landing page: "Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) levels in blood and tissues are widely proposed to decline with age, yet evidence in human blood is inconsistent. Using a rigorously validated ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry system that accounts for real-world analytical variability, we quantify NAD+ across seven independent human cohorts. We find that whole-blood NAD+ levels remain remarkably stable with age and across lifestyle interventions, but change in response to nicotinamide riboside supplementation, as expected. Our results challenge the utility of blood NAD+ levels as a biomarker of ageing or lifestyle factors." FOUR CORRECTIONS. (1) ARTICLE TYPE: the page label is "Brief Communication", not a full Article — a short-format paper, which caps how much method detail is on the record. (2) NOT A CONSORTIUM: it is a multi-institution collaboration led by the Houtkooper lab at Amsterdam UMC, with no consortium name; and the four institutions listed are an incomplete set. OpenAlex affiliations give: Amsterdam UMC / University of Amsterdam, Universitat de València, INCLIVA, CIBER, Universidad Católica de Murcia, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, University of Helsinki, University of Oulu, Leiden UMC, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences, Deakin University (Australia). Write "including", not a closed list. (3) BLOOD ONLY — this is the load-bearing caveat: the paper measured WHOLE BLOOD (plus plasma only in the pre-analytical-handling validation, Extended Data Fig. 1). Fig. 2 is titled "Whole-blood NAD+ levels remain unchanged across age and lifestyle interventions." There is NO human tissue (skin, brain, muscle) measurement in it. It therefore does NOT contradict Massudi's skin data or Zhu's brain data; it refutes blood NAD+ as an ageing biomarker, not the tissue-decline hypothesis. Saying it "contradicted" the founding premise overstates it — it contradicts the blood-based version of the premise, which is the version the supplement industry sells tests for. (4) The paper also found NAD+ DOES rise with nicotinamide riboside supplementation, which is the positive control showing the assay was not simply insensitive (Extended Data Fig. 3, "Validation of assay sensitivity in a twin-pair NR supplementation cohort"). Include this or a critic will say the null is an assay artifact. No erratum, correction, comment or rebuttal exists as of 2026-07-28 (Europe PMC citation list for PMID 42135539 returns hitCount 0). A companion Research Briefing, "Whole-blood NAD+ levels do not reflect healthy ageing", Nat Metab 2026;8:1260-1261, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01540-w, is by Trętowicz and Houtkooper themselves — it is NOT independent commentary.

- **(d) total N and the identity of the seven cohorts** — `unreachable`
  I could NOT verify the total N or the seven cohort identities against the primary document. The paper is fully closed access (Unpaywall: is_oa false, oa_status "closed", has_repository_copy false; no PMCID; the ResearchGate PDF returns HTTP 403). The nature.com landing page shows only the abstract, figure titles, and Data availability — it states the rest is "a preview of subscription content" and no Methods with participant descriptions is visible. Sample sizes I could see literally quoted on the visible page: "younger (<30 years, n = 20), older (>60 years, n = 20)", plus n = 70, n = 26, n = 24, n = 15 in figure legends. One fetch pass additionally returned cohort labels (CardioHT n=26; ELITE athletes n=23 / <40 n=12 / >40 n=12; Leiden Longevity Study n=70; TEAMS n=31+34; MEJNES2019 n=7+9+15; twin-pair NR n=24; summing to roughly 300) — I am flagging these as NOT VERIFIED because a second, stricter fetch of the same page could not reproduce the cohort names verbatim, and this pipeline has previously had fetch summarizers fabricate exactly this kind of detail. DO NOT print a specific total N or specific cohort names in the article on my authority. If a number is needed, the defensible statement is "seven independent human cohorts" (verbatim from the abstract) with no total.

- **(e) Independent expert review in Nature Metabolism (Oct 2025) says the decline has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies** — `corrected`
  The QUOTE IS RIGHT; "INDEPENDENT" IS WRONG, and this is the most damaging error in the group. Verified verbatim from the PubMed abstract of Vinten KT, Trętowicz MM, Coskun E, van Weeghel M, Cantó C, Zapata-Pérez R, Janssens GE, Houtkooper RH. "NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges." Nat Metab 2025;7(10):1974-1990, published online 13 Oct 2025, PMID 41083806, DOI 10.1038/s42255-025-01387-7, publication type Review. Exact sentence: "However, evidence for an age-related decline in NAD+ levels in humans has been consistently observed only in a limited number of studies." WRONG: describing this as an "independent expert review" — SEVEN of its eight authors (Vinten, Trętowicz, Coskun, van Weeghel, Zapata-Pérez, Janssens, Houtkooper) are also authors of the May 2026 whole-blood paper in item (d), and both come out of the same Laboratory Genetic Metabolic Diseases, Amsterdam UMC (Houtkooper lab). RIGHT: it is the same group's own review, published seven months before their data paper, in the same journal — it is the authors' framing of the field, not third-party corroboration. Presenting (d) and (e) as two converging independent sources would be a genuine misrepresentation a hostile reader will catch immediately. Separately, co-author Carles Cantó is at Nestlé Research, an industry NAD+-precursor stakeholder — worth a footnote if the article leans on this review, since it cuts the other way (an industry-affiliated review conceding the evidence is thin is more, not less, telling).

**修正:**
- Do not call the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review (Vinten et al., Nat Metab 2025;7(10):1974-1990, PMID 41083806) 'independent'. Seven of its eight authors — Vinten, Trętowicz, Coskun, van Weeghel, Zapata-Pérez, Janssens and Houtkooper — are also authors on the May 2026 whole-blood paper, and both come from the Houtkooper lab at Amsterdam UMC. Describe it as the same group's own prior review of the field, not as third-party corroboration, and do not present (d) and (e) as two converging sources.
- Replace 'the entire in-vivo human BRAIN evidence is a single 31P-MRS study' with an accurate version. The n=17 occipital study (Zhu XH et al., PNAS 2015;112(9):2876-2881, PMID 25730862) is the foundational and most-cited one, and its numbers are exactly as stated — 17 volunteers, 21–68 y, 10 male / 7 female, bins of 7 (21–26 y), 4 (33–36 y) and 6 (59–68 y), occipital lobes. But at least three further in-vivo human brain 31P NAD studies exist: Lu, Zhu & Chen, NMR Biomed 2016 (PMID 27257783); Zhu XH et al., Metabolites 2021;11(3):145 (PMID 33804401); and Guo R et al., Front Neurosci 2024;18:1389111 (PMID 38911598), a whole-brain 7T 31P-MRSI study in 7 then 14 subjects that also reported NAD declining above age 30. The honest framing is that the literature is a handful of small studies from essentially one group (Zhu/Chen at Minnesota) — a single-source problem, not a single-study one.
- Correct the description of the May 2026 paper: it is a Brief Communication in Nature Metabolism 2026;8(6):1282-1290 (PMID 42135539, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01537-5), published online 14 May 2026, with exactly 32 authors — that count is confirmed. But it is not a named 'consortium'; it is a Houtkooper-lab-led multi-institution collaboration. And the institution list is incomplete: besides Amsterdam UMC, Helsinki, Leiden and Valencia it includes Universidad Católica de Murcia, INCLIVA and CIBER (Spain), University of Oulu (Finland), Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences, and Deakin University (Australia). Use 'including' rather than a closed list of four.
- State explicitly that the May 2026 paper measured WHOLE BLOOD only (plasma appears only in the pre-analytical validation, Extended Data Fig. 1); it contains no human tissue measurement. Fig. 2 is titled 'Whole-blood NAD+ levels remain unchanged across age and lifestyle interventions.' It therefore does not contradict Massudi's skin data or Zhu's brain data — it refutes blood NAD+ as an ageing biomarker. Soften 'has been contradicted' to something like: the blood-based version of the premise — the version consumer NAD+ tests actually sell — has been contradicted, while the tissue-level question remains open and thinly evidenced.
- Add the paper's positive control when citing the null result: whole-blood NAD+ did change in response to nicotinamide riboside supplementation ('but change in response to nicotinamide riboside supplementation, as expected' — abstract; Extended Data Fig. 3 is titled 'Validation of assay sensitivity in a twin-pair NR supplementation cohort'). Without this, the null reads as a possible assay-insensitivity artifact.
- Do not state a total N or name the seven cohorts of the May 2026 paper. It is fully closed access (Unpaywall: closed, no repository copy, no PMCID) and the Methods are not visible; only 'seven independent human cohorts' is verifiable verbatim from the abstract. Sample sizes literally visible on the landing page are limited to a young-vs-old cross-section of n = 20 versus n = 20, plus n = 70, n = 26, n = 24 and n = 15 in figure legends. Note also that the age comparison in the cross-sectional cohort is only 20 versus 20 participants.
- Fix the Massudi 2012 description: the n = 49 is not 49 adults. The abstract reads 'Human pelvic skin samples were obtained from consenting patients aged between 15–77 and newborn babies (0–1 year old) (n = 49) previously scheduled for an unrelated surgical procedure', and the Methods add that the skin came from 'non-sun exposed areas of the pelvic region'. The cohort mixes newborns with a 15–77 adult range, the subjects were surgical patients rather than healthy volunteers, and there is no pooled decline statistic — results are split by sex (males p = 0.001, r = −0.706; females p = 0.01, r = −0.537). The paper is also internally inconsistent, reporting r = −0.706 for males in the abstract but 'r = 0.769 males, versus r = 0.537 females' in the Results.
- Do not assert Massudi 2012 is 'the most-cited' human tissue datapoint as a verified fact — no citation ranking was checked. Say 'the most frequently cited' only if the article is willing to carry it as an impression, or drop the superlative.
- For the '~50% by age 50' figure, phrase the negative carefully: neither Massudi 2012 nor Zhu 2015 PNAS reports any percentage decline — Massudi gives only per-sex correlation coefficients and a categorical newborn-versus-adult contrast, and Zhu gives only pooled concentrations ([NAD+] 0.30 ± 0.02 mM, [NADH] 0.06 ± 0.01 mM, total NAD 0.37 ± 0.02 mM across all 17 subjects) plus correlation coefficients. Write 'we could not locate a human primary source reporting this figure', not 'there is none'.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Guo R, Yang S, Wiesner HM, Li Y, Zhao Y, Liang ZP, Chen W, Zhu XH. 'Mapping intracellular NAD content in entire human brain using phosphorus-31 MR spectroscopic imaging at 7 Tesla.' Front Neurosci 2024;18:1389111, PMID 38911598, PMC11190064 — a second, later in-vivo human brain NAD dataset (7 volunteers plus 14 subjects, whole brain rather than occipital only) that directly contradicts sub-claim (b)'s 'entire in-vivo human brain evidence is a single study'. Verbatim from the paper: 'Cluster of the data with ages below 30 showed the highest overall NAD levels, and the NAD levels declined with ages above 30. The linear regression curve also confirmed this trend of NAD decline as age increases.'
- Two further in-vivo human brain 31P NAD studies also contradict (b): Lu M, Zhu XH, Chen W, NMR Biomed 2016 (PMID 27257783), and Zhu XH et al., Metabolites 2021;11(3):145 (PMID 33804401), which measured occipital NAD in Parkinson's patients and controls at 7T.
- The May 2026 paper's own abstract undercuts the article's use of it as a blanket refutation: 'NAD+ levels in blood AND TISSUES are widely proposed to decline with age, yet evidence IN HUMAN BLOOD is inconsistent' — the authors scope their own null to blood, and Fig. 2 is titled 'Whole-blood NAD+ levels remain unchanged across age and lifestyle interventions'. No human tissue was measured.
- The companion piece Trętowicz MM & Houtkooper RH, 'Whole-blood NAD+ levels do not reflect healthy ageing', Nat Metab 2026;8:1260-1261, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01540-w, is a Research Briefing written by the study authors themselves — if the article treats it as external validation of the finding, that is wrong.
- Co-author Carles Cantó on the October 2025 Nature Metabolism review is affiliated with Nestlé Research, a commercial stakeholder in NAD+ precursors. This does not weaken the review's concession that the evidence is limited, but it does further disqualify the word 'independent'.

## V19 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I did not rely on any web-fetch summary for the load-bearing numbers. I downloaded the raw Europe PMC full-text XML for both papers (PMC6702140 Elhassan; PMC7398770 Remie), stripped tags locally, and regex-grepped for every quoted string, printing surrounding context. Every quoted sentence below was seen as an exact substring in that local text.

Elhassan (Cell Rep 2019;28:1717-1728, doi 10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.043, NCT02950441), verified verbatim: title exactly as claimed; 'Twelve aged (median age of 75 years) ... men ... orally supplemented with 1-g NR per day for 21 days in a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, crossover design, with 21 days' washout period between phases'; '...a 2-fold increase in muscle NAAD (NR 0.73 pmol/mg versus placebo 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.004), without an increase in NAD+ (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22)'; 'No differences were detected between the NR and placebo groups in skeletal muscle complex I- and complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and maximal respiratory capacity'; 'we did not observe any differences in the participants' peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96)'. Statistics section confirms paired t tests, mean ± SEM, alpha 0.05, and no formal power calculation ('Sample size ... decided upon based on previous experience'); no primary endpoint is declared. Blood NAD+ rose >2-fold (47.75 vs 20.90 uM, p < 0.001) — an important qualifier the claim omits.

Remie (Am J Clin Nutr 2020, doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqaa072, NCT02835664), verified verbatim: 13 healthy overweight/obese men and postmenopausal women, 45-65 y, BMI 27-35, 1000 mg/d NR for 6 wk, crossover with 4-7 wk washout; muscle NAD+ unchanged by enzymatic assay (1.019 ± 0.126 vs 1.125 ± 0.106 nmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.34, n = 8) and by MS (P = 0.91, n = 12); NAAD +677 ± 155% and MeNAM +299 ± 62%, both P < 0.01, n = 12; acetylcarnitine 4558 ± 749 vs 3025 ± 316 pmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.04. Remie's Discussion explicitly aligns itself with Elhassan, so it corroborates rather than contradicts.

Adversarial search: with WebSearch quota exhausted I queried the Europe PMC REST search API directly via curl/urllib (not the summarising fetch tool) for other human trials measuring muscle NAD+ in older adults, then downloaded and grepped the three best candidates' full texts. This is what broke the exclusivity claim — Jensen 2022 JCI Insight, elderly 55-80, muscle biopsies, LC-MS NAD+, verbatim 'NAD+, NADH, NADP+, and NADPH were not affected by NRPT supplementation'. I also checked and eliminated Lapatto 2023 (gene expression only, median age 39.7) and the 2024 acipimox trial in 65-75 y men (transcriptomics/respirometry; no direct muscle NAD+ quantification found). No erratum, correction or retraction is attached to the Elhassan record.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: (1) Elhassan's Figure S4 and Figure 3A/3B underlying values are in supplementary files I could not open, so I could not independently check the dispersion behind the grip-strength p = 0.96 or extract per-state respirometry numbers — my objection to that p-value is arithmetic inference from n=12 and a 2.2 kg mean difference plus the fact that the identical p = 0.96 is printed for three different comparisons, not a document I read. (2) I did not open Dollerup 2020 J Physiol in full (no open PMC record surfaced); my characterisation of it rests on Remie's and Jensen's descriptions of it plus its title, so treat that one as second-hand. (3) Whether 'aged' in the article means 70+ or 55+ decides how badly the exclusivity claim fails — at 70-80 it survives if narrowed, at 55+ it is simply false.

- **Elhassan et al. 2019 is the ONLY trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans** — `refuted`
  WRONG as stated. Jensen JB, Dollerup OL, ... Farup J, Jessen N, JCI Insight 2022 (10.1172/jci.insight.158314, PMC9675477) randomised 32 elderly individuals aged 55-80 to 1,000 mg NR + 200 mg pterostilbene vs placebo, took vastus lateralis biopsies (pre, 2 h, 2, 8, 30 d post experimental injury) and measured muscle NAD+ directly by UHPLC-MS. Verbatim from that paper: 'In skeletal muscle, NAD+, NADH, and NADPH increased in response to injury, but NAD+, NADH, NADP+, and NADPH were not affected by NRPT supplementation (Figure 3B).' Whole-blood NAD+ DID rise in the same trial. Remie 2020 also measured muscle NAD+ directly (enzymatic cycling assay AND MS) in 45-65 y olds, and Dollerup et al. 2020 J Physiol did so in obese insulin-resistant men. RIGHT version: Elhassan is the only randomised trial of NR alone in adults aged 70-80 (median 75) to measure the muscle NAD+ metabolome directly in biopsies — 'only trial ... in aged humans' full stop is false.

- **12 aged men, 1 g NR/day for 21 days, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled** — `corrected`
  Numbers right, design descriptor incomplete. Verbatim: 'Twelve aged (median age of 75 years) and marginally overweight (median BMI of 26.6 kg/m2; range 21-30), but otherwise healthy, men were recruited and orally supplemented with 1-g NR per day for 21 days in a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, CROSSOVER design, with 21 days' washout period between phases.' WRONG impression: 'randomised double-blind placebo-controlled' with 'NR vs placebo groups' reads as parallel-arm. RIGHT: it was a CROSSOVER — all 12 men received both NR and placebo, analysed by paired t tests; inclusion age 70-80 y; NR chloride (Niagen) 500 mg twice daily, capsules supplied by ChromaDex. (The paper's own Results text sloppily says 'the NR and placebo groups' for respirometry; do not inherit that.)

- **Muscle NAD+ did not rise significantly: 210 vs 197 pmol/mg, p=0.22** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim against the raw Europe PMC full-text XML of PMC6702140: '...we found that oral NR resulted in a 2-fold increase in muscle NAAD (NR 0.73 pmol/mg versus placebo 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.004), without an increase in NAD+ (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22).' 210 = NR, 197 = placebo, paired t test, n=12, mean ± SEM. Caveat worth carrying: BLOOD NAD+ did rise >2-fold in the same trial (NR 47.75 uM vs placebo 20.90 uM; p < 0.001), so the null must always be labelled as MUSCLE NAD+.

- **Paper title says NR 'augments the NAD+ metabolome'; the title refers to other metabolites, not NAD+ itself** — `confirmed`
  Title verbatim: 'Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD+ Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures.' The interpretation is correct and is the paper's own: what rose in muscle was NAAD (0.73 vs 0.35 pmol/mg, p=0.004), MeNAM (1.45 vs 0.35 pmol/mg, p=0.006) and other NAM clearance products, while NAD+ itself did not (p=0.22) and muscle NAM did not (92.0 vs 86.5 pmol/mg, p=0.96). Conclusion verbatim: 'The targeted NAD+ metabolome analysis suggests pre-existing NAD+ sufficiency...'

- **No difference in complex I- or complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'No differences were detected between the NR and placebo groups in skeletal muscle complex I- and complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and maximal respiratory capacity, with (Figure 3A) and without (Figure 3B) the prior addition of the fatty acid conjugate octanoyl-carnitine.' No p-values are given in text; the claim is figure-based (high-resolution respirometry, Oroboros O2k, permeabilized fibres). Citrate synthase activity, mtDNA copy number and ETC resident proteins were likewise unchanged, which strengthens rather than weakens the null.

- **No difference in peak hand-grip strength: NR 32.5 kg vs placebo 34.7 kg; p=0.96** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'After 3 weeks of supplementation, we did not observe any differences in the participants' peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96) or body-weight-adjusted relative strength (NR 2.4 versus placebo 2.3; p = 0.96) between NR and the placebo (Figure S4).' TWO caliber cautions the article must respect: (a) grip strength was an exploratory surrogate, NOT a pre-specified primary endpoint — the paper states no primary endpoint, calls itself an 'experimental medicine study', and its sample size was 'decided upon based on previous experience' with no formal power calculation; the authors themselves write 'one cannot expect hand-grip strength to change after 3 weeks of NR supplementation and without muscle training'. (b) The identical p = 0.96 is reported for three different comparisons in this paper (muscle NAM, peak grip, relative grip), and a 2.2 kg mean difference in 12 paired subjects cannot plausibly give p = 0.96 — treat that p-value as unreliable and quote 'no significant difference' rather than leaning on '0.96' as a precision figure.

- **Remie et al. 2020: 13 healthy overweight/obese participants, 1,000 mg/day NR, 6 weeks, crossover** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from raw full-text XML of PMC7398770 (Am J Clin Nutr 2020;112:413-426, doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqaa072, NCT02835664): 'A randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, crossover intervention study was conducted in 13 healthy overweight or obese men and women. Participants received 6 wk NR (1000 mg/d) and placebo supplementation...' Add for precision: inclusion 45-65 y, BMI 27-35, men and postmenopausal women, 4-7 wk washout; muscle NAD+ analyses were run on n=8 (enzymatic assay) and n=12 (MS), not all 13; muscle NAD+ metabolites were a SECONDARY outcome (primary focus was insulin sensitivity and muscle mitochondrial function).

- **Remie DID raise a muscle NAD+ metabolite — does it contradict Elhassan?** — `corrected`
  Half right, and the framing 'counterpart / contradiction' is WRONG. What rose was NAAD (+677 ± 155% vs placebo, P < 0.01, n=12) and methylnicotinamide/MeNAM (+299 ± 62%, P < 0.01, n=12) — plus muscle acetylcarnitine (4558 ± 749 vs 3025 ± 316 pmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.04). Muscle NAD+ ITSELF did NOT rise, by either method: enzymatic cycling assay 1.019 ± 0.126 vs 1.125 ± 0.106 nmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.34, n=8; MS P = 0.91, n=12. Verbatim: 'We confirmed that NR supplementation had no effect on skeletal muscle NAD+ content itself (P = 0.91, n = 12)' and 'In agreement with findings by Elhassan et al. (19) and Dollerup et al. (23), we have shown that NR supplementation increased the NAD+ metabolites NAAD and MeNAM in skeletal muscle, but without an increase in total NAD+ content itself.' Remie also found no effect on muscle mitochondrial respiration. So Remie REPLICATES Elhassan; it does not contradict it.

- **Later correction, erratum, retraction or failed replication of Elhassan 2019** — `confirmed`
  None found. Europe PMC returns no erratum, correction or retraction notice linked to PMID 31412242 / PMC6702140; the record's pubType list is 'randomized controlled trial; journal article' with no correction flag. The muscle-NAD+ null has since been independently reproduced in Remie 2020 (n=13, 6 wk), Dollerup 2020 J Physiol (2,000 mg/d, 12 wk, obese insulin-resistant men) and Jensen 2022 JCI Insight (NRPT, 55-80 y). Contrary evidence checked and found NOT to apply: Lapatto et al. Sci Adv 2023 (NR 250-1000 mg/d for 5 months, BMI-discordant monozygotic twins) is often cited as showing NR raised muscle NAD+ — it did not measure muscle NAD+ concentration at all. It measured whole-blood NAD metabolites plus mRNA expression of muscle NAD+ biosynthetic enzymes (NAMPT, NRK1, NMNAT3); and its participants had a median age of 39.7 years, so it is not an aged cohort.

**修正:**
- Delete or narrow the exclusivity claim. Elhassan 2019 is NOT 'the only trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans'. Jensen et al., JCI Insight 2022 (doi 10.1172/jci.insight.158314) measured muscle NAD+, NADH, NADP+ and NADPH by mass spectrometry in vastus lateralis biopsies from 32 elderly individuals aged 55-80 given 1,000 mg NR + 200 mg pterostilbene, and found muscle NAD+ unaffected by supplementation even though whole-blood NAD+ rose. Remie 2020 and Dollerup 2020 also measured muscle NAD+ directly in biopsies. Replace with: 'the only randomised trial of NR alone in adults aged 70-80 to measure the muscle NAD+ metabolome directly in biopsies'.
- Add 'crossover' to the Elhassan design description. It was a placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind CROSSOVER trial: all 12 men (median age 75, inclusion 70-80 y) received both 1 g/day NR and placebo for 21 days each with a 21-day washout, analysed by paired t tests. Do not describe it as NR and placebo 'groups' — that wording appears in the paper's own Results but misdescribes the design.
- Always label the null as MUSCLE NAD+. In the same trial, whole-blood NAD+ more than doubled (NR 47.75 uM vs placebo 20.90 uM; p < 0.001). The point is tissue-specific: the supplement is bioavailable systemically but does not move steady-state NAD+ in muscle.
- Do not present Remie 2020 as a contradiction of Elhassan. Remie raised muscle NAAD (+677 ± 155%, P < 0.01) and methylnicotinamide (+299 ± 62%, P < 0.01) — flux/turnover markers — while muscle NAD+ itself was unchanged (enzymatic assay 1.019 ± 0.126 vs 1.125 ± 0.106 nmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.34, n=8; MS P = 0.91, n=12). Remie's own Discussion states the result is 'In agreement with findings by Elhassan et al. and Dollerup et al.' Remie also found no effect on muscle mitochondrial respiration.
- If the article states what Remie 'raised', name the metabolites: NAAD and MeNAM (and separately, muscle acetylcarnitine, 4558 ± 749 vs 3025 ± 316 pmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.04). The bare phrase 'raised a muscle NAD+ metabolite' will be read by most readers as 'raised muscle NAD+', which is the opposite of what happened.
- Downgrade the reliance on the grip-strength p-value. The quoted figures (NR 32.5 kg vs placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96) are verbatim correct, but grip strength was an exploratory surrogate, not a pre-specified primary endpoint (the trial declares no primary endpoint and had no formal power calculation), and the paper's authors write that 'one cannot expect hand-grip strength to change after 3 weeks of NR supplementation and without muscle training'. The identical p = 0.96 is also printed for three different comparisons in the paper and is arithmetically implausible for a 2.2 kg paired difference at n=12. Say 'no significant difference in peak hand-grip strength (NR 32.5 vs placebo 34.7 kg)' and drop the p-value, or footnote it as reported-as-published.
- Note that Remie's participants were 45-65 y with BMI 27-35, i.e. overweight/obese middle-aged, not an aged cohort — so it cannot be used to generalise the Elhassan finding to older adults, only to corroborate the mechanism.
- If the article elsewhere cites Lapatto et al. Sci Adv 2023 (NR in BMI-discordant twins) as evidence that longer NR dosing raises muscle NAD+, correct it: that study did not measure muscle NAD+ concentration. It measured whole-blood NAD metabolites and mRNA expression of muscle NAD+ biosynthetic enzymes, and its twins had a median age of 39.7 years.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Jensen JB et al., 'A randomized placebo-controlled trial of nicotinamide riboside and pterostilbene supplementation in experimental muscle injury in elderly individuals', JCI Insight 2022, PMC9675477 — 32 elderly individuals aged 55-80, 1,000 mg NR + 200 mg pterostilbene, serial vastus lateralis biopsies, muscle NAD+ measured directly by UHPLC-MS. Directly refutes the 'only trial in aged humans' exclusivity claim, while independently reproducing the null: whole-blood NAD+, NAAD and Me2/4PY all rose, but muscle NAD+, NADH, NADP+ and NADPH were unaffected by supplementation.
- Remie 2020 measured muscle NAD+ by TWO independent methods (enzymatic cycling assay, n=8, P = 0.34; mass spectrometry, n=12, P = 0.91) and found no change by either — so it is a second-method replication of the Elhassan null rather than a counterpoint to it, which is the opposite of how the claim frames it.
- Dollerup et al. 2020 J Physiol (2,000 mg/d NR for 12 weeks in obese insulin-resistant men) is a third independent dataset with muscle biopsies showing raised NAD+ metabolites without a rise in muscle NAD+ or any change in mitochondrial respiration, content or morphology — relevant because it doubles the Elhassan dose and quadruples the duration and still shows nothing.
- Lapatto et al. Sci Adv 2023 does NOT provide the contrary 'long-duration NR raises muscle NAD+' result it is often cited for: it measured muscle NAD+ biosynthetic gene expression (NAMPT, NRK1, NMNAT3), not muscle NAD+ concentration, and its participants had a median age of 39.7 years.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I reached both primary documents as raw text rather than relying on fetch summarizers. My first WebFetch of the Elhassan PMC page returned a summary containing apparent quotes; per the pipeline warning I discarded it as evidence and re-downloaded the full PMC HTML with curl, stripped tags to plain text, and grepped for each exact string myself. Every quote marked verbatim above is a string I read in that extracted text (files retained at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/scratchpad/elhassan.txt, remie.txt, connell.txt).

Confirmed verbatim in Elhassan (PMC6702140): the full title; 'without an increase in NAD + (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22)'; 'No differences were detected between the NR and placebo groups in skeletal muscle complex I- and complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and maximal respiratory capacity'; 'we did not observe any differences in the participants' peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96)'. The title-vs-NAD+ reading is correct and is stated by the paper's own abstract, which attributes the 'metabolome' increase to NAAD and nicotinamide clearance products.

Three things the article gets wrong or under-specifies. First, the design is crossover with 21-day washout, not parallel — I confirmed this in the paper text and against the registry record NCT02950441 pulled from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API. Second, that same registry record shows muscle NAD+ and respirometry were CO-PRIMARY endpoints while grip strength was secondary; this makes the NAD+/OXPHOS nulls stronger than the article claims and the grip null weaker, and the authors explicitly disclaim the grip test in their discussion. Third and most serious, the Remie counterpart is framed as a contrast when Remie is a replication: Remie found muscle NAD+ itself flat at P = 0.91 and only NAAD (+677%) and MeNAM (+299%) raised, and says in its own discussion that this agrees with Elhassan and Dollerup.

Searching for refutation, I found no correction, erratum or retraction linked to Elhassan (Europe PMC citation query returned zero). But the exclusivity claim does not survive: Connell et al. 2021 in J Nutr measured muscle NAD+ by biopsy in 14 adults aged ~73 and found the identical pattern.

Tooling limitation, stated plainly: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I made any call, so I could not do open-ended discovery. I worked around it with direct HTTP to the Europe PMC REST search API and the ClinicalTrials.gov API, which is how I found Connell. That is a decent but not exhaustive sweep — my literature queries were keyword-bounded, so I cannot rule out a further aged-human muscle-biopsy NAD+ trial (particularly anything published 2023-2026, or indexed with unusual phrasing) that my queries missed. Since one counterexample already refutes the 'only trial' claim, this residual uncertainty does not change the verdict, but it does mean the article should avoid any exclusivity framing rather than merely narrowing it to a different superlative. I did not verify Dollerup et al. against its own primary text; I am reporting it only as cited by Remie, and it is flagged as such.

- **Elhassan et al. 2019 (Cell Reports) is the ONLY trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans** — `refuted`
  WRONG: 'the only trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans.' RIGHT: it is the only such trial using nicotinamide riboside in the 70-80 age band. A direct counterexample exists: Connell NJ et al., J Nutr 2021 (PMC8485915), 'NAD+-Precursor Supplementation With L-Tryptophan, Nicotinic Acid, and Nicotinamide Does Not Affect Mitochondrial Function or Skeletal Muscle Function in Physically Compromised Older Adults' — randomized double-blind controlled crossover, 14 community-dwelling older adults (age 72.9 +/- 4.0 y; BMI 25.2 +/- 2.3), 207.5 mg niacin equivalents/day for 32 days, with vastus lateralis biopsies. I read verbatim from that paper: skeletal muscle NAD+ was '7.5 +/- 1.9 compared with 7.9 +/- 1.6 AU' in INT vs CON, 'not significantly different', while 'skeletal muscle methyl-nicotinamide levels were significantly higher under NAD+-precursor supplementation [INT, 0.098 +/- 0.063 compared with CON, 0.025 +/- 0.014; P = 0.001]'. I also confirmed biopsies were used ('permeabilized muscle fibers obtained from skeletal muscle biopsies'). So a second aged-human muscle-biopsy NAD+ measurement exists — and it reproduces the same pattern (NAD+ flat, MeNAM up).

- **12 aged men, 1 g NR/day for 21 days, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled** — `corrected`
  N, sex, dose and duration are exactly right; the design descriptor is incomplete. WRONG (as implied): a parallel randomised placebo-controlled trial with an 'NR group' and a 'placebo group'. RIGHT: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled CROSSOVER trial with a 21-day washout — all 12 men received both NR and placebo. Verbatim from the paper: 'We supplemented 12 aged men with 1 g NR per day for 21 days in a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, crossover trial' and 'in a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, crossover design, with 21 days' washout period between phases.' Registry NCT02950441 lists interventionModel CROSSOVER, allocation RANDOMIZED, masking QUADRUPLE, enrollment 12. Participants: median age 75 (range 70-80), median BMI 26.6. Because it is a crossover, '210 vs 197' are within-subject phase means, not two independent arms — the article's 'NR ... vs placebo ...' phrasing (which mirrors the paper's own wording) should not be read as 6-vs-6.

- **Muscle NAD+ did NOT rise significantly: 210 vs 197 pmol/mg, p=0.22** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in the Cell Reports full text (PMC6702140). Exact string I read: 'without an increase in NAD + (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22).' Units pmol/mg, direction and p-value all match. STRENGTHENING FACT the article may use: this was a PRE-SPECIFIED CO-PRIMARY outcome, not a post-hoc null — NCT02950441 lists as primary outcomes both 'Skeletal muscle NAD+ levels in vastus lateralis biopsy using targeted metabolomics' and 'Mitochondrial function assessment in skeletal muscle using high resolution respirometry.'

- **The paper's title says NR 'augments the NAD+ metabolome'; the title refers to other metabolites, not NAD+ itself** — `confirmed`
  Title verified verbatim: 'Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD+ Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures' (Cell Reports 2019). The interpretation is correct and the paper states it explicitly. Abstract verbatim: 'Targeted metabolomics showed that NR elevated the muscle NAD+ metabolome, evident by increased nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide and nicotinamide clearance products.' The specific movers, verbatim: 'a 2-fold increase in muscle NAAD (NR 0.73 pmol/mg versus placebo 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.004)' and '5-fold increases in the products of NAM methylation clearance pathways; N-methyl nicotinamide (MeNAM; NR 1.45 pmol...'. Muscle nicotinamide itself was flat: 'NR supplementation did not affect muscle nicotinamide (NAM) (NR 92.0 pmol/mg versus placebo 86.5 pmol/mng; p = 0.96)' (the 'pmol/mng' typo is in the source).

- **No difference in complex I- or complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: 'No differences were detected between the NR and placebo groups in skeletal muscle complex I- and complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and maximal respiratory capacity, with (Figure 3A) and without (Figure 3B) the prior addition of the fatty acid conjugate octanoyl-carnitine.' Section heading verbatim: 'Three Weeks of Oral NR Does Not Alter Skeletal Muscle Mitochondrial Bioenergetics or Hand-Grip Strength.' Citrate synthase activity and mtDNA copy number were also unchanged. This too was a pre-specified co-primary outcome (NCT02950441).

- **No difference in peak hand-grip strength: NR 32.5 kg vs placebo 34.7 kg; p=0.96** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: 'After 3 weeks of supplementation, we did not observe any differences in the participants' peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96) or body-weight-adjusted relative strength (NR 2.4 versus placebo 2.3; p = 0.96) between NR and the placebo (Figure S4).' CALIBER CAVEAT the article should not omit: grip strength was a pre-specified SECONDARY outcome (NCT02950441, 'Muscle strength - grip testing'), and the authors pre-emptively disclaim it verbatim: 'one cannot expect hand-grip strength to change after 3 weeks of NR supplementation and without muscle training' and 'Our data suggest that 3 weeks of NR supplementation without concomitant muscle training is insufficient for increased strength.' Citing this null as evidence of 'no functional benefit' overstates it — a 21-day untrained grip test is not powered to show a functional effect. The OXPHOS null is the load-bearing functional evidence; the grip null is decorative.

- **Remie et al. 2020: 13 healthy overweight/obese participants, 1,000 mg/day NR, 6 weeks, crossover** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from Am J Clin Nutr 2020 (PMC7398770), 'Nicotinamide riboside supplementation alters body composition and skeletal muscle acetylcarnitine concentrations in healthy obese humans': 'we performed a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, crossover study with detailed metabolic phenotyping in which we provided healthy overweight or obese men and women 1000 mg NR/d for 6 wk.' n = 13 confirmed in figure legends; note the muscle NAD+ metabolomics were reported at n = 12, not 13.

- **Remie DID raise a muscle NAD+ metabolite — and whether this contradicts Elhassan** — `corrected`
  The literal statement is true but the implied contrast with Elhassan is FALSE, and this is the most consequential error in the group. WRONG framing: Remie as a counterpart/counterexample where NR succeeded and Elhassan failed. RIGHT: Remie found exactly what Elhassan found. Verbatim from Remie: 'We confirmed that NR supplementation had no effect on skeletal muscle NAD + content itself ( P = 0.91, n = 12). However, oral NR supplementation significantly increased 2 main markers of enhanced NAD + metabolism—nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide (NAAD, 677 +/- 155% increase in NR compared to placebo, P < 0.01, n = 12) and methylnicotinamide (MeNAM, 299 +/- 62% increase in NR compared to placebo, P < 0.01, n = 12), confirming that indeed NR was amplifying skeletal muscle NAD + metabolism without affecting the steady state.' Remie names the agreement itself, verbatim: 'In agreement with findings by Elhassan et al. ( 19 ) and Dollerup et al. ( 23 ), we have shown that NR supplementation increased the NAD + metabolites NAAD and MeNAM in skeletal muscle, but without an increase in total NAD + content itself.' So what rose in Remie is NAAD and MeNAM — precisely the two metabolite classes that also rose in Elhassan (NAAD 2-fold p=0.004; MeNAM 5-fold). Remie does not contradict Elhassan; it replicates it, and a third study (Dollerup) makes it three-for-three.

**修正:**
- Drop or narrow the exclusivity claim. 'The only trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans' is false. Connell et al., J Nutr 2021 (PMC8485915) did the same in 14 older adults (72.9 +/- 4.0 y) using vastus lateralis biopsies, with muscle NAD+ 7.5 +/- 1.9 vs 7.9 +/- 1.6 AU (not significant) and MeNAM significantly raised (0.098 +/- 0.063 vs 0.025 +/- 0.014, P = 0.001). Safe rewrite: 'the only nicotinamide riboside trial to measure muscle NAD+ directly by biopsy in adults aged 70-80.'
- Add 'crossover' to the Elhassan design descriptor. It was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled CROSSOVER trial with a 21-day washout (NCT02950441: interventionModel CROSSOVER, masking QUADRUPLE, enrollment 12).
