All 12 men received both NR and placebo; '210 vs 197 pmol/mg' are within-subject phase means, not two independent arms of six.
- Fix the Remie framing — this is a false contrast, not a counterpoint. Remie et al. 2020 found muscle NAD+ itself UNCHANGED (P = 0.91, n = 12); what rose was NAAD (+677 +/- 155%, P < 0.01) and MeNAM (+299 +/- 62%, P < 0.01). Remie states it agrees with Elhassan verbatim: 'In agreement with findings by Elhassan et al. and Dollerup et al., we have shown that NR supplementation increased the NAD+ metabolites NAAD and MeNAM in skeletal muscle, but without an increase in total NAD+ content itself.' Present Remie as an independent REPLICATION of the Elhassan pattern (precursor metabolites and clearance products rise; the NAD+ pool does not), not as a study that succeeded where Elhassan failed.
- Strengthen the Elhassan null by naming its endpoint status: muscle NAD+ by targeted metabolomics on vastus lateralis biopsy AND mitochondrial function by high-resolution respirometry were both PRE-SPECIFIED CO-PRIMARY outcomes in NCT02950441. These are primary-endpoint nulls, not post-hoc or secondary nulls — a materially stronger grading claim than the article currently makes.
- Demote or caveat the hand-grip result. Grip strength was a pre-specified SECONDARY outcome, and the authors disclaim it in the paper itself: 'one cannot expect hand-grip strength to change after 3 weeks of NR supplementation and without muscle training.' Do not cite the 32.5 vs 34.7 kg / p = 0.96 result as primary evidence of 'no functional benefit'; the complex I/II oxidative phosphorylation null is the load-bearing functional finding.
- If quoting Remie's participant count, note that n = 13 overall but the skeletal muscle NAD+ metabolomics were reported at n = 12.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Connell NJ et al., J Nutr 2021;151(10):2917-2931 (PMC8485915) is a second aged-human muscle-biopsy NAD+ measurement, directly refuting the 'only trial' exclusivity claim: 14 older adults aged 72.9 +/- 4.0 y, randomized double-blind controlled crossover, 207.5 mg niacin equivalents/day x 32 days, skeletal muscle NAD+ 7.5 +/- 1.9 vs 7.9 +/- 1.6 AU (ns), MeNAM significantly up (P = 0.001), and no improvement in ADP-stimulated (P = 0.716) or maximally uncoupled (P = 0.495) mitochondrial respiration.
- Remie et al. 2020 contradicts the article's implied Elhassan-vs-Remie contrast rather than supporting it: Remie's own discussion places its result 'In agreement with findings by Elhassan et al. ... and Dollerup et al.', all three showing NAAD and MeNAM up with total muscle NAD+ unchanged.
- Dollerup et al. (cited in Remie as ref 23; J Physiol 2020, 'Nicotinamide riboside does not alter mitochondrial respiration, content or morphology in skeletal muscle from obese and insulin-resistant men') is a third independent muscle-biopsy dataset showing the same dissociation, further undercutting any framing in which one of these trials is the outlier.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

I reached primary documents for every quantitative sub-claim. WebSearch was exhausted at session start (200/200), so I worked entirely through WebFetch against Europe PMC REST, PMC, and the ClinicalTrials.gov API.

Guarding against the fabrication failure mode: I verified every load-bearing Elhassan and Remie number in TWO independent renderings — the PMC HTML article page and the Europe PMC `fullTextXML` endpoint — issued with different prompts. The XML fetches returned strings carrying intact JATS markup (`<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>`, `<sup>+</sup>`) and even a source typo ('86.5 pmol/mng'), which is positive evidence the text is genuine extraction rather than a model reconstruction. ScienceDirect (403) and bioRxiv (403) were blocked, so my two channels both ultimately derive from PMC deposits; that is a residual limitation, though the JATS artifacts make fabrication unlikely.

Confirmed verbatim in Elhassan (PMID 31412242, PMC6702140, Cell Rep 28:1717-1728.e6): the exact title including the words 'Aged Human'; the design sentence (twelve men, median age 75, median BMI 26.6, 1 g/day, 21 days, CROSSOVER with 21-day washout); 'without an increase in NAD+ (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22)'; the complex I/complex II OXPHOS null sentence; and 'peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96)'. All the article's numbers are exactly right.

Two things the article gets wrong. First, and decisively: I searched for later trials specifically to refute the exclusivity claim, and found the NICE trial (McDermott 2024, Nat Commun) — 90 PAD patients, mean age 71.2, open gastrocnemius biopsies at baseline and 6 months, muscle NAD+ by HPLC. That is a larger, longer, older-cohort NR trial with direct muscle-biopsy NAD+, so 'the only trial ... in aged humans' is false as written. Damgaard & Treebak's 2023 review independently lists four biopsy trials measuring muscle NAD+. Second, the Remie counterpart is misframed: I confirmed via two fetches that Remie's muscle NAD+ was null by both assays (P = 0.34, n = 8 enzymatic; P = 0.91, n = 12 mass-spec), and that what rose was NAAD (+677%) and MeNAM (+299%) — exactly the metabolites Elhassan also found elevated. Remie replicates Elhassan rather than contradicting it.

One finding that helps the article: I pulled ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02950441 and confirmed that muscle NAD+ (vastus lateralis, targeted metabolomics) and high-resolution respirometry were both listed PRIMARY outcome measures, with grip strength secondary. The article should say so — these are pre-specified primary-endpoint nulls, not post-hoc ones.

Remaining uncertainty: I could not retrieve an independent non-PMC copy of either full text. I found no erratum, correction, or retraction attached to DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.043. I did not independently verify the Dollerup 2020 and Stocks 2021 primary papers — those come from the Damgaard & Treebak review and are cited here only as secondary support; the NICE refutation, which I did verify against the primary article, is sufficient on its own to overturn the exclusivity sub-claim.

- **Elhassan et al. 2019 Cell Reports is the ONLY trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans** — `refuted`
  WRONG: 'the only trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans.' RIGHT: it is not the only one, and this is false even with the 'aged' qualifier. McDermott et al. 2024, the NICE trial (Nat Commun, PMC11176364, PMID 38871717), randomised 90 people with peripheral artery disease, 'mean age was 71.2 years (standard deviation (SD): 9.1)', to 6 months of NR. Verbatim from the paper: 'An open muscle biopsy was performed in the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle after subcutaneous lidocaine administration at baseline and 6-month follow-up', and muscle NAD+ was assayed — 'For measurement of NAD+ abundance, nucleotides were measured by High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC)'. Result was null (combined NR groups vs placebo -35.13, one-sided 90% CI -81.20 to +infinity, P = 0.84). NICE is larger (n=90 vs 12), longer (6 months vs 21 days) and in an older mean-age cohort. Separately, at least three other NR trials took muscle biopsies and measured muscle NAD+ in non-aged cohorts (Dollerup 2020, obese insulin-resistant men, 2000 mg/d 12 wk; Remie 2020; Stocks 2021, recreationally active men), so the unqualified 'only trial ... with biopsies' half of the sentence is false outright. Safe rewrite: 'one of the few trials, and the first, to measure muscle NAD+ directly by biopsy in aged humans.'

- **Design: 12 aged men, 1 g NR/day for 21 days, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled** — `corrected`
  Numbers all correct but the design descriptor is incomplete. Verbatim: 'Twelve aged (median age of 75 years) and marginally overweight (median BMI of 26.6 kg/m2; range 21-30), but otherwise healthy, men were recruited and orally supplemented with 1-g NR per day for 21 days in a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind, crossover design, with 21 days' washout period between phases.' WRONG (by omission): stating '12 aged men ... randomised double-blind placebo-controlled' invites the reader to assume a parallel design with ~6 per arm. RIGHT: it was a CROSSOVER — all 12 men received both NR and placebo, with 21 days' washout. Registry NCT02950441 confirms male-only, minimum age 70, enrolment 12.

- **Muscle NAD+ did NOT rise significantly: 210 vs 197 pmol/mg, p=0.22** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in two independent renderings (PMC6702140 HTML and the Europe PMC fullTextXML): 'Consistent with nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide (NAAD) as a highly sensitive biomarker of NR supplementation and an enhanced rate of NAD+ synthesis, we found that oral NR resulted in a 2-fold increase in muscle NAAD (NR 0.73 pmol/mg versus placebo 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.004), without an increase in NAD+ (NR 210 pmol/mg versus 197 pmol/mg; p = 0.22).' STRENGTHENER the article should use: this was a PRE-SPECIFIED PRIMARY endpoint, not a post-hoc null. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02950441 ('Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide and Skeletal Muscle Metabolic Phenotype', NADMet) lists as primary outcome measures both 'Mitochondrial function assessment in skeletal muscle using high resolution respirometry' and 'Skeletal muscle NAD+ levels in vastus lateralis biopsy using targeted metabolomics'.

- **The title says NR 'augments the NAD+ metabolome' but refers to other metabolites, not NAD+ itself** — `confirmed`
  Title verified verbatim via Europe PMC core record (PMID 31412242, PMCID PMC6702140, DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.043, Cell Reports 28:1717-1728.e6): 'Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD+ Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures.' Note the exact title contains 'Aged Human', which the claim's paraphrase drops. The interpretation is correct and can be evidenced: the muscle analytes that actually rose were NAAD (NR 0.73 vs placebo 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.004), MeNAM (1.45 vs 0.35 pmol/mg; p = 0.006), Me-2-py (6.6 vs 1.1 pmol/mg; p < 0.001) and Me-4-py (1.6 vs 0.3 pmol/mg; p < 0.001) — i.e. one upstream biosynthetic intermediate and three degradation/clearance products — while NAD+ itself did not move.

- **No difference in complex I- or complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in two independent renderings: 'No differences were detected between the NR and placebo groups in skeletal muscle complex I- and complex II-mediated oxidative phosphorylation and maximal respiratory capacity, with (Figure 3A) and without (Figure 3B) the prior addition of the fatty acid conjugate octanoyl-carnitine.' As with muscle NAD+, this was a pre-specified PRIMARY outcome per NCT02950441 ('Mitochondrial function assessment in skeletal muscle using high resolution respirometry'), which makes the null stronger than the article currently implies.

- **No difference in peak hand-grip strength: NR 32.5 kg vs placebo 34.7 kg; p=0.96** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in two independent renderings: 'After 3 weeks of supplementation, we did not observe any differences in the participants' peak hand-grip strengths (NR 32.5 kg versus placebo 34.7 kg; p = 0.96) or body-weight-adjusted relative strength (NR 2.4 versus placebo 2.3; p = 0.96) between NR and the placebo.' One caliber caveat the article should not overstate: unlike the NAD+ and respirometry nulls, grip strength is a SECONDARY outcome in NCT02950441, and with n=12 over 21 days the trial is not powered to exclude a functional effect — this is an absence of evidence at very low power, not evidence of absence.

- **Counterpart: Remie et al. 2020, 13 participants, 1,000 mg/day NR, 6 weeks, crossover — DID raise a muscle NAD+ metabolite** — `corrected`
  Design and the 'metabolite rose' half are correct; the implied CONTRAST with Elhassan is wrong. Remie et al. 2020, Am J Clin Nutr (PMID 32320006, PMCID PMC7398770), title verbatim: 'Nicotinamide riboside supplementation alters body composition and skeletal muscle acetylcarnitine concentrations in healthy obese humans.' Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, 'Thirteen participants completed the study', inclusion '45-65 y of age, BMI (in kg/m2) 27-35', 'Each participant received 2 interventions, each of which lasted 6 wk' at '1000 mg/d'. What rose, verbatim: 'oral NR supplementation significantly increased 2 main markers of enhanced NAD+ metabolism—nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide (NAAD, 677 +/- 155% increase in NR compared to placebo, P < 0.01, n = 12) and methylnicotinamide (MeNAM, 299 +/- 62% increase in NR compared to placebo, P < 0.01, n = 12)'. CRITICAL: muscle NAD+ ITSELF did NOT rise in Remie either, by either assay — 'NAD+ content was not different between NR and placebo (1.019 +/- 0.126 compared with 1.125 +/- 0.106 nmol/mg dry weight in NR and placebo, respectively; change: 0.106 +/- 0.105 nmol/mg dry weight, P = 0.34, n = 8)' and 'We confirmed that NR supplementation had no effect on skeletal muscle NAD+ content itself (P = 0.91, n = 12)'. WRONG framing: presenting Remie as a counterpart that contradicts or offsets Elhassan. RIGHT: Remie REPLICATES Elhassan. Elhassan itself already reported the same NAAD rise (2-fold, p = 0.004) and MeNAM rise (p = 0.006) alongside a flat NAD+. Both trials show the identical pattern: NR reaches muscle and moves flux/clearance markers, while the NAD+ pool does not measurably change.

**修正:**
- Delete the exclusivity claim. Elhassan 2019 is NOT 'the only trial that measured muscle NAD+ directly with biopsies in aged humans.' McDermott et al. 2024 (the NICE trial, Nature Communications, PMID 38871717) randomised 90 peripheral-artery-disease patients of mean age 71.2 years (SD 9.1) to 6 months of NR, took open medial-gastrocnemius biopsies at baseline and 6-month follow-up, and measured muscle NAD+ abundance by HPLC — also null (combined NR vs placebo -35.13, one-sided 90% CI -81.20 to +infinity, P = 0.84). At least three further NR trials (Dollerup 2020, Remie 2020, Stocks 2021) also measured muscle NAD+ by biopsy in younger cohorts. Rewrite as: 'Elhassan 2019 was the first trial to measure muscle NAD+ directly by biopsy in aged humans.'
- Describe Elhassan's design as a CROSSOVER, not just 'randomised double-blind placebo-controlled.' The exact design was: twelve aged (median age 75 years), marginally overweight (median BMI 26.6 kg/m2) but otherwise healthy MEN, 1 g NR/day for 21 days, placebo-controlled randomised double-blind crossover with a 21-day washout between phases. All 12 received both arms — writing '12 aged men' without 'crossover' misleads readers into assuming ~6 per arm.
- Add that the muscle NAD+ null and the respirometry null were PRE-SPECIFIED PRIMARY endpoints, which materially strengthens the article's point. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02950441 (NADMet) lists two primary outcome measures: 'Mitochondrial function assessment in skeletal muscle using high resolution respirometry' and 'Skeletal muscle NAD+ levels in vastus lateralis biopsy using targeted metabolomics.' These are not post-hoc nulls.
- Downgrade the grip-strength point. Peak hand-grip strength is a SECONDARY outcome in NCT02950441, not primary, and with n=12 over 21 days the trial cannot exclude a functional effect. Present it as 'no signal on a secondary functional endpoint in an underpowered 21-day study,' not as evidence that NR does not help function.
- Fix the Remie framing — it does not contradict Elhassan, it replicates it. Remie 2020 found muscle NAD+ itself UNCHANGED by both assays ('NAD+ content was not different between NR and placebo ... P = 0.34, n = 8' and 'We confirmed that NR supplementation had no effect on skeletal muscle NAD+ content itself (P = 0.91, n = 12)'). What rose in Remie were NAD+ METABOLOME markers: NAAD +677 +/- 155% (P < 0.01, n = 12) and MeNAM +299 +/- 62% (P < 0.01, n = 12). Elhassan reported the very same pattern (muscle NAAD up 2-fold, p = 0.004; MeNAM 1.45 vs 0.35 pmol/mg, p = 0.006). The correct statement is that two independent trials converge: oral NR demonstrably reaches skeletal muscle and shifts flux and clearance metabolites, but does not measurably raise the muscle NAD+ pool.
- Correct the Remie participant descriptor if the article calls them 'aged' or uses them as an aging cohort: inclusion was 45-65 years, BMI 27-35, men and women, mean age 59 +/- 5 — middle-aged overweight/obese, not aged. (The paper's own title says 'healthy obese humans'; the text says overweight/obese.) Also note the crossover had a 4-7 week washout.
- Quote Elhassan's title exactly if quoting it — it is 'Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD+ Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures.' The words 'Aged Human' are in the title and should not be dropped. The article's reading of the title is correct and can be made concrete: the muscle analytes that actually rose were NAAD (0.73 vs 0.35 pmol/mg, p = 0.004), MeNAM (1.45 vs 0.35, p = 0.006), Me-2-py (6.6 vs 1.1, p < 0.001) and Me-4-py (1.6 vs 0.3, p < 0.001) — one biosynthetic intermediate plus three degradation products — while NAD+ itself did not move.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- McDermott et al. 2024, 'Nicotinamide riboside for peripheral artery disease: the NICE randomized clinical trial', Nature Communications, PMID 38871717 / PMCID PMC11176364. Directly contradicts the 'only trial ... in aged humans' assertion: 90 randomised participants, 'mean age was 71.2 years (standard deviation (SD): 9.1)', 6 months of NR, with 'An open muscle biopsy ... performed in the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle ... at baseline and 6-month follow-up' and muscle NAD+ abundance measured by HPLC. Its NAD+ result was also null (-35.13, one-sided 90% CI -81.20 to +infinity, P = 0.84), so it reinforces the article's substantive conclusion while destroying its exclusivity framing.
- Remie et al. 2020 does not function as a counterpoint to Elhassan — it independently reproduces Elhassan's central null. Muscle NAD+ was unchanged on both the enzymatic assay (P = 0.34, n = 8) and targeted mass spectrometry (P = 0.91, n = 12). Any sentence contrasting Remie's 'positive' muscle NAD+ result against Elhassan's negative one is a misreading: Remie's positive findings are NAAD and MeNAM, which Elhassan also found elevated.
- Damgaard & Treebak 2023, 'What is really known about the effects of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans', Sci Adv, PMID 37478182 / PMCID PMC10361580, tabulates four NR trials that took muscle biopsies and measured muscle NAD+ — Dollerup 2020 (obese insulin-resistant men, 2000 mg/d, 12 wk), Elhassan 2019, Remie 2020, and Stocks 2021 (recreationally active men, 1000 mg/d, 7 d) — all null for muscle NAD+. This both refutes the 'only trial with biopsies' wording and gives the article a much stronger, better-sourced generalisation than a single-study claim.
- Caliber note on the NICE trial if the article cites it elsewhere: its efficacy analysis used ONE-SIDED 90% confidence intervals (reported as '+1.8,+infinity'), not two-sided 95% intervals. Its headline 6-minute-walk benefit should not be quoted as if it met a conventional two-sided 95% threshold.

## V20 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

I reached and read all five primary documents myself rather than trusting fetch summaries. This mattered: my first four WebFetch attempts returned a reCAPTCHA wall, an unrelated Science Advances paper on protein NMR, an unrelated page about dementia-friendly gardens, and an HTTP 402 -- and in each case the summarizer model produced fluent prose about what it had NOT read. Given the pipeline's known fabrication incident, I abandoned WebFetch for the load-bearing verification and switched to curl via Bash, pulling raw XML and raw MEDLINE text that I stripped and grepped locally. Every string I have marked verbatim above was matched by grep in a file on disk, not read out of a model summary.

Sources actually obtained: PMC5876407 (Martens 2018, Nat Commun, CC BY), PMC10361580 (Damgaard & Treebak 2023, Sci Adv), PMC12022230 (Prokopidis 2025, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, CC BY) -- all three as full text via the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint; and raw MEDLINE abstracts via NCBI efetch for PMIDs 39531138, 29992272, 39185644, 39116016, 32320006, 30911774, 41901064, 42514320. PMIDs were mapped to PMCIDs through the NCBI ID converter. Dollerup 2018 is not deposited in PMC, so item (d) rests on the publisher-supplied structured abstract from MEDLINE rather than the full text -- the design, dose, N, clamp method and conclusion are all in that abstract verbatim, but I did not see the full results tables, so I could not check per-arm completer counts or whether the clamp analysis was the pre-specified primary endpoint. That is the one residual gap in an otherwise fully sourced verification.

Findings. Sub-claims (b) and (d) are clean -- every number, dose, duration, N and conclusion matches the source word for word. Sub-claim (e) is the strongest item in the group: the incriminating sentence 'Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made' exists exactly as quoted, and I additionally recovered the subgroup denominator (N=13), the completer count (24 of 30 randomized, 60 consented), the null whole-group figures (-3.9 and -2.0 mmHg on one-sided CIs, failing Bonferroni at alpha=0.006), the absence of any washout, and the ChromaDex funding. Its only defect is the word 'pre-specified,' which is wrong -- blood pressure was never pre-specified; the only pre-specified primary outcomes were NAD+ metabolites, and all physiological outcomes were exploratory and one-sided.

Sub-claim (a) carries a genuine numeric error: the article assigns the all-trials duration range (3-24 weeks) to the NMN subset, when the 3-week trial is Elhassan 2019, an NR study; the NMN range is 4-24 weeks. It also conflates pooled with narrative, since only NMN was meta-analysed and the NR narrative was mixed, not null. Sub-claim (c) is right on the article count (25, confirmed verbatim and by counting the review's own table) but hardens the authors' 'unfortunate tendency ... to exaggerate' into 'systematically overstates' and omits their explicit hedge about inflammation and severe disease.

I actively hunted for refutations and found no erratum, correction, or critical comment registered against any of the five sources. The Diabetologia letter 'Underpowered or negative?' initially looked like an attack on Dollerup 2018 but is authored BY the Dollerup group about a different paper. The real problem for the article is not falsification but currency and unanimity: a 2025 meta-analysis (PMID 39185644) reaches the opposite conclusion on gait speed from the one cited in (a), and two 2026 Nutrients meta-analyses (PMIDs 42514320, 41901064) supersede the 8-RCT analysis in (b) and report a small but statistically significant diastolic blood pressure reduction. An article dated mid-2026 that cites only the null results, without acknowledging the disagreeing pooled analyses, would be presenting a contested literature as settled -- which is a milder version of the same selective-reporting fault the article accuses the NAD field of.

- **(a) 2025 meta-analysis of NR and NMN on skeletal muscle: 10 RCTs; NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks in 6 RCTs, NR 500-1000 mg/d for 3-12 weeks in 4 RCTs; mean age 60.9-83; no effect on skeletal muscle index/mass or strength** — `corrected`
  Source located and read in full: Prokopidis K, Moriarty F, Bahat G, McLean J, Church DD, Patel HP. 'The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.' J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025;16(3):e13799. PMID 40275690, PMC12022230 (CC BY full text read via Europe PMC fullTextXML). CONFIRMED verbatim: '10 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1), from which, six used nicotinamide mononucleotide ... and four used nicotinamide riboside'; 'The mean age range of the included participants was 60.9-83 years'; null pooled NMN results for SMI (MD -0.42, 95%CI -0.99-0.14, I2=63%, p=0.14), left HGS (MD 0.61, 95%CI -0.89-2.10, p=0.42), right HGS (MD 0.45, 95%CI -1.06-1.96, p=0.56), gait speed (MD -0.01, 95%CI -0.08-0.06, p=0.79), 5CST (MD -0.21, 95%CI -0.70-0.29, p=0.41). Verbatim bottom line: 'Current evidence does not support NMN and NR supplementation for preserving muscle mass and function in adults with mean age of over 60 years.' TWO ERRORS. (1) DURATION MISATTRIBUTED. WRONG: 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks.' RIGHT: NMN was 4-24 weeks. The paper states an OVERALL range across all ten studies -- 'Treatment dosage was between 250 to 2000 mg/day and treatment duration between 3 and 24 weeks among studies' -- and the article has split that pooled range onto the NMN arm. Table 1 shows the six NMN trials at 250 mg/d x 24 wk; 250 mg/d x 12 wk (Kim 2022 AM and PM arms); 250 mg/d x 12 wk (Morifuji 2024); 250 mg/d x 12 wk (Igarashi 2022); 250 mg/d x 10 wk (Yoshino 2021); 2000 mg/d x 4 wk (Pencina 2023). The 3-week figure belongs to Elhassan 2019, an NR trial (1 g/d x 3 wk). The NR half of the claim is exactly right: Elhassan 1 g/d 3 wk, Martens 2018 1 g/d 6 wk, Orr 2024 1 g/d 10 wk, McDermott 2024 500 mg/d 12 wk = 500-1000 mg/d, 3-12 weeks. (2) POOLED-VS-NARRATIVE CONFLATION. Only NMN was meta-analysed. NR was narrative synthesis only -- no NR pooling for SMI, grip, or gait speed -- and the NR narrative was NOT uniformly null: 'NR supplementation was associated with a longer 6MWD among individuals with peripheral artery disease. However, lower scores in the SPPB and slower 5CST were observed in those with mild cognitive impairment.' Saying 'the meta-analysis found no effect on muscle index/mass or strength' for both compounds overstates what was pooled. No erratum, correction, or comment is registered on PMID 40275690.

- **(b) 2024/2025 meta-analysis of NMN on metabolic endpoints: 8 RCTs, n=342 middle-aged/older adults, 250-2000 mg/day for 14 days to 12 weeks, no significant benefit** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim against the raw MEDLINE record (NCBI efetch, not a summarizer). Chen F, Zhou D, Kong AP, Yim NT, Dai S, Chen YN, Hui LL. 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide on Glucose and Lipid Metabolism in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.' Curr Diab Rep 2024 Nov 12;25(1):4. PMID 39531138, PMC11557618. Verbatim: 'Eight RCTs on NMN (dosage ranged 250-2000 mg/d for a duration of 14 days to 12 weeks) involving a total of 342 middle-age/older adults (49% females, mainly non-diabetic) reporting at least one outcome on glucose control or lipid profile published in 2021-2023 were reviewed. The random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile.' Verbatim bottom line: 'Based on the small number of RCTs involving mainly relatively healthy adults, short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.' Every element checks out. Two precision notes, neither a factual error: the 2024/2025 ambiguity is real and benign (published online 12 Nov 2024, assigned to volume 25 issue 1, nominally 2025); and 'metabolic endpoints' should be read narrowly -- the pooled outcomes were glucose control and lipid profile only, not body weight, BMI, or blood pressure. No erratum or comment registered.

- **(c) Damgaard & Treebak assessed all 25 published human NR research articles and concluded effects are few and clinically marginal and that the literature systematically overstates them** — `corrected`
  Source located and read in full: Damgaard MV, Treebak JT. 'What is really known about the effects of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans.' Sci Adv 2023;9(29):eadi4862. PMID 37478182, PMC10361580 (full text read via Europe PMC fullTextXML). The article count is CONFIRMED verbatim: 'This review endeavors to summarize and critically assess the 25 currently published research articles on human nicotinamide riboside supplementation to identify any poorly founded claims and assist the field in elucidating the actual future potential for nicotinamide riboside.' I also counted the 25 trials in the review's own overview table. Bottom line verbatim: 'Collectively, oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation has displayed few clinically relevant effects, and there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects.' TWO CALIBER SLIPS, both hardening the source. (1) 'systematically overstates' is stronger than the source's 'an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate'; a tendency is not a systematic property. (2) The article omits the review's own hedge, which immediately follows the sentence quoted: 'Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases. The putative clinical potential of oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans remains to be understood.' Presenting this as a flat negative verdict misrepresents a review that explicitly leaves the door open on inflammation and severe disease. Also note 'few clinically relevant effects' in the source reads as few in NUMBER; 'clinically marginal' (about magnitude) is a defensible but not identical gloss. Finally, this is a narrative critical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis -- 'most complete' is an editorial judgement, defensible because it covers the entire human corpus as of 2023, but it should not be phrased so as to imply systematic-review methodology. No erratum or comment registered.

- **(d) 40 obese insulin-resistant men, 2,000 mg/day NR for 12 weeks, hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, no effect on insulin sensitivity** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim against the raw MEDLINE record (NCBI efetch). Dollerup OL, Christensen B, Svart M, Schmidt MS, Sulek K, Ringgaard S, Stodkilde-Jorgensen H, Moller N, Brenner C, Treebak JT, Jessen N. 'A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial of nicotinamide riboside in obese men: safety, insulin-sensitivity, and lipid-mobilizing effects.' Am J Clin Nutr 2018 Aug 1;108(2):343-353. PMID 29992272, NCT02303483. Verbatim design: 'forty healthy, sedentary men with a body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m2, age-range 40-70 y were randomly assigned to 12 wk of NR (1000 mg twice daily) or placebo. We determined the effects of NR supplementation on insulin sensitivity by a hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp.' Verbatim results: 'Insulin sensitivity, endogenous glucose production, and glucose disposal and oxidation were not improved by NR supplementation.' Verbatim conclusion: '12 wk of NR supplementation in doses of 2000 mg/d appears safe, but does not improve insulin sensitivity and whole-body glucose metabolism in obese, insulin-resistant men.' 2000 mg/d is correct (1000 mg twice daily). Design is parallel-group, 20 NR / 20 placebo (confirmed independently in the Damgaard & Treebak trial table: 'Dollerup 2018 Obese, insulin resistant 20 20 2000 12 weeks'). The 'most rigorous' framing survives scrutiny: I searched for every NR trial using a clamp and found only two others -- Remie 2020 (Am J Clin Nutr 112:413-426, PMID 32320006, n=13 crossover, 1000 mg/d x 6 wk, also null: 'no effects of NR were found on insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial function...') and Dollerup's own follow-ups on the same cohort. At n=40 this is the largest, and the only 2000 mg/d one. I specifically hunted for a critical letter attacking this null and found none: the Diabetologia 2019 letter 'Underpowered or negative? A crucial distinction' (PMID 30911774) is BY Dollerup, Treebak and Jessen about a different paper, not a criticism of this trial. No erratum, correction, or comment is registered on PMID 29992272.

- **(e) 'NR lowers blood pressure by 9 mmHg' (Martens 2018) is a post-hoc exploratory subgroup of a 24-completer crossover about which the authors wrote that no statistical inferences can be made; the pre-specified whole-group results were null** — `corrected`
  Substantively CONFIRMED word-for-word against the full text: Martens CR, Denman BA, Mazzo MR, Armstrong ML, Reisdorph N, McQueen MB, Chonchol M, Seals DR. 'Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD+ in healthy middle-aged and older adults.' Nat Commun 2018;9:1286. PMID 29599478, PMC5876407 (CC BY full text read via Europe PMC fullTextXML). Verbatim: 'Of particular note, mean SBP was 9 mmHg lower after NR vs. placebo in individuals with elevated/stage I hypertension, whereas no change was observed in subjects with initial SBP in the normal range (Fig. 3d). Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made.' That exact string exists -- I read it in the source, not in a fetch summary. Completers verbatim: 'resulting in a total of 24 subjects who completed the trial' (60 consented, 30 randomized, 24 completed). Design: 2 x 6-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, 500 mg twice per day. Subgroup sizes: elevated/stage I hypertension N=13 vs normal BP N=11 -- so the celebrated 9 mmHg rests on THIRTEEN people. Whole-group result verbatim: 'Supplementation with NR tended to lower mean systolic (SBP; mean change = -3.9 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.058)) and diastolic (DBP; mean change = -2.0 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.26)) blood pressure (BP) in all subjects as a group (Fig. 3a-c); however, these comparisons were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons.' ONE CALIBER SLIP: the article calls the whole-group BP analysis 'pre-specified,' which makes the trial sound more rigorous than it was. The pre-specified PRIMARY outcomes were NAD+ metabolites only -- verbatim: 'With the exception of our primary outcome variables (NAD+ metabolites: NAD+, NAAD, NADP, NaM, NMN), in which inferences were based on an unadjusted alpha level set at 0.05, all inferences of significance are based on the Bonferroni-adjusted alpha level (alpha = 0.006).' BP was never a pre-specified endpoint; verbatim: 'Because the physiological outcomes in this study were designed to be exploratory in nature, the associated statistical inferences for those variables were based on one-sided hypothesis testing and the alpha level was set at a conservative P < 0.006 to account for multiple testing.' So the whole-group BP result was itself exploratory and ONE-SIDED, and still failed. Two further weaknesses the article can use: there was no washout -- verbatim: 'A formal washout period was not included in the study design' -- and the trial was part-funded by ChromaDex, which supplied the NIAGEN study pills. Damgaard & Treebak's independent assessment corroborates: 'These findings have not been supported by other reports.' No erratum or comment registered.

**修正:**
- In sub-claim (a), change the NMN duration range from '3-24 weeks' to '4-24 weeks'. Prokopidis et al. (J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025;16(3):e13799) report '3 and 24 weeks' as the range across ALL TEN included trials, not for the NMN subset. The six NMN trials ran 4, 10, 12, 12, 12 and 24 weeks; the 3-week study is Elhassan 2019, which is an NR trial. The NR half of the claim (500-1000 mg/d, 3-12 weeks, 4 RCTs) is correct as written and needs no change.
- In sub-claim (a), stop describing the null as covering both compounds equally. Only NMN was meta-analysed (pooled nulls for skeletal muscle index, left and right handgrip strength, gait speed, and 5-time chair stand test). NR was handled by narrative synthesis only, with no pooled estimate, and the NR narrative was mixed rather than null: longer 6-minute walk distance in peripheral artery disease, but lower SPPB scores and slower 5-time chair stand in mild cognitive impairment. Recommended phrasing: 'pooled NMN results were null across muscle index, grip strength, gait speed and chair-stand; the four NR trials were too heterogeneous to pool and gave mixed results.'
- In sub-claim (c), soften 'the literature systematically overstates them' to match the source. Damgaard & Treebak (Sci Adv 2023;9(29):eadi4862) wrote 'there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects.' A tendency is not a systematic property; quote the authors' wording rather than hardening it.
- In sub-claim (c), do not present Damgaard & Treebak as a flat negative verdict. Their abstract adds, immediately after the sentence about few clinically relevant effects: 'Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases. The putative clinical potential of oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans remains to be understood.' Include this hedge.
- In sub-claim (c), if the article calls this 'the most complete critical review,' make clear it is a NARRATIVE critical review covering the full corpus as of 2023 -- not a systematic review or meta-analysis. Also date-stamp the count: 'the 25 human NR research articles published as of mid-2023,' since the corpus has grown since (e.g. Norheim et al., Nature Aging 2024, NR in COPD).
- In sub-claim (e), delete the word 'pre-specified' from 'the pre-specified whole-group results were null.' Blood pressure was never a pre-specified endpoint in Martens 2018. The only pre-specified primary outcomes were the NAD+ metabolites (NAD+, NAAD, NADP, NaM, NMN); the paper states 'the physiological outcomes in this study were designed to be exploratory in nature.' Correct phrasing: 'the whole-group result -- itself an exploratory, one-sided analysis -- was null (SBP -3.9 mmHg, DBP -2.0 mmHg, not significant after Bonferroni correction at alpha = 0.006).'
- In sub-claim (e), add the subgroup denominator, which is the strongest single fact against the 9 mmHg figure: the elevated/stage I hypertension subgroup contained just 13 people (N=13), versus N=11 with normal baseline BP, out of 24 completers. Optionally add that no formal washout period was included in the crossover, and that ChromaDex supplied the NIAGEN study pills and provided partial funding.
- In sub-claim (b), specify the endpoints rather than saying 'metabolic endpoints' generally. Chen et al. (Curr Diab Rep 2024;25(1):4) pooled fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated haemoglobin, HOMA-IR and lipid profile only -- not body weight, BMI or blood pressure. Cite it as 2024 (published online 12 Nov 2024; volume 25 issue 1 is nominally 2025), and note the included trials were published 2021-2023 in mainly non-diabetic adults, 49% female.
- In sub-claim (d), give the full participant descriptor from the source: 'forty healthy, sedentary men with a body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m2, age-range 40-70 y,' randomised 20/20 in a parallel-group design (not crossover), NCT02303483. If the article calls this 'the most rigorous insulin-sensitivity test of NR,' support it by noting it is the largest and highest-dose NR clamp trial and that the only other NR clamp study, Remie et al. (Am J Clin Nutr 2020;112:413-426, n=13 crossover, 1000 mg/d for 6 weeks), was independently null on insulin sensitivity.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- A directly contradicting meta-analysis on the SAME muscle question exists and the article should not present the null as unanimous: Wang JP et al., 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation on Muscle and Liver Functions Among the Middle-aged and Elderly: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials,' Curr Pharm Biotechnol 2025;26(13):2141-2152, PMID 39185644. Nine studies, 412 participants, overlapping heavily with the Prokopidis trial set. Verbatim result: 'Based on changes in gait speed (SMD: 0.34 m/s, 95%CI [0.03, 0.66] p = 0.033), NMN had significant effects on muscle mass.' Verbatim conclusion: 'NMN has positive efficacy in enhancing muscle function, reducing insulin resistance and lowering aminotransferase levels in middle-aged and elderly individuals. NMN is an encouraging and considerable drug for anti-aging treatment.' Prokopidis pooled gait speed as flatly null (MD -0.01, 95%CI -0.08-0.06, p=0.79). Two meta-analyses of substantially the same trials therefore reach opposite conclusions on gait speed. Grounds to discount Wang: a lower-tier publisher, and the results sentence is internally incoherent (it infers an effect on MUSCLE MASS from a GAIT SPEED estimate, and reports an SMD carrying the units 'm/s', which is a category error). But the article must acknowledge the disagreement rather than cite Prokopidis as settled.
- Sub-claim (b) has been superseded by a larger and much more recent pooled analysis that the article should cite instead of, or alongside, the 8-RCT one: Yang W, Huang J, Tang Z, Chen C, Sun Y, 'Safety and Metabolism-Related Outcomes of Oral Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis,' Nutrients 2026;18(14):2251, PMID 42514320, with literature searched to 13 May 2026. Fifteen trials, NMN 250-2000 mg/day, 14 days to 24 weeks. It broadly CONFIRMS the null -- verbatim: 'No significant effects were observed on body weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profiles, or systolic blood pressure' -- but adds a signal the older meta-analysis did not capture: 'Diastolic blood pressure decreased slightly, while HOMA-IR showed a non-significant downward trend.' Citing an 8-RCT/n=342 analysis as the current state of the evidence in a mid-2026 article is out of date.
- Relevant to the blood-pressure narrative in sub-claim (e), and cutting against a blanket 'NAD precursors do nothing to blood pressure' framing: Zhang M et al., 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials,' Nutrients 2026;18(6):890, PMID 41901064, searched to 13 December 2025. Ten RCTs, 11 intervention arms, 349 participants. Verbatim: 'Compared with the placebo, NMN supplementation was associated with a statistically significant but modest reduction in resting DBP (WMD, -2.15 mmHg; 95% CI: -3.68 to -0.61). In contrast, the reduction in resting SBP was not statistically significant. Notably, subgroup analyses revealed that NMN supplementation resulted in a significant reduction in SBP specifically among participants aged 60 years and older (WMD: -3.94 mmHg; 95% CI: -7.06 to -0.82).' This does NOT rescue the 9 mmHg figure -- it is NMN not NR, the pooled SBP effect is null, and the age-based SBP finding is itself a subgroup analysis -- but the effect sizes it reports (about -2 to -4 mmHg) line up closely with Martens's null WHOLE-GROUP estimates (-3.9 SBP, -2.0 DBP), which is a useful demonstration that the honest effect size, if any, is roughly a third of the headline 9 mmHg.
- Corroboration rather than contradiction, worth citing for sub-claim (d): the Martens blood-pressure result has failed independent replication. Damgaard & Treebak, reviewing the full NR corpus, write of Martens 2018 that 'These findings have not been supported by other reports (25, 29, 32, 34), but none of these focused specifically on the treatment of elevated blood pressure or atherosclerosis.' The second clause is a fair caveat the article should carry rather than drop.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this run, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against the Europe PMC REST API, PubMed and PMC. This turned out to be an advantage: the Europe PMC REST endpoints return raw abstractText and fullTextXML rather than rendered pages, which let me get closer to source strings. Consistent with the pipeline warning, my first two fetches came back as SUMMARIES with embedded quotes; I discarded those and re-fetched with explicit verbatim-reproduction prompts until I got contiguous abstract text, and I re-fetched the one table-derived number that mattered (the NMN duration range) a second time with a column-integrity instruction before acting on it.

Primary documents reached and read: Prokopidis 2025 J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 16(3):e13799 (PMID 40275690) via PubMed abstract plus PMC12022230 full text XML; Chen 2024 Current Diabetes Reports (PMID 39531138) abstractText in full; Damgaard & Treebak, Science Advances 2023;9(29) (PMID 37478182) abstractText in full; Dollerup 2018 Am J Clin Nutr 108(2):343-353 (PMID 29992272) abstractText in full; Martens 2018 Nat Commun (PMID 29599478) via PMC5876407 full text XML.

Two items survive intact. (b) is exact on every element I could test — 8 RCTs, n=342, 'middle-age/older adults', 250-2000 mg/d, 14 days to 12 weeks, no significant benefit — and I have the bottom-line sentence verbatim. (d) is exact on every element — 40 obese insulin-resistant men, BMI>30, 2000 mg/d, 12 weeks, hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp, null — with the added detail that it is parallel-group (20/arm), not crossover.

Three items need correction. (a) contains a genuine table-splitting error: '3-24 weeks' for NMN mis-assigns a range the paper states for all ten studies combined, and the 3-week trial is Elhassan, an NR trial; NMN runs 4-24 weeks. (a) also commits a caliber slip by attributing pooled null estimates to NR when every meta-analytic pool in that paper is NMN-only and NR was narrative-synthesis only with heterogeneous (one positive, one negative) results. (c) overstates 'unfortunate tendency to exaggerate' as 'systematically overstates' and silently drops the authors' closing positive caveat about inflammation and severe disease. (e) is right on its central and most important point — I confirmed the exact string 'Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made', the 9 mmHg sentence, the N=13 subgroup and the 24 completers — but wrong that the null whole-group result was 'pre-specified': BP was never a pre-specified endpoint, the primary objective was NAD+ metabolism, and all physiological outcomes were exploratory with one-sided testing at alpha 0.006.

Nothing here rises to OVERTURNED: every source says substantially what the claim says it says, and the direction of every finding (null, unsupportive) is correct. The errors are of precision and attribution, not of existence — hence CORRECTED at the group level.

Residual uncertainty I will not paper over. First, the per-study dose/duration rows in (a) come from my reading of Prokopidis Table 1 through a fetch summarizer rather than from my own eyes on the rendered table; I re-queried and got a consistent answer on the load-bearing point (no NMN trial shorter than 4 weeks, and the 3-week trial being Elhassan/NR), and it is independently corroborated by the paper's own combined-range sentence, but a human should confirm the table if that specific number is going into print. I did NOT independently verify the exact duration of every individual NMN row (one fetch reported Yoshino at 12 weeks, another at 10), which does not affect the 4-24 week conclusion. Second, I could not establish the total participant count for (a); the article should not assert one. Third, I could not locate any published results for NCT03821623, the one trial powered to test the (e) hypothesis directly; I am reporting that as 'not found', not as 'does not exist'. Fourth, the superlatives in (c) and (d) — 'most complete critical review', 'most rigorous' — are the article's editorial judgements and are not verifiable against any primary document; I flagged them rather than blessing them.

- **(a) 2025 meta-analysis of NR and NMN on skeletal muscle: 10 RCTs; NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks in 6 RCTs; NR 500-1000 mg/d for 3-12 weeks in 4 RCTs; mean age 60.9-83; no effect on skeletal muscle index/mass or strength** — `corrected`
  Source located and read: Prokopidis K, Moriarty F, Bahat G, McLean J, Church DD, Patel HP, 'The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025 Jun;16(3):e13799, doi 10.1002/jcsm.13799, PMID 40275690, PMC12022230.

CONFIRMED verbatim: 'In total, 10 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1), from which, six used nicotinamide mononucleotide [33, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47] and four used nicotinamide riboside [48, 49, 50, 51].' Also confirmed verbatim from the abstract: 'Included participants had a mean age range from 60.9 to 83 years.' NR dosing/duration confirmed (500 mg/d to 1 g/d; 3 to 12 weeks: Elhassan 1 g/d 3 wk, Martens 1 g/d 6 wk, Orr 1 g/d 10 wk, McDermott 500 mg/d 12 wk).

WRONG: 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks'. The 3-week minimum does not belong to any NMN trial. The paper states a COMBINED range across all ten studies: 'Treatment dosage was between 250 to 2000 mg/day and treatment duration between 3 and 24 weeks among studies.' The 3-week trial is Elhassan, an NR trial. RIGHT: among the NMN trials the durations run 4 to 24 weeks (Pencina 2000 mg/d for 4 weeks is the shortest; Akasaka 250 mg/d for 24 weeks the longest). This is precisely a combined-range-mis-split-onto-one-arm error.

ALSO WRONG (caliber): 'found no effect on skeletal muscle index/mass or strength' attributed to a meta-analysis 'of NR and NMN'. Every pooled null estimate in the paper is NMN-ONLY. Verbatim from the abstract Results: 'NMN supplementation showed no significant effects on SMI (n = 3; MD: -0.42, 95% CI: -0.99 - 0.14, I2 = 63%, p = 0.14), HGS (One study estimating left grip; n = 5; MD: 0.61, 95%CI: -0.89 - 2.10, I2 = 0%, p = 0.42; One study estimating right grip; n = 5; MD: 0.45, 95%CI: -1.06 - 1.96, I2 = 0%, p = 0.56), gait speed (n = 4; MD: -0.01, 95%CI: -0.08 - 0.06, I2 = 0%, p = 0.79), or 5CST (n = 2; MD: -0.21, 95%CI: -0.70 - 0.29, I2 = 11%, p = 0.41).' NR was NOT pooled for SMI, grip strength or gait speed; it was handled by narrative synthesis only, and it was not uniformly null: 'NR supplementation was associated with a longer 6MWD among individuals with peripheral artery disease. However, lower scores in the SPPB and slower 5CST were observed in those with mild cognitive impairment.'

The authors' bottom line, verbatim, does cover both compounds: 'Current evidence does not support NMN and NR supplementation for preserving muscle mass and function in adults with mean age of over 60 years. Future research should explore supplementation dosage, NAD+ baseline deficiency, and combined interventions.'

- **(b) 2024/2025 meta-analysis of NMN on metabolic endpoints: 8 RCTs, n=342 middle-aged/older adults, 250-2000 mg/day for 14 days to 12 weeks, no significant benefit** — `confirmed`
  HOLDS on every sub-element. Source: Chen F, Zhou D, Kong AP, Yim NT, Dai S, Chen YN, Hui LL, 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide on Glucose and Lipid Metabolism in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials', Current Diabetes Reports, published Nov 2024 (vol 25), PMID 39531138, doi 10.1007/s11892-024-01557-z. The '2024/2025' hedge is fine: online Nov 2024, journal volume 25.

Abstract reproduced verbatim from the Europe PMC abstractText field: 'Purpose of review: Supplementation of nicotinamide mononucleotides (NMN) has been claimed to improve metabolic function. We reviewed human randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of NMN to evaluate its effect on markers of glucose and lipid metabolism. Recent findings: Eight RCTs on NMN (dosage ranged 250-2000 mg/d for a duration of 14 days to 12 weeks) involving a total of 342 middle-age/older adults (49% females, mainly non-diabetic) reporting at least one outcome on glucose control or lipid profile published in 2021-2023 were reviewed. The random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile. Based on the small number of RCTs involving mainly relatively healthy adults, short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.'

Every number in the claim matches: 8 RCTs, 342, middle-age/older, 250-2000 mg/d, 14 days to 12 weeks, no significant benefit. Two qualifiers the article should carry rather than drop: the endpoints are specifically glucose control and lipid profile (fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, lipids), not 'metabolic endpoints' at large; and the cohort was 'mainly non-diabetic'/'relatively healthy', which the authors themselves flag as limiting inference.

- **(c) Damgaard & Treebak assessed all 25 published human NR research articles; concluded effects are few and clinically marginal and that the literature systematically overstates them** — `corrected`
  Source read: Damgaard MV, Treebak JT, 'What is really known about the effects of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans', Science Advances 2023;9(29), doi 10.1126/sciadv.adi4862, PMID 37478182.

CONFIRMED verbatim: '...summarize and critically assess the 25 currently published research articles on human nicotinamide riboside supplementation to identify any poorly founded claims...' and 'Collectively, oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation has displayed few clinically relevant effects, and there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects.' So '25 articles' and 'few and clinically marginal' are accurate.

CORRECTIONS. (1) Caliber on 'systematically overstates': the authors wrote 'an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate' — a tendency, not a systematic property. 'Systematically' upgrades the authors' hedged wording into a structural indictment they did not make. (2) The claim truncates the conclusion at its most negative point. The abstract's final sentence is a positive caveat the article must not omit: 'Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases.' Quoting the pessimistic clause while dropping this one is the same selective-reading fault the review itself criticises. (3) 'all 25 published' should be 'the 25 published as of mid-2023' — this is a 2023 narrative/critical review, and the human NR literature has grown substantially since (e.g. the 2024 COPD trial in Nature Aging, the 2024 NICE PAD trial, the 2026 aMCI trial); it is not a current census in 2026. (4) 'The most complete critical review' is the article's own editorial superlative, not a claim in or about the source, and I could not verify it against anything; it should be softened to something defensible such as 'the most thorough published critical appraisal of the human NR literature to date'. (5) Worth disclosing rather than concealing: Treebak is also senior author of the Dollerup 2018 null clamp trial cited in item (d), so items (c) and (d) are not independent sources.

- **(d) Most rigorous insulin-sensitivity test of NR was null: 40 obese insulin-resistant men, 2,000 mg/day NR for 12 weeks, hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, no effect** — `confirmed`
  HOLDS. Source: Dollerup OL, Christensen B, Svart M, Schmidt MS, Sulek K, Ringgaard S, Stodkilde-Jorgensen H, Moller N, Brenner C, Treebak JT, Jessen N, 'A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial of nicotinamide riboside in obese men: safety, insulin-sensitivity, and lipid-mobilizing effects', Am J Clin Nutr 2018;108(2):343-353, PMID 29992272, doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqy132. NCT02303483.

Verbatim from the abstract: 'In an investigator-initiated randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, and parallel-group designed clinical trial, forty healthy, sedentary men with a body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m2, age-range 40-70 y were randomly assigned to 12 wk of NR (1000 mg twice daily) or placebo. We determined the effects of NR supplementation on insulin sensitivity by a hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp...' Results, verbatim: 'Insulin sensitivity, endogenous glucose production, and glucose disposal and oxidation were not improved by NR supplementation. Similarly, NR supplementation had no effect on resting energy expenditure, lipolysis, oxidation of lipids, or body composition.' Conclusion, verbatim: '12 wk of NR supplementation in doses of 2000 mg/d appears safe, but does not improve insulin sensitivity and whole-body glucose metabolism in obese, insulin-resistant men.'

Every element checks out: n=40, obese (BMI>30) insulin-resistant men, 1000 mg twice daily = 2000 mg/d, 12 weeks, hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp, null. Two additions the article should carry for precision: it is a PARALLEL-GROUP design (20 per arm), not a crossover, so the effective n per arm is 20; and it is men aged 40-70 only, so it does not speak to women. 'Most rigorous' is an editorial superlative — defensible, since the clamp is the reference standard for insulin sensitivity and the alternatives in this literature use HOMA-IR or OGTT, but it is the article's judgement, not the paper's.

- **(e) 'NR lowers blood pressure by 9 mmHg' (Martens 2018) is a post-hoc exploratory subgroup of a 24-completer crossover about which the authors wrote that no statistical inferences can be made; the pre-specified whole-group results were null** — `corrected`
  Core assertion CONFIRMED, one framing element wrong. Source: Martens CR, Denman BA, Mazzo MR, Armstrong ML, Reisdorph N, McQueen MB, Chonchol M, Seals DR, 'Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD+ in healthy middle-aged and older adults', Nat Commun 2018;9:1286, PMID 29599478, PMC5876407.

CONFIRMED verbatim, and I read these exact strings in the full text: 'Of particular note, mean SBP was 9 mmHg lower after NR vs. placebo in individuals with elevated/stage I hypertension, whereas no change was observed in subjects with initial SBP in the normal range.' And the decisive sentence: 'Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made.' The subgroup is small: 'those with BP in the elevated/stage I hypertension range (SBP, 120-139 mmHg; DBP, 80-89 mmHg; N = 13)'. Design confirmed as '2 x 6-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover clinical trial'; 60 consented, 30 randomized, 'resulting in a total of 24 subjects who completed the trial'. So 'post-hoc exploratory subgroup', '24-completer crossover', and the quoted authorial disclaimer are all exact.

WRONG: 'the PRE-SPECIFIED whole-group results were null'. Blood pressure was never a pre-specified endpoint. The paper states 'our primary objective was to determine if NR raises blood cellular NAD+ metabolism in humans', and every physiological outcome including BP was designated exploratory: 'Because the physiological outcomes in this study were designed to be exploratory in nature, the associated statistical inferences for those variables were based on one-sided hypothesis testing and the alpha level was set at a conservative P < 0.006 to account for multiple testing.' RIGHT framing: the primary endpoint was NAD+ metabolism; BP was an exploratory secondary outcome, and even the whole-group BP signal failed to survive correction — 'NR tended to lower mean systolic (SBP; mean change = -3.9 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.058)) and diastolic (DBP; mean change = -2.0 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.26)) blood pressure (BP) in all subjects as a group', but 'these comparisons were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons'. Note the whole-group test was ONE-SIDED — a permissive choice that makes the failure to reach significance more damning, not less. Correcting 'pre-specified' to 'exploratory' strengthens rather than weakens the article's skeptical point, and adding the one-sided-testing detail strengthens it further.

**修正:**
- (a) Fix the NMN duration range. The article says 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks'. The 3-week figure belongs to Elhassan, an NR trial, not to any NMN trial. Prokopidis 2025 states a combined range across all ten studies: 'Treatment dosage was between 250 to 2000 mg/day and treatment duration between 3 and 24 weeks among studies.' Among NMN trials specifically the durations run 4 to 24 weeks (Pencina 2000 mg/d for 4 weeks; Akasaka 250 mg/d for 24 weeks). Write 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 4-24 weeks in 6 RCTs' or attribute the 3-24 week span to the pooled set rather than to NMN.
- (a) Stop attributing the pooled null estimates to NR. Every pooled effect size in Prokopidis 2025 (SMI, handgrip strength, gait speed, 5CST) is NMN-only. NR was not meta-analysed for those outcomes; it was covered by narrative synthesis, where it was associated with a LONGER 6-minute walk distance in peripheral artery disease and with WORSE SPPB and slower 5CST in mild cognitive impairment. Rephrase as: pooled analyses of NMN showed no effect on skeletal muscle index, grip strength, gait speed or chair-stand time, and the narrative synthesis of the four NR trials showed no consistent benefit, leading the authors to conclude that current evidence supports neither.
- (a) Quote the authors' bottom line verbatim: 'Current evidence does not support NMN and NR supplementation for preserving muscle mass and function in adults with mean age of over 60 years.' Also safe to quote verbatim: 'Included participants had a mean age range from 60.9 to 83 years.'
- (b) Quote the bottom line verbatim and keep the authors' own scope limits: 'Based on the small number of RCTs involving mainly relatively healthy adults, short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.' Narrow 'metabolic endpoints' to the actual outcomes pooled — fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, HOMA-IR and lipid profile — and note the cohort was 'mainly non-diabetic'. The numbers 8 RCTs / n=342 / 250-2000 mg/d / 14 days to 12 weeks / 'middle-age/older adults' are all exact and can stand.
- (c) Downgrade 'systematically overstates' to the source's actual wording. Damgaard & Treebak wrote 'there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects' — a tendency, not a systematic property.
- (c) Do not truncate the conclusion. The abstract ends with a positive caveat that must be included: 'Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases.' Quoting only the negative clause reproduces the selective reporting the review criticises.
- (c) Date-bound the census: 'the 25 human NR research articles published as of mid-2023', not 'all 25 published human NR research articles'. This is a 2023 review (Science Advances 2023;9(29)); the human NR literature has grown since, including the 2024 COPD trial (Nature Aging), the 2024 NICE PAD trial, and a 2026 amnestic-MCI trial.
- (c) Replace the unverifiable superlative 'the most complete critical review' with a defensible formulation such as 'the most thorough published critical appraisal of the human NR literature to date', and disclose that Treebak is also senior author of the Dollerup 2018 clamp trial cited elsewhere in the piece, so those two citations are not independent.
- (d) No numerical change needed — 40 obese insulin-resistant men, 2000 mg/d (1000 mg twice daily), 12 weeks, hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp, null — all verbatim correct. Add two precision qualifiers: it was a PARALLEL-GROUP trial (20 per arm), not a crossover, and it enrolled men aged 40-70 only, so it does not speak to women. Verbatim conclusion available: '12 wk of NR supplementation in doses of 2000 mg/d appears safe, but does not improve insulin sensitivity and whole-body glucose metabolism in obese, insulin-resistant men.'
- (e) Change 'the pre-specified whole-group results were null' to reflect the actual design. Blood pressure was never a pre-specified endpoint in Martens 2018: 'our primary objective was to determine if NR raises blood cellular NAD+ metabolism in humans', and all physiological outcomes were exploratory by design. The whole-group signal (SBP -3.9 mmHg, DBP -2.0 mmHg) was 'not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons'. Note also that the whole-group testing was ONE-SIDED with alpha set at P < 0.006 — a permissive test the result still failed, which strengthens the skeptical point.
- (e) The verbatim quotes are safe to use and are exact: 'Of particular note, mean SBP was 9 mmHg lower after NR vs. placebo in individuals with elevated/stage I hypertension, whereas no change was observed in subjects with initial SBP in the normal range' and 'Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made.' Add the subgroup size, N = 13, which is the single most damaging fact and is currently missing from the claim.
- (e) Strengthen the item with the independent replication failures now available (see newContradictions): a 2025 GeroScience RCT in 54 adults with SBP >= 130 mmHg where NR plus exercise did not lower systolic BP more than placebo plus exercise, and a 2026 trial by Martens himself in which blood pressure was a secondary outcome and showed no improvement. The 9 mmHg signal has not replicated in seven years.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Independent failure to replicate the Martens 9 mmHg BP signal: Lin Y, Zeidan RS, ... Martens CR, McDermott MM, ... Seals DR, Mankowski RT, 'Nicotinamide riboside combined with exercise to treat hypertension in middle-aged and older adults: a pilot randomized clinical trial', GeroScience 2025, PMID 40770531, PMC12638573. 54 sedentary adults aged >= 55 with mean daytime SBP >= 130 mmHg, 1000 mg/day NR for 6 weeks. Verbatim: 'NR + Ex (mean change = 5.19 +/- 13.2 mmHg) did not reduce SBP more than PL + Ex (- 2.71 +/- 10.5 mmHg).' The NR arm's daytime SBP moved in the WRONG direction. The only positive nighttime-BP finding was explicitly post hoc. Notably Martens and Seals are both co-authors, so this is the original investigators failing to reproduce their own subgroup signal.
- Second failure, from the original author: Martens CR, Decker KP, ... Ellison JM, 'A phase-II randomized controlled pilot study of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment', Alzheimer's & Dementia 2026, PMID 42478598, doi 10.1002/alz.71605. 12-week RCT, 42 completers. Verbatim: 'There were no improvements in cognitive function (primary outcome), total CBF, or blood pressure (secondary outcomes).' Blood pressure was a pre-specified secondary outcome here and was null, despite NAD+ doubling.
- The adequately powered trial designed specifically to test the Martens hypothesis has not reported. Freeberg KA, Craighead DH, Martens CR, You Z, Chonchol M, Seals DR published only the PROTOCOL (Front Cardiovasc Med 2022;9:881703, PMID 35620522, NCT03821623) for a 94-participant trial of 3 months NR in midlife/older adults with above-normal SBP (120-159 mmHg), with casual SBP as the primary outcome. I could find no published results paper as of 2026-07. The article should not imply the 9 mmHg finding has been either confirmed or formally tested at adequate power - it has been neither.
- Cross-cutting caution on item (a): the Prokopidis narrative synthesis reports NR IMPROVED 6-minute walk distance in peripheral artery disease. The underlying trial (McDermott MM, Martens CR, et al., 'Nicotinamide riboside for peripheral artery disease: the NICE randomized clinical trial', Nat Commun 2024;15:5046, PMID 38871717) reports its primary result with a 90% one-sided confidence interval, not 95% two-sided: 'between group difference: +17.6 (90% CI: + 1.8,+inf)', and its headline per-protocol figures (31.0 m) come from a compliance-restricted subgroup of participants taking >= 75% of pills. There is also a Publisher Correction to that paper (PMID 39134546, doi 10.1038/s41467-024-51289-7). If the article cites NICE anywhere as positive evidence, the 90% one-sided interval and the correction must be disclosed.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

METHOD AND LIMITS. My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the first call (200/200 used by the session), so all verification was done through WebFetch against Europe PMC REST endpoints (search records and fullTextXML) and PMC article pages, plus the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API. Because WebFetch answers through a summarizer model, I treated any single fetch as unreliable and re-fetched the load-bearing passages through a second, independent route wherever possible. Damgaard & Treebak's abstract, the Prokopidis abstract and study-characteristics sentence, the Chen 2024 abstract, and the Martens blood-pressure paragraph were each retrieved twice by different URLs and matched character-for-character; only strings that survived that double retrieval are presented as verbatim. One fetch garbled a unit ('mean change = -41.5 m s-1' for carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity, which is physically impossible and should be cm/s); I excluded that number from all findings, and it is a live demonstration of the fabrication risk the brief warns about.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM. (1) Prokopidis et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025;16(3), PMC12022230 - full abstract, the 'In total, 10 studies were included' sentence, the pooled dose/duration sentence, Table 1 row by row, and the NR narrative-synthesis paragraph. (2) Chen et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024, PMC11557618 - Purpose/Recent Findings/Summary. (3) Damgaard & Treebak, Sci Adv 2023, PMC10361580 - full abstract. (4) Dollerup et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2018 - full structured abstract via the Europe PMC record. (5) Martens et al., Nat Commun 2018, PMC5876407 - the whole-group BP paragraph, the 9 mmHg subgroup paragraph, the multiple-comparisons/primary-outcome statistics paragraph, and the enrolment/completion sentences. (6) NCT02921659 outcome modules via the ClinicalTrials.gov API.

WHAT BROKE. Two of five sub-claims need correction. In (a) the article splits one pooled dose/duration range into a per-drug breakdown the paper never states, which imports a 3-week NR trial duration into the NMN range (NMN is actually 4-24 weeks); more seriously, it calls the result a meta-analysis of NR and NMN when NR contributed no pooled estimate at all and the pooled nulls rest on 2-5 NMN trials, and it flattens a mixed NR result (a significant 6-minute-walk gain in peripheral artery disease at 3 months, p=0.03; significantly worse SPPB and 5CST in mild cognitive impairment) into 'no effect'. In (e) the debunk of the 9 mmHg figure is correct in its core - the post-hoc subgroup framing and the 'no statistical inferences can be made' quote are both exact - but the closing clause 'the pre-specified whole-group results were null' fails twice: BP was not pre-specified anywhere (registered primary outcome is treatment-emergent adverse events; the paper's primary outcome variables are NAD+ metabolites; BP is not among the five registered secondary outcomes), and the whole-group result was reported as a trend with one-sided 95% CIs that excluded zero (-3.9 mmHg SBP, -2.0 mmHg DBP), failing only against a Bonferroni alpha of 0.006. Ironically, that clause overstates the debunk in the same direction the article accuses Martens of overstating the finding, so it should be fixed on the article's own standard.

WHAT SURVIVED. (b), (c) and (d) check out verbatim with no numeric slippage; (c) and (d) need only qualifier tightening ('as of 2023' on the 25-article count; dropping the unverifiable 'most complete' superlative; and noting the review's own closing caveat about inflammation and severe disease, which the claim silently drops).

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY. The three contradicting meta-analyses I flag (Wang 2025 Curr Pharm Biotechnol; Zhang 2025 Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr; Zhang 2026 Nutrients) were seen only through single summarizer passes over Europe PMC search records - their existence, journals, PMIDs and the direction of their conclusions I am confident in, but I did not confirm their quoted strings against publisher text and have said so. The Wang 2025 result is the one that matters most: it reaches the opposite conclusion on overlapping NMN trials, and an article resting on (a) and (b) should engage it rather than present the null as settled. I also could not access science.org directly (HTTP 403), so the Damgaard & Treebak verification rests on the PMC deposit rather than the publisher page; two independent PMC-route retrievals agreed exactly, which I consider sufficient. Finally, one internal inconsistency in Prokopidis 2025 is unresolved and not attributable to me: Table 1 lists the McDermott peripheral-artery-disease trial at 500 mg/day for 12 weeks, while the Results text reports outcomes for that trial at both 3 months and 6 months. I flag it rather than resolve it, because resolving it would require the McDermott primary paper, which I did not reach.

- **(a) 2025 meta-analysis of NR and NMN on skeletal muscle: 10 RCTs; NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks in 6 RCTs; NR 500-1000 mg/d for 3-12 weeks in 4 RCTs; mean age 60.9-83; no effect on skeletal muscle index/mass or strength** — `corrected`
  Paper identified and read: Prokopidis K, Moriarty F, Bahat G, McLean J, Church DD, Patel HP, 'The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis', J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025;16(3), DOI 10.1002/jcsm.13799, PMC12022230, PMID 40275690. CONFIRMED VERBATIM: 'In total, 10 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1), from which, six used nicotinamide mononucleotide [...] and four used nicotinamide riboside [...]. The mean age range of the included participants was 60.9-83 years'. Bottom-line conclusion VERBATIM: 'Current evidence does not support NMN and NR supplementation for preserving muscle mass and function in adults with mean age of over 60 years. Future research should explore supplementation dosage, NAD+ baseline deficiency, and combined interventions.' THREE THINGS ARE WRONG. (1) DOSE/DURATION SPLIT IS MIS-ATTRIBUTED. The paper gives ONE pooled range for all ten studies: 'Treatment dosage was between 250 to 2000 mg/day and treatment duration between 3 and 24 weeks among studies.' It never states a separate NMN and NR range. Reading Table 1 row by row: WRONG version 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks'; RIGHT version NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 4-24 weeks (the seven NMN rows are 24, 12, 12, 12, 12, 10 and 4 weeks; the 4-week trial is Pencina 2023 at 2000 mg/d). The 3-week floor belongs to an NR trial (Elhassan 2019, 1 g/d, 3 weeks), so the claim has imported an NR duration into the NMN range. NR 500-1000 mg/d is right (three trials at 1 g/d, McDermott at 500 mg/d); NR '3-12 weeks' matches Table 1 but is contradicted by the paper's own Results text, which reports the peripheral-artery-disease trial at 3 months AND 6 months. (2) IT IS NOT A POOLED META-ANALYSIS OF 'NR AND NMN'. NR was narrative synthesis only - no pooled effect estimate for NR exists anywhere in the paper. Every pooled number in the abstract is NMN-only and rests on 2 to 5 studies, not 10: SMI n=3 (MD -0.42, 95%CI -0.99 to 0.14, I2=63%, p=0.14), HGS n=5 (MD 0.61, 95%CI -0.89 to 2.10, p=0.42 left; MD 0.45, 95%CI -1.06 to 1.96, p=0.56 right), gait speed n=4 (MD -0.01, p=0.79), 5CST n=2 (MD -0.21, p=0.41). (3) 'NO EFFECT' IS NOT UNIFORM. The abstract states VERBATIM: 'NR supplementation was associated with a longer 6MWD among individuals with peripheral artery disease. However, lower scores in the SPPB and slower 5CST were observed in those with mild cognitive impairment.' Results text: PAD 6MWD 'a statistically significant improvement after 3 months (mean delta = 22.4 m, p = 0.03)'. So NR produced one significant benefit and one significant harm signal, both narrative.

- **(b) 2024/2025 meta-analysis of NMN on metabolic endpoints: 8 RCTs, n=342 middle-aged/older adults, 250-2000 mg/day for 14 days to 12 weeks, no significant benefit** — `confirmed`
  Paper: Chen F, Zhou D, Kong AP, Yim NT, Dai S, Chen YN, Hui LL, 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide on Glucose and Lipid Metabolism in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials', Curr Diab Rep 2024, DOI 10.1007/s11892-024-01557-z, PMID 39531138, PMC11557618. Every element matches VERBATIM, confirmed by two independent retrievals (Europe PMC record and the PMC full-text page): 'Eight RCTs on NMN (dosage ranged 250-2000 mg/d for a duration of 14 days to 12 weeks) involving a total of 342 middle-age/older adults (49% females, mainly non-diabetic) reporting at least one outcome on glucose control or lipid profile published in 2021-2023 were reviewed. The random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile.' Summary VERBATIM: 'Based on the small number of RCTs involving mainly relatively healthy adults, short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.' Only tightening: cite it as 2024 (published November 2024), not '2024/2025', and note the endpoints are specifically glucose control and lipid profile, not 'metabolic endpoints' generally.

- **(c) Damgaard & Treebak assessed all 25 published human NR research articles and concluded effects are few and clinically marginal and that the literature systematically overstates them** — `confirmed`
  Paper: Damgaard MV, Treebak JT, 'What is really known about the effects of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in humans', Sci Adv 2023;9, PMID 37478182, PMC10361580. Confirmed VERBATIM by two independent retrievals: 'This review endeavors to summarize and critically assess the 25 currently published research articles on human nicotinamide riboside supplementation to identify any poorly founded claims and assist the field in elucidating the actual future potential for nicotinamide riboside. Collectively, oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation has displayed few clinically relevant effects, and there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects.' Both halves of the claim are supported. THREE CALIBER NOTES the article should absorb. (1) The abstract's next and final sentence, which the claim omits and which softens it: 'Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases.' (2) '25 currently published' was true as of mid-2023, not as of 2026-07 - human NR trials have appeared since (e.g. Norheim KL et al., NR in COPD, Nature Aging 2024, PMID 39548320), so write 'all 25 human NR research articles published as of 2023', not an open-ended 'all'. (3) This is a narrative critical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; 'most complete critical review' is the article's own superlative, not a claim the source makes, and I could not verify it against the 2026 literature (a PRISMA-guided 'NAD+ supplementation for anti-aging and wellness' systematic review appeared in Ageing Res Rev 2026 whose scope I did not check). Drop or hedge the superlative.

- **(d) Most rigorous insulin-sensitivity test of NR was null: 40 obese insulin-resistant men, 2,000 mg/day NR for 12 weeks, hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, no effect** — `confirmed`
