  Paper: Dollerup OL et al., 'A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial of nicotinamide riboside in obese men: safety, insulin-sensitivity, and lipid-mobilizing effects', Am J Clin Nutr 2018, DOI 10.1093/ajcn/nqy132, PMID 29992272, NCT02303483. Abstract retrieved VERBATIM from the Europe PMC record. Design: 'forty healthy, sedentary men with a body mass index (BMI) > 30 kg/m2, age-range 40-70 y were randomly assigned to 12 wk of NR (1000 mg twice daily) or placebo. We determined the effects of NR supplementation on insulin sensitivity by a hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp'. Results: 'Insulin sensitivity, endogenous glucose production, and glucose disposal and oxidation were not improved by NR supplementation.' Conclusion: '12 wk of NR supplementation in doses of 2000 mg/d appears safe, but does not improve insulin sensitivity and whole-body glucose metabolism in obese, insulin-resistant men.' N, sex, dose, duration, method and null result all check out with no slippage. Two small precision points: 1000 mg twice daily equals 2000 mg/d, so state it that way; and the enrolment criterion in the abstract is BMI >30 and age 40-70, with 'insulin-resistant' being the authors' own descriptor of the cohort in the Objective and Conclusion rather than a stated screening threshold. 'Most rigorous' is the article's editorial judgement, not a source claim.

- **(e) 'NR lowers blood pressure by 9 mmHg' (Martens 2018) is a post-hoc exploratory subgroup of a 24-completer crossover about which the authors wrote that no statistical inferences can be made; the pre-specified whole-group results were null** — `corrected`
  Paper: Martens CR et al., 'Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD+ in healthy middle-aged and older adults', Nat Commun 2018;9:1286, DOI 10.1038/s41467-018-03421-7, PMID 29599478, PMC5876407, NCT02921659. CONFIRMED VERBATIM: 'Of particular note, mean SBP was 9 mmHg lower after NR vs. placebo in individuals with elevated/stage I hypertension, whereas no change was observed in subjects with initial SBP in the normal range (Fig. 3d). Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made.' Also confirmed: 2 x 6-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover; 'Sixty healthy middle-aged and older men and women between the ages of 55 and 79 years were consented', ClinicalTrials.gov actual enrollment 30, 'a total of 24 subjects who completed the trial'; subgroups were normal BP (SBP/DBP < 120/80 mmHg; N = 11) versus elevated/stage I hypertension (SBP 120-139, DBP 80-89 mmHg; N = 13). THE LAST CLAUSE IS WRONG IN TWO WAYS. (1) WRONG version: 'the pre-specified whole-group results were null'. RIGHT version: blood pressure was never a pre-specified endpoint. The registered primary outcome on NCT02921659 is 'Incidence of treatment emergent adverse events'; the paper states its primary outcome variables were the NAD+ metabolites ('With the exception of our primary outcome variables (NAD+ metabolites: NAD+, NAAD, NADP, NaM, NMN), in which inferences were based on an unadjusted alpha level set at 0.05, all inferences of significance are based on the Bonferroni-adjusted alpha level (alpha = 0.006)'), and the five registered secondary outcomes are endothelium-dependent dilation, arterial stiffness (aortic PWV), cognitive function, motor function, and markers of oxidative stress/inflammation. BP is not among them. (2) WRONG version: whole-group result was 'null'. RIGHT version, VERBATIM: 'Supplementation with NR tended to lower mean systolic (SBP; mean change = -3.9 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.058)) and diastolic (DBP; mean change = -2.0 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.26)) blood pressure (BP) in all subjects as a group (Fig. 3a-c); however, these comparisons were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons.' Note these are ONE-SIDED 95% CIs and both excluded zero; the finding fails only against the Bonferroni-adjusted alpha of 0.006. Accurate phrasing: 'the whole-group change was -3.9 mmHg systolic, reported with a one-sided 95% CI and not statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (alpha = 0.006)'. The 9 mmHg figure itself carries no CI or p-value in the paper.

- (a) Change 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 3-24 weeks in 6 RCTs' to 'NMN 250-2000 mg/d for 4-24 weeks in 6 RCTs'. Per Table 1 of Prokopidis 2025, the shortest NMN trial is Pencina 2023 at 4 weeks (2000 mg/d); the 3-week floor belongs to an NR trial (Elhassan 2019, 1 g/d). The paper itself gives only one pooled range covering all ten studies: 'Treatment dosage was between 250 to 2000 mg/day and treatment duration between 3 and 24 weeks among studies.'
- (a) Do not describe Prokopidis 2025 as a pooled meta-analysis of NR and NMN. NR was handled by narrative synthesis only and contributes no pooled effect estimate. Every pooled null in the abstract is NMN-only and rests on 2-5 studies, not 10: SMI n=3 (MD -0.42, 95%CI -0.99 to 0.14, I2=63%, p=0.14); handgrip n=5 (MD 0.61, 95%CI -0.89 to 2.10, p=0.42); gait speed n=4 (MD -0.01, 95%CI -0.08 to 0.06, p=0.79); 5CST n=2 (MD -0.21, 95%CI -0.70 to 0.29, p=0.41).
- (a) Do not say the meta-analysis found 'no effect' across the board. Quote the paper's actual mixed NR finding: 'NR supplementation was associated with a longer 6MWD among individuals with peripheral artery disease. However, lower scores in the SPPB and slower 5CST were observed in those with mild cognitive impairment.' The PAD 6-minute-walk gain was statistically significant at 3 months (mean delta = 22.4 m, p = 0.03).
- (a) Use the paper's verbatim bottom line: 'Current evidence does not support NMN and NR supplementation for preserving muscle mass and function in adults with mean age of over 60 years.' Cite as Prokopidis K et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025;16(3), DOI 10.1002/jcsm.13799.
- (b) Cite as a 2024 paper, not '2024/2025': Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024, DOI 10.1007/s11892-024-01557-z. Use the verbatim bottom line: 'Based on the small number of RCTs involving mainly relatively healthy adults, short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.' Narrow 'metabolic endpoints' to the actual endpoints: fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, HOMA-IR and lipid profile.
- (c) Write 'all 25 human NR research articles published as of 2023', not 'all 25 published human NR research articles'. The review's scope sentence is time-stamped ('the 25 currently published research articles') and human NR trials have been published since, e.g. Norheim KL et al., NR in COPD, Nature Aging 2024 (PMID 39548320).
- (c) Drop or hedge 'the most complete critical review'. Damgaard & Treebak 2023 is a narrative critical review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, and the superlative is unverifiable against the 2024-2026 literature.
- (c) If the article quotes the conclusion, use it verbatim and do not truncate the caveat: 'Collectively, oral nicotinamide riboside supplementation has displayed few clinically relevant effects, and there is an unfortunate tendency in the literature to exaggerate the importance and robustness of reported effects. Even so, nicotinamide riboside may play a role in the reduction of inflammatory states and has shown some potential in the treatment of diverse severe diseases.'
- (e) Delete 'the pre-specified whole-group results were null'. Blood pressure was not a pre-specified endpoint of Martens 2018. The registered primary outcome (NCT02921659) is 'Incidence of treatment emergent adverse events'; the paper's stated primary outcome variables are the NAD+ metabolites; the five registered secondary outcomes are endothelium-dependent dilation, aortic pulse wave velocity, cognitive function, motor function, and oxidative stress/inflammation markers. BP appears among none of them.
- (e) Replace 'null' with the paper's actual whole-group wording: 'Supplementation with NR tended to lower mean systolic (SBP; mean change = -3.9 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.058)) and diastolic (DBP; mean change = -2.0 mmHg; one-sided 95% CI (-inf, -0.26)) blood pressure (BP) in all subjects as a group; however, these comparisons were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons.' Note that these are ONE-SIDED 95% CIs which excluded zero, and significance was denied only against the Bonferroni-adjusted alpha of 0.006.
- (e) Add the subgroup sizes, which are the strongest part of the debunk: the 9 mmHg came from N = 13 participants in the elevated/stage I hypertension range, versus N = 11 in the normal range, inside a 24-completer crossover (60 consented, 30 randomized). The 9 mmHg figure is reported with no confidence interval and no p-value.
- (e) Quote the authors' caveat exactly: 'Because this post-hoc subgroup analysis was exploratory, no statistical inferences can be made.'
- (d) State the dose as administered: NR 1000 mg twice daily (2000 mg/d) for 12 weeks. Note the enrolment criteria in the abstract are BMI > 30 kg/m2 and age 40-70 y; 'insulin-resistant' is the authors' descriptor of the cohort in the Objective and Conclusion, not a stated screening threshold. Cite Dollerup OL et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2018, DOI 10.1093/ajcn/nqy132, NCT02303483.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- A directly opposing meta-analysis on overlapping trials exists and the article should not present the null result as uncontested: Wang JP, Wang L, Wang T, Zhang YD, Zhou AJ, Wang ZP, Xiong ZE, 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation on Muscle and Liver Functions Among the Middle-aged and Elderly: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials', Curr Pharm Biotechnol 2025, PMID 39185644, DOI 10.2174/0113892010306242240808094303. It pooled 9 RCTs and 412 participants and concluded NMN 'has positive efficacy in enhancing muscle function, reducing insulin resistance and lowering aminotransferase levels' in middle-aged and elderly individuals - contradicting both (a) and (b). CAVEAT: I retrieved this abstract only through a fetch summarizer and could not confirm the quoted string character-for-character against the publisher text, so treat that quote as unverified; the opposing direction of the conclusion is nonetheless clear and independently reported.
- A larger metabolic meta-analysis than the 8-RCT/342-participant pool cited in (b) exists: Zhang J, Poon ET, Wong SH, 'Efficacy of oral nicotinamide mononucleotide supplementation on glucose and lipid metabolism for adults', Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr 2025, PMID 39116016, DOI 10.1080/10408398.2024.2387324, covering 12 studies and 513 participants. Its direction reportedly agrees with (b) (most clinically relevant outcomes not significantly different), but if the article implies the Chen 2024 pool is the definitive metabolic synthesis, this larger one supersedes it on size. I did not verify its abstract verbatim.
- A 2026 meta-analysis complicates any blanket 'NAD precursors do not move blood pressure' framing adjacent to (e): Zhang M, Chen Y, Jiang N, Zeng J, Zhang J, Wu C, Liu Y, Nie Z, Yang J, Han S, 'Effects of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials', Nutrients 2026, PMID 41901064, DOI 10.3390/nu18060890. Reported as 10 RCTs, 349 participants, with a statistically significant reduction in resting diastolic BP (WMD -2.15 mmHg, 95% CI -3.68 to -0.61) and no significant systolic effect overall. This is NMN, not NR, so it does not rescue the Martens 9 mmHg claim, but it post-dates the article's evidence base. Abstract not verified verbatim.
- Superseding-scope risk for (c): 'NAD+ supplementation for anti-aging and wellness: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of preclinical and clinical evidence', Ageing Res Rev 2026, and a bioRxiv 2026 preprint 'Mapping Evidence Gap Between NMN and NR for Metabolic Outcomes: A Systematic Review, Transitivity Assessment, and Indirect Comparison Meta-Analysis'. I did not verify either one's scope or conclusions, but their existence means the article's superlative 'the most complete critical review' for a 2023 narrative review is an unverified claim in 2026.
- No refutation found against the claims themselves: I searched Europe PMC for corrections, errata, retractions, letters or comments attached to Prokopidis 2025 (jcsm.13799) and Damgaard & Treebak 2023 (sciadv.adi4862) and found none. Dollerup 2018 and Martens 2018 likewise show no correction notices in the records I retrieved.

## V21 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

Primary documents reached and read: (1) Yoshino et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229 full text via PMC8550608 -- I pulled the abstract randomisation sentence, the 250 mg/day dose string, the Figure 2A legend n's and three-way interaction P=0.022, the 25+/-7% result sentence, and Table 1's complete column header row (Placebo Before/After, NMN Before/After, Pgroup, Ptime, Pgroup x time) with the intrahepatic triglyceride row. I deliberately re-fetched Table 1 with a targeted prompt after a first pass returned only the interaction P and silently dropped the Pgroup column -- exactly the multi-column misread failure mode flagged in the brief. The second read surfaced Pgroup=0.003, which independently reconciles with Brenner. (2) Brenner C, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj1696 -- complete published abstract retrieved byte-identical from two independent metadata sources (PubMed PMID 34326206 and the Semantic Scholar graph API), so the quoted string is genuinely verbatim. The BODY of the comment is unreachable: science.org returns 403, Semantic Scholar reports openAccessPdf CLOSED, no PMCID, no preprint. (3) Klein S & Yoshino M, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj7375 -- full abstract from PubMed PMID 34326209. (4) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 raw JSON for NCT03151239 and NCT04571008, including the verbatim outcomeMeasuresModule JSON object for the follow-up trial's primary outcome, its interventionsModule (300 or 450 mg/day), participantFlowModule (28 started / 20 completed per arm), and resultsFirstPostDateStruct (2026-03-11). (5) Chen F et al. 2024 meta-analysis via PMC11557618 to enumerate every published NMN RCT. Replication hunt: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted at 200/200), so I worked entirely through structured primary APIs -- Europe PMC REST (title search, RCT publication-type filters, 2024-2026 date-windowed search, author search on Klein S), Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API. That is arguably more reliable than search here, but it does mean I did not sweep grey literature, conference abstracts, or non-English registries, so a replication outside PubMed/Europe PMC/ClinicalTrials.gov would have been missed. What remains uncertain: (a) whether Brenner's comment body advances the 'liver fat depresses muscle insulin sensitivity' argument the article attributes to him -- I can only verify his abstract, which gives a different rationale; (b) the meaning of the '0.05' pValue field in the NCT04571008 posted analysis, which is almost certainly a threshold rather than a computed statistic and should not be quoted; (c) whether NCT04571008 will be published with a different analysis than the registry posting. The headline finding of this verification is item (b) of the replication check: the article's 'no replication' line is literally true but conceals a null primary-outcome result from the original investigators' own larger confirmatory trial, posted four months ago.

- **Arm sizes: 13 on NMN, 12 on placebo (25 total)** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against two independent primary sources. Yoshino et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229 (PMC8550608) abstract: 'Twenty-five postmenopausal women with prediabetes based on criteria proposed by the American Diabetes Association who were overweight or obese completed this study; 12 were randomized to the placebo group and 13 to the NMN group'. Figure 2A legend independently states 'NMN (n=13) and placebo (n=12)'. Brenner's Science comment independently states 'the 13 women who received NMN' and 'the 12 in the placebo group'. Note 25 is the COMPLETER count, not the randomised count; the article should not imply 25 were randomised.

- **Dose and duration: 250 mg/day NMN for 10 weeks** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the paper: 'randomized to the placebo group and 13 to the NMN group (250 mg/day; Oriental Yeast Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan)' and 'participants were randomly assigned to 10 weeks of treatment with placebo or NMN'. Registered as NCT03151239.

- **Population: postmenopausal women with prediabetes** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, but incomplete as stated. The full inclusion is postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were ALSO overweight or obese ('who were overweight or obese completed this study'). The article omits the adiposity criterion.

- **Hepatic lipid imbalance: 6.3 +/- 1.2% NMN vs 14.8 +/- 2.0% placebo, P=0.003** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim, and stronger than the article implies. Brenner's abstract (identical string retrieved independently from PubMed PMID 34326206 and the Semantic Scholar API): 'the 13 women who received NMN had hepatic lipid content of 6.3 +/- 1.2%, whereas the 12 in the placebo group had 14.8 +/- 2.0% (P = 0.003)'. I then traced this to the paper's own Table 1, row 'Intrahepatic triglyceride content (%)': Placebo Before 14.8 +/- 2.0, After 15.7 +/- 2.5; NMN Before 6.3 +/- 1.2, After 6.8 +/- 1.3; Pgroup 0.003, Ptime 0.385, Pgroup x time 0.461. So P=0.003 is the RM-ANOVA main effect of group printed in Yoshino et al.'s own Table 1, not a number Brenner computed himself. Caution: the values are SEM, not SD, and Table 1 contains no column giving a baseline-only between-group P.

- **The challenge was published in Science; find the comment and the authors' response** — `confirmed`
  Both located. Comment: Brenner C, 'Comment on "Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women"', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj1696, doi 10.1126/science.abj1696, PMID 34326206. Response: Klein S, Yoshino M, 'Response to Comment on...', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj7375, doi 10.1126/science.abj7375, PMID 34326209. Response abstract verbatim: 'In evaluating any randomized clinical trial, it is important to determine whether baseline differences between groups could have affected the primary outcome. In our study, muscle insulin sensitivity, which was identical in both groups at baseline, improved after nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), not placebo, therapy. Differences in baseline intrahepatic triglyceride content between groups do not negate the effects of NMN observed in muscle.' The article currently presents the challenge without the rebuttal; the rebuttal exists and should be named.

- **Brenner's stated reason why the imbalance matters ('liver fat itself depresses muscle insulin sensitivity')** — `corrected`
  WRONG version (as written in the article): the arms were imbalanced 'since liver fat itself depresses muscle insulin sensitivity'. RIGHT version (Brenner's actual stated rationale, verbatim from his abstract): 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial.' Brenner's published argument is about NMN's own mechanism of action being liver-fat clearance -- i.e. the placebo arm had far more of the substrate NMN is supposed to act on -- not about liver fat suppressing muscle insulin sensitivity. The full body of eabj1696 is paywalled (science.org returned HTTP 403) so I cannot exclude that he also makes the muscle argument in the body, but the article must not attribute the muscle-suppression rationale to him as if it were his stated ground.

- **No independent replication published in the five years since** — `corrected`
  The literal sentence survives, but it is materially misleading and must be replaced with a stronger and more accurate fact. (a) Literal check holds: the 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of NMN RCTs on glucose/lipid metabolism (Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep, PMC11557618) includes 8 NMN trials (Yoshino 2021, Pencina 2023, Okabe 2022, Igarashi 2022, Fukamizu 2022, Huang 2022, Yi 2023, Katayoshi 2023) and only Yoshino 2021 used a hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp; its conclusion is 'short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile'. No NMN clamp trial has been published since. (b) BUT: the same Washington University group ran a larger, longer confirmatory trial, NCT04571008, 'Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) Supplementation on Organ System Biology' -- prediabetes, both sexes, age >=45, BMI 25-50, NMN 300 or 450 mg/day for at least 16 weeks, 28 randomised per arm, 20 completers per arm -- with the pre-specified PRIMARY outcome 'Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity' by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp. Results were posted to ClinicalTrials.gov on 2026-03-11 and are NULL: placebo +19.0 +/- 95.0 vs NMN +13.5 +/- 88.4 (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL), i.e. NMN numerically WORSE than placebo. It has no journal publication (Europe PMC author search on Klein S + nicotinamide mononucleotide returns nothing after 2022). So it is neither 'independent' nor 'published', but writing only 'no replication exists' hides a failed self-replication that is far more damaging to the NMN case.

- **Was muscle insulin sensitivity the pre-specified primary endpoint?** — `confirmed`
  Not asserted by the article but checked because it bears on caliber. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03151239 lists the primary outcome as 'Muscle insulin sensitivity change', and Klein/Yoshino's Response calls it 'the primary outcome'. However, the Science paper's own text contains no sentence using the word 'primary' (searched: NOT FOUND) -- it frames three co-equal aims. So the endpoint was pre-registered as primary but not labelled as such in the publication.

- **Effect size of the flagship result** — `confirmed`
  For accuracy if the article quantifies it: 'Muscle insulin sensitivity, assessed as the rate of insulin-stimulated glucose disposal per kg of fat-free mass during the clamp procedure, was 25+/-7% greater after than before 10 weeks of NMN supplementation (p<0.01), but was not different after than before placebo treatment'. The supporting between-group statistic is a three-way mixed-model ANOVA (time x condition x group) with 'A significant three-way interaction (P =0.022)'. The headline 25% is a WITHIN-group before/after change in the NMN arm, not a between-group difference.

- **Full text of Brenner's technical comment (body, beyond the abstract)** — `unreachable`
  science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abj1696 returned HTTP 403 Forbidden; Semantic Scholar reports openAccessPdf status CLOSED with no URL; no PMCID exists and no preprint or repository copy was located. I read the complete published abstract (verified identical from two independent metadata sources) but not the body. Any characterisation of arguments Brenner makes beyond his abstract is unverified.

**修正:**
- Replace the attributed rationale. Brenner did not argue that liver fat depresses muscle insulin sensitivity. His published ground, verbatim, is: 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial.' Rewrite as: the placebo arm carried more than twice the liver fat of the NMN arm, and liver fat clearance is one of NMN's own putative targets, so the arms differed at baseline on a variable central to the drug's mechanism.
- Add the authors' rebuttal, which the article currently omits. Klein S and Yoshino M, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj7375, replied that muscle insulin sensitivity -- the pre-registered primary outcome -- 'was identical in both groups at baseline' and that 'Differences in baseline intrahepatic triglyceride content between groups do not negate the effects of NMN observed in muscle.' Presenting the challenge without the response overstates how settled the objection is.
- Attribute P=0.003 correctly. It is not an outside recalculation; it is the RM-ANOVA main-effect-of-group P printed in Yoshino et al.'s own Table 1 for intrahepatic triglyceride content. State that the +/- figures are SEM, not SD.
- Replace 'No independent replication has been published in the five years since' with the sharper and verifiable fact: the same Washington University group's larger confirmatory trial (NCT04571008: prediabetic men and women aged 45+, NMN 300 or 450 mg/day for at least 16 weeks, 28 randomised per arm, 20 completers per arm) had 'Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity' by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp as its pre-specified primary outcome and posted null results to ClinicalTrials.gov on 11 March 2026: placebo +19.0 +/- 95.0 versus NMN +13.5 +/- 88.4 (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL) -- NMN numerically worse than placebo. Flag explicitly that these are registry-posted results with no peer-reviewed publication as of July 2026, and that this is a self-replication by the original investigators, not an independent one. Do NOT quote a p-value from the registry: the posted analysis field reads '0.05' for both the primary and the secondary outcome, which is implausible as a computed statistic given the means and SDs and is almost certainly a significance-threshold entry.
- If the article states arm sizes as a total, say 25 COMPLETERS (13 NMN / 12 placebo), not 25 randomised -- the paper reports only completers.
- If the article quantifies the effect, use: 25 +/- 7% greater insulin-stimulated glucose disposal after versus before NMN (p<0.01), a within-group before/after change; the between-group support is a three-way mixed-model ANOVA interaction, P=0.022. Do not present 25% as a placebo-adjusted difference.
- Add the adiposity criterion: participants were postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were also overweight or obese.
- Optional but accurate context: the 2024 meta-analysis of NMN RCTs (Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep, PMC11557618) covering 8 trials found that only Yoshino 2021 used a clamp at all, and concluded that 'short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.'

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04571008 (Washington University School of Medicine), results posted 2026-03-11, is a failed self-replication of the flagship result. Larger (28 randomised per arm, 20 completers per arm vs 13/12), longer (>=16 weeks vs 10), higher dose (300 or 450 mg/day vs 250), broader population (prediabetic men and women aged 45+, BMI 25-50 vs postmenopausal women only), same pre-specified primary outcome measured the same way ('Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity', hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp with stable isotope tracer). Posted primary result: placebo +19.0 +/- 95.0, NMN +13.5 +/- 88.4 (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL). NMN is numerically worse than placebo. Posted secondary 'Changes in Glucose Tolerance' also favours placebo: placebo -9.0 +/- 38.0 (n=19) vs NMN +14 +/- 42 (n=20) mg/dL x 3 Hr (lower is better for a glucose AUC). No journal publication exists for this trial as of 2026-07-28.
- The enormous SDs in the follow-up trial (~90 on a mean change of ~15) indicate the clamp-derived muscle insulin sensitivity change is a very noisy measure at these sample sizes, which retrospectively undercuts the precision implied by the original n=13 vs n=12 result.
- The only other registered trial that could bear on this, NCT06627868 (University of Turku, NAD+ metabolism in human brown adipose tissue, whole-body insulin sensitivity as primary outcome, n=68), is still recruiting with completion scheduled 2027-08-31 -- so no independent clamp replication is even in the pipeline to report before 2027.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

Note on tooling: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I started, so all work was done via direct WebFetch against primary and primary-adjacent hosts (PMC, PubMed, EuropePMC REST API, ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, Semantic Scholar API). I could not reach science.org (HTTP 403), so the full body text of Brenner's comment and of the Klein/Yoshino response are unreachable; I verified both abstracts instead, and I obtained Brenner's abstract from TWO independent hosts (PubMed 34326206 and the EuropePMC REST API) which returned character-identical text, which is my guard against the fabricated-quote failure mode.

Primary documents reached verbatim: (1) Yoshino et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229 via PMC8550608 — abstract, Results sentences, Methods statistical paragraph, and Table 1 including its footnote; (2) Brenner's Science comment abstract (two hosts); (3) Klein & Yoshino response abstract (EuropePMC); (4) ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03151239 full record; (5) ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04571008 full record INCLUDING the posted results module; (6) Pencina et al. JCEM 2023 full abstract via EuropePMC; (7) Chen et al. Curr Diab Rep 2024 abstract.

What checks out exactly: 13 NMN / 12 placebo; 250 mg/day; 10 weeks; postmenopausal, overweight/obese, prediabetic women; hepatic lipid 6.3 +/- 1.2 vs 14.8 +/- 2.0 with P=0.003; publication of the challenge and the reply in Science on 30 July 2021. The three hepatic-lipid numbers appear identically in Brenner's abstract and in Table 1 of the original paper, so they are cross-confirmed rather than taken from a single summarizer pass.

What is off: (a) the figures are BASELINE values and are SEM not SD (Table 1 legend verbatim: 'Values are means +/- SEM'); (b) P=0.003 is Brenner's computation, absent from the Science paper; (c) the article's mechanistic gloss — 'liver fat itself depresses muscle insulin sensitivity' — is NOT Brenner's published argument, which is instead that liver fat clearance is a target of NMN, so the arms were unbalanced on the drug's own substrate.

The consequential finding, and the reason this is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS: the replication statement is stale. Searching ClinicalTrials.gov for NMN trials with insulin-sensitivity outcomes surfaced NCT04571008 — the same Washington University group's larger 16-week confirmatory trial with clamp-measured muscle insulin sensitivity as the registered primary outcome — which posted results on 2026-01-06 showing no effect (placebo +19.0 SD 95.0 vs NMN +13.5 SD 88.4). This is unpublished and easy to miss via literature search alone. Combined with the independent Pencina 2023 null and the 2024 meta-analysis null, the honest statement is not 'nobody has tried to replicate' but 'it has been tried and it did not replicate, including by the original investigators.'

Remaining uncertainty: (i) the NCT04571008 posted pValue field reads exactly 0.05 for both the primary and the secondary outcome, which I judge to be a threshold entry rather than a computed p — I flag it and recommend the article quote the means rather than that field; (ii) I could not read Brenner's or Klein's full comment bodies, so I cannot rule out that the muscle-insulin-sensitivity mechanism appears there even though it is absent from the abstract; (iii) I could not confirm from Science's own page whether the section is formally headed 'Technical Comment' — PubMed's publication type is simply 'Comment'. No erratum, correction, expression of concern, or retraction is attached to the 2021 Science paper.

- **Arm sizes: 13 women on NMN, 12 on placebo** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against two primary documents. Yoshino et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229 (PMC8550608) Results: 'Twenty-five postmenopausal women with prediabetes based on criteria proposed by the American Diabetes Association who were overweight or obese completed this study; 12 were randomized to the placebo group and 13 to the NMN group'. Brenner's Science comment abstract independently states 'the 13 women who received NMN' and 'the 12 in the placebo group'. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03151239 lists actual enrollment 25. Caveat worth noting: 25 is the number who COMPLETED; the paper describes randomization of completers, so 13/12 are the analyzed arm sizes.

- **250 mg/day NMN for 10 weeks, postmenopausal prediabetic overweight/obese women, endpoint = muscle insulin sensitivity** — `confirmed`
  Dose, duration and population confirmed verbatim in the Science abstract: 'We conducted a 10-week, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial to evaluate the effect of NMN supplementation on metabolic function in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese.' NCT03151239 lists the intervention as 250 mg total daily (two capsules) and the PRE-SPECIFIED primary outcome as 'Change in muscle insulin sensitivity' by 'hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp procedure in conjunction with stable isotopic tracer infusion' — so this was the registered primary endpoint, not a post-hoc finding. Registration first posted 2017-05-12, before the 2017-07-01 start.

- **Hepatic lipid content 6.3 +/- 1.2% (NMN) vs 14.8 +/- 2.0% (placebo), P=0.003** — `corrected`
  The three numbers are exactly right but two qualifiers are missing. WRONG (as written): 'hepatic lipid content was 6.3 +/- 1.2% in the NMN arm versus 14.8 +/- 2.0% in placebo (P=0.003)' — reads as if these are trial values reported by Yoshino et al. RIGHT: these are BASELINE (pre-treatment) values, they are means +/- SEM not SD (Table 1 legend, verbatim: 'Values are means +/- SEM'), the variable is labelled 'Intrahepatic triglyceride content (%)' in the paper (Table 1 row: placebo before 14.8 +/- 2.0, after 15.7 +/- 2.5; NMN before 6.3 +/- 1.2, after 6.8 +/- 1.3), and the P=0.003 is Brenner's own computed between-group baseline comparison — the Science paper reports no baseline between-arm p-value for this variable. Brenner's abstract verbatim (identical text retrieved independently from PubMed 34326206 and EuropePMC): 'However, the 13 women who received NMN had hepatic lipid content of 6.3 +/- 1.2%, whereas the 12 in the placebo group had 14.8 +/- 2.0% (P = 0.003).'

- **The challenge was published in Science (technical comment + authors' response)** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed. Comment: Brenner C, 'Comment on "Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women"', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj1696, DOI 10.1126/science.abj1696, PMID 34326206 (author affiliation: Department of Diabetes and Cancer Metabolism, City of Hope National Medical Center). Response: Klein S, Yoshino M, 'Response to Comment on...', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj7375, DOI 10.1126/science.abj7375, PMID 34326209. Response abstract verbatim (EuropePMC): 'In evaluating any randomized clinical trial, it is important to determine whether baseline differences between groups could have affected the primary outcome. In our study, muscle insulin sensitivity, which was identical in both groups at baseline, improved after nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), not placebo, therapy. Differences in baseline intrahepatic triglyceride content between groups do not negate the effects of NMN observed in muscle.' No erratum, correction, expression of concern or retraction is attached to PMID 33888596. Minor unverified detail: science.org returned HTTP 403, so I could not confirm the exact section header ('Technical Comment' vs 'Comment'); PubMed's publication type is 'Comment'.

- **Stated reason for the challenge: 'liver fat itself depresses muscle insulin sensitivity, so the arms were imbalanced on the variable most likely to drive the endpoint'** — `corrected`
  WRONG (as written): attributes to Brenner the argument that liver fat depresses muscle insulin sensitivity. RIGHT: Brenner's published rationale, verbatim from his abstract, is 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial' — i.e. the NMN arm had far less liver fat available for NMN to act on, so the arms were not exchangeable with respect to the drug's own target. The full text is paywalled (science.org 403), so I could not verify whether the liver-fat-to-muscle-insulin-sensitivity mechanism appears in the body; on the reachable text it does not. Rewrite to Brenner's own framing, or drop the mechanistic gloss.

- **No independent replication has been published in the five years since** — `corrected`
  Literally true but materially understated, and it omits evidence published since. WRONG (as written): 'No independent replication has been published in the five years since' — implies an evidentiary vacuum. RIGHT: the finding has been actively tested and has FAILED to replicate. (1) Independent trial: Pencina KM et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023 (PMID 36740954, PMCID PMC11491622), Bhasin group, 30 overweight/obese adults >=45y randomized 2:1 to MIB-626 (microcrystalline beta-NMN) 1000 mg/day vs placebo for 28 days; abstract verbatim: 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group.' (2) Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024 (PMID 39531138), meta-analysis of 8 RCTs / 342 adults: 'random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile.' (3) Decisive: the ORIGINAL investigators' own larger, longer follow-up — NCT04571008, 'Effect of NMN Supplementation on Organ System Biology', PI Samuel Klein, Washington University, prediabetic adults 45-75y, 300-450 mg/day for >=16 weeks, 56 randomized / 40 completers (20 per arm), pre-specified primary outcome 'Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity' by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp — posted results to ClinicalTrials.gov on 2026-01-06 showing a null effect: placebo mean change +19.0 (SD 95.0) vs NMN +13.5 (SD 88.4) (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL), i.e. NMN numerically LOWER than placebo. Secondary OGTT outcome: placebo -9.0 (SD 38.0) vs NMN +14 (SD 42) mg/dL x 3 hr, also favouring placebo. No peer-reviewed publication of NCT04571008 exists as of 2026-07 (no PubMed or EuropePMC record cites it as a results publication).

- **Framing of the headline effect ('raising muscle insulin sensitivity')** — `corrected`
  Not stated in the claim group but a caliber trap the article should not fall into. The headline number is a WITHIN-GROUP before/after change, verbatim: 'Muscle insulin sensitivity, assessed as the rate of insulin-stimulated glucose disposal per kg of fat-free mass during the clamp procedure, was 25+/-7% greater after than before 10 weeks of NMN supplementation (p<0.01), but was not different after than before placebo treatment'. The statistical model, verbatim from Methods: 'A three-way mixed model ANOVA with time (before- vs after- treatment), condition (basal vs insulin infusion), and group (placebo vs NMN) as factors, was used to compare the effect of NMN (n=13) and placebo (n=12) treatment on insulin-stimulated glucose disposal rate', with 'A significant three-way interaction (P =0.022) was followed by Tukey's post-hoc test'. The paper reports no direct between-arm comparison of the CHANGE in glucose disposal. The significant-in-one-arm / not-significant-in-the-other pattern is a difference-of-significance, not a demonstrated between-group difference.

**修正:**
- Add 'at baseline' when citing the hepatic lipid figures: at baseline, intrahepatic triglyceride content was 6.3% in the NMN arm versus 14.8% in the placebo arm. These are pre-treatment values from Table 1 of the Science paper, not on-treatment values.
- State that the +/- figures are SEM, not SD. Table 1's legend reads verbatim: 'Values are means +/- SEM.' With n=13 and n=12, SEMs of 1.2 and 2.0 correspond to SDs of roughly 4.3 and 6.9 — the spread is much wider than '+/- 1.2' suggests to a reader who assumes SD.
- Attribute the P=0.003 to Brenner, not to Yoshino et al. The Science paper reports no baseline between-arm p-value for intrahepatic triglyceride; P=0.003 is Brenner's own computation, published in his comment.
- Replace the mechanistic gloss with Brenner's actual argument. He does not argue that liver fat depresses muscle insulin sensitivity; his published sentence is: 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial.' The point is that the NMN arm had little liver fat for the drug to clear, so the arms were not exchangeable with respect to the drug's own target.
- Give the full citation pair so readers can find both sides: Brenner C, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj1696 (30 July 2021), and the reply, Klein S & Yoshino M, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj7375. Klein and Yoshino do not dispute the imbalance; they argue baseline muscle insulin sensitivity was identical and that 'Differences in baseline intrahepatic triglyceride content between groups do not negate the effects of NMN observed in muscle.'
- Replace 'no independent replication has been published' with the stronger and now-documented statement: the result has failed to replicate. Cite (a) Pencina et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023 — independent RCT, 1000 mg/day NMN for 28 days in 30 overweight/obese adults >=45y, 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group'; (b) Chen et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024 — meta-analysis of 8 RCTs / 342 adults finding no significant benefit on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c or HOMA-IR.
- Add the decisive 2026 update the article is currently missing: the same Washington University group (PI Samuel Klein) ran a larger, longer confirmatory trial — NCT04571008, 300-450 mg/day NMN for at least 16 weeks in prediabetic adults aged 45-75, 56 randomized and 40 completers (20 per arm), with clamp-measured muscle insulin sensitivity as the pre-specified primary outcome — and posted null results to ClinicalTrials.gov on 6 January 2026: mean change +19.0 in placebo versus +13.5 in NMN (units (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL)), with NMN numerically worse than placebo. It has not been published in a journal as of July 2026.
- Do NOT quote a p-value from the NCT04571008 results posting. The pValue field reads '0.05' for both the primary and the secondary outcome, which is almost certainly a significance-threshold entry rather than a computed p (the secondary outcome's means run in the opposite direction). Quote the mean changes and note the p-value field is uninformative as entered.
- If the article describes the 2021 finding as 'NMN raised muscle insulin sensitivity', flag that the 25+/-7% figure is a within-arm before/after change (p<0.01) that was significant in the NMN arm and not in placebo; the paper reports a three-way time x condition x group interaction of P=0.022 with Tukey post-hoc, but no direct between-arm comparison of the change. Significant-in-one-arm-only is not a demonstrated between-group effect.
- Note that the trial's primary endpoint was pre-registered (NCT03151239, first posted 12 May 2017, before the 1 July 2017 start), listing 'Change in muscle insulin sensitivity' by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp. This is a genuine strength of the study and should be stated alongside the criticisms — the finding is not post-hoc.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04571008 posted results on 2026-01-06 (retrieved from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API): the original investigators' own follow-up trial — Washington University, PI Samuel Klein, DoD-funded, prediabetic adults 45-75y, 300-450 mg/day NMN for >=16 weeks, 56 randomized (28/28), 40 completers (20/20) — reports for the pre-specified primary outcome 'Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity' (hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp, ANCOVA): placebo mean change 19.0 (SD 95.0) vs NMN 13.5 (SD 88.4) (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL). This is a null result with NMN numerically below placebo, in a trial roughly 1.6x larger and 60% longer than the Science trial. It is unpublished as of 2026-07.
- Pencina KM et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023 (PMID 36740954): independent RCT, 30 overweight/obese adults >=45y, 2:1 randomization to MIB-626 beta-NMN 1000 mg/day vs placebo for 28 days. Abstract verbatim: 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group.' Four times the daily dose of the Science trial, no insulin-sensitivity signal.
- Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024 (PMID 39531138): meta-analysis of 8 RCTs, 342 middle-aged/older adults. Verbatim: 'random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile' and 'short-term supplementation of NMN of 250-2000 mg/d did not show significantly positive impacts on glucose control and lipid profile.'
- The Science paper's own Table 1 legend states, verbatim, 'The effect of NMN on these variables was not different from placebo' — i.e. every body-composition and basal metabolic variable in the table, including intrahepatic triglyceride, was unmoved by NMN. The claimed mechanism (NMN clearing liver fat) did not occur in this trial: NMN arm 6.3 -> 6.8, placebo 14.8 -> 15.7.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Note on constraints: this session's WebSearch budget was fully exhausted before I began, so every source below was reached by direct WebFetch against primary or near-primary endpoints (PubMed, PMC, the Europe PMC REST API, the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, Semantic Scholar). I compensated for the loss of search by using PubMed and Europe PMC query URLs and the ClinicalTrials.gov API as structured search substitutes.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED. (1) Yoshino M et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229 via PMC8550608 - I extracted the randomization sentence, the dose/duration, the Table 1 intrahepatic triglyceride row (14.8 +/- 2.0 / 15.7 +/- 2.5 / 6.3 +/- 1.2 / 6.8 +/- 1.3, Pgroup 0.003), and the clamp result sentence. (2) Brenner's technical comment abstract, retrieved verbatim and character-identically from two mutually independent endpoints - the PubMed record for PMID 34326206 and the Europe PMC REST core JSON. That cross-endpoint agreement is why I treat the 6.3/14.8/0.003 figures and the 13/12 arm sizes as verbatim-verified rather than summarizer-reported. (3) The Klein/Yoshino response abstract from PubMed PMID 34326209. (4) The ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API records for NCT03151239 and NCT04571008, including a raw-JSON dump of the NCT04571008 primary outcome object so I could inspect actual field names rather than a prose rendering.

GUARDING AGAINST THE KNOWN FABRICATION FAILURE MODE. Because I was warned that fetch summarizers invent quotes and misread multi-column tables, I deliberately re-fetched the Science paper a second time with a string-hunting prompt rather than accepting the first fetch's tidy table, and the four-column Table 1 row it returned is corroborated externally by Brenner quoting the same two values with the same P. For NCT04571008 I explicitly demanded the raw JSON, which mattered: the prose fetch had presented 'p-Value: 0.05' as a result, but the raw object shows a bare pValue field alongside nonInferiorityType 'OTHER', and with means of 19.0 and 13.5 against SDs near 90 at n=20 per arm an exact p of 0.05 is arithmetically implausible. I therefore report the means and refuse to report that p as a finding.

WHAT I COULD NOT REACH. The body text of Brenner's one-page comment is paywalled (science.org HTTP 403; Europe PMC isOpenAccess N; Semantic Scholar returned no openAccessPdf). I verified his abstract only, which is why I flag the article's mechanistic gloss as an unsupported attribution rather than asserting it is absent from the paper. I also could not reach the Methods of Pencina 2023 (JCEM full text behind reCAPTCHA; Europe PMC fullTextXML 404 for PMC11491622), so I cannot confirm whether its insulin sensitivity measure was clamp-derived, and I have graded it accordingly as a non-strict null rather than a replication. Separately, the three-way interaction P=0.022 in the 2021 paper is single-sourced from one PMC fetch and should be re-checked before it is printed.

WHERE THE CLAIM GROUP STANDS. The verifiable core is solid: arm sizes, dose, duration, population, the hepatic lipid figures and P value, and the existence of a formal Science technical comment plus authors' response all check out verbatim. Two things need fixing. The smaller is a misattributed rationale - Brenner's published argument is that NMN targets liver fat clearance, not that liver fat confounds muscle insulin sensitivity. The larger is that the 'no replication' line is stale in a way that understates the article's own case: I found, by sweeping the ClinicalTrials.gov API rather than the literature, that the originating lab ran a bigger, longer, better-powered confirmatory trial with the clamp endpoint pre-specified as primary, and posted null results four months before today's date. Because it is registry-only and from the same group, no literature search would surface it and the article's sentence is not technically false - but an article assessing evidence grading that omits a null pre-specified primary endpoint from the same investigators is misleading by omission. Verdict CORRECTED rather than OVERTURNED, since every number the group asserts survives; what fails is one attribution and the currency of the replication claim.

- **Arm sizes: 13 women on NMN, 12 on placebo** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against two independent primary sources. The Science paper (Yoshino M et al., Science 2021;372(6547):1224-1229, doi 10.1126/science.abe9985, PMID 33888596) states: '25 postmenopausal women with prediabetes...completed this study; 12 were randomized to the placebo group and 13 to the NMN group'. Brenner's published abstract independently states 'the 13 women who received NMN' and 'the 12 in the placebo group'. Registry NCT03151239 lists actual enrollment 25. Note these are completers; the analysis n per arm in the stats text is likewise n=13 NMN / n=12 placebo.

- **Dose and duration: 250 mg/day for 10 weeks** — `confirmed`
  Paper reports '250 mg/day' and '10 weeks of treatment'. Registry NCT03151239 confirms '250 mg total daily' and a primary outcome time frame of 'at least 8 weeks of treatment'. Population confirmed as postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese.

- **Hepatic lipid imbalance: 6.3 +/- 1.2% NMN vs 14.8 +/- 2.0% placebo, P=0.003** — `confirmed`
  Numbers are exactly right. Brenner's abstract, retrieved verbatim and identically from two independent endpoints (PubMed PMID 34326206 and the Europe PMC REST API core record), reads: 'However, the 13 women who received NMN had hepatic lipid content of 6.3 +/- 1.2%, whereas the 12 in the placebo group had 14.8 +/- 2.0% (P = 0.003).' The underlying source is Table 1 of the Science paper, row 'Intrahepatic triglyceride content (%)', with four values 14.8 +/- 2.0 (placebo before) / 15.7 +/- 2.5 (placebo after) / 6.3 +/- 1.2 (NMN before) / 6.8 +/- 1.3 (NMN after), and Pgroup = 0.003. One caliber note: 0.003 is the group main effect (Pgroup) from the paper's mixed model across before/after, not a standalone baseline t-test; both Brenner and Klein nonetheless treat it as the baseline between-group difference, so the article's usage tracks the disputants.

- **The challenge was published in Science; technical comment and authors' response located** — `confirmed`
  Both located. Comment: Brenner C, 'Comment on "Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women"', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj1696, doi 10.1126/science.abj1696, PMID 34326206. Response: Klein S, Yoshino M, 'Response to Comment on...', Science 2021 Jul 30;373(6554):eabj7375, doi 10.1126/science.abj7375, PMID 34326209. The response abstract verbatim: 'In evaluating any randomized clinical trial, it is important to determine whether baseline differences between groups could have affected the primary outcome. In our study, muscle insulin sensitivity, which was identical in both groups at baseline, improved after nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), not placebo, therapy. Differences in baseline intrahepatic triglyceride content between groups do not negate the effects of NMN observed in muscle.' No erratum, correction, or retraction is attached to the 2021 paper; PubMed lists four 'Comment in' items and no 'Erratum in'.

- **Rationale attributed to the challenge: 'liver fat itself depresses muscle insulin sensitivity', so the arms were imbalanced on the variable most likely to drive the endpoint** — `corrected`
  WRONG as attribution. The article puts a mechanism in Brenner's mouth that his published abstract does not state. RIGHT: Brenner's stated reason is that NMN's own target is liver fat, not that liver fat confounds muscle insulin sensitivity. Verbatim: 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial.' The full body text of the one-page comment is paywalled (science.org returned HTTP 403; Europe PMC records it as not open access; Semantic Scholar returns no open-access PDF), so I could not confirm or exclude that the muscle-insulin-sensitivity confounding argument appears in the body. The article should quote Brenner's actual stated rationale rather than supply its own.

- **No independent replication has been published in the five years since** — `corrected`
  Literally defensible but materially out of date, and it omits the single most decisive item. WRONG as written: 'No independent replication has been published in the five years since', with the implication that the 2021 result simply stands untested. RIGHT: no POSITIVE replication exists, and three lines of later evidence now cut against the result. (1) The originating lab's own larger confirmatory trial has posted NULL results. NCT04571008, 'Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) Supplementation on Organ System Biology', sponsor Washington University School of Medicine, PI Samuel Klein (same senior author): randomized, quadruple-masked, 56 enrolled (28 placebo / 28 NMN), adults 45-75 of both sexes with prediabetes, 300-450 mg/day for at least 16 weeks, PRIMARY outcome 'Change in Muscle Insulin Sensitivity' by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp. Completed 2025-03-04; results first posted 2026-03-11. Posted primary result, n=20 analysed per arm: placebo mean change 19.0 (SD 95.0) vs NMN mean change 13.5 (SD 88.4) (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL) - the NMN arm improved LESS than placebo. The registry statistical-analysis object lists statisticalMethod 'ANCOVA' and pValue '0.05'; I do not trust that as a computed p-value (a 5.5-unit difference with SDs near 90 and n=20/arm cannot yield p=0.05) and read it as a threshold entry, so cite the means, not the p. No journal publication of this trial exists as of 2026-07 (Europe PMC returns zero hits from the Klein/Yoshino group citing NCT04571008). (2) Independent trial finding no effect: Pencina KM et al., 'Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide Augmentation in Overweight or Obese Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A Physiologic Study', J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(8):1968-1980, doi 10.1210/clinem/dgad027, PMID 36740954 - 30 overweight/obese adults >=45 randomized 2:1 to MIB-626 microcrystalline beta-NMN 500 mg x2 twice daily (2000 mg/day) or placebo for 28 days; abstract verbatim: 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group.' I could not reach its Methods to confirm whether insulin sensitivity was clamp-derived (JCEM full text behind reCAPTCHA; Europe PMC full-text XML 404), so this is a different-population, different-dose null, not a strict replication. (3) Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024;25(1):4, doi 10.1007/s11892-024-01557-z, PMID 39531138, meta-analysis of 8 NMN RCTs, 250-2000 mg/d, 14 days to 12 weeks, 342 adults: 'The random-effects meta-analyses indicated no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile.' A PubMed RCT-filtered sweep of all 16 human NMN trials through 2026 found no other trial with clamp-measured muscle insulin sensitivity.

- **Statistical caliber of the flagship result itself (context check, not asserted by the article)** — `corrected`
  Worth adding because it strengthens the article. The headline effect is a WITHIN-group before-vs-after change, not a reported between-arm difference: 'Muscle insulin sensitivity, assessed as the rate of insulin-stimulated glucose disposal per kg of fat-free mass during the clamp procedure, was 25+/-7% greater after than before 10 weeks of NMN supplementation (p<0.01), but was not different after than before placebo treatment.' The between-arm anchor is a three-way mixed-model ANOVA (time x condition x group) with a reported significant three-way interaction of P=0.022, followed by Tukey post-hoc. CAVEAT: that methods sentence and the 0.022 came from a single WebFetch of the PMC full text (PMC8550608) and I did not corroborate it against a second endpoint, so treat 0.022 as single-sourced. The 25+/-7% and p<0.01 figures were returned consistently across two separate fetches.

**修正:**
- Do not attribute to Brenner the argument that liver fat depresses muscle insulin sensitivity. His published rationale is that NMN's own target is liver fat clearance. Use his exact wording: 'Given that a target of NMN is liver fat clearance, this was not an effectively randomized trial.' (Brenner C, Science 2021;373(6554):eabj1696.)
- Delete or rewrite 'No independent replication has been published in the five years since.' As of 2026-07 the accurate statement is: no positive replication exists, and the originating lab's own larger confirmatory trial has posted null results. Replace with language to this effect: 'The Washington University group's larger follow-up trial (NCT04571008) - 56 prediabetic adults of both sexes, 300-450 mg/day for at least 16 weeks, with clamp-measured muscle insulin sensitivity as the pre-specified primary endpoint - completed in March 2025 and posted results in March 2026 showing no benefit: mean change 13.5 (SD 88.4) in the NMN arm versus 19.0 (SD 95.0) on placebo, n=20 per arm. It has not yet been published in a journal.'
- When citing the NCT04571008 null result, cite the arm means and SDs, not a p-value. The registry's statistical-analysis block lists pValue '0.05' with method 'ANCOVA', but that figure is not credible as a computed p given the dispersion and sample size and is most likely a significance-threshold entry.
- Add the independent null: Pencina KM et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(8):1968-1980 (MIB-626 beta-NMN 2000 mg/day, 28 days, 30 overweight/obese adults randomized 2:1) reported 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group.' Flag it as a different population, dose and duration rather than a strict replication.
- Add the pooled evidence: Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024;25(1):4 - meta-analysis of 8 NMN RCTs (250-2000 mg/d, 14 days to 12 weeks, 342 adults) found 'no significant benefit of NMN on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, glycated hemoglobin, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and lipid profile.'
- If the article characterises the 2021 effect size, make the within-group nature explicit: the 25 +/- 7% improvement (p<0.01) is an after-versus-before change inside the NMN arm, with placebo unchanged; the between-arm support is a three-way mixed-model interaction, not a directly reported arm-versus-arm difference in glucose disposal.
- Optionally sharpen the source label: the paper's Table 1 row is 'Intrahepatic triglyceride content (%)' and the 0.003 is the group main effect (Pgroup) from the mixed model. Brenner's 'hepatic lipid content' phrasing is his own, and both he and Klein treat 0.003 as the baseline between-group difference.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- DECISIVE, and apparently unknown to the article: NCT04571008 posted null primary results on 2026-03-11. This is the same lab (Washington University, PI Samuel Klein), a larger and longer version of the flagship trial - 56 prediabetic adults aged 45-75 of both sexes, randomized quadruple-masked to 300-450 mg/day NMN or placebo for at least 16 weeks, with change in muscle insulin sensitivity by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp as the pre-specified PRIMARY outcome. Posted result (n=20 analysed per arm): placebo mean change 19.0 (SD 95.0) vs NMN mean change 13.5 (SD 88.4) (nmol/kg FFM/min)/(uU/mL). The NMN arm improved numerically LESS than placebo. Trial completed 2025-03-04; results submitted 2026-01-06, posted 2026-03-11; no journal publication as of 2026-07.
- Pencina KM et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(8):1968-1980 (PMID 36740954): independent randomized trial of beta-NMN (MIB-626, 2000 mg/day, 28 days, N=30, 2:1) that measured insulin sensitivity and reported 'Insulin sensitivity and hepatic and intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group', despite substantial increases in circulating NAD.
- Chen F et al., Curr Diab Rep 2024;25(1):4 (PMID 39531138): random-effects meta-analysis of 8 NMN RCTs (342 adults) found no significant benefit on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, HOMA-IR or lipids.
- The headline 2021 effect is reported as a within-arm before-versus-after change (25 +/- 7%, p<0.01) with placebo unchanged, rather than as a directly reported between-arm difference in glucose disposal - a weaker construction than 'NMN raised insulin sensitivity relative to placebo' implies.

## V22 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

Method: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I began, so I bypassed the summarizing fetch layer entirely after one bad result. My first WebFetch of the Martens 2018 PMC page returned an unrelated article (Chinese NSFC/Shenzhen funding, "no conflicts of interest") — a clear misfetch of exactly the kind the task warned about. I discarded it and switched to curl against the Europe PMC REST API, pulling raw JATS XML and grepping the strings myself with Python. Every quotation in this report was read by me in the raw XML, not relayed by a model.

Primary documents reached verbatim: Martens 2018 (PMC5876407, 142 KB XML), Trammell 2016 (PMC5062546), NICE trial (PMC11176364, 143 KB) plus its Publisher Correction (PMC11319328) in full, NR-SAFE (PMC10684646), the Geroscience 2025 Florida hypertension trial (PMC12638573), and the EClinicalMedicine 2025 long-COVID trial (PMC12675013).

Confirmed exactly as claimed: the Martens 2018 juxtaposition (ChromaDex acknowledgement and "The authors declare no competing interests" separated only by the Author contributions section); the Trammell 2016 ChromaDex funding/employment/equity nexus; and every NICE number the article cites — n=90, PAD, 6 months, NR 1,000 mg daily, the pre-specified one-sided P<0.10 (stated eight times in the paper), and the +17.6 m primary ITT effect with 90% CI +1.77 to +infinity, P=0.08.

Three things do not survive. First, the MCID: the NICE Methods define ~8 m as the small MCID and 20 m as the LARGE MCID, so the article's "~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important" mislabels the threshold and inverts the reading — +17.6 m clears the small MCID twofold. Second, NICE is AHA-funded, not ChromaDex-funded; ChromaDex donated product only. Third, the load-bearing absence is refutable as literally worded: I attacked it through the ClinicalTrials.gov API rather than the literature (108 interventional NR studies ranked by actual enrollment), which surfaced NOPARK at 410 actual enrollment, publicly sponsored, completed June 2025, and a cluster of large trials tied to Elysium Health rather than ChromaDex.

What remains uncertain: NOPARK's funding and product-sourcing statements are UNREACHABLE — no results posted, no primary publication findable in Europe PMC as of 2026-07. I did not fill that gap from memory. I also could not reach the full text of the Lancet Neurology 2026 Friedreich's ataxia trial (paywalled; the XML endpoint returned zero bytes), so its NR sourcing is unverified — though at 66 randomized and NIH R01HL149722-funded it is not "large" by the article's own standard and does not bear on the claim. The thesis is sound and I found two fresh instances that strengthen it; the corrections are about caliber and scope, not about the underlying argument.

- **Martens 2018 declares "The authors declare no competing interests" in the same document that discloses ChromaDex supplied study pills, standards and partial funding** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED VERBATIM from the JATS full text of Nat Commun 2018;9:1286 (PMC5876407, PMID 29599478, DOI 10.1038/s41467-018-03421-7), fetched as raw XML via Europe PMC and read directly (not via a summarizer). Acknowledgements, final sentence: "Study pills, NR standards for metabolite analyses and partial funding support were provided by ChromaDex, Inc." Two sections later, verbatim: "Competing interests The authors declare no competing interests." The two statements are separated only by the Author contributions section — the article's characterization is exact. Additional detail the article may use: NR was NIAGEN, 500 mg twice per day (1,000 mg/day), 2 x 6-week crossover; other funding was NIH AG000279 and TR001082.

- **Trammell 2016 carries ChromaDex money/product/equity ties** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED VERBATIM from Nat Commun 2016;7:12948 (PMC5062546, PMID 27721479). This one is stronger than the article implies — it is disclosed, not concealed. Footnotes, verbatim: "F.J., R.W.D. and C.B. own stock in ChromaDex, the supplier of NR and sponsor of the clinical study. F.J. and R.W.D. are employees of ChromaDex. M.E.M. has received research grants and serves as a consultant for ChromaDex. C.B. has received a research grant and serves on the scientific advisory board of ChromaDex." Also verbatim: "C.B. is the chief scientific adviser of ProHealthspan, which sells NR supplements." Acknowledgments, verbatim: "This study was supported by grants from the Roy J. Carver Trust, ChromaDex and National Institutes of Health (R21-AA022371) to C.B." Affiliation 3 on the byline is literally "ChromaDex, Inc., 10005 Muirlands Blvd, Suite G, Irvine, California 92618, USA". So Trammell 2016 hits money AND product AND equity AND employment — but note it DISCLOSES all of it, unlike Martens 2018. If the article groups the two as equivalent failures of disclosure, that is unfair to Trammell.

- **NICE trial: n=90, peripheral artery disease, 6 months, NR 1,000 mg +/- resveratrol** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED from Nat Commun 2024;15:5046 (PMC11176364, PMID 38871717, DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-49092-5), raw XML. Verbatim: "Eligible participants were randomized to one of three groups: nicotinamide riboside 1,000 mg daily, nicotinamide riboside 1000 mg + 125 mgs resveratrol daily, or placebo." Dosing verbatim: "Two 250 mgs of NR (or placebo) pills twice daily and one 125 mg resveratrol (or placebo) once daily." N=90, Northwestern, enrollment 12/13/2018-9/14/2022, final follow-up 4/3/2023, NCT03743636, 6-month intervention. Resveratrol dose is 125 mg — specify it if the article states a dose. Caveat the article should not blur: only the NR-ALONE arm met the threshold; verbatim, "Compared to placebo, NR+ resveratrol did not significantly improve 6-" the primary endpoint. The "+/- resveratrol" phrasing describes the arms, not two positive results.

- **NICE was declared positive only against a PRE-SPECIFIED ONE-SIDED p<0.10 threshold** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED VERBATIM, and the paper repeats it in eight separate places (Results, Fig. 2 legend, Tables 2-5 footnotes, Methods). Exact string: "The a priori statistical analysis plan defined a one-sided P value of <0.10 to define statistical significance." Methods add verbatim: "One-sided 90% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for between group differences. Because the clinical trial was a Phase II trial, to help ensure that a true beneficial effect of the interventions was not dismissed due to lack of statistical significance, the pre-specified P value for statistical significance was more liberal than a P value of <0.05." Power calc was also built on it: "a one-sided significance level of 0.10". The observed P was 0.08, so the result would NOT clear a conventional two-sided alpha=0.05 (two-sided p is roughly 0.16). The article's characterization is accurate and well supported.

- **NICE intention-to-treat effect of +17.6 m on the 6-minute walk** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED VERBATIM, Primary outcomes section: "Compared to placebo, NR improved 6-min walk by 17.6 meters (90% CI: + 1.77, +infinity, P = 0.08) at 6-month follow-up, meeting the pre-specified criterion for statistical significance (Table 2 and Fig. 2A)." The abstract rounds the bound: "between group difference: +17.6 (90% CI: + 1.8,+infinity)". This is the pre-specified primary endpoint analyzed by MMRM on all N=90. Calling it ITT is substantively correct — verbatim, "Pre-specified analyses were performed according to each participant's assigned group, irrespective of pill adherence" — but note the paper itself never uses the phrase "intention-to-treat", so do not put that term in quotation marks. Contrast values the article should keep straight: the 31.0 m and 26.9 m figures are labeled by the paper as "Post-hoc analyses" in the >=75%-adherence subgroup (n=60), NOT ITT.

- **+17.6 m is below the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important** — `corrected`
  CALIBER SLIPPAGE — the article mislabels the threshold. WRONG version: "+17.6 m ... below the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important." RIGHT version, from the NICE paper's own Methods, verbatim: "In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters." So 20 m is the LARGE MCID, not the MCID. Against the paper's own cited small MCID of ~8 m, +17.6 m EXCEEDS the threshold by more than twofold; it falls short only of the large MCID. Presenting 20 m as "the" MCID makes a result that clears the conventional small MCID read as sub-threshold. The honest formulation is: the ITT effect cleared the small MCID (~8 m) but not the large MCID (20 m), and was significant only under a pre-specified one-sided alpha=0.10.

- **NICE funding/COI statement** — `corrected`
  NICE is NOT ChromaDex-funded — it is ChromaDex-SUPPLIED. Acknowledgements verbatim: "Funded by the American Heart Association, Grant Numbers 18SFRN33900097, 18SFRN33900136, and 18SFRN33970010. Nicotinamide riboside was provided by ChromaDex. Resveratrol was provided by ReserveAge". So if the article says NICE carries ChromaDex money, that is WRONG; the right version is that AHA paid for it and ChromaDex donated the product. Separately, the article's core disclosure point is ALSO true here and is worth using: Competing interests verbatim reads "Dr. McDermott reports research funding from Helixmith and other research support from ArtAssist, and Mars. The remaining authors report no competing interests." — i.e., no ChromaDex entry in the COI section despite ChromaDex supplying the investigational product, the same Martens-2018 pattern, and Martens (C.R.M.) is himself a NICE co-author. Also verified: the Publisher Correction (PMC11319328, DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-51289-7, 12 Aug 2024) is purely clerical — it restored a truncated abstract sentence adding "Clinical Trials.gov registration: NCT03743636". No scientific correction, no erratum to the numbers; do not imply otherwise.

- **No large independent (non-ChromaDex-linked) NR trial exists — the load-bearing absence** — `corrected`
  PARTIALLY REFUTED as literally worded; survives if narrowed. I attacked this via the ClinicalTrials.gov API (108 interventional NR studies, ranked by actual enrollment) rather than the literature, to catch trials the publication record hides. Findings: (a) NOPARK, NCT03568968, "A Randomized Controlled Trial of Nicotinamide Riboside Supplementation in Early Parkinson's Disease" — ACTUAL enrollment 410, status COMPLETED 2025-06-17, lead sponsor Haukeland University Hospital with ten Norwegian public hospitals as collaborators and NO industry collaborator listed. That is 4.5x the size of NICE and is publicly sponsored. Its results are NOT posted (hasResults False) and I could not find a primary publication in Europe PMC as of 2026-07, so its funding/product statement is UNREACHABLE — I will not guess it. The same group's smaller sister trial NR-SAFE (PMC10684646) states verbatim "We are grateful to ChromaDex (Irvine, California) for providing the NR and placebo capsules for the study" while being funded by "The Research Council of Norway (288164, C.T.), Trond Mohn Foundation (BFS2017REK05, C.T.) and the Western Norway Regional Health Authority" — so the likely NOPARK pattern is public money + donated ChromaDex product, which the article's net does catch, but only via "product". (b) A second, cleaner problem: several LARGE registered NR trials name Elysium Health — a rival NR vendor, not ChromaDex — as collaborator: NO-ALS NCT04562831 (n=380), NADAPT NCT06162013 (n=330), NCT05483465 Oklahoma/Penn (n=214), NAD-HD NCT06853743 (n=120), Slow Age NCT05593939 (n=80). None has posted results yet, but when they publish, a claim keyed literally to "ChromaDex/Niagen" fails while the underlying "industry-dependent" thesis survives. So the sentence must be scoped to PUBLISHED trials and widened past ChromaDex to "an NR vendor". Everything I could actually read does support the thesis: the largest published NR RCTs all carry a ChromaDex/Niagen tie.

- **Independent search for further ChromaDex-linked trials (corroboration)** — `confirmed`
  I found two additional instances that strengthen the article beyond the three trials it names. (1) Lin, Zeidan et al., Geroscience 2025, NR + exercise for hypertension (PMC12638573, NCT04112043): Methods verbatim "NR and matching placebo (microcrystalline cellulose) capsules for this study were provided by Niagen Bioscience (previously ChromaDex, Corp) (Los Angeles, CA)" and Acknowledgements verbatim thank "the Niagen Bioscience (former ChromaDex, Corp) for excellent collaboration on this project by providing NR product and matching placebo" — yet the Declarations read verbatim "Competing interests The authors declare no competing interests." This is the exact Martens-2018 pattern recurring in 2025, and its author list includes C.R.M. (Martens), M.M.M. (McDermott) and D.R.S. (Seals). Note for accuracy: this trial randomized 54, not the 147 registered. (2) EClinicalMedicine 2025 long-COVID NR RCT (PMC12675013, NCT04809974, n=58 randomized): Funding verbatim "This work was supported by Niagen Bioscience, the MGH McCance Center for Brain Health..."; Declaration of interests verbatim "Drs. Brenner and Tanzi are on the scientific advisory board and hold equity in Niagen Bioscience"; and Role of the funding source verbatim "Team members of Niagen Bioscience reviewed the manuscript." Result was null on the primary cognitive endpoints. Useful to the article as a well-disclosed contrast case.

- Scope the universal claim. Change "Every large or landmark NR human trial" to "Every large or landmark NR trial that has actually been published," and widen "ChromaDex/Niagen Bioscience" to "an NR vendor (ChromaDex/Niagen, or its competitor Elysium Health)." Trammell 2016 disclosed its ties in full and explicitly, including "F.J., R.W.D. and C.B. own stock in ChromaDex, the supplier of NR and sponsor of the clinical study." The concealment point applies to Martens 2018 (and to the 2025 Geroscience hypertension trial), not to Trammell.

- Note that the NICE Publisher Correction (DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-51289-7, 12 Aug 2024) was purely clerical: it restored a truncated abstract sentence adding the registration number. Do not imply a substantive erratum.
