### 票 2(CORRECTED)

My WebSearch budget was exhausted before I began, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against primary documents and structured APIs (PMC, the Europe PMC REST/fullTextXML endpoints, and the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API), which turned out to be an advantage: JATS XML gives literal element text rather than a summarizer's gloss. Because a previous run of this pipeline caught a fetch summarizer fabricating quotes, I treated single-source quotes as provisional and pulled every load-bearing string from two independent renderings.

Double-sourced and confirmed character-for-character: the Martens 2018 acknowledgement ("Study pills, NR standards for metabolite analyses and partial funding support were provided by ChromaDex, Inc.") against its competing-interests line ("The authors declare no competing interests"), via PMC5876407 HTML and the Europe PMC fullTextXML; and the NICE MCID sentence ("In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters"), via the same two routes. Single-sourced but from primary full text: the Trammell 2016 competing-interests block, the NICE one-sided p<0.10 statement, the 17.6 m result with its one-sided 90% CI, the NR-SAFE ChromaDex sourcing sentence, and the Norheim 2024 Elysium statements. nature.com is behind an IdP redirect and cell.com returned 403, so Nature-hosted and Cell-hosted copies were unreachable; PMC mirrors covered everything except NADPARK (no PMCID, full text unavailable) and the 2026 Friedreich's ataxia trial (PMC record returned only front matter, XML 404).

The two named COI claims survive intact, and the Martens 2018 juxtaposition is the group's strongest item - I checked for a correction or erratum and found none, so it stands uncorrected in the literature. The NICE statistical claims also survive verbatim. What does not survive is the universal quantifier. Fetching the COPD trial produced a clean counterexample: a landmark NR trial funded and supplied by Elysium Health with no ChromaDex involvement whatsoever, sitting atop a whole Elysium-sponsored NR+pterostilbene trial family. The article's underlying thesis - that the NR evidence base is structurally non-independent - is if anything strengthened by this, since Elysium is also an NR seller; but the specific "ChromaDex" framing is factually wrong and would be easy for a critic to knock down.

On the load-bearing absence I found the thing the claim did not anticipate: NOPARK, a completed phase 3 trial with 410 actual participants, sponsored by a Norwegian public hospital with no commercial collaborator in the registry, finished 17 June 2025. It is roughly 4.5x the NICE trial and the largest NR RCT ever run. I could find no published results anywhere as of today, so the absence should be restated as "none has reported" rather than "none exists." I deliberately did NOT infer NOPARK's drug sourcing from the sister NR-SAFE trial's explicit ChromaDex donation, even though that inference is probably correct - that sub-fact is marked unreachable and needs rechecking when NOPARK publishes. Two smaller caliber errors also turned up in passing: the "+/- resveratrol" phrasing hides a null arm, and the 20 m figure is the paper's LARGE MCID, not the minimal one, so the article as drafted understates the result it is trying to criticize while using a number that a careful reader can refute.

- **Trammell 2016 (Nat Commun 7:12948, PMC5062546) carries ChromaDex money and author equity** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from the PMC full text. Acknowledgements: "This study was supported by grants from the Roy J. Carver Trust, ChromaDex and National Institutes of Health (R21-AA022371) to C.B." Competing financial interests: "F.J., R.W.D. and C.B. own stock in ChromaDex, the supplier of NR and sponsor of the clinical study. F.J. and R.W.D. are employees of ChromaDex. M.E.M. has received research grants and serves as a consultant for ChromaDex. C.B. has received a research grant and serves on the scientific advisory board of ChromaDex... C.B. is the chief scientific adviser of ProHealthspan, which sells NR supplements." So money, product, employees, equity and advisory ties are all present and openly declared. Note the article should not imply concealment here: Trammell 2016 disclosed fully.

- **Martens 2018 declares "The authors declare no competing interests" in the same document that discloses ChromaDex supplied study pills, standards and partial funding** — `confirmed`
  This is the strongest item in the group and it checks out exactly. Verified from TWO independent renderings of the primary document (PMC HTML at PMC5876407 and the Europe PMC JATS fullTextXML), which agree character-for-character. Acknowledgements end: "This work was supported by NIH grants AG000279 and TR001082 and was completed while C.R.M. was a Glenn/AFAR Postdoctoral Fellow. Study pills, NR standards for metabolite analyses and partial funding support were provided by ChromaDex, Inc." Competing interests section reads in full: "The authors declare no competing interests." I searched for a correction, erratum, addendum or retraction to this paper and found none as of 2026-07, so the contradiction stands uncorrected in the literature.

- **NICE trial pre-specified a one-sided p<0.10 threshold** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim in the primary paper (McDermott MM et al., Nat Commun 2024;15:5040, doi 10.1038/s41467-024-49092-5, PMC11176364): "The a priori statistical analysis plan defined a one-sided P value of <0.10 to define statistical significance." Also verbatim: "One-sided 90% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for between group differences" and "Because the clinical trial was a Phase II trial, to help ensure that a true beneficial effect of the interventions was not dismissed due to lack of statistical significance, the pre-specified P value for statistical significance was more liberal than a P value of <0.05." The authors are transparent about this; it was pre-specified, not chosen after the fact.

- **NICE trial n=90, 6 months, effect of +17.6 m on 6-minute walk in the intention-to-treat analysis** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: "Compared to placebo, NR improved 6-min walk by 17.6 meters (90% CI: + 1.77, +∞, P = 0.08) at 6-month follow-up, meeting the pre-specified criterion for statistical significance." And: "Ninety participants were randomized and 89 (98.9%) completed 6-month follow-up." Primary outcome verbatim: "The primary outcome was 6-month change in 6-min walk distance." One caliber caveat: the paper never uses the phrase "intention-to-treat"; the closest verbatim wording is "Pre-specified analyses were performed according to each participant's assigned group, irrespective of pill adherence." That is ITT in substance, so the article's label is fair, but it is the article's word, not the paper's. Also note the interval quoted is a ONE-SIDED 90% CI (+1.77, +infinity), not a conventional two-sided 95% CI.

- **The positive NICE result was for "NR 1,000 mg +/- resveratrol"** — `corrected`
  WRONG as written: the "+/- resveratrol" formulation implies both active arms were positive. RIGHT: only the NR-alone arm met the threshold (+17.6 m, P = 0.08). The NR + resveratrol arm was null, verbatim: "Compared to placebo, NR+ resveratrol did not significantly improve 6-min walk at 6-month follow-up (+3.65 meters (90% CI:-11.2, +infinity, P = 0.38))". The trial randomized three arms, verbatim: "nicotinamide riboside 1,000 mg daily, nicotinamide riboside 1000 mg + 125 mgs resveratrol daily, or placebo." The article must say NR alone was positive and the resveratrol co-arm failed.

- **+17.6 m is "below the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important"** — `corrected`
  WRONG as written: it misrepresents 20 m as the minimal important difference. RIGHT, per the NICE paper's own verbatim sentence (confirmed from two renderings, the Europe PMC XML and the PMC HTML): "In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters." So 17.6 m sits BETWEEN the small MCID (~8 m, which it exceeds) and the large MCID (20 m, which it misses) - the paper accordingly calls it "consistent with a clinically meaningful effect." A far stronger and fully defensible version of the article's point is the power calculation: verbatim, "Ninety participants provided more than 80% power to detect a 30-meter difference between NR + resveratrol and placebo and between NR alone and placebo at follow-up" and "30 participants randomized per group provided 80% power to detect a difference of 0.58 standard deviation (SD) of change in 6-min walk distance at a one-sided significance level of 0.10 based on a two-sample t-test." The observed 17.6 m is well under the 30 m the trial was designed to detect.

- **EVERY large or landmark NR human trial carries ChromaDex money, product, or an author with ChromaDex equity/advisory ties** — `refuted`
  The universal quantifier is false. Counterexample reached in primary text: Norheim KL et al., "Effect of nicotinamide riboside on airway inflammation in COPD," Nature Aging 2024 (PMID 39548320, PMC11645284), n=40, 2 g NR for 6 weeks. Verbatim acknowledgement: "Elysium Health (New York) provided the NR and placebo capsules and funded and carried out the DNA methylation analyses." Verbatim competing interests: "D.S. and R.W.D. are employees of Elysium Health and own shares in the company. The other authors declare no competing interests." Its public funding is Novo Nordisk Foundation, Nordea, Lundbeck, etc. - no ChromaDex link at all. A whole family of NR trials is Elysium-linked rather than ChromaDex-linked (the NR+pterostilbene / "Basis" trials: Simic 2020 BMC Nephrol, Jensen 2022 JCI Insight, Dellinger 2023 Hepatology). Sharp detail the article can use: R. W. Dellinger appears as a ChromaDex employee-shareholder in Trammell 2016 and as an Elysium Health employee-shareholder in Norheim 2024. The defensible claim is COMMERCIAL NAD-precursor sponsorship (ChromaDex OR Elysium), not ChromaDex specifically.

- **No large independent (non-ChromaDex-linked) NR trial exists - the load-bearing absence** — `corrected`
  Overstated. NOPARK exists: NCT03568968, "A Randomized Controlled Trial of Nicotinamide Riboside Supplementation in Early Parkinson's Disease: the NOPARK Study," phase 3, ENROLLMENT 410 ACTUAL, NR 500 mg twice daily vs placebo for 52 weeks, primary outcome MDS-UPDRS total score, lead sponsor Haukeland University Hospital (sponsor class OTHER), collaborators all Norwegian public hospitals, status Completed, completion date 17 June 2025. I searched the registry record for "ChromaDex"/"Niagen"/"Elysium" and found NO commercial supplier or industry collaborator listed. This is roughly 4.5x the size of the NICE trial and is the largest NR RCT ever run. TWO honest caveats that keep the article's point alive: (1) results are not published or indexed anywhere I could find as of 2026-07-28, so the absence is really "no large independent trial has REPORTED," not "none exists"; (2) the same Bergen group's NR-SAFE trial (Nat Commun 2023, PMC10684646) states verbatim "The study drug nicotinamide riboside chloride (NR; Tru Niagen) and placebo were provided by ChromaDex, USA" and "We are grateful to ChromaDex (Irvine, California) for providing the NR and placebo capsules for the study," so NOPARK very likely received ChromaDex product too - but I could NOT verify NOPARK's drug sourcing from any primary document, so I mark that specific sub-fact unverified rather than assume it. Note also that this group is not disinterested: NR-SAFE's competing interests declare pending patents PCT/EP2022/067408, PCT/EP2022/067412 and PCT/EP2023/060962 on NR as a Parkinson's treatment with C.T. and C.D. as inventors.

- **NOPARK's nicotinamide riboside supplier / whether ChromaDex donated product** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach any primary document stating who supplied the NR and placebo for NOPARK. The ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT03568968) names no commercial supplier, results are not posted (hasResults false), and no results publication is indexed in Europe PMC as of 2026-07-28. I am explicitly NOT filling this gap from memory or from the sister trial. If the article rests weight on NOPARK, this must be checked again once NOPARK publishes.

  Pattern holds broadly even where the specific sponsor differs. Szarvas Z et al., J Pharmacol Exp Ther 2025 (PMC13095416), NR in PAD, is NOT ChromaDex-linked (no ChromaDex or Niagen mention; NIH/AHA/Hevolution funded) but had only 8 participants and its COI still discloses industry NAD ties: "Joseph A. Baur has received research funding and materials from Pfizer, Elysium Health, and Metro International Biotech and consulting fees from Pfizer, Elysium Health, Cytokinetics, and Altimmune. ### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Web search quota was exhausted at the start of this session, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against primary sources: PMC full texts, the Europe PMC REST search and full-text-XML endpoints, PubMed records, and the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API. To guard against the fabricated-quote failure mode, I verified the load-bearing Martens 2018 strings through two independent endpoints (the PMC HTML article and the Europe PMC full-text XML for PMC5876407) and got byte-identical text both times; the NICE numbers I pulled in three separate passes over PMC11176364 plus the Europe PMC core record and the PubMed abstract, and they agree.

What I reached verbatim: Martens 2018 acknowledgements and competing-interests sentences; Trammell 2016 acknowledgements and the full competing-financial-interests paragraph; the NICE trial's statistical-analysis sentence ("The a priori statistical analysis plan defined a one-sided P value of <0.10 to define statistical significance"), its power calculation, its primary ITT result (+17.6 m, 90% CI +1.77 to +infinity, P=0.08), its dosing (two 250 mg NR pills twice daily = 1,000 mg/day, plus 125 mg resveratrol), its arm sizes (28/33/29), its manufacturer sentence (ChromaDex for NR, ReserveAge for resveratrol), its funding line, its COI statement, and every occurrence of MCID/clinically meaningful in the paper; the Conze/Brenner/Kruger 2019 n=140 competing-interests paragraph; the Dellinger 2017 Elysium funding, supply and equity statements; the Norheim 2024 COI; the Christen 2026 Nestlé COI and NR product identity; the Lin 2025 GeroScience funding, COI and Niagen Bioscience supply sentences; the NADPARK COI; and the full CT.gov record for NOPARK.

Three of the four sub-claims survive intact. Martens 2018 is exactly as described — the "no competing interests" line and the ChromaDex supply/funding line sit in the same paper. The NICE one-sided p<0.10 pre-specification and the +17.6 m ITT effect are verbatim correct. What fails is the MCID gloss: the paper itself puts the small MCID at ~8 m and 20 m as the LARGE MCID, so calling 20 m "the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important" inverts the source and overstates the shortfall. The universality claim also fails as literally written: Dellinger 2017 (n=120, Elysium-funded, all-Elysium equity), Norheim 2024 and Christen 2026 are NR trials with no ChromaDex money or authorship. The underlying thesis — that the NR base is sponsor-saturated — survives and is arguably stronger once Elysium and Nestlé are folded in, and once you note that even the null Danish trial has Brenner on it.

Two things I want the article to treat as uncertain. First, I could not reach the printed disclosure text of Dollerup 2018 (OUP 404, Elsevier 403, no PMC deposit); I verified only its author list and funders, so nothing from that paper's disclosure should be quoted. Second, the "no large independent trial" absence is real today but fragile: NOPARK, n=410, Phase 3, publicly funded across eleven Norwegian centres, completed 17 June 2025, is unpublished as of 28 July 2026 across every index I searched. That is a sentence with a fuse on it, and I could not determine whether ChromaDex donated NOPARK's study drug — the CT.gov record is silent and I did not retrieve the NADPARK supply sentence, so the Bergen group's NR sourcing remains an open question that could change how that trial counts when it reports.

- **Martens 2018 declares "The authors declare no competing interests" in the same document that discloses ChromaDex supplied study pills, standards and partial funding** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim twice via two independent endpoints (PMC HTML article PMC5876407 and the Europe PMC full-text XML for the same PMCID), which returned identical strings. Acknowledgements, final sentence: "Study pills, NR standards for metabolite analyses and partial funding support were provided by ChromaDex, Inc." Competing-interests section, in full: "The authors declare no competing interests." Paper: Martens CR, Denman BA, Mazzo MR, Armstrong ML, Reisdorph N, McQueen MB, Chonchol M, Seals DR, "Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD+ in healthy middle-aged and older adults", Nat Commun 2018 (NCT02921659; CT.gov lists ChromaDex, Inc. as collaborator, enrollment 30). The claim is exact.

- **Trammell 2016 carries ChromaDex money/equity/advisory ties** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim from PMC5062546 (Trammell et al., "Nicotinamide riboside is uniquely and orally bioavailable in mice and humans", Nat Commun 2016). Competing Financial Interests, verbatim: "F.J., R.W.D. and C.B. own stock in ChromaDex, the supplier of NR and sponsor of the clinical study. F.J. and R.W.D. are employees of ChromaDex. M.E.M. has received research grants and serves as a consultant for ChromaDex. C.B. has received a research grant and serves on the scientific advisory board of ChromaDex. S.A.J.T. and C.B. have an intellectual property interest in detecting NAAD as a biomarker of elevated NAD metabolism. C.B. is the chief scientific adviser of ProHealthspan, which sells NR supplements." Acknowledgements, verbatim: "This study was supported by grants from the Roy J. Carver Trust, ChromaDex and National Institutes of Health (R21-AA022371) to C.B. ... We thank Dale Wilson and staff at KGK Synergize, Inc. (London, Ontario, Canada) for conducting the n=12 clinical study." Note this trial declares its ties openly — unlike Martens 2018 — so it is an example of disclosure, not of concealment; do not lump the two under the same rhetorical point.

- **NICE trial: n=90, PAD, 6 months, NR 1,000 mg +/- resveratrol** — `confirmed`
  Verified from PMC11176364 (McDermott MM et al., "Nicotinamide riboside for peripheral artery disease: the NICE randomized clinical trial", Nat Commun 2024;15:5046, NCT03743636). Dosing verbatim: "Participants were asked to take five pills daily: Two 250 mgs of NR (or placebo) pills twice daily and one 125 mg resveratrol (or placebo) once daily." That is 1,000 mg/day NR — correct. Ninety randomized, but NOT 30/30/30: NR alone N=28, NR+resveratrol N=33, placebo N=29. "NR (250 mg pills) and matching placebo were manufactured by ChromaDex. Resveratrol capsules (125 mgs of 98% pure trans-resveratrol) and matching placebo were manufactured by ReserveAge." Funding: American Heart Association SFRN grants 18SFRN33900097, 18SFRN33900136, 18SFRN33970010; "Nicotinamide riboside was provided by ChromaDex." So the ChromaDex-product link holds for NICE.

- **NICE was declared positive only against a pre-specified one-sided p<0.10 threshold** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim: "The a priori statistical analysis plan defined a one-sided P value of <0.10 to define statistical significance." and "One-sided 90% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for between group differences." Power calc verbatim: "Anticipating a 90% follow-up rate, 30 participants randomized per group provided 80% power to detect a difference of 0.58 standard deviation (SD) of change in 6-min walk distance at a one-sided significance level of 0.10 based on a two-sample t-test." Result verbatim: "Compared to placebo, NR improved 6-min walk by 17.6 meters (90% CI: + 1.77, +∞, P = 0.08) at 6-month follow-up, meeting the pre-specified criterion for statistical significance." P=0.08 one-sided corresponds to roughly p=0.16 two-sided, i.e. not significant at conventional 0.05 two-sided. The article's characterization is accurate.

- **NICE ITT effect of +17.6 m on the 6-minute walk** — `confirmed`
  Verified. Abstract verbatim: "NR significantly improved 6-min walk (+7.0 vs. -10.6 meters, between group difference: +17.6 (90% CI: + 1.8,+∞)". Body reports the same difference with CI lower bound +1.77 (the abstract rounds to +1.8). The 31.0 m and 26.9 m figures the article may be tempted to cite are described by the authors themselves as post-hoc: "In post-hoc analyses, compared to placebo, NR alone significantly improved 6-min walk by 31.0 meters and NR + resveratrol improved 6-min walk by 26.9 meters among people with at least 75% adherence to study pills."

- **+17.6 m is "below the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important"** — `corrected`
  WRONG version: that ~20 m is the MCID usually cited for 6-minute walk in PAD, so 17.6 m fell short of clinical importance. RIGHT version: the NICE paper itself states, verbatim in Methods, "In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters" (citing ref 18). So 20 m is the LARGE MCID; the small/standard MCID is ~8 m, which +17.6 m exceeds by more than double. The authors accordingly write in the Discussion, verbatim: "compared to placebo, NR improved 6-min walk distance by 17.6 meters at 6-month follow-up, consistent with a clinically meaningful effect". The honest criticism is not that 17.6 m is sub-MCID but that (a) it clears only the SMALL MCID, (b) the lower bound of the one-sided 90% CI is +1.77 m, i.e. the data are compatible with an effect well below even the 8 m small MCID, and (c) significance depended on a one-sided 0.10 threshold. Rewrite the sentence on those grounds, not on the 20 m claim.

- **NICE authors' COI statement** — `corrected`
  WRONG version (if the article implies NICE also said flatly "no competing interests"): the NICE statement is not a blanket denial. RIGHT version, verbatim: "Dr. McDermott reports research funding from Helixmith and other research support from ArtAssist, and Mars. The remaining authors report no competing interests." No ChromaDex relationship is disclosed under competing interests despite ChromaDex having manufactured and provided the study drug and placebo — that disclosure appears only in the funding line. Same structural pattern as Martens 2018, but the wording differs, so quote it correctly.

- **No large independent (non-ChromaDex-linked) NR trial exists** — `corrected`
  WRONG version: "Every large or landmark NR human trial carries ChromaDex/Niagen money, product, or an author with ChromaDex equity or advisory ties." RIGHT version: no large NR trial is free of NAD-supplement-industry sponsorship, but the sponsor is not always ChromaDex. Verified counterexamples: (1) Dellinger RW, Santos SR, Morris M, Evans M, Alminana D, Guarente L, Marcotulli E, npj Aging Mech Dis 2017 (PMC5701244), 120 randomized 1:1:1 to placebo / NRPT 1X / NRPT 2X — verbatim: "NRPT (commercially known as Basis) is a supplement marketed by Elysium Health, which funded the trial"; "The matched placebo pills and the investigational product (NRPT) were provided by Elysium Health (New York, NY)"; "R.W.D., S.R.S., M.M., D.A., L.G., and E.M. are all employees of Elysium Health and all own shares in the company." No ChromaDex link stated. (This is an NR+pterostilbene combination, and it is MORE conflicted, not less.) (2) Norheim KL et al., Nat Aging 2024 (PMID 39548320, NR in COPD, n=40) — verbatim COI: "D.S. and R.W.D. are employees of Elysium Health and own shares in the company. The other authors declare no competing interests." (3) Christen S et al., Nat Metab 2026 (PMC12855009, n=67 randomized, 14 days, four arms) — funded and run by Nestlé (all COI entries are Nestlé Research / Nestlé Health Science employees), no ChromaDex money or authors, though the product used was "NR (TRU NIAGEN Pro; daily dose of 1,000 mg, 3.4 mmol)", i.e. ChromaDex's branded material. Reframe the claim as industry-capture generally (ChromaDex/Niagen Bioscience plus Elysium plus Nestlé), with ChromaDex dominant, rather than ChromaDex-universal.

- **Whether a genuinely large, publicly funded, ChromaDex-free NR outcome trial exists as of 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  Holds, with an expiry date the article must flag. The largest published NR-only RCT I could find is Conze D, Brenner C, Kruger CL, Sci Rep 2019 (PMC6611812), n=140 randomized 35 per arm to placebo / 100 / 300 / 1000 mg NR per day — verbatim competing interests: "Claire Kruger and Dietrich Conze are employees of ChromaDex. Charles Brenner is the inventor of intellectual property licensed by ChromaDex and serves as their chief scientific adviser. ChromaDex funded the study." The one genuinely large, publicly funded, ChromaDex-independent trial is NOPARK (NCT03568968), "A Randomized Controlled Trial of Nicotinamide Riboside Supplementation in Early Parkinson's Disease: the NOPARK Study", lead sponsor Haukeland University Hospital with ten Norwegian hospital collaborators, actual enrollment 410, Phase 3, primary outcome MDS-UPDRS total, start 6 May 2020, primary completion 17 June 2025, status COMPLETED. As of 2026-07-28 I could find NO results publication: Europe PMC searches on "NOPARK" AND "nicotinamide riboside", on NR+Parkinson 2025-2026, and on all 2025-2026 publications by senior author Tzoulis C (20 records) return no phase 3 NR-in-PD trial. The article should therefore say "as of July 2026 no large independent NR outcome trial has REPORTED", and should name NOPARK (n=410, completed June 2025) as the pending test — otherwise the sentence will be falsified without warning.

- **Dollerup 2018 AJCN as a nominally independent European NR trial** — `corrected`
  Not in the claim as written, but load-bearing for the independence argument, so flagging. WRONG assumption a reader might make: the Danish trial (Dollerup OL et al., "A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial of nicotinamide riboside in obese men: safety, insulin-sensitivity, and lipid-mobilizing effects", Am J Clin Nutr 2018;108(2):343-353, PMID 29992272, NCT02303483, n=40, 2000 mg/d for 12 weeks, funded by Novo Nordisk Foundation and the Danish Council for Independent Research) is a fully independent negative trial. RIGHT version: its author list, verified via the Europe PMC core record, includes Charles Brenner — i.e. even this nominally independent, publicly funded, NULL-result trial has a ChromaDex-equity/advisory author. That is a stronger version of the article's point than the one currently made, and it comes attached to a NEGATIVE result, which blunts the "sponsorship buys positive findings" reading.

- **Verbatim COI/disclosure text of Dollerup 2018 AJCN** — `unreachable`
  Could not reach. The OUP URL (academic.oup.com/ajcn/article/108/2/343/5051352) returns 404 and the DOI now redirects to Elsevier (linkinghub/sciencedirect PII S0002916522029409), which returned 403 Forbidden; no PMC deposit exists. I verified the author list (Brenner is a co-author) and the funders from the Europe PMC core record, but I did NOT see the printed author-disclosure sentence. Do not quote it.

- **Whether the NICE result has been corrected, retracted or superseded** — `confirmed`
  A Publisher Correction exists — McDermott MM et al., Nat Commun 2024;15:6890, PMID 39134546, PMCID PMC11319328, DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-51289-7 — but it is cosmetic: it restores the trial registration "Clinical Trials.gov registration: NCT03743636" that had been truncated from the abstract. No numbers, endpoints or disclosures were changed. I found no erratum, retraction, critical correspondence or failed replication touching the 17.6 m figure, and no larger NR PAD trial. Note NCT06534944 ("NAD Supplementation and Vascular Health in PAD", University of Oklahoma, n=8, Phase 1/2) is the only other PAD-NR record and is far too small to supersede. The article should cite the corrected version and include the NCT number.

**修正:**
- Fix the MCID sentence. The NICE paper states verbatim: "In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters." 20 m is the LARGE MCID, not the ordinary minimally-important difference, and +17.6 m is more than twice the ~8 m small MCID. Delete "below the ~20 m usually cited as minimally clinically important." Replace with the defensible criticism: the effect cleared only the small MCID, and the one-sided 90% CI runs from +1.77 m to infinity, so the data remain compatible with an effect far below even the 8 m small MCID.
- Do not say the NICE authors declared no competing interests. The exact statement is: "Dr. McDermott reports research funding from Helixmith and other research support from ArtAssist, and Mars. The remaining authors report no competing interests." The point to make is narrower and still valid: no ChromaDex relationship appears under competing interests even though ChromaDex manufactured and supplied the drug and placebo; that fact surfaces only in the funding line, "Nicotinamide riboside was provided by ChromaDex."
- Weaken "every large or landmark NR human trial carries ChromaDex money, product, or an author with ChromaDex equity or advisory ties" to an industry-capture claim rather than a ChromaDex-universal claim. Verified counterexample: Dellinger et al., npj Aging Mech Dis 2017, 120 participants randomized 1:1:1 to placebo / NRPT 1X / NRPT 2X, funded by Elysium Health, product supplied by Elysium Health, and all six industry authors are Elysium employees and shareholders — no ChromaDex link. Same for Norheim et al., Nat Aging 2024 (COPD, n=40; two authors are Elysium employees and shareholders) and Christen et al., Nat Metab 2026 (n=67, entirely Nestlé-staffed, though it used ChromaDex's TRU NIAGEN Pro product). Accurate framing: the NR trial base is sponsored end to end by NAD-supplement sellers — ChromaDex/Niagen Bioscience overwhelmingly, with Elysium and Nestlé filling the remainder — and no large trial is free of all of them.
- Add an expiry date to the "no large independent trial" sentence and name the pending trial. NOPARK (NCT03568968), "A Randomized Controlled Trial of Nicotinamide Riboside Supplementation in Early Parkinson's Disease", lead sponsor Haukeland University Hospital with ten Norwegian public hospital collaborators, actual enrollment 410, Phase 3, primary outcome MDS-UPDRS total, completed 17 June 2025, has no results publication indexed in PubMed or Europe PMC as of 28 July 2026. Write "as of mid-2026 no large independent NR trial has reported" and flag NOPARK as the imminent test, or the sentence will be falsified on publication.
- State the size ceiling of the field explicitly, since it is the strongest form of the argument: the largest published NR-only RCT is Conze, Brenner & Kruger, Sci Rep 2019, n=140 (35 per arm, placebo / 100 / 300 / 1000 mg/day), whose competing-interests statement reads verbatim: "Claire Kruger and Dietrich Conze are employees of ChromaDex. Charles Brenner is the inventor of intellectual property licensed by ChromaDex and serves as their chief scientific adviser. ChromaDex funded the study." A field whose biggest trial is a 140-person, 8-week, sponsor-run safety study is the point.
- Correct the NICE arm sizes if the article states them: randomization was not balanced. NR alone N=28, NR + resveratrol N=33, placebo N=29, total 90. The 30-per-group figure appears only in the power calculation, which assumed "30 participants randomized per group provided 80% power to detect a difference of 0.58 standard deviation."
- If the article cites the 31.0 m adherent-subgroup figure, label it as the authors do: "In post-hoc analyses ... among people with at least 75% adherence to study pills." It is not a pre-specified per-protocol analysis.
- Cite the corrected NICE record and include the registration number NCT03743636. A Publisher Correction (Nat Commun 2024;15:6890, PMID 39134546) restored that registration line to the truncated abstract; nothing substantive changed, so the correction does not undermine the trial, but the article should reference the corrected version.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Dellinger RW, Santos SR, Morris M, Evans M, Alminana D, Guarente L, Marcotulli E, npj Aging and Mechanisms of Disease 2017 (PMCID PMC5701244): 120 participants randomized 1:1:1, verbatim "NRPT (commercially known as Basis) is a supplement marketed by Elysium Health, which funded the trial", "The matched placebo pills and the investigational product (NRPT) were provided by Elysium Health (New York, NY)", and "R.W.D., S.R.S., M.M., D.A., L.G., and E.M. are all employees of Elysium Health and all own shares in the company." A large NR-containing trial with no ChromaDex money, product or authors — contradicting the literal universality of the ChromaDex claim.
- Norheim KL et al., Nature Aging 2024 (PMID 39548320, PMCID PMC11645284), NR in stable COPD, n=40: verbatim COI "D.S. and R.W.D. are employees of Elysium Health and own shares in the company. The other authors declare no competing interests." Again Elysium, not ChromaDex.
- Christen S et al., Nature Metabolism 2026 (PMCID PMC12855009), 67 randomized to NR (n=17), NMN (n=15), nicotinamide (n=17), placebo (n=18) for 14 days: every conflicted author is a Nestlé Research or Nestlé Health Science employee, with no ChromaDex funding or authorship, although the NR used was "NR (TRU NIAGEN Pro; daily dose of 1,000 mg, 3.4 mmol)".
- The NICE paper's own MCID sentence contradicts the article's 20 m framing: "In PAD, a small minimum clinically important difference (MCID) was defined as ~8 meters and a large MCID as 20 meters."
- NOPARK (NCT03568968), enrollment 410, Phase 3, lead sponsor Haukeland University Hospital with ten Norwegian public hospital collaborators, no industry collaborator listed, status COMPLETED with primary completion 17 June 2025 — a large, publicly funded, ChromaDex-independent NR trial that exists and has finished, even though its results are not yet published. The absence the article leans on is an absence of published results, not an absence of trials.
- Dollerup OL et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2018;108(2):343-353 (n=40, Novo Nordisk Foundation and Danish Council for Independent Research funded) lists Charles Brenner as a co-author yet reported a fully null result: "12 wk of NR supplementation in doses of 2000 mg/d appears safe, but does not improve insulin sensitivity and whole-body glucose metabolism in obese, insulin-resistant men." ChromaDex-linked authorship did not produce a positive finding here, which cuts against a simple sponsorship-bias reading.

## V23 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

Primary documents reached and read directly: (1) the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 record for NCT00427193 — identification, design, outcomes, participant-flow and outcome-measures results modules, fetched four separate times with different framings to guard against summarizer error; (2) Ravussin et al. 2015, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci, full text at PMC4841173 — abstract reproduced verbatim, Methods definition of 'RMR residual', Results sentences, Figure 3 legend, and Table 1 rows with column headers; (3) Kraus et al. 2019, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, abstract via PubMed 31303390; (4) Waziry et al. 2023, Nature Aging, full text at PMC10148951; (5) the Waziry Author Correction at PMC10275750; (6) Europe PMC REST search for CALERIE errata/corrections/reanalyses.

Every verbatim string I have quoted was returned to me inside a reproduction of the source text, and the load-bearing ones were confirmed across at least two independent retrievals. The single most important finding came from cross-checking two different documents against each other rather than trusting either alone: the four numbers ClinicalTrials.gov publishes as the 'RMR Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' primary outcome (-83/-1 at 12 mo, -71/-7 at 24 mo) are exactly the raw 'RMR, kcal/d' row of Table 1 in Ravussin 2015. That identity is what exposes the registry posting as unadjusted data under an adjusted-sounding title, and it is what rescues the article's thesis from a registry record that otherwise flatly contradicts it. I read the registry outcome block three times with different prompts before relying on it, because a misread multi-column table here would have inverted the verdict.

Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS because of one real overstatement and one real omission. The overstatement: 'failed BOTH registered primary endpoints' is not what the record shows — the RMR endpoint was met at 12 months (p=.04) and there are four registered primary outcome measures, not two. The omission: the 11.7% mean is a two-year average over 19.5% (months 0-6) and 9.1% (months 7-24), which the article should state. Everything else in the group survived: the registry outcome titles, the p=.04-then-null RMR residual pattern, the verbatim phrase 'differed little between groups', 11.7±0.7% SE and 11.9% (SE 0.7), 'under half the target', the 'exploratory outcomes' title, 2:1 randomisation, and the 2-year duration. The N question is fully resolved (238 assessed / 220 randomized / 218 started and analysed) and the apparent 218-vs-220 conflict is an artifact of Ravussin and Kraus both loosely calling the 218 starters 'randomized'.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: I could not verify the uniqueness qualifier 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans'. My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task, so I worked entirely through direct WebFetch on known URLs and the Europe PMC REST API. That was sufficient for every documentary check, but not for the exhaustive literature sweep a universal negative requires, and no CALERIE document asserts the exclusivity itself. I have marked it unreachable rather than guessing. I also could not retrieve the registry's version history, so I verified the primary outcomes as they stand in the current record and corroborated them against the paper's own prespecification sentence rather than against the original 2007 registration.

- **(a) Registered primary outcomes were change in core body temperature and change in RMR corrected for body composition, at 12 and 24 months** — `confirmed`
  Verified against the ClinicalTrials.gov API record for NCT00427193 (read twice, independently). The registry lists FOUR primary outcome measures, verbatim: 'Change in Core Body Temperature, Baseline to 12 Months'; 'Change in Core Temperature, Baseline to 24 Months'; 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition, Baseline to 12 Months'; and 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' (timeFrame 'Baseline, 24 months'). All four carry type=PRIMARY. Ravussin 2015 agrees: 'The two prespecified primary outcomes were selected to test the hypothesis that CR would induce metabolic adaptations, specifically (a) decrease in resting metabolic rate (RMR) adjusted for changes in body composition and (b) decrease in core body temperature.' Caveat worth noting: the paper's own ABSTRACT describes the endpoint as 'resting metabolic rate adjusted for weight change ("RMR residual")' while its Methods say 'adjusted for changes in body composition' — the paper is internally inconsistent on the adjustment. Say 'two prespecified primary outcomes, each assessed at 12 and 24 months' rather than implying two registry entries.

- **(b) RMR residual decreased more in CR at 12 months (p=0.04) but NOT at 24 months** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the Ravussin 2015 abstract (PMC4841173): 'RMR residual decreased significantly more in CR than AL at 12 months (p = .04) but not 24 months (M24).' Results section, verbatim: 'RMR residual decreased significantly more in CR compared with AL at 12 months (48±9 vs 14±12 kcal/d in AL, p = .04)' and 'decreases did not differ significantly between CR and AL at 24 months.' No p-value is printed for the 24-month residual comparison — do not invent one. Methods define the endpoint verbatim: 'Change in RMR was defined as "RMR residual," that is, the difference between an individual's RMR measured by indirect calorimetry during the intervention and RMR predicted from a regression of RMR as a function of fat mass and fat-free mass in participants at baseline.'

- **(b) Core temperature 'differed little between groups' — i.e. null** — `confirmed`
  The quoted phrase is real and I saw the exact string. Ravussin 2015 abstract, verbatim: 'Core temperature change differed little between groups.' Note the sentence subject is 'Core temperature CHANGE', not 'core temperature' — quote it in full. Corroborated by hard numbers from two independent documents. Table 1 of the paper: 24-h core temperature, delta Month 12, AL -0.03 (0.02) vs CR -0.05 (0.02), between-group p=.70; delta Month 24, AL -0.02 (0.02) vs CR -0.05 (0.02), between-group p=.84. The registry's own posted results match exactly: 12-month p=0.70 (two-sided, 95% CI, difference in mean change 0.02 [-0.019, 0.059]); 24-month p=0.84 (mean net difference 0.03 [-0.0092, 0.069]). The core-temperature endpoint is unambiguously null at both timepoints, by both the paper and the registry.

- **(b) The trial 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints'** — `corrected`
  WRONG as stated. RIGHT: it failed the core-temperature endpoint at both 12 and 24 months, and failed the RMR endpoint at 24 months — but the RMR endpoint WAS met at 12 months (p=.04), which is one of the four registered primary outcome measures. 'Failed both primary endpoints' asserts 0 for 4 (or 0 for 2); the actual record is 1 hit out of 4 registered primary outcome measures, and that one hit was a marginal p=.04 that did not persist. Correct framing: 'neither primary endpoint held at 24 months; core temperature was null throughout, and the RMR effect was significant only at 12 months and had dissipated by 24.'

- **ClinicalTrials.gov POSTED RESULTS for the RMR primary outcome directly contradict the 'failed' framing** — `corrected`
  This is the biggest exposure in the claim group and the article must pre-empt it. The registry's posted results for the primary outcome titled 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' report: 12 months, CR -83 (10) vs AL -1 (13), p<0.001, mixed models, two-sided, 95% CI, net difference -82 [-103.8, -60.2]; 24 months, CR -71 (12) vs AL -7 (16), p<0.0001, net difference -64 [-90.5, -37.5]. Read off the registry alone, the RMR primary endpoint was met overwhelmingly at BOTH timepoints. RESOLUTION (I verified this by matching against Table 1 of Ravussin 2015): those four numbers -83/-1 and -71/-7 are character-for-character the RAW, UNADJUSTED 'RMR, kcal/d' row of Table 1 (delta M12: AL -1 (13), CR -83 (10), between-group p<.001; delta M24: AL -7 (16), CR -71 (12), between-group p<.001). So ClinicalTrials.gov posted the UNADJUSTED RMR change under an outcome title that claims correction for body composition. The body-composition-adjusted analysis — the actual prespecified endpoint, the 'RMR residual' in Figure 3 — is the one that is null at 24 months. Also note the registry tags the dispersion as 'Standard Deviation' when these are plainly standard errors. Any reader who checks the registry will think the article is wrong unless this mislabelling is stated explicitly.

- **(c) Achieved restriction 11.7 +/- 0.7% (Ravussin 2015)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the Ravussin 2015 abstract: 'The CR group achieved 11.7±0.7 %CR (mean ± standard error) and maintained 10.4±0.4% weight loss.' The ± is a STANDARD ERROR, not SD — the paper says so in-line, so write 'SE' explicitly. Measured by the intake-balance method with doubly labeled water plus body-composition change.

- **(c) The 11.7% two-year mean conceals a large front-loading** — `corrected`
  Missing qualifier that materially changes the reading. Ravussin 2015 Results, verbatim: 'resulting in CR averaging 11.7±0.7 %CR (19.5±0.8% during the first 6 months and 9.1±0.7% on average for the remainder of the study)'. So the trial did NOT deliver a flat ~12% for two years: it delivered ~19.5% for the first 6 months and ~9.1% for the remaining 18. The sentence 'Every effect attributed to 25% CR in humans was produced by about 12%' is directionally right but should acknowledge the dose declined over time — for the 24-month endpoints the operative dose was closer to 9%, which strengthens rather than weakens the argument. Waziry 2023 adds, verbatim: 'the %CR achieved by participants in the treatment group varied, with most participants achieving doses below the prescribed 25% (mean = 11.9, s.e.m. = 0.7%)'.

- **(c) Achieved restriction 11.9 +/- 0.7% (Kraus 2019); under half the 25% target** — `confirmed`
  Kraus 2019 abstract, verbatim: 'Individuals in the calorie restriction group achieved a mean reduction in calorie intake of 11·9% (SE 0·7; from 2467 kcal to 2170 kcal).' Note the paper writes '(SE 0·7)', not '±0.7' — prefer the paper's own notation. 'Under half the target' checks out arithmetically: 11.7/25 = 46.8%, 11.9/25 = 47.6%. The 11.7 vs 11.9 gap is real and reflects different derivations (Ravussin: %CR by intake-balance/DLW; Kraus: mean reduction in calorie intake) — attribute each figure to its own paper rather than presenting them as a discrepancy.

- **(d) Cardiometabolic results are labelled 'exploratory outcomes' in the paper's own title; N=218, 2:1, 2 years** — `confirmed`
  Title verbatim (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, 2019 Sep; PMID 31303390): '2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial.' The word 'exploratory' is in the title, and the Methods repeat it: 'Exploratory cardiometabolic risk factor responses to a prescribed 25% calorie restriction diet for 2 years were evaluated... analysed in the intention-to-treat population.' Findings verbatim: 'of 238 participants that were assessed, 218 were randomly assigned to and started a 25% calorie restriction diet (n=143, 66%) or an ad libitum control diet (n=75, 34%)'. Randomisation 2:1 confirmed. One small caliber point: the title reads 'cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE)', not 'cardiometabolic results' — if you paraphrase the title, do not put it in quotation marks.

- **Adjudication of N: 218 vs 220 vs 238** — `confirmed`
  Fully resolved from the registry participant-flow module, verbatim: '238 Participants were eligible, 18 participants withdrew prior to randomization, 220 participants were randomized to the study, and 2 participants withdrew prior to initiating the intervention.' So: 238 = assessed/eligible, and this is what ClinicalTrials.gov records as 'Enrollment: 238 (ACTUAL)'. 220 = randomized — Waziry 2023 verbatim: 'Of 238 eligible individuals, CALERIE randomized N = 220 participants (145 CR intervention and 75 AL control'. 218 = started the intervention and the ITT analysis population — registry participant flow shows STARTED 143 CR / 75 AL, COMPLETED 117 CR / 71 AL, and baseline analysis population 218 (143 + 75). CAUTION for the article: both Ravussin 2015 ('218 persons were randomized') and Kraus 2019 ('218 were randomly assigned to and started') describe 218 as randomized, which is loose — 220 were randomized and 2 CR participants withdrew before starting. Waziry's 220 is not an inconsistency with 218; it is the correct randomized count. Waziry's own analytic sample is smaller still: 'Blood DNAm data were generated at baseline and at least one follow-up timepoint for n = 197 participants (128 CR and 69 AL)'.

- **CALERIE-2 is 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans'** — `unreachable`
  I could not test this universal negative. My WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before I could run the literature sweep needed to rule out other long-term randomized CR trials in healthy non-obese adults, and a universal 'only' cannot be established from the CALERIE documents themselves — none of them make that claim in the text I read. Nothing I found contradicts it, and CALERIE-2 is plainly the largest and longest such trial, but 'only' is unverified. Recommend hedging to a claim that IS documented ('the only two-year randomized trial of caloric restriction in healthy non-obese humans' or 'the largest and longest') unless another verifier reaches a source that states the exclusivity.

- **Search for corrections, errata, failed replications superseding these numbers up to 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  No erratum or correction to Ravussin 2015 or Kraus 2019 was found in the Europe PMC index. The one CALERIE correction that exists is 'Author Correction: Effect of long-term caloric restriction on DNA methylation measures of biological aging in healthy adults from the CALERIE trial' (Nature Aging 2023, PMID 37161091) — and it is trivial: it corrects D. W. Belsky's first affiliation to 'Butler Columbia Aging Center, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, New York, NY, USA.' It does NOT touch any result. Do not cite it as a substantive correction. The 11.7% / 11.9% figures and the null core-temperature result are unsuperseded as of 2026-07.

**修正:**
- Replace 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints' with an accurate scorecard: the core-temperature endpoint was null at both 12 and 24 months (between-group p=.70 and p=.84), and the body-composition-adjusted RMR endpoint was significant at 12 months (p=.04) but no longer significant at 24 months. That is one marginal hit out of four registered primary outcome measures, and the hit did not persist — not 0 for 2.
- MANDATORY caveat, or the article will read as falsified by its own cited registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193 posts the RMR primary outcome as CR -83 vs AL -1 kcal/d at 12 months (p<0.001) and CR -71 vs AL -7 kcal/d at 24 months (p<0.0001) — apparently a resounding success. Those figures are identical to the RAW, UNADJUSTED 'RMR, kcal/d' row of Table 1 in Ravussin 2015, i.e. the registry posted unadjusted RMR under an outcome title that says 'Corrected for Changes in Body Composition'. The genuinely body-composition-adjusted analysis is the 'RMR residual' (Figure 3), and that is the one that dies by 24 months. State this explicitly.
- Quote the core-temperature sentence in full and correctly: Ravussin 2015 says 'Core temperature change differed little between groups.' — the subject is 'core temperature change', not 'core temperature'.
- State that the ± on 11.7% is a standard error, not a standard deviation (the paper writes 'mean ± standard error'), and render the Kraus figure in the paper's own notation: '11.9% (SE 0.7)', not '11.9 ± 0.7%'.
- Add the dose trajectory, which the flat '~12%' figure hides: Ravussin 2015 reports CR averaging 11.7±0.7 %CR, comprising 19.5±0.8% during the first 6 months and 9.1±0.7% on average for the remainder. The 24-month endpoints were therefore tested against a dose nearer 9%, not 12%.
- Fix the N attributions: 238 = participants assessed/eligible (this is ClinicalTrials.gov's 'Actual Enrollment'); 220 = randomized (145 CR + 75 AL); 218 = started the intervention and the ITT analysis population (143 CR + 75 AL). Note that Ravussin 2015 and Kraus 2019 both loosely call 218 'randomized'; Waziry's 220 is the correct randomized count, not a contradiction.
- Do not put the Kraus 2019 title in quotation marks unless quoted exactly. It reads '2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial' — 'cardiometabolic risk', not 'cardiometabolic results'.
- Soften 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans' to a defensible form such as 'the only two-year randomized trial of caloric restriction in healthy non-obese humans' or 'the largest and longest', unless a source stating the exclusivity is located. No CALERIE document I read asserts it.
- If the Waziry 2023 Author Correction is mentioned at all, note it corrects only an author affiliation and no result — do not imply the DNA methylation findings were corrected.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- ClinicalTrials.gov's own posted results for NCT00427193 report the RMR primary outcome as met at BOTH timepoints with p<0.001 (12 mo, net -82 kcal/d, 95% CI -103.8 to -60.2) and p<0.0001 (24 mo, net -64 kcal/d, 95% CI -90.5 to -37.5), two-sided mixed models, n=143 CR / 75 AL. Taken at face value this refutes 'failed both primary endpoints'. It is reconcilable only once you notice the registry posted UNADJUSTED RMR under a title claiming body-composition correction — but the article must say so, because the registry is the document a skeptical reader will check first.
- The RMR primary endpoint was in fact met at 12 months (p=.04), so the claim of failing 'both' endpoints is false at 12 months even on the paper's own adjusted analysis.
- Ravussin 2015 states that unadjusted RMR reductions in CR did significantly exceed AL at 24 months ('decreases from baseline in absolute RMR in CR (5.9±0.7% and 5.0±0.9% at 12 and 24 months, respectively) significantly exceeded those in AL'). An adversary can cite this to claim the RMR endpoint succeeded; the rebuttal is that the prespecified endpoint was the body-composition-adjusted residual, not absolute RMR.
- The registry lists FOUR primary outcome measures (two constructs x two timepoints), not two, so 'BOTH primary endpoints' misdescribes the registered structure.
- The ClinicalTrials.gov posting labels its dispersion values 'Standard Deviation' when the matching Table 1 values are standard errors — the registry record is demonstrably unreliable on metadata, which is itself worth one sentence if the article leans on the registry.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I could not use WebSearch — this session's budget was already exhausted (200/200) before my first query — so I reached every primary document by direct curl to raw endpoints and parsed the text myself. Nothing below came from a web-fetch summarizer; every quoted string was grepped out of a file on disk.

Documents reached verbatim: (1) the full ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193 record as raw JSON from the v2 API, including outcomesModule, participantFlowModule, outcomeMeasuresModule with per-outcome analyses and denominators, and moreInfoModule; (2) the registry's internal version-history API plus reconstructed records at versions 6 (2008-05-12), 9 (2009-07-17) and 13 (2015-03-25), which let me distinguish prospectively registered outcome wording from the 2018 results-posting revision; (3) Ravussin 2015 (PMC4841173) full text scraped from PMC and stripped to 48.9k characters of plain text, including the abstract, Methods, the CONSORT figure legend, the Results paragraphs on adherence and on the primary outcomes, and the raw cell values of Table 1; (4) the Ravussin 2015 erratum (PMC4888401) scraped the same way; (5) Kraus 2019's published Lancet abstract via PubMed efetch plus the PMC author manuscript (PMC6707879); (6) Waziry 2023's abstract via PubMed efetch and its Author Correction full text via Europe PMC.

The central finding is the erratum. I found it by pulling the MEDLINE record for Ravussin 2015 and checking the EIN field, which pointed to doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056. It states in one sentence that 11.7 +/- 0.7% was wrong and 11.9 +/- 0.7% is correct. The claim group treats 11.7 and 11.9 as a discrepancy between two papers; in fact there is one number, and the article was about to cite a retracted figure. Both the PMC copy of Ravussin and the PMC author manuscript of Kraus still display 11.7% in their body text, so this is reachable only via the erratum — exactly the failure mode the pipeline is guarding against.

The second finding is a genuine registry-versus-paper conflict on the RMR endpoint. The registry's posted results report p<0.001 and p<0.0001 for RMR at 12 and 24 months. I established that the posted values (-83/-1 and -71/-7 kcal/day) are byte-identical to Ravussin's Table 1 row for absolute RMR, not the residual, and cross-checked them against the paper's stated percentage declines (5.9% and 5.0% of the CR baseline RMR of 1,418 kcal/day give 84 and 71 kcal/day). So the registry posted the wrong measure under the right title. Either way, the claim's 'failed BOTH primary endpoints' does not survive: even on the paper's own analysis, RMR residual was significant at 12 months (p=.04), and 12-month RMR is a separately registered primary outcome entry.

The N question resolved cleanly and all three figures are legitimate: 238 eligible/baseline-assessed (which is what the registry's 'Actual Enrollment' field means here, a common misreading), 220 randomized, 218 ITT who started. I also flagged that both the Ravussin and Kraus abstracts say '218 randomized', contradicting Ravussin's own CONSORT text, so the abstracts are the wrong citation for that number, and that the month-24 analyses rest on 191 observed participants with 18.2% versus 5.3% differential dropout.

What remains uncertain: I could not test 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans'. It is a universal negative, no primary source asserts it, and without search I had no way to survey the trial literature. I marked it unreachable rather than guessing. I also did not open Ravussin's online Supplementary Material (the RMR-residual computation details) or Kraus's supplementary appendix; the residual figures I report come from the Figure 3A caption text and the Results paragraph in the main article, not from the supplement. Finally, I checked for retractions and errata across the CALERIE corpus via a PubMed publication-type search and found only the two correction notices reported above; neither the Kraus 2019 paper nor the registry record carries an erratum.

- **(a) Registered primary outcomes were change in core body temperature and change in RMR (corrected for body composition) at 12 and 24 months** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim against the ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193 record (fetched as raw JSON via curl, not summarizer-mediated). The current record (last update 2022-03-14) lists exactly four primary outcome entries: 'Change in Core Body Temperature, Baseline to 12 Months'; 'Change in Core Temperature, Baseline to 24 Months'; 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition, Baseline to 12 Months'; and 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' (timeFrame 'Baseline, 24 months'). Only ONE secondary outcome is registered: change in TNF-alpha at 12 months. VERSION CAVEAT the article should know: the four-entry, 12-and-24-month structure was created on 2018-12-04, the same submission that posted results. The prospectively registered versions (v6 2008-05-12 through v13 2015-03-25) listed only TWO primary outcomes, with broader windows: 'Core body temperature' (timeFrame 'Baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months') and 'Resting metabolic rate (RMR) corrected for changes in body composition' (timeFrame 'Baseline, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months'). The measures never changed; only the timepoint parsing did. Ravussin 2015 independently states the two prespecified primary outcomes and that assessment had 'a primary focus on baseline, 12 months, and 24 months', so the claim is fair — but 'at 12 and 24 months' is the 2018 wording, not the 2008 wording.

- **(b) At 24 months RMR residual fell more in CR at 12 mo (p=0.04) but NOT at 24 mo; core temperature 'differed little between groups'** — `corrected`
  The quoted paper language is exactly right; the 'failed BOTH primary endpoints' framing wrapped around it is wrong. VERBATIM from the Ravussin 2015 abstract (PMC4841173, text extracted by me from raw HTML): 'RMR residual decreased significantly more in CR than AL at 12 months ( p = .04) but not 24 months (M24). Core temperature change differed little between groups.' Discussion, verbatim: 'For our two primary outcomes, the intervention did not significantly affect core temperature, and its lowering of RMR residual (indicative of metabolic adaptation) differed significantly from AL only in the first year of the intervention.' Table 1 core temperature: Delta M12 AL -0.03(.02) vs CR -0.05(0.02), between-group p=.70; Delta M24 AL -0.02(0.02) vs CR -0.05(0.02), p=.84 (Bonferroni-corrected per the table footnote). Registry-posted analyses agree on core temperature: p=0.70, two-sided 95% CI -0.019 to 0.059; and p=0.84, 95% CI -0.0092 to 0.069. WRONG version: 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints.' RIGHT version: core temperature failed at both 12 and 24 months; the RMR endpoint was MET at 12 months (p=.04) and failed at 24 months. One of two endpoints hit significance at one of two registered timepoints. SEPARATE LANDMINE the article must defuse: ClinicalTrials.gov's own posted results for the RMR primary outcome report CR -83 (SE 10) vs AL -1 (13) at 12 months, net difference -82 (95% CI -103.8 to -60.2), p<0.001; and CR -71 (12) vs AL -7 (16) at 24 months, net -64 (95% CI -90.5 to -37.5), p<0.0001, n=143/75. Read at face value, the registry says the RMR primary endpoint was met at BOTH timepoints. Those posted numbers are however identical to the Ravussin Table 1 row for ABSOLUTE RMR in kcal/d (Delta M12: AL -1 (13), CR -83 (10), p<.001; Delta M24: AL -7 (16), CR -71 (12), p=.001), not the RMR residual — cross-check: CR baseline RMR 1,418 kcal/d, and the paper reports absolute RMR fell 5.9% at 12 mo (=84 kcal/d) and 5.0% at 24 mo (=71 kcal/d). So the registry posted absolute RMR under an outcome titled 'Corrected for Changes in Body Composition'. The paper's actual primary analysis, the RMR residual, is reported only in Figure 3A: 48+/-9 kcal/d in CR vs 14+/-12 in AL at 12 months, p=.04, and non-significant at 24 months.

- **(c) Prescribed 25% CR but achieved 11.7 +/- 0.7% (Ravussin 2015) / 11.9 +/- 0.7% (Kraus 2019); every '25% CR' effect was produced by about 12%** — `refuted`
  The 11.7% half of this is a retracted number and the implied Ravussin-vs-Kraus discrepancy does not exist. A formal erratum (J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2016 Jun;71(6):839-840, doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056, PMID 27059599, PMC4888401) states VERBATIM, in text I extracted myself from the raw PMC HTML: 'In Volume 70, Issue 9 of The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences , DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glv057 , the value for the degree of CR achieved in the study was incorrectly stated as 11.7 +/- 0.7% in the Abstract and the Results section (page 1100). The correct value is 11.9 +/- 0.7%.' WRONG version: '11.7 +/- 0.7% (Ravussin 2015) / 11.9 +/- 0.7% (Kraus 2019)', presented as two sources giving two figures. RIGHT version: there is one figure, 11.9 +/- 0.7% (the 0.7 is a standard ERROR, not SD); 11.7% is an erratum-corrected error in Ravussin 2015 and must not be cited. THE TRAP: the publisher/PMC copy of Ravussin 2015 still displays '11.7+/-0.7 %CR' in both the abstract and Results, and the PMC author manuscript of Kraus 2019 also still says 'averaged 11.7% (+/-0.7%)' in its Results text — both are uncorrected. Only the erratum and the published Lancet abstract carry the right value. Kraus 2019 published abstract, verbatim: 'Individuals in the calorie restriction group achieved a mean reduction in calorie intake of 11.9% (SE 0.7; from 2467 kcal to 2170 kcal) versus 0.8% (1.0) in the control group'. Independent recent confirmation up to 2026: a 2026 CALERIE diet-quality paper (PMID 41475553) reports 'Average CR achieved during the 2-y intervention was 11.9% +/- 7.2%' — the 7.2% being the SD, which shows the between-participant spread the +/-0.7 SE conceals. SURVIVING SUB-CLAIMS: 'prescribed 25%' is confirmed (registry arm description: '25% caloric restriction'; Kraus: 'randomly assigned (2:1) to a 25% calorie restriction diet'). 'Under half the target' survives at the corrected value: 11.9/25 = 47.6%. 'Did not deliver its nominal dose' is confirmed by the sponsor itself — the registry's Limitations and Caveats field reads verbatim: 'The Caloric Restriction (CR) group fell short of achieving the 25% CR goal specified in the protocol.' Ravussin's Discussion says the same. NEEDED REFINEMENT to 'about 12% throughout': it was not flat. Ravussin, verbatim: energy intake in CR fell 'by 480+/-20 kcal/d during the first six months, then stabilized at approximately 234+/-19 kcal/d below baseline for the remainder of the trial', i.e. '19.5+/-0.8% during the first 6 months and 9.1+/-0.7% on average for the remainder of the study'. The 24-month cardiometabolic effects were produced by ~19.5% CR for six months followed by ~9% for eighteen.

- **(d) The cited cardiometabolic results are labelled 'exploratory outcomes' in the paper's own title (N=218, 2:1 randomisation, 2 years)** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim on every element. Title, exactly as indexed: '2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial.' Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019 Sep;7(9):673-683, doi:10.1016/S2213-8587(19)30151-2, PMID 31303390. Abstract, verbatim: 'Participants were randomly assigned (2:1) to a 25% calorie restriction diet or an ad libitum control diet'; 'Exploratory cardiometabolic risk factor responses to a prescribed 25% calorie restriction diet for 2 years were evaluated ... analysed in the intention-to-treat population'; '218 were randomly assigned to and started a 25% calorie restriction diet (n=143, 66%) or an ad libitum control diet (n=75, 34%)'. Actual allocation ratio 143:75 = 1.91:1. The claim is STRENGTHENED by a source the article is not yet using: Ravussin 2015 pre-specified these as exploratory in the Methods, verbatim — 'Exploratory outcomes included risk factors for age-related conditions and psychological responses.' So 'exploratory' is not retrospective self-deprecation in a 2019 title; it is the 2015 prespecified analysis tier.

- **N adjudication: 218 (Kraus 2019) vs 220 (Waziry 2023) vs 238 (registry actual enrollment)** — `confirmed`
  All three are correct and denote different things; the article can state this cleanly. Ravussin 2015 CONSORT figure legend, verbatim: 'After an extensive screening process (10), 238 individuals were eligible and 220 individuals were randomized. Two individuals, both assigned to the CR group, dropped out prior to starting the intervention, resulting in an ITT cohort of 218 participants; 75 in the AL control and 143 in the CR group.' Registry participant-flow preAssignmentDetails, verbatim: '238 Participants were eligible, 18 participants withdrew prior to randomization, 220 participants were randomized to the study, and 2 participants withdrew prior to initiating the intervention.' Therefore: 238 = screened-eligible who began baseline assessments, which is what ClinicalTrials.gov posts as 'Actual Enrollment: 238' (enrollment on that registry field does NOT mean randomized); 220 = randomized, which is the number Waziry 2023 uses ('a randomized controlled trial in which n = 220 adults without obesity were randomized to 25% CR or ad libitum control diet for 2 yr'); 218 = ITT cohort who started the intervention, 143 CR + 75 AL, which is Kraus 2019's N and Ravussin's analysis population. CAUTION the article should absorb: the Ravussin 2015 ABSTRACT says '218 persons were randomized', contradicting its own CONSORT text, and Kraus's abstract says '218 were randomly assigned to and started' — both conflate randomized with started. Cite the CONSORT text, not the abstracts, for the randomization count. ALSO: neither 218 nor 220 is the number analyzed at 24 months. Ravussin, verbatim: 'Across the time points, there were observations from 211 participants at month 6, 201 at month 12, 193 at month 18, and 191 at month 24.' Differential dropout was severe and asymmetric: 30 withdrew, '4 (5.3%) in the AL control group and 26 (18.2%) in the CR group ( p = .01)'. The registry results tables nonetheless post denominators of 143/75 for all four primary outcomes.

- **Framing: CALERIE-2 is 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans'** — `unreachable`
  I could not verify 'the only' against any primary document, and no primary source asserts it. A universal-negative claim of this kind cannot be established by reading the CALERIE papers, and my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this task (200/200 used before I ran a single query), so I could not run the systematic-review-style search that would be needed to test it. What the primary source does support, verbatim from Ravussin 2015: 'To our knowledge, no previous study in any population, not to mention a normal weight population, has demonstrated this degree of sustained CR and weight loss for this length of time', and 'this study provides the first evidence from a randomized controlled trial that sustained CR is both feasible and without adverse effects on quality of life in nonobese humans'. Note also that CALERIE Phase 1 comprised earlier randomized CR trials in overweight-but-non-obese people at 6-12 months (Ravussin cites one as reference 7), so 'only randomized CR trial' is false without the duration qualifier. Recommend the article narrow the wording rather than defend 'only'.

**修正:**
- Delete the figure '11.7 +/- 0.7% (Ravussin 2015)' entirely. It was formally retracted by an erratum: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2016 Jun;71(6):839-840, doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056 (PMID 27059599), which states that the achieved CR 'was incorrectly stated as 11.7 +/- 0.7% in the Abstract and the Results section (page 1100). The correct value is 11.9 +/- 0.7%.' Cite a single achieved-restriction figure: 11.9 +/- 0.7% (the 0.7 is a standard error, not an SD).
- Remove the implied disagreement between Ravussin 2015 and Kraus 2019 on achieved restriction. There is none: both report 11.9 +/- 0.7% once the 2016 erratum is applied. If the article wants a dispersion figure that conveys how variable adherence actually was, use the SD from the 2026 CALERIE diet-quality paper (PMID 41475553): 'Average CR achieved during the 2-y intervention was 11.9% +/- 7.2%'.
- Do not write that CALERIE-2 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints'. Core body temperature failed at both timepoints (between-group p=.70 at 12 months, p=.84 at 24 months). The RMR endpoint was MET at 12 months: RMR residual fell 48 +/- 9 kcal/d in CR vs 14 +/- 12 in AL, p=.04, and failed only at 24 months. Correct formulation: CALERIE-2 missed its core-temperature primary endpoint at both timepoints and its RMR primary endpoint at 24 months, with the RMR effect reaching significance only in year one.
- Pre-empt the registry contradiction on RMR. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193's posted results report the RMR primary outcome as significant at BOTH timepoints (12 months: CR -83 [SE 10] vs AL -1 [13], net -82, p<0.001; 24 months: CR -71 [12] vs AL -7 [16], net -64, p<0.0001). Those posted values are the ABSOLUTE RMR change from Ravussin Table 1, not the body-composition-corrected residual that the endpoint title names and that the paper actually analysed. State this explicitly, or a reader who opens the registry will conclude the article misreported the endpoint.
- Give the achieved restriction as a two-phase profile, not a flat ~12%. Ravussin 2015: energy intake in the CR arm fell 19.5 +/- 0.8% during the first 6 months and averaged 9.1 +/- 0.7% for the remaining 18 months, yielding the 11.9% two-year average. The 24-month cardiometabolic results were therefore produced by roughly 19.5% restriction for six months followed by roughly 9% for eighteen.
- Define the three participant counts rather than picking one. 238 = screened-eligible who began baseline assessments (this is what ClinicalTrials.gov posts as 'Actual Enrollment', which does not mean randomized); 220 = randomized (the number Waziry 2023 uses); 218 = intention-to-treat cohort who started the intervention, 143 CR + 75 AL (Kraus 2019's N and Ravussin's analysis population). Source the randomization count to Ravussin's CONSORT figure legend, not to the Ravussin or Kraus abstracts, both of which incorrectly say 218 were randomized.
- If the article quotes N=218 alongside 24-month results, add that only 191 participants contributed month-24 observations (201 at month 12), and that dropout was strongly asymmetric: 26 of 143 CR participants (18.2%) vs 4 of 75 controls (5.3%), p=.01.
- Narrow 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans' to 'the only two-year randomized controlled trial of sustained caloric restriction in healthy non-obese adults'. No primary source supports the unqualified 'only', and CALERIE Phase 1 included earlier randomized CR trials of 6-12 months in non-obese participants.
- When stating that the trial under-delivered its dose, attribute it to the sponsor rather than to inference: the ClinicalTrials.gov results record's own 'Limitations and Caveats' field reads 'The Caloric Restriction (CR) group fell short of achieving the 25% CR goal specified in the protocol.'
- Optional strengthening for the 'exploratory outcomes' point: the cardiometabolic measures were designated exploratory prospectively, not just in the 2019 title. Ravussin 2015 Methods states 'Exploratory outcomes included risk factors for age-related conditions and psychological responses.' Note also that the registry lists exactly one secondary outcome (change in TNF-alpha at 12 months), so everything cardiometabolic sits below that tier.
- If the article describes the registered endpoints as being specified 'at 12 and 24 months', note that this is the wording of the December 2018 results-posting revision. The prospectively registered versions (2008 through 2015) listed two primary outcomes with wider windows: core body temperature at 'Baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months' and RMR corrected for changes in body composition at 'Baseline, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months'. The measures themselves never changed.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- DECISIVE: Erratum, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2016 Jun;71(6):839-840, doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056, PMID 27059599, PMC4888401. Verbatim, from raw HTML I extracted myself: 'In Volume 70, Issue 9 of The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences , DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glv057 , the value for the degree of CR achieved in the study was incorrectly stated as 11.7 +/- 0.7% in the Abstract and the Results section (page 1100). The correct value is 11.9 +/- 0.7%.' This retracts the claim's Ravussin figure and dissolves the claimed 11.7-vs-11.9 discrepancy between the two papers.
- ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193's posted results contradict the claim that the RMR primary endpoint failed. The registry reports, for the outcome titled 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition': 12 months, CR -83 (SE 10) vs AL -1 (13) kcal/day, mean net difference -82 (two-sided 95% CI -103.8 to -60.2), p<0.001; 24 months, CR -71 (12) vs AL -7 (16), mean difference -64 (95% CI -90.5 to -37.5), p<0.0001; n=143/75 both times. These are the same values Ravussin Table 1 gives for ABSOLUTE RMR, so the registry appears to have posted the uncorrected measure under the corrected measure's title — but the discrepancy is real and public and will be used against an unqualified 'failed both endpoints' claim.
- Within Ravussin 2015 itself the RMR primary endpoint was not a clean null: the paper reports that absolute RMR fell significantly more in CR than AL at BOTH 12 and 24 months (Table 1 between-group p<.001 and p=.001), and that RMR residual fell significantly more in CR at 12 months (48 +/- 9 vs 14 +/- 12 kcal/d, p=.04). Only the 24-month residual comparison was null.
- The single 'positive' primary-endpoint result rests on p=.04, obtained under a hierarchical gatekeeping procedure in which non-significant gate tests trigger Bonferroni correction ('Type I error was controlled using a hierarchical gatekeeping strategy'). An article leaning on the 12-month RMR result, or on its absence at 24 months, should not treat p=.04 as robust.
- The +/-0.7 attached to the achieved-restriction figure is a standard error, not a standard deviation. Ravussin states results are 'reported as mean +/- standard error' and Kraus's abstract writes '(SE 0.7)'. The corresponding SD is roughly ten times larger: a 2026 CALERIE publication (PMID 41475553) gives 'Average CR achieved during the 2-y intervention was 11.9% +/- 7.2%'. Presenting 11.9 +/- 0.7% without saying it is an SE overstates how uniformly the dose was delivered across participants.
- The Waziry 2023 Nature Aging DNA-methylation paper carries an Author Correction (Nat Aging 2023, doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y, PMID 37161091). I read it in full: it corrects only D. W. Belsky's first affiliation and changes no data. Recording it so the article is not blindsided by the existence of a correction notice. That paper also self-describes verbatim as 'a post hoc analysis'.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

I reached every primary document myself rather than relying on fetch summarizers. Because a prior run of this pipeline caught summarizer models fabricating quotes, I downloaded the sources with curl into the scratchpad, stripped the HTML to plain text locally, and grepped the raw text — every string I quote above was matched against bytes I pulled down, not against a model's paraphrase. Files: /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/scratchpad/{ravussin2015.txt, kraus2019.txt, waziry.txt, errata.html, ctg.json}.

DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM: (1) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 record for NCT00427193, parsed as raw JSON — protocol section (4 primary outcome measures, 1 secondary, 2 other; enrollment 238 ACTUAL), participant-flow module (preAssignmentDetails narrating 238 -> 220 -> 218; STARTED 143/75; COMPLETED 117/71), and the posted outcome-measures module with per-arm values and p-values. (2) Ravussin 2015 full text (PMC4841173) — abstract, CONSORT paragraph, statistical-methods paragraph, primary-outcome results paragraph, Table 1 rows for RMR and 24-h core temperature, and Discussion. (3) The 2016 Erratum full text (PMC4888401). (4) Kraus 2019 author manuscript (PMC6707879) plus the published title and abstract confirmed independently via PubMed EFetch and the Crossref API. (5) Waziry 2023 full text (PMC10148951) and its Author Correction (PMC10275750).

THE DECISIVE FINDING is the erratum. The claim treats 11.7% (Ravussin) and 11.9% (Kraus) as two independent estimates that happen to agree — a construction that reads as corroboration. They are not: 11.7% was a printing error in Ravussin 2015 that the journal formally corrected to 11.9% in 2016. PMC still serves the uncorrected body text under a correction banner, which is almost certainly how 11.7 entered the article's source chain. This is the kind of slippage the article must not ship.

The second finding is a landmine for anyone auditing the article: ClinicalTrials.gov's posted results show the RMR primary outcome as highly significant at BOTH timepoints, because the posted numbers are absolute RMR (matching Ravussin Table 1's 'RMR, kcal/d' rows exactly), not the body-composition-corrected residual that the outcome title names and that the paper actually analysed. A reader who checks the registry will conclude the article is wrong. The article needs to name this discrepancy rather than assert 'failed both registered primary endpoints' flatly.
