The claim's core thesis survives intact and is well supported: core temperature was null between groups at both timepoints (p=0.70, p=0.84); RMR residual was significant only at 12 months; achieved restriction was roughly half the 25% prescription; the cardiometabolic results carry 'exploratory outcomes' in the published title and were never registered as primary or secondary outcomes. The N question resolves cleanly (238 assessed / 220 randomized / 218 ITT), and Waziry's 220 is a description of the parent trial rather than that paper's analytic N of 197 — worth fixing, since the article's own framing implies Waziry analysed 220 people.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY, stated plainly. My WebSearch budget was exhausted before I began (200/200 consumed by an earlier session), so I could not run open-ended adversarial sweeps. I compensated with structured API queries against Europe PMC, PubMed EFetch and Crossref, which is how I found the erratum and confirmed the absence of retractions or critical correspondence. But absence of evidence here is weaker than it would be with full search: I verified no erratum/retraction exists on Kraus 2019 via PubMed's CommentsCorrections field and found no critical letters in a Europe PMC letter/comment sweep for 2019-2026, yet I cannot rule out a critique indexed elsewhere. The 2015 accompanying editorial (Di Francesco & de Cabo, PMID 26187232) is paywalled and not in Europe PMC — unreachable, though it is commentary rather than a data source. The superlative 'only long-term randomized CR trial in healthy non-obese humans' is the one claim I could not test properly: proving a negative over the trial literature needs search I did not have, and the primary sources say 'first', not 'only'. I flag it as unverified rather than guess.

- **Headline: CALERIE-2, the only long-term randomized CR trial in healthy non-obese humans, failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints and did not deliver its nominal dose** — `corrected`
  WRONG as written: 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints' is unqualified. RIGHT: both primary endpoints were null at 24 months, but the RMR-residual endpoint WAS met at 12 months. Ravussin 2015's own Discussion says verbatim: 'For our two primary outcomes, the intervention did not significantly affect core temperature, and its lowering of RMR residual (indicative of metabolic adaptation) differed significantly from AL only in the first year of the intervention.' Note also the registry lists FOUR primary outcome measures (temp at 12mo, temp at 24mo, RMR at 12mo, RMR at 24mo), so 'BOTH' should be 'both prespecified primary outcomes' (the paper's framing), not 'both registered endpoints' (there are four). Separately, 'only' is an editorial superlative the primary sources do not make — Ravussin 2015 says 'the first evidence from a randomized controlled trial that sustained CR is both feasible and without adverse effects on quality of life in nonobese humans' (first, not only). I could not exhaustively verify 'only' (WebSearch budget exhausted); treat as unverified. 'Did not deliver its nominal dose' HOLDS.

- **(a) Registered primary outcomes were change in core body temperature and change in RMR corrected for body composition, at 12 and 24 months** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim from the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 record for NCT00427193 (raw JSON parsed locally, not via a summarizer). The four primaryOutcomes measure strings are exactly: 'Change in Core Body Temperature, Baseline to 12 Months'; 'Change in Core Temperature, Baseline to 24 Months'; 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition, Baseline to 12 Months'; 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' (timeFrame 'Baseline, 24 months'). Ravussin 2015 matches: 'The two prespecified primary outcomes were selected to test the hypothesis that CR would induce metabolic adaptations, specifically (a) decrease in resting metabolic rate (RMR) adjusted for changes in body composition and (b) decrease in core body temperature.'

- **(b) At 24 months RMR residual significant at 12mo (p=0.04) but not 24mo; core temperature 'differed little between groups'** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim in Ravussin 2015. Results: 'RMR residual decreased significantly more in CR compared with AL at 12 months (48±9 vs 14±12 kcal/d in AL, p = .04) ... but decreases did not differ significantly between CR and AL at 24 months.' Abstract: 'Core temperature change differed little between groups.' Adding the numbers the claim omits, from Table 1 and confirmed independently in the registry's posted results: core temperature between-group p = .70 at 12 months and p = .84 at 24 months — unambiguously null. IMPORTANT QUALIFIER the article must not blur: the WITHIN-group core-temperature declines in the CR arm WERE nominally significant (−0.05 °C, p=.006 at 12mo; −0.05 °C, p=.02 at 24mo); the null is strictly between-group (AL fell −0.03 and −0.02 °C). Note also all p values in that table 'reflect Bonferroni corrections, truncated at 1.0, as appropriate'; Type I error used 'a hierarchical gatekeeping strategy'. No one-sided testing is described anywhere in the statistical methods.

- **(c) Prescribed 25% CR but achieved 11.7 ± 0.7% (Ravussin 2015) / 11.9 ± 0.7% (Kraus 2019)** — `refuted`
  REFUTED as stated — these are NOT two independent estimates from two papers. WRONG: '11.7 ± 0.7% (Ravussin 2015) / 11.9 ± 0.7% (Kraus 2019)'. RIGHT: a single value, 11.9 ± 0.7%. A formal erratum (J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2016 Jun;71(6):839-840; doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056; PMID 27059599; PMC4888401) states verbatim: 'In Volume 70, Issue 9 of The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences, DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glv057, the value for the degree of CR achieved in the study was incorrectly stated as 11.7 ± 0.7% in the Abstract and the Results section (page 1100). The correct value is 11.9 ± 0.7%.' The PMC copy of Ravussin 2015 still displays the uncorrected '11.7±0.7' in both abstract and Results while carrying the banner 'This article has been corrected. See J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2016 Apr 8;71(6):839.' — which is exactly how the stale 11.7 figure keeps propagating. Kraus 2019 (published Lancet Diab Endocrinol abstract) independently reports 'a mean reduction in calorie intake of 11·9% (SE 0·7; from 2467 kcal to 2170 kcal) versus 0·8% (1·0) in the control group'; Waziry 2023 also cites 'mean = 11.9, s.e.m. = 0.7%'. The substantive point (under half the 25% target: 11.9/25 = 48%) HOLDS. But 'about 12%' is a 2-year AVERAGE, not a steady dose — Ravussin 2015 reports '19.5±0.8% during the first 6 months and 9.1±0.7% on average for the remainder of the study'. Sustained weight loss 10.4±0.4% (Ravussin) / 7.5 kg (Kraus).

- **(d) Cardiometabolic results labelled 'exploratory outcomes' in the paper's own title (N=218, 2:1, 2 years)** — `corrected`
  Substance CONFIRMED; the title is misquoted. WRONG: 'exploratory outcomes of the CALERIE Phase 2 randomised controlled trial'. RIGHT (confirmed identically by PubMed PMID 31303390 and Crossref DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(19)30151-2): '2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial', Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019;7(9):673-683. N=218, 2:1 randomisation, 2 years all CONFIRMED from the paper. The point is actually STRONGER than the article states: the NCT00427193 registry lists exactly ONE secondary outcome — 'Change in Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α), Baseline to 12 Months' — and two 'other' outcomes (change in fat mass). No blood pressure, lipid, insulin, CRP or metabolic-syndrome measure was ever registered as primary or secondary. Caveat for citation hygiene: the free PMC author manuscript (PMC6707879) is titled 'Two Years of Calorie Restriction and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors' and does NOT contain the word 'exploratory' — quote the published Lancet title only.

- **N adjudication: 218 (Kraus 2019) vs 220 (Waziry 2023) vs 238 (registry actual enrollment)** — `confirmed`
  ESTABLISHED, all three are correct and denote different things. 238 = individuals screened eligible who began baseline assessments; this is what ClinicalTrials.gov posts as enrollmentInfo {count: 238, type: ACTUAL}, and the registry's own preAssignmentDetails says verbatim: '238 Participants were eligible, 18 participants withdrew prior to randomization, 220 participants were randomized to the study, and 2 participants withdrew prior to initiating the intervention.' 220 = number randomized (145 CR / 75 AL) — this is what Waziry 2023 refers to ('Of 238 eligible individuals, CALERIE randomized N = 220 participants (145 CR intervention and 75 AL control)'); it is NOT Waziry's own analytic N. 218 = ITT cohort that started the intervention (143 CR / 75 AL) — the analysis population of Ravussin 2015 and Kraus 2019, and the registry's participant-flow STARTED counts (FG000 143, FG001 75) and baseline denominator (218). Waziry 2023's actual DNAm analysis sample was N=197 (128 CR / 69 AL), of whom 164 had all three timepoints. Trial target sample size was 225. Completion: 117/143 CR and 71/75 AL (82% CR, 95% AL). Do not cite 220 as 'Waziry's N'.

- **Adversarial search for corrections, refutations, failed replications up to 2026-07** — `corrected`
  One material correction found and applied above (the 2016 Ravussin erratum, 11.7 → 11.9). Waziry 2023 also carries an Author Correction (Nat Aging 2023;3(6):753, doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y) but it is NON-SUBSTANTIVE: it corrects only D. W. Belsky's first affiliation — no data changed. No erratum, retraction or expression of concern on Kraus 2019. A Europe PMC sweep of letters/comments citing CALERIE 2019-2026 turned up no critical correspondence, reanalysis or failed replication — only secondary analyses (e.g. two 2026 Diabetes Obes Metab papers on predicted CVD/T2D risk and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic health). The accompanying 2015 editorial (Di Francesco & de Cabo, 'Two-Year Trial of Human Caloric Restriction', J Gerontol A 2015;70(9):1095-6, PMID 26187232) is paywalled and not in Europe PMC — UNREACHABLE, but it is a commentary, not a data source, and nothing rests on it.

**修正:**
- Replace '11.7 +/- 0.7% (Ravussin 2015) / 11.9 +/- 0.7% (Kraus 2019)' with a single figure: 11.9 +/- 0.7%. The 11.7% in Ravussin 2015 was a reporting error formally corrected by an erratum (J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2016;71(6):839-840, doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056, PMID 27059599). Presenting 11.7 and 11.9 as two independent measurements from two papers is wrong — they are the same number before and after correction. If the erratum is worth a sentence, note that the PMC copy of Ravussin 2015 still shows the uncorrected 11.7 in its abstract, which is why the stale figure circulates.
- Qualify 'failed BOTH of its registered primary endpoints'. Accurate version: both prespecified primary outcomes were null at 24 months; core temperature was null at BOTH timepoints (between-group p=0.70 at 12 months, p=0.84 at 24 months); RMR residual was nominally significant at 12 months (48+/-9 vs 14+/-12 kcal/d, p=0.04) and null at 24 months. Ravussin 2015's Discussion is the safest formulation to cite: the RMR-residual effect 'differed significantly from AL only in the first year of the intervention.'
- Add the trap that a fact-checker will hit: the ClinicalTrials.gov posted RESULTS for NCT00427193 report the primary outcome 'Change in Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) Corrected for Changes in Body Composition' as CR -83 vs AL -1 kcal/d (p<0.001) at 12 months and CR -71 vs AL -7 kcal/d (p<0.0001) at 24 months — i.e. significant at both timepoints. Those posted numbers are the ABSOLUTE RMR values from Ravussin 2015 Table 1, not the body-composition-corrected RMR residual the outcome title names. Anyone auditing the registry will see the opposite of 'failed'; the article should say the endpoint failed as analysed in the trial's own primary paper, and flag the registry-posting discrepancy.
- State that core temperature was null BETWEEN GROUPS specifically. Within the CR arm the decline was nominally significant (-0.05 degrees C, within-group p=0.006 at 12 months; -0.05 degrees C, p=0.02 at 24 months); the AL arm fell -0.03 and -0.02 degrees C. Writing 'core temperature did not fall' would be wrong; 'core temperature change differed little between groups' (the paper's own abstract wording) is right.
- Quote the Kraus 2019 title exactly: '2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial', Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019;7(9):673-683. The article's rendering ('exploratory outcomes of the CALERIE Phase 2 randomised controlled trial') is a paraphrase, and the free PMC author manuscript is titled 'Two Years of Calorie Restriction and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors' with no 'exploratory' in it.
- Strengthen claim (d) with the registry fact: NCT00427193 registers exactly ONE secondary outcome (change in TNF-alpha, baseline to 12 months) plus two 'other' outcomes (change in fat mass). No blood pressure, lipid, insulin, CRP or metabolic-syndrome measure was ever registered as primary or secondary — so 'exploratory' is the registry's status for them too, not just the journal's label.
- Fix the N sentence to assign each number its denotation: 238 = screened-eligible participants who began baseline assessments (this is ClinicalTrials.gov's 'Actual Enrollment'); 220 = randomized (145 CR / 75 AL); 218 = ITT cohort that started the intervention (143 CR / 75 AL), the analysis population of both Ravussin 2015 and Kraus 2019. Do not attribute 220 to Waziry 2023 as 'their N' — Waziry cites 220 to describe the parent trial; Waziry's own DNA-methylation analytic sample was N=197 (128 CR / 69 AL).
- Do not present '~12% CR' as a steady two-year dose. Ravussin 2015 reports 19.5 +/- 0.8% during the first 6 months and 9.1 +/- 0.7% on average thereafter; 11.9% is the two-year mean. The rhetorical point ('every effect attributed to 25% CR was produced by roughly half that') survives, but the front-loaded profile should be stated so the claim is not vulnerable to a one-line rebuttal.
- Soften 'the only long-term randomized caloric restriction trial in healthy non-obese humans' to 'the first and, to date, the only' or attribute it. The primary sources claim 'first', not 'only': Ravussin 2015 says the study 'provides the first evidence from a randomized controlled trial that sustained CR is both feasible and without adverse effects on quality of life in nonobese humans.'

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Erratum, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2016;71(6):839-840 (doi:10.1093/gerona/glw056, PMID 27059599, PMC4888401), verbatim: 'In Volume 70, Issue 9 of The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences, DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glv057, the value for the degree of CR achieved in the study was incorrectly stated as 11.7 +/- 0.7% in the Abstract and the Results section (page 1100). The correct value is 11.9 +/- 0.7%.' This directly contradicts the claim's presentation of 11.7% and 11.9% as two separate source figures.
- ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193 posted results contradict the 'failed both primary endpoints' framing on its face: the RMR primary outcome is posted as CR -83 (10) vs AL -1 (13) kcal/day, p<0.001 at 12 months, and CR -71 (12) vs AL -7 (16) kcal/day, p<0.0001 at 24 months, method 'Mixed Models Analysis'. These are the uncorrected absolute-RMR values from Ravussin Table 1, posted under an outcome titled 'Corrected for Changes in Body Composition'. The registry as posted therefore records the RMR primary endpoint as MET at both timepoints.
- Registry/paper unit-of-dispersion mismatch: ClinicalTrials.gov tags every posted primary-outcome spread as dispersionType 'Standard Deviation', but Ravussin 2015 states 'Results are reported as mean +/- standard error' and Table 1 is headed 'Mean (SE)'. The values are identical (e.g. core temp -0.05 (0.02)), so the registry is mislabelling SEs as SDs. Do not cite the registry spreads as SDs.
- Internal arithmetic tension left unresolved by the erratum: the sub-period figures in Ravussin 2015 (19.5 +/- 0.8% over months 0-6, 9.1 +/- 0.7% thereafter) time-average to 11.7%, not the corrected 11.9%. The erratum changed only the headline value and left the sub-period numbers standing. The erratum is authoritative, but an article that quotes both the 11.9% average and the 19.5%/9.1% split should not imply they were derived the same way.
- Kraus 2019's abstract states 'of 238 participants that were assessed, 218 were randomly assigned to and started a 25% calorie restriction diet (n=143, 66%) or an ad libitum control diet (n=75, 34%)' — collapsing randomization and initiation, and thereby erasing the 220-randomized step documented in Ravussin 2015's CONSORT text ('238 individuals were eligible and 220 individuals were randomized. Two individuals, both assigned to the CR group, dropped out prior to starting the intervention, resulting in an ITT cohort of 218') and in the registry's own preAssignmentDetails. Citing Kraus alone for '218 randomized' would be inaccurate.

## V24 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the outset (200/200 used), so I worked entirely through WebFetch and direct HTTP retrieval — which turned out to be better for this task. Rather than trust a summarizer (the pipeline's prior fabrication incident), I downloaded primary documents as raw bytes with curl and grepped the exact strings myself.

Documents reached verbatim: (1) the full JATS XML of Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023;3:248-257, doi 10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y, via the Europe PMC REST fullTextXML endpoint for PMC10148951 (143,987 bytes; tag-stripped to plain text at /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/scratchpad/waziry.txt). (2) The Supplementary Information PDF from Springer static content (1,751,029 bytes, 43587_2022_357_MOESM1_ESM.pdf), converted with pdftotext -layout and read as a laid-out table so I could see the ITT and TOT column groups separately — this is where Horvath, Hannum and Skin & Blood results live, and it is the item the main text does not contain. (3) The full XML of the Author Correction, PMC10275750 / doi 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y / PMID 37161091.

Every quoted string in my verdict was matched by regex against those raw files, not read from a fetch summary. An early WebFetch summary of the PMC page did return the overlap and gold-standard sentences; I treated those as unverified until I reproduced them byte-for-byte from the XML, which they were.

The claim group is substantially accurate — unusually so. The overlap sentence, the gold-standard sentence, the two unknown-clinical-benefit sentences, N=197/220, d=-0.29 (-0.45,-0.13), the post-hoc characterisation, the banked-specimen characterisation, and the administrative nature of the Author Correction all check out verbatim. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS on four points: (a) the clock count is understated — eleven measures, ten of them clocks, not 'about five', and the Horvath Skin & Blood clock is missing from the article's null list; (b) DunedinPACE is miscategorised as a clock when the paper explicitly classes it as a pace-of-aging measure; (c) the mortality translation is attributed to downstream repetition when it is the authors' own Discussion sentence, and the article drops the paper's 'as much as' hedge; (d) the smoking-cessation comparator is a randomized trial (Anthonisen 2005), not an observational cohort. I also flag, in fairness to the source, that DunedinPACE was one of three pre-designated primary measures and that the paper used a strict p<0.005 two-sided threshold — the article should not imply pure post-hoc fishing past a lax bar.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: my search for later refutations rests on Europe PMC indexing alone, because I could not run open-web queries. A citation query and a title query both returned only the single affiliation erratum and unrelated downstream CALERIE work through 2026 — no Matters Arising, rebuttal, or failed replication. Non-indexed criticism would not have surfaced, so I cannot claim an exhaustive refutation search. I also did not open Belsky et al., eLife 2022 to check the observational hazard ratios underlying the 10-15% figure, so whether that number is itself well-founded is unverified here — I only verified that Waziry et al. state it and where they source it.

- **Post-hoc analysis of banked specimens** — `confirmed`
  Abstract states verbatim: 'Here we report the results of a post hoc analysis of the influence of CR on DNAm measures of aging in blood samples from the Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy (CALERIE) trial'. Methods state verbatim: 'We conducted new DNAm assays of stored blood biospecimens collected from the CALERIE Phase 2 randomized controlled trial and merged these data with existing secondary data from the trial.' Both strings read directly from the Europe PMC raw JATS XML.

- **N=197 with DNA methylation data out of 220 randomised** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: 'Of 238 eligible individuals, CALERIE randomized N = 220 participants (145 CR intervention and 75 AL control'. And: 'we analyzed data from all participants for whom blood DNAm data were available at baseline and at least one follow-up timepoint (N = 197; CR n = 128, AL n = 69).' Precision point the article should not lose: the per-timepoint analytic samples are smaller than 197 — 'baseline to 12-month change was measured for n = 125 CR and n = 66 AL participants and baseline to 24-month change was measured for n = 117 CR and n = 68 AL participants' (i.e. n=191 at 12mo, n=185 at 24mo). The headline d=-0.29 rests on n=191, not 197.

- **DunedinPACE d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.13)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from Results: 'CR treatment reduced participants' DunedinPACE by the 12-month follow-up and this reduction was maintained through follow-up at 24 months (12-month d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13), 24-month d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09), P < 0.003 for both).' Supplementary Table S4 Panel C gives ITT 12mo d=-0.29 [-0.45,-0.13], p=4.83E-04 and 24mo d=-0.25 [-0.41,-0.09], p=0.002. The quoted figure is specifically the 12-month ITT estimate — the article should say so, since an unlabelled '-0.29' silently drops the 24-month value. 95% CI (not 90%), and the supplement states 'All tests reported were two-sided.'

- **The other clocks tested (PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum) did NOT move significantly** — `corrected`
  Direction is right, enumeration is incomplete. WRONG: the null clocks were 'PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum'. RIGHT: five clock families were tested, each in an original and a principal-component version — Horvath, Hannum, Horvath Skin & Blood, PhenoAge, GrimAge — i.e. ten clock variants, and ALL ten were null in ITT at both 12 and 24 months. The article omits the Horvath Skin & Blood clock entirely. Main text reports only PhenoAge and GrimAge ('for PhenoAge, 12-month d = -0.03 (95% CI -0.19, 0.12), 24-month d = 0.05 (95% CI -0.11, 0.20), P > 0.50 for both; for GrimAge, 12-month d = -0.04 (95% CI -0.16, 0.07), 24-month d = 0.05 (95% CI -0.07, 0.17), P > 0.40 for both'); Horvath/Hannum/Skin & Blood appear only in Supplementary Table S4. From S4 (ITT, 12mo/24mo): Horvath Clock d=0.07 p=0.457 / d=0.05 p=0.599; PC Horvath d=0.01 p=0.771 / d=0.04 p=0.341; Hannum Clock d=0.03 p=0.758 / d=0.00 p=0.986; PC Hannum d=0.00 p=0.964 / d=0.04 p=0.501; Skin & Blood Clock d=-0.09 p=0.316 / d=-0.14 p=0.139; PC Skin & Blood d=0.02 p=0.647 / d=0.06 p=0.156; PhenoAge Clock d=0.04 p=0.719 / d=0.16 p=0.104; GrimAge Clock d=-0.10 p=0.170 / d=-0.01 p=0.898. Note the paper's declared threshold is strict: 'Bolded entries fall below the significance threshold of p < 0.005.' Nothing but DunedinPACE is bolded.

- **'One clock out of about five'** — `corrected`
  Undercounts the multiple-comparison surface and miscategorises DunedinPACE. WRONG: 'one clock out of about five'. RIGHT: DunedinPACE was the only one of ELEVEN DNAm measures of aging to show a significant effect — ten epigenetic clocks (Horvath, Hannum, Horvath Skin & Blood, PhenoAge, GrimAge, each in original and PC form) plus DunedinPACE. Separately, DunedinPACE is not a clock in the paper's own taxonomy: Table S4 puts clocks in Panels A and B and DunedinPACE alone in 'Panel C. Pace of Aging', and the text distinguishes clocks (which 'estimate biological age') from pace-of-aging measures (which 'estimate the rate of biological aging'). So the accurate formulation is 'zero of ten epigenetic clocks moved; the single pace-of-aging measure did'. Countervailing nuance the article should concede: this was not pure fishing — the paper pre-designated three measures as primary ('Primary analysis focused on the PhenoAge and GrimAge second-generation DNAm clocks and the DunedinPACE measure of pace of aging'), and DunedinPACE was one of the three.

- **Authors state treatment and control DunedinPACE trajectories overlap by close to 90%** — `confirmed`
  Verified verbatim, character for character, from the raw Europe PMC JATS XML (not a summarizer): 'Moreover, changes in DunedinPACE over follow-up showed substantial overlap between the CR treatment group and the AL control group; effect-size estimates imply close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups.'

- **Authors state no gold-standard measure of biological aging exists** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the Discussion limitations paragraph: 'We acknowledge limitations. There is no gold standard measure of biological aging.' (cites ref 37 = Ferrucci L et al., 'Measuring biological aging in humans: a quest', Aging Cell 2020). Note the paper writes 'gold standard' unhyphenated — the string 'gold-standard' does not appear.

- **Authors state whether the slowing translates to health outcomes is unknown** — `confirmed`
  Two separate verbatim sentences support this. (1) 'Follow-up in the CALERIE Trial did not extend beyond the intervention. It is therefore unclear if the changes in DunedinPACE observed during the 2-yr intervention will translate into reduced morbidity and mortality over the long term.' (2) 'CALERIE follow-up is, so far, limited to the end of the intervention period. Whether treatment and any slowing in biological aging that resulted from it translated to long-term clinical benefit is currently unknown.'

- **The Author Correction is administrative (first-affiliation fix), not scientific** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed from the full text of the Author Correction (Nat Aging 2023;3:753, doi 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y, PMID 37161091, PMCID PMC10275750), read as raw XML. Entire substantive body verbatim: 'Correction to: Nature Aging 10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y. Published online 9 February 2023. In the version of this article initially published, the first affiliation listed for D. W. Belsky was incorrect; it should have been shown as Butler Columbia Aging Center, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, New York, NY, USA. The error has been corrected in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.' No data, figure, or result was changed. A Europe PMC query on the article title returns exactly one erratum, so this is the only correction.

- **The 2-3% / 10-15% mortality / smoking-cessation translation is imported from DunedinPACE observational validation cohorts, and no mortality was measured in CALERIE** — `corrected`
  Substance holds but the attribution and the caliber are both off. WRONG (as implied): this is a 'widely repeated' media/secondary translation grafted onto the trial from outside. RIGHT: the translation is in the paper's own Discussion, in the authors' own words: 'These previous studies suggest that the CALERIE treatment effect of 2-3% slower pace of aging corresponds to a reduction in mortality risk of as much as 10-15%, similar in magnitude to the effect of smoking cessation intervention.' Second error — WRONG: '10-15% lower mortality risk' stated as a point range. RIGHT: the paper says 'as much as 10-15%', an explicit upper bound. Third error — WRONG: the smoking-cessation benchmark comes from DunedinPACE's observational validation cohorts. RIGHT: it cites ref 36 = Anthonisen NR et al., 'The effects of a smoking cessation intervention on 14.5-year mortality: a randomized clinical trial', Ann Intern Med 2005 — a randomized trial, not an observational cohort. What DOES hold: the mortality linkage itself is observational and external, flagged as such verbatim ('In observational studies with long-term follow-up, individuals with slower DunedinPACE are better-off on a range of healthspan metrics, including showing reduced incidence of morbidity and increased survival', citing ref 24 = Belsky et al., DunedinPACE, eLife 2022 and ref 29 = Sugden et al., Neurology 2022); and no mortality was measured in CALERIE, since 'Follow-up in the CALERIE Trial did not extend beyond the intervention.' Worth noting ref 29 (Sugden) concerns cognitive impairment and dementia, not mortality, so the mortality figure rests essentially on ref 24 alone. The '2-3%' figure is confirmed verbatim: 'Standardized treatment effects on DunedinPACE correspond to a reduction in the pace of aging of 2-3%.'

- **Search for later refutation, failed replication, or critical correspondence through 2026-07** — `confirmed`
  No refutation found. A Europe PMC citation query (CITES:37118425_MED restricted to CALERIE/caloric-restriction/DunedinPACE titles) returns 7 records through 2026, none of them a Matters Arising, rebuttal, or failed replication; the closest related items are 'The CALERIE Genomic Data Resource' (Nat Aging 2025) and downstream CALERIE analyses. A title query for CALERIE + methylation/aging returns only the article, its one erratum, and a conference abstract. Caveat on reachability: my WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could run open-web queries, so this null result rests on Europe PMC indexing alone — non-indexed critiques (blogs, preprint commentary, journal correspondence not deposited) would not surface. I did not verify the DunedinPACE eLife 2022 mortality hazard ratios at source, so the internal validity of the 10-15% figure itself remains unchecked.

**修正:**
- Replace 'one clock out of about five' with the accurate count: DunedinPACE was the only one of eleven DNAm measures of aging to show a treatment effect. Ten epigenetic clocks were tested — Horvath, Hannum, Horvath Skin & Blood, PhenoAge and GrimAge, each in an original and a principal-component (PC) version — and all ten were null at both 12 and 24 months.
- Do not call DunedinPACE a 'clock'. The paper's own taxonomy separates clocks (which estimate biological age; Supplementary Table S4 Panels A and B) from pace-of-aging measures (which estimate the rate of aging; Panel C, DunedinPACE alone). The sharpest true formulation is: zero of ten epigenetic clocks moved, and the single pace-of-aging measure did.
- Add the Horvath Skin & Blood clock to the list of clocks that did not move. The article's list (PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum) omits it. ITT: Skin & Blood Clock d=-0.09 p=0.316 (12mo), d=-0.14 p=0.139 (24mo); PC Skin & Blood d=0.02 p=0.647 (12mo), d=0.06 p=0.156 (24mo).
- Label the -0.29 with its timepoint: d=-0.29 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.13) is the 12-month intent-to-treat estimate. The 24-month estimate was d=-0.25 (95% CI -0.41 to -0.09). Both were two-sided, at 95% confidence.
- Concede that DunedinPACE was one of three PRE-DESIGNATED primary measures, not a post-hoc winner picked from the full panel: 'Primary analysis focused on the PhenoAge and GrimAge second-generation DNAm clocks and the DunedinPACE measure of pace of aging.' The paper is post hoc relative to the CALERIE trial, but the measure selection within it was declared. Overstating this as pure multiple-comparison fishing would be unfair to the source.
- Note the paper's significance threshold was strict, not lax: Supplementary Table S4 states 'Bolded entries fall below the significance threshold of p < 0.005' and 'All tests reported were two-sided.' DunedinPACE cleared it (p=4.83E-04 at 12 months); nothing else did. This strengthens the article's point rather than weakening it.
- Stop attributing the '2-3% = 10-15% lower mortality, like smoking cessation' translation to downstream media. It appears in the authors' own Discussion, verbatim: 'These previous studies suggest that the CALERIE treatment effect of 2-3% slower pace of aging corresponds to a reduction in mortality risk of as much as 10-15%, similar in magnitude to the effect of smoking cessation intervention.' The framing should be that the authors themselves imported it, which is a stronger and more accurate criticism.
- Restore the hedge: the paper says mortality risk reduction of 'AS MUCH AS 10-15%' — an explicit upper bound. Rendering it as a flat '10-15%' is caliber inflation.
- Correct the source of the smoking-cessation comparator. It is not from DunedinPACE's observational validation cohorts; it cites Anthonisen NR et al., 'The effects of a smoking cessation intervention on 14.5-year mortality: a randomized clinical trial', Ann Intern Med 2005;142:233-239 — a randomized trial. Only the DunedinPACE-to-mortality link is observational, citing Belsky et al., eLife 2022 (DunedinPACE) and Sugden et al., Neurology 2022 (the latter about cognitive impairment and dementia, not mortality).
- Keep 'no mortality was measured in CALERIE' but source it to the paper's own sentence: 'Follow-up in the CALERIE Trial did not extend beyond the intervention. It is therefore unclear if the changes in DunedinPACE observed during the 2-yr intervention will translate into reduced morbidity and mortality over the long term.'
- When quoting the gold-standard line, use the paper's unhyphenated wording: 'There is no gold standard measure of biological aging.' The string 'gold-standard' does not appear in the paper.
- Optional precision: if the article implies the -0.29 rests on all 197 participants, tighten it. The 12-month change was measured in n=125 CR + n=66 AL (191); the 24-month change in n=117 CR + n=68 AL (185). N=197 is the union of anyone with baseline plus at least one follow-up.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The '2-3% / 10-15% / smoking cessation' translation is not an external media artifact — it is in the paper's own Discussion, in the authors' voice. This contradicts the article's framing that the translation was 'imported' or 'widely repeated' by others, and is a materially stronger criticism than the one the article currently makes.
- The smoking-cessation benchmark is sourced to a RANDOMIZED trial (Anthonisen 2005, Lung Health Study, 14.5-year mortality), not to an observational cohort, contradicting the article's claim that the whole translation comes from DunedinPACE's observational validation cohorts.
- The paper tested eleven DNAm measures (ten clocks plus DunedinPACE), not 'about five' — the multiple-comparison surface is roughly twice what the article states, because every clock family was run in both original and PC versions. This cuts in the article's favour but the stated number is wrong.
- The paper's own significance threshold was p < 0.005 with two-sided tests, which is stricter than the conventional 0.05 the article's framing implicitly assumes. DunedinPACE's p=4.83E-04 clears it comfortably. The article should not imply the result squeaked past a lax bar.
- Countervailing to the article's 'fishing' implication: DunedinPACE was one of three pre-designated primary-analysis measures, not selected after the fact from the full panel.

### 票 2(CORRECTED)

I reached the primary documents directly and read the numbers myself rather than relying on any summarizer. Documents reached: (1) the full text of Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023, via PMC10148951 rendered HTML AND independently via the raw JATS XML at the EBI Europe PMC REST endpoint (www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10148951/fullTextXML); (2) the Supplementary Information PDF (43587_2022_357_MOESM1_ESM.pdf) downloaded from Springer static content and extracted to text LOCALLY with pdftotext -layout, so Supplementary Table S4 was read off the actual table, not summarized — local file at /Users/cissychen/.claude/projects/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/tool-results/supp.txt; (3) Supplementary Data 2 (MOESM4 CSV) of mixed-model change estimates, reproduced in full, which independently corroborates that DunedinPACE is the only measure whose CR and AL confidence intervals separate (pace 12mo AL +0.0107 [0.0000431, 0.0214] vs CR -0.0151 [-0.0243, -0.0059]) while all ten clock measures overlap heavily; (4) the Author Correction full text via PMC10275750 raw XML.

Guarding against the fabrication failure mode flagged in my instructions: I treated no quote as verbatim unless I saw the exact string. The load-bearing ~90% overlap sentence was fetched from two independent hosts (PMC HTML and EBI raw XML) and came back character-identical, and the Table S4 numbers were extracted locally from the PDF binary rather than through any summarizer, which is why I can assert them as read. Where a WebFetch returned only a summary (the first PMC pass), I re-derived the same facts from raw XML or local extraction before relying on them.

Overall the claim group is substantially accurate and its skeptical thrust is well founded — the post hoc framing, N=197/220, d=-0.29 (-0.45, -0.13), the null results on the other clocks, the ~90% overlap quote, the no-gold-standard quote, the unknown-clinical-benefit quote, the administrative-only correction, and the observational provenance of the mortality translation all check out against primary text. Verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS because of four caliber slips: the clock count is eleven measures / six families rather than "about five" and omits the Skin & Blood clock; d=-0.29 needs its 12-month ITT label; "10-15% lower mortality" drops the paper's "as much as" upper-bound qualifier; and the "one of five" framing misdescribes the multiplicity structure, since DunedinPACE was 1 of 3 pre-designated primary measures clearing a p<0.005 threshold.

Remaining uncertainty, stated plainly: (a) I could not reach the full citations for references 24, 29 and 36 — the Europe PMC XML reference list is truncated and nature.com sits behind an idp.nature.com auth redirect — so I did not verify which specific validation papers underpin the mortality extrapolation, and I did not guess. (b) This session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before my first search, so my refutation sweep is Europe PMC REST-only. It found zero Comment/Letter/Erratum records for DunedinPACE+CALERIE and no reanalysis or failed replication through 2026-07, but it would not surface preprints or non-indexed critiques. A future pass with search budget should re-check that specific gap.

- **Post-hoc analysis of banked specimens** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the Abstract: "Here we report the results of a post hoc analysis of the influence of CR on DNAm measures of aging in blood samples from the Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy (CALERIE) trial, a randomized controlled trial in which n = 220 adults without obesity were randomized to 25% CR or ad libitum control diet for 2 yr." Verbatim from Methods: "Illumina Infinium Methylation EPIC BeadChip arrays were used to assay genome-wide DNAm data from banked DNA samples extracted from blood collected at the baseline, 12-month and 24-month follow-ups." and "DNA extracted from blood samples was obtained from the CALERIE Biorepository at the University of Vermont." Both 'post hoc' and 'banked' are the paper's own words.

- **N=197 with DNA methylation data out of 220 randomised** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim: "Of 238 eligible individuals, CALERIE randomized N = 220 participants (145 CR intervention and 75 AL control" and "Blood DNAm data were generated at baseline and at least one follow-up timepoint for n = 197 participants (128 CR and 69 AL)." One addition worth carrying: the per-timepoint analytic N is smaller than 197 — verbatim: "Of the n = 197 participants for whom DNAm data were available from baseline and at least one follow-up assessment, baseline to 12-month change was measured for n = 125 CR and n = 66 AL participants and baseline to 24-month change was measured for n = 117 CR and n = 68 AL participants." So the headline d=-0.29 rests on 191 people, not 197.

- **DunedinPACE d=-0.29 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.13)** — `corrected`
  The numbers are exactly right but the timepoint label is missing. RIGHT: d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13) is the 12-month intent-to-treat estimate, p = 4.83E-04. Read directly off Supplementary Table S4 Panel C in the Supplementary PDF: "Dunedin 12mo -0.29 [-0.45 , -0.13] 4.83E-04" and "PACE 24mo -0.25 [-0.41 , -0.09] 0.002". The 24-month ITT effect is d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09). Main text verbatim: "CR treatment reduced participants' DunedinPACE by the 12-month follow-up and this reduction was maintained through follow-up at 24 months (12-month d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13), 24-month d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09), P < 0.003 for both)." Table S4 note confirms "All tests reported were two-sided" and that the paper used a strict threshold: "Bolded entries fall below the significance threshold of p < 0.005." So this is a two-sided, 95% CI, and it clears even the stricter 0.005 bar.

- **One clock out of about five** — `corrected`
  WRONG: 'about five' clocks. RIGHT: Supplementary Table S4 reports ELEVEN DNAm measures spanning SIX distinct algorithm families. Panel A (first-generation): Horvath Clock, PC Horvath Clock, Hannum Clock, PC Hannum Clock, Skin & Blood Clock, PC Skin & Blood Clock. Panel B (second-generation): PhenoAge Clock, PC PhenoAge Clock, GrimAge Clock, PC GrimAge Clock. Panel C: DunedinPACE. The claim's undercount is in the article's own favour — more clocks failed to move than it says — but it is still wrong, and it omits the Horvath Skin & Blood clock entirely. Countervailing nuance the article must not drop: within this (post hoc) DNAm paper, DunedinPACE was not one lucky hit fished from eleven. Table S4's footnote reads verbatim: "Table entries for measurements included in primary analysis (PC PhenoAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE) are highlighted in black text." Main text: "Our primary analysis focused on the PC versions of the PhenoAge and GrimAge second-generation clocks and DunedinPACE, all of which show exceptional test-retest reliability in technical replicates." So it was 1 of 3 pre-designated primary measures, with the other 8 as supplementary. Framing it as '1 of ~5' implies a multiplicity problem of the wrong shape.

- **PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum did NOT move significantly** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed, and the true picture is stronger than claimed. Every one of the ten non-DunedinPACE measures was null on ITT. Verbatim from Supplementary Table S4 (ITT column, Cohen's d [95% CI] p): Horvath Clock 12mo 0.07 [-0.11 , 0.25] 0.457 / 24mo 0.05 [-0.14 , 0.24] 0.599; PC Horvath 12mo 0.01 [-0.06 , 0.09] 0.771 / 24mo 0.04 [-0.04 , 0.12] 0.341; Hannum Clock 12mo 0.03 [-0.15 , 0.21] 0.758 / 24mo 0.00 [-0.18 , 0.18] 0.986; PC Hannum 12mo 0.00 [-0.11 , 0.11] 0.964 / 24mo 0.04 [-0.08 , 0.15] 0.501; Skin & Blood 12mo -0.09 [-0.26 , 0.08] 0.316 / 24mo -0.14 [-0.32 , 0.04] 0.139; PC Skin & Blood 12mo 0.02 [-0.07 , 0.11] 0.647 / 24mo 0.06 [-0.02 , 0.15] 0.156; PhenoAge Clock 12mo 0.04 [-0.17 , 0.24] 0.719 / 24mo 0.16 [-0.03 , 0.36] 0.104; PC PhenoAge 12mo -0.03 [-0.19 , 0.12] 0.663 / 24mo 0.05 [-0.11 , 0.20] 0.550; GrimAge Clock 12mo -0.10 [-0.23 , 0.04] 0.170 / 24mo -0.01 [-0.14 , 0.12] 0.898; PC GrimAge 12mo -0.04 [-0.16 , 0.07] 0.461 / 24mo 0.05 [-0.07 , 0.17] 0.432. Smallest p among all ten is 0.104 — null at 0.05, not just at the paper's 0.005 threshold. Note also several point estimates run in the FASTER-aging direction under CR (e.g. PhenoAge 24mo d = +0.16). Main-text abstract verbatim: "but did not lead to significant changes in biological age estimates measured by various DNAm clocks including PhenoAge and GrimAge." Horvath/Hannum/Skin & Blood results appear only in Supplementary, per verbatim: "In the interest of comparability across studies, we report results for so-called 'first-generation' clocks developed to predict chronological age and the original versions of the PhenoAge and GrimAge clocks in the Supplementary Information."

- **Authors state treatment and control DunedinPACE trajectories overlap by close to 90%** — `confirmed`
  VERBATIM CONFIRMED, character-for-character, and independently re-verified from two separate hosts (PMC rendered HTML at PMC10148951, and the raw JATS XML from the EBI Europe PMC REST endpoint) returning identical strings: "Moreover, changes in DunedinPACE over follow-up showed substantial overlap between the CR treatment group and the AL control group; effect-size estimates imply close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups."   Verbatim, opening the limitations paragraph: "We acknowledge limitations. There is no gold standard measure of biological aging". Followed verbatim by: "Nevertheless, these measures are acknowledged to be incomplete summaries of biological changes that occur with aging and to have technical limitations".

- **Authors state whether the slowing translates to health outcomes is unknown** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim, two separate statements. Discussion: "Follow-up in the CALERIE Trial did not extend beyond the intervention. It is therefore unclear if the changes in DunedinPACE observed during the 2-yr intervention will translate into reduced morbidity and mortality over the long term." - **The Author Correction is administrative (first-affiliation fix), not scientific** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim in full. Author Correction, Nature Aging, DOI 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y, PMID 37161091, PMCID PMC10275750; the parent article's change-history note reads "5/9/2023 A Correction to this paper has been published: 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y". - **2-3% slower pace = 10-15% lower mortality, comparable to smoking cessation, is imported from observational cohorts; no mortality measured in CALERIE** — `corrected`
  The provenance claim is fully confirmed; only the number's caliber is off. WRONG: '10-15% lower mortality risk' stated as a point estimate.   None found. **修正:**
- Replace 'one clock out of about five' with the actual count: Supplementary Table S4 reports ELEVEN DNA methylation measures across SIX algorithm families — Horvath, PC Horvath, Hannum, PC Hannum, Skin & Blood, PC Skin & Blood (Panel A); PhenoAge, PC PhenoAge, GrimAge, PC GrimAge (Panel B); DunedinPACE (Panel C). The article's list of 'the other clocks tested' must add the Horvath Skin & Blood clock, which it currently omits.
- Do not imply DunedinPACE was one lucky hit fished out of eleven. Table S4's footnote states verbatim: 'Table entries for measurements included in primary analysis (PC PhenoAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE) are highlighted in black text.' DunedinPACE was 1 of 3 pre-designated primary measures within the paper; the other 8 were supplementary. The correct multiplicity criticism is that the entire DNAm paper is post hoc relative to the CALERIE trial — not that the primary analysis scanned eleven clocks.
- Label the timepoint on the headline effect: d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13), p = 4.83E-04 is the 12-month intent-to-treat estimate. The 24-month ITT estimate is d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09), p = 0.002. Both are two-sided, 95% CI.
- Change '10-15% lower mortality risk' to the paper's actual wording, 'a reduction in mortality risk of AS MUCH AS 10-15%'. The paper states an upper bound; the widely repeated version silently converts it into a point estimate. The article should flag that conversion as part of the caliber slippage it is documenting.
- Strengthen the null result rather than leaving it vague: all ten non-DunedinPACE measures were null with smallest p = 0.104 (PhenoAge Clock, 24 months, d = +0.16), so they fail at conventional p<0.05 and not merely at the paper's stricter threshold. Table S4 states verbatim 'Bolded entries fall below the significance threshold of p < 0.005' and 'All tests reported were two-sided.' Several point estimates, including PhenoAge at 24 months, ran in the FASTER-aging direction under caloric restriction.
- If the article cites N=197, note that the per-timepoint analytic sample is smaller: baseline-to-12-month change was measured for n=125 CR and n=66 AL (191 total), and baseline-to-24-month change for n=117 CR and n=68 AL (185 total). The d=-0.29 headline rests on 191 participants, not 197.
- When quoting the overlap sentence, use it in full and verbatim: 'Moreover, changes in DunedinPACE over follow-up showed substantial overlap between the CR treatment group and the AL control group; effect-size estimates imply close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups.'
- The Author Correction characterization is correct and can be stated with specificity: Nature Aging, 9 May 2023, DOI 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y, correcting only the first affiliation listed for D. W. Belsky to 'Butler Columbia Aging Center, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health'. No result, figure, or number was altered.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The claim's own clock count is wrong in a direction that understates the article's case: eleven measures were tested, not about five, and the Horvath Skin & Blood clock (both original and PC versions) is missing from the claim's list of non-movers entirely.
- Countervailing evidence against a pure 'multiple comparisons' reading: DunedinPACE was one of only three pre-designated primary measures (PC PhenoAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE), and it survived a stricter-than-conventional significance threshold of p<0.005 with p=4.83E-04, two-sided. An article that frames this as one hit out of five clocks is attacking a multiplicity problem the primary analysis did not have.
- The dose-response and instrumental-variable analyses cut in the result's favour and are not mentioned in the claim: verbatim, 'In IV analysis, the effect of 20% CR on DunedinPACE was d = -0.43 (95% CI -0.67, -0.19) at 12 months and d = -0.40 (95% CI -0.67, -0.12) at 24 months (P < 0.005 for both). IV effect-size estimates for PhenoAge and GrimAge were small (d = -0.13-0.01; P > 0.15).' Also 'For DunedinPACE, the treatment effect in the >10% CR group was d = -0.33 at 12 months and d = -0.33 at 24 months, as compared with d = -0.19 at 12 months and d = -0.14 at 24 months in the <10% CR group.'
- A limitation the paper raises that runs opposite to the article's skeptical framing: 'measurement error due to technical limitations of DNAm assays may bias effect estimates towards the null. Treatment effect estimates may therefore represent a lower-bound of the true impact of CALERIE intervention on biological aging.'
- Independent supporting evidence published since: Moulds et al., 'Graded Calorie Restriction Causes Graded Slowing of Epigenetic Ageing in Mice', Aging Cell 2026 — a dose-response replication of the direction of effect in a different species. No failed replication or reanalysis of Waziry was found.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

Web search budget was exhausted, so I bypassed the summarizing fetch layer entirely and downloaded raw primary documents with curl, then grepped the raw text myself — every string quoted below was read by me in the raw source, not relayed by a summarizer. Documents reached verbatim: (1) the full JATS XML of Waziry et al., Nature Aging 3:248-257, 2023, doi 10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y, via the Europe PMC REST fullTextXML endpoint for PMC10148951; (2) Supplementary Information PDF 43587_2022_357_MOESM1_ESM.pdf from static-content.springer.com, converted with pdftotext -layout, which contains Supplementary Table S4 with the full eleven-measure ITT and TOT results; (3) the full text of the Author Correction, PMC10275750, doi 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y; (4) the PubMed EFetch XML for PMID 37118425 to enumerate all CommentsCorrections; (5) the eLife 2022 DunedinPACE abstract (doi 10.7554/eLife.73420) to confirm its validation cohorts are observational; (6) the full text of the HUNT mortality paper, PMC13188620, 2026. Confirmed exactly as claimed: N=197 (128 CR, 69 AL) out of 220 randomised (145 CR, 75 AL); DunedinPACE 12-month d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13); PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath and Hannum all null in every specification; the 'close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories' sentence verbatim; 'There is no gold standard measure of biological aging' verbatim; the 'currently unknown' clinical-benefit caveat verbatim; and the Author Correction as a pure first-affiliation fix for D. W. Belsky. Three things are off. First, the clock count: Supplementary Table S4 reports eleven measures across six families, and the claim's list omits the Skin & Blood clock, so 'about five' understates the multiplicity. Second, the post-hoc framing slips: the DNAm study is post hoc relative to the trial, but DunedinPACE was one of three measures the authors designated as the primary analysis (with PC PhenoAge and PC GrimAge), so 'one clock out of about five' wrongly implies selection after the fact — though the paper contains no pre-registration language anywhere, which limits how much credit that designation earns. Third, the mortality translation is not a media artifact: the authors themselves write it in the Discussion, hedged as 'as much as 10-15%', with the observational DunedinPACE-mortality mapping from Belsky eLife 2022 but the smoking-cessation comparator from Anthonisen 2005, which is a randomized trial. I searched actively for refutation and found none directed at the paper: exactly one erratum, no retraction, no expression of concern, and zero Matters Arising, comments or replies in Europe PMC as of 2026-07. What I did find is that the downstream mortality extrapolation is shaky — the HUNT cohort gives DunedinPACE a significant per-SD HR of 1.99 in one wave and a null 1.15 in the other. Remaining uncertainty: I read Supplementary Table S4 from a text-layout extraction of a multi-column PDF, which is exactly the failure mode flagged in the brief, so I cross-checked the DunedinPACE row against the independently-stated main-text values (-0.29 / -0.25 with matching CIs) and they agree, and the Horvath/Hannum rows are internally consistent across Tables S4 and S5; I did not independently verify the CALERIE trial registration record (NCT00427193) or the underlying Dunedin cohort mortality estimates that generate the 10-15% figure.

- **N=197 with DNA methylation data out of 220 randomised** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim in the paper: 'Blood DNAm data were generated at baseline and at least one follow-up timepoint for n = 197 participants (128 CR and 69 AL).' And: 'Of 238 eligible individuals, CALERIE randomized N = 220 participants (145 CR intervention and 75 AL control; Fig. 1).' Randomisation ratio 2:1. Caveat the article should not lose: 197 means baseline plus AT LEAST ONE follow-up; only n=105 CR (82%) and n=59 AL (86%) had all three timepoints. Per-timepoint analysable N: 12-month change n=125 CR / 66 AL; 24-month change n=117 CR / 68 AL.

- **Post-hoc analysis of banked specimens** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verbatim: 'Here we report the results of a post hoc analysis of the influence of CR on DNAm measures of aging in blood samples from the ... CALERIE ... trial'. Methods verbatim: 'We analyzed blood biospecimens collected from the CALERIE Phase 2 randomized controlled trial and merged these data with existing secondary data from the trial. The assays of the biospecimens were conducted blind to the conditions of the trial.'

- **DunedinPACE d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.13)** — `corrected`
  The numbers are exact but the timepoint is unstated. WRONG (as written): a bare 'd = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.13)'. RIGHT: that is the 12-MONTH intent-to-treat estimate; the 24-month estimate is d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09). Verbatim: 'CR treatment reduced participants DunedinPACE by the 12-month follow-up and this reduction was maintained through follow-up at 24 months (12-month d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13), 24-month d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09), P < 0.003 for both).' Supplementary Table S4 Panel C gives exact p = 4.83E-04 (12mo) and 0.002 (24mo). Tests two-sided, 95% CIs, and the significance threshold used was the conservative P < 0.005, not 0.05 — this strengthens rather than weakens the sceptical framing.

- **The other clocks tested (PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum) did NOT move significantly** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed for all four, at both timepoints, in ITT and in TOT/instrumental-variable analysis, and in both original and principal-component versions. Main text verbatim: 'change in PhenoAge and GrimAge values did not differ between CR and AL groups (for PhenoAge, 12-month d = -0.03 (95% confidence interval (95% CI) -0.19, 0.12), 24-month d = 0.05 (95% CI -0.11, 0.20), P > 0.50 for both; for GrimAge, 12-month d = -0.04 (95% CI -0.16, 0.07), 24-month d = 0.05 (95% CI -0.07, 0.17), P > 0.40 for both).' Supplementary Table S4 Panel A (read directly from the supplementary PDF) gives Horvath Clock 12mo d = 0.07 [-0.11, 0.25] p = 0.457, 24mo d = 0.05 [-0.14, 0.24] p = 0.599; Hannum Clock 12mo d = 0.03 [-0.15, 0.21] p = 0.758, 24mo d = 0.00 [-0.18, 0.18] p = 0.986. Not one non-DunedinPACE measure came near p < 0.005; the smallest null p-value anywhere in Table S4 is 0.104.

- **One clock out of about five** — `corrected`
  Undercount, and the list is incomplete. WRONG: 'about five' clocks, namely DunedinPACE, PhenoAge, GrimAge, Horvath, Hannum. RIGHT: Supplementary Table S4 reports ELEVEN DNAm measures — Horvath, PC Horvath, Hannum, PC Hannum, Skin & Blood, PC Skin & Blood, PhenoAge, PC PhenoAge, GrimAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE — i.e. six clock families. The claim silently drops the Skin & Blood clock, which was also tested and also null (ITT 12mo d = -0.09 [-0.26, 0.08] p = 0.316; 24mo d = -0.14 [-0.32, 0.04] p = 0.139). One of eleven measures moved; ten did not.

- **Implication that DunedinPACE was a post-hoc-selected winner among the clocks** — `corrected`
  WRONG (implied by 'one clock out of about five, in a post-hoc analysis'): that the authors ran five clocks and reported the one that hit. RIGHT: within this post-hoc DNAm study the authors designated three measures as primary in advance of reporting. Main text verbatim: 'Our primary analysis focused on the PC versions of the PhenoAge and GrimAge second-generation clocks and DunedinPACE, all of which show exceptional test-retest reliability in technical replicates.' Supplementary Table S4 footnote verbatim: 'Table entries for measurements included in primary analysis (PC PhenoAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE) are highlighted in black text.' So DunedinPACE was 1 of 3 primary measures (2 of the 3 were null), with Horvath/Hannum/Skin & Blood and the original non-PC versions relegated to supplement. Counter-caveat the article may keep: the words 'pre-registered', 'preregistered', 'pre-specified' and 'analysis plan' appear NOWHERE in the paper, so the 'primary analysis' designation is author-asserted in the report, not a verifiable pre-registration.

- **Authors state treatment and control DunedinPACE trajectories overlap by close to 90%** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim, read by me in the raw JATS XML: 'Moreover, changes in DunedinPACE over follow-up showed substantial overlap between the CR treatment group and the AL control group; effect-size estimates imply close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups.' Exact string confirmed including 'close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups'.

- **Authors state no gold-standard measure of biological aging exists** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim, immediately after the overlap sentence: 'We acknowledge limitations. There is no gold standard measure of biological aging' (citing ref 37, Ferrucci et al., Aging Cell 2020). Note the paper writes 'gold standard' unhyphenated. Continues: 'Nevertheless, these measures are acknowledged to be incomplete summaries of biological changes that occur with aging'.

- **Authors state whether the slowing translates to health outcomes is unknown** — `confirmed`
  Two verbatim statements. Limitations: 'CALERIE follow-up is, so far, limited to the end of the intervention period. Whether treatment and any slowing in biological aging that resulted from it translated to long-term clinical benefit is currently unknown.' Discussion: 'Follow-up in the CALERIE Trial did not extend beyond the intervention. It is therefore unclear if the changes in DunedinPACE observed during the 2-yr intervention will translate into reduced morbidity and mortality over the long term.' The phrase 'health outcomes' does not itself appear; the paper says 'long-term clinical benefit' and 'reduced morbidity and mortality'.

- **The Author Correction is administrative (a first-affiliation fix), not scientific** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim from the correction notice (Nat Aging 3, 753, 2023; doi 10.1038/s43587-023-00432-y; PMID 37161091; published online 9 May 2023): 'Correction to: Nature Aging 10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y. Published online 9 February 2023. In the version of this article initially published, the first affiliation listed for D. W. Belsky was incorrect; it should have been shown as Butler Columbia Aging Center, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, New York, NY, USA. The error has been corrected in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.' PubMed CommentsCorrections for PMID 37118425 lists exactly one ErratumIn and nothing else — no retraction, no expression of concern, no Matters Arising, no published critical comment (Europe PMC citation search for comments/replies on this paper returns 0 hits as of 2026-07).

- **'2-3% slower pace of aging = 10-15% lower mortality, comparable to smoking cessation' is imported from DunedinPACE observational validation cohorts; no mortality measured in CALERIE** — `corrected`
  Substance right, attribution and caliber wrong. WRONG: framing it as a 'widely repeated' downstream translation, stated flatly as '= 10-15% lower mortality risk'. RIGHT: it is the authors' own sentence in the Discussion, and it is hedged as an upper bound. Verbatim: 'In observational studies with long-term follow-up, individuals with slower DunedinPACE are better-off on a range of healthspan metrics, including showing reduced incidence of morbidity and increased survival(24,29). These previous studies suggest that the CALERIE treatment effect of 2-3% slower pace of aging corresponds to a reduction in mortality risk of as much as 10-15%, similar in magnitude to the effect of smoking cessation intervention(36).' The mortality mapping is indeed observational — ref 24 is Belsky et al., eLife 2022, the DunedinPACE validation paper (Dunedin 1972-73 birth cohort plus five additional observational datasets); note ref 29 (Sugden et al., Neurology 2022) is about cognitive impairment and dementia, not mortality. But ref 36, the smoking-cessation comparator, is Anthonisen et al., Ann Intern Med 2005 — a RANDOMIZED trial (Lung Health Study, 14.5-year mortality), not observational. And no mortality was measured in CALERIE: confirmed by the authors ('CALERIE follow-up is, so far, limited to the end of the intervention period') and by the absence of any CALERIE mortality follow-up publication in Europe PMC as of 2026-07. The 2-3% figure itself checks out arithmetically: baseline DunedinPACE SD in CALERIE is 0.09 (Supplementary Table S4 note), so d = -0.29 x 0.09 = ~0.026 on a ~1.0 scale.

- **Independent check on the durability of the 10-15% mortality import** — `confirmed`
  Searched for post-2023 contradicting evidence. The per-SD DunedinPACE-mortality association that the 10-15% figure rests on is not stable across independent cohorts. Read directly from the full text of Nguyen et al., Clin Epigenetics 2026 (HUNT study, PMC13188620): adjusted per-SD all-cause mortality HR for DunedinPACE was 1.99 (95% CI 1.09-3.64) in HUNT2 but 1.15 (95% CI 0.70-1.89), i.e. null, in HUNT3; the authors note 'a 23% higher risk reported in a Finnish study' for comparison. Nothing overturns Waziry et al., but the mortality translation should be presented as an unstable observational extrapolation, not a fixed conversion rate.

**修正:**
- Do not write 'one clock out of about five'. The paper reports ELEVEN DNAm measures in Supplementary Table S4 — Horvath, PC Horvath, Hannum, PC Hannum, Skin & Blood, PC Skin & Blood, PhenoAge, PC PhenoAge, GrimAge, PC GrimAge, and DunedinPACE (six clock families). Write 'one of eleven DNA methylation measures moved; the other ten did not.' The current list omits the Skin & Blood clock, which was tested and null (12mo d = -0.09 [-0.26, 0.08] p = 0.316).
- Do not imply DunedinPACE was cherry-picked from a panel after the fact. The paper states verbatim: 'Our primary analysis focused on the PC versions of the PhenoAge and GrimAge second-generation clocks and DunedinPACE', and Supplementary Table S4 footnotes 'measurements included in primary analysis (PC PhenoAge, PC GrimAge, DunedinPACE)'. The accurate framing: the DNAm study as a whole is post hoc relative to the trial, but within it DunedinPACE was 1 of 3 designated primary measures — and 2 of those 3 were null. The article may add that the paper contains no pre-registration statement (the words 'pre-registered', 'pre-specified' and 'analysis plan' do not appear), so the primary-analysis designation is author-asserted rather than externally verifiable.
- Specify the timepoint on the effect size: d = -0.29 (95% CI -0.45, -0.13) is the 12-month intent-to-treat estimate; the 24-month estimate is d = -0.25 (95% CI -0.41, -0.09). Exact p-values from Supplementary Table S4 Panel C are 4.83E-04 and 0.002.
- Note that the main-text 'PhenoAge' and 'GrimAge' results are the principal-component (PC) versions of those clocks, not the original ones; the original versions are reported only in the Supplementary Information (and are also null).
- Add that the significance threshold used was the conservative P < 0.005 (the authors write: 'We use P < 0.005 as a conservative threshold for statistical significance following guidance from leaders in the field'), with two-sided tests and 95% CIs. This makes the null results on the other clocks more, not less, robust — the smallest p-value among all null measures in Table S4 is 0.104.
- Attribute the '2-3% = 10-15% mortality, comparable to smoking cessation' translation to the authors' own Discussion, not to downstream popularisers, and preserve the hedge. The paper says the effect 'corresponds to a reduction in mortality risk of as much as 10-15%, similar in magnitude to the effect of smoking cessation intervention' — 'as much as' is an upper bound and must not be rendered as a flat equality.
- Correct the sourcing of the smoking-cessation comparator: the DunedinPACE-to-mortality mapping is indeed observational (ref 24, Belsky et al., eLife 2022, the Dunedin birth cohort plus five additional observational datasets), but the smoking-cessation reference (ref 36) is Anthonisen et al., Ann Intern Med 2005 — a randomized trial (Lung Health Study, 14.5-year mortality). Also note that the paper's other cited support, ref 29 (Sugden et al., Neurology 2022), concerns cognitive impairment and dementia, not mortality.
- Keep 'no mortality was measured in CALERIE' — it is correct and the authors say so ('CALERIE follow-up is, so far, limited to the end of the intervention period'), and no CALERIE mortality follow-up has been published as of 2026-07.
- Quote the overlap sentence exactly as printed: 'Moreover, changes in DunedinPACE over follow-up showed substantial overlap between the CR treatment group and the AL control group; effect-size estimates imply close to 90% overlap of DunedinPACE trajectories between the two groups.'
- Quote the gold-standard sentence exactly, unhyphenated: 'There is no gold standard measure of biological aging.' If quoting the health-outcomes caveat, use the paper's actual wording: 'Whether treatment and any slowing in biological aging that resulted from it translated to long-term clinical benefit is currently unknown.'
- If describing the sample, note that N=197 means baseline plus at least one follow-up; only 105 of 128 CR (82%) and 59 of 69 AL (86%) participants had data at all three timepoints, and the 24-month analysis rests on n=117 CR / 68 AL.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Nguyen et al., Clinical Epigenetics 2026 (HUNT study, PMC13188620, doi 10.1186/s13148-026-02070-8): the observational per-SD DunedinPACE-to-mortality association underpinning the '10-15%' figure does not replicate stably. Adjusted all-cause mortality HR per SD of DunedinPACE was 1.99 (95% CI 1.09-3.64) in HUNT2 but a null 1.15 (95% CI 0.70-1.89) in HUNT3; the paper cites a Finnish cohort at 1.23. In the same cohort GrimAge2 was the consistently significant predictor (HR 2.42 and 2.30), i.e. the clock that did NOT move in CALERIE is the one with the more reproducible mortality signal.
- The claim's own clock list is contradicted by the paper's supplementary material: the Skin & Blood clock and PC Skin & Blood clock were also tested (and null), so 'about five' clocks understates the multiplicity that the article is trying to highlight.

## V25 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

Primary documents reached: (1) Villareal DT et al., 'Effect of Two-Year Caloric Restriction on Bone Metabolism and Bone Mineral Density in Non-Obese Younger Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial,' J Bone Miner Res 2016;31(1):40-51, PMID 26332798, PMC4834845 — abstract obtained verbatim via TWO independent routes (PubMed record and the Europe PMC REST API, query EXT_ID:26332798) and the two strings matched character-for-character, so the BMD numbers, p-values, N per arm, BMI, age and the 'potential limitation' sentence are solidly verified. (2) Kraus WE et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019, PMID 31303390 / PMC6707879 — abstract obtained verbatim from Europe PMC REST; the 71% sentence including its parenthetical derivation is exactly as claimed. (3) Shen W et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2021, PMID 34159359 / PMC8645192 — abstract obtained verbatim from Europe PMC REST; n=43 (28/15) and 'intended, 25%; actual, 13.7%' confirmed, and the 68.4/7.4/2.2 depot breakdown confirmed. (4) Romashkan SV et al., Oncotarget 2016, PMID 26992237 — abstract verbatim from Europe PMC REST. (5) Das SK et al., AJCN 2017, PMID 28275127 — abstract read; no bone outcome. (6) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 outcomes module for NCT00427193. (7) Europe PMC citation query for comments/letters/errata on PMID 26332798 — empty result set, so no correction or published rebuttal exists.

Limits I will not paper over. WebSearch quota was exhausted at the start of this session, so all retrieval was direct WebFetch against PubMed, Europe PMC REST, PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov; I could not run open-web sweeps for grey-literature criticism. More importantly, the Villareal FULL TEXT was reachable only through PMC's HTML on a single host: Europe PMC's fullTextXML endpoint 404s for PMC4834845 (JBMR is not in the OA subset), the PMC PDF route returned only an interstitial, and the Oxford Academic copy is paywalled. The Discussion quotes I rely on — the FRAX/T-score sentence, 'modest but significant decline in BMD, expected on the basis of the weight lost', 'predicted from their decrease in body weight', 'central sites of the spine and hip but not at the peripheral site of the wrist or whole body', the 'secondary outcomes of CALERIE phase 2' sentence, and the Table 2 baseline BMD values (1.042 / 0.984 / 0.839 g/cm2) — were returned identically across three separately-worded extraction prompts, and the FRAX line carried an intact inline reference marker to R46, which is a signature of genuine extraction rather than generation. I nonetheless flag them as single-host and recommend the writer confirm the FRAX sentence and the Table 2 baselines against the PDF before printing any percent BMD figure. The three-site BMD numbers, the p-values, the 'potential limitation' wording, the 71% and the 68.4/7.4/2.2 breakdown are NOT subject to this caveat — those are all double-sourced or came from the REST API directly.

Net: the claim group is substantially right on the bone finding and on the 71% figure, and right that no long-term bone follow-up exists. It is wrong on the 13.7% CR figure in the MRI ancillary, wrong to attribute '78%' to that paper as a reported result, and it commits caliber slippage three times over — by omitting that BMD was a non-registered secondary outcome, by omitting the authors' own 'modest' / 'expected from weight loss' / '<0.5% fracture risk' qualifiers while keeping only their 'potential limitation' phrase, and by implying general skeletal loss when wrist and whole-body BMD were unchanged. Hence CORRECTED rather than HOLDS or OVERTURNED.

- **Villareal et al. 2016 (J Bone Miner Res 31(1):40-51, PMID 26332798) reported significant BMD loss at lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck after 2 years of CR** — `confirmed`
  Abstract verified verbatim via two independent routes (PubMed record and Europe PMC REST /search?query=EXT_ID:26332798, identical strings): 'Compared with AL, the CR group had greater changes in BMD at 24 months: lumbar spine (-0.013 ± 0.003 versus 0.007 ± 0.004 g/cm(2); p < 0.001), total hip (-0.017 ± 0.002 versus 0.001 ± 0.003 g/cm(2); p < 0.001), and femoral neck (-0.015 ± 0.003 versus -0.005 ± 0.004 g/cm(2); p = 0.03).' All three sites significant between-group. CAVEAT the article must not flatten: femoral neck is p=0.03, an order of magnitude weaker than the other two, and the AL control group ALSO lost femoral-neck BMD (-0.005), so the CR-vs-AL femoral-neck gap is only ~0.010 g/cm2. Independently corroborated by the CALERIE safety paper (Romashkan 2016, Oncotarget, PMID 26992237): 'At months 12 and 24, bone mineral densities at the lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck of participants in the CR group were significantly lower than in those in the AL group.'

- **Effect sizes / magnitude of the BMD loss** — `corrected`
  The paper reports ONLY absolute g/cm2 changes in text and tables — it does not state percent BMD changes in the text. Against Table 2 CR-group baselines (lumbar spine 1.042, total hip 0.984, femoral neck 0.839 g/cm2) the CR-group 24-month changes correspond to roughly -1.2%, -1.7% and -1.8%. If the article quotes percentages it must label them as derived, not as reported figures. The paper's own magnitude statement is materially softer than 'significant BMD loss': 'At the femoral neck, the average BMD loss was -0.015 g/cm2 (-0.16 T-score units). Using the WHO Fracture Risk Assessment Tool, this degree of BMD loss in a 50-year-old woman without risk factors corresponds to <0.5% increase in 10-year risk of fracture.' (Table-2 baselines and the FRAX sentence come from PMC4834845 full-text extraction, consistent across three separately-worded fetches, but I could not corroborate them via a second independent host — Europe PMC fullTextXML returns 404 and the OUP copy is paywalled. Treat as high-but-not-certain confidence.)

- **'all three clinically important fracture sites' — i.e. bone loss was general** — `corrected`
  WRONG if read as generalized bone loss. The three named sites are correct, but the paper explicitly limits the finding: 'BMD decreased at the central sites of the spine and hip but not at the peripheral site of the wrist or whole body.' Whole-body and wrist (radius) BMD did NOT decline. The article must not imply system-wide skeletal loss.

- **'about 12% caloric restriction', 2 years, healthy non-obese adults, mean age about 38** — `confirmed`
  Villareal abstract verbatim: 'Two-hundred eighteen non-obese (body mass index [BMI] 25.1 ± 1.7 kg/m(2)), younger (age 37.9 ± 7.2 years) adults were randomly assigned to 25% CR (CR group, n = 143) or ad libitum (AL group, n = 75) for 2 years.' Prescribed CR was 25%; ACHIEVED CR was 11.9% (Kraus 2019 verbatim: 'a mean reduction in calorie intake of 11·9% (SE 0·7; from 2467 kcal to 2170 kcal)'). Villareal reports the trajectory: '19.5±0.8% over the first 6 months, 10.8±0.7% over the second 6 months, and 8.3±0.8% over the remaining 12 months.' So ~12% is the 2-year mean, but by the second year CR was only ~8%. The article should say 'prescribed 25%, achieved ~12%' — writing only '12% CR' hides that this was a failed-adherence 25% arm.

- **BMD was an investigator-reported outcome — pre-specification status** — `corrected`
  NOT a pre-specified primary endpoint. The paper itself states: 'The data reported here were obtained as secondary outcomes of CALERIE phase 2, which has the overall aim of examining the effects of sustained ~25% CR on slowing aging in non-obese humans.' The registry (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00427193) lists primary outcomes as change in core body temperature and change in resting metabolic rate at 12 and 24 months; bone mineral density does not appear in the registered outcome list at all. The abstract's phrase 'Main outcomes were BMD and markers of bone turnover' refers to this report's outcomes, not the trial's registered primary endpoint.

- **Authors characterise the bone loss as a limitation/concern — verbatim** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim in the abstract Conclusions (verified on two independent hosts): 'Therefore, bone loss at clinically important sites of osteoporotic fractures represents a potential limitation of prolonged CR for extending life span.' The word is 'potential limitation'. BUT the Discussion's own concluding sentence is markedly hedged and the article must not omit it: 'In conclusion, our results demonstrate that 2-years sustained CR in non-obese younger adults increases bone resorption while decreasing bone formation (i.e. uncoupling of bone turnover) and causes a modest but significant decline in BMD, expected on the basis of the weight lost, at clinically important sites of osteoporotic fractures.' Also: 'The decreases in spine and hip BMD in our participants, however, were predicted from their decrease in body weight.' And the companion CALERIE safety paper concluded 'Two-years of CR at levels achieved in CALERIE was safe and well tolerated. Close monitoring for excessive bone loss and anemia is important.'

- **71% of the weight lost was fat (Kraus 2019)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from Kraus WE et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019 (PMID 31303390, PMC6707879), abstract Findings: 'a sustained mean weight reduction of 7·5 kg (SE 0·4) versus an increase of 0·1 kg (0·5) in the control group, of which 71% (mean change in fat mass 5·3 kg [SE 0·3] divided by mean change in weight 7·5 kg [0·4]) was fat mass loss.' The complementary 'about 29% was not fat' is arithmetically correct and matches Villareal's DXA fat-free-mass change (-2.2 ± 0.2 kg), but note 29% of weight lost is fat-free MASS, which includes water and glycogen — it is not 29% muscle.

- **MRI ancillary study (n=43), about 13% CR over 24 months, 78% of tissue loss as fat** — `corrected`
  Source is Shen W et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2021;114(4) (PMID 34159359, PMC8645192). n=43 CONFIRMED verbatim: '43 healthy adults [25-50 y; BMI (kg/m2): 22-28] randomly assigned to 25% CR (n = 28) or ad libitum (AL) eating (n = 15)'. TWO corrections. (1) CR dose: WRONG as 'about 13%' — the paper says 'Twenty-four months of CR (intended, 25%; actual, 13.7%)'. 13.7% rounds to 14%, not 13%.
