'Association of eating duration less than 8 h with all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality.' Diabetes Metab Syndr. 2025;19(7):103278. DOI 10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103278. PMID 40849219. Abstract Methods verbatim: 'included from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in 2003-2018 (n = 19,831). Mortality status as of December 2019 was obtained through linkage to the National Death Index.' Confirmed independently via two separate Europe PMC REST queries (EXT_ID and DOI).

- **(a) The published numbers are NOT the ones in circulation** — `corrected`
  TRUE, but the article must state the direction, because the natural reading is backwards. WRONG version (if the article implies publication deflated/walked back the scary headline): the published CV result is NOT smaller than 1.91. RIGHT version: the published hazard ratio for cardiovascular mortality is HR 2.35 (95% CI, 1.39-3.98) for eating duration <8 h versus the 12-14 h reference — i.e. +135%, substantially LARGER than the abstract's 1.91 (+91%). Published Results verbatim: 'compared with eating duration of 12-14 h, eating duration <8 h was robustly associated with higher cardiovascular mortality (HR, 2.35 [95 % CI, 1.39-3.98]), but not with all-cause and cancer mortality.' Two further real divergences the article can legitimately use: (i) the reference group CHANGED between abstract and paper, from 12-16 h to 12-14 h, so the two HRs are not strictly the same contrast; (ii) the all-cause mortality signal did attenuate — published Results verbatim: 'However, the association with all-cause mortality did not survive many sensitivity analyses.' The CV association, by contrast, 'remained consistent across 8 subgroups ... and survived 14 sensitivity analyses.' The paper's own conclusion is hedged, verbatim: 'further research is required to understand whether this risk is attributed to the short eating duration itself or residual confounding resulting from its contributing factors.'

- **(b) The FMD '2.5 years biologically younger' is a within-group pre-post comparison inside the FMD arm, not a randomised between-group contrast** — `confirmed`
  Brandhorst S, Levine ME, Wei M, Shelehchi M, Morgan TE, Nayak KS, Dorff T, Hong K, Crimmins EM, Cohen P, Longo VD. Nat Commun 2024, PMID 38378685, PMC10879164. Full text verbatim: 'After 3 FMD cycles, median biological age in the 52 study participants decreased by nearly 2.5 years' — this is baseline vs 3-month within the FMD arm only. The abstract itself frames the whole analysis verbatim as 'secondary and exploratory analysis of blood samples from a randomized clinical trial (NCT02158897)', so biological age was not a pre-specified primary endpoint. Control data are reported only descriptively: verbatim 'Over the intervention period control study participants exhibited a non-significant average biological age increase of 0.78 years (SD = 3.57; p = 0.76; Fig. 3B).' Biological age was computed for only 19 controls, though 48 were randomised to control. No formal FMD-vs-control statistical test of the biological-age change is reported. Added precision the article should carry: 2.5 years is a MEDIAN, from trial NCT02158897; the second trial NCT04150159 gave 2.7 years; the pooled figure across both trials (N = 86) is verbatim 'a median decrease in biological age of 2.6 years'.

- **(b) Both parent trials had control arms** — `confirmed`
  NCT02158897: FMD arm n = 52, control arm n = 48, controls instructed to 'continue their normal diet for 3 months'. NCT04150159 (ClinicalTrials.gov record, official title 'Evaluation of a Fasting Mimicking Diet and the Effect on Endothelial Function, Body Composition and Vascular Markers'): randomized, open-label, parallel, 80 enrolled, 40 per arm; experimental arm FMD, active-comparator control arm Mediterranean diet; sponsor Hypertension Institute, Nashville; collaborator L-Nutra Inc. So yes, control arms existed in both and were not used for the headline biological-age contrast.

- **(b) The '11 years younger' figure is not a measured result but a 20-year simulation assuming continued efficacy** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the Nat Commun full text: 'A simulation of the effect of 3 FMD cycles for twenty years assuming continued efficacy of this dietary intervention suggests a potential decrease in biological age of about 11 years.' This is exactly as the claim describes — a projection, not an observation. Related simulated (not measured) figures in the same paper: 20-year all-cause mortality risk at age 70 'reduced from 81.1% to 57.5%', and 20-year heart-disease mortality risk 'reduced from 29.1% to 15.4%'. These are model outputs and should never be reported as trial results.

- **(b) Valter Longo's commercial relationship with L-Nutra** — `corrected`
  Confirmed but INCOMPLETE as usually stated, and the omitted half is material. Competing interests section of the Nat Commun paper, verbatim in full: 'The experimental FMD was provided by L-Nutra Inc. USC has licensed intellectual property to L-Nutra that is under study in this research. As part of this license agreement, the University has the potential to receive royalty payments from L-Nutra. V.D.L. and T.E.M., who have equity interest in L-Nutra, did not participate in the collection and analysis of the data. One-hundred percent of V.D.L.'s equity will be assigned to charitable organizations and companies including the Create Cures Foundation. The remaining authors declare no competing interests.' WRONG version: 'Longo has an equity stake in L-Nutra, the company that sells the diet' full stop. RIGHT version: that, PLUS (i) co-author Todd E. Morgan also holds equity, (ii) USC itself stands to receive royalties, (iii) both equity-holding authors state they did not participate in data collection or analysis, and (iv) Longo states 100% of his equity is assigned to charitable organizations including the Create Cures Foundation. Note separately that L-Nutra is also a named ClinicalTrials.gov collaborator on NCT04150159, and Methods state verbatim: 'The FMD provided by L-Nutra to this study participants comprises proprietary formulations belonging to USC and L-Nutra.'

- **Verbatim text of the AHA conference abstract body itself (to confirm HR 1.91 and abstract N)** — `unreachable`
  I could not reach the abstract body. ahajournals.org returned HTTP 403 on both /doi/ and /doi/abs/ paths. The '91% higher risk' figure is therefore verified only from (i) the AHA's own newsroom press release and (ii) the Crossref metadata record for the DOI — not from the abstract text. I did NOT see the string 'HR 1.91' or '1.91' in any primary document; the 91% is the press release's phrasing. Likewise, the frequently cited abstract sample size of N=20,078 came back only through a Semantic Scholar response that was a paraphrase rather than the source text, so I treat it as UNVERIFIED and the article should not quote it as verbatim. Also note WebSearch quota was exhausted at the start of this run, so all sourcing above is via direct WebFetch of Crossref, Europe PMC REST, PubMed, PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov API, and the AHA newsroom.

- **Later corrections, errata, or failed replications** — `confirmed`
  No erratum, comment, or letter indexed in Europe PMC against either paper (searched PUB_TYPE Comment/Letter/Published Erratum for the eating-duration topic, and CITES:38378685_MED for commentary on Brandhorst; both returned hitCount 0). Independent dataset found that does NOT overturn (a): Mao Z, Grant H, Kritchevsky SB, Newman AB, Farsijani S. 'Association of Eating Window With Mortality Among US Adults.' Aging Cell 2025, PMID 40944446 — a larger overlapping NHANES 2003-2018 sample (n = 33,052, two complete 24-h recalls, median 8 years) reporting a U-shaped association with ~11-12 h/day optimal, shorter windows linked to elevated all-cause mortality and >50% higher CV mortality in some strata. This broadly corroborates rather than refutes the direction, though it is the same NHANES source and so is not statistically independent confounding-wise.

**修正:**
- Replace any implication that the peer-reviewed publication softened the 91% headline. The published hazard ratio for cardiovascular mortality is HR 2.35 (95% CI, 1.39-3.98) for an eating duration under 8 hours versus a 12-14 hour reference — larger, not smaller, than the abstract's 91% (1.91). Cite: Chen M, et al., Diabetes Metab Syndr. 2025;19(7):103278, doi:10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103278.
- State the reference-group change explicitly: the 2024 conference abstract compared <8 h against a 12-16 h eating window; the 2025 paper compared <8 h against 12-14 h. The two hazard ratios are therefore not the same contrast, which is part of why the numbers differ.
- Relocate the genuine attenuation to the correct endpoint. What weakened on publication was ALL-CAUSE mortality, not cardiovascular. Published wording: the <8 h group was 'not' associated with all-cause and cancer mortality, and 'the association with all-cause mortality did not survive many sensitivity analyses.' By contrast the CV association 'remained consistent across 8 subgroups ... and survived 14 sensitivity analyses.'
- Do not present '1.91' as a hazard ratio quoted from the abstract. The abstract body is paywalled (ahajournals returns 403); the only reachable primary sourcing for the figure is the AHA press release's phrase '91% higher risk of death due to cardiovascular disease.' Attribute it to the press release, or state the HR without implying you read it in the abstract.
- Do not cite N=20,078 as the abstract's sample size unless the article can reach the abstract itself. That figure could not be verified against a primary document. The verified sample size is the published one: n = 19,831.
- Change 'averaging ~8 years of follow-up' to 'a median 8.1 years of follow-up' (the paper reports a median, not a mean). Also note the two 24-h recalls were required of all participants and collected within the first year of enrollment, so 'as little as two days' is better phrased as 'exactly two days of dietary recall, collected in year one, used to classify an exposure over the following eight years.'
- Correct the citation form for the abstract to 'Circulation. 2024;149(Suppl_1):P192' (doi:10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.P192), or note that 'AP192' is AHA's abstract-numbering convention for the same record. Authors on the DOI record are Meng Chen and Victor W Zhong; Zhong is the senior author, not the first author, of both the abstract and the 2025 paper.
- Add that the FMD biological-age analysis was, in the authors' own words, a 'secondary and exploratory analysis' of NCT02158897 — biological age was not a pre-specified primary endpoint. This is a stronger and more defensible point than the within-group framing alone.
- Specify the 2.5-year figure precisely: it is a MEDIAN decrease among the 52 participants of the FMD arm of NCT02158897. The second trial (NCT04150159) gave 2.7 years and the pooled estimate across both trials (N = 86) was 2.6 years. Cite Brandhorst S, et al., Nat Commun 2024, PMC10879164.
- Strengthen the within-group point with the control-arm numbers the paper does report: controls showed 'a non-significant average biological age increase of 0.78 years (SD = 3.57; p = 0.76)', and biological age was computed for only 19 controls even though 48 were randomised to the control arm. No formal between-group statistical test of the biological-age change is reported anywhere in the paper.
- Name both control arms when saying 'both parent trials had control arms': NCT02158897 used a normal-diet control (n = 48); NCT04150159 used a Mediterranean-diet active comparator (80 enrolled, 40 per arm), with L-Nutra Inc listed as a study collaborator on the registry record.
- Quote the 11-year figure with its conditional intact: 'A simulation of the effect of 3 FMD cycles for twenty years assuming continued efficacy of this dietary intervention suggests a potential decrease in biological age of about 11 years.' Note that the companion 20-year mortality-risk reductions cited in coverage (all-cause 81.1% to 57.5%; heart disease 29.1% to 15.4%) are outputs of the same simulation, not trial results.
- Report the L-Nutra disclosure in full rather than as 'Longo has equity in L-Nutra.' The paper discloses that co-author Todd E. Morgan also holds equity, that USC licensed the IP and may receive royalties, that both equity-holding authors state they did not participate in data collection or analysis, and that 100% of Longo's equity is assigned to charitable organizations including the Create Cures Foundation. Omitting the last two makes the disclosure sound more damning than the primary document supports.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The single largest problem with this claim group is a directional trap. The claim says 'the published numbers are NOT the ones in circulation', which is literally true but invites the opposite-of-correct inference. The published cardiovascular hazard ratio is 2.35 (95% CI, 1.39-3.98), i.e. a 135% increase, versus the 91% in the press release. Peer review made the cardiovascular signal bigger, not smaller. Any article using this as a 'the scary headline evaporated on publication' example would be factually inverted.
- The abstract-vs-paper comparison is not apples-to-apples in a second way that the claim does not mention: the reference category moved from 12-16 h to 12-14 h. Part of the 1.91 to 2.35 shift is definitional, not a change in evidence.
- An independent (though overlapping-source) NHANES analysis published after the Zhong paper corroborates rather than contradicts the short-window signal: Mao Z, et al., Aging Cell 2025 (PMID 40944446), n = 33,052 NHANES 2003-2018 adults with two complete 24-h recalls, median 8 years follow-up, found a U-shaped association with ~11-12 h/day optimal and elevated mortality at both extremes. An article implying the short-eating-window mortality finding is an isolated, discredited artifact would be overstating the case.
- The FMD conflict-of-interest point is weaker than commonly asserted, in the specific respect that the paper states Longo and Morgan 'did not participate in the collection and analysis of the data' and that 100% of Longo's equity is assigned to charity. The stronger, cleaner criticism is methodological, not financial: the biological-age result is an explicitly 'secondary and exploratory' analysis with no pre-specification and no reported between-arm test, in trials that had control arms available.

Primary documents I reached and read: (1) the Crossref deposit for DOI 10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.P192, returning the full JATS-tagged abstract body, and the Semantic Scholar record for the same DOI, returning byte-identical text — this is what let me catch that the abstract says HR 1.96, not the 1.91 everyone quotes; (2) the AHA newsroom press release of 18 March 2024, retrieved in full including the 03/19/24 editor's note, the study-details block, and Christopher Gardner's critique; (3) the abstract of record for Diabetes Metab Syndr. 2025;19(7):103278 as raw <abstractText> XML from Europe PMC, corroborated by an independent NCBI efetch that returned the same HR 2.35 (1.39-3.98); (4) the full text of Nat Commun 2024;15:1309 via Europe PMC's fullTextXML for PMC10879164, plus the PMC HTML page, which between them gave me the within-group 2.5-year sentence with its p-value and test, the control-arm n=19 result, both trial designs, the 20-year simulation sentence, and the complete Competing interests block.

Where I could not get to a primary document I have said so rather than guessed: the AHA poster (ahajournals.org 403s) and the full text of the 2025 paper beyond its abstract (ScienceDirect 403, no OA deposit).

On the fabrication risk flagged in the brief: my highest-confidence strings are the ones that arrived as escaped raw JSON/XML with markup intact (the JATS `<jats:bold>` tags in the Crossref abstract, the `<h4>` headers in the Europe PMC abstract) — those are passthrough, not summary. The FMD in-text quotes and the Competing interests block came through summarizer renderings that asserted verbatim status; the L-Nutra/ProLon sentence appeared identically across two different URLs, and one fetch explicitly refused to over-quote on fair-use grounds while still surfacing the 2.5-year sentence with its test name, which reads as genuine extraction rather than confabulation. Still, if the article is going to print the Competing interests paragraph as a block quote, someone should eyeball the PMC page directly first.

What remains genuinely uncertain: whether the '91%' traces to a superseded poster model or is a straightforward error in the AHA release. I can prove the deposited abstract says 1.96 and cannot prove what the poster said. The safe framing for the article is to attribute 91% to the release and give 1.96 as the abstract's own figure — which is also the more damning framing, since it means the number that circulated globally never matched any document in the scientific record.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The abstract of record does not contain the number the article attributes to it. Two independent metadata sources — Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.P192) and Semantic Scholar, returning byte-identical JATS text — give HR 1.96 (95% CI, 1.23-3.13), not 1.91. The '91%' exists only in the AHA news release. The AHA also appended a 03/19/24 editor's note that the authors 'shared their full poster presentation for updated details about their research abstract' and that 'the most current statistics... are in the poster and the news release', which suggests the release and the deposited abstract were never reconciled. I could not reach the poster to settle which is which.
- The published effect is BIGGER, not smaller. Anyone writing the standard 'preprint hype deflates on peer review' arc will get this backwards: 1.91/1.96 in the abstract, 2.35 in the peer-reviewed paper. What weakened was not the point estimate but the comparator's definition and the all-cause result's robustness.
- An independent NHANES re-analysis using the same survey years and the same NDI cutoff reaches partly different conclusions on a nearly 70% larger sample: Mao Z, Grant H, Kritchevsky SB, Newman AB, Farsijani S. 'Association of Eating Window With Mortality Among US Adults: Insights From a Nationally Representative Study.' Aging Cell. 2025 (PMID 40944446, DOI 10.1111/acel.70230). NHANES 2003-2018 linked through December 2019, N = 33,052 with two complete 24-h recalls — versus Zhong's 19,831, because Zhong additionally restricted to participants who reported 'usual intake' in both recalls, a sample-selection choice that removes roughly 40% of eligible adults and is never mentioned in coverage of either study. Mao et al. find a U-shaped curve with the nadir at ~11-12 h/day, eating windows of 8 h or less linked to '≥30% higher all-cause mortality' — where Zhong's published paper found all-cause mortality null — and >50% higher cardiovascular mortality only in subgroups (older adults, men, Whites), a much smaller effect than HR 2.35. The two studies agree on direction and disagree on magnitude and on whether all-cause mortality moves at all.
- The FMD paper's second trial (NCT04150159) is not a placebo comparison at all — the comparator is a Mediterranean diet, an active intervention with its own cardiometabolic effects. A between-group contrast there would understate the FMD effect relative to a do-nothing control, which cuts against reading the pooled 2.6-year figure as a clean effect size in either direction.
- Europe PMC shows no erratum, correction, or critical letter attached to the Brandhorst 2024 Nature Communications paper as of July 2026 — so the FMD critique in this article is a design critique, not a documented post-publication dispute. Do not imply the paper has been formally challenged the way the Zhong paper has.

### 票 3(CORRECTED)

My WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against structured APIs (Crossref, Europe PMC REST, NCBI E-utilities/BioC, ClinicalTrials.gov API v2) rather than search engines. This turned out to be an advantage: those endpoints return raw JSON/XML, so I could get literal field contents rather than summarizer prose. Where a fetch returned an obvious summary instead of the document text, I re-fetched the same content by a different route and only trusted strings that reproduced identically.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS I ACTUALLY REACHED VERBATIM:
1. The Circulation abstract's raw JATS XML, via api.crossref.org/works/10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.p192. I have the complete Introduction/Hypothesis/Methods/Results/Conclusions text with all six HRs. This is the decisive document for the '91 vs 96' finding. Two independent Crossref/Semantic Scholar fetches both returned HR 1.96 [1.23-3.13], and the geometric-mean-of-CI check (1.962) rules out a transcription error.
2. The published paper's structured abstract, via Europe PMC resultType=core (abstractText field), cross-checked against an NCBI efetch call that independently returned the same HR 2.35 [1.39-3.98] and n=19,831.
3. The Nature Communications 2024 full text, fetched twice by different routes — the NCBI BioC RESTful full-text API and the PMC HTML article page (PMC10879164). The competing-interests paragraph, the 'decreased by nearly 2.5 years' sentence, and the twenty-year/11-year simulation sentence came back byte-identical both times. Given the pipeline's history of fabricated quotes, I treated dual-route reproduction as my bar for calling something verbatim, and I only quote strings that cleared it.
4. The ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API record for NCT04150159, which settled the 'both trials had control arms' question.
5. The AHA newsroom press release, fetched twice with different prompts.

WHAT I COULD NOT REACH: the ahajournals.org page for the abstract returned HTTP 403, and ScienceDirect returned 403 for the Manoogian letter, so I have the letter's full bibliographic record and 35-author list but not one word of its argument. I have deliberately not characterized its content. Likewise I could not read the authors' reply. I also could not verify the widely repeated claim that Longo founded L-Nutra — the disclosure says only 'equity interest', and I refuse to upgrade that from memory.

NET ASSESSMENT: the claim group is directionally sound and its two structural criticisms — that the TRE scare rests on two days of recall promoted through a non-peer-reviewed abstract, and that the FMD rejuvenation numbers are a within-arm pre-post change plus a twenty-year extrapolation — both survive contact with the primary sources, the FMD half almost word for word. But the group contains one genuine factual error (the 91% figure is not the abstract's; the abstract says 1.96) and one misleading implication (that publication deflated the number, when it rose to 2.35 against a re-cut reference). Those two must be fixed before the article runs, which is why this is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS. The residual uncertainty I would flag to the editor: I cannot explain WHY the press release said 91% when the abstract says 1.96 — I can only document that they disagree.

- **(a) The claim originated as an AHA EPI|Lifestyle 2024 conference ABSTRACT, Circulation 2024;149:AP192, not peer reviewed, promoted worldwide by press release** — `confirmed`
  Reached the abstract of record via Crossref: 'Abstract P192: Association Between Time-Restricted Eating and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality', Meng Chen and Victor W Zhong, Circulation vol 149, issue Suppl_1, published 19 March 2024, DOI 10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.p192. The AHA newsroom release confirms it was 'Abstract P192' at the 'Epidemiology and Prevention|Lifestyle and Cardiometabolic Scientific Sessions 2024' and states verbatim that 'research abstracts are considered preliminary until published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal' and that 'Abstracts presented at the Association's scientific meetings are not peer-reviewed'. The 'AP192' page identifier is the standard AHA supplement convention (A + abstract number) and is consistent with the DOI suffix suppl_1.p192.

- **(a) The figure was '91% higher cardiovascular mortality'** — `corrected`
  WRONG as attributed to the abstract. RIGHT: the 91% figure comes from the AHA PRESS RELEASE, not from the abstract. The press release says verbatim: 'People who followed a pattern of eating all of their food across less than 8 hours per day had a 91% higher risk of death due to cardiovascular disease.' But the Circulation abstract of record reports, verbatim: 'eating duration <8 hours was significantly associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality (HR, 1.96 [95% CI, 1.23-3.13])' — i.e. 96%, not 91%. This is not a transcription slip on my side: the geometric mean of the CI bounds, sqrt(1.23 x 3.13) = 1.962, confirms 1.96 is the internally consistent point estimate. The press release page carries no hazard ratio at all. So the number that went around the world (91%) does not match the number printed in the abstract it was supposedly based on.

  Substantively right, caliber loose on two points. WRONG: 'as little as two days' implies a minimum; 'averaging ~8 years' implies a mean. RIGHT: it was EXACTLY two days — the abstract's Methods say verbatim 'Participants aged at least 20 years who completed two valid 24-hour dietary recalls and reported usual intake in both recalls were included' and 'The average duration of two recall days defined typical eating duration'. Two valid recalls were an inclusion requirement, not a floor. And follow-up was a MEDIAN of 8.0 years (IQR, 4.2-11.8) in the abstract, median 8.1 years in the published paper — not an average. Supporting: the AHA's own release concedes 'categorization into the different windows of time-restricted eating was determined on the basis of just two days of dietary intake', and an eating occasion was defined as consuming more than 5 kcal.

Abstract Methods verbatim: 'Adult participants who reported usual intake from two valid 24-h dietary recalls were included from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in 2003-2018 (n = 19,831).   The claim is TRUE but the article will mislead if it implies the full publication walked the finding back. WRONG framing: that the published HR is a retreat from 1.91. RIGHT: the published CVD hazard ratio is HIGHER, not lower. Verbatim from the published abstract: 'compared with eating duration of 12-14 h, eating duration <8 h was robustly associated with higher cardiovascular mortality (HR, 2.35 [95 % CI, 1.39-3.98]), but not with all-cause and cancer mortality.' (Geometric-mean check: sqrt(1.39 x 3.98) = 2.352, internally consistent.) What actually changed between abstract and paper: (i) point estimate 1.96 -> 2.35; (ii) the REFERENCE CATEGORY was re-cut from '12-16 (reference group; mean duration in US adults)' to '12-14 h (mean duration)', so the two HRs are not comparing the same contrast; (iii) N 20,078 -> 19,831; (iv) the published paper states the all-cause association 'did not survive many sensitivity analyses' while the CVD association 'survived 14 sensitivity analyses' and held across 8 subgroups; (v) the published conclusion is heavily hedged verbatim: 'further research is required to understand whether this risk is attributed to the short eating duration itself or residual confounding resulting from its contributing factors.'   Confirmed verbatim, and independently reproduced across two separate retrieval routes (NCBI BioC full-text API and the PMC HTML article page), which is why I trust the string. The 52 participants are the FMD arm only, so this is a pre-vs-post change within one arm, tested with a within-sample rank test — no comparison to the control arm. - **(b) Both parent trials had control arms** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed. Trial 1, NCT02158897: the paper states verbatim 'Arm 1 (n = 48), the control group' and 'Participants in arm 2 (n = 52) started the FMD' out of 100 randomized participants. Trial 2, NCT04150159 (this is the second trial the Nature Communications abstract names — flag for the article: it is NCT04150159, NOT NCT02710721): the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API record shows an interventional RANDOMIZED two-arm parallel design, 'Evaluation of a Fasting Mimicking Diet and the Effect on Endothelial Function, Body Composition and Vascular Markers', FMD (ProLon) arm vs an ACTIVE COMPARATOR Mediterranean diet arm, enrollment 80, lead sponsor Hypertension Institute Nashville, collaborator L-Nutra Inc. The Nature Communications paper analyzed only the 44 participants 'instructed to consume the FMD for 4 consecutive months' — again the FMD arm alone. So in both trials a randomized control arm existed and was not used for the biological-age contrast.

- **(b) The circulated '11 years younger' figure is not a measured result — it is a 20-year simulation assuming continued efficacy** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed essentially word for word, and this is the strongest-supported item in the group. The Discussion states verbatim: 'A simulation of the effect of 3 FMD cycles for twenty years assuming continued efficacy of this dietary intervention suggests a potential decrease in biological age of about 11 years.' The claim's phrasing '20-year simulation assuming continued efficacy' matches the source almost exactly. Additional detail the article can use: the simulation was not run on trial participants at all — verbatim, 'A simulation of the effect of continued FMD (3 cycles annually up until age 70) was run using the NHANES IV population ages 20-59 (n = 7733), given that it is the closest representation of the current U.S. population.' So 11 years is a model output projected onto a national survey sample, extrapolating a within-arm 2.5-year pre-post change out over two decades.

- **(b) Valter Longo's commercial relationship with L-Nutra** — `corrected`
  Real and disclosed, but the claim as stated is incomplete and would be unfair if printed without the mitigating clauses. RIGHT (full verbatim competing-interests statement, reproduced identically by two independent fetch routes): 'The experimental FMD was provided by L-Nutra Inc. USC has licensed intellectual property to L-Nutra that is under study in this research. As part of this license agreement, the University has the potential to receive royalty payments from L-Nutra. V.D.L. and T.E.M., who have equity interest in L-Nutra, did not participate in the collection and analysis of the data. One-hundred percent of V.D.L.'s equity will be assigned to charitable organizations and companies including the Create Cures Foundation. The remaining authors declare no competing interests.' So: Longo holds equity in L-Nutra, L-Nutra supplied the test product, and USC stands to collect royalties — but the disclosure also states Longo was walled off from data collection and analysis and that 100% of his equity is pledged to charitable organizations including Create Cures Foundation. I did NOT verify the commonly repeated assertion that Longo FOUNDED L-Nutra; the competing-interests statement says only 'equity interest'. Do not assert founder status on the strength of this document. Separately, the second parent trial (NCT04150159) lists L-Nutra as an industry collaborator, and a related Longo FMD trial in Diabetologia 2024 (PMID 38546821) discloses it was 'co-funded by Health~Holland, Top Sector Life Sciences & Health, the Dutch Diabetes Foundation and L-Nutra.'

- **Independent check: is there a published critique or contradicting dataset?** — `confirmed`
  Two relevant items found, both of which the article should know about. (1) A formal published critique exists and is signed by essentially the entire chrononutrition field: Manoogian ENC, Peterson CM, Sears DD, Playdon M, Banks S, Bonham M, Chaix A, Chow LS, Coletta A, De Cabo R, Desplats P, Dibner C, Gabel K, Johnson SL, Kriegsfeld LJ, Hardikar S, Hawley JA, Heilbronn LK, Hogenesch J, James DL, Kleckner AS, Laferrere B, Marinac C, Panda S, Parr E, Pendergast JS, Quist JS, Ravussin E, Scheer FAJL, Swiatkiewicz I, Takahashi JS, Taub PR, Termannsen AD, Varady KA, Wilkinson MJ, Zee PC, Collet TH. 'Short-term 24h dietary recalls from observational studies cannot support claims on mortality.' Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome 2025;19(10):103316, DOI 10.1016/j.dsx.2025.103316, PMID 41218440. The authors replied: Chen M, Xu L, Zhong VW, 'Authors' Reply to Letter to the Editor by Emily N.C. Manoogian et al.', Diabetes Metab Syndr 2025;19(12):103330, PMID 41365209. (2) A second NHANES analysis, Mao Z, Grant H, Kritchevsky SB, Newman AB, Farsijani S, 'Association of Eating Window With Mortality Among US Adults', Aging Cell 2025, PMID 40944446, N=33,052, reports verbatim a U-shaped association with 'the lowest risk at ~11-12 h/day' and that 'Shorter windows (<= 8 h) were linked to >= 30% higher all-cause mortality, especially in older adults, and > 50% higher cardiovascular mortality in older adults, men, and Whites.' CAUTION: this is NOT an independent replication — it uses the same NHANES 2003-2018 cycles and the same two-24h-recall instrument, so it inherits the identical exposure-measurement weakness and largely overlapping participants.

- **Full text of the Manoogian et al. letter's specific arguments** — `unreachable`
  I could confirm the letter's existence, exact title, complete 35-author list, journal, volume, issue, page, DOI and PMID, but I could NOT read its body text. Europe PMC returns no abstract for it (letters typically carry none), and the ScienceDirect full-text page (S1871402125002206) returned HTTP 403 Forbidden. The same applies to the authors' reply (103330), which also has no abstract. So I can tell the article that a major field-wide methodological rebuttal was published and answered, but I cannot quote what either side actually argued. Do not paraphrase their arguments from the title alone.

**修正:**
- Do not attribute the '91%' figure to the conference abstract. The Circulation abstract of record (Circulation 2024;149, Suppl_1, Abstract P192, DOI 10.1161/circ.149.suppl_1.p192) reports HR 1.96 (95% CI 1.23-3.13) — i.e. 96% higher cardiovascular mortality. The '91%' appears only in the AHA press release, which carries no hazard ratio at all. The correct statement is: the AHA press release headlined a 91% figure that does not match the 1.96 hazard ratio printed in the abstract it summarized.
- Correct the direction of the abstract-vs-published divergence. The published paper did NOT attenuate the finding: the CVD hazard ratio went UP, to 2.35 (95% CI 1.39-3.98). Any sentence implying the peer-reviewed version shrank or retracted the effect is false.
- State that the reference category changed between abstract and paper, so the two hazard ratios are not the same contrast: the abstract used '12-16 h (reference group; mean duration in US adults)'; the published paper used '12-14 h (mean duration)'. Sample size also changed from 20,078 to 19,831.
- Replace 'as little as two days of 24-hour dietary recall' with 'exactly two 24-hour dietary recall days'. Two valid recalls were an inclusion requirement, not a minimum, and the exposure was the average of those two days.
- Replace 'averaging ~8 years of follow-up' with 'a median of 8.0 years (IQR 4.2-11.8)' for the abstract, or 'a median of 8.1 years' for the published paper. It is a median, not a mean.
- Report what the published paper actually found beyond the CVD signal: no association with all-cause or cancer mortality; the CVD association survived 14 sensitivity analyses and 8 subgroups, while the all-cause association 'did not survive many sensitivity analyses'. Quote the authors' own hedge: 'further research is required to understand whether this risk is attributed to the short eating duration itself or residual confounding resulting from its contributing factors.'
- Give the full published citation: Chen M, Xu L, Van Horn L, Manson JE, Tucker KL, Du X, Feng N, Rong S, Zhong VW. Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome 2025;19(7):103278 (PMID 40849219). Note it is a mid-tier Elsevier journal, not a leading cardiology or nutrition venue.
- If the article names the second FMD parent trial, it is NCT04150159 (FMD vs an active-comparator Mediterranean diet, enrollment 80, sponsor Hypertension Institute Nashville, collaborator L-Nutra) — not NCT02710721. The first is NCT02158897 (control arm n=48, FMD arm n=52).
- Quantify the FMD within-group point precisely: 'After 3 FMD cycles, median biological age in the 52 study participants decreased by nearly 2.5 years (p = 0.0007, Wilcoxon).' The 52 are the FMD arm alone; the randomized control arm was never used for this contrast; and the paper self-describes as 'secondary and exploratory analysis'.
- Add that the 11-year simulation was not run on trial participants: it was projected onto 'the NHANES IV population ages 20-59 (n = 7733)', assuming 3 FMD cycles annually up until age 70. The source sentence is: 'A simulation of the effect of 3 FMD cycles for twenty years assuming continued efficacy of this dietary intervention suggests a potential decrease in biological age of about 11 years.'
- When describing Longo's L-Nutra tie, include the mitigating half of the disclosure or the article will be unfair: he and T.E. Morgan 'did not participate in the collection and analysis of the data', and 'One-hundred percent of V.D.L.'s equity will be assigned to charitable organizations and companies including the Create Cures Foundation.' Do not call Longo the FOUNDER of L-Nutra on the strength of this paper — the disclosure says only 'equity interest'.
- Do not present the Aging Cell 2025 study (Mao et al., N=33,052) as independent corroboration. It draws on the same NHANES 2003-2018 cycles and the same two-24h-recall instrument, so it shares the exposure-measurement flaw and most of the participants.
- Mention that a 35-author rebuttal was published — Manoogian ENC, Peterson CM, Sears DD, ... Panda S, Varady KA, Scheer FAJL, Takahashi JS, et al., 'Short-term 24h dietary recalls from observational studies cannot support claims on mortality', Diabetes Metab Syndr 2025;19(10):103316 — with an authors' reply at 19(12):103330. Do not characterize the letter's specific arguments; its full text was not retrievable.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The single most important thing this verification turned up, which the claim group did not anticipate: the famous '91%' is not the abstract's number. The Circulation abstract reports HR 1.96 (95% CI 1.23-3.13). I confirmed 1.96 is not a typo by checking internal consistency — the geometric mean of the CI bounds, sqrt(1.23 x 3.13) = 1.962, matches the stated point estimate. So the worldwide '91% higher cardiovascular death' headline traces to the AHA press release, which itself contains no hazard ratio, and is inconsistent with the primary document.
- The claim's implied narrative — that peer review deflated the scary abstract number — is contradicted by the published paper. Peer review produced a LARGER estimate (HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.39-3.98; geometric-mean check sqrt(1.39 x 3.98) = 2.352). What peer review actually changed was the reference category (12-16 h to 12-14 h), the sample (20,078 to 19,831), and above all the rhetoric: the published conclusion explicitly refuses to claim causation and flags residual confounding.
- The abstract already reported that the all-cause mortality finding was null; the published paper repeats this and adds that even the all-cause association 'did not survive many sensitivity analyses.' Any article implying the original claim was about overall mortality is wrong — it was cardiovascular-specific from the start.
- The 2.5-year and 11-year FMD figures are not two versions of one result. The 11-year figure was generated from a completely different population — 7,733 NHANES IV respondents aged 20-59 — and never involved anyone who took the FMD. It is a model output stacked on top of a within-arm pre-post change, i.e. an extrapolation of an exploratory secondary analysis.
- The Nature Communications paper's second cohort is NCT04150159, not NCT02710721. Anyone citing NCT02710721 as the second FMD parent trial for the biological-age result is citing the wrong registry record.

## V29 — 组级判决:OVERTURNED(票型 OVERTURNED/OVERTURNED/OVERTURNED)

### 票 1(OVERTURNED)

Method: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted at 200/200 before my first call), so every document below was retrieved directly by HTTP from primary sources and parsed locally — no summarizer stood between me and the text, and every quoted string below was read from the raw JSON/XML.

(1) ClinicalTrials.gov API v2. I reproduced the article's query exactly and got totalCount = 1472 on 2026-07-28, then downloaded all 1,472 full records (two pages, saved to ctg_cr.json) and regex-scanned every primaryOutcomes[].measure for hard-endpoint vocabulary (mortality, death, survival, incident/incidence, fracture, MI, stroke, cancer, dementia, diagnosis, onset, event, morbid). 109 records tripped the broad filter; I read them all. Almost all are disease-population trials (chemo toxicity, PFS/DFS in cancer, perioperative composites, diabetes remission) or adverse-event safety primaries, which correctly fall outside the article's boundary. Two do not: NCT02960711 (MeMeMe) and NCT01777893 (PREVIEW). I pulled both full records and, for MeMeMe, the published primary-results paper (Diabetes Care 2025;48(2), PMC11770154, full text from Europe PMC) to check the pre-specified endpoint and the nature of the diet arm.

(2) ISRCTN API (the CTG-only method's blind spot). 184 unique records across seven CR/fasting/TRE terms; scanning primary outcomes surfaced PREDIMED-Plus (ISRCTN89898870), whose registered primary endpoint is a hard CVD composite in a CVD-free primary-prevention population of 6,874. I then confirmed PREDIMED-Plus has no ClinicalTrials.gov registration (query for the ISRCTN id returns 0 studies), so the article's scan could not have found it — the absence claim rests on a method that cannot see the strongest counterexample.

(3) BMJ NMA. Full text of PMC12175170 read and grepped: 99 trials / 6,582 adults / body weight primary / intermediate cardiometabolic outcomes only; zero hits for 'mortality' or 'cardiovascular event'. I also chased the correction notice (BMJ 2025;390:r1737, PMC12359177) and confirmed it changes only a coauthor affiliation, not the numbers.

(4) CALERIE Legacy. NCT05651620 record parsed from the API: both primary outcomes and the '11-16 years post CALERIE trial' time frame match the article verbatim; the one caliber error is that it is an observational follow-up study, not a trial.

Remaining uncertainty: ANZCTR (error page) and ChiCTR (HTTP 405) refused my requests, and with no WebSearch I could not query WHO ICTRP, UMIN/jRCT, CTIS or the Iranian/Indian registries. So I cannot certify how many further counterexamples exist outside CTG and ISRCTN — but exhaustiveness only matters for upholding the claim, and the claim is already dead. I also did not find any CR/fasting/TRE trial anywhere with all-cause mortality as the primary endpoint; that narrower statement appears to survive, and is what the article should say instead.

- **No caloric restriction, fasting, or time-restricted-eating trial in a healthy or general population anywhere in the world has mortality or incident age-related disease as a primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  WRONG as an absolute. Decisive counterexample: PREDIMED-Plus, ISRCTN89898870 (NOT registered on ClinicalTrials.gov — a CTG query for 'ISRCTN89898870' returns 0 studies). Registry record read verbatim via the ISRCTN API: title 'Effect of an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet, physical activity and behavioral intervention on the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease'; intervention arm = 'Intensive intervention with an energy-restricted Mediet ... together with promotion of physical activity, behavioral support and weight loss goals' vs control 'a 14-item Mediet ... without energy-restriction, without weight loss goals and without a physical activity program'; primaryOutcome (as of 04/06/2018) = '1. A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke 2. Changes in body weight'; inclusion = men 55-75 / women 60-75, BMI >=27 and <40, >=3 metabolic syndrome criteria, 'No cardiovascular disease (CVD) at enrolment' (<=25% may have diabetes); totalFinalEnrolment 6874; recruitment 2013-09-05 to 2016-12-05, overall end 2024-12-22. That is a caloric-restriction intervention with incident hard cardiovascular disease (including CV death) as the pre-specified primary endpoint in a primary-prevention, non-diseased population — exactly what the article says does not exist anywhere. Secondary outcomes there also include 'Death of any cause', dementia, type 2 diabetes, osteoporotic fractures, cancer. Second counterexample INSIDE ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02960711 (MeMeMe, Italy, N=1600 actual, Phase 3, healthyVolunteers=True, ages 55-74, metabolic syndrome, diabetes/cancer excluded), primary outcome verbatim 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases', description 'We will retrieve records for all Age related chronic diseases but we will first concentrate the analysis on cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, and diabetes', time frame 5 years; secondary 'Effect of the intervention on total mortality and on the incidence of specific chronic diseases.' The narrow half of the claim that DOES survive: I found no CR/fasting/TRE trial in a general population with all-cause MORTALITY as its sole/primary endpoint.

- **Researcher scanned all 1,472 ClinicalTrials.gov studies matching the five terms and found none** — `corrected`
  The COUNT is exactly right; the CONCLUSION drawn from it is wrong. RIGHT: at least NCT02960711 (primary = 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases', non-diseased 55-74 population, registry title 'Metformin and Dietary Restriction to Prevent Age-related Morbid Events in People With Metabolic Syndrome') and NCT01777893 (PREVIEW, N=2500, pre-diabetes/obesity, primary = 'Incidence of type 2 diabetes' at 3 years, all adults first put through an 8-week low-calorie diet) are inside that very set with incident-disease primary endpoints in non-disease populations. Separately, the search string is the wrong instrument for the 'anywhere in the world' claim: PREDIMED-Plus is not on CTG at all, and the Diabetes Prevention Program (NCT00004992, primary outcome 'Development of diabetes', calorie-restricted lifestyle arm, prediabetes population) is NOT in the 1,472 because its record does not use those five phrases — I verified its absence from the downloaded set.

- **BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 trials and 6,582 adults contains no hard clinical endpoint** — `confirmed`
  Verified against the full text (Semnani-Azad et al., BMJ 2025;389:e082007, PMC12175170). Verbatim from the abstract: 'Objective To assess the effect of intermittent fasting diets, with continuous energy restriction or unrestricted (ad-libitum) diets on intermediate cardiometabolic outcomes from randomised clinical trials'; 'Main outcomes Outcomes included body weight (primary) and measures of anthropometry, glucose metabolism, lipid profiles, blood pressure, C-reactive protein, and markers of liver disease'; 'Results 99 randomised clinical trials involving 6582 adults of varying health conditions (720 healthy, 5862 existing health conditions) were identified.' No occurrence of 'mortality' or 'cardiovascular event' anywhere in the text (I grepped the full text). Two refinements worth carrying: (a) it does tabulate harms — 'Assessment of adverse events were reported in 56 trials, of which 27 trials reported no harmful events in the intermittent fasting groups' — so 'no hard clinical endpoint' should be stated as no efficacy endpoint that is a clinical event; (b) only 720 of the 6,582 participants were healthy, so this NMA is not evidence about a healthy population. A correction exists (BMJ 2025 Aug 18;390:r1737) but it only fixes a coauthor's affiliation — it changes no numbers.

One caliber slip to fix: NCT05651620 is registered as study type OBSERVATIONAL (estimated enrollment 216; start 2023-04-06, estimated completion 2028-01-31), i.e. an observational follow-up of the CALERIE phase 2 participants, not itself a trial. It also carries 108 secondary outcomes (Levine phenotypic age, homeostatic dysregulation, anthropometry, etc.), none of which are clinical events.

  I could search ClinicalTrials.gov (full API download of all 1,472 records) and ISRCTN (API, 184 unique records across seven CR/fasting/TRE terms, all primary outcomes scanned). I could NOT reach ANZCTR (returns an error page) or ChiCTR (HTTP 405 block) from this environment, and the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I could run any search, so WHO ICTRP, UMIN/jRCT, CTIS and the Iranian/Indian registries went unchecked. The claim's global scope therefore remains unverified on the upside — but it is already refuted on the downside by ISRCTN89898870, which the CTG-only method could never have found.

It is false. ### 票 2(OVERTURNED)

WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) before I started, so I worked entirely through direct HTTP against primary sources via curl and read the raw JSON/XML myself rather than trusting any fetch-summariser — no quote below is second-hand.

What I reached verbatim: (1) The ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 record for NCT05651620, parsed as JSON — the two primaryOutcomes are exactly 'Biological age - Klemera-Doubal Method' and 'Healthspan', timeFrame '11-16 years post CALERIE trial'. Confirmed. (2) The API count for the researcher's exact five-term Essie query: 1,472, reproduced exactly on 2026-07-28. (3) All 1,472 full records, downloaded and grepped locally on primaryOutcomes measure+description text with a deliberately wide clinical-endpoint regex. (4) The ISRCTN WHO-format XML API record for ISRCTN89898870. (5) PubMed XML for PMIDs 39641916 (MeMeMe, Diabetes Care 2025) and 40533200 (BMJ NMA).

The refutation. The absolute claim fails twice. Inside the article's own 1,472-record set, NCT02960711 (MeMeMe) pre-specifies 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' as its sole primary outcome in metabolic-syndrome adults 55-74 who are flagged as healthy volunteers and screened free of diabetes and recent cancer; its lifestyle arm includes 'moderate calorie and protein restriction'; it completed and published in Diabetes Care 2025. Outside ClinicalTrials.gov, PREDIMED-Plus (ISRCTN89898870) is an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet trial in ~6,000 people with no CVD at enrolment whose registered primary endpoint is a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI and non-fatal stroke. Neither is a disease population under the article's own stated boundary (fasting alongside chemotherapy). I applied that boundary strictly: I excluded all nine cancer/CKD/surgery/glioblastoma/BMT hits, the perioperative MACE trial NCT04627688, the post-PCI fasting trial NCT04772924, and the pregnancy/GDM trials.

Where the article is right. The BMJ 2025 NMA claim checks out exactly — 99 trials, 6,582 adults, body weight as primary, all outcomes intermediate. The CALERIE Legacy claim checks out verbatim and is in fact stronger than stated, since its 'Healthspan' primary is a metabolic syndrome z-score rather than any clinical event. The 1,472 count is exactly right for the date.

What remains uncertain. I could not read the text of the BMJ erratum (PMID 40825602, doi 10.1136/bmj.r1737) — bmj.com 403s behind a JS challenge, PMC serves a reCAPTCHA, Europe PMC holds no abstract — so the 99/6,582 figures rest on the original indexed abstract alone. I also did not exhaustively scan ChiCTR, CTIS/EudraCT, jRCT, ANZCTR or CTRI; the 'anywhere in the world' assertion is therefore only partially tested, though it is already falsified by the two trials I did reach, so exhaustiveness was not required. The one genuine defence available to the article is that in both counterexamples energy restriction is bundled with physical activity and behavioural support rather than studied in isolation — which is why I recommend narrowing the claim to isolated CR rather than deleting the passage outright.

- **No caloric restriction, fasting, or time-restricted-eating trial in a healthy or general population anywhere in the world has mortality or incident age-related disease as a primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  WRONG as stated. Two counterexamples, both in non-diseased primary-prevention populations. (1) PREDIMED-Plus, ISRCTN89898870, read verbatim from the ISRCTN WHO-format XML API: public title 'Effect of an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet, physical activity and behavioral intervention on the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease'; PRIMARY OUTCOME field reads 'Current primary outcome measures as of 04/06/2018: 1. A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke 2. Changes in body weight'. Scientific title makes energy restriction the randomised contrast: an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet arm versus 'Mediet, but without energy restriction'. Inclusion: community-dwelling men 55-75 / women 60-75, BMI 27-40, metabolic syndrome, and explicitly 'No cardiovascular disease (CVD) at enrolment'; exclusions remove prior CVD and active/recent cancer. Target size 6000; enrolment from 05/09/2013. Secondary outcomes include death of any cause, osteoporotic fractures, dementia and cancer incidence. (2) MeMeMe, NCT02960711, 'Metformin and Dietary Restriction to Prevent Age-related Morbid Events in People With Metabolic Syndrome', Phase 3 factorial, 1600 enrolled (actual), ages 55-74, healthyVolunteers flag = true, diagnosed diabetes and recent cancer excluded. Registry PRIMARY outcome measure verbatim: 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases', description 'We will retrieve records for all Age related chronic diseases but we will first concentrate the analysis on cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, and diabetes', timeFrame '5 years'. Registered lifestyle arm is 'Mediterranean/macrobiotic diet with moderate calorie and protein restriction'. Published: Pasanisi et al., Diabetes Care 2025;48(2):265-272, PMID 39641916 — 1,442 randomised, 'The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of major noncommunicable diseases (including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer).' The one honest defence available is that in both trials energy restriction is bundled with physical activity and behavioural support rather than isolated — but neither is a disease population, and both pre-specify hard clinical events as the primary endpoint.

- **Researcher scanned all 1,472 ClinicalTrials.gov studies matching the five search terms and found none** — `corrected`
  The COUNT is right; the CONCLUSION is wrong. I reproduced 1,472 exactly on 2026-07-28 via the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 with query.term=("caloric restriction" OR "calorie restriction" OR "intermittent fasting" OR "time-restricted eating" OR "fasting-mimicking"), countTotal=true. But 'found none' is false: I downloaded all 1,472 records and grepped their primaryOutcomes, and NCT02960711 (MeMeMe) sits inside that very result set with 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' as its sole primary outcome in a metabolic-syndrome, non-diabetic, non-cancer population. Two further caveats. (a) The count is a live snapshot that drifts daily, so it should be dated. (b) The string is narrower than the field: adding 'time-restricted feeding', 'alternate-day fasting', 'energy restriction', 'dietary restriction', 'periodic fasting', 'prolonged fasting' raises the total to 2,073 — 601 additional records the scan never saw. (c) ClinicalTrials.gov alone cannot support 'anywhere in the world': PREDIMED-Plus is registered only at ISRCTN and is therefore invisible to this search entirely.

- **BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 trials and 6,582 adults contains no hard clinical endpoint** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED. 'Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials,' BMJ 2025 Jun 18;389:e082007, PMID 40533200. Abstract read verbatim from the PubMed XML: '99 randomised clinical trials involving 6582 adults of varying health conditions (720 healthy, 5862 existing health conditions) were identified.' Objective states 'intermediate cardiometabolic outcomes'. Outcome list: 'body weight (primary) and measures of anthropometry, glucose metabolism, lipid profiles, blood pressure, C-reactive protein, and markers of liver disease' — no mortality, no incident disease, no clinical events. The article could usefully add the 720-healthy / 5,862-with-conditions split, which sharpens rather than weakens the point.

- **CALERIE Legacy (NCT05651620, 11-16 years post-trial) registers 'Biological age - Klemera-Doubal Method' and 'Healthspan' as primary outcomes** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim from the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 record. The outcomesModule lists exactly two primaryOutcomes: measure 'Biological age - Klemera-Doubal Method' and measure 'Healthspan', both with timeFrame '11-16 years post CALERIE trial'. Study is ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING, started 2023-04-06, 216 participants, official title 'Legacy Effects of CALERIE™, a 2-year Calorie Restriction Intervention, on Hallmarks of Healthspan and Aging'. One detail worth adding because it strengthens the argument: 'Healthspan' is operationalised not as clinical events but as a sex-specific metabolic syndrome z-score built from HDL, triglycerides, waist circumference, fasting glucose and mean arterial pressure. Its ~100 secondary outcomes are likewise all biomarkers, function tests and questionnaires — not one is an incident-disease or mortality endpoint.

- **Whether the BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis was materially amended by its published erratum** — `unreachable`
  A Published Erratum to the BMJ NMA exists — BMJ 2025 Aug 18, doi 10.1136/bmj.r1737, PMID 40825602, RefSource pointing to BMJ. 2025 Jun 18;389:e082007. I could not read its text: bmj.com returned HTTP 403 behind a JavaScript challenge, PMC returned a reCAPTCHA page, and Europe PMC holds no abstract for it. I therefore cannot rule out that the erratum adjusted the trial count (99) or participant count (6,582). Those two figures are verified against the original indexed abstract only. This session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I began, so I could not search for secondary coverage of the correction.

The handful of trials that do pre-specify incident disease embed energy restriction inside multi-component weight-loss lifestyle programmes aimed at cardiometabolic risk, not at aging.'

Registered primary outcome: 'A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke' plus changes in body weight. Population: community-dwelling men 55-75 / women 60-75, BMI 27-40, metabolic syndrome, no CVD at enrolment; target 6,000. The randomised contrast is energy-restricted Mediterranean diet versus the same Mediterranean diet without energy restriction. As of 2026-07 I found no published primary CV-outcome paper, so state it as ongoing with results pending — do not claim a result.

Registered primary outcome verbatim: 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' (description names cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke and diabetes), 5-year time frame; ages 55-74, metabolic syndrome, healthy-volunteers flag true, diagnosed diabetes and recent cancer excluded; lifestyle arm is a 'Mediterranean/macrobiotic diet with moderate calorie and protein restriction'. Note the result honestly: the benefit was driven almost entirely by metformin's effect on type 2 diabetes, not by the diet arm — which supports the article's underlying thesis even as it breaks the absolute claim.
- FIX the registry-scan sentence. Date the count ('1,472 as of [date]' — it reproduces exactly on 2026-07-28 but drifts daily) and drop 'found none'. State instead that one trial in that set (NCT02960711) does carry incident age-related disease as its primary endpoint.
