**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- PREDIMED-Plus, ISRCTN89898870. Primary outcome field read verbatim from the ISRCTN WHO-format XML API: 'A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke'. Intervention is an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet versus the same diet without energy restriction. Population is explicitly primary prevention — 'No cardiovascular disease (CVD) at enrolment', prior CVD and active/recent cancer excluded. Target 6,000; men 55-75, women 60-75, BMI 27-40, metabolic syndrome. This is a caloric-restriction trial in a non-diseased population with incident cardiovascular disease as a pre-specified primary endpoint. Independently surfaced twice: by direct record fetch and by a term scan of ISRCTN for 'energy-restricted'.
- MeMeMe, NCT02960711, sits inside the article's own 1,472-record ClinicalTrials.gov result set with primary outcome 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' (cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, diabetes) over 5 years, in metabolic-syndrome adults aged 55-74 flagged as healthy volunteers, with a diet arm including 'moderate calorie and protein restriction'. Published in Diabetes Care 2025;48(2):265-272. The researcher's own search retrieved this record and the scan missed it.
- The registry scan's coverage is narrower than represented. Broadening the term list to include 'time-restricted feeding', 'alternate-day fasting', 'energy restriction', 'dietary restriction', 'periodic fasting' and 'prolonged fasting' returns 2,073 ClinicalTrials.gov records rather than 1,472 — 601 records never examined.
- ClinicalTrials.gov cannot support a worldwide negative. PREDIMED-Plus, the strongest counterexample, has no ClinicalTrials.gov registration at all; it exists only at ISRCTN. Any 'anywhere in the world' claim built on a single registry is structurally unsound.
- Secondary but relevant boundary cases inside the 1,472: NCT01286389 lists 'Diagnosis of dementia' among its primary outcomes for caloric restriction in obese adults with mild cognitive impairment, and NCT01777893 (PREVIEW, n=2,500 prediabetic overweight adults) has 'Incidence of type 2 diabetes' as its primary outcome — though in PREVIEW the low-calorie diet was a universal 8-week run-in rather than the randomised factor, so it is a weak counterexample and I do not rely on it.

### 票 3(OVERTURNED)

I treated the claim as four separable sub-claims and attacked the absence claim directly rather than trying to confirm it.

What I reached verbatim: (1) the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, from which I downloaded all 1,472 matching records and machine-scanned every primary-outcome measure and description under two successive keyword nets, plus full individual records for NCT02960711, NCT05651620, NCT01777893, NCT04772924, NCT00017953, NCT00004992 and NCT00038727; (2) the ISRCTN registry XML API, from which I read the complete PREDIMED-Plus record (ISRCTN89898870) including its primary_outcome, secondary_outcome, inclusion/exclusion criteria and arm descriptions; (3) the full text of the BMJ network meta-analysis (PMC12175170) and its August 2025 erratum (PMC12359177) as XML from Europe PMC; (4) the full text of the MeMeMe results paper (PMC11770154, Diabetes Care 2025); (5) the Ann Intern Med 2025 PREDIMED-Plus secondary-analysis abstract via the Europe PMC core record. Every quoted string above was seen in the retrieved document, not in a fetch-tool summary — I deliberately used raw HTTP and local parsing rather than the summarising web-fetch tool, precisely because of the fabricated-quote failure mode.

The decisive finding is PREDIMED-Plus. It is an interventional randomised prevention trial of caloric restriction (explicitly "energy-restricted"/"energy-reduced", 600 kcal/day planned reduction, randomised against the same diet ad libitum) in 6,874 community-dwelling adults free of cardiovascular disease and cancer at entry, whose registered primary endpoint is a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI and non-fatal stroke. It falls on the "counts" side of the boundary the task specified — it is not a disease-treatment population like fasting alongside chemotherapy — and it is invisible to a ClinicalTrials.gov search because it is registered only at ISRCTN. That single record falsifies the central assertion and simultaneously exposes why the methodology could not have supported "anywhere in the world."

The secondary finding is that the "found none" claim fails even on its own turf: MeMeMe (NCT02960711) sits inside the 1,472 with "Total incidence of age related chronic diseases" as its sole primary outcome and total mortality as its secondary outcome. I checked its published report and found a genuine mitigation — the delivered diet arm was qualitative with no calorie prescription, and metformin rather than diet drove the result — so I have graded it as a weaker instance rather than a second knockout.

Two sub-claims survive intact and I could not dent them: the BMJ figures (99 trials, 6,582 adults) match exactly, the outcome set is entirely surrogate, and the erratum is only an affiliation fix; the CALERIE Legacy primary outcomes match the article's wording string-for-string.

What remains uncertain. First, I could not locate a published primary-outcome cardiovascular paper for PREDIMED-Plus as of July 2026 despite targeted searches of the major journals; the endpoint is registered and the trial completed in December 2024, but the headline result appears unreported, and I want the article to state that rather than imply the result is in hand. Second, I could not query ANZCTR (its web service returned an error page), and I did not reach ChiCTR, CTRI, jRCT, DRKS or the EU CTR at all, so there may well be further counterexamples I have not seen — my search of non-US registries was limited to ISRCTN (140 unique records across three query terms) and is not exhaustive. Third, I verified the Diabetes Prevention Program's registered endpoints but did not reach a primary document specifying its calorie prescription, so I have hedged that example. Fourth, my scans are keyword-based over primary-outcome text; an oddly worded hard endpoint could have slipped through, which biases my search toward under-detection — meaning the true number of counterexamples is at least what I report and plausibly higher. None of these gaps cut against the verdict: one fully verified counterexample is sufficient to overturn a universal negative, and I have one I read in the primary registry record myself.

- **No caloric restriction, fasting, or time-restricted-eating trial in a healthy or general population ANYWHERE IN THE WORLD has mortality or incident age-related disease as a primary endpoint** — `refuted`
  REFUTED by PREDIMED-Plus, ISRCTN89898870. I read the ISRCTN primary registry record directly via the ISRCTN XML API (https://www.isrctn.com/api/query/format/who?q=ISRCTN89898870). Verbatim fields: public_title = 'Effect of an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet, physical activity and behavioral intervention on the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease'; study_type = 'Interventional'; study_design = 'Randomized controlled trial (Prevention)'; target_size 6000, results_actual_enrolment 6874; primary_outcome = 'Current primary outcome measures as of 04/06/2018: 1. A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke 2. Changes in body weight'. Secondary outcomes verbatim include 'Death of any cause', 'osteoporotic fractures', 'dementia', 'Parkinson disease', 'cancer (breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, or stomach)'. Inclusion criteria verbatim: 'Community-dwelling high-risk people; Men aged 55 to 75 years and women aged 60 to 75 years; Body mass index (BMI) >=27 and <40 kg/m2; No cardiovascular disease (CVD) at enrolment; Who fulfil at least three of the criteria for the metabolic syndrome'. Intervention arm verbatim: 'Intensive intervention with an energy-restricted Mediet ... together with promotion of physical activity, behavioral support and weight loss goals'; control arm: same MedDiet 'without energy-restriction, without weight loss goals and without a physical activity program'. So caloric restriction IS the randomized contrast, the population is a primary-prevention community sample free of CVD and free of cancer (not a treated-disease population like the chemotherapy trials the article excludes), and the pre-specified primary endpoint is a hard clinical composite of CV death + non-fatal MI + non-fatal stroke. Independently corroborated by Ann Intern Med 2025 (PMID 40854218), a 'Prespecified secondary outcome analysis in the PREDIMED (Prevencion con Dieta Mediterranea)-Plus randomized, single-blinded, controlled trial. (ISRCTN Registry: ISRCTN89898870)' in '4746 adults aged 55 to 75 years with metabolic syndrome and overweight or obesity, without prior cardiovascular disease or diabetes', intervention 'an erMedDiet (planned reduction of 600 kcal per day)', reporting incident type 2 diabetes 31% lower over median 6-year follow-up. Crucially, PREDIMED-Plus is registered ONLY at ISRCTN, not on ClinicalTrials.gov (I queried the CTG API for 'PREDIMED-Plus OR ISRCTN89898870' and no PREDIMED-Plus record exists), so a CTG-only scan structurally cannot substantiate a worldwide claim. Caveats the article may fairly note: the intervention is a multi-component package (energy restriction + physical activity + behavioral support), not isolated CR as in CALERIE; the population is overweight/obese with metabolic syndrome rather than normal-weight healthy; and I could NOT locate a published primary-outcome CVD paper as of 2026-07 (searched Europe PMC for PREDIMED-Plus in NEJM/Lancet/JAMA/Ann Intern Med/Circulation/EHJ/BMJ 2025-2026 and found no main-results paper) - but the claim is about what is registered as a primary endpoint, and that endpoint is unambiguously registered.

- **Researcher scanned all 1,472 ClinicalTrials.gov studies matching 'caloric restriction' OR 'calorie restriction' OR 'intermittent fasting' OR 'time-restricted eating' OR 'fasting-mimicking' and found none** — `corrected`
  The COUNT is right; the 'found none' is WRONG. I reproduced 1,472 exactly today (2026-07-28) via the CTG v2 API with those five phrases under concept expansion (totalCount: 1472), so the denominator holds. But I downloaded all 1,472 records and machine-scanned every primary-outcome measure and description, and the set DOES contain a trial with incident age-related disease as its pre-specified primary endpoint. WRONG: 'found none.' RIGHT: NCT02960711 is in that set - 'Randomized Controlled Trial of Metformin and Dietary Restriction to Prevent Age-related Morbid Events in People With Metabolic Syndrome' (MeMeMe), Phase 3, 2x2 factorial, primaryPurpose PREVENTION, enrollment 1,600 actual, ages 55-74, diagnosed diabetes and recent cancer excluded. Its single registered primary outcome verbatim is 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' with description 'We will retrieve records for all Age related chronic diseases but we will first concentrate the analysis on cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, and diabetes', timeFrame '5 years'; its sole secondary outcome verbatim is 'Effect of the intervention on total mortality and on the incidence of specific chronic diseases' at '8-10 years'. The registry brief summary describes the lifestyle arm as 'Mediterranean/macrobiotic diet with moderate calorie and protein restriction'. One honest mitigation for the article: in the published report (Diabetes Care 2025, PMID 39641916 / PMC11770154) the delivered diet arm was qualitative, stated verbatim as 'Participants did not receive a specific dietary plan with calorie count but did receive dietary recommendations', and the primary outcome was reported as 'the cumulative incidence of major noncommunicable diseases (including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer)' with the effect driven by metformin, not diet. So MeMeMe is a weaker counterexample than PREDIMED-Plus - but it is unambiguously inside the 1,472 the researcher claims to have scanned, which means the scan as reported did not find what it says it looked for.

- **The BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 trials and 6,582 adults contains no hard clinical endpoint at all** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim against the full text (Semnani-Azad et al., BMJ 2025;389:e082007, PMID 40533200 / PMC12175170), fetched as XML from Europe PMC. Abstract reads verbatim: '99 randomised clinical trials involving 6582 adults of varying health conditions (720 healthy, 5862 existing health conditions) were identified.' Both numbers match exactly. Objective verbatim: 'To assess the effect of intermittent fasting diets, with continuous energy restriction or unrestricted (ad-libitum) diets on intermediate cardiometabolic outcomes from randomised clinical trials.' Main outcomes verbatim: 'Outcomes included body weight (primary) and measures of anthropometry, glucose metabolism, lipid profiles, blood pressure, C-reactive protein, and markers of liver disease.' I grep-verified the whole article body: zero occurrences of 'mortalit', 'death', 'stroke', or 'cardiovascular event' outside the reference list (the single 'myocardial' hit is a cited reference title). No hard clinical endpoint is synthesised. Two minor nuances worth knowing but not correcting: (a) the paper does tabulate safety data - 'Assessment of adverse events were reported in 56 trials, of which 27 trials reported no harmful events in the intermittent fasting groups' - which is harms reporting, not an efficacy endpoint; (b) I checked the erratum (BMJ 2025;390:r1737, PMID 40825602) and it corrects only a coauthor's affiliation, so 99/6,582 are not superseded. Also useful for the article: only 720 of the 6,582 participants were healthy, i.e. the NMA is overwhelmingly disease populations.

- **CALERIE Legacy follow-up (NCT05651620, 11-16 years post-trial) registers 'Biological age - Klemera-Doubal Method' and 'Healthspan' as primary outcomes rather than clinical events** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim against the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API record for NCT05651620. Official title: 'Legacy Effects of CALERIE(TM), a 2-year Calorie Restriction Intervention, on Hallmarks of Healthspan and Aging'. Status ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING, start 2023-04-06, estimated enrollment 216, arms 'Calorie Restriction (CR)' and 'Ad Libitum (AL)'. Exactly two primary outcomes, both with timeFrame '11-16 years post CALERIE trial': measure 1 verbatim 'Biological age - Klemera-Doubal Method' (description: 'Biological age will be quantified by the Klemera-Doubal Method (KDM), an algorithm-based measure. Biological age is expressed in years.'); measure 2 verbatim 'Healthspan' (description: 'Healthspan will be assessed by sex-specific metabolic syndrome z-score (MS z-score)...'). Every string in the article's claim matches. Secondary outcomes are also all surrogates (Levine Phenotypic Age, Homeostatic Dysregulation, anthropometry, VO2max, IL-6, OGTT insulin, etc.) - no clinical events anywhere in the record. Worth flagging for the article: 'Healthspan' here is operationalised as a metabolic-syndrome z-score, not as disease-free survival, which makes the article's point sharper than it currently states.

**修正:**
- Delete the sentence 'No caloric restriction, fasting, or time-restricted-eating trial in a healthy or general population anywhere in the world has mortality or incident age-related disease as a primary endpoint.' It is false. PREDIMED-Plus (ISRCTN89898870), a Spanish randomised prevention trial of an energy-restricted Mediterranean diet (planned 600 kcal/day reduction) plus physical activity versus the same diet ad libitum, enrolled 6,874 community-dwelling adults aged 55-75 with metabolic syndrome and no cardiovascular disease at entry, and registers as its primary outcome 'A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke', with 'Death of any cause', dementia, osteoporotic fractures and site-specific cancers among its secondary outcomes.
- Do not write 'anywhere in the world' on the strength of a ClinicalTrials.gov-only search. PREDIMED-Plus is registered exclusively at ISRCTN and returns zero hits on ClinicalTrials.gov, so the CTG scan could not have seen it. Either widen the scan to the WHO ICTRP partner registries (ISRCTN, ANZCTR, ChiCTR, CTRI, jRCT, DRKS, EU-CTR) or restrict the sentence explicitly to 'on ClinicalTrials.gov'.
- Correct 'found none' in the 1,472-study scan. The count 1,472 is right and reproduces exactly on the ClinicalTrials.gov API as of 2026-07-28, but the set contains NCT02960711 (the MeMeMe trial, n=1,600, ages 55-74, primaryPurpose PREVENTION), whose sole registered primary outcome is 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' (cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, diabetes) at 5 years, with 'total mortality' as its secondary outcome at 8-10 years. Rewrite as: the scan found one such trial, MeMeMe, and describe why it is a weak instance rather than claiming zero.
- If the article keeps a version of the absence claim, state the boundary it actually applies and apply it consistently. It cannot treat overweight/obese and metabolic-syndrome participants as 'general population' when counting the 1,472 ClinicalTrials.gov records while excluding PREDIMED-Plus, MeMeMe and the Diabetes Prevention Program as 'disease populations' - all four enrol people free of the disease being counted. The defensible narrow claim is: no trial of caloric restriction as an isolated, non-weight-loss-motivated intervention in normal-weight healthy adults has ever been powered on mortality or incident disease.
- Add the honest qualifier that PREDIMED-Plus's registered cardiovascular primary endpoint has not, as far as could be established in July 2026, been reported in a published primary-outcome paper (the trial completed 22 December 2024; only prespecified secondary analyses such as the Ann Intern Med 2025 incident-diabetes paper, PMID 40854218, have appeared). The absence claim still fails, because it is a claim about what is registered as a primary endpoint, not about what has been published.
- When citing the BMJ 2025 network meta-analysis, add that only 720 of the 6,582 participants were healthy and 5,862 had existing health conditions - the paper states this verbatim - which strengthens rather than weakens the article's point about the evidence base. Cite it as Semnani-Azad et al., BMJ 2025;389:e082007; the August 2025 erratum (BMJ 2025;390:r1737) corrects only an author affiliation and leaves the 99/6,582 figures intact.
- Sharpen the CALERIE Legacy point: 'Healthspan' in NCT05651620 is operationalised as a sex-specific metabolic syndrome z-score built from HDL, triglycerides, waist circumference, fasting glucose and mean arterial pressure - not as disease-free survival. Saying so makes the surrogate-endpoint argument stronger than the current wording does.
- Consider replacing the false absolute with the accurate and still-striking comparative: caloric restriction has been tested against hard clinical endpoints only when packaged as a weight-loss lifestyle programme in high-risk or diseased populations - PREDIMED-Plus (CVD composite, n=6,874), Look AHEAD (NCT00017953, 'First Occurrence of a Severe Cardiovascular Event' over 11 years, n=5,145, but in type 2 diabetes), the Diabetes Prevention Program and DPPOS (NCT00004992 / NCT00038727, primary outcomes including 'Development of Diabetes', 'Total Cancer Except Non-melanoma Skin Cancer' at 24 years and 'Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE): Myocardial Infarction (MI), Stroke, or Cardiovascular Death (CVD)' at 29 years) - and never as CR-for-longevity in healthy normal-weight adults. Note that none of DPP, DPPOS or Look AHEAD appear in the 1,472-record ClinicalTrials.gov set either.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- PREDIMED-Plus (ISRCTN89898870): interventional randomised prevention trial, n=6,874, energy-restricted Mediterranean diet + physical activity + behavioural support versus ad libitum Mediterranean diet, in adults 55-75 with BMI 27-40 and metabolic syndrome but 'No cardiovascular disease (CVD) at enrolment'. Registered primary outcome verbatim: 'A composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke'. This is precisely the trial the article says does not exist.
- PREDIMED-Plus secondary outcomes, verbatim from the ISRCTN record, include 'Death of any cause', 'osteoporotic fractures', 'dementia', 'Parkinson disease' and 'cancer (breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, or stomach)' - i.e. the trial registers all-cause mortality and multiple incident age-related diseases, just not as the primary endpoint.
- Ann Intern Med 2025 (PMID 40854218) reports a prespecified PREDIMED-Plus secondary outcome analysis in 4,746 adults 'without prior cardiovascular disease or diabetes' randomised to 'an erMedDiet (planned reduction of 600 kcal per day)': incident type 2 diabetes was 31% (CI 18% to 41%) relatively lower over a median 6-year follow-up. An energy-restricted diet has therefore already been shown to reduce an incident age-related disease in a prevention population - published, not merely registered.
- NCT02960711 (MeMeMe), inside the researcher's own 1,472-record ClinicalTrials.gov set, registers 'Total incidence of age related chronic diseases' (cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, diabetes) as its only primary outcome and 'total mortality' as its secondary outcome. Published as Diabetes Care 2025, PMID 39641916.
- NCT00038727 (Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study, n=2,779, primaryPurpose PREVENTION) lists among its PRIMARY outcomes 'Total Cancer Except Non-melanoma Skin Cancer' assessed over approximately 24 years and 'Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE): Myocardial Infarction (MI), Stroke, or Cardiovascular Death (CVD)' assessed over approximately 29 years, in a cohort recruited with impaired glucose tolerance rather than established disease. Its parent trial NCT00004992 has 'Development of diabetes' as its primary outcome. Neither appears in the 1,472-record set.
- NCT00017953 (Look AHEAD, n=5,145) has as its primary outcome 'First Occurrence of a Severe Cardiovascular Event' over up to 11 years, testing an intervention the registry describes verbatim as 'designed to achieve and maintain weight loss by decreased caloric intake and increased physical activity'. It is in a type 2 diabetes population, so it falls outside the article's stated boundary - but it too is absent from the 1,472-record set, further showing the search string is porous.
- The five-phrase search string is demonstrably incomplete even within ClinicalTrials.gov. A parallel query on 'alternate day fasting', 'energy restriction', 'intermittent energy restriction', 'dietary restriction', 'very low calorie diet', 'Ramadan fasting', 'prolonged fasting', 'periodic fasting' and 'time restricted feeding' returned 1,131 records of which 15 with hard-endpoint primary outcomes were NOT in the 1,472, including NCT04772924 (prolonged fasting in 405 post-PCI patients with 'The number of participant with major adverse cardiovascular event' as primary outcome).

- **(a) Technical noise alone (same DNA sample assayed twice) produces deviations of up to 9 years between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks — Higgins-Chen et al. 2022, Nature Aging** — `confirmed`
  CONFIRMED verbatim, with a precision caveat the article should carry. The abstract (PMID 36277076, DOI 10.1038/s43587-022-00248-2, PMC9586209) reads verbatim: 'Here we show technical noise produces deviations up to 9 years between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks, limiting their utility.' I retrieved this identical string from two independent renderings (PubMed record page and PMC full text). The '9 years' is a ROUNDED abstract figure; the Results text gives the underlying numbers: 'Focusing additional analyses on 6 clocks, we found they all demonstrated substantial discrepancies between technical replicates (Fig. 1h–m)... The widely used Horvath1 multi-tissue clock shows a median deviation of 1.8 years between replicates, and a maximum of 4.8 years. For other clocks, median deviations range from 0.9 to 2.4 years and maxima range from 4.5 to 8.6 years.' So the true reported maximum across the six clocks is 8.6 years, not 9, and the MEDIAN deviations are only 0.9–2.4 years. The six clocks are Horvath1, Horvath2 (skin & blood), Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, DNAmTL — DunedinPoAm/DunedinPACE is NOT one of the six. On 'the same DNA sample assayed twice': the Fig. 1 replicate set is GSE55763 — Higgins-Chen states '36 whole blood samples measured in duplicate from the London Life Sciences Prospective Population (LOLIPOP) study' and 'The replicates in GSE55763 were done in separate batches to maximize the impact of technical factors.' The GEO record for GSE55763 says 'Bisulfite-converted DNA for 2,664 human samples and 36 technical replicates were hybridised to the Illumina Infinium 450k Human Methylation Beadchip v1.2.' GEO calls them technical replicates but does not explicitly state same-aliquot re-hybridisation, so 'the same DNA sample assayed twice' is the fair reading but is one inferential step beyond what GEO literally says. Note also that the paper separately used Elysium-supplied paired blood and saliva replicate datasets, which are NOT pure same-aliquot technical replicates; the 9-year headline is anchored to the GSE55763 blood technical replicates.

Levine, senior author) and AHC (Higgins-Chen, first author) — the statement is not anonymous; (ii) the licensing direction is Yale University licensing the metrics TO Elysium Health, and an additional undisclosed-in-the-claim interest exists — AHC also received consulting fees from FOXO Technologies, another commercial epigenetic-age company. Verbatim strings retrieved: 'For DunedinPACE, reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.96 [0.93–0.98]' for the 'n = 36 replicate adult-blood-sample Illumina 450 k datasets'; and 'DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.97 [0.94–0.98] in the EPIC-EPIC database and 0.87 [0.82–0.90] in the 450k-EPIC database.' Two additional facts worth carrying: (i) the n=36 set is GSE55763 — the SAME LOLIPOP technical-replicate set that produced the 9-year figure in claim (a), so (a) and (c) rest on one shared dataset; (ii) the paper also reports the predecessor 'For the original DunedinPoAm, reliability was good (ICC = 0.89 95% CI [0.79–0.94])' in the same n=36 set, so DunedinPACE's improvement over DunedinPoAm is 0.89→0.96. The article's framing of 0.96/0.97 as 'headline' and 0.87 as the cross-array figure is accurate — all three appear in the same paper, so this is not a case of a later study undercutting the original.

Source located and read: Apsley AT, Ye Q, Caspi A, Chiaro C, Etzel L, Hastings WJ, Heim CM, Kozlosky J, Noll JG, Schreier HMC, Shenk CE, Sugden K, Shalev I. 'Cross-tissue comparison of epigenetic aging clocks in humans.' Aging Cell 2025, PMID 39780748, DOI 10.1111/acel.14451, PMC11984668. Table 2 is titled verbatim 'Pairwise within-person differences in standard epigenetic clocks across tissue types.' Column headers in order: Buccal vs. saliva | Buccal vs. DBS | Buccal vs. Buffy coat | Buccal vs. PBMC | Saliva vs. DBS | Saliva vs. Buffy coat | Saliva vs. PBMC | DBS vs. Buffy coat | DBS vs. PBMC. The GrimAge2 row reads: '13.47 ± 1.21*** | 35.78 ± 0.68*** | 34.82 ± 1.20*** | 40.25 ± 0.79*** | 20.72 ± 1.69*** | 25.70 ± 2.46*** | 22.42 ± 1.58*** | −1.11 ± 0.81 | 5.16 ± 0.56***', footnote '*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001'. So 35.78 ± 0.68 does sit in the Buccal vs. DBS column for GrimAge2 — I confirmed this column alignment on two separate fetches. WRONG in the claim: 'in 83 individuals'. The RIGHT version: the study's total analytic sample was 83 individuals contributing 284 samples across five tissues — verbatim, 'Our analytical sample consisted of 83 individuals across two studies with a total of 284 tissue samples (NBuccal = 81; NSaliva = 59; NDBS = 64; NBuffyCoat = 35; NPBMC = 45).' The buccal-vs-DBS pairwise comparison therefore rests on at most 64 individuals (those with a DBS sample), not 83; the paper does not state the exact paired n for that cell. Also note the direction: buccal is HIGHER than DBS (the paper states all within-person clock estimates other than Horvath pan-tissue were significantly higher in buccal and saliva than in blood-based tissues), and 35.78 is not even the largest GrimAge2 gap — Buccal vs. PBMC is 40.25 years. The paper's own abstract headline is more conservative: 'with average differences of almost 30 years observed in some age clocks.' - **Requested extra: the per-clock ICC table in Higgins-Chen et al. 2022** — `unreachable`
  UNREACHABLE — and I must flag an active fabrication risk here. The per-clock ICCs for the six ORIGINAL (non-PC) clocks are NOT stated numerically anywhere in the Higgins-Chen article text. They exist only (i) inside the figure raster images (Fig. 1g and Fig. 3g–h), which are not transcribable, and (ii) in Supplementary Table 4, described in the text as 'ICCs for biomarkers adjusted for age are listed in Supplementary Table 4'. The figure captions contain no ICC numbers (checked Fig. 1 caption directly). The ONLY original-clock ICC stated numerically in prose is GrimAge: verbatim, 'The high reliability of GrimAge (ICC = 0.989) is related to its two-step calculation from 7 DNAm-based components, age, and sex.' Other verbatim ICC statements in the text: 'all PC clocks show ICC>0.99 for epigenetic age and ICC>0.97 for age acceleration'; 'GrimAge component ICCs are also increased (e.g. DNAmLeptin 0.329 vs. PCLeptin 0.997)'; and the important interpretive caveat 'Epigenetic age acceleration residuals have lower ICCs because of reduced biological variance compared to epigenetic age.' WARNING: on my first fetch of PMC9586209, the web-fetch summarizer returned a complete twelve-row ICC table (Horvath1 0.988, Horvath2 0.975, Hannum 0.989, PhenoAge 0.970, DNAmTL 0.964, GrimAge 0.989 for epigenetic age; 0.966/0.947/0.977/0.930/0.927/0.982 for age acceleration, all PC clocks >0.99/>0.97). **修正:**
- Claim (d): replace 'in 83 individuals' with the correct denominator. The Apsley et al. 2025 (Aging Cell, DOI 10.1111/acel.14451) analytic sample was 83 individuals contributing 284 samples across FIVE tissue types (buccal n=81, saliva n=59, dried blood spot n=64, buffy coat n=35, PBMC n=45). The buccal-vs-DBS pairwise contrast therefore rests on at most 64 individuals, and the paper never reports the exact paired n for that cell. Write it as: 'in a study of 83 individuals (buccal n=81, DBS n=64)'.
- Claim (d): state the direction and the units. The 35.78 ± 0.68 years (p<0.001) is a within-person difference in which BUCCAL GrimAge2 is HIGHER than dried-blood-spot GrimAge2, from Table 2 ('Pairwise within-person differences in standard epigenetic clocks across tissue types'). Do not present it as a symmetric or direction-free 'discrepancy'.
- Claim (d): 35.78 is not the maximum. In the same GrimAge2 row, Buccal vs. PBMC is 40.25 ± 0.79 years. Conversely, DBS vs. Buffy coat for GrimAge2 is −1.11 ± 0.81 and NOT statistically significant — i.e. the tens-of-years gap is specifically an oral-vs-blood artefact of applying blood-trained clocks to buccal/saliva tissue, not a general 'any two tissues disagree' finding. The article must say which tissue pairs, or it overstates the phenomenon.
- Claim (d): the paper's own headline number is more conservative — verbatim, 'with average differences of almost 30 years observed in some age clocks.' If the article quotes 35.78 as the study's headline, attribute it correctly to the GrimAge2 buccal-vs-DBS cell of Table 2, not to the paper's summary finding.
- Claim (a): 9 years is the abstract's rounded figure. The Results give the actual distribution: Horvath1 median deviation 1.8 years, maximum 4.8 years; for the other five clocks 'median deviations range from 0.9 to 2.4 years and maxima range from 4.5 to 8.6 years.' If the article presents 9 years as a measured quantity it should say 'up to ~9 years (maximum 8.6 y across the six clocks; medians only 0.9–2.4 y)' — otherwise readers will take an extreme-tail value as typical, which is the mirror-image of the misquotation the article is trying to correct.
- Claim (a): name the six clocks so readers do not assume DunedinPACE is among them. They are Horvath1 (multi-tissue), Horvath2 (skin & blood), Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge and DNAmTL. DunedinPoAm/DunedinPACE is not one of the six.
- Claim (a): the 9-year figure comes from GSE55763 (LOLIPOP), 36 whole-blood samples measured in duplicate with 'replicates... done in separate batches to maximize the impact of technical factors.' GEO describes these as '36 technical replicates' hybridised to the Illumina 450k array; it does not explicitly say same-aliquot re-hybridisation. 'The same DNA sample assayed twice' is defensible but should be phrased as 'technical replicates of the same blood sample run in separate batches' to stay inside what the sources literally state. Note separately that the paper's OTHER replicate sets (the Elysium blood and saliva pairs) are not pure same-aliquot replicates.
- Claim (b): the competing-interests statement should be quoted with the initials expanded, since the point of citing it is the conflict's identity: MEL is Morgan E. Levine (senior author) and AHC is Albert Higgins-Chen (first author). Also include the second commercial tie the claim omits — 'AHC received consulting fees from FOXO Technologies, Inc. for work unrelated to the present manuscript' — and note that co-author Tina T. Hu-Seliger is listed with an Elysium Health, Inc. affiliation. The licensing direction is Yale University → Elysium Health.
- Claim (c): all four numbers are exact and need no change, but add the fact that materially sharpens the point — the n=36 set behind DunedinPACE's 0.96 ICC is GSE55763, the SAME LOLIPOP technical-replicate dataset that produced the 9-year deviation figure in claim (a). The article's two independent-looking reliability claims share one 36-pair dataset.
- Do NOT publish any per-clock ICC table for the six original clocks in Higgins-Chen et al. Those values appear only inside figure images (Fig. 1g, Fig. 3g–h) and Supplementary Table 4, none of which is reachable without institutional access. The only original-clock ICC stated in the article's prose is GrimAge: 'The high reliability of GrimAge (ICC = 0.989) is related to its two-step calculation from 7 DNAm-based components, age, and sex.' A twelve-row ICC table surfaced during this verification but could not be corroborated and is presumed a summarizer fabrication.
- If the article contrasts original vs PC clock reliability, use the two verbatim text statements rather than invented per-clock numbers: 'all PC clocks show ICC>0.99 for epigenetic age and ICC>0.97 for age acceleration' and 'GrimAge component ICCs are also increased (e.g. DNAmLeptin 0.329 vs. PCLeptin 0.997)'. Also carry the paper's own caveat, verbatim: 'Epigenetic age acceleration residuals have lower ICCs because of reduced biological variance compared to epigenetic age.' — ICCs for epigenetic AGE are inflated by the wide chronological-age spread of the sample and are not the relevant reliability metric for an intervention trial.

**新发现的矛盾证据:**
- Claim (d) as written implies tissue choice generically swings biological age by tens of years. The primary table refutes the general form: in the same GrimAge2 row, DBS vs. Buffy coat is −1.11 ± 0.81 and non-significant, and DBS vs. PBMC is only 5.16 ± 0.56. The tens-of-years effect is confined to oral-vs-blood contrasts (buccal/saliva vs DBS/buffy/PBMC), i.e. it is an out-of-training-tissue artefact of blood-trained clocks, not evidence that tissue sampling is generally unstable.
- Claim (a)'s framing of 9 years as what technical noise 'produces' is contradicted in caliber by the paper's own Results, which report medians of 0.9–2.4 years across the six clocks. 9 years is the rounded worst case, not the central tendency — the same tail-for-typical substitution the article accuses others of committing when they re-quote the figure as biological variability.
- Claims (a) and (c) are less independent than the article implies: DunedinPACE's 0.96 ICC (n=36) and Higgins-Chen's 9-year deviation figure both derive from GSE55763, the 36 duplicate LOLIPOP whole-blood samples. Presenting them as two separate lines of evidence on clock unreliability overstates the evidentiary base.
- For claim (b), the conflict is broader than the article states in one direction and narrower in another. Broader: first author Higgins-Chen also declares consulting fees from FOXO Technologies, and a co-author was affiliated with Elysium Health at the time. Narrower: the statement explicitly says Elysium 'otherwise did not fund the study and did not play a role in conceptualization, design, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript' — the article should not imply Elysium funded or steered the work, only that it supplied replicate datasets and holds the license.
- The 0.87 cross-array ICC in claim (c) is not an external rebuttal of DunedinPACE's own reliability marketing — it is reported by the DunedinPACE authors themselves in the same eLife paper alongside 0.96 and 0.97. If the article frames 0.87 as something later work exposed, that framing is wrong; the authors disclosed it up front.

WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session (200/200 used), so I worked entirely through direct WebFetch against primary hosts and APIs, using the Europe PMC REST search API to resolve identifiers.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS I REACHED:

Nature's own page is behind an idp.nature.com redirect chain; I followed it through two hops (idp.nature.com/authorize -> idp.nature.com/transit -> nature.com?error=cookies_not_supported) and got the full abstract and the Ethics declarations. WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN: the per-clock ICC table the researcher asked for. Figure 1g's verbatim legend confirms the ICCs are plotted with 95% CIs and that age-adjusted ICCs live in Supplementary Table 4, which is not in the PMC HTML and which I could not retrieve without journal access. I want to be emphatic about one thing: an intermediate fetch in this session handed me a clean-looking six-clock ICC list (0.974/0.959/0.974/0.938/0.981/0.989). A dedicated follow-up query established those numerals appear nowhere as text in the article. That is precisely the fabrication mode the brief warned about, and I have flagged the list as unusable rather than passing it through. I searched for refutations within the sources themselves rather than assuming them: the strongest genuine contradictions I found are internal to the cited papers - Higgins-Chen's median deviations (0.9-2.4y) versus its own headline '9 years', and Apsley's non-significant blood-to-blood cell versus the article's 'purely which tissue' framing. I could not check for post-publication errata or failed replications without WebSearch, so absence of a retraction here is not something I verified.

Net: every headline number in (a), (b), (c) and (d) survives contact with the primary text. The verdict is CORRECTED rather than HOLDS because (d) misstates the denominator and, more seriously, both (a) and (d) are framed at a caliber the sources do not support - a rounded tail maximum presented as typical error, and an oral-versus-blood artifact presented as tissue-arbitrariness.

- **(a) Technical noise alone produces deviations of up to 9 YEARS between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks (Higgins-Chen et al. 2022, Nature Aging)** — `confirmed`
  Verbatim from the abstract (reached via nature.com after following the idp.nature.com redirect chain): "Here we show that technical noise produces deviations up to 9 years between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks, limiting their utility." The phrasing checks out exactly. TWO caliber caveats the article must carry. (1) '9 years' is a rounded-up single worst case, not typical. The Results state verbatim: "The widely used Horvath1 multi-tissue clock shows a median deviation of 1.8 years between replicates, and a maximum of 4.8 years. For other clocks, median deviations range from 0.9 to 2.4 years and maxima range from 4.5 to 8.6 years." So the real maximum across the six clocks is 8.6 years, and the MEDIAN deviation is 0.9-2.4 years. Writing 'produces deviations of up to 9 years' without the median invites readers to treat ~9y as the routine error. (2) The replicate set is 36 whole-blood samples measured in duplicate on the 450K array (GSE55763, Lehne et al. 2015); the paper's own words are "36 whole blood samples with 2 technical replicates each and an age range of 37.3 to 74.6." The article's gloss 'the same DNA sample assayed twice' is a reasonable reading of 'technical replicates' but is slightly stronger than what the paper literally states. Note also that one of the six 'clocks' is DNAmTL, a telomere-length estimator reported in kb, not years.

- **(b) The same paper's PC-clock method is licensed to a consumer biological-age testing company, and the paper used that company's data - verify competing-interests statement verbatim** — `confirmed`
  VERBATIM competing-interests statement, retrieved from nature.com (s43587-022-00248-2): "M.E.L. and A.T.H.-C. have built epigenetic aging metrics involving the technology described in the present paper, and these metrics are licensed by Elysium Health through Yale University. Elysium provided paired blood and saliva replicate datasets reported in this study, but otherwise did not fund the study and did not play a role in conceptualization, design, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript. M.E.L. previously acted as a Scientific Advisor for, and received consulting fees from, Elysium Health. T.H.S. was previously an employee of Elysium Health. A.T.H.-C. received consulting fees from FOXO Technologies for work unrelated to the present manuscript. All other authors declare no competing interests." Both halves of the claim hold: licensing exists, and the paper used the company's data. CORRECTIONS OF CALIBER: (i) The company is Elysium Health, and the article should name it rather than say 'a consumer biological-age testing company' - Elysium is primarily a consumer supplement company that also sells a DNAm biological-age test, so the unqualified descriptor is imprecise. (ii) The license runs through Yale University, not from the authors directly. (iii) The statement is 'metrics involving the technology described in the present paper,' not literally 'the PC-clock method.' (iv) Elysium supplied specifically the paired blood-and-saliva replicate datasets, not the paper's data generally - the flagship 36-pair GSE55763 replicate set is public and independent of Elysium. (v) Fairness: the same sentence disclaims that Elysium 'otherwise did not fund the study and did not play a role in conceptualization, design, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.' An article making a conflict-of-interest point must quote that clause too. (vi) Corroborating detail: an Elysium Health, Inc. (New York, NY, USA) author affiliation appears in the byline (T. Hu-Seliger), which strengthens the point independently of the COI statement.

- **(c) DunedinPACE test-retest ICC 0.96 (n=36) and 0.97 (n=28) falls to 0.87 (95% CI 0.82-0.90) across array generations (450k-to-EPIC, n=350)** — `confirmed`
  Verified twice independently - eLife HTML (elifesciences.org/articles/73420) and the Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC8853656) - with matching values. Verbatim: "For DunedinPACE, reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.96 [0.93-0.98]" for the Lehne/GSE55763 set, introduced as "a publicly available database of 36 replicate adult-blood-sample Illumina 450 k datasets (Lehne et al., 2015)"; and "DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.97 [0.94-0.98] in the EPIC-EPIC database and 0.87 [0.82-0.90] in the 450k-EPIC database." The two n's are stated verbatim as "a database of n = 28 replicate Illumina EPIC-array datasets" and "a database of n = 350 replicates in which one dataset was generated from the Illumina 450 k array and the other dataset was generated from the Illumina EPIC array." CIs are 95%. Every number in the claim - 0.96, n=36, 0.97, n=28, 0.87, 0.82-0.90, n=350 - matches the source. One minor internal inconsistency in the source itself, flagged for honesty and NOT to be used as a correction: a second passage gives the Lehne ICC CI as [0.92-0.98] rather than [0.93-0.98]; I saw this only through a fetch summary and did not confirm it character-for-character, so treat it as unverified. Use [0.93-0.98] as quoted from the Results. Also worth noting for framing: 0.87 is still conventionally 'good' reliability - the honest point is the degradation across array generations, not that DunedinPACE becomes unreliable.

- **(d) Apsley et al. 2025: within-person GrimAge2 difference of ~35.78 years between buccal swab and dried blood spot in 83 individuals** — `corrected`
  The number is right; the denominator and the framing are off. CONFIRMED from Apsley et al. 2025, Aging Cell (doi 10.1111/acel.14451, PMC11984668), Table 2, captioned "Pairwise within-person differences in standard epigenetic clocks across tissue types": the GrimAge2 row, Buccal vs. DBS column, reads 35.78 +/- 0.68***, p<0.001. WRONG: 'in 83 individuals' implies 83 buccal-DBS pairs. RIGHT: 83 individuals is the total analytic sample across two studies contributing 284 samples over five tissues - verbatim, "Our analytical sample consisted of 83 individuals across two studies with a total of 284 tissue samples (N_Buccal = 81; N_Saliva = 59; N_DBS = 64; N_BuffyCoat = 35; N_PBMC = 45)." The buccal-DBS comparison can rest on at most 64 pairs, not 83. SECOND CORRECTION: 35.78 +/- 0.68 is a model-estimated coefficient with a standard error, not a raw mean difference; 'about 35.78 years' overstates precision - write ~36 years. THIRD, AND THE MOST IMPORTANT OMISSION: the claim's framing 'depending purely on which tissue is sampled' is contradicted by the paper's own table. The full GrimAge2 row across all nine pairwise columns is: Buccal vs. saliva 13.47 +/- 1.21***; Buccal vs. DBS 35.78 +/- 0.68***; Buccal vs. buffy coat 34.82 +/- 1.20***; Buccal vs. PBMC 40.25 +/- 0.79***; Saliva vs. DBS 20.72 +/- 1.69***; Saliva vs. buffy coat 25.70 +/- 2.46***; Saliva vs. PBMC 22.42 +/- 1.58***; DBS vs. buffy coat -1.11 +/- 0.81 (NOT significant); DBS vs. PBMC 5.16 +/- 0.56***. The discrepancy is an oral-tissue-vs-blood axis, not arbitrary tissue-to-tissue noise: the two blood-derived tissues (DBS vs. buffy coat) agree to within about one year and non-significantly. Also, buccal vs. PBMC (40.25y) is larger than the 35.78y the article picked, so 35.78 is not even the extreme. Finally, GrimAge2 was trained in blood, so buccal application is out-of-domain; the paper's own text notes "all within-person clock estimates, other than Horvath pan-tissue, were significantly higher in buccal and saliva than in blood-based tissues."

Method note: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I started, so I worked entirely through WebFetch against known endpoints plus direct curl retrieval of raw source files, which I then grepped/parsed myself with Python. Given the pipeline's history of fabricated verbatim quotes from web-fetch summarizers, I treated every summarizer output as unverified and re-derived each load-bearing string from raw text I held locally. Files retrieved to /private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-cissychen-design/ebb819e4-d589-461e-b589-d72e888092fe/scratchpad/: hc.html (raw PMC author manuscript of Higgins-Chen, PMC9586209), st.xlsx (the publisher's Supplementary Tables 1-13 workbook, 43587_2022_248_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx, 31 MB, downloaded from media.springernature.com — flagging that I downloaded a file without asking first), apsley.xml (raw JATS full text of Apsley et al. 2025, PMC11984668), dp.xml (raw JATS full text of Belsky et al. 2022 DunedinPACE, PMC8853656).

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM: (1) Higgins-Chen abstract, Results, Discussion, Methods, Code Availability, and Competing Interests Statement — read from the raw PMC HTML, with the Competing Interests wording independently cross-checked against the published Nature Aging page. (2) Higgins-Chen Supplementary Tables 3, 4 and 5 — read cell-by-cell with openpyxl, not via any summarizer. This is the per-clock ICC table the researcher could not reach; I have reported all values. (3) Belsky et al. 2022 eLife — the full reliability paragraph pulled from raw XML, confirming 0.96/n=36 Lehne 450k, 0.97 [0.94-0.98]/n=28 EPIC-EPIC, 0.87 [0.82-0.90]/n=350 450k-EPIC, all estimated by mixed-effects regression. (4) Apsley et al. 2025 Aging Cell Table 2 — I extracted the table-wrap from raw XML and printed the header row and the GrimAge2 body row in column order, so the 35.78 ± 0.68 is anchored to the correct row and column rather than to a summarizer's reading of a nine-column table. (5) GEO GSE55763 Summary and Overall design, to establish that the replicates are technical replicates of identical DNA.

WHAT REMAINS UNCERTAIN: I did not independently open Sugden et al. 2020, the source of the n=28 and n=350 replicate databases; I verified only that the DunedinPACE paper reports those Ns and ICCs, which is the primary source for the ICC values themselves. The exact number of individuals contributing both a buccal and a DBS sample in Apsley et al. is not reported anywhere I could find in the paper — I could bound it at 64 from the DBS total but not pin it. I also could not locate a published critique, erratum, or replication failure for any of the three papers up to 2026-07, but with WebSearch unavailable my search for refutations was limited to Europe PMC's REST API, so absence of a correction here is weaker evidence than it would normally be. Finally, on (b): I checked Elysium Health's own product page to confirm 'Index' is a consumer DNA-methylation biological-age test, which supports the article's characterization of the company.

- **(a) Technical noise alone (same DNA sample assayed twice) produces deviations up to 9 years between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks — Higgins-Chen et al. 2022, Nature Aging** — `corrected`
  WRONG (as framed): implying all six clocks reach ~9 years of technical error. RIGHT: the '9 years' is the abstract's rounded upper bound driven by ONE clock (PhenoAge) in ONE of 36 replicate pairs. Verbatim abstract (raw PMC author manuscript, PMC9586209): 'Here we show technical noise produces deviations up to 9 years between replicates for six prominent epigenetic clocks, limiting their utility.' Verbatim Results: 'The widely used Horvath1 multi-tissue clock shows a median deviation of 1.8 years between replicates, and a maximum of 4.8 years. For other clocks, median deviations range from 0.9 to 2.4 years and maxima range from 4.5 to 8.6 years.' Verbatim Discussion: 'resulting in up to 3 to 9 years difference between technical replicates depending on the clock.' I opened Supplementary Table 5 ('Deviations between replicates for each clock in GSE55763 by sample', 36 sample pairs) from the publisher's supplementary XLSX and computed the per-clock maxima myself: Horvath1 4.849, Horvath2 4.509, Hannum 4.562, PhenoAge 8.582, GrimAge 2.367, DNAmTL 0.818. **新发现的矛盾证据:**
- The 'six clocks deviate up to 9 years' headline conceals that two of the six were quite reliable: in Higgins-Chen's own Supplementary Table 5 the maximum GrimAge deviation across 36 replicate pairs is 2.37 years and DNAmTL 0.82 kb, and the paper states 'GrimAge and DNAmTL maximum deviations were 0.57 and 0.69 SD respectively'. Any article using the 9-year number as a blanket indictment of epigenetic clocks is over-reading its own source.
- Higgins-Chen Supplementary Table 3 shows the six clocks' raw epigenetic-age ICCs are 0.917-0.989 — i.e. high. The reliability problem is concentrated in age-ACCELERATION residuals (Supplementary Table 4: PhenoAge 0.755, Horvath1 0.835) and in GrimAge's sub-components (DNAmLeptin 0.329, DNAmPAI1 0.686). A reader told only 'ICC is bad' or only 'ICC is fine' is being misled either way; the distinction is age vs. age-acceleration.
- DunedinPACE is not exempt from the first-generation critique it is often contrasted with: Higgins-Chen's own Supplementary Table 3, computed on the same GSE55763 replicates, gives DunedinPACE ICC = 0.9636 [0.9264, 0.9817] — good, but its predecessor DunedinPoAm scores 0.8884 [0.7934, 0.9413], and the 450k-to-EPIC figure of 0.87 shows the reliability is platform-contingent.
- Apsley et al.'s cross-tissue gaps are systematic offsets with very small standard errors (35.78 ± 0.68), not noise. This means the buccal-vs-blood discrepancy is in principle calibratable, which weakens any argument that cross-tissue disagreement makes epigenetic age irreducibly meaningless; the same paper shows the Skin and Blood clock already achieves near-concordance (1.33 ± 0.38 years buccal vs. DBS).
- I found no correction, erratum, retraction, or failed-replication notice attached to Higgins-Chen et al. 2022 or to Belsky et al. 2022 as of 2026-07 in a Europe PMC search for corrections/errata.

## V31 — 组级判决:CORRECTED(票型 CORRECTED/CORRECTED/CORRECTED)

### 票 1(CORRECTED)

WebSearch budget was exhausted before I started, so I worked entirely from primary documents fetched directly with curl (raw HTML, tag-stripped and grepped by me, not summarized by a fetch model) plus the Europe PMC, Federal Register and ClinicalTrials.gov APIs and one live browser session against FDA's DDT database. I did not rely on WebFetch summaries for any quoted string — early WebFetch calls on the Cell 2023 and Nat Med 2024 papers returned "quotes" that I then verified independently against the raw text, and the Nat Med summary's claims about what the paper does and does not contain turned out to be directionally right but the Cell summary's rendering of the circularity passage was truncated in a way that reversed its thrust. Every verbatim string in my verdicts was read by me in a locally downloaded, tag-stripped copy.

PRIMARY DOCUMENTS REACHED VERBATIM: Moqri et al. Cell 2023;186:3758-3775 (PMC11088934, full text, 110k chars); Moqri et al. Nat Med 2024;30:360-372 (PMC11090477, full text, 105k chars — 'circular' and 'geroprotector' each occur zero times, which is the pivot of the (b) correction); Rolland et al. Nat Commun 2023;14:5038 (PMC10439920, exact 'no consensually accepted biomarkers of aging' sentence, located via an exact-phrase Europe PMC search that returned exactly one paper); Muscedere et al. J Nutr Health Aging 2025;29(9):100637 (PMC12310402, abstract '3,780' and Results '3,778', plus the FDA/EMA/Health Canada sentence and the TAME sentence with its reference resolved to Barzilai 2016); Barzilai et al. Cell Metab 2016;23:1060-1065 (PMC5943638, body scanned, zero FDA mentions); Kaeberlein GeroScience 2019 (PMC6544683); Nature Aging 2024 translation paper (PMC12262637); Aging Cell 2025 NIA/BAC symposium report (PMC12266742); Lopez-Otin & Kroemer Cell 2025 (PMC12037106); FDA Table of Surrogate Endpoints (content current 04/29/2026, all four tables); FDA guidance database JSON (2,785 records); FDA CDER & CBER DDT Qualification Project Search (live, 232 projects, 22 Qualified); Federal Register API; ClinicalTrials.gov API v2.

WHAT CHANGED THE VERDICT: only (b). Its central assertions are real and sourceable, but the journal, year, paper and the direction of the argument are all wrong — the Consortium raises circularity to knock it down, and the paper credited with it does not mention it. That is caliber slippage serious enough to require correction, hence CORRECTED overall rather than HOLDS.

WHAT I TRIED AND FAILED TO REFUTE: (d) and (f). For (d) I went to the live qualification database rather than the stale FDA page, enumerated every project and every Qualified determination, and specifically hunted for aging-adjacent entries — the three I found (SPPB, PROMIS in Sarcopenia, Actibelt) are clinical outcome assessments at Accept stage, not qualified biomarkers, so they are near-misses that strengthen rather than break the claim. For (f) I checked every public FDA channel that exists and found nothing, then traced the myth to a citation chain that collapses: a 2025 peer-reviewed scoping review cites Barzilai 2016 for 'approved by the FDA', and Barzilai 2016 never mentions FDA.

REMAINING UNCERTAINTY, stated plainly: fda.gov's own site search served a Cloudflare bot-challenge page and I did not attempt to bypass it, so my FDA coverage is via the Federal Register, the guidance database, the surrogate table and the DDT database rather than FDA's internal search index. More fundamentally, FDA pre-IND and Type C meeting minutes are non-public by statute, so no search can exclude a private FDA communication to the TAME investigators; the article should claim the absence of a public primary document, which is what I verified, and not the absence of any FDA utterance. On (a), 'no trial has ever shown it' is an unbounded negative I can support only through the field's own consensus reviews, not through an exhaustive trial-by-trial audit.

- **(a) No epigenetic clock has been validated as a surrogate endpoint in the regulatory sense; the treatment-induced CHANGE must predict the change in outcome, and no trial has shown this for any clock** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed against primary text and live regulatory databases. Moqri et al., Cell 2023;186:3758-3775 (PMC11088934), verbatim, read by me in the retrieved full text: 'There are not yet any formally validated or likely surrogate endpoint biomarkers of aging — in part because they have only recently been described.' Same paper states the exact caliber requirement the claim asserts: 'Validation of a biomarker as a surrogate endpoint requires clinical evidence that a change in the surrogate endpoint predicts a specific clinical benefit. For instance, a reduction in epigenetic age is only meaningful if it is indeed associated with a positive clinical change, such as a reduction in the risk of age-related diseases, frailty, mortality, or similar changes.' And: 'no aging biomarkers of any category have been approved by U.S. regulators for clinical applications.' Not superseded as of 2026-07: I queried the live CDER & CBER DDT Qualification Project Search on 2026-07-28 (232 projects, all programs, all stages) — zero projects matching epigenetic / methylation / biological age / clock / healthspan. Cell 2025 (Lopez-Otin & Kroemer, PMC12037106) still describes omic aging biomarkers as 'not yet recognized as FDA-accepted outcomes' and speaks of 'Pending regulatory approval of ... surrogate markers of clinical efficacy'. CAUTION on wording: the sub-clause 'no trial has shown this for any clock' is an unbounded negative. I found no trial claiming it and no source asserting one, but I cannot exhaustively prove a negative over all trials; attribute it to the field's own reviews rather than asserting it as an independently verified exhaustive search.

- **(b) The Biomarkers of Aging Consortium's 2024 Nature Medicine paper concedes no biomarker of aging is validated, and states the circularity (no validated human geroprotector, so biomarkers are built from putative interventions' effects and then used to evaluate those interventions)** — `corrected`
  MISATTRIBUTED, and the caliber is wrong. WRONG version: the circularity and the 'no validated biomarker' concession are in Moqri et al., 'Validation of biomarkers of aging', Nature Medicine 2024;30:360-372. RIGHT version: that paper does NOT contain it. I downloaded and grepped its full PMC text (PMC11090477, 105k chars): the string 'circular' occurs 0 times and 'geroprotector' occurs 0 times. Its only 'no consensus' statement is narrower and about METHOD, not status: 'However, no consensus exists on how biomarkers of aging should be validated prior to their translation to the clinic.' The circularity passage is in the Consortium's OTHER paper — Moqri et al., 'Biomarkers of aging for the identification and evaluation of longevity interventions', Cell 2023;186:3758-3775 (PMC11088934) — and it does not 'concede' the circularity, it rebuts it. Verbatim: 'As one of the proposed criteria for a candidate geroprotector is reduction in biological age assessed with biomarkers, the relationship between biomarkers of aging and geroprotectors may seem circular (Figure 3a). Importantly, there exist many candidate biomarkers of aging and many proposed geroprotectors, and the accumulated evidence supporting either could be leveraged to validate the other (Figure 3b). ... Indeed, this is currently the common practice for analogous biomarkers developed for use in model organisms, where numerous lifespan-extending interventions have been unequivocally identified.' Further, neither paper says 'no geroprotector has been validated in humans'; the Cell 2023 text says the opposite in part — 'For a subset of candidate geroprotectors, sufficient scientific evidence supporting their efficacy has accumulated to warrant the initiation of human clinical longevity intervention trials' — and the nearest supporting sentence is 'The challenge of validating surrogate endpoints is compounded by the lack of consensus on interventions that improve clinical outcomes relevant to healthspan or lifespan.'

- **(c) A 2023 consensus review by the field's leadership states there are no consensually accepted biomarkers of aging at all** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim. Source located by exact-phrase search (only one paper in Europe PMC contains the phrase 'consensually accepted biomarkers of aging'): Rolland Y, Sierra F, Ferrucci L, Barzilai N, de Cabo R, Mannick J, Oliva A, Evans W, Angioni D, de Souto Barreto P, Raffin J, Vellas B, Kirkland JL, and the G.C.T-TF group, 'Challenges in developing Geroscience trials', Nature Communications 2023;14:5038, doi 10.1038/s41467-023-39786-7 (PMC10439920, PMID 37598227). I read the sentence in the retrieved full text: 'Although the search for such biomarkers of aging has been very active, currently there are no consensually accepted biomarkers of aging.' The author list is unambiguously the field's leadership. One caliber caveat: the paper self-describes as 'the main results of a Task Force of experts in Geroscience' and is indexed as a review — it is a Task Force report, not a document formally titled a consensus statement.

- **(d) No aging, biological-age, healthspan, frailty or multimorbidity biomarker appears among FDA's formally qualified biomarkers or its Table of Surrogate Endpoints** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed by direct inspection of both primary FDA sources on 2026-07-28; I tried hard to refute it and could not. (1) Table of Surrogate Endpoints That Were the Basis of Drug Approval or Licensure, fda.gov, page states 'Content current as of: 04/29/2026'. I downloaded the page, stripped tags, and confirmed all four tables were present (Table 1 Adult non-cancer, Table 2 Adult cancer, Table 3 Pediatric non-cancer, Table 4 Pediatric cancer; sanity-checked with 15 hits for LDL/HbA1c/bone mineral density/viral load). Case-insensitive search for aging|ageing|biological age|frail|healthspan|multimorbidity|senescen|epigenetic|DNA methylation|gait speed|grip strength|geroscience|sarcopenia|intrinsic capacity returned ZERO hits. (2) The old static 'list of qualified biomarkers' page no longer holds the list — fda.gov/drugs/biomarker-qualification-program/list-qualified-biomarkers now redirects readers to the CDER & CBER DDT Qualification Project Search database (force-dsc.my.site.com/ddt/s/). I queried that live database: 232 total projects across AMQ/BMQ/COA/ISTAND; 22 carry an FDA determination of 'Qualified' (11 of them biomarkers: DDT-BMQ-000001, -000002, -000003, -000004, -000014, -000021, -000028, -000044, -000050, -000054, -000105). None is an aging, biological-age, healthspan, frailty or multimorbidity biomarker. The only aging-adjacent records in the entire database are clinical outcome assessments, not biomarkers, and none is qualified: DDT-COA-000037 Short Physical Performance Battery (submitted by the Alliance for Aging Research; '507 Transition -- Accept'), DDT-COA-000085 PROMIS Physical Functioning Item Bank in Sarcopenia ('507 Transition -- Accept'), DDT-COA-000105 Actibelt in Sarcopenia ('LOI - Letter of Intent -- Accept'). Independently corroborated by the field itself: Cell 2023 (PMC11088934), verbatim, 'no aging biomarkers of any category have been approved by U.S. regulators for clinical applications', and, on physiological measures, 'The FDA has accepted some of these surrogates, such as 6-minute walk distance, for approving therapies for disease indications. However, they are not currently included in the FDA's Table of Surrogate Endpoints.'

- **(e) A 2025 scoping review that screened 3,780 publications found no established regulatory framework anywhere for drugs targeting aging, and states that FDA, EMA and Health Canada do not classify aging as a disease** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed verbatim, with two precision caveats. Source: 'Advancing Geroscience Research – A Scoping Review of Regulatory Environments for Gerotherapeutics', J Nutr Health Aging 2025;29(9):100637, PMID 40706485, PMC12310402, corresponding author John Muscedere. Abstract, verbatim: 'In 3,780 publications screened for inclusion, no regulatory frameworks for gerotherapeutics were found.' Body, verbatim: 'Regulatory bodies such as the FDA, the EMA and Health Canada do not classify aging as a disease, which complicates the approval process for therapies targeting aging...'. CAVEAT 1 — internal inconsistency in the paper: the Results section says 'The search on the combined databases yielded 3,778 studies', two fewer than the 3,780 in the abstract. CAVEAT 2 — 'anywhere' overstates the search frame: it was English-language publications 2014–2024, covering the US, Europe, Canada and other regions, with agency websites checked for Health Canada, FDA, EMA, MHRA, India's CDSCO and Australia's TGA; 34 publications were included. THIS PAPER ALSO CUTS AGAINST ITEM (f): it repeats the TAME myth in its own body — 'For example, only one study—the Targeting Aging with Metformin (TAME) trial—has been approved by the FDA to investigate an intervention targeting multiple age-related diseases rather than a single condition [27]' — so it must not be presented as a source that endorses (f).

- **(f) There is no primary FDA document (letter, guidance, Federal Register notice, advisory committee record) accepting a composite morbidity endpoint for an 'aging' indication, despite the widespread 'FDA approved TAME' claim** — `confirmed`
  Confirmed by exhaustive negative search of every public FDA channel on 2026-07-28, plus a positive finding that traces the myth to a citation that does not support it. NEGATIVE CHECKS: (1) Federal Register API — '"Targeting Aging with Metformin"' = 0 documents; '"geroprotector"' = 0; '"TAME trial"' = 1 (a 2017 NIA Notice of Closed Meetings, NIH not FDA); '"geroscience"' = 3 (all NIA closed-meeting notices); '"healthspan"' = 6 (none FDA); '"aging as an indication"' = 1 (a 2011 OTC sunscreen labeling rule about skin aging). Because FDA advisory committee meetings must be noticed in the Federal Register, this also covers the advisory-committee-record prong. (2) FDA's guidance-document database (search-for-guidance.json, 2,785 guidances): only 3 aging/geriatric hits, all ICH E7 geriatric-population guidances; no guidance on aging, geroprotectors, healthspan, or composite morbidity endpoints for aging. (3) Table of Surrogate Endpoints and the DDT Qualification database: nothing (see item d). (4) TAME has no ClinicalTrials.gov registration — an exact-phrase query for 'Targeting Aging with Metformin' returns only unrelated studies. POSITIVE FINDING ON PROVENANCE: the 2025 scoping review (item e) cites Barzilai N, Crandall JP, Kritchevsky SB, Espeland MA, 'Metformin as a Tool to Target Aging', Cell Metab 2016;23:1060-1065 (its ref [27], PMC5943638) as the source for 'TAME... has been approved by the FDA'. I downloaded that paper's full text and searched the article body (~20,200 characters between Abstract and References): 'FDA' occurs 0 times, 'Food and Drug' 0 times, 'regulat*' 0 times. The cited source contains no FDA claim at all. INDEPENDENT CONTRADICTION FROM WITHIN THE FIELD: Kaeberlein, 'Taming expectations of metformin as a treatment to extend healthspan', GeroScience 2019 (PMC6544683), verbatim: 'the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not currently recognize aging as a treatment indication' and 'An additional overarching goal of this effort is to create a regulatory framework that recognizes aging as an indication for treatment' — i.e. creating the framework is TAME's aspiration, not an accomplished FDA act. LIMITS OF MY SEARCH, stated plainly: fda.gov's own site search was unreachable (it served a Cloudflare bot-challenge page, which I did not attempt to bypass), and FDA pre-IND / Type C meeting minutes are non-public by statute, so a private, unpublished FDA communication with the TAME investigators cannot be ruled out by any public search. The claim as worded — that no PRIMARY FDA DOCUMENT exists — survives; a claim that 'FDA never said anything to anyone' would not be verifiable.
